en: Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart, from whose lotus-bud of a mouth the world drinks the nectar of sacred speech. He is the tree whose roots are firmly established in Dharma, whose trunk is the Veda, and who is richly adorned with the branches of the Purāṇas.

Victorious is Viṣṇu, the wish-fulfilling tree whose flowers are sacrifices and whose fruit is liberation. They proclaim him as the sixth great seer, endowed with inexhaustible majesty, beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā).
I bow to Dvaipāyana, the son of Nārāyaṇa’s portion and his only son, who is a treasure-house of the Vedas.
[I bow to] the stainless lotus of Pārāśarya’s words, intense with the fragrance of the meaning of the Gītā.

May this *Bhārata-lotus*, whose filaments are various narratives awakened by the fragrance of the stories of Hari, and which is joyfully sipped day after day by the bees that are the virtuous in this world, destroy the impurities of the Kali age and lead to our supreme welfare.
He who attained whiteness in the Kṛta age, redness in the Tretā age,
tawny hue in the Dvāpara age, and who, as the Blessed One, has assumed blackness in the Kali age—
he who is praised by the sages and celebrated by the yogis.
Whether he be Brahmā, or Hara, or Śiva— whosoever he may be— to him I bow.
I pay homage to that elephant-faced one, by whose grace the lords of speech and other wise beings, having attained their purpose, become successful in all their aims.

I bow to Vyāsa, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha, the great-grandson of Śakti, the sinless son of Parāśara, the father of Śuka, and a treasure-house of asceticism; [he who was] Brahmā without four faces and with two arms...
Śambhu, the Blessed One Bādarāyaṇa, whose eye is in his forehead, [says]:
"For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon the Lord who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a gracious countenance."

We worship Hayagrīva, the god consisting of knowledge and bliss, stainless and crystalline in form, the source of all sciences. Salutations to Vyāsa, who is Viṣṇu in form, and to Viṣṇu, who is Vyāsa in form.
01,000.000*0011_02 Homage indeed to Vasiṣṭha, the treasure-house of Brahman; salutations again and again.
01,000.000*0012_01 Homage to the Great Dharma; homage to Kṛṣṇa, the Ordainer. 01,000.000*0012_02 Having paid obeisance to the Brāhmaṇas, I shall proclaim the eternal Dharmas.
Dark as a cloud, with his mass of matted hair bound in a topknot, tall and carrying a staff, clad in the skin of a black antelope,
that foremost of poets was visibly purifying the worlds.

May the son of Parāśara reveal his form during the sacred festivals. That which, when merely remembered by men, drives away inauspicious things and extends a succession of auspicious ones—that, they know, is Brahman; that is the source of blessing.
Dharma increases by the recitation of Yudhiṣṭhira;
evil is destroyed by the recitation of Vṛkodara;
and the enemy perishes by the recitation of Dhanañjaya.
May the two sons of Mādrī declare that diseases do not exist [for those who hear this]. I salute Sarasvatī, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Umā,
the Lord of Radiance, Gaṇapati, and the sages headed by Bṛhaspati.
To Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the gods, the sole lord of the world,
who is dear to his devotees, honored by all the worlds,
free from the three qualities, unborn, all-pervading, the primordial Lord;
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, who destroys worldly existence and is worshipped by asuras, gods, and siddhas, and likewise to Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then proclaim the *Jaya*.

Once, Ugraśravas, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a Sūta well-versed in the Purāṇas, approached the Brahman-sages of rigid vows who were seated at the twelve-year sacrificial session of the patriarch Śaunaka in the Naimiṣa forest; having bowed low with humility, the son of the Sūta presented himself before them.
When he arrived at that hermitage, the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest spoke to all those sages: "We are blessed today by the sight of you;
we know all the discourses of Vyāsa’s son, which are composed of dharma and artha."
"I shall speak to you, O best of the twice-born; listen today, you whose wealth is asceticism.
Having heard those words of his, the ascetics dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest gathered around there to hear his various stories.
Having saluted all those sages with palms joined in reverence,
and being greeted by those virtuous ones, he inquired after their increase in ascetic merit.
Then, when all those ascetics had taken their seats...
Lomaharṣaṇi took the seat pointed out to him with humility. Then, observing that he was comfortably seated and rested,
a certain ṛṣi there began to speak and asked him about various stories.
"O Sauti, from where have you come, and where have you spent this time? O lotus-eyed one, tell this to me as I ask.
Thus questioned, Lomaharṣaṇi spoke correctly and in due order.
In that vast assembly of sages of purified souls, he who was perfected in speech spoke words concerning their conduct.
Sūta said:
At the snake sacrifice of the high-souled royal seer Janamejaya,
the lord of kings and son of Parikṣit,
there were various most meritorious stories proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana in his presence.
Having heard those stories of manifold meanings contained within the Mahābhārata, which were indeed related by Vaiśampāyana according to the prescribed rules,
and having wandered extensively among many sacred fords and holy shrines, I [have come here].
I went to that meritorious region named Samantapañcaka, frequented by the twice-born, where in ancient times the battle took place between the Pāṇḍavas,
the Kurus, and all the lords of the earth.
Therefore, desiring to see you, I have come here into your presence;
for all of you, long-lived ones, are in my view truly become Brahman.
O highly fortunate ones, you possess the splendor of the sun and fire in this sacrifice.

"O twice-born ones, having performed your ablutions, being pure, having completed your prayers, and having offered oblations into the fire, you sit here at ease; what shall I say to you? Shall I relate meritorious stories based on the Purāṇas or those centered upon Dharma?"
I have heard this account of the deeds of kings and high-souled sages, known as the Bhārata narrative, which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa;
it was spoken by Vaiśampāyana when he was questioned by Janamejaya.
There, in the presence of the great-souled sages who were most righteous,
Vaiśampāyana then recited that narrative known as the Bhārata, which had been heard by him at the command of Vyāsadeva and was augmented by the meanings of the Vedas.
"Therein, I have understood the entire narrative of the Bharatas from the beginning.
The sages said:
"That which was formerly proclaimed by the supreme seer Dvaipāyana as the Purāṇa..."
Having heard that which was praised by the gods and the Brahman-sages, [I shall relate] this most excellent narrative, which possesses wonderful words and sections,
is endowed with subtle meanings and logic, and is adorned with the meanings of the Vedas.
[He studied] the holy history of Bhārata, endowed with both text and meaning, refined by grammatical purification, composed in the Brāhmī language, and augmented by various sciences—
[that history] which Vaiśampāyana recited for King Janamejaya.
Just as that sage was satisfied at the sacrifice by the command of Dvaipāyana,
we wish to hear the righteous compendium (*saṃhitā*) of Vyāsa, the performer of wondrous deeds, which is equal to the four Vedas and removes the fear of sin.
Sūta said:
[He is] the primordial Puruṣa, the Lord, invoked by many and praised by many;
the Truth, the single syllable, the Brahman, both manifest and unmanifest, eternal.
He who is both the unreal and the real, the universe itself, yet beyond both the real and the unreal; the creator of the high and the low, the ancient, supreme, and imperishable;
the auspicious one, the source of all auspiciousness, Viṣṇu, the most excellent, the sinless, and the pure.
Having paid homage to Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary,
I shall proclaim the entire doctrine of the high-souled Great Seer Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, who is honored here in all the worlds.
Homage to that Blessed One, Vyāsa, of immeasurable splendor,
by whose grace I shall relate this narrative of Nārāyaṇa;
[a narrative which is] equivalent to visiting all stages of life and bathing in all sacred fords.
The narrative of Nārāyaṇa does not yield fruit in such a manner as this [story] does. There has been nothing equal to Nārāyaṇa, nor will there ever be;
by these words of truth, I shall accomplish all my aims.
Some poets have recounted it, others are recounting it now,
and others likewise will recount this history on earth;
for this great knowledge is established throughout the three worlds.
That which is maintained by the twice-born both in detail and in summary,
adorned with auspicious words and divine and human conventions, endowed with various poetic meters, and beloved by the wise.
On the auspicious foothills of the Himalayas, in a pure mountain cave-dwelling,
the righteous-souled Vyāsa— pure, self-restrained, tranquil in spirit, and established in austerity— purified his body and sat upon a bed of darbha grass.
Having investigated that course of the history of Bhārata through dharma, he entered into yoga by means of knowledge and perceived everything in its ultimate reality;
[he saw] this world devoid of luster, without light, and enveloped on all sides by darkness.

In the beginning of the age, there was a single vast egg, the inexhaustible seed of all creatures; that great and divine cause is proclaimed as that in which the eternal Brahman, the light of truth, is heard to reside.
It is wondrous and inconceivable, having attained a state of equality everywhere;
it is the unmanifest, subtle cause, which consists of both being and non-being,
from which the Grandfather was born— the one Lord, Prajāpati.
Brahmā, the preceptor of the gods, Sthāṇu, Manu, Ka, and Parameṣṭhin; likewise Prācetasa, Dakṣa, and the seven sons of Dakṣa;
from them there arose the twenty-one Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis).
And the Person of immeasurable self, whom all the seers know—
the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and also the two Aśvins;
the Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and likewise the Pitṛs.
From him were born the learned, disciplined, and stainless Brahman-sages,
as well as many royal sages endowed with all virtues;
likewise, the waters, heaven, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and the directions.
The years, seasons, months, fortnights, days and nights, in their proper order;
the moments (kṣaṇa), divisions (lava), hours (muhūrta), twinklings of an eye (nimeṣa), and the cycles of the yugas—
all these, and whatever else exists, have come into being with the world as their witness.
Whatever is seen here, whether stationary or moving,
this entire world is withdrawn again when the end of the age arrives,
just as the various signs of the seasons disappear with the change of the season.
Those very same things are seen to appear in such a manner at the beginnings of the ages;
thus this wheel, which effects the destruction of beings, revolves throughout the world without beginning or end, and without beginning or finality.
Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred,
and thirty-three is the concise description of the creation of the gods. Divasputra, Bṛhadbhānu, Cakṣus, Ātman, and Vibhāvasu— [these are their names].
Savitṛ, Ṛcīka, Arka, Bhānu, Āśāvaha, and Ravi—
these were all the sons of Vivasvat, with Mahya being the youngest among them. Devabhrāj was his son, and for that reason he is known as Subhrāj.
Subhrāja had three sons who were prolific and highly learned:
Daśajyotis, Śatajyotis, and the self-possessed Sahasrajyotis. The high-souled Daśajyotis had ten thousand sons.
Then there were ten times as many other sons of Śatajyotis here;
furthermore, the sons of Sahasrajyotis were ten times more numerous than those.
From them descended this lineage of the Kurus, as well as that of the Yadus and of Bharata.

The lineage of Yayāti and Ikṣvāku, as well as all the lineages of the royal sages (rājarṣis), have been fully described; likewise, the many lineages and the detailed accounts of the creation of beings,
all the abodes of beings, and that which is the threefold secret.

The sage beheld the Vedas along with the Yoga and its specialized knowledge (vijñāna), as well as Dharma, Artha, and Kāma; he saw the treatises on Dharma, Kāma, and Artha, various other sciences, and the established rules for the conduct of worldly life.
The policy of the Bharata lineage and its expansion in every respect,
the historical narratives with their commentaries, and various sacred scriptures—
all this has been set forth here in due order; thus has the characteristic of the work been described.
01,001.048d After this, I shall speak of the history in detail;
01,001.049a having expanded this great knowledge, the Seer spoke it in brief.
01,001.049c For in this world, the learned desire both the concise and the detailed exposition.

Some [Brahmins] study the Bhārata beginning with Manu, others likewise beginning with Āstīka, and still others beginning with Uparicara; thus these wise men thoroughly master and illuminate the various branches of the knowledge of the Saṃhitās.
Some are skilled at explaining, while others are capable of merely retaining the text. Having divided the eternal Veda through austerity and celibacy,
the son of Satyavatī composed this meritorious history.
Know that the learned Brahmarṣi, the son of Parāśara, who is firm in his vows,
is the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa;
for who else but the lotus-eyed one could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
It shines in all the Vedas; it brings delight to all living beings;
it is the means of crossing over for all the worlds—therefore it is called the Bhārata.
By the command of his mother and of the wise son of Gaṅgā, the righteous-souled one [set out].
In former times, the powerful Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana begot three Kauravas in the field of Vicitravīrya, like the three sacred fires;
having procreated Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.
The wise one returned once more to the hermitage for the sake of asceticism. When they had been born, grown old, and had departed to the supreme goal—
thus indeed was this chapter on the summary previously composed by the great seer.
For it is indeed joined with stepping-stones that are exceedingly difficult to traverse;
and for this very purpose, this collection has been compiled exactly as it was heard,
so that when all of this is proclaimed, human beings in the world shall come to know it.
In this world of men, O Bhārata, the great Ṛṣi, having been questioned by Janamejaya and by thousands of Brāhmaṇas, spoke to his disciple Vaiśampāyana, who was seated nearby. He commanded him thus:

Seated together with the members of the assembly, he caused the *Bhārata* to be heard during the intervals of the sacrifice, being urged again and again [to recite] the detailed account of the Kuru lineage and the virtuous character of Gāndhārī.
The venerable seer Dvaipāyana correctly described the wisdom and fortitude of Vidura, the nobility of Kuntī,
the greatness of Vāsudeva, the truthfulness of the Pāṇḍavas,
and the wicked conduct of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

This supreme Bhārata, consisting of one hundred thousand verses of meritorious deeds, together with its sub-narratives, is to be known as that which is to be heard. He composed the Bhārata-saṃhitā in twenty-four thousand [verses].
First, the *Bhārata* is recited by the wise without the sub-narratives (*upākhyānas*).
Then, the seer further condensed it into one hundred and fifty [verses],
composing the chapter on the table of contents (*anukramaṇī*) which summarizes the events of the various sections (*parvans*).
Sūta:
Having composed that most excellent of narratives, the lord Dvaipāyana reflected thus: "How shall I teach this here to my disciples?"
While the seer Dvaipāyana was thus reflecting,
the blessed Brahmā, the teacher of the worlds, himself arrived, having remembered him out of affection for the great seer and with a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

Having seen him, he was filled with wonder; with palms joined in reverence, he stood bowing. He prepared a seat for Hiraṇyagarbha, who was seated upon that supreme throne together with all the hosts of gods.
Turning back, Vāsudeva stood bowed down near the seat;
then, permitted by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa sat down near the seat, feeling joyful and greatly amazed.
01,001.062 That one of great splendor spoke to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord:
"O Blessed One, this poem of supreme honor has been composed by me;
O Brahman, it contains the secret of the Vedas and whatever else has been proclaimed by me."

The detailed exposition of the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and Upaniṣads; the expansion and contraction of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; and that which is designated as the threefold time—past, present, and future.
The determination of the existence and non-existence of old age, death, fear, and disease;
the characteristics of various dharmas and the stages of life (āśramas);
the ordinance for the four castes, and the entire meaning of the Purāṇas.
The measure of austerity, of celibacy, of the earth, of the moon and the sun, of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, along with the duration of the *yugas*;
likewise, the *ṛg*, *yajus*, and *sāman* verses, and the inner self (*adhyātma*) of the Vedas.
Logic, grammar, medicine, and likewise the Pāśupata knowledge—
thus there was a birth based on many sources, pertaining to both divine and human realms,
as well as the glorification of sacred fords and holy regions.
[He knows] the skill in battle regarding rivers, mountains, forests, and the ocean; the divine cities and the cycles of kalpas;
the specific distinctions of speech and lineage; and the course of worldly affairs.
O Lord, you ought to forgive even that which is an all-pervading offense;
for I consider you today to be the most excellent even among Vasiṣṭha, that bull among sages distinguished by his asceticism, because of your realization of the knowledge of the secret doctrine.
"Since birth we have known you as a truthful speaker of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinī*). You yourself have declared, 'It shall be poetry (*kāvyam*'); therefore, it will indeed be poetry.
Other poets are not capable of excelling this poetry."

If the world were not illuminated by you with the fire of knowledge, the remaining three stages of life would be like the state of a householder alone; the world would become dull, blind, deaf, and insane, shrouded in darkness.
For the world blinded by darkness and entangled by its own actions,
a festival for the eyes of the intellect has been created by means of the ointment-stick of knowledge,
through concise and detailed expositions on the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By you, the sun of the Bharatas, the darkness of men has been destroyed;
by you, the full moon of the Purāṇas, illuminating with the moonlight of the Vedas,
the awakening of the intellect has been brought about for those men who are as gentle as water-lilies.
By means of this lamp of history, which destroys the veil of delusion,
the entire inner chamber of the world has been correctly illuminated. Indeed, it has the chapter on the summary as its seed, Pauloma and Āstīka as its roots, and is firmly established.
The *Saṃbhava-parvan* is its trunk and its expansion; it possesses the *Sabhā* and *Āraṇyaka-parvans* as its ornamental gables;
it is enriched with the form of the *Araṇī-parvan* as its joints; it has the *Virāṭa* and *Udyoga-parvans* as its vital sap;
the *Bhīṣma-parvan* is its great branch, and the * Droṇa-parvan* is its foliage.
It is adorned with the flowers gathered in the Karṇaparvan, fragrant with the Śalyaparvan;
it finds its rest in the Eṣīka section of the Strīparvan and bears the great fruit of the Śāntiparvan.
It possesses the nectar-like essence of the Aśvamedha and takes its refuge in the stations of the Āśramavāsika.
This summary of the Mausala-parvan, frequented by disciplined twice-born ones,
shall be the source of sustenance for all the foremost poets;
like the rain-cloud to living beings, this inexhaustible tree of the Bharata shall flourish.

Having addressed him thus, Brahmā, the Blessed One and creator of the world, departed for his own abode together with the hosts of ṛṣis and gods. I shall now describe the perpetual production of flowers and fruits of that tree.
Endowed with a sweet and pure flavor, and indestructible even by the immortals,
Dvaipāyana formerly taught this to his son Śuka;
thereafter, the Lord bestowed it upon other worthy disciples.
The *saṃhitās* of the *Bhārata* were proclaimed by them individually;
he composed another *saṃhitā* consisting of six million verses,
and thirty million verses were established in the world of the gods.
Fifteen thousand are said to be in the realm of the ancestors (pitrya), fourteen thousand among the Rakṣasas and Yakṣas,
and one hundred thousand are established among human beings.
Nārada recited this to the gods, and Asita Devala to the ancestors.
Śuka indeed caused the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas to hear it;
however, in this world of humans, Vaiśampāyana—
disciple of Vyāsa, righteous-souled, and the best among those who know all the Vedas— recited it.
"Listen indeed to this one hundred thousand [verses] that have been spoken by me;
the brahmin-sage Vaiśampāyana caused it to be heard by the mighty-armed king, the son of Parīkṣit, named Janamejaya."
Duryodhana is a great tree composed of wrath;
Karṇa is its trunk, Śakuni its branches,
and Duḥśāsana its abundant flowers and fruit.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lacking wisdom, is the root;
Yudhiṣṭhira is the great tree composed of dharma;
Arjuna is its trunk, and Bhīmasena its branches.
The two sons of Mādrī are like a tree abundant with flowers and fruit;
Kṛṣṇa is its root, as are the Veda and the Brahmins. Pāṇḍu, having conquered many lands through battle and valor, [attained his goal].
At that time, he lived with his people in the forest, devoted to the sport of hunting.
Through the killing of deer during their mating season, he encountered a dire calamity.
Therein lies the sequence of the rules of conduct for the sons of Pṛthā from their very birth.
And she attended upon her two mothers regarding the secret doctrine of Dharma—
of Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and likewise the two divine Aśvins.
Then, having become a vessel for the secret doctrine of Dharma, Pṛthā became dear to her husband.
Desiring sons, she invoked Dharmarāja, Vāyu, and Indra with those [mantras];
and Mādrī, having been given the secret mantra by him, invoked the Aśvins.
Then all the Pārthas were born from Kuntī and Mādrī through the power of the incantation.
When all those high-souled Pāṇḍavas had been born, Pāṇḍu,
having united with Mādrī on the greatly meritorious great mountain Śataśṛṅga, died due to the power of a sage’s curse.
Reared together with ascetics and protected by their two mothers in sacred forests and the great hermitages of the sages,
they were then personally brought by the seers to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Children, handsome ones, with matted hair and living as celibate students—
these are your sons, brothers, disciples, and friends,
the Pāṇḍavas," having said this, the sages then vanished.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas thus announced by them, the Kauravas,
the remaining castes, and the citizens then cried out loudly with joy.
Some said, "These are not his," while others said, "These are indeed his."
"When Pāṇḍu died long ago, how can this be his? so asked others.
"Welcome! By good fortune, we behold the progeny of Pāṇḍu!"—thus were words of welcome heard on all sides.
When that sound had ceased, a tumultuous roar from invisible beings arose, making all the quarters of the sky resound;
there was a shower of flowers, auspicious fragrances, and the blaring of conchs and drums.
At the entrance of the Pārthas, that [event] was like a marvel;
and because of their affection for them, a great sound arose among all the citizens, born of joy, reaching to the heavens, and increasing their fame.
Having studied all the Vedas and various treatises,
those Pāṇḍavas lived there, honored and free from fear;
the subjects became delighted by Yudhiṣṭhira’s purity.
The entire world was gratified by the fortitude of Bhīmasena, the prowess of Arjuna,
Kuntī’s service to her elders, the humility of the twins,
and their quality of heroism.
Then, at an assembly of kings, Arjuna obtained Kṛṣṇā as his bride by choice after performing a most difficult feat;
from that time forward, he has been honored in this world as the foremost among all archers.
He became as difficult to behold in battles as the sun;
having conquered all the kings and all the great hosts,
Arjuna brought [the wealth] for the king to perform the great Rājasūya sacrifice.
Abounding in food and sacrificial fees, and endowed with all excellent qualities,
Yudhiṣṭhira has successfully accomplished the great Rājasūya sacrifice through the wise guidance of Vāsudeva and the strength of Bhīma and Arjuna.
Having caused Jarāsaṃdha and the King of Cedi, who was proud of his strength, to be slain,
they approached Duryodhana with offerings gathered from here and there—
jewels, gold, gems, and wealth consisting of cattle, elephants, and horses.
And seeing those various garments, both outer robes and inner coverings,
precious woolen blankets and skins, as well as rugs made of *rāṅkava* wool,
and observing that abundant prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas at that time—

A very great anger, born of envy, arose within him. Seeing the assembly hall of the Pāṇḍavas, which was like a celestial chariot and had been skillfully constructed by Maya and brought there for them, he was consumed with grief.
Where he was mocked by Bhīma, who acted with the impetuosity of one leaping forward out of agitation, right before the eyes of Vāsudeva as if he were lacking noble birth;
yet he continued to enjoy various pleasures and various jewels.
It was reported that Dhṛtarāṣṭra had become pale, wan, and emaciated;
then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, out of affection for his son, authorized the gambling match.
Upon hearing this from Vāsudeva, a great anger arose within him.
He was not at all pleased in mind, yet he consented to disputes;
he overlooked those terrible and increased vices such as gambling and other forms of misconduct.
Having cast out Vidura, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, [he acted thus].

In that tumultuous conflict, while the sons of Pāṇḍu were victorious, the kṣatriyas slaughtered one another. Having heard this most grievous news and having learned the intentions of Duryodhana, as well as those of Karṇa and Śakuni...
01.001.095 Having reflected for a long time, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to Sañjaya:
01.001.096 "Listen, Sañjaya, to all of this from me; you ought not to be displeased with me.
You have heard much, you are intelligent, wise, and esteemed by the learned."
My mind is not set on conflict, nor do I take pleasure in the destruction of the Kurus;
I have no distinction between my own sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu. Yet my sons, devoted to wrath, show malice toward me, though I am old.
But I, being blind, endure that out of wretchedness and love for my son;
and I am deluded along with the senseless Duryodhana as he becomes deluded,
having seen the splendor of the mighty Pāṇḍava at the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having encountered that derision during the spectacle of ascending the assembly hall,
he was filled with indignation; yet, being unable himself to conquer the Pāṇḍavas in battle,
and lacking the energy to attain prosperity like one who is not a kṣatriya, he remained despondent.
Accompanied by the King of Gāndhāra, he proposed a fraudulent game of dice.
Listen, Sañjaya, to everything that was understood by me there and exactly how it occurred;
for having heard my words, which are endowed with wisdom and grounded in reality, you shall understand them.
"Then, O Sauti, you shall know me as one whose eye is wisdom,
when I heard that he had drawn his wonderful bow, pierced the target, and indeed caused it to fall to the earth."
When I heard that while all the kings looked on, Kṛṣṇā was carried away, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory. When I heard that Subhadrā [was brought] to Dvārakā;
When Mādhavī was forcibly carried off by Arjuna,
and the two Vṛṣṇi heroes went to Indraprastha, then,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the king of the gods, while pouring down rain,
was warded off by Arjuna with divine arrows,
and likewise that Agni was gratified at Khandava;
Then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the five Pārthas, together with Kuntī, had escaped from the house of lac.
And when I heard that Vidura had been sent by them for the sake of achieving their own purpose,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Draupadī was dragged into the midst of the assembly hall...
When Arjuna had pierced the target and defeated the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas— those heroic warriors who were so well-prepared— then,
O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Jarāsaṃdha, the most eminent of the Magadhas, blazing in the midst of the warrior class,
had been slain by Bhīmasena after he went [to him] with his two arms;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory when I heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu,
by force, had brought the rulers of the earth under their control during their conquest of the quarters.
When I heard that the great Rājasūya sacrifice had been performed,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory;
when I heard that he was the essence of the entire universe.
O Saṃjaya, when I heard that Maya had out of affection fashioned for the king that fierce mace which was then given to Bhīmasena, I had no hope of victory.
When I heard that Yudhiṣṭhira had been deprived of his kingdom,
defeated at dice by the son of Subala,
and followed by his immeasurable brothers;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that Draupadī— distressed, with tears in her throat, and clad in a single garment— had been led into the assembly hall.
When I heard that the one with a protector was treated as if she were unprotected while she was menstruating, then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory— when I heard of that heap of garments there.
The gambler of dull intellect, Duḥśāsana, provoked him and did not stop; at that time,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
O dear one, when I heard of the various deeds of the virtuous Pāṇḍavas as they set out for the forest, enduring hardships out of love for their eldest brother;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard Draupadī speaking of her exile, weeping with a throat choked by tears.

"When I heard that she was devoted to her husband and that it was not dharma for her to dwell there, then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory— when I heard that [he was surrounded] by thousands of *snātaka*s."
When I heard that the King of Dharma had followed [the forest] and was dwelling in the woods,
subsisting on alms among the high-souled Brahmins, then,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that all the sons of Pṛthā had gathered in their forest dwellings,
being attended by ancient and eminent sages together with their hosts at times.
Then, O Sañjaya,
I had no hope of victory when I heard that Arjuna, having gratified Tryambaka, the god of gods, in battle while he was in the form of a hunter, [had obtained his weapons].
When I heard that Dhananjaya, while staying in the third heaven, had obtained that great Pashupata weapon, then, O Sanjaya, I had no hope for victory.
O Sañjaya, when I heard that he was properly studying the divine weapon from Śakra himself— that praiseworthy one who is true to his promise— then I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the Kālakeyas and the Paulomas— who were arrogant because they had been granted boons and were unconquerable by the gods— were utterly defeated by Arjuna; then...
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the diadem-adorned one, the crusher of enemies, had set out for the sake of slaying the Asuras.
And when I heard that he had returned from the world of Śakra with his purpose accomplished,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory;
yet when I heard that he had set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords...
When I heard that the son of Pāṇḍu was accompanied by Romaśa,
and that Arjuna had obtained the celestial weapons from him,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Bhīma and the other Pārthas had met with Vaiśravaṇa in that region inaccessible to mortals;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that those who had gone on the cattle-expedition were captured by the Gandharvas and subsequently liberated by Arjuna.
When I heard that Draupadī had been seized by the ruler of the Sindhus, while my own sons were intent on the counsel of Karṇa, then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
Jayadratha, who had not been brought [back] and was released by Arjuna,
was spared with his life remaining.
"Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard, O Sūta, that Dharma had met with Dharmarāja in the form of a Yakṣa."
When I heard him answering correctly the questions that were posed,
and that my men did not know them, then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
O Sañjaya, when I heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu were living in disguise in the kingdom of Virāṭa together with Kṛṣṇā, I had no hope then for victory.
When I heard that those skillful sons of Pṛthā, who are like fires, were living in concealment and could not be seen by various means, even though they were searching for them.
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the most excellent of the Kīcakas had been slain along with his hundred brothers.
O Sañjaya, when I heard that Bhīmasena had [fought] for the sake of Draupadī in battle at that time, I had no hope for victory, even as I heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu were dwelling [in exile].
When I heard that the skillful Pārthas had become invisible through various means in battle by means of Bhīmasena,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the most excellent of my men had been broken by Dhanañjaya on a single chariot,
while the high-souled one was dwelling in the kingdom of Virāṭa;
Then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the daughter of the Matsya king, Uttarā, who was duly honored, had been given to Arjuna as his wife.
And Arjuna accepted her for the sake of a son; at that time,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory— when I heard that he was defeated and deprived of his wealth.
When Yudhiṣṭhira had gone forth as a renunciant and fallen away from his kinsmen, and yet possessed seven akṣauhiṇīs,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard from Nārada that those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, were Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, I said,
"I shall see them in the world of Brahmā."
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that Vāsudeva Mādhava was devoted with his whole soul to the cause of the Pāṇḍavas.
When I heard that they called this earth "the one stride" of his,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory— when I heard that Kṛṣṇa had acted for the welfare of the world.
O Sañjaya, when he who seeks peace approached the Kurus,
and while seeking peace departed without having achieved his purpose,
then I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Karṇa and Duryodhana had resolved upon the capture of Keśava,
and that he was manifesting himself in many forms;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory, when I heard that as Vāsudeva was departing,
[Kṛṣṇā] stood alone at the front of the chariot.
O Sañjaya, when I heard that Vāsudeva had departed after Keshava had consoled the distressed Pṛthā, then I had no hope for victory.
O Sañjaya, even when Phalguna, with the wheel of his chariot in hand, was present there, I had no hope for victory at that time, seeing my son desiring to seize him on his elephant.
When I heard that Vāsudeva was their counselor,
as well as Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu, and the son of Bharadvāja pronouncing blessings upon them;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory when I heard that Karṇa said to Bhīṣma,
"I will not fight while you are fighting."
Having abandoned the army, he indeed retreated; at that time,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory when I heard that Vāsudeva and Arjuna were both there.
Likewise, when the immeasurable bow Gāṇḍīva and those three of fierce prowess had come together, then,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Arjuna, overcome by dejection, was sinking down upon the seat of his chariot, and that Kṛṣṇa was showing him the worlds within his own body;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory when I heard that Bhīṣma, the scorcher of enemies,
was slaughtering ten thousand chariot-warriors in battle.
When not a single one among them appeared to be slain,
then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory—
when I heard that [the son of] Ganga had been struck down in battle.
When the sons of Pāṇḍu joyfully carried out that death ordained for the righteous man by himself,
then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Bhīṣma,
the exceedingly heroic and unassailable in battles, had been slain by Pārtha after Śikhaṇḍin was placed in front of him;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the aged hero was lying upon a bed of arrows, struck down by shafts with variegated feathers.
When I heard that the Somakas had been reduced to a small remnant after Bhīṣma was laid low,
then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the son of Śantanu was lying on his bed of arrows;
When Arjuna, urged by the need for water,
pierced the earth to satisfy Bhīṣma there, then,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Venus and the Sun were conjoined,
favorable for the victory of the sons of Kuntī,
and that beasts of prey were constantly howling at us;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when Droṇa, a versatile warrior, displayed various paths of weaponry in battle.
When I heard that he did not slay the most excellent Pāṇḍavas,
then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory;
and when I heard of our own great chariot-warriors—
When I heard that the Saṃśaptakas, who were stationed for Arjuna’s destruction,
had been slain by Arjuna,
then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the son of Subhadrā, a single hero, having broken through the impenetrable array protected by Bhāradvāja with weapon in hand, had entered it;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory, when they surrounded the youth Abhimanyu and,
having slain him, became joyful in appearance.
When I heard that they were unable to overcome the son of Pṛthā, though they were great chariot-warriors, then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory;
and when I heard that Abhimanyu had been slain.
O Sañjaya, when I heard the Dhārtarāṣṭras crying out in joy and delusion, and that Arjuna had released his wrath upon the ruler of the Sindhus, then I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Arjuna had made a vow for the sake of the King of Sindhu, and that he had fulfilled that vow for his slaughter in the midst of the enemy;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that Dhanañjaya’s horses were exhausted, and that he had unyoked them, watered them, and let them rest.
When I heard that Vāsudeva had again joined him as he set forth,
then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory; and when I heard that his mounts were taking rest.
O Sañjaya, when all the warriors were held back by Arjuna with his Gāṇḍīva bow as he stood upon the seat of his chariot, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Yuyudhāna, having crushed Droṇa’s army— which was difficult even for the hosts of Nāgas to withstand—
had gone to where those two, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, were;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that Karna,
having encountered Bhima, had released him from death after reviling him with words.
When Karṇa, with the tip of his bow, struck that hero,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory—
when Droṇa, Kṛtavarman, and Kṛpa were [all failing him].
O Sañjaya, when Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and the heroic king of Madra could not endure the slaughter of the ruler of the Sindhus,
then I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the divine spear given by the king of the gods had been rendered futile by Mādhava against the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca of terrible form;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that in battle the Sūtaputra had released the *śakti* weapon against Karṇa and Ghaṭotkaca.
When I heard that Savyasācin was to be slain by her in battle, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope for victory. When I heard that the preceptor Droṇa was alone—
When Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having transgressed dharma,
slaughtered him as he sat upon the seat of his chariot intent on death,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that in the midst of the world, the son of Droṇa had fought Nakula, the son of Mādrī, a Pāṇḍava, as his equal in a single-chariot combat; and while he was fighting, [the son of Droṇa]...
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory, when Drona’s son, after Drona was slain,
began to discharge the divine Narayana weapon.
"O Sañjaya, when I heard that Bhīmasena had drunk [the blood], I had no hope for victory over those Pāṇḍavas, even though no one had reached the end of them."
When the blood of my brother Duḥśāsana was being drunk in battle by Bhīma, and no one else could restrain him,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
O charioteer, when I heard that the fierce Bhīma of terrible deeds had drunk blood in battle after piercing the chest of the crown prince;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory when I heard that Karṇa— the exceedingly heroic one,
unassailable in battles— had been slain by Pārtha.
When I heard of that secret of the gods— the conflict among the brothers— then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory. When I heard [of the deaths] of the son of Droṇa and Kṛpa;
When Duḥśāsana and the fierce Kṛtavarman were assailing Yudhiṣṭhira while he was alone,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
O Sūta, when I heard that the heroic King of Madra had been slain in battle by Dharmarāja—
he who always vied with Kṛṣṇa in combat— [I was overcome].
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the son of Subala, who relied on the power of illusion, was defeated by the Pāṇḍava at the root of the quarrel and the gambling match.
When I heard that the wicked one had been slain in battle by Sahadeva, then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory. When I heard that he was alone, exhausted, and lying down;
O Sañjaya, when he had gone to the lake and solidified those waters, leaving Duryodhana carless and his pride shattered,
I then had no hope for victory.
When I heard that the Pāṇḍavas,
together with Vāsudeva, were staying at the pool of the Gaṅgā,
and that they were insulting my intolerant son;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard, my dear, that he was moving in various maneuvers,
traversing circles in the mace-duel.
When I heard that Vasudeva had been struck down through [Duryodhana’s] own intellect,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory— when I heard that he had been slain by those led by the son of Droṇa.
When the Pāñcālas and the sons of Draupadī were slain while asleep—
a loathsome and disgraceful deed— then,
O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory.
When I heard that Aśvatthāman, following Bhīmasena, discharged the supreme weapon— the *aiṣīka*—
in his anger, by which he destroyed the fetus;
Then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory,
when I heard that the Brahmashira weapon discharged by Arjuna was neutralized by the Svasti weapon.
When Aśvatthāman gave me the jewel-gem,
then, O Sañjaya, I had no hope for victory— when I heard that the son of Droṇa [had cast it] into the womb.
O Saṃjaya, when that great weapon was being hurled by the son of Virāṭa, I had no hope for victory, thinking of Hari’s vow: "I shall restore him to life."
Dvaipāyana and Keśava both cursed the son of Droṇa with mutual imprecations;
and having realized this, O Sūta, I am now deprived of my wits.
Burning with grief and deprived of my sons and grandsons, I now reflect with a ruined intellect;
O Sūta, I do not know what ought to be done.
Gāndhārī is to be pitied, deprived of her sons and grandsons;
likewise are the daughters-in-law, separated from their fathers and brothers.
A difficult task has been accomplished by the Pāṇḍavas.
The kingdom has been regained by them without a rival;
alas, I have heard that only ten remain in this war—
three of us and seven of the Pāṇḍavas.
In that battle, a conflict among the Kṣatriyas, eighteen Akṣauhiṇīs were struck down;
it was a gathering of great-souled men overtaken by time.
The son who was my cause for joy has been destroyed;
overwhelmed by darkness, delusion seems to enter me. O charioteer, I perceive no consciousness; my mind is as if reeling.
Having spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lamenting and deeply distressed, fainted; then, having recovered his breath, he addressed these words to Sañjaya:
"O Sañjaya, since things have come to this pass, I wish to give up my life without delay."
"For I do not see even the slightest fruit in maintaining this life.
To the lord of the earth, who was speaking thus, dejected, lamenting,
sighing like a serpent, and fainting again and again—
The wise son of Gavalgaṇa spoke these words of great significance:
"You have indeed heard from the words of Dvaipāyana and the wise Nārada about kings of great energy and great strength."
Born into great royal lineages and endowed with all virtues, they were skilled in divine weapons and possessed splendor equal to that of Śakra;
having conquered the earth through righteousness, they performed sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having attained fame in this world, they subsequently fell under the power of time:
the great chariot-warrior Vainya, the hero Sṛñjaya, the best among victors,
Suhotra, Rantideva, Kakṣīvān, and likewise Auśija.
Bāhlīka, Damana, Śaibya, the unconquered Śaryāti, Viśvāmitra the slayer of enemies, the mighty Ambarīṣa,
Marutta, Manu, Ikṣvāku, Gaya, and Bharata as well.
Rāma, son of Daśaratha, Śaśabindu, Bhagīratha,
the highly fortunate Kṛtavīrya, as well as Janamejaya,
and Yayāti of auspicious deeds, whom the gods themselves officiated at his sacrifice.
"This earth, marked by sacrificial altars and pillars and containing places of sacrifice,"—
thus were the twenty-four kings described in former times by the celestial sage Nārada to Śaibya, who was consumed by grief for his son.
And before them, other kings who were even more powerful had passed away—
great chariot-warriors, high-souled, and endowed with all virtues:
Pūru, Kuru, Yadu, Śūra, Viṣvagaśva, and Mahādhṛti.
Anenas, Yuvanāśva, Kakutstha, the valiant Raghu,
Vijitī, Vītihotra, Bhava, Śveta, Bṛhadguru, Uśīnara, Śataratha, Kaṅka, Duliduha, and Druma.
Dambhodbhava, Para, Vena, Sagara, Saṃkṛti, Nimi, Ajeya, Paraśu, Puṇḍra, Śambhu, Devāvṛdha, Anagha,
Devāhvaya, Supratima, Supratīka, and Bṛhadratha.
Nala, the king of Niṣadha, was possessed of great energy, a disciplined soul, and excellent wisdom;
he was devoted to truth, free from fear, a friend to his people, and a powerful lord.
He had long shanks, was known as Anaraṇya, was like the sun, was kind to his servants, and was firm in his auspicious vows.
Balabandhu, Nirāmarda, Ketuśṛṅga, Bṛhadbala,
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Bṛhatketu, Dīptaketu, Nirāmaya,
Avikṣit, Prabala, Dhūrta, Kṛtabandhu, and Dṛḍheṣudhi.
The Mahāpurāṇa, the Saṃbhāvya, the Pratyanga, and the Parahā-śruti—
these and many others are heard of by the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and even by the millions (padma).
Having abandoned vast enjoyments, wise and mighty kings who were even greater than your sons have met their end— kings whose deeds were divine, as was their prowess and their generosity.
Greatness, faith in the existence of the divine, truthfulness, purity, and straightforwardness—
these are proclaimed in the world by the learned, the ancient ones, and the best of poets; yet even they, though endowed with all prosperity and virtues, have gone to their destruction.
Your sons were evil-minded, tormented by wrath, greedy, and largely of wicked conduct; you ought not to grieve for them. You are learned, wise, intelligent, and esteemed by the prudent.
O Bhārata, those whose intellect follows the scriptures do not fall into delusion.
O lord of men, you too understand both restraint and favor;
yet it is heard that you have not been excessively devoted to protecting your son.
That which was destined to be has come to pass; therefore, you ought not to grieve. Who is able to turn back destiny by means of superior wisdom?
No one can overstep the path ordained by the Creator.
All this—existence and non-existence, pleasure and pain—has Time as its root.
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures. Time again extinguishes Time itself as it consumes all creatures.
Time transforms all things in the world, both auspicious and inauspicious;
Time withdraws all creatures and emits them again.
While others sleep, Time remains awake; for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Saṃjaya said:
O Indra among kings, the wise do not grieve for those who have passed away, nor for those yet to come, nor for those currently living; for Time is the ender of the world.
Time moves unimpeded and impartially through all beings. Having understood that past, future, and present entities are fashioned by time, you ought not to lose your composure.
Having thus consoled Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, who was afflicted by grief for his son, Sūta Gāvalgaṇi then restored him to composure;
and having spoken thus to the king, Sañjaya became silent.
Having heard that, Dhṛtarāṣṭra also took recourse in fortitude alone; considering, "By fate this has come to pass," that best of wise men [remained steadfast].
Sūta said:
Regarding this, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana has declared this meritorious Upaniṣad:
"From the meritorious study of the Mahābhārata, even for one who studies but a single foot [of a verse] with faith, all sins are purified without remainder."
For the sake of the welfare of the worlds and out of compassion, the Best of Sages [composed this];
for if these three— the Bhārata, the Sun, and the Moon— did not exist,
what would be the condition of the world blinded by the darkness of ignorance?
Having churned the ocean of the Vedas with the churning-stick of his intellect,
he brought forth for the welfare of the world the moon of the Mahābhārata;
for herein are found the meritorious celestial sages, as well as the Brahman-sages and royal sages.
The performers of auspicious deeds, as well as the yakṣas and mahoragas, are celebrated here;
and the eternal Lord Vāsudeva is also celebrated herein,
for he is indeed truth, righteousness, purity, and merit itself.
The eternal Brahman, supreme, fixed, the ancient light,
whose divine deeds the wise proclaim; from whom that God proceeds both the non-existent and the existent, and indeed both the existent and the non-existent.
Continuity, worldly activity, birth, death, and rebirth—

that which is heard regarding the internal self and that which consists of the qualities of the five elements, as well as that which is beyond the unmanifest (avyakta)— all this is proclaimed to be that very [Brahman].
That which the best of ascetics, disciplined and endowed with the power of meditation and yoga,
perceive as established within themselves like a reflection in a mirror—
he who is full of faith, ever-striving, and devoted to the true Dharma [attains it].
By studying this chapter, a person is liberated from evil. By constantly listening from the beginning to this table of contents of the *Bhārata*, a believer never sinks under difficulties.
By reciting even a small portion during both twilights, one is immediately liberated from sin—
whatever may have been accumulated during the day and night through the *Anukramaṇī*.
For this is the very body of the *Bhārata*, consisting of truth and immortality itself.
All divine sacrifices, Viṣṇu, and the great Upaniṣads are like the nectar extracted from herbs by the Āraṇyakas from the Vedas;
they are like butter from curds, or like the Brāhmaṇa among bipeds.
As the ocean is the best among lakes and the cow is the most excellent among quadrupeds,
so too is the Bhārata said to be the most preeminent. Furthermore, whoever should cause even a single quarter-verse of this to be heard by Brahmins at a *śrāddha* ceremony—
That inexhaustible food and drink attends upon his ancestors.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me."
A learned man who causes this Veda of Kṛṣṇa to be heard attains his purpose;
he would even cast off the sin committed by killing an embryo— of this there is no doubt—
who, being pure, recites this chapter on every lunar festival.
"It is my conviction that by him the entire Bhārata has been studied,
who would constantly listen to this work of the seers with faith;
such a man shall attain long life, fame, and the path to heaven."

In ancient times, when the four Vedas were placed on one side and the *Bhārata* alone on the other, the assembled celestial sages weighed them together; for it was found that the *Bhārata* surpassed the four Vedas along with their secret Upanishads.
From that time forth, it has been called the Mahābhārata in this world;
because it maintains greatness and weightiness, it is even more than that. Due to its greatness and its possession of weight, it is called the Mahābhārata.
He who knows its etymological derivation is liberated from all evils. Austerity is not a defilement, study is not a defilement, and the natural injunctions of the Veda are not a defilement.
The forcible seizure of wealth is not *kalka*; rather, those very acts when corrupted by intention (*bhāva*) constitute *kalka*.
— Śrī Sūta.
Know that the all-pervading Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana is Nārāyaṇa himself;
for who else but the lotus-eyed one could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
It was by churning the great ocean of the Vedas with the churning-stick of his intellect that he [produced it].
The moon of the Mahābhārata was produced for the welfare of the world;
what else could there be worthy of praise for him who desires the welfare of all the worlds? By him, the Vedas were divided, and the wonderful Mahābhārata was composed.
"May all cross over difficulties; may everyone behold auspicious things.
Having spoken thus, he revealed therein the meanings of all the Vedas. Listen now to this lion’s roar of the high-souled Ṛṣabha.
O supreme bull among men, regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa:
whatever exists here may exist elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
For this world is by its very nature attached to artha and kāma.
Therefore, I shall compose this compendium devoted to the liberation through Dharma;
for what fruit does a man obtain by describing desire to those who lust, or describing greed to the greedy— thereby casting them, like a blind man, into a well?
Even the Sage, recognizing that sensual pleasure and material wealth captivate the world,
maintained these two— though they are censurable— with the intention of teaching the Dharma and liberation;
otherwise, they would have been the causes for the terrible bondage of saṃsāra for all people.
How could the wise Sage, possessed of great compassion, describe them? Having described those two for the sake of introducing people to reflection on the world,
he then censured them right here by means of various historical narratives (itihāsas).

If these three— the Bhārata, the Sun, and the Moon— did not exist, what state would there be for the world blinded by the darkness of ignorance? Having understood this, the wise, ever endowed with faith, [should study it].

This collection of history from the Bhārata is to be studied; whatever verses are found anywhere within the Bhārata that have identical meaning, I shall indeed incorporate them into this meritorious compendium.
Who is capable of extracting all those verses from the *Bhārata*?
It would be like attempting to extract every jewel from the great ocean through yoga;
yet he has undertaken this task out of mere pride in his own wisdom.
"But it was my devotion to Bhārata that urged me on, even against my will.
The sages said:
"O son of a Sūta, regarding that which was called 'Samantapañcaka'—"
"We wish to hear all of this according to the proper method.
Sūta said:
"O Brahmins, if you have a desire to listen, I shall speak auspicious stories."
O best of beings, you ought to hear about that which is called Samantapañcaka. At the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, Rāma, the foremost of weapon-wielders,
impelled by indignation, repeatedly struck down the royal kṣatriyas.

Having exterminated the entire warrior class by his own prowess, that son of Jamadagni, blazing with the splendor of fire, created five lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka, each one a yojana in length and breadth, O powerful one.
01.002.005 In those lakes of blood, he, overcome by rage, offered libations to the ancestors with blood; so we have heard.
01.002.006 Then the ancestors, headed by Ṛcīka, approached that bull among Brahmins.
Rāma said:
"O Rāma, O Rāma, O highly fortunate one of the Bhṛgu lineage! We are pleased with you, O Lord, because of this devotion to your father and because of your prowess."
"Choose a boon— may it be well with you— what do you desire, O one of great splendor?
If my ancestors are pleased, and if I am worthy of your favor,
[then grant that] which was destroyed by me when I was overcome by wrath."
"Therefore, may I be released from this sin; this is the boon I request.
And may these lakes of mine become renowned on earth as sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
"So shall it be," said the ancestors, those bulls among Brahmins.
"Forgive him," they entreated; thereupon he desisted.
The region near those lakes of bloody waters is celebrated as the sacred Samantapañcaka.
The wise declare that a region should be designated by the very name of the characteristic feature with which it is observed to be endowed.
And when the interval between the Dvāpara and Kali ages had arrived, there came into being...
In Samantapañcaka, the battle between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas took place;
in that most righteous region, free from defects of the soil,
eighteen akṣauhiṇīs assembled, desiring to fight.
Having gathered there, those twice-born ones and they all met their end right then and there. O twice-born ones, it was thus that the name of that region arose;
indeed, that region has been described to you as both meritorious and delightful.
"O best of sages, all this has been told by me to you,
regarding how that region became renowned and famous throughout the three worlds.
The Ṛṣis said:
"O son of a Sūta, regarding that which was mentioned by you as an *akṣauhiṇī*,
we wish to hear all of it exactly as it is—
the measurement of an *akṣauhiṇī* in terms of chariots, horses, men, and elephants."
"Tell us exactly as it is, for everything is known to you.
Sūta said:
"One chariot, one elephant, five men, and foot-soldiers."
Three horses and one foot-soldier, as known by those skilled in the matter, are designated as a *patti*. The wise declare that three times this *patti* is a *senāmukha*,
and three *senāmukhas* are designated as one *gulma*.
Three *gulmas* are called a *gaṇa*; three *gaṇas* are known as a *vāhinī*; three *vāhinyas* are designated as a *pṛtanā* by the wise;
three *pṛtanās* are a *camū*; and three *camūs* are an *anīkinī*.
The wise say that ten times an *anīkinī* is an *akṣauhiṇī*.
O best of the twice-born, the calculation of chariots in an *akṣauhiṇī*,
according to those who know the principles of numerical computation, is twenty-one thousand.
One hundred and eight, and furthermore seventy more;
this indeed should be specified here as the total measure of elephants.
It should be known that there are one hundred thousand and nine thousand.
O sinless ones, they say that the number of men here was exactly three hundred and fifty;
likewise, the number of horses was sixty-five thousand six hundred and ten.

01.002.023 Those who know the truth of calculation call this an *akṣauhiṇī*, which I have described to you in detail, O best of the twice-born. 01.002.024 For it was by this reckoning that the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas stood arrayed.
O best of the twice-born, eighteen akṣauhiṇīs in total were assembled in that region,
and they all met their destruction right there,
with the Kauravas as the cause, by Time of wondrous deeds.
Bhīṣma, the knower of supreme weapons, fought for ten days;
Droṇa, however, protected the Kuru army for five days;
and Karṇa, the crusher of enemy forces, fought for two days.
Śalya fought for half a day, but after that,
there was a mace-duel between Duryodhana and Bhīma for the remaining half of the day.
At the end of that very day, however, the son of Hṛdika, the son of Droṇa, and the son of Gautama [engaged in combat].
They slaughtered the army of Yudhiṣṭhira while it was sleeping and unsuspecting at night.
As for that extensive narrative of the Bhārata which you heard at Śaunaka’s sacrifice— that was recited at Janamejaya’s sacrifice by the wise disciple of Vyāsa.
The fame and prowess of the rulers of the earth have been recounted in detail;
the entire, supreme narrative of the Mahābhārata has been told. Therein, I shall further relate from the beginning the narrative of Pauloma.
It is a narration of diverse meanings and words, endowed with many traditional doctrines; it is embraced by wise men as detachment is by those seeking liberation,
as the self is among things to be known, and as life is among dear things.
This history, whose primary purpose is the ultimate truth, is the most excellent among all sacred scriptures;
for upon this supreme history is grounded the highest intelligence,
just as all speech— comprising both vowels and consonants— is based upon the world and the Vedas.
Listen now to the summary of the sections (*parvasaṃgraha*) of this history of the *Bhārata*, which is permeated by wisdom and composed of diverse chapters and divisions. First,
the *Ādiparva* was proclaimed of old by the wise son of Parāśara.
First is the Table of Contents of the Parvas, and second is the Summary of the Parvas.
Then follow the Pauṣya, the Pauloma, the Āstīka, and the Descent of the Original Lineage;
after that, the Sambhava Parva is declared, which is marvelous and fashioned by the gods.
The burning of the house of lac is told here, and the section concerning the son of Hiḍimbā is spoken of; then follows the section on the slaying of Baka, then the Caitraratha section,
and thereafter the section on the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of the princess of Pañcāla is recounted.
Having conquered them according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, the marriage rites were then performed;
this constitutes the Vidurāgamana Parva and likewise the acquisition of the kingdom.
Then follows the forest-dwelling of Arjuna and the abduction of Subhadrā.

After the abduction of Subhadrā, the section known as the Haraṇahārika should be known; then follows that called the Khāṇḍavadāha, wherein occurs the appearance of Maya. After that, the Sabhāparvan is proclaimed, and following that, the Mantraparvan.
The Jarāsaṃdhavadha Parva, and likewise the Digvijaya Parva; after the Digvijaya Parva, the Rājasūyika Parva is told. Then follows the Arghābhiharaṇa, and after that, the Śiśupālavadha.
Then the Dyūtaparva (The Book of the Gambling Match) is proclaimed, and after that, the Anudyūta (The Subsequent Gambling).
Following that is the Āraṇyakaparva (The Forest Book), as well as the Kirmīravadha (The Slaying of Kirmīra).
After this, the Arjunābhigamana (The Return of Arjuna) is to be known as the next Parva.
The section concerning the battle between Īśvara and Arjuna is known as the Kairāta-parvan;
following that, the Indralokābhigamana-parvan is to be known;
and after that, the Tīrthayātrā-parvan of the wise Kuru king.
The section on the slaying of Jaṭāsura; following that, the battle with the Yakṣas;
then Arjuna’s acquisition of divine weapons and his arrival;
then the battle with the Nivātakavacas and the Ājagara Parvan.
Likewise, the section immediately following that should be known as the Ājagara-parvan;
after that, the section called Mārkaṇḍeya-samasyā is mentioned;
and then follows the section containing the dialogue between Draupadī and Satyabhāmā.
Then follows the Ghoṣayātrā Parvan, and after that the Mṛgasvapnabhaya;
then the Rāmopākhyāna Parvan and the Sāvitrī-upākhyāna,
which contains the wonderful majesty of the devoted wife Sāvitrī.
01,002.046b Herein, the Rāmopākhyāna (Episode of Rāma) is to be known as the next section;
01,002.046c immediately following that, the narrative of the Vrihidraunikam is told.
01,002.046d Having reached a decision regarding the counsel and reflecting upon the task at hand, [he spoke].

01.002.046 Following this is the section called the Nalākhyāna, and after that, the Mṛgasvapna; thereafter, the narrative of Nahuṣa is told immediately next. 01.002.047 Then follows the Draupadīharaṇa section, concerning [her] abduction from the forest by the ruler of the Sindhus.
Next, the Kuṇḍalāharaṇa Parva is here described;
after that is the Āraṇeya Parva, and immediately following that is the Vairāṭa Parva,
which includes the entry of the Pāṇḍavas and their observance of the agreement.
The section on the slaughter of the Kīcakas, then the section on the seizure of the cattle,
and the marriage section concerning Abhimanyu and the daughter of Virāṭa are recorded;
after this, the most wonderful Udyoga Parva is to be known.
Next, the section known as Saṃjayayāna should be known;
following that is the Prajāgara section, concerning Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s anxiety;
and then the Sānatsujāta section, which contains secret teachings on the vision of the supreme self.
The section on the junction of the vehicles, followed by the Bhagavad-yāna;
then the narrative of Mātali, the life of Gālava,
the Sāvitra, the Vāmadevya, and the narrative of Vainya.
The Jāmadagnya episode, the Parva of the Sixteen Kings,
the entry of Kṛṣṇa into the assembly hall, the instruction of Vidulā’s son,
the Udyoga, the departure of the armies, and the Śveta episode.
01.002.052a Herein is to be known the section concerning the dispute of the high-souled Karṇa; 01.002.052b having reached a decision on the counsel, the task was thoroughly deliberated upon;
and also the narrative of his consecration as commander-in-chief is recounted.
Then follows the *Śvetopākhyāna*, which is wonderful and based on many stories, told by Vāsudeva;
then the *Niryāṇaparvan*, concerning the departure of the armies of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas;
and immediately after that, the *Rathātirathasaṃkhyāparvan* is declared.
The section on the arrival of the owl-messenger, which increases indignation;
and thereafter, the Ambopākhyāna section is to be known.
In this [latter], the great seer granted divine vision to Sañjaya.
The Bhīṣmābhiṣecana Parva, which contains marvelous causes, should be known [as the next]; immediately after that, the Jambūkhaṇḍavinirmāṇa Parva is stated;
thereafter, the Bhūmiparva should be known, which is a proclamation of the extent of the continents.
The Bhagavadgītā Parva has been described; after that, the Bhīṣmavadha [Parva];
the Droṇābhiṣeka Parva has been described; after that, the Saṃśaptakavadha [Parva];
the Abhimanyuvadha Parva; and the Pratijñā Parva is also mentioned.
The Jayadrathavadha Parva, followed by the Ghaṭotkacavadha;
thereafter, the Droṇavadha Parva, which causes the hair to stand on end, should be known;
and immediately after that, the Mokṣa of the Nārāyaṇa-weapon is declared as the next Parva.
Then the Karṇaparva is to be known, and after that the Śalyaparva;
then the Hradapraveśana-parva, and after that the Gadāyuddha-parva;
then the Sārasvata-parva, which possesses the qualities of the lineage of sacred fords (tīrtha).
After this, however, the section called Sauptika, which is loathsome, is told;
after that, the most terrible Aiṣīka section is indicated;
then follows the Jalapradānika section, and after that, the Strīparva.
Then follows the Śrāddhaparvan, concerning the funeral rites for the Kurus;
then the Ābhiṣecanikaparvan, regarding the consecration of the wise Dharmarāja;
and the Cārvākanigrahaparvan, concerning the subduing of the Rākṣasa who had assumed the form of a Brahmin.
01.002.063c Immediately following that, the section on the classification of houses was spoken.

01.002.064a Then comes the Śānti Parva, wherein the duties of kings (rājadharma) are proclaimed; 01.002.064c the section on duties in times of distress (āpaddharma) is spoken, and after that, the Mokṣadharma.
The arrival for the parrot’s questions, the instruction on the questions of Brahmā, the manifestation, and the dialogue with Durvāsas through his illusory power—
thereafter, the supreme Parva known as the Ānuśāsanika is to be understood.
Then follows the Svargārohaṇika Parva, and then the Bhīṣma Parva of the wise one;
then the Aśvamedhika Parva, which destroys all sins;
and thereafter the Anugītā Parva is to be known as that which speaks of the supreme self (adhyātma).
The section named Āśramavāsa and the section on the Vision of the Sons;
thereafter, the section on the Arrival of Nārada is spoken of here.
Following that, the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) and the enumeration of the stages of life (āśrama) are to be known.
Then follows the vision of the deceased by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds;
thereafter, the terrible Mausala-parvan is described,
followed by the Mahāprasthānika-parvan and the Svargārohaṇika-parvan.
After that, the Svargārohaṇika Parva is to be known;
following that is the Harivaṃśa Parva, the Purāṇa known as the Khila. It contains the Viṣṇu Parva, the childhood deeds of Viṣṇu, and likewise the slaying of Kaṃsa.
The *Saubhavadha-parvan*, the *Bāṇa-parvan*, and the *Naraka-parvan*; at Janamejaya’s sacrifice, the *Nakula-ākhyāna* itself;
and the wonderful and great *Bhaviṣyat-parvan*—these are also declared among the *Khilas*.
This complete collection of one hundred sections was spoken by the high-souled Vyāsa; it was then recounted exactly as it is by Lomaharṣaṇa, the son of a Sūta,
in the Naimiṣa forest, consisting indeed of eighteen books.
01,002.071c This summary of the *Bhārata*, spoken therein as a compendium of its sections (*parvas*), is as follows:
01,002.071d*0093_01 The *Pauṣya*, the *Pauloma*, the *Āstīka*, and the descent of the original lineage;
01,002.071d*0093_02 the *Saṃbhava*, that which is called the *Jatuveśman* (the House of Lac), and the slaying of Hiḍimba and Baka.
Likewise, the Svayaṃvara of the princess of Pañcāla at Caitraratha; then, having conquered according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, the marriage is recorded;
as well as the arrival of Vidura and the acquisition of the kingdom.
The forest-dwelling of Arjuna, the abduction of Subhadrā thereafter,
the taking and not taking [of her], the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, and the vision of Maya— all this is narrated in the Ādi-parvan.
In the Pauṣya Parvan, the greatness of Uttaṅka is described;
in the Pauloma, the expansion of Bhṛgu’s lineage is proclaimed. [This section] consists of one thousand one hundred and fifty verses.
Likewise, eight chapters are proclaimed in this section;
in the Āstīka-parvan, there is the origin of all the nāgas and of Garuḍa,
as well as the churning of the Ocean of Milk and the birth of Uccaiḥśravas.
This narrative concerning the high-souled Bhāratas came into being during the performance of the Sarpasattra sacrifice by the king, the son of Parikṣit.
It consists of one thousand three hundred and ten verses.
And likewise, there are eighty-four verses in this Parvan;
furthermore, forty chapters were proclaimed therein by the Great Seer.
In the Sambhava Parvan, the various origins of kings are recounted.
Furthermore, the partial incarnations (*aṃśāvataraṇa*) of other brahmins, as well as of the seer Dvaipāyana,
and of the gods,
Daityas, Dānavas, and the highly powerful Yakṣas, are proclaimed here.
Then, the origin of the *nāgas*, serpents, *gandharvas*, birds,
and various other beings occurred within the hermitage of the great seer Kaṇva, the ascetic.
From Duṣyanta, Bharata was born of Śakuntalā,
after whose name this lineage became celebrated throughout the worlds as the Bhārata; furthermore,
there was the rebirth of the high-souled Vasus from the Bhāgīrathī.
The ascent of them once more into heaven within the palace of Śantanu; the birth of Bhīṣma here from the aggregation of portions of their splendor;
his renunciation of the kingdom and his steadfastness in the vow of celibacy.
The fulfillment of his promise, the protection of Citrāṅgada,
and upon Citrāṅgada’s death, the protection of his younger brother Vicitravīrya and the subsequent establishment of him in the kingdom.
The birth of Dharma among men arose from the curse of Aṇīmāṇḍavya;
and his birth from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana resulted from the granting of a boon.
This is the account of the origin of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and the Pāṇḍavas.
The journey to Vāraṇāvata and the counsel of Duryodhana;
and the beneficial instruction given on the road by the wise Vidura to the intelligent Dharmarāja for his welfare, using the language of the Mlecchas.
By the word of Vidura, the undertaking of the tunnel was carried out; furthermore,
the burning of the sleeping Niṣāda woman with her five sons in the house of lac,
as well as the burning of Purocana right there, has been fully described.
The meeting of the Pāṇḍavas with Hiḍimbā in the terrible forest, the slaying of Hiḍimba by the mighty Bhīma,
and the birth of Ghaṭotkaca are all celebrated in this very section.
And the meeting with the great seer Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor;
then, by his command, the Pandavas lived in the house of a brahmin in Ekacakrā,
dwelling there in disguise within the home of a brahmin.
The death of Baka, the amazement of the city-dwellers,
the birth of Kṛṣṇā and Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
and [the account of] having heard [this] from a Brahmin, impelled by the words of Vyāsa—
Desiring Draupadī and wishing to witness the *svayaṃvara*, they set out for the Pañcālas from all sides, filled with curiosity; meanwhile,
Kūṭa was dispatched by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to the Pāṇḍavas.
Having defeated Aṅgāraparṇa on the banks of the Gaṅgā, Arjuna then formed a friendship with him; from that very person, he heard [of the Pāñcālas] and,
accompanied by all his brothers, marched toward the Pāñcāla kingdom.
Then follow the Tāpatya, the Vāsiṣṭha, and the excellent narrative of Aurva;
and also how Dhanañjaya, having pierced the target in the city of Pañcāla,
obtained Draupadī there in the midst of all the kings of the earth.
Where Bhīmasena and Arjuna, having swiftly conquered the enraged lords of the earth as well as Śalya and Karṇa in that great battle,
displayed such immeasurable and superhuman prowess.
Suspecting those Pāṇḍavas [to be the true Kṛṣṇas], the two high-minded ones, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
went to the hall in the house of Bhārgava to meet with them,
and to witness the self-choice ceremony (*svayaṃvara*) of the princess of Pañcāla and the breaking of the mechanical bow.
The great and wonderful battle of the kings with the Pāṇḍavas;
herein is told the marvelous account of the five Indras,
as well as Drupada’s deliberation regarding the five brothers having a single wife.
The superhuman marriage of Draupadī ordained by the gods;
the dispatching of Vidura to the Pāṇḍavas by Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
the arrival of Vidura; and the appearance of Keśava.
The dwelling at Khāṇḍavaprastha and likewise the governance of half the kingdom;
by the command of Nārada, the establishment of the agreement with Draupadī,
and therein the narrative of Sunda and Upasunda is proclaimed.
Immediately thereafter, Phalguna, having approached Yudhiṣṭhira as he sat with Draupadī, took up his weapon for the sake of the brahmins;
having resolved to rescue them, he went home.
01.002.090d–01.002.091a: While the hero was observing his vow, he went to the forest;
there followed Pārtha’s dwelling in the woods, his meeting with Ulūpī on the way, his journey to sacred fords, and the birth of Babhruvāhana.
Right there, he liberated five beautiful apsarases who had attained the state of crocodiles due to the curse of an ascetic Brahmin;
this was followed by the meeting of Pārtha with Kṛṣṇa at the Prabhāsa tīrtha.
In Dvārakā, while Vāsudeva gave his consent, Subhadrā— the object of desire— was won by Kirīṭin as he yearned for her; and when Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, had arrived after taking her away.
Filled with supreme joy, the mighty-armed one dwelt at Śakraprastha together with Pārtha, the doer of noble deeds;
[this section contains] the acquisition of the discus and the bow, and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.
The birth of Abhimanyu of supreme splendor from Subhadrā,
as well as the birth of Draupadī’s sons, is recounted right here; likewise,
the journey of the two Kṛṣṇas along the Yamunā for the sake of recreation.
The liberation of Maya from the fire, the rescue of the serpent,
and the birth of sons for the great seer Mandapāla through Śārṅgin—
this first book, the Ādi-parvan, has thus been described in great detail.
Two hundred chapters were enumerated by the supreme seer;
however, eighteen chapters were composed by Vyāsa of unsurpassed splendor. There are seven thousand and nine hundred verses.
There are eighty-four verses, and this book was composed by the Great-souled One.
The second, however, is called the Sabhā Parva, which contains many narratives;
it describes the construction of the assembly hall for the Pāṇḍavas and the appearance of the Kiṃkaras.
The narration of the assembly of the world-protectors from Nārada, who had seen the gods;
the commencement of the Rājasūya sacrifice; likewise, the slaying of Jarāsaṃdha;
and the liberation by Kṛṣṇa of the kings imprisoned at Girivraja.
Likewise, the conquest of the quarters by the Pāṇḍavas is proclaimed right here;
as well as the arrival of kings with their tributes at the great sacrifice,
the Rājasūya, and the slaying of Śiśupāla during the dispute over the guest-offering (arghya).
Having witnessed that splendor at the sacrifice, Duryodhana was filled with grief and indignation; and when Bhīma mocked him in the assembly hall,
his wrath was kindled, which led him to arrange the game of dice.
Where the gambler Śakuni defeated the Son of Dharma at dice;
where Draupadī, like a boat from the ocean, rescued those submerged in the sea of gambling;
and where the highly wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra [consoled] his daughter-in-law who was in extreme distress.
Having learned that they had crossed over, King Duryodhana caused them to be ferried across;
then he once again challenged the Pāṇḍavas to a game of dice.
Having won, he then sent them away to dwell in the forest.
This entire Sabhā Parva has been narrated by the high-souled one;
it should be known that there are seventy-two chapters here in number,
and two thousand five hundred verses.
It should be known that eleven verses are proclaimed in this parvan.
Beyond this, the great third [parvan], the Āraṇyaka, should be known;
it begins when the high-souled Pāṇḍavas have set out for their forest dwelling.
