And the following of the citizens by the wise son of Dharma;
where the wise Dharmarāja obtained boons from the Sun; and for the sake of food and medicinal herbs, [the boon] was granted by the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
The performance of worship to the Sun for the sake of maintaining the twice-born;
the abandonment by the son of Ambikā of Vidura as he spoke what was beneficial;
and likewise, the departure of the one thus abandoned to the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu.
The return [of the Pāṇḍavas] at the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the instigation of Karṇa by the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
and the counsel of Duryodhana to slay the Pāṇḍavas while they were dwelling in the forest.
Having recognized that evil disposition, [the account of] Vyāsa’s swift arrival,
the prohibition against departure, and the narrative of Surabhī; as well as Maitreya’s arrival here and the instruction given to the king.
The casting of the curse upon King Duryodhana by that very same person;
the slaying of Kirmīra by Bhīmasena in combat;
and the production of food through the instruction of Dhaumya and the grace of the Sun.
The utterance of Maitreya’s curse and the exile of Vidura;
the arrival of the Vṛṣṇis and all the Pāñcālas there,
having heard that they had been defeated by Śakuni through deceit at the game of dice.
The pacification of the enraged Hari by Kirīṭin;
the lamentation of the princess of Pañcāla in the presence of Vāsudeva; and the consolation proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa for her who was afflicted with grief.

The arrival of the kinsmen and the shedding of tears by Draupadī; the narrative of the slaying of Kirmīra, as well as the arrival of the Vṛṣṇis and all the Pāñcālas, and likewise the narrative of Saubha.
Wherein is the narrative of the slaying of Saubha and the slaying of Kirmīra; and indeed,
the carrying away of Subhadrā together with her sons by Kṛṣṇa to the city of Dvārakā, as well as that of the sons of Draupadī by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then follows the entry of the Pāṇḍavas into the beautiful Dvaitavana forest;
here also is recorded the conversation of Dharmarāja with Kṛṣṇā,
as well as the conversation of Bhīma with the King.
The arrival of Vyāsa near the sons of Pāṇḍu; then, through the power of his recollection, the great seer’s gift of knowledge to the king; and the departure for Kāmyaka forest once Vyāsa had departed.
The exile of the infinitely radiant Pārtha for the sake of the celestial weapon,
his battle with Mahādeva in the form of a Kirāta,
the vision of the world-protectors, and his ascent to heaven.
The journey of Arjuna (Kirīṭin) to the realm of Mahendra for the sake of weapons,
wherein great anxiety arose in Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
and the meeting with the great seer Bṛhadaśva, whose soul was purified.

The lamentation of the distressed Yudhiṣṭhira during his calamity; herein also is the most righteous and pathos-inducing story of Nala, wherein is described the steadfastness of Damayantī upon the arrival of Nala’s misfortune.

Likewise, from that very same great seer, Lomaśa, they obtained the secret of the dice; and here is recorded his arrival from heaven to visit the sons of Pāṇḍu while those high-souled Pāṇḍavas were dwelling in the forest.
01.002.110c The journey to heaven was indeed described by Lomaśa to Arjuna; 01.002.110d*0125_01 here, at his command, is the account of the act of visiting the sacred fords (tīrtha),
01.002.110d*0125_02 as well as the attainment of the fruits of those fords and their sanctity that has been proclaimed.
The pilgrimage to the sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) undertaken by the great seer Nārada with Pulastya,
as well as the pilgrimage of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
and the slaying of Jaṭāsura are described therein.
Bhimasena was also commissioned by Draupadi to go to Gandhamadana,
where he seized that lotus-pond for the sake of Mandara flowers;
there, a very great battle took place between him and the Rakshasas.
Also [the account] of the Yakṣas of great prowess, headed by Maṇimat;
and likewise the narrative concerning Agastya, wherein is described the devouring of Vātāpi and the sage’s union with Lopāmudrā for the sake of offspring.
Then follows the narrative of the hawk and the pigeon,
wherein Indra and Agni, along with Dharma, sought to test King Śibi; having become a hawk and a pigeon, they approached him at his sacrifice.
The life-story of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, who was a celibate from his youth;
the life-story of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who possessed immense splendor;
and wherein the slaying of Kārtavīrya and the Haihayas is described.
Also the narrative of Saukaneya, wherein Cyavana Bhārgava,
at the sacrifice of Śaryāti, made the two Nāsatyas drinkers of soma;
and how that sage was restored to youth by them.
In this very section is the narrative of Jantu, wherein King Somaka performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son and obtained a hundred sons;
and here also is the story of Aṣṭāvakra, concerning the debate with Bandi.

Having conquered the ocean and reached his father, the Rishi heard that his father had previously been cast into the salt waters. Having acquired the divine weapons for the sake of his preceptor, Savyasācin [returned].
The battle with the Nivātakavacas who dwell in Hiraṇyapura;
the meeting of Pārtha with his brothers on Mount Gandhamādana;
and the cattle-expedition where Kirīṭin fought with the Gandharvas.
Furthermore, their return to the Dvaitavana lake;
the abduction of Draupadī from the hermitage by Jayadratha;
and how Bhīma, equal to the wind in speed, pursued him there.
In the section concerning the parable of Mārkaṇḍeya, there are various sub-narratives;
the meeting with Kṛṣṇa and his dialogue with Satyabhāmā;
the narrative of Vrihidraunika, and likewise that of Indradyumna.
The two Sāvitrī episodes, the story of Auddālaki, and the narrative of Vainya;
here also is the Rāmāyaṇa episode in great detail. Herein is also the seizure of Karṇa’s earrings by Purandara.
Likewise, the greatness of Gaya’s sacrifice is proclaimed here;
also the narrative of Agastya, wherein he devours Vātāpi,
and the sage’s approach to Lopāmudrā for the sake of offspring.
The life-story of Ṛśyaśṛṅga, who was a celibate from his youth;
the life-story of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who possessed immense splendor;
and wherein the slaying of Kārtavīrya and the Haihayas is described.
At the sacred ford of Prabhāsa, there was the meeting of the Pāṇḍavas with the Vṛṣṇis;
also the narrative of Śaukeya, wherein Cyavana Bhārgava made the two Nāsatyas drinkers of Soma at the sacrifice of Śaryāti.
And in that very place where the sage was restored to youth by those two,
the legend of King Māndhātṛ is also proclaimed;
and right here is the legend of Jantu, wherein Somaka [was tested] by his son.

The king performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son, and he obtained a hundred sons. Immediately following that is the narrative of the hawk and the pigeon, wherein Indra, Agni, and Dharma tested King Śibi.
In this very context is the *Aṣṭāvakrīya*, where a dispute took place between the brahmin-sage Aṣṭāvakra and Bandi at the sacrifice of Janaka,
involving the foremost of logicians, the son of Varuṇa.
Where the bard was defeated in debate by that Great-Souled One;
how the Rishi, having conquered the ocean, recovered his father;
and the narrative of Yavakrīta and the Great-Souled Raibhya.
The journey to Gandhamādana and the stay at the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa;
Bhīmasena was commissioned by Draupadī to go to Gandhamādana,
and while traveling on the path, the mighty-armed one saw the son of the Wind-god.
There, amidst a grove of plantain trees, stood the mighty Hanumān;
there he violated that lotus pond for the sake of Mandāra flowers,
and there his great battle with the Rākṣasas took place.
And likewise, the encounter with the immensely powerful Yakṣas headed by Maṇimat;
the slaying of the Rākṣasa Jaṭāsura by Vṛkodara;
and thereafter, the visit to the royal sage Vṛṣaparvan is recorded.
01,002.126d*0128_32 Their journey to and stay at the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa;
01,002.126d*0128_33 And the encouragement of the high-souled Bhīma by the princess of Pañcāla;
01,002.126d*0128_34 And the ascent of Kailāsa is described, where he was challenged by the Yakṣas of fierce strength.
There was a most terrible battle with Maṇimān and others; there was the meeting of the Pāṇḍavas with Vaiśravaṇa,
and right there, Arjuna’s reunion with his brothers.
Having obtained divine weapons for the sake of his preceptor, Savyasācin fought with the Nivātakavacas,
the inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura—
those terrible Dānavas, the enemies of the gods.
Wherein the battle of the Diademed One (Arjuna) with the Paulomas and Kālakeyas is told,
as well as their slaughter by that very wise king;
and the commencement of the display of celestial weapons in the presence of Dharmarāja.
The prohibition of Pārtha by the great seer Nārada;
the descent of the Pāṇḍavas once again from Gandhamādana; and the capture of Bhīma there by one whose stature was as vast as a mountain range.
In that very dense forest, Yudhiṣṭhira was liberated by the powerful lord of serpents after he had answered the questions;
and [the text recounts] the return of those high-souled ones once again to the Kāmyaka forest.
Furthermore, the arrival of Vāsudeva right there in order to see the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, is proclaimed in this very section;
as well as all the various sub-narratives within the Mārkaṇḍeya-samāsyā.
The narrative of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, as told by the supreme seer; the dialogue between Sarasvatī and the high-souled seer Tārkṣya;
and immediately following that, the story of the fish is recounted here.

The Mārkaṇḍeya-samasyā is proclaimed as a Purāṇa; likewise, there is the episode of Indradyumna and the Dhaundhumāra story. Furthermore, the narrative of the devoted wife (Pativratā) and that of Aṅgiras are recorded.
01,002.126d*0128_59(125ab) Herein is recounted the conversation between Draupadī and Satyabhāmā; 01,002.126d*0128_60(123ab) And again, the Pāṇḍavas returned to the Dvaitavana forest;
01,002.126d*0128_61(122cd) And the cattle-expedition (*ghoṣayātrā*), wherein Suyodhana was captured by the Gandharvas.
But that dull-witted one, while being carried away, was rescued by Kirīṭin;
and here, in this very place, is the account of the dream of the deer seen by Dharmarāja,
as well as his return once more to the Kāmyaka, the best of forests.
In this very place, the extensive narrative of Vṛīhidrauṇika is told;
likewise, the episode concerning Durvāsas is proclaimed here. Also included is the abduction of Draupadī from the hermitage by Jayadratha.
Wherein Bhīma, equal to the wind in speed, pursued him;
and where the mighty Bhīma made him five-crested;
and wherein the narrative of Rāmāyaṇa is told here at great length.
Where Rāvaṇa was slain in battle by Rāma through his prowess;
and here also the narrative of Sāvitrī is fully recounted,
as well as that of Mārkaṇḍeya and the celestial sage Nārada.
In this [section], there is the theft of Karna’s earrings from Purandara,
where the gratified god gave him the Śakti weapon for the sake of slaying a singular hero;
and here is the Āraṇeya episode, wherein Dharma instructed his son.
Having obtained their boons, they went toward the western direction where the Pāṇḍavas were.
This is proclaimed as the third book, the Āraṇyaka Parva.
Here, two hundred chapters have been counted by the supreme ṛṣi.
Likewise, sixty-nine chapters have been proclaimed;
this section is celebrated as containing eleven thousand six hundred and sixty-four verses.
01.002.130a After this, learn of the extensive Vairāṭa Parvan.
01.002.130c Having gone to the city of Virāṭa and seeing a large Śamī tree in the cremation ground, the Pāṇḍavas deposited their weapons there.
Where, having entered the city, they lived in disguise;
where, as he pursued Pāñcālī with his mind struck by lust,
the wicked-souled Kīcaka was slain by Vṛkodara.
And for the purpose of searching for the Pāṇḍavas and King Duryodhana,
clever spies were dispatched here in every direction;
yet no news of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas was obtained by them.
And first, Virāṭa’s seizure of cattle was carried out by the Trigartas,
where he had a great battle with them that caused the hair to stand on end;
and there, while he was being carried away, he was liberated by Bhīmasena.
01.002.132a Where the Kurus were defeated in battle by Pārtha during the cattle-raid; 01.002.132b where the wealth of cattle was recovered through the prowess of Kirīṭin;
01.002.132c and where the cattle-wealth of Virāṭa was liberated by the Pāṇḍavas.
Immediately thereafter, the Kurus carried off his cattle;
and there, Virāṭa gave Uttarā as a daughter-in-law to Kirīṭin for the sake of Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadrā and slayer of enemies.
This fourth extensive book, the Vairāṭa Parva, has been described;
here too, the number of chapters has been calculated by the Great-Souled One as sixty-seven. Now hear from me the total number of verses as well.
Two thousand and fifty verses have been declared by the supreme seer in this Parvan by way of enumeration;
know this to be the fifth Parvan, the Udyoga Parva, and listen to what follows.
When the Pāṇḍavas were encamped at Upaplavya with the desire for victory,
Duryodhana and Arjuna both approached Vāsudeva,
saying: "You ought to grant us assistance in this battle."
When these words had been spoken, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa said to those two bulls among men, who were not fighting but acting as ministers:
"Whose akṣauhiṇī of troops shall I provide, or what shall I give?"
Where the dull-witted and evil-minded Duryodhana chose the army,
Dhanañjaya chose Kṛṣṇa as his non-combatant counselor;
and [Duryodhana] chose the King of Madra as king, who was advancing against the Pāṇḍavas.
Having deceived him with offerings right on the road, Suyodhana chose a boon from that granter of boons, saying, "Let assistance be rendered to me.
Having promised this to him, Śalya set out toward the Pāṇḍavas.
He spoke with conciliatory words concerning the defeat of Indra and the dispatch of the family priest by the Pāṇḍavas to the Kauravas, having received the command of the son of Vicitravīrya.
Likewise, he dispatched Indravijaya, the charioteer of the family priest, and Sañjaya to the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of peace—
where the majestic Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sent his messenger.
And having heard that the Pāṇḍavas were there with Vāsudeva at their head,
a sleepless anxiety arose in Dhṛtarāṣṭra due to his reflection;
it was then that Vidura spoke various words that were both wonderful and beneficial.
He caused the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra to hear that unsurpassed teaching on the supreme self (adhyātma) as it was spoken by Sanatsujāta;
thus was the king, who was consumed by grief and overwhelmed by mental anguish, made to listen.
At dawn, in the assembly of kings, Sañjaya spoke there, O Lord,
of the oneness of Vāsudeva and Arjuna;
and how the highly illustrious Kṛṣṇa, moved by compassion and desiring peace, [approached].
He came in person to the city called after the elephant (Hastināpura) to bring about peace;
yet King Duryodhana rejected Kṛṣṇa,
even though he was entreating for peace for the sake of the welfare of both sides.
In this very place, the narrative of Dambhodbhava is fully proclaimed;
here also is the search for a bride by the high-souled Mātali,
and the life-story of the great seer Gālava is told.
The instruction given to Vidula’s son is also recounted there; furthermore,
having perceived the wicked counsel of Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the others,
Kṛṣṇa demonstrated his mastery over yoga (Yogeśvaratva) among the kings.

01.002.148a Where Kṛṣṇa, having placed Karṇa upon the chariot, exhorted him; 01.002.148c and how he was refused by Karṇa out of pride, despite the former’s skillful approach; 01.002.148d*0138_01 the wonderful and extensive account of Śveta’s consecration as told by Kṛṣṇa.

Having arrived at Upaplavya from Hastinapura, Hari, the subduer of enemies, related everything concerning the Pāṇḍavas exactly as it had occurred. Having heard his words and deliberated upon what was beneficial, they [acted accordingly].
Then those subduers of enemies made all their war equipment ready;
thereafter, they set out from the city of Hastināpura with a vast number of chariots, horses, men, and elephants, and conducted a census of their forces.

Therein is described the king’s dispatching of Ulūka as an envoy to the Pāṇḍavas on the eve of the great battle; his harsh speech in his capacity as a messenger, the slander against the Pāṇḍavas, and the delay in the appearance of the next day.
The enumeration of Rathas and Atirathas, as well as the Ambopākhyāna;
this latter, the Ambopākhyāna, occurs right here during the encounter between Rāma and Bhīṣma. This fifth book in the Mahābhārata contains many such episodes.
The Udyoga Parva is specified as being concerned with peace and war;
it is recorded here as having one hundred and eighty-six chapters,
and its verses number exactly six thousand six hundred.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, ninety-eight verses have been proclaimed by the high-souled Vyāsa of noble intellect in this Parvan.
Following this, they declare the Bhīṣma Parvan, which contains manifold meanings.
01.002.154–155. Therein is described the formation of the Jambūkhaṇḍa by Sañjaya;
there the terrible battle took place for ten days, most cruel, wherein the army of Yudhiṣṭhira fell into the deepest despair.
There, the high-minded Vāsudeva destroyed the dejection born of delusion that had come upon Pārtha by means of arguments revealing the path to liberation;
for Adhokṣaja, devoted to the welfare of Yudhiṣṭhira, quickly perceived [the situation].
Leaping from the chariot with speed, the noble-minded Kṛṣṇa himself,
whip in hand and free from fear, ran toward Bhīṣma to slay him— there,
where the Pāṇḍava had been struck by the whip of Kṛṣṇa’s words.
There, in battle, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the best among all bearers of weapons,
that great archer Pārtha, placing Śikhaṇḍin in front,
struck down Bhīṣma from his chariot with sharpened arrows.
And where Bhīṣma lay upon his bed of arrows—
this is proclaimed as the sixth great parvan in the Mahābhārata;
it is said to contain one hundred and seventeen chapters.
Five thousand eight hundred and eighty-four verses have been proclaimed in this Bhīṣma Parva, as counted by Vyāsa, the knower of the Vedas.
Then follows the wonderful Droṇaparva, which contains many episodes. Therein, the powerful teacher,
an expert in great weapons, was consecrated to the generalship and, for the sake of pleasing Duryodhana, made a solemn vow.
The capture of the wise Dharmarāja, the son of Pāṇḍu,
wherein the Saṃśaptakas drew Pārtha away from the field of battle;
and where the great king Bhagadatta, who was equal to Śakra in combat, [was encountered].

There, the youth Abhimanyu— a hero who had not yet reached full maturity— was slain by many great chariot-warriors of the world led by Jayadratha, even as he fought alongside the elephant Supratīka and the diadem-wearing Arjuna.
When Abhimanyu had been slain in battle by the enraged Pārtha,
King Jayadratha was killed after seven *akṣauhiṇīs* had been destroyed;
there, the mighty-armed Bhīma and the great car-warrior Sātyaki [remained].
By the command of King Yudhiṣṭhira, they entered the Bharata army— which was unassailable even by the gods— in order to search for Pārtha;
and in that battle, they completely annihilated the remnants of the Saṃśaptakas.
Nine crores of high-souled heroes among the Saṃśaptakas were dispatched to the abode of Yama by Kirīṭin after he had emerged from his concealment;
Jiṣṇu, emboldened by the slaughter of the Saṃśaptakas, was nonetheless tormented by the memory of his son’s death.
Having made a great vow, Alambusa, Śrutāyus, the valiant Jalasandha, Saumadatti, Virāṭa, and the great car-warrior Drupada were all overcome by the illusory power of the Lord of Śrī.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as well as those who fought with stones,
the Nārāyaṇas, the cowherds who fought with diverse tactics,
and others such as Ghaṭotkaca, were slain in the Droṇaparvan.
And at that very moment, when Droṇa had been struck down in battle,
the indignant Aśvatthāman manifested the fierce Nārāyaṇa weapon; therein is celebrated the supreme majesty of Rudra as the Āgneya weapon.
The arrival of Vyāsa, the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna,
the Śatarudrīya, and the great hymn of praise to Śaṅkara—
this is proclaimed as the seventh great Parvan of the Mahābhārata.
In this [section], most of those protectors of the earth met their end;
these were the heroes, the bulls among men, who were specified in the Droṇaparvan. One hundred and seventy chapters have been declared [to be contained therein].
Eight thousand, nine hundred,
and likewise nine verses have been counted here in the Droṇaparvan by the sage Pārāśarya, the seer of truth, after he had reflected upon them.
After this, the most wonderful Karṇaparva is proclaimed,
wherein is told the appointment of the wise King of Madra as a charioteer,
and the ancient narrative of the destruction of Tripura.
In this [section], there is the harsh dialogue between Karṇa and Śalya during the departure; here also is the narrative of the swan and the crow, which includes a reproach;
and likewise, the slaying of Pāṇḍya by the high-souled Aśvatthāman.
The slaying of Daṇḍasena and likewise the slaying of Daṇḍa; where, in a single combat with Karṇa, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira was brought into a state of peril in battle while all the archers looked on.
The mutual anger between Yudhiṣṭhira and Kirīṭin (Arjuna),
wherein Mādhava indeed spoke words of conciliation to Arjuna,
and also [the account] of Duḥśāsana’s chest [being torn open] according to his vow.
Where Vṛkodara, having torn open [the chest], drank the blood in battle;
and where the slaying of both Duḥśāsana and Vṛṣasena took place;
and where the son of Karṇa was killed by Pārtha while Karṇa himself looked on.
The son of the Wind (Hanumān) described the army and its strength exactly as it was;
filling his joined palms to the brim, he declared that no such flavor exists even in curds,
nor in any other flavors, for his resolve regarding this promise was firm.
While that terrifying single combat between Karṇa and Arjuna was taking place,
the discus fell to the earth due to Karṇa’s own curse; then Karṇa released at Phālguna a weapon capable of reaching as far as a nāga and measuring a *valīka*.

Out of fear of that, Keśava caused the chariot to enter the earth at the spot where the great car-warrior Karṇa was slain by Pārtha in a duel of chariots. This is designated as the eighth book by those who contemplate the Mahābhārata.
Seventy-nine chapters are declared in the Karṇaparvan;
four thousand and nine hundred verses,
along with sixty-four additional verses— this is the extent of this book as it has been proclaimed.
After this, the Śalyaparvan is proclaimed, containing manifold themes. When the heroes of the army had been slain, the Lord of Madra became their leader;
therein is the narrative of Kumāra and the rite of consecration.
In this [section], the various chariot battles are recounted in their respective parts;
the destruction of the leaders of the Kurus is proclaimed in the Śalyaparvan,
as well as the death of Śalya at the hands of the great car-warrior Dharmarāja.
And right here, Śakuni was slain in battle by Sahadeva;
and when the army was mostly destroyed and only a small remnant remained, Suyodhana entered a lake, where he stayed, having solidified its waters.
Therein is described the encounter with the hunters and the speech full of reproach addressed by them to the wise Dharmarāja;
and there, the highly intolerant son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra rose up from the lake.
The battle with the mace that he fought there with Bhīma,
and the arrival of Rāma at the assembly of the war, are recorded;
the tumultuous mace-duel is celebrated right here.
Then, in that battle, the two thighs of King Duryodhana were forcibly broken by Bhīma with his mace of terrible velocity;
and the sanctity of the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) along the Sarasvatī was proclaimed.
This wonderful and meaningful ninth book has been described; there, according to those skilled in calculation, fifty-nine chapters have been counted,
containing many narratives, and the total number of verses here is praised.
Three thousand two hundred and twenty verses were thus composed by the Sage for the sake of the illustrious Kauravas. Hereafter,
I shall proclaim the terrible Sauptika Parva.
Where King Duryodhana, the intolerant one, lay with his thighs broken,
while the sons of Pṛthā had retreated, three chariot-warriors approached him in the evening— Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa— all drenched in blood.
Having gathered together, they beheld him fallen upon the earth at the head of the battle,
where the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, firm in his wrath,
had vowed that he would not rest until he had slain all the Pāñcālas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
"I shall not release the Pāṇḍavas along with their ministers from my grasp. Having spoken thus to the king, three chariots departed and reached a great forest at the time of sunset.
There, beneath a great banyan tree where they were stationed,
the son of Droṇa, filled with rage as he recollected the slaughter of his father, saw many crows being killed by an owl during the night.
He set his mind upon the slaughter of the Pāñcālas while they were fast asleep;
having gone to the gate of the camp, he beheld there a Rākṣasa of terrible form, difficult to look upon, standing there pervading the sky.
And seeing that the neutralization of his weapons was being effected by him,
the son of Droṇa quickly propitiated Rudra Virūpākṣa; it was there,
during the night, that those bulls among men were sleeping in trustful repose.
Led by the son of Droṇa, they slaughtered the Pāñcālas along with their followers;
together with Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa, he struck them down,
whereupon those five sons of Pṛthā were rescued by relying on the power of Kṛṣṇa.
The great archer Sātyaki and the rest have met their end;
for there, while the Pāñcālas were fast asleep, their slaughter at the hands of Droṇa’s son was reported to the Pāṇḍavas by the charioteer of Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
01,002.183a There, Draupadī, afflicted by grief for her sons and tormented by the slaughter of her father and brothers,
sat down before her husbands after having resolved to fast unto death.
01,002.184a It was at Draupadī’s word that Bhīma, of terrible prowess, [acted].
Desiring to do what was pleasing to her, the valiant one took up his mace and,
filled with rage, pursued the son of his preceptor, the descendant of Bharadvāja,
as he had been impelled by fate out of fear of Bhīmasena.
"May there be no more Pāṇḍavas!"—with these words, the son of Droṇa released a weapon in rage.
"Do not do this! Kṛṣṇa said, pacifying his speech;
and Phālguna neutralized that weapon with a weapon of his own.
Having observed the malicious intent of the wicked-souled son of Droṇa,
as well as the mutual curses exchanged between the son of Droṇa, Dvaipāyana, and the others;
and likewise, having taken up the jewel from the great chariot-warrior, the son of Droṇa—
The Pāṇḍavas, appearing victorious and filled with joy, presented these [garments] to Draupadī.
This is indeed declared to be the tenth book, the Sauptika-parvan,
concerning the water-rites and the offering of water for all the kings.
The tenth book here, the *Sauptika*, recounts the secret birth of Karṇa and his declaration of himself as the son of Pṛthā;
eighteen chapters are said to be contained in this book by the Great-Souled One.
The total number of verses stated here is eight hundred and seventy,
as correctly calculated by the one of immeasurable intellect for this Parvan concerning the connection between the *Sauptika* and the *Aiṣīka*.
01,002.191a After this, they speak of the Strīparvan, which evokes compassion;
01,002.191b where the lord of men, whose eye was wisdom, tormented by grief for his son,
[beheld] that firm iron image brought forth by Kṛṣṇa.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra shattered his intent to harm Bhīmasena;
likewise, for the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra who was scorched by the fire of grief,
he demonstrated the departure from worldly existence through reasoning that reveals liberation.
In this section, it is related how Vidura offered consolation to the king, as well as the departure of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his inner apartments, afflicted by grief, from the Kuru battlefield.
Wherein the exceedingly piteous lamentation of the wives of the heroes is recorded; where the outburst of wrath and the subsequent pacification of Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra occur;
and where those heroic Kṣatriyas, who never retreated, have reached their appointed end.
They beheld their sons, brothers, and fathers slain in battle;
likewise, the distress of Gāndhārī due to the slaughter of her sons and grandsons was proclaimed right there, as was the act of pacifying her anger by Kṛṣṇa.

Wherein the highly wise king, the best among all upholders of dharma, caused those bodies of the kings to be cremated according to the sacred precepts. This eleventh book is declared to be a great and most piteous parvan.
Twenty-seven chapters are declared in this parvan;
seven hundred and seventy-five verses are said here by the high-souled author of the Bhārata narrative.
This excellent section causes distress in the minds of the virtuous and brings forth tears;
following this is the twelfth book, the Śāntiparvan, which increases the intellect,
wherein Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira fell into a state of despondency.
Having caused his fathers, brothers, sons, kinsmen, and relatives to be slain,
the duties regarding the bed of arrows (*śaratalpika*) were explained in the *Śāntiparvan*; these should be correctly understood by kings who desire to know the principles of policy (*naya*).
In that very place, the duties for times of distress (*āpaddharma*) were taught, demonstrating the proper times and causes;
by understanding these correctly, a person may attain omniscience.
Furthermore, the diverse and extensive duties pertaining to liberation (*mokṣadharma*) were expounded.
This twelfth book has been described as dear to wise people; in this book,
O ascetics, three hundred and thirty-nine chapters are to be known.
Fourteen thousand,
five hundred, and twenty-five verses have been proclaimed;
beyond this, however, the supreme Ānuśāsana is to be known.

01.002.201c Where Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, having returned to his natural state after hearing the determination of dharma from Bhīṣma, the son of Bhagīrathī, 01.002.202a the judicial procedure pertaining to dharma and artha is here demonstrated in its entirety.

The various applications of the fruits of diverse gifts, as well as the distinctions among worthy recipients and the supreme rules for giving; the application of the rules of conduct, and the ultimate goal of truth.
The great majesty of cows and likewise of Brahmins,
as well as the secret of the dharmas associated with place and time—
this is the supreme instruction containing many narratives.
In this very section, the attainment of heaven by Bhīṣma is fully described.
This is the thirteenth book, which establishes the determination of dharma;
it contains one hundred and forty-six chapters.
There are six thousand seven hundred verses;
then the fourteenth book is declared, named the Aśvamedhika,
wherein is the unsurpassed narrative concerning Saṃvarta and Marutta.
The recovery of the golden treasure-chest and the birth of Parikṣit were told— how he,
previously consumed by the fire of the weapon, was restored to life again through Kṛṣṇa;
and how the horse was released during the sacrificial rite as the Pāṇḍava followed it.
In various places, there were battles with indignant princes; and here, Dhanañjaya was brought into a state of peril in combat by Babhruvāhana, the son of Citrāṅgadā’s daughter.
Likewise, the Anugītā was duly proclaimed again by the Blessed One;
the eternal Dharma was told by Kṛṣṇa in the presence of Arjuna,
as well as the Brāhmaṇagītā, which is a dialogue between a teacher and a pupil.
The Sudarśana, the Vaiṣṇava-dharma,
and the narrative of Nakula at the great horse-sacrifice—
thus has this most wonderful Parva, the Āśvamedhika, been described.
In this [work], one hundred and thirty-three chapters have been declared; three thousand,
three hundred,
and twenty verses have likewise been counted by the Seer of Reality.
Then follows the fifteenth book, known as the Āśramavāsika Parvan,
wherein King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having renounced his kingdom, went to the hermitage accompanied by Gāndhārī and Vidura.
Seeing him set forth, the virtuous Pṛthā then followed him,
having renounced the kingdom for her sons in order to devote herself to the service of her elders.
There, the king [beheld] his slain sons, grandsons, and other kings.
Having seen that unsurpassed marvel by the grace of the seer Kṛṣṇa— the heroes who had gone to the other world returning once more—
he cast off his grief along with his wife and attained supreme perfection.
Where Vidura, having relied upon the Dharma, attained a happy rebirth;
where the wise and self-controlled great minister Saṃjaya, the son of Gavalgaṇa, [did likewise];
and where Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira beheld Nārada.

And from Nārada he heard of the great slaughter of the Vṛṣṇis. This [section], called Āśramavāsa, which was previously described as most wonderful, consists of forty-two chapters by count; this constitutes a Parvan.
One thousand and five hundred and six verses have been counted by the seer of truth.
Beyond this, learn now of the terrible Mausala Parva.
There, those tigers among men, who were capable of enduring the touch of weapons in battle,
were crushed by the staff of Brahma near the salt waters; driven by fate, they had become intoxicated at the drinking bout.
With *vajras* that had taken the form of *eraka* grass, they struck one another; there,
having brought about the destruction of all, both Rāma and Keśava did not transcend the all-consuming Time that had arrived equally for them both.

01.002.223 When Arjuna, that bull among men, arrived at Dvāravatī and saw it bereft of the Vṛṣṇis, he fell into despondency and experienced the utmost distress. 01.002.224 Having paid his respects to his maternal uncle Śauri, the best of the Yadus, [he departed].
He beheld the great carnage at the drinking bout of the Yadu heroes;
he then caused the funeral rites to be performed for the bodies of Vāsudeva and the high-souled Rāma, as well as for the principal members of the Vṛṣṇis.
Taking with him the people of Dvārakā, including the old and the young,
he then beheld the failure of the Gāṇḍīva bow in that dire calamity,
as well as the lack of efficacy of all his divine weapons.
Having witnessed the destruction of the Vṛṣṇi women and the impermanence of all powers, and having fallen into a state of world-weariness prompted by the words of Vyāsa,
he approached Dharmarāja and resolved to take up renunciation.
Thus is this sixteenth book, the Mausala-parvan,
proclaimed. It is said to consist of eight chapters and three hundred and twenty verses, as counted by the seer of truth.
After that, the seventeenth is known as the Mahāprasthānika,
wherein the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, having renounced their kingdom along with Queen Draupadī, attained the highest perfection.
Where they beheld Agni after reaching the Lauhitya ocean; there,
when urged by Agni, Pārtha, having honored that high-souled one, gave him that divine and supreme bow, Gāṇḍīva.
Where Yudhiṣṭhira, having seen his brothers and Draupadī fallen,
departed alone, leaving them all behind without looking back—
this is remembered as the seventeenth book, the Mahāprasthānika Parva.

01,002.231 Here, three chapters have been declared, as well as one hundred and twenty verses; thus have they been counted by the seer of truth. 01,002.232 Thereafter, the Svargaparva is to be known, which is divine and superhuman.
The King of Dharma had arrived with the celestial chariot from heaven,
but that man of great wisdom, out of compassion, did not wish to ascend it without the dog.
Perceiving that unwavering steadfastness in dharma of that high-souled one, [Yama spoke].
Having abandoned his own true nature there, he was endowed with [the fruits of] his karma;
thus he attained heaven, and likewise experienced intense and vast torment where hell was shown by the divine messenger under a pretext.
There, the righteous-souled one heard the piteous words of his brothers,
who remained obedient to his command while staying in that very land; and the Pāṇḍava was further instructed in dharma by both Dharma and the King of the Gods.
Having bathed in the celestial Gaṅgā and cast off his human body,
that King of Dharma attained a station in heaven won by his own righteous conduct;
honored by all the hosts of gods led by Indra, he rejoiced.
This eighteenth Parva was proclaimed by the wise Vyāsa;
herein is celebrated Karna’s descent into hell and his liberation,
as well as the reunion of the high-souled heroes in the heavenly world.
Wherein the conversation regarding heaven is recounted according to the rules,
and where those bulls among men attained their respective stations;
and wherein Yudhiṣṭhira, having beheld the splendor of Duryodhana and the others—
Having attained supreme detachment, the great chariot-warrior of immense splendor no longer longed for the imperishable heaven where he had cast off his body at the word of the gods; instead,
that majestic one went to the forest, his own eternal abode.
The chapters are numbered as five; by this calculation,
O you whose wealth is asceticism, two hundred verses have been counted,
and likewise nine other verses have been enumerated by the supreme seer.
Thus, these eighteen sections have been described in their entirety.
Following that is the Harivaṃśa section, known as the supplement (khila) to the Purāṇa;
it contains the Viṣṇu-parvan, the account of Viṣṇu’s childhood deeds, and likewise the slaying of Kaṃsa.
The Bhaviṣya Parva is also declared among the Khilas as a great and wonderful section;
following that is the Viṣṇu Parva, which is cited as a major Parva,
wherein the human birth of the lotus-navelled Lord occurs.
Born in the lineage of Vasudeva, he was nurtured in the family of the cowherd Nanda; there,
in his childhood, he performed his own wondrous and delightful deeds,
and having slain Kaṃsa, he drew him about in the midst of the arena.
Through many alliances and by the slaying of Jarāsandha,
that slayer of enemy heroes, having recovered Queen Rukmiṇī through his prowess,
examined various sites and established Dvārakā as his residence.

Having displayed his prowess in battle, Kṛṣṇa slew Kaliṅga and Dantavakra; then he married Satyabhāmā, the princess who was his rightful bride-price. Urged by Satyabhāmā, Adhokṣaja then departed for heaven.
Where he, having conquered the Lord of the Immortals, brought away the *pārijāta* tree;
where the mighty-armed one slew Dhenuka at the front of the battle;
and [where he slew] the Dānavas Naraka, Asura, Kālīya, and Hayagrīva.
In that battle, he severed the thousand arms of Bāṇa of wondrous deeds— along with Keśin, Sakāliya, and Kālanemi—
and released his grandson together with his wife.
Wherein the Indian narrative is told, and the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis is celebrated;
it is called the *Bhaviṣya*, the *Harivaṃśa*, and the *Khilas*.
Likewise, there are the *Vārāha*, the *Nārasiṃha*, the *Vāmana*, and the *Pauṣkara*.
Having conquered the kings and abandoned his chariots, O Bhīmasena, your lord [has reached this state].
Ten thousand verses and two thousand verses have been counted by the great seer in the *Khilas* and the *Harivaṃśa*.
01,002.233b Here too, the enumeration has been declared by Tattvabuddhi;
O best of the twice-born, one thousand chapters have indeed been proclaimed,
and eighteen thousand verses have indeed been recited.
Eighteen thousand verses,
as well as one hundred and eighty-four verses, are proclaimed in the *Harivaṃśa*.
The *Harivaṃśa* and the *Bhaviṣya* are proclaimed among the *Khilas*.
In the *Khilas* of the *Harivaṃśa*, the supreme seer has explained those places where divine,
meritorious, and sin-destroying narratives are celebrated, and where various wonderful accounts of the gods and asuras are recounted.
Furthermore, there is a wondrous narrative that increases merit,
wherein the deeds of Kṛṣṇa are heard along with his birth;
its chapters are declared to be seventy-nine less one.
The great seer spoke thirteen thousand and three hundred verses, including all those beginning with the Pauloma, as well as the Purāṇas and the final secret doctrine.
Thus, these eighteen sections have been declared by the wise one;
[the work consists] of two thousand chapters and exactly one hundred sections,
and nine thousand and ten verses.
This indeed is the enumeration of the sections (*parvan*) and the verses (*śloka*) in the book according to their sequence,
as spoken by the seer Vyāsa of supreme splendor,
for the sake of the wise Janamejaya who desired to witness the horse sacrifice.
There, the horse sacrifice was commenced, wherein he was challenged by Śakra;
there also arose a conflict between that king and the Brahmins who served as his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Brought from the city of Viśvāvasu, the king ruled over the kingdom.
This indeed is the enumeration of the sections; after that, he spoke of the supplementary passages (khilas). This entire Bhārata has been recounted according to the summary of its sections.
Eighteen akṣauhiṇī divisions assembled with a desire to fight.
That great and terrible battle lasted for eighteen days.
A twice-born man who knows the four Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences and Upaniṣads,
yet does not know this narrative, cannot truly be considered wise.
"This is declared to be the science of polity (*artha-śāstra*), this is the great science of dharma (*dharma-śāstra*),
and this is declared to be the science of pleasure (*kāma-śāstra*) by Vyāsa of immeasurable intellect.
Having heard this narrative, no other tale is pleasing to hear."
Hearing the song of the male cuckoo, it is like the harsh cry of a crow.
O bull of the Bharatas, regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—whatever exists here elsewhere also exists; whatever does not exist here exists nowhere else.
Having understood this, the wise who know the truth declare that the great birth of the Bharatas is indeed called the Mahābhārata;
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins.

"From the merit of studying the *Bhārata*, even for one who studies but a single quarter-verse with faith, all sins are purified; of this there is no doubt. After three years, the illustrious and auspicious Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana [completed it]."
The blessed Lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana composed this work, the Mahābhārata; he first taught it to his son Śuka,
as well as to Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and Vaiśampāyana.
And they, in turn, revealed it to those Brahmins whose intellects were focused on nothing else. Whatever ritual action is performed, and whatever rule of action exists—
all this proceeds for the delight of listeners upon the earth.

A twice-born man who knows the Veda and upholds the Veda should study this according to the prescribed rule. This supreme narrative, equal to the four Vedas, shall be a source of sustenance for poets like food.
And there shall be no poets at all capable of describing his excellence;

for in the case of a householder, there are only three [other] stages of life as his qualifications. [This stage] is auspicious, conducive to health and long life, meritorious, and the means for accomplishing virtuous deeds.
One who desires prosperity should, from the very beginning, hold this great narrative in high regard;
for it was then properly studied by the best of the twice-born from the most excellent of the twice-born,
and was subsequently recounted by those foremost brahmins, headed by Vaiśampāyana.
From this supreme history arise the insights of poets,
just as the three worlds arise from the five elements.
O twice-born ones, within the scope of this narrative, the Purāṇa exists.
In the realm of the intermediate space, like the fourfold classes of living beings,
this narrative is the substratum for all the qualities of action,
just as the various activities of the mind are for all the sense organs.
Without relying on this narrative, no story exists upon the earth,
just as the maintenance of the body is impossible without depending on food. This narrative is the very sustenance upon which all the best of poets depend.
Like a noble lord surrounded by servants seeking his advancement,
the poets are not capable of fully describing the excellence of this poem,
just as the other three stages of life cannot equal that of the virtuous householder.
May your minds be ever-attentive toward the Dharma;
for that alone is the kinsman who follows one to the next world.
Wealth and women, even when pursued by the most skillful, [are not].
It does not lead to personal existence, nor does it possess permanence;
yet this immeasurable merit, flowing from the lips of Dvaipāyana,
is purifying, auspicious, and a destroyer of sin.
For one who masters the *Bhārata* as it is being recited,
what need is there for ablutions with the waters of Puṣkara?
Whatever sin a Brahmin commits in a single day through the activity of his senses—
By reciting the Mahābhārata at the evening twilight,
one is released from the sin committed during the night through action, mind, or speech; by reciting the Mahābhārata at the morning twilight, one is liberated from that [sin].
He who gives a hundred cows with horns adorned with gold to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and possessed of great erudition,
and who constantly listens to the meritorious narrative of the *Bhārata*, [attains the highest reward].
The fruit for both of them is exactly the same.
This unsurpassed narrative, which possesses great significance, has been set forth here in this summary of the major sections.
"Having first heard it, it becomes easy for men to comprehend,
just as the vast salt ocean is [crossed] by means of a boat.
Sūta said:
Janamejaya, the son of Parikshit, together with his brothers, was performing a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) at Kurukṣetra.
He had three brothers: Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
While they were engaged in that sacrificial session, a dog—a puppy—approached them there.
Struck by the brothers of Janamejaya, he approached his mother while wailing piteously. To him, as he was wailing, his mother said:
"Why do you weep?"
"By whom has he been struck?
Thus addressed, he replied to his mother:
"I have been struck by the brothers of Janamejaya."
His mother replied to him:
"Clearly you have committed some offense there, since he has struck you.
He spoke to her again:
"I have committed no offense;
I have neither looked at the sacrificial offerings nor licked them.
Hearing this, his mother Saramā, afflicted with grief for her son, went to that sacrificial session where Janamejaya was performing a long-term sacrifice together with his brothers.
They said nothing at all.
She spoke to them.
He was addressed there by her in anger.
"This son of mine has committed no offense at all;
for what reason has he been struck?
"Because this innocent man has been struck, therefore unseen danger shall come upon you."
01.003.009 Thus addressed by Saramā, Devaśunī, Janamejaya became deeply agitated and despondent.
01.003.010 When that sacrifice was completed, he returned to Hastināpura and made a supreme effort in search of a suitable priest, thinking, "May he pacify this sinful deed of mine.
01.003.011 Once, while out hunting, Janamejaya, the son of Parikṣit, saw a hermitage in a certain region of his own territory.
There, a certain seer named Śrutaśravas lived;
he had a beloved son named Somaśravas. Janamejaya, the son of Parikṣit, approached that son and chose him for the office of domestic priest.
Having paid homage to that seer, he said,
"O Blessed One, let this son of yours be my domestic priest.
Thus addressed, he replied:
"O Janamejaya, this son of mine was born of a female serpent;
he is a great ascetic, perfected in the study of the Vedas, and nurtured in her womb by the power of my own austerities after she had drunk my seed.
He is capable of pacifying all your sinful deeds, with the sole exception of those committed against Mahādeva."
However, he has one secret vow:
if any brahmin should beg him for anything, he must give it to him, saying,
"If you can endure this, then take him away."
Thus incited by him, Janamejaya replied to him,
"Venerable sir, it shall be so.
Taking that priest with him, he returned and said to his brothers:
"I have chosen this man as my preceptor; whatever he says must be done by you without hesitation. Having been addressed thus by him, his brothers did exactly so.
Having thus instructed his brothers, he set out toward Takṣaśilā and brought that region under his control.
In the meantime, there was a certain seer named Dhaumya, a descendant of Ayoda.
He had three disciples: Upamanyu, Āruṇi, and Veda.
He sent one disciple, Āruṇi of Pañcāla, saying, "Go and repair the breach in the irrigation channel."
Instructed by his teacher, Āruṇi Pāñcālya went there, but he was unable to dam that breach in the field. While struggling, he perceived a means and thought, "Let it be; I shall do this."
He lay down there upon a breach in the field,
and while he was lying there, the water remained still.
Then, on one occasion, the preceptor Dhaumya Āyoda asked his disciples:
"Where has Āruṇi Pāñcālya gone? They replied, "He was sent by the Blessed One himself with the words: 'Go and repair the breach in the irrigation trench.'"
Having been addressed thus, he replied to those disciples:
"Therefore, let us all go there, to where he is.
Having gone there, he made a sound to call him.
"O Āruṇi Pāñcālya, where are you?
Come, my child!
Hearing those words of his teacher, Āruṇi rose up suddenly from that field-plot and approached his teacher.
And he said to him:

"I am here, having lain down in this breach of the field-dyke to stop the water that was flowing out and could not be restrained; but upon hearing the word 'Bhagavat,' I suddenly tore open the breach of the field-dyke and have come before you."
"I pay homage to the Blessed One;
may your lordship command me:
what shall I do?"
The teacher said to him:
"Since you have arisen after tearing open a gap in a field, therefore you shall be known by the name Uddālaka.
Thus he was favored by his teacher.
"Because you have carried out my word, you shall attain prosperity;
all the Vedas and all the treatises on Dharma shall be revealed to you.
Having been addressed thus by his teacher, he went to the desired region.
Now, there was another disciple of that very Ayoda Dhaumya named Upamanyu. The teacher sent him forth, saying,
"Child Upamanyu, guard the cows."
01,003.034A At his teacher’s command, he tended the cattle.
01,003.034B Having tended the cattle during the day, at the end of the day he returned, stood before his teacher, and paid homage.
01,003.035A The teacher saw that he was fat.
And he said to him:
"O child Upamanyu, by what means do you provide for your livelihood?
For you are very stout."
He replied to his preceptor,
"I shall maintain my livelihood by means of alms.
Having said, "So be it," he went out to beg for alms and presented it to his preceptor.
From that point on, the preceptor took all the alms-food for himself.
The preceptor said to him:
"The alms-food must not be consumed without first being offered to me."
Having said, "So be it," he again protected the cows;
and having returned after protecting them, he stood before his teacher as before and paid homage.
Seeing that he was still just as fat, the teacher said to him:
"O Vatsa Upamanyu, I have taken all your alms without exception;
by what means will you now maintain yourself?
When he was addressed thus by his preceptor, he replied:
"Having first offered [the fruit] to the Blessed One, I eat the remainder;
by that means I provide for my livelihood.
To him, the preceptor replied:
"This is not the proper conduct toward a teacher;
by acting in this way, you are obstructing the livelihood of others as well.
You are greedy."
Having said, "So be it," he tended the cows. After tending them, he returned to the teacher's house, stood before the teacher, and paid his respects.
Seeing that he was still as fat as before, the teacher spoke to him again.
"I take all your alms-food and you do not go out to beg for anything else;
yet you are stout. By what means do you maintain your livelihood?"
He replied to his preceptor:
"Sir, I shall provide my livelihood with the milk of these cows.
The preceptor replied to him:

"It is not right for me to consume this milk without your permission. Having agreed, saying "So be it," he guarded the cows and returned again to the teacher's house; standing before his guru, he paid homage.
The teacher saw that he was indeed fat.
And he said to him:
"You do not eat alms-food, nor do you go about seeking anything else; you do not drink milk."
"You are fat; by what means do you provide for your livelihood? Having been addressed thus, he replied to his teacher.
"O, I am drinking the froth that these calves, while suckling at their mothers' teats, spit out. To him the teacher replied:
"It is out of compassion for you that these virtuous calves are spitting out such an abundance of froth."
"Even so, by acting in this manner, you are indeed causing an obstruction to the livelihood of the calves;
therefore, you ought not to drink even the froth.
Having promised "So be it," he protected those cows while abstaining from food.
Thus forbidden, he does not eat alms-food, nor does he go out for it; he does not drink milk,
nor does he consume froth.
Once, while in the forest, being oppressed by hunger, he ate the leaves of the *arka* plant.
Because those *arka* leaves—which were alkaline, pungent, and hot in their digestion—had been consumed, his eyes were impaired and he became blind.
Even though he was blind, as he was wandering about, he fell into a well.
"Upamanyu has not returned.
They said,
"He went to the forest to tend the cows."
The teacher said to them:
"Now, while he was not coming, the teacher spoke to his disciples: 'I have forbidden Upamanyu from all sides.'"
"He must certainly be angry;
therefore he does not come, or perhaps he has gone far away.
Having spoken thus, he went into the forest and called out to Upamanyu.
"O Upamanyu, where are you?
Come, my child!
Hearing this call from his teacher, he replied loudly:
"O Preceptor, here I am, fallen into a well. The preceptor replied to him,
"How have you fallen into a well?"
He replied to him:
"Having eaten the leaves of the *arka* plant, I have become blind;
therefore, I fell into the well."
The preceptor replied to him:
"Praise the Aśvins;
those two physicians of the gods will restore your sight."

Thus addressed by his preceptor, he began to praise the two divine Aśvins with words and *ṛc*-verses: "I extol with my song the two who go before, the first-born, of wondrous luster, the two scorching ones who are infinite."
Two divine, well-winged, stainless celestial chariots,
dwelling above all worlds— golden birds that carry one across to the hereafter.
The two Nasatyas, the Dasras, with beautiful noses, the victorious ones, weaving the bright [thread] with speed, well-guided,
spreading over the dark [night] while shining forth.
The Aśvins released the quail that was seized by the power of Suparṇa for the sake of her well-being; they,
being well-conducted, bowed down through their creative power (māyā).
Seven ruddy cows brought him forth;
sixty and three hundred milch-cows give birth to a single calf, and they milk that one.
Various stalls are established for milking at one time;
those two Aśvins milk the Ukthya Gharma. There is a single nave to which seven hundred spokes are attached.
Twenty spokes are fixed upon the two hubs;
the wheel revolves without rim and without decay;
the Aśvins, through their creative power, anoint it for all people.
A single wheel revolves, with twelve spokes, a felly,
six naves, and one axle— the support of immortality—
upon which all the gods are fastened.

Rumaṇvat, Suṣeṇa, Vasu, and likewise Viśvāvasu.

Rāma, the son of Reṇukā, was his youngest; he was a master of great weapons, by whom the earth was cleared of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times. There was also a son of Bhṛgu named Cyavana, a descendant of Bhṛgu who was very dear to him.
The heir of Cyavana was the righteous Pramati; and from Pramati, through Ghṛtācī, was born a son named Ruru. From Ruru also was born a son, Śunaka, who had mastered the Vedas.
From your great-grandfather, the righteous-souled one begot Pramadvarā;
he was an ascetic, illustrious, learned in the Vedas, the foremost among those who know Brahman,
most virtuous, truthful, self-restrained, and possessed of controlled senses.
Śaunaka said:
O son of a Sūta, tell me, who am asking you, how that high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu became renowned as Cyavana.
Sūta said:
Bhṛgu’s most beloved wife was renowned by the name Pulomā;
in her was conceived a fetus produced from the seed of Bhṛgu.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, when that embryo had been conceived in Pulomā— the illustrious and virtuous lawful wife of equal character— and while Bhṛgu,
the best among the upholders of dharma, had gone out for his ritual ablution, [the following occurred].
Then the Rākṣasa Puloman came to his hermitage.
Having entered that hermitage and seen Bhṛgu’s blameless wife,
he was overcome by lust and became distraught.
When that Rākṣasa had arrived, the beautiful Pulomā then invited him with wild fruits, roots, and other forest fare. But then,
O Brahmin, that Rākṣasa was tormented by lust for her.
Seeing her there, he became joyful, desiring to carry off that blameless woman;
delighted and wishing to seize the auspicious lady, he said, "The task is accomplished. For she, the one of pure smiles, had previously been chosen by Puloman.
Then his father gave her to Bhṛgu according to the sacred scriptures;
yet that offense remained constantly in the heart of the descendant of Bhṛgu,
and he then set his mind on seizing her, thinking, "This is the opportunity."
Then, in the fire-sanctuary, he saw the blazing Jātavedas.
Thereupon, the Rākṣasa questioned the flaming Pāvaka:
"Tell me truly, O Agni, whose wife is she?"
"You are truth; speak the truth to me who asks you, O Purifier.
For this woman of excellent complexion was first chosen by me for the sake of a wife, but later her father gave her to Bhrigu, who acted falsely."
"If this woman of beautiful limbs is indeed Bhṛgu’s wife staying here in secret, tell me the truth; I wish to take her away from this hermitage.
For my anger stands today as if burning my very heart."

"Since Bhṛgu has obtained this slender-waisted woman, who was previously my wife, he has today done what is displeasing to me; I shall take her away from this hermitage. Having thus addressed the blazing fire, that Rākṣasa—
Suspecting [the identity of] Bhṛgu’s wife, he questioned her again and again:
“O Agni, you always move within all living beings.
Like a witness regarding merits and sins, O Sage, speak the truth.”
"My former wife was carried off by Bhṛgu, who acted falsely.
If this is indeed so, you ought to tell me the truth.
Having heard from you that she is Bhṛgu's wife, I shall take her away from the hermitage."
"O Jātavedas, speak a truthful word to me while you are looking on.
Having heard those words of his, the seven-flamed one was deeply distressed;
"I speak the truth," he thought, "if only my curse might fall upon this best of knowers of Brahman."
"If I speak what is untrue, I shall fall into the hells one after another.
Fearing both falsehood and the curse of Bhṛgu, he spoke thus softly.
Agni said:
"O son of the Dānavas, this Pulomā was previously chosen by you;
however, she was not previously chosen by you according to the ritual with the sacred mantras. This illustrious Pulomā was instead given by her father to Bhṛgu."
"O Dānava, it was not out of greed for a boon that your highly illustrious father gave her to you; rather,
the sage Bhṛgu obtained me as his wife through a rite prescribed by the Vedas and performed according to the rules, having placed me at the forefront."
"I understand this to be so; I cannot bring myself to speak a falsehood, for falsehood is never honored in the world, O best of Dānavas.
Sūta said:
Then, having heard the words of Agni, that Rākṣasa carried her away in the form of a boar,
possessing the speed of thought and the wind, O Brahmin.
Thereupon, that embryo dwelling within his womb, O scion of Bhrigu’s lineage, [was cast forth].
Because he fell from his mother’s womb out of anger, he became known as Cyavana.
Seeing him fallen from his mother’s belly, radiant as the sun,
that *rākṣasa* released her and fell down, reduced to ashes.
Taking him, O Brahmin, that woman of beautiful hips,
Pulomā, fainted with grief, followed after Cyavana Bhārgava, the descendant of Bhrigu;
then Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds, beheld her.
The Blessed Lord Brahmā, the Grandfather, consoled the blameless wife of Bhṛgu as she wept with eyes full of tears;
from her teardrops there issued forth a great river.
Following the path of that illustrious wife of Bhrigu,
when the Grandfather of the Worlds saw the river flowing along her course, he then gave that river its name.
"O Vadhūsara," the Blessed One said, heading toward the hermitage of Cyavana.
Thus was that powerful Cyavana born as the son of Bhṛgu;
there his father beheld Cyavana and that beautiful woman.
Then Bhrigu, filled with anger, questioned his wife Puloma:
"By whom were you revealed here to that Rākṣasa who desired to carry you away? For that Rākṣasa did not know you, my wife of lovely smiles."
"Tell me that, for today I wish to curse him in my wrath. Who does not fear my curse, and who has committed this transgression?
Puloma said:
"O Blessed One, I was delivered to that Rākṣasa by Agni;
then the Rākṣasa carried me away as I cried out like a female osprey.
Thus have I been liberated by the splendor of this son of yours."
"And that Rākṣasa, reduced to ashes, fell away after releasing me.
Sūta said:
"Having heard this from Pulomā, Bhṛgu was filled with supreme wrath."
Enraged, he cursed Agni: "You shall become a consumer of all things.
Sūta said:
Having been thus cursed by Bhṛgu, Agni, filled with wrath, then spoke these words.
"O Brahmin, what is this rash act you have now committed? While I was striving for righteousness and speaking the truth with impartiality,
what transgression is there on my part in that I spoke the truth when asked?"
For a witness who, when questioned, speaks otherwise than the truth while knowing the facts of the testimony,
he destroys seven ancestors of his own lineage as well as seven descendants; and so too does he who,
knowing the true nature of the matter at hand, fails to speak.
He too will be tainted by that very same sin; of this there is no doubt.
Though I am capable of cursing you, I hold the Brahmins in high esteem.
Even though I already know [the truth], I shall speak clearly to you; listen to it.
By means of yoga, I divide myself into many forms and abide within various manifestations— in the maintenance of sacred fires, in sacrificial sessions, in ritual acts, and in great sacrifices.
Whatever oblation is offered into me according to the injunctions declared in the Vedas, [I am that].
By that, indeed, the deities and the ancestors become satisfied.
All the hosts of gods are water, and likewise the hosts of ancestors;
the new moon and the full moon sacrifices belong to the gods together with the ancestors.
Therefore, the deities are the ancestors, and the ancestors are also the deities;
they are worshipped both as one and separately on the sacred festival days (parvan). Indeed, the deities and the ancestors always offer oblations into me.
I am thus remembered as the mouth of the thirty gods and of the ancestors.
On the new moon day, the ancestors, and on the full moon day, the deities,
are offered oblations through my mouth alone, and they consume the sacrificed sacrificial offering.

"How shall I become a consumer of all things and yet remain their mouth? Having reflected thus, Agni then brought about his own withdrawal from the *agnihotra* rites of the twice-born and from the performance of sacrifices and sacrificial sessions (*satra*).
Devoid of the utterances of *niḥ*, *oṃkāra*, and *vaṣaṭ*, and deprived of *svadhā* and *svāhā*,
all creatures were consequently filled with great suffering in the absence of fire. Then the sages, deeply distressed, went to the gods and spoke these words.
"O sinless ones, because of the disappearance of the fire and the resulting lapse in ritual action, the three worlds have become bewildered.
Perform here whatever task must be done so that there may be no further delay.
Then the ṛṣis and the gods, having approached Brahmā, [spoke].
He reported to Agni the curse and the withdrawal of ritual acts:
"O highly fortunate one, Agni was indeed cursed by Bhṛgu for a certain reason;
how is it that, being the mouth of the gods and the consumer of the first portion of the sacrifice, he has become thus?"
"01,007.016e The consumer of oblations shall become the devourer of all things in all worlds.
01,007.017a Having heard those words of theirs, the Creator of the World summoned Agni and spoke these gentle words to the imperishable source of all beings:
01.007.018a You are the creator and indeed the end of all these worlds here;
01.007.018c you sustain the three worlds and are the promoter of ritual actions. 01.007.018e Therefore, O Lord of the World, act in such a way that these ritual actions may not be destroyed.
01.007.019 Why are you so deluded, O Agni, though you are the Lord?

Since you are the purifier in the world and reside within all beings, you shall not consume everything with your entire body. 01.007.020 You shall not attain the state of devouring all things with your whole physical form.
Those flames of yours that are in the fuel shall burn everything, O Flaming One;
and that body of yours which devours raw flesh shall consume all things.
Just as everything touched by the rays of the sun is perceived as pure, so shall it be.
In that way, everything consumed by your radiance shall become pure. Therefore, O Agni, you who have emerged from your own great splendor through your own power,
O Lord, make the curse of the seer true by means of your own brilliance.
"Take for yourself a portion of the gods' own share, offered into your mouth.
"So be it," the Fire replied to the Grandfather,
and he departed to carry out the command of the Supreme Lord.
The celestial sages, filled with joy, then departed as they had come; and the [other] sages performed all their rites as before. In heaven the gods rejoiced, as did the hosts of beings in the world.
And Agni, his impurities destroyed, attained supreme joy.
Thus did the Blessed One, Agni, receive a curse from Bhṛgu in ancient times.
Such is this ancient history concerning the origin of Agni’s curse.
The destruction of Puloman and the birth of Cyavana.
Sūta said:
And that Cyavana, O Brahmin, the descendant of Bhṛgu, begot a son.
Upon Sukanyā, he begot the high-souled Pramati, who was radiant with splendor.
Pramati, in turn, begot one named Ruru upon Ghṛtācī;
and Ruru begot Śunaka upon Pramadvarā.
The highly fortunate Śaunaka was the son of Śunaka;
that great being Śaunaka, the delighter of all the Bhṛgus,
was born established in intense austerity and remained thereafter firm in his renown.

O Brahmin, I shall relate in detail the entire life of that Ruru of immense splendor; listen to it from beginning to end. Formerly, there was a great sage endowed with ascetic power and sacred knowledge.
Known as Sthūlakeśa, he was devoted to the welfare of all beings. At that very time, O brahmin sage, the king of the Gandharvas, renowned as Viśvāvasu, begot a son upon Menakā.
Then, O descendant of Bhrigu, that Apsaras Menakā,
at the proper time, cast off that fetus near the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa.
Having abandoned the fetus on the bank of the river, she departed.
O Brahmin, the great seer beheld that maiden, who was like the offspring of an immortal and blazing as if with splendor, abandoned on the riverbank by the merciless and shameless Apsaras Menakā.
The radiant Sthūlakeśa saw that maiden, who was alone and deprived of kinsmen; then, O best of the twice-born,
that foremost of sages, filled with compassion, took her and raised her.

That beautiful woman of noble limbs grew up in his hermitage; and the highly fortunate and great seer Sthūlakeśa performed her birth-rites and other ceremonies according to the rules and in due order.
She was indeed the most excellent among women, endowed with every beauty and virtue;
therefore, the great seer gave her the name Pramadvārā. Having seen that Pramadvārā in his hermitage, Ruru—
It is said that he was indeed righteous-souled, yet his mind was entirely devoted to Madana.
Then that descendant of Bhṛgu caused his father to recite [the mantras] with his friends.
And having heard of the illustrious Sthūlakeśa, Pramati approached him and made a request.
He requested that maiden of excellent complexion for the sake of a son.
Then the father gave that maiden Pramadvarā to Ruru,
having first fixed the marriage under the lunar mansion presided over by Bhaga.
Then, when the wedding was imminent after a few days had passed,
that maiden of excellent complexion, while playing with her friends,
did not see a serpent lying asleep across her path.
Driven by Time and desiring death, she stepped upon him with her foot. Urged by the law of Time,
he violently pressed his venom-smeared fangs into the body of that heedless woman.
Bitten suddenly, she fell to the ground unconscious;
her complexion turned pale, her beauty vanished, and her ornaments and senses were lost.
With her hair disheveled, she brought no joy to her kinsmen.
Though her life-force had departed and she was no longer fit to look upon, her form remained most beautiful to behold; like one fallen asleep on the ground, afflicted by the venom of a serpent,
that slender-waisted woman became even more captivating to the mind.
Her father and those other ascetics beheld her fallen upon the ground, writhing, yet possessing the luster of a lotus.
Then all those best of the twice-born, filled with compassion, gathered together.
Svastyaatreya, Mahajanu, Kushika, Shankhamekhala,
Uddalaka, Katha, and likewise Shvetaketu;
Bharadvaja, Kaunakutsa, Arstishena, and then Gautama.
Pramati, along with his son, as well as other forest-dwellers,
seeing that maiden lifeless and afflicted by the serpent's venom,
wept, overcome with compassion; Ruru, however, went outside in distress.
And all those best of the twice-born then sat down right there.
Sūta said:
While those Brāhmaṇas were seated there on all sides...
Having entered the dense forest, Ruru, deeply afflicted by grief, cried out.
Stricken by sorrow, he then lamented piteously at great length;
grieving and thinking of his beloved Pramadvarā, he spoke these words.

That slender-limbed woman, whose face resembles the full moon, lies upon the earth increasing my grief; she who has broad and shapely hips and eyes like lotus petals seems to be stealing away my very life.
Even as I am on the verge of death, he will depart swiftly, taking my life-breaths away.
For me, whose offerings of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to my father, mother, friends,
and all my kinsmen have been cut off— what indeed could be more painful than this?

"If I have given gifts, if I have practiced austerities, or if my gurus have been properly honored by me— by that merit, let my beloved come back to life! Just as I have indeed been self-restrained and firm in my vows since birth..."
"May the beautiful Pramadvarā likewise rise up this very day!
While he was thus lamenting in his grief for the sake of his wife,
the divine messenger approached him in the forest and spoke these words to Ruru.

"If my devotion remains unshakable toward Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Lord of the World, the enemy of the Asuras, may that beloved wife of mine live. While Ruru was thus lamenting, all the gods were moved with compassion.
Having instructed him with words for his benefit, they dispatched a messenger.
That pure messenger, acting for the pleasure of the gods, arrived in haste and,
addressing the sorrowful Ruru, spoke the words of the gods.
"O Brahmin, I have been sent to your presence by all the gods. O best of the twice-born, listen to these words spoken for your benefit by those who wish you well.
[They spoke thus] to Ruru, who was then lamenting, deeply distressed, and most miserable."
01,009.005d A divine messenger, having arrived, spoke these words:
01,009.006 The divine messenger said:
01,009.006a "O Ruru, that which you utter with your voice out of sorrow is indeed false."
"O righteous one, there is no life remaining for a mortal whose lifespan has expired.
This piteous daughter of a Gandharva and an Apsaras has reached the end of her life;
therefore, my dear son, do not let your mind be overcome by grief in any way whatsoever."
"A means for this has already been ordained by the high-souled gods;
if you wish to perform it, you shall regain this Pramadvarā.
Ruru said:
"O sky-traveler, tell me truly what means has been employed by the gods;
having heard it, I shall act accordingly. You ought to save me.
The messenger of the gods said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, grant half of your own life to the maiden;
in this way, O Ruru, your wife Pramadvarā shall rise up.
Ruru said:
"O best of sky-dwellers, I grant half of my life to the maiden;
let my beloved rise up, adorned with the beauty of passion,
endowed with the excellence of conversation, and possessing a face like the full moon."
"He will dispel his grief with the water of his words.
Sūta said:
"Then the king of the Gandharvas and the messenger of the gods, those two most excellent beings—"
Approaching Dharmarāja, they addressed him with these words:
"O Dharmarāja, let Ruru’s wife Pramadvarā rise up by means of half of your own lifespan;
let the auspicious lady arise, even if you consider her as already dead."
The King of Dharma said:
"O messenger of the gods, if you so desire, let Pramadvārā, the wife of Ruru,
rise up endowed with half of Ruru's own lifespan."
Sūta said:
When this had been spoken, the maiden Pramadvarā then rose up;
that woman of excellent complexion arose as if from sleep, restored by half of Ruru’s life-span.
"This was indeed foreseen regarding Ruru of supreme splendor,
that when his lifespan had greatly increased, half of it should be diminished for the sake of a wife.
Then, on an auspicious day, his parents joyfully performed the rites for them both.
Having performed the marriage ceremony, the two of them, desiring each other's welfare, took their pleasure together.
Having obtained that rare wife, who possessed the radiance of the filaments of a lotus, he—
firm in his vows— undertook a penance for the destruction of the serpents.
Seeing all those serpents gliding crookedly, he was filled with intense anger;
seizing whatever weapon was at hand, he would always strike them down as they approached.
Once, that brahmin Ruru entered a vast forest.
There he saw a young *ḍuṇḍubha* snake lying down;
then, raising his staff which resembled the staff of Death, the enraged Brahmin struck it. Thereupon, the *ḍuṇḍubha* spoke to him.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I have not offended you at all today;
why then, filled with wrath, do you strike me out of agitation?
Ruru said:
"My wife, who was as dear to me as my own life, has been bitten by a serpent. O snake, a terrible vow was made by me there: 'I shall always slay whichever serpent I may see.'"
"Therefore, I wish to kill you; you shall be deprived of life.
The *ḍuṇḍubha* said:
"O Brahmin, those snakes are different who bite human beings here."

"You ought not to harm the *duṇḍubha* snakes by means of the scent of a snake, for they are not truly snakes. Having become one who knows the Dharma, you ought not to harm these *duṇḍubhas*, who share a single purpose but have separate purposes, and share a single suffering but have separate pleasures."
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of that serpent, Ruru was then agitated by fear; he did not kill it, for he considered the *ḍuṇḍubha* to be a seer (*ṛṣi*).
And the blessed Ruru spoke to him as if to soothe him:
"By what ripening of karma have you come to this state of being a serpent?
O serpent, tell me out of a desire to know: who has undergone this transformation?"
The Dundubha said:
"O Ruru, in former times I was a sage named Sahasrapāt;
by the curse of a brahmin, I have come to this state of being a serpent."
"However, by the curse of a brahmin, I have undergone this transformation,
even though I am always engaged in and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Ruru said:
"O best of serpents, for what reason did the twice-born one curse you in his anger?
And for how long will this body of yours remain so?
The *ḍuṇḍubha* said:
"O dear one, formerly I had a friend, a twice-born man named Khagama,
who was very firm in his speech and endowed with the power of asceticism. While playing in my childhood, I once made a snake out of grass."
While engaged in the Agnihotra sacrifice, being terrified, he indeed fainted. Having regained consciousness, that ascetic spoke to me:
"Friend, do not cause such distress with this serpent; fear has entered me."
"And you, O brahmin, were cursed by me: 'I shall never rejoice.
Because of that very curse, I was repeatedly urged by the serpent toward my own self, O twice-born one, while I was seated at the *agnihotra* sacrifice; thus, being deluded, I entered [the fire]."
As if burning with rage, he whose word is truth and whose vows are firm said:
"O serpent, just as this snake has been rendered powerless by you out of fear of me,
so shall you, O snake, become powerless through my anger."
O ascetic, knowing the power of his austerity, I,
that ascetic, sighing repeatedly and hotly,
became greatly agitated; with a deeply distressed heart, I spoke to that forest-dweller.

"Self-restrained, out of sheer agitation, standing with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, I said to you, 'Friend,' and laughed; this was done by me merely for sport. O Brahmin, you ought to forgive me; let this curse be withdrawn."
Then, seeing me with a deeply agitated mind, that ascetic, greatly distressed, sighed hotly again and again and said to me:
"What I have spoken shall certainly not prove false in any way."
"O you who are firm in your vows, listen to these words that I shall speak to you. Having heard them, O one rich in asceticism, let this speech remain in your heart;
for by addressing and beholding him, you shall be released from this curse."
"A pure son named Ruru shall be born to Pramati;
upon seeing him, you will be released from the curse almost immediately.
Having been addressed thus by him, I attained the state of a serpent.
"You are known as Ruru, the pure son of Pramati;
O best of the twice-born, your release from the curse will occur before long. Having regained my own form, I shall today speak for your benefit."
Then that bull among brahmins, the one of great renown, having cast off his form as a *ḍauṇḍubha*,
once again assumed his own radiant form and spoke these words to Ruru of incomparable vigor:
Having quickly grasped his true nature, the charioteer addressed that seer with these words:
"Non-violence is declared to be the supreme duty for all living beings."
