Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should never harm any living beings whatsoever. O dear one, the supreme Vedic revelation declares that a Brāhmaṇa is born here as one who is inherently gentle, a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and a bestower of fearlessness upon all creatures.

Non-violence, truthful speech, and forbearance— these are determined to be the supreme duty of a Brahmin, even more so than the memorization of the Vedas. As for the duty of a Kshatriya, that indeed shall not be desired by you here.
"O twice-born one, that which is the duty of a kṣatriya is certainly not suitable for you.
The wielding of the rod, severity, and the protection of subjects—this is the work of a kṣatriya; listen to me, O Ruru."
O virtuous-souled one, [you have heard] of the slaughter of the serpents in the past by Janamejaya,

and the protection of those terrified snakes even from the brahmin who was endowed with the power of asceticism and strength, and who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O best of the twice-born, [having heard] from Āstīka, the foremost of the twice-born, regarding the snake-sacrifice,
Ruru said:
"How indeed did the Kṣatriya Janamejaya slay the snakes?"
"O dear one, why were the serpents harmed, O best of the twice-born?
And for what reason were those snakes liberated by him? Tell me that;
relate everything concerning Āstīka, for I wish to hear it in its entirety."
The seer said:
"O Lord, when that best of seers had spoken thus and vanished through his yogic power,
the seer, his heart filled with agitation, marveled at that wonder."
"O Ruru, you shall hear the entire great life-story of Āstīka as it is being told by the Brahmins," having said this, he vanished. Sūta said:

Ruru, too, ran all around through the entire forest in every direction, seeking to find that ṛṣi; utterly exhausted, he collapsed upon the ground. Having fallen into a state of extreme delusion, he became as if deprived of consciousness.
Reflecting again and again upon those truthful words of the seer, Ruru regained his composure and went to his father;
then that twice-born one related everything to his father exactly as it had happened.
Having related to his father all the meaningful words of the Dundubha,
he then questioned his father further regarding those words of Astika which had been recounted in their entirety by the Dundubha.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear that which is being proclaimed in its true essence.
When his father was asked about this narrative, he related it all.
[The son asked: "O tiger among kings, for what purpose did King Janamejaya [perform the sacrifice]?"
"Tell me how he brought about the end of the serpents by means of the snake-sacrifice. Homage to Śrī Rāma!
Homage to the venerable gurus!
Salutation to Śrī Vedavyāsa.
Whatever syllable may have been omitted, or whatever may be deficient in its prosodic measure (mātrā), the learned ought to forgive it; for who is free from transgression?
Auspicious one, auspicious one! O Kapardin, O capable Lord of Beings, O destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes!
O Blessed One, Śaṅkara, you ought to forgive my transgression.
Homage to Nārāyaṇa!
Salutations to Śrī Vedavyāsa.
Salutations to Gaṇapati.
May there be no obstacles.
Śaunaka said:
"O tiger among kings, tell me why that King Janamejaya brought about the end of the serpents through a snake-sacrifice."
O Sauti, relate everything in its entirety, according to the facts and without omission:
for what reason did Āstīka, the best of the twice-born and foremost among those who recite prayers,
liberate the serpents from that blazing fire?
Whose son was that king who performed the snake-sacrifice?
And whose son was that foremost of the twice-born? Tell me this.
Sūta said:
"O twice-born one, this great narrative called Āstīka is being recited here;
listen to all of it in its entirety from me as I speak, O best of speakers.
Śaunaka said:
"I wish to hear this delightful story in its entirety—
the ancient tale of the illustrious Brahmin Āstīka.
Sūta said:
The elders dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest relate this ancient history (itihāsa) proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
formerly, my father Lomaharṣaṇa was urged to speak as a Sūta.
The intelligent disciple of Vyāsa, having been addressed thus by the Brahmins, said:
"Therefore, having heard it from him, I shall relate this narrative of Āstīka exactly as it is to you, O Śaunaka, who have asked for it."
I shall describe in its entirety that which destroys all sins.
For Āstīka’s father was a lord equal to Prajāpati;
he was a celibate student, restrained in diet, and always devoted to fierce austerity.
The great sage known as Jaratkāru was one whose vital seed was drawn upward;
he was a knower of dharma, the foremost among the Yāyāvaras, and firm in his vows. Once, that highly fortunate one, endowed with the power of asceticism, [set out].
The sage wandered over the entire earth, making his home wherever evening found him; performing ritual ablutions at sacred fords, he roamed everywhere,
practicing a vow of great splendor that is difficult for those of undisciplined minds to perform.
Subsisting on air, taking no food, withering away, the sage remained with unblinking eyes; wandering here and there, radiant as a blazing fire,
he once beheld his own ancestors as they roamed about.
Seeing those ancestors hanging in a great chasm with their feet upward and their faces downward,
Jaratkāru addressed them:
"Who are you that hang here in this pit with your heads down?"

When the clump of vīraṇa grass, upon which they were clinging, was completely devoured on all sides by a mouse dwelling constantly in this hole and remaining hidden, the ancestors said: The ancestors said: [as follows].
"We are sages named Yāyāvaras, firm in our vows. O Brahmin, due to the extinction of our lineage, we are descending to the earth.
For those who have no progeny, there is no source of happiness in the world of mortals."

"Even those who observe meritorious vows do not obtain a dwelling in heaven. Among our lineage, there is one known as Jaratkāru; unfortunate among the unfortunate, he has devoted himself solely to asceticism."
"That fool does not wish to take a wife in order to procreate sons;
because of him, we hang here in this pit due to the extinction of our lineage. With him as our protector, we are as helpless as evildoers."

"O best of beings, who are you that grieves for us like a kinsman? O Brahmin, we wish to know: who are you stationed here, and for what reason do you deign to show compassion for us who are so pitiable?"
Jaratkāru said:
"You are indeed my ancestors, my fathers and grandfathers;
tell me, what shall I do today? I am Jaratkaru himself."
The ancestors said:
"O dear son, we are your ancestors; deliver our lineage yourself. Strive with diligence, my son, for the sake of the continuity of our family."
"O Lord, for one's own sake and for the sake of us, [one should practice] dharma alone. Indeed,
O dear one, neither by the fruits of dharma nor by well-accumulated austerities do those who possess sons attain in this world that destination which those who have sons reach."
"Therefore, apply yourself to taking a wife and set your mind upon progeny;
O son, at our command, do this, for it is our supreme welfare.
Jaratkāru said:
"My mind has always been resolved that I shall not take a wife; however,
for the sake of your welfare, I shall take a wife according to the prescribed rites and under this agreement."
"If I obtain such a girl as this, I shall do so and not otherwise;
for that maiden who shall bear my name and is offered by her kinsmen,
I shall marry according to the prescribed rite, even as if she were alms."
"For who will give a wife to one as poor as me, especially?
However, I shall accept alms if anyone should offer them.
O ancestors, for the sake of marriage, I shall thus strive."
"By this method, I shall never act otherwise;
and there a being shall arise for the sake of delivering you all.
Having attained the eternal station, may my ancestors rejoice."
Sūta said:
As soon as these words were spoken, the Grandfathers replied, "So be it," and all vanished; the sage was filled with wonder.

Then, for the sake of settling down, that brahmin of rigid vows wandered the earth seeking a wife, yet he found no wife. Once, having gone to the forest, the brahmin remembered the words of his father.
Seeking alms from the maiden, he uttered three words very softly;
Vāsuki then offered his sister to him,
but he did not accept her, reflecting that she was not of the same name as his own.
"May I take as my wife one who is of the same name and who offers herself," such was the thought that took hold in the mind of the high-souled Jaratkāru.
Then the immensely wise and great ascetic Jaratkāru spoke to him.
"O serpent, tell me truly, what is the name of this sister of yours?
Vāsuki replied:
"Jaratkāru, Jaratkaru—this is my younger sister."
"Accept this woman of slender waist, given by me for the sake of a wife;
she was previously preserved for your sake, O best of the twice-born—please accept her.
Having spoken thus, he then gave that woman of excellent complexion to him as a wife.
Sūta said:
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, the serpents were indeed cursed by their mother in the past:
'At Janamejaya’s sacrifice, the one whose chariot is drawn by the wind (Agni) shall consume you.'"
To pacify that curse, the best of the serpents gave his sister to that rishi, who was firm in his vows and devoted to asceticism;
and he accepted her according to the rites prescribed by tradition.
And from that [wife] was born a son of that high-souled one named Āstīka;
he was an ascetic, a great soul, a master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
impartial toward all the world, and a remover of fear for his father and mother.

Then, after a long time, the son of Pāṇḍu, the lord of men, performed a great sacrifice known as the Sarpasattra; so it is heard. When that sacrificial session for the destruction of the serpents had commenced, indeed—
The highly illustrious Āstīka released him from that curse;
he likewise delivered the snakes, his maternal uncles, and other kinsmen,
and he saved his ancestors through his progeny as well as through his asceticism.
O Brahmin, he became free from debt through various vows and the study of the Vedas;
he gratified the gods with sacrifices accompanied by diverse sacrificial fees,
the sages through his practice of celibacy, and his ancestors through the procreation of offspring.
Having removed the heavy burden of his ancestors,
Jaratkaru, firm in his vows, ascended to heaven together with his forefathers; and having obtained a son, Āstīka, as well as the highest dharma, the sage [attained his goal].
After a very long time, Jaratkāru ascended to heaven.
This narrative of Āstīka has been recounted by me exactly as it occurred. Speak, O tiger among the Bhṛgus: what more should be told?
Śaunaka said:
"O Sauti, tell us again that story in detail;
for we have the highest desire to hear it concerning the wise and virtuous Āstīka."
"O gentle one, you speak sweetly, with smooth syllables and words;
we are greatly pleased, dear one, for you speak just like a father. Indeed, your father was always devoted to our service."
"Tell this exactly as your father related it; you must speak it thus.
Sūta said:
"I shall relate to you this life-prolonging narrative of Āstīka."
O Brahmin, long ago, in the age of the gods, I heard from my father as he recounted it how there were two auspicious daughters of Prajāpati,
sisters endowed with wonderful beauty and free from all blemish.
Kadru and Vinata were the two wives of Kaśyapa;
their husband, equal to Prajāpati, being pleased, granted a boon to those two lawful wives,
filled with supreme joy.
Upon hearing from Kaśyapa that those excellent boons had been granted, those two noble women attained incomparable joy and delight. Kadrū chose a thousand sons who were nāgas of equal splendor.
Vinatā chose two sons who would be superior in strength to the sons of Kadrū;
two sons who would be superior in vigor, splendor, and prowess. "By your grace, may these two sons be endowed with such qualities."
Her husband granted her the boon she desired: a son who would be superior by half.
Vinatā then said to Kaśyapa, "So be it.
When this had been spoken, she then conceived and bore these two embryos with focused devotion.

Having obtained the boon exactly as requested, Vinatā was then filled with joy; having secured two sons superior in prowess, she felt her purpose was fulfilled. And Kadrū, for her part, obtained a thousand sons of equal splendor.
"Both embryos must be preserved with great care," said that great ascetic Kaśyapa; having spoken thus, he entered the forest while his two wives were filled with joy at their good fortune.
After a long time, Kadrū gave birth to one hundred and ten eggs.
Then, O best of Brahmins, Vinatā gave birth to two eggs;
the delighted attendants placed those eggs in warm vessels for five hundred years.
Then, after five hundred years had passed, the sons of Kadrū emerged from their eggs;
however, no pair was seen from the two eggs of Vinatā.
Thereupon, that ascetic goddess, seeking her sons, was filled with shame.

Vinatā split the egg and there she beheld her son; he was fully formed in the upper half of his body, while the other half remained unmanifest. According to tradition, that son, filled with rage, cursed her.
"O mother, since you, overcome by greed, have treated me thus,
I shall today remain incomplete in body; therefore, you shall become her slave for five hundred years, she with whom you are vying."
"And this son of yours, O mother, will liberate you from slavery;
provided that you do not, O mother, deprive him of his body or leave him crippled through the breaking of his egg, just as you have done to me, poor wretch."
"You must wait with patience for his time of birth,
which will occur after five hundred years, if you desire him to possess superior strength.
Having thus cursed Vinatā, her son departed through the air.
"O Brahmin, Aruṇa is always seen at the time of dawn;
he performed the duty of charioteer for the sun's chariot.
Then, as he was rising, the thousand-rayed Lord, having seen that Aruṇa,"
Blazing with his own splendor and equal in brilliance to himself,
the dispeller of darkness, being well-pleased, appointed him to the office of charioteer;
and he too, having ascended that chariot of the sun of immeasurable luster...
Indeed, even Aruṇa became immortal as the lamp of all the worlds;
and Garuḍa, the slayer of serpents, was born at the proper time. As soon as he was born, he abandoned Vinatā and entered the sky.
"O tiger among the Bhṛgus, he was about to take for himself that food which had been ordained by the Creator for him to eat while he was hungry and desiring to feed.
Sūta said:
At that very time, O ascetic, those two sisters saw Uccaiḥśravas approaching nearby—
the one whom all the hosts of gods, appearing joyful, had worshipped.
While the nectar was being churned, there arose the unsurpassed jewel among horses,
possessing the strength of a great torrent, the best of swift steeds,
glorious, ageless, divine, and endowed with every auspicious mark.
Śaunaka said:
"Tell me how that nectar was churned by the gods and where it was;
and tell me the reason for the churning, and what else arose from the nectar."
Therein was born that horse-king of great heroism and immense splendor.
Sūta said:
[He was like] the blazing, immovable Mount Meru, an unsurpassed mass of radiance.
Formerly, all the hosts of gods and likewise all the Daityas,
overcome by hunger and old age, approached Brahmā;
[they were] eclipsing the splendor of the sun with their own peaks, radiant with gold.
It was adorned with variegated golden ornaments and frequented by gods and gandharvas;
it was immeasurable and unassailable by people abounding in unrighteousness,
inhabited by fierce beasts of prey, and illuminated by divine medicinal herbs.
It stood covering the heavens with its height, a great mountain inaccessible even to the minds of others, filled with rivers and trees,
and made most enchanting by the songs of various flocks of birds.
Having ascended its back— which was auspicious, strewn with many jewels, towering,
and enduring for infinite kalpas— all the gods of great power,
those inhabitants of heaven, sat there and began to deliberate.
Having assembled for the sake of the nectar (*amṛta*), they remained established in asceticism and self-restraint.

While the gods were thus reflecting and deliberating on all sides, the divine Nārāyaṇa spoke these words to Brahmā: [While the gods were thus reflecting and deliberating on all sides,] the divine Nārāyaṇa spoke this to Brahmā.
"Let the gods and the hosts of asuras churn the ocean-jar;
while that great ocean is being churned, the nectar of immortality will appear there,
once all medicinal herbs and all precious gems have been cast into it."
"O gods, churn the ocean; you shall find the nectar therein.
Sūta said:
Then [the mountain] adorned with mountain peaks shaped like the summits of clouds...
Mandara, the best of mountains, covered with networks of creepers,
resounded with the cries of various birds and teemed with diverse fanged beasts; it was frequented by kinnaras, apsaras, and even gods.
It rises eleven thousand yojanas high and is established in the same number of thousands below the earth. At that time, all the hosts of gods were indeed unable to uproot it.
Approaching Viṣṇu as he sat with Brahmā, they said this:
"May you two both apply your supreme intellect here toward our ultimate welfare;
let an effort be made for our benefit in the lifting of Mount Mandara."
"So be it," Viṣṇu replied to Bhārgava along with Brahmā.
Then the lotus-eyed one of immeasurable soul urged the lord of serpents.
Thereupon, Ananta, being exhorted by Brahmā, rose up.
And having been addressed by Nārāyaṇa regarding that task,
the valiant and immensely powerful Ananta, O Brahmin, then forcibly uprooted that king of mountains along with its forests and its forest-dwellers.
Then, with ease, Madhusūdana [approached] that divine [ocean] frequented by perfected sages (siddharṣi);
thereafter, together with the gods, he drew near to the ocean.
They said to him, "We shall churn the waters for the sake of the nectar.
Then the Lord of Waters said, "In that case, let there be a share for me as well;
I shall endure the immense pressure from the churning of Mount Mandara."
And the gods and the asuras said to Akūpāra, the king of tortoises: "You ought to become the foundation for this mountain. Having replied, "So be it," the tortoise offered his back to him.
Indra pressed down upon the summit of that mountain with a mechanical device;
having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
the gods began to churn the ocean, the reservoir of waters.
Then, O Brahmin, the Daityas and Dānavas seeking the nectar,
those great Asuras, took hold of one end of the serpent king together;
all the gods stood together at the place where the tail was.
The great asuras clung to the head of Vāsuki, the king of serpents;
for where the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa was, there was Ananta.
Raising up the serpent’s head, he cast it down again and again.
Then, as the nāga Vāsuki was being violently pulled by the gods,
O descendant of Bhṛgu, at that time, as Vāsuki was being churned by Mount Mandara with the arms of the gods and the Dānavas, the water became mixed with the poison that issued forth.
A fierce poison arose, known as Hālāhala;
indeed, both the gods and the Dānavas were scorched by that poison.
Terrified, they fled from there and fell into despair.
The gods, having assembled with the foremost of sages, said to Brahmā:

"While the nectar was being churned, poison was produced, possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction. By that very poison the worlds have been tormented; therefore, provide a remedy for it."
Thus addressed, Brahmā then meditated upon Hara, the Lord of the World—
the three-eyed, trident-bearing Rudra, the God of gods, the consort of Umā. Then, having perceived his thought, the God arrived swiftly.
Then Prajāpati, the god, explained all of that to him.
Having heard it, Rudra, the lord of the gods of gods, desiring the welfare of this world,
drank that poison which possessed a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
The Lord placed it around his neck out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
because of that blueness on his neck, he is therefore remembered as Nīlakaṇṭha.
As soon as the poison was swallowed there by Rudra of immeasurable splendor, [it turned his throat blue].

The gods, being gratified, departed once more; they indeed performed that task accordingly. As the nectar was being churned again by the gods and the Dānavas, those masses of smoke became masses of clouds accompanied by lightning.
The hosts of gods rained down upon those who were emaciated by exhaustion and heat;
and showers of flowers falling from the peaks of that mountain crest scattered garlands everywhere over the hosts of gods and asuras.
There arose a great roar, like the sound of massive clouds,
as the ocean was churned by Mount Mandara with the gods and asuras;
there, various aquatic creatures were crushed by the great mountain.
Hundreds of aquatic creatures perished in the salt waters,
and the mountain brought to destruction various beings belonging to Varuṇa who dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
And as that mountain was being whirled about, great trees together with their birds fell down from the mountain peaks, rubbing against one another;
and from their friction, a fire arose, repeatedly blazing up with its flames.
Like lightning enveloping a dark cloud, it covered Mount Mandara;
it consumed the elephants and the lions that had emerged,
as well as all the various creatures whose lives were departed.
Then Indra, the best of the immortals, extinguished that fire burning here and there on all sides with water born from the clouds. Thereupon,
various kinds [of creatures] flowed forth there into the waters of the ocean.
The resinous exudations of great trees and the juices of many medicinal herbs— through the essence of those liquids possessing the potency of nectar,
as well as through milk and the flow of gold, the gods attained immortality.

Then, that water which had arisen in the ocean became milk mixed with the finest essences; from that milk, clarified butter (ghṛta) was produced. In the meantime, [the nectar] arose from the mouth of Vāsuki as he emerged.
The terrible Kālakūṭa poison, which strikes fear into all living beings—
when that dreadful poison, radiant as the fire of cosmic destruction, had arisen,
the hosts of gods and asuras were terrified and fled in all directions.
At that time, Viṣṇu was rendered black by a great poison;
thereupon the entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
Then, at the word of Brahmā, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [acted].
He drank that terrible poison in the very presence of the gods. While that poison was being drunk by Hara of immeasurable splendor,
the gods, sages, and dānavas were struck with supreme wonder.
Then, seeing that the poison had reached Hara’s throat, Brahmā said to the Lord of Gods: “O Lord, please hold it in your throat. At the word of the Self-born One, Śambhu held that supreme poison.
Because the terrible *hālāhala* poison was in his throat, he was thereafter known as Nīlakaṇṭha.
Then the gods spoke to Brahmā, who was seated there as the granter of boons:
"O Brahmā, we are utterly exhausted, yet that nectar does not emerge."
Except for the god Nārāyaṇa, the Daityas and the best of the Nāgas were likewise overcome;
this churning of the ocean, though undertaken long ago,
has brought exhaustion upon us, yet the nectar has not yet emerged.
Having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, then spoke these words to the god Nārāyaṇa:
"O Viṣṇu, bestow strength upon them; you are the ultimate refuge in this matter."
Viṣṇu said:
"I shall grant strength to all of you who are intent upon this task. Let the jar be churned by everyone; let Mount Mandara be turned."
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, those mighty ones together once again made the waters of the great ocean extremely turbulent.

There, poison had previously arisen; for the sake of protecting the world, Śiva first swallowed it by the word of Brahmā. Then the goddess Jyeṣṭhā arose, assuming a dark form and adorned with all ornaments.
Then, like the sun with its hundred thousand rays emerging from the ocean,
the bright, cool-rayed, and radiant Soma arose;
immediately thereafter, Śrī appeared, clothed in white garments, rising from the clarified butter.
The goddess Surā was born, as was the pale-white horse;
and the divine Kaustubha jewel, produced from the nectar of immortality, emerged,
radiant with spreading rays, from the chest of Nārāyaṇa.
O great sage, O Brahmin, at that very time the Pārijāta and the Surabhi were born there, both bestowing the fruits of all desires;
thereafter, O illustrious one, the great elephant with four tusks was born.
Śrī, Surā, Soma, and the horse Manojava;
after these arose the great-bodied, four-tusked,
and exceedingly fierce Airāvaṇa, the lord of the Nāgas, born from the nectar.
Poison, the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, Soma, Śrī, Surā, and likewise the horse;
the Kaustubha gem and the Apsarases, as well as the great elephant Airāvata; Kapilā, the wish-fulfilling tree, the Kaustubha, and the hosts of Apsarases.
That elephant Airāvata was indeed the most excellent and auspicious among elephants; possessing four white tusks and a massive body,
he thereafter became the great elephant Airāvaṇa, borne by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
From that very intense churning, the Kālakūṭa poison emerged thereafter,
suddenly blazing like a smoky fire, pervading the world;
by smelling its scent, the three worlds were rendered unconscious.
Then the Blessed One, Maheśvara, whose form is the mantra, held it in his throat;
from that time forth, the god is known by the name Nīlakaṇṭha, according to tradition. In the meantime, the Daityas completely defeated the gods.
The gods took the divine nectar and became despondent;
however, at the word of Brahmā, Śiva first swallowed it for the sake of protecting the world.
Having witnessed this marvel, the Dānavas stood there in despair.
For the sake of the nectar and for the sake of sovereignty, they resorted to great enmity;
from where the gods were, they departed, taking to the path of the sun.
But as Mount Mandara was being whirled around, its droplets [fell].
In them were born sixty crores of excellent women, each possessing eight apsarases;
they were free from old age and death, possessed beautiful forms, and had full hips and breasts—
such that at the mere sight of them, a mortal would become like one driven mad.
Then the god Dhanvantari arose in a magnificent form, bearing a white water-pot in which the nectar of immortality was contained. Seeing this most wonderful sight, the Dānavas rose up.

While they were clamoring, "This is mine! This is mine! for the sake of the nectar, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, resorting to his power of illusion (māyā), assumed a wonderful female form and approached the Dānavas.
Then those Dānavas and Daityas, their minds deluded and all intent upon it, gave that nectar to her, the woman;
for she was the illusory power (māyā) of Nārāyaṇa, carrying a water-pot.
While the Daityas were being seated in rows by the Dānavas, the Goddess caused the gods to drink [the amṛta], but not the Daityas; and they cried out.
Sūta said:
Then, seizing their principal shields and various weapons, the Daityas and Dānavas together rushed toward the gods. Thereupon,
the powerful god Viṣṇu took up that nectar.
Accompanied by Nara, the Lord took [the nectar] from the lords of the Dānavas; then,
while a tumultuous commotion prevailed, all the hosts of gods obtained that nectar from the presence of Viṣṇu and drank it.
With the strength of his arms, Hari causes the gods to drink the nectar,
and with his bow, he restrains them by driving away other archers;
then, at that moment, while the gods were drinking the desired nectar—
Whosoever drank the nectar, they all fought with the Dānavas.
At that time, the Dānava Rāhu, assuming the form of a god, drank it;
and when the nectar had reached the throat of that Dānava, [the gods struck him].

This was recounted by the Moon and the Sun out of a desire for the welfare of the gods. Then, while he was drinking the nectar with his vital power, the Blessed One severed his adorned head with his discus weapon.
That great head of the Dānava, resembling a mountain peak,
was severed by the discus and fell, shaking the surface of the earth;
severed by the discus, it leapt into the sky and let out an exceedingly terrifying roar.
That headless trunk of the Daitya fell, quivering upon the surface of the earth, making the world— along with its mountains, forests, and islands—
tremble for thirteen thousand *yojanas* in every direction.

Then, indeed, a persistent enmity was established by the face of Rāhu toward the moon and the sun; even today he still swallows them both. And the Blessed Lord Hari, having abandoned his incomparable female form, [resumed his own].
With various terrifying weapons, he made the Dānavas tremble;
then a great battle, the most formidable of all, commenced between the gods and the Asuras near the salt waters of the ocean.
Thousands of massive, sharp spears fell down,
along with javelins with extremely sharp points and various other weapons.
Then the asuras, pierced by the discus, vomited copious amounts of blood.
Mangled by swords, spears, and maces, they fell upon the surface of the earth;
and heads, severed by sharp-edged spears (*paṭṭiśa*) in that dreadful battle,
as well as nets of refined gold, fell incessantly at that time.
With their limbs smeared with blood, the slain great asuras lay prostrate like mountain peaks stained with red minerals. Then, a tumultuous roar arose from all sides.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there by the thousands as they struck one another with weapons while the sun turned blood-red;
they fought with yellow iron clubs and with fists in close combat.
As they struck one another in battle, the sound seemed to touch the very heavens.
"Cut! Pierce! Run forward! Strike down!
Attack!"—such most terrible cries were heard there on all sides.
While that tumultuous and terrifying battle was thus proceeding,
the two gods, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, entered the fray. There,
the Blessed One also beheld the divine bow of Nara.
Viṣṇu then thought of his discus, the destroyer of Dānavas. Then, as soon as it was thought of, the discus of great luster, which torments enemies, arrived from the sky.
Equal to the sun, with its unimpeded disc,
the Sudarśana— terrible, invincible, and supreme—
had arrived, possessing the radiance of a blazing fire.
The formidable Acyuta, whose arms were like the trunks of elephants,
released that swift, fiercely impetuous,
and greatly radiant weapon capable of shattering the cities of enemies.
Then, blazing with a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon,
it fell again and again with great force,
tearing asunder thousands of the sons of Diti and the Danavas.
Stirred by the Best of Men in the battle,
he burned in some places like a leaping fire,
and forcibly cut down those hosts of asuras.
Then, repeatedly cast into the sky and onto the earth,
he drank blood in battle like a *piśāca*;
meanwhile, the Asuras, with undaunted hearts, [assailed him] with mountains.
Then, repeatedly afflicting the hosts of gods,
those of great strength, possessing the luster of clouds that have dispersed,
ascended into the sky by the thousands.
Then, from the sky, great mountains— inspiring terror,
accompanied by trees, and possessing the forms of various clouds—
fell down with their peaks and ridges crumbling away.
Having struck one another swiftly with a roar,
the earth, along with its forests, then trembled,
being struck on all sides by the falling of great mountains.
As they roared fiercely at one another for a moment on the battlefield where the combat was intensely underway,
men [clashed] with ornaments of excellent gold upon their heads.
He completely covered the path of the sky with great arrows,
tearing apart mountain peaks with his feathered shafts during that time of great terror, the battle between the hosts of asuras.
Then, oppressed by the gods, the great asuras entered the earth and the salt-water ocean;
they fled into the sky, which possessed the brilliance of a blazing sacrificial fire.
And having observed Sudarśana to be enraged,
the gods then achieved victory and returned Mount Mandara to its own place, having honored it well.
Having made the earth, the sky, and even the heavens resound on all sides with their roar,
the clouds then departed as they had come;
thereafter, they carefully secured the nectar of immortality.
The gods, having attained abundant and supreme joy,
then, together with the immortals, entrusted that treasure of nectar to the Diademed One (Arjuna) for protection, as the Destroyer of Bala (Indra).
Sūta said:
"All this has been narrated to you, how the nectar was churned,
and how that glorious horse of incomparable prowess was produced therein."
Having observed him at that time, Kadrū said this to Vinatā:
"O blessed lady, find out without delay what color Uccaiḥśravas is.
Vinatā replied:
"This king of horses is indeed white; or what do you think, O beautiful one? Tell me its color as well, and then let us bargain here. Kadrū replied:
"O lady of radiant smiles, I consider this horse to have black tail-hair;
come, play with me for the sake of slavery, O beautiful woman.
Sūta said:
Having thus made an agreement with one another regarding their mutual status as slaves,
they both went to their own homes, thinking, "We shall see each other tomorrow.
Then Kadrū, desiring to act deceitfully, [conceived] a thousand sons.
Then, assuming the forms of young girls with the luster of collyrium, she commanded them:
"Enter this horse quickly, so that I may no longer be a slave.
They did not comply with those words, and she cursed those serpents.
"While a snake-sacrifice is being performed, the fire shall consume you all at the sacrifice of the wise royal sage Janamejaya, the descendant of Pāṇḍu. The Grandfather himself heard this curse.
Indeed, because Kadrū had made an exceedingly cruel request,
all the hosts of gods,
out of a desire for the welfare of their subjects and observing the great number of serpents, approved those words.
For these venomous serpents are of fierce power and great strength; indeed,
because of their sharp poison, it is for the welfare of all creatures that a measured amount of this was prepared for them, even though they are prone to inflicting harm upon others.
"Furthermore, for those other beings who are constantly intent on fault-finding, the punishment of death shall be inflicted by fate. Having spoken thus, the god then honored Kadrū.

Having summoned Kaśyapa, the god spoke these words: "O sinless one, O scorcher of foes, these venomous serpents with great coils, who were born from you, have been cursed by their mother with virulent poison."
"In this matter, my dear son, you must not feel any resentment whatsoever;
for this ancient destruction of the serpents at the sacrifice has already been witnessed.
Having spoken thus, the God who created the universe appeased that Prajāpati.
He bestowed the knowledge of neutralizing poison upon the high-souled Kāśyapa. O best of the twice-born, when the Nāgas had been thus cursed by Kadrū,
Karkoṭaka, agitated by her curse, spoke to Kadrū.

Then, filled with supreme joy, that best of serpents entered his mother’s preeminent horse; having become a colt with the luster of collyrium, he said, "I shall reveal myself there; have confidence as you wish."
"So be it," the illustrious lady replied to her son.
Sūta said:
Then, when the night had passed and the sun had risen at dawn...

O ascetic, Kadrū and Vinatā were sisters; at that time, they were both indignant and highly agitated after having made a wager regarding servitude. [They went] to the far shore of the ocean, adorned with forest groves on its edge.
They went to see the horse Ucchaiḥśravas nearby;
there they beheld the ocean,
the reservoir of waters— vast, bottomless, agitated, and roaring with a great sound.
It was crowded with *timiṃgila* fish and likewise filled with *makaras*,
and it was teeming with many thousands of beings of various forms,
as well as other terrifying, deformed, and dreadful aquatic creatures.
It is eternally unassailable by fierce beings, teeming with tortoises and crocodiles;
it is a mine of all jewels, the abode of Varuṇa,
the delightful dwelling of the nāgas, and the supreme lord of rivers.
The ocean is the abode of the subterranean fire, the prison of the asuras,
and a source of terror to all living beings;
yet it is the auspicious, divine repository of the immortals and the supreme mine of nectar.
Immeasurable and inconceivable, with its wonderful waters of great merit; terrible, with the fierce cries of aquatic creatures and a terrifying roar;
thick with deep whirlpools, it strikes fear into all living beings.
Moving with the wind on its shores like a swing, it was stirred up by agitation and turbulence; with its moving hands of waves, it seemed to dance in every direction,
difficult to approach due to its surging billows that rose and fell with the waxing and waning of the moon.
The birth of Pāñcajanya, the unsurpassed mine of jewels,
[was described] by the Blessed One, Govinda of immeasurable splendor,
who, assuming the form of a boar, agitated the waters of the ocean until they were turbid.
And by the Brahmarṣi Atri, performing austerities for a hundred years,
the bottomless and imperishable depths of Pātāla were reached;
as was the state of the Yogic sleep of the Lotus-navelled One (Viṣṇu).
The sleep of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor at the beginning of the Yuga;
the bestower of fearlessness upon Maināka, who was terrified by the falling of the thunderbolt;
and the ultimate refuge for the Asuras afflicted by the tumultuous battle.
The auspicious lord of rivers, whose waters serve as a sacrificial offering for the blazing fire of the Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha),
is vast, shoreless, immeasurable,
and flows with thousands of great rivers as if in emulation.
They beheld the great ocean being incessantly filled, overflowing to an extreme degree as if dancing with its waves— deep and teeming with formidable whales and sea-monsters.
They beheld that vast, bottomless, and infinite reservoir of waters, roaring with the fierce sounds of aquatic creatures and as expansive as the sky.
Thus, that ocean— crowded with large fish, crocodiles,
and waves, deep, expansive, and bright as the sky, illuminated by the flames of the subterranean fire— [was seen].
Seeing them, they then quickly rushed forward.
Sauti said:
O best of the twice-born, having thus made their wager, the two sisters—
Filled with supreme joy, Kadrū and Vinatā, the two daughters of Dakṣa, traveled through the sky to the far shore of the great ocean,
gazing upon the unshakeable sea, the treasury of waters.
It was being violently agitated by a great wind, making a massive roar;
it was crowded with *timiṅgila* fish, covered with *makara* monsters,
and filled with many thousands of various kinds of creatures.
Terrible, formidable, unassailable, profound, and exceedingly fearsome;
the source of all jewels and the abode of Varuṇa,
as well as the dwelling place of the Nāgas, it is the most beautiful lord of rivers.
The abode of the subterranean fire, the dwelling place of the asuras, the refuge of terrifying beings, the inexhaustible treasury of waters,
auspicious, divine, the supreme source of nectar for the immortals.
Immeasurable and inconceivable, it is like a vast reservoir of merit;
filled to the brim by thousands of great rivers from here and there, it seems to dance with its waves.
Sūta said:
Having reached an agreement that those words must be carried out, the snakes declared:
"A mother who has failed to fulfill her desires shall indeed burn without affection."
"Once she is pleased, that beautiful woman will release us from that curse. We shall undoubtedly make Kṛṣṇa the tail of the horse.
Having spoken thus, they went and remained upon his tail like hairs.
In the meantime, while those two co-wives were thus wagering,
Kadrū, together with Vinatā, having crossed that ocean,
descended near the horse as if she had been traveling swiftly for no long time.
Then those two beheld that best of horses, possessed of great speed,
with a tail as dark as the rays of the moon; and they observed the many black hairs gathered together at its end.
There, Kadru’s face became dejected and she was bowed down on all sides;
seeing the tail of the king of horses, Kṛṣṇa, she was struck with amazement.
With her head cast down and her mind distressed, Kadru fell into a state of servitude.
Kadrū subjected the dejected Vinatā to slavery.
Then, having been defeated by that wager, Vinatā became consumed by grief, having entered into the state of servitude.
In the meantime, when the time had arrived, the immensely radiant Garuḍa, endowed with great being and strength, burst through the egg and was born without his mother,
illuminating all the directions.
Capable of assuming any form at will, moving at will, possessing the vigor of desire, he was a bird-like ranger;
blazing like a mass of fire kindled into a flame, he was exceedingly terrifying.
With tawny eyes made vivid by lightning, his radiance was equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
Suddenly growing large, that bird of massive body took to the sky—
terrible, with a fearsome roar, as fierce as another Aurva fire.
Seeing him, all creatures went for refuge to Vibhāvasu.
Having prostrated themselves before him as he sat there in his universal form, they said to him:
"O Agni, do not increase further; surely you wish to consume us?
For that very great mass of fuel is spreading toward you."
Agni said:
"O destroyers of the Asuras, it is not as you think;
this Garuḍa is powerful and equal to me in his own splendor."
Born with supreme splendor, he increased the joy of Vinatā.
Seeing this mass of radiance, delusion has entered you.
Indeed, this mighty son of Kaśyapa is the destroyer of the Nāgas.
"You are intent on the welfare of the gods and harmful to the Daityas and Rākṣasas;
you should not feel fear here in any way—behold me all together!
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, the gods, together with the hosts of sages, then approached Garuḍa from nearby and praised him with these words:
"You are a seer; you are highly blessed; you are a god, O Lord of Birds!"
You are the Lord, resplendent like the sun; you are our unsurpassed protection. You are the All-pervading One, the Heated One, the Sun, the Supreme Abider, and the Lord of Creatures.
You are Indra, you are the horse-headed one, you are the arrow, and you are the Lord of the World.
You are the lotus-born mouth, you are the Brahmin, and likewise you are Agni and Vāyu;
for you are the Ordainer and the Disposer, you are Viṣṇu, the best of gods;
you are the Great One, the Overcomer, the eternal Immortality, and the Great Glory.
You are the light, you are our desired goal, you are our unsurpassed protection;
you are our constant refuge—how could fear ever come upon us from you?
You are the one possessed of the power of waves, the virtuous one of undaunted spirit.
O you of undiminished fame, you alone are prosperous and difficult to overcome; all austerity and sacred learning are yours,
as are all things both yet to come and already arrived.
You are the supreme one; you illuminate this entire world of moving and unmoving beings, like the sun with its rays,
repeatedly eclipsing the splendor of luminous bodies.
You are the End-maker of all this, both the permanent and the impermanent;
like the sun when it is enraged,
you burn all creatures, O one who possesses the splendor of fire.
Terrifying like a fire risen at the time of universal dissolution, destroying all as it brings about the end of the eon’s cycle—
we have come to the Lord of Birds for refuge.
Having approached the mighty Garuḍa, who possesses great splendor, is free from darkness, ranges through the clouds, is possessed of great strength, moves through the sky,
is both supreme and subordinate, bestows boons, and is invincible in his prowess;
Possessing a radiance equal to fire and the brilliance of lightning,
this entire world is scorched by your power.
O Lord of the World, those traveling in celestial chariots through the sky, filled with fear at your splendor like that of molten gold,
are humbled and forced to take a deviant course.
O Lord, best of birds, you are indeed the son of the compassionate and high-souled sage Kaśyapa; therefore,
do not be angry, but show supreme compassion for the world.
O Lord, attain tranquility; protect us! By the sound of your voice, which is like the crash of a great thunderbolt, the quarters, the sky, the heavens, and this earth [are filled].
O bird, our hearts tremble incessantly;
restrain this body of yours which resembles fire,
for its brilliance is like that of the enraged God of Death.
Having heard this, our steady mind wavers;
be gracious to us who implore you, O Lord of Birds! Be auspicious to us, O Blessed One, and bringer of happiness.
"Protect all the great-souled gods as well.
Thus praised then by the gods together with the hosts of sages, Suparṇa withdrew his own splendor.
Sauti said:
Suparṇa said:
Sauti said.
Ruru said;
Pramati said;
the gods said.
The Grandfather said: Pramati said:
Having heard this and having himself beheld his own body, Suparṇa...
He then proceeded to withdraw his own body from view, thinking:
"May all beings not be terrified by the sight of my body; therefore, I shall withdraw this brilliance that causes such agitation due to its fearsome form."
Then, placing Aruṇa upon his back, that bird— who could travel at will and possessed of the power to assume any form— departed from his father’s home and returned to his mother with supreme joy.

There, that great chariot-warrior of immense splendor, Aruṇa, was stationed facing the eastern direction; for what purpose did the Blessed Sun then intend to burn the worlds, which had already been scorched by the sun's own brilliance?

"O sinless one, what offense has been committed against him by the gods that this wrath has entered him? For when Rāhu was declared by Candra and Āditya to be drinking the nectar, he then established a persistent enmity toward Candra and Āditya."
Then, as the sun was being eclipsed by Rāhu, wrath took possession of him: "This anger of Rāhu, arisen for the sake of the gods, is directed toward me;
may I alone incur this great evil that causes so much misfortune."
Not even a single companion arises for me in my difficult undertakings.
The denizens of heaven, together with the gods, behold me being swallowed up;
therefore, I shall undoubtedly remain here for the destruction of the worlds.
Having thus resolved his mind, the sun indeed went down to the mountain of setting;
then, at the time of midnight, there shall arise a great conflagration, bringing fear to all the world and destroying the three realms.
Then the gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis, approached the Grandfather and said:
"O Blessed One, what is this great and terrifying conflagration that has arisen today?
The sun is not to be seen, and even this night does not shine."
"O Blessed One, now that the sun has risen, how will this come to pass?
This sun is prepared to rise for the destruction of the world;
for as soon as it is seen, it will reduce the worlds to a heap of ashes."
Indeed, a remedy for that has already been ordained:
the learned son of Kaśyapa, renowned as Aruṇa,
possessed of a massive body and great splendor, shall stand before the Sun.
He will act as the charioteer and will take away his splendor;
in this way, there shall be peace for the worlds, for the seers, and for the dwellers of heaven.
Then, commanded by the Grandfather (Brahmā), Aruṇa did all of that.
And the sun rose, enveloped by Aruṇa;
all this has been told to you regarding how wrath entered Sūrya,
and how the lord Aruṇa acted as his charioteer.
"Listen further to another question previously mentioned.
Sūta said:
"Then there was a bird, capable of going wherever it wished, possessed of great heroism and great strength."
He went to his mother’s side, to the further shore of the great ocean,
where Vinatā, having been defeated by that wager, dwelt,
consumed by extreme grief and fallen into the state of a slave.
Then, on one occasion, Kadrū summoned Vinatā— who was inclined toward her presence— into the vicinity of their sons, and at that time spoke these words:
"O blessed lady, there is the abode of the Nāgas, most delightful and beautiful."
"Carry me there, O Vinatā, to a secluded spot within the belly of the ocean. Then Suparṇa’s mother carried that mother of the serpents,
and Garuḍa, impelled by his mother's word, [carried] the pannagas as well.
That bird Vainateya flew all around the sun;
and the serpents, enveloped by the sun’s rays, became faint.
Seeing her sons in that condition, Kadrū then offered praise to Śakra.
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage to you, O slayer of Bala! Homage be to you, O destroyer of Namuci, O thousand-eyed Lord of Śacī!
May you be a raft with water for the serpents scorched by the sun.
"You alone, O best of the immortals, are our supreme protection;
for you, O Purandara, are the lord capable of creating no small amount of water.
You are the cloud, you are the wind, and you are the lightning-fire in the sky."
You are the disperser of the thick clouds; they call you the cloud once again.
You are the incomparable and terrible thunderbolt; you are the resonant rain-cloud.
You alone are the creator of the worlds, and the unconquered destroyer as well.

You are the light of all beings; you are the sun, the source of radiance. You are the great and wondrous being; you are the king, the supreme among gods. You are Viṣṇu, you are the thousand-eyed one; you are the god, the ultimate refuge.
O God, you are all immortality; you are Soma, most highly honored.
You are the muhūrta and the lunar day (tithi); you are indeed the lava and the kṣaṇa. You are the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, as well as the kalā, the kāṣṭhā, and the truṭi.
The years, seasons, months, nights, and days;
you are the supreme earth with its mountains and forests,
as well as the sky with the sun, free from darkness.
Like the great ocean, which contains timis and timiṅgilas, possesses mighty waves,
abounds in makaras, and is the dwelling place of large fish,
you are always worshipped as one of great fame.
With a joyful mind, praised by wise great seers, you drink the soma at the sacrifice,
and you consume the oblations consecrated with the cry of "vaṣaṭ" for the welfare of all beings.
O you of incomparable mass of power, you are constantly worshipped here by the Brahmins for the sake of fruit, and you are praised in the Vedāṅgas;
for your sake, the best of the twice-born are devoted to sacrifice.
They cause one to master the Vedāṅgas through all the Vedas.
Sūta said:
Thus praised then by Kadrū, the Blessed One whose vehicle is green horses—
He commanded the clouds, "Rain down auspicious water," and with masses of dark-blue clouds, he completely covered the entire sky. Those clouds, flashing with lightning, released abundant water.
Roaring excessively at one another as if in the sky, the most wonderful clouds— releasing incomparable water incessantly with great thunderous sounds— seemed to have completely filled the atmosphere.
The sky seemed as if it were dancing, with its many waves of rain-showers;
the firmament became filled with the roar of thundering clouds,
trembling with lightning and wind.
Then, as those clouds rained down a continuous downpour incessantly,
the rays of the moon and sun were lost from view;
at that time, while Indra was raining, the best of the Nāgas rejoiced.
The earth was filled with water on all sides,
and cool, pure water reached down to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
At that time, the earth became covered by numerous waves of water.
01.022.005d Coming to the delightful place together with their mother, the serpents [were there].
01.023.001 Sūta said:
01.023.001* Then the Nāgas were greatly delighted, having been drenched by the streams of water.
Being carried by Suparṇa, they quickly reached that region,
that island— the abode of sea-monsters— constructed by Viśvakarman;
there they beheld the entire formidable expanse, possessing a strength equal to Indra's.
The serpents, accompanied by the *suparṇas*, beheld the enchanting forest,
surrounded on all sides by the waters of the ocean and resounding with the cries of flocks of birds;
it was covered with rows of groves filled with various fruits and flowers.
It was surrounded by delightful palaces as well as lotus ponds,
adorned with various lakes of clear water,
and fanned by holy breezes carrying divine fragrances.
The sky was adorned by even the sandalwood trees,
which, stirred by the wind, were shedding showers of flowers while their fragrance seemed to kiss the air; likewise, it was graced by other trees whose blossoms were scattered by the breeze.
As if showering the serpents dwelling there with rains of flowers and water,
it was holy and heart-gladdening, dear to the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
resounded by swarms of intoxicated bees, and lovely to behold in its form.
Delightful, auspicious, and meritorious, it was enchanting to all people; filled with the songs of various birds, it was lovely and brought great joy to the sons of Kadrū.
Having reached that forest, those serpents sported there with delight.
And they spoke to the immensely powerful Suparṇa, the best of birds:
"Carry us to another island that is most beautiful and possesses abundant water;
for as you fly, O sky-traveler, you behold many delightful regions."
Having reflected, that bird then said to his mother Vinatā:
"O Mother, for what reason must I do what was spoken by the serpents?
And for what purpose do we carry those weak and base snakes?"
Thus addressed by him at that time, Vinatā spoke to her son, the sky-ranger who was endowed with all virtues and possessed of great heroism, strength, and steadfastness. Vinatā said:
"O best of birds, I have become a slave to my ignoble sister,
having entered into a false wager made by the serpents through deception.
Sūta said:
When that reason had been told by his mother, the sky-walker,
distressed by that sorrow, spoke these words to the serpents:
"What, having brought it or having learned it, or what human effort having performed here..."
"O licking ones, tell me the truth so that I may be released from slavery to you.
Having heard him, the serpents said, "Bring the nectar by your power;
then, O sky-goer, there will be your release from slavery."
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by the serpents, Garuḍa then spoke to his mother:
"I am going to fetch the nectar; I wish to know what food I may eat."
Vinatā said:
"O best of the twice-born, in a secluded spot within the belly of the ocean, there is an excellent dwelling of the Niṣādas; the palaces of the Niṣādas are located there."
"Having devoured many thousands of those sinners— those who have lost their worlds, the merciless, and the evil-minded— bring back the nectar.
But you must never, under any circumstances, set your mind on killing a Brahmin."
For a Brāhmaṇa is indestructible by all beings, indeed like fire;
when provoked to anger, a Brāhmaṇa becomes fire, the sun, poison, or a weapon.
It is by such characteristics as these that a Brāhmaṇa is truly regarded by the virtuous.
"O dear one, he must never be killed by you, even when you are provoked to anger. One must never, under any circumstances, commit an injury against Brahmins;
for neither fire nor the sun can reduce them to ashes in such a way, O sinless one."
Just as an enraged Brāhmaṇa of firm vows might act,
you shall recognize that best of the twice-born by these various signs;
for the Brāhmaṇa is proclaimed to be the teacher of all living beings.
"In that case, I shall state the clear reason; listen to it.
The Brahmin is the first-eater among beings, the best of the castes, the father, and the preceptor.
Garuḍa said:
"O Mother, you ought to tell me, who am asking for the reason, so that I may recognize a brahmin by his auspicious marks:
what is the form of a brahmin, O Mother, what is his character, and what is his power?"
"What indeed shines like fire? What indeed has a gentle appearance?
Vinatā said:
"One should recognize a religious student (*brahmacārī*) by his girdle, deerskin, and staff."
Wearing white garments, pure, self-controlled, and adorned with golden earrings,
carrying a bamboo staff, a sacred thread, and a water-pot—
one should recognize a householder by these characteristics.

One should recognize as a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) a Brahmin who is covered with nails and hair, who wears rags, skins, and matted locks, and who is constantly devoted to dwelling in the forest. An ascetic (yati) is one who is shaven-headed, carries a triple staff, wears saffron robes, and holds a water-pot.
"O son, by these characteristics you should recognize those upright Brāhmaṇas.
He who, having reached your throat like a swallowed hook,
would burn like a coal, O son— know him to be a bull among Brāhmaṇas."
Sūta said:
Out of affection for her son, Vinatā spoke these words to him:
"Know that he who cannot be digested within your belly is the best of the twice-born."
Although she knew his incomparable prowess and was endowed with blessings,
Vinatā, being afflicted by supreme sorrow and wronged by the Nāgas, spoke then to Garuḍa out of maternal affection for her son, being both pleased and pained.
"May the Wind-god protect your two wings; may the Moon protect your back, my son.
May Agni protect your head, and may the Sun protect your entire body. And may Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, protect all your limbs."

And I, my son, shall always be devoted to your peace and well-being; seated here, I shall remain ever intent on performing rites for your welfare. Restrained by vows and fasts, I shall come from the world of the gods.
"There will be no doubt regarding this until your return;
travel the path safely, my child, for the successful accomplishment of your purpose.
Then, having heard his mother’s words;
Spreading his wings, he flew up into the sky;
then the powerful one approached the Niṣādas like the great, hungry God of Death at the end of time.
Then, as he was subduing those Niṣādas,
he raised a great cloud of dust that touched the sky and dried up the waters within the belly of the ocean.
Then, agitating the nearby mountains,
the king of birds opened his great mouth, blocking the path of the Niṣādas.
Then, descending with the fierce prowess of a thunderbolt,
he spread his wings and approached the Niṣāda.
Thereupon, the Niṣādas fled away in haste.
The mouth of that eater of serpents was then opened wide to an immense size,
like the sky when birds, being oppressed, fly toward it.
By the thousands, they were bewildered by the dust stirred up by the wind in that forest where the trees were shaken by a great gale;
then the bird, the scorcher of his enemies, opened his mouth.
Then the lord of the sky-dwellers, the mighty one, being hungry and exceedingly restless, gathered together and destroyed those who eat many kinds of fish.
Sūta said:
Having reached his throat along with his wife, the Brahmin,
glowing like a burning ember, spoke to him while remaining in the sky.
"O best of the twice-born, come out quickly from my open mouth;
for a Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed by me, even if he is constantly engaged in sinful deeds.
And how have you come here to this great abode of the Niṣādas?"
"O twice-born one, tell me truly: why are those who perform sacrifices always untouchable?
As Garuḍa was speaking thus, the brahmin addressed him.
The brahmin said:
Having come from the Middle Country, wandering the earth in search of wealth,
he then arrived among the Niṣādas and found pleasure here;
[he obtained] cattle, gold, riches, grain, as well as jars and bracelets.
"O best of birds, those Niṣādas who always act for my benefit constantly provide me with Niṣāda women; here, a beautiful Niṣāda woman became my wife,
and living with her, I have always attained the highest delight."
"This Niṣāda woman is my wife; let her go out with me, and then I shall depart;
otherwise, I will not leave.
Garuḍa said:
"Take even this Niṣāda woman and depart quickly;
save yourself at once before you are consumed by my fiery energy.
Sūta said:

Then that brahmin, accompanied by the Niṣāda woman, departed; and having offered his blessings to Garuḍa, he went to his desired destination. When that brahmin had gone out with his wife, that king of birds—
Spreading his wings, he flew into the sky with the speed of thought.
Then he saw his father; when questioned, he reported it to his father.
That great seer of immeasurable soul spoke to him in accordance with what was right.
"Is all well with you always, my son, regarding your abundant food?
And is there plenty of food for you in the world of men?
Having thus risen and rested, he then approached his father.
The best of birds paid homage to Brahmā, the lord of those who know the Veda.
And when questioned by his father, the powerful and majestic son of Vinatā said with haste: "Where are you going? You ought to tell me."
Garuḍa said:
"My mother is always well, as is my brother, and likewise myself;
yet, dear father, it is not well for me when there is always an abundance of food."
"For I have been dispatched by the serpents and am intent on fetching the Soma;
today I shall indeed bring it for the sake of liberating my mother from her servitude. Furthermore, I have been commanded by my mother: 'Devour the Niṣādas!'"
"And even after eating it by the thousands, I did not reach satiety.
Therefore, O Blessed One, please point out another thing for me to eat,
O Lord, such that having eaten it, I shall be capable of bringing back the nectar."
"01,025.009d *0328_01 Please tell me, sir, what food may be eaten for the sake of dispelling hunger and thirst.
Kaśyapa said:
"01,025.010 *0329_01 This lake is of great merit and is renowned even in the world of the gods."
Where the elephant, with his face turned downward, constantly drags the elder tortoise;
I shall relate to you in due order their entire birth,
and you should understand from me the truth regarding what their dimensions are considered to be.
"Listen, my child, may it be well with you; hear this story that increases dispassion, O bird of ancient lineage, concerning a dispute over the division of wealth between two parents in the past.
There was a great seer named Vibhāvasu who was exceedingly prone to anger."
He had a younger brother named Supratīka, who was a man of great asceticism.
That great sage did not desire to have his wealth held in common with his brother;
instead, Supratīka constantly insisted upon a formal division of the property.
Then his brother Vibhāvasu said to Supratīka,
"O you of great asceticism, there will be many faults in partitioning;
many people always desire to make a division out of delusion."
Then, divided from one another and deluded by wealth, they pay no heed to each other.
Then, perceiving them to be fools intent on their own interests, separated by their respective riches, enemies disguised as friends incite them to further discord.
Having perceived them divided, others then fall upon the gaps;
for those who are divided, incomparable destruction quickly ensues.
Therefore, the wise do not praise division.
Thus addressed, Supratīka incessantly proclaimed his share.
Being thus pressed, Vibhāvasu cursed him—
those who are bound by the precepts of their teacher and yet harbor mutual suspicion.
Among them, you too are one who acts with deceit; though you cannot be restrained by those great-souled ones through sowing dissension, since you desire wealth,
therefore, O Supratīka, you shall obtain the state of an elephant.
Thus cursed, Supratīka then spoke to Vibhāvasu:
"You too shall become a tortoise dwelling within the water.
In this way, through their mutual cursing, those two—Supratīka and Vibhāvasu—were transformed.
Having become an elephant and a tortoise for the sake of wealth, those two of deluded mind,
through the persistence of the fault of anger, were born even into the animal realm; there,
intoxicated by their size and strength, they took delight in mutual hatred.
In this lake there are two large-bodied creatures who follow their former enmity.
One of them, a majestic great elephant, is approaching;
by the sound of his trumpeting, even the tortoise dwelling within the water [is alerted].

Rising up, that massive-bodied creature agitated the entire lake. Seeing him, this powerful elephant fell into the water with his trunk coiled, using the force of his tusks, the tip of his trunk, his tail, and his feet.

As he agitated that lake, which was teeming with many fish, the powerful tortoise also rose up with his head uplifted and advanced for battle. The elephant stood six yojanas high and twice that length.
The tortoise is three *yojanas* in height and ten *yojanas* in circumference.
These two, intoxicated by battle and each desiring victory over the other,
should quickly employ him and accomplish this desired task of yours.
"Bring that nectar after eating [it], [the elephant] which resembles a great mass of clouds,
which is like a massive mountain, and which possesses a terrifying form.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Garuḍa, the sage then performed an auspicious rite for him:
"May there be prosperity for you as you fight with the gods in battle!
May the full water-pot, the twice-born, the cows, and whatever else is most excellent [bring you luck]."
O bird of great strength, as you fight in battle alongside the gods, there shall be auspiciousness and prosperity for you;
[I shall grant] the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, and the purifying oblations.
"All secrets and all the Vedas shall be your strength. Having been addressed thus by his father, Garuḍa went to the vicinity of that lake;
he saw its pure water, crowded with various birds.
At that very time, those two sages, greedy for wealth,
were born as an elephant and a tortoise and fought with one another.
Hearing those words of his father, Bhīmavega traveled through the sky.
With one claw he seized an elephant and with the other a tortoise;
then that bird soared high into the sky. Reaching Alamba-tīrtha, he approached the celestial trees.

Struck by the wind from his wings, those divine golden trees trembled in fear; "May he not break us," they thought then. Seeing them with their limbs trembling—those sprouts that were the fruits of their desires—[he approached].
The sky-traveler approached other trees of incomparable form—
great, radiant trees surrounded by the waters of the ocean, possessing branches of lapis lazuli and fruits of gold and silver.
In their midst there was a great, most enchanting tree,
a thousand yojanas in height and endowed with many branches;
it was a divine abode for birds, known by the name Rohiṇa-pādapa.
Relying upon whose shade one immediately becomes tranquil—
that exceedingly vast and ancient Rohiṇa tree spoke there to the best of birds as he approached with the speed of thought.
"This great branch of mine extends for a hundred yojanas;
taking hold of this branch, you may eat these two, the elephant and the tortoise. Then [you shall reach] the tree frequented by thousands of birds."
The best of birds, possessing a body like a mountain, swooped down swiftly with great speed, shaking the earth,
and shattered that tree which was covered with dense foliage.
Sūta said:
As soon as she was touched by the feet of the mighty Garuḍa, that branch of the tree broke; and he supported it once it was broken.
Smiling as he looked at that great branch which had been broken,
he then saw the Vālakhilyas hanging there with their faces turned downward;
"For the sages are hanging here— let me not kill those seers," he thought.
Seeing those Brahman-sages devoted to austerity hanging there,
as well as the Vaikhānasas hanging head-downward from the branch, he thought,
"This falling fruit might kill them. Then, reflecting thus, he [acted].
Firmly seizing the elephant and the tortoise with his talons,
the mighty Vainateya, the lord of birds, being overcome by fear as they performed their penance,
pursued them out of terror that they might destroy him.
Out of a desire to look upon them, he seized a branch with his beak;
seeing that act of his, which surpassed even the divine, the great seers,
their hearts trembling with wonder, gave the name "Mahākhaga" (Great Bird) to him.
Having encountered this heavy burden, this bird has flown up;
for Garuḍa is the best of winged creatures and the consumer of serpents. Slowly the bird circled about, shattering the mountains.

Thus, accompanied by the elephant and the tortoise, he traversed many lands out of compassion for the Vālakhilyas, yet he found no place to stay. Having reached the inexhaustible Gandhamādana, the best of mountains, he [rested].
There he saw his father Kaśyapa, established in ascetic penance;
and the father also beheld that bird of divine form,
endowed with splendor, heroism, and strength, and possessing the speed of thought and the wind.
Resembling a mountain peak, like the raised staff of Brahmā,
it was inconceivable, unknowable, and a source of terror to all beings;
possessing the power of illusion, it stood like a blazing fire manifest before one's eyes.
Invincible and unconquerable by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas; a shatterer of mountain peaks and a dryer of river waters;
a terrible agitator of the world, appearing like the God of Death himself.
Seeing him arrived, the venerable Kaśyapa then understood his intention and spoke these words:
"Son, do not commit this rash act; do not suffer immediate pain."
"Let not the Vālakhilyas, who subsist on the rays of the sun, consume you in their wrath.
For the sake of his son, Kaśyapa propitiated those Vālakhilyas, who were perfected through asceticism, with these words regarding this matter.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, this undertaking of Garuḍa is for the sake of the welfare of all creatures;
you ought to grant your permission for him to perform this great deed. Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, those sages approached him.
Having left the branch for the sacred Himavat mountain to seek ascetic merit,
when they had departed, the son of Vinatā, his face still entangled in the branch, questioned Kaśyapa regarding his father.
"O Blessed One, where shall I release this tree branch?
May the Blessed One point out to me a place that is avoided by Brahmins.
Thereupon [he pointed to] a mountain devoid of men, its caves blocked by snow.
Kaśyapa told him that it was inaccessible even to the minds of others;
having mentally entered the vast interior of that mountain,
Tārkṣya, the bird, flew toward it with speed, carrying branches, elephants, and tortoises.
Neither a large leather thong nor even a hundred small ones could encircle that branch—
the great branch of a tree which the bird had seized and by which he traveled. Then he arrived at a distance of a hundred thousand *yojanas*.
In no great length of time, Garuḍa, the best of birds,
having gone to that mountain in an instant at his father’s command,
released a massive, resounding branch there.
Struck by the wind from his wings, that king of mountains trembled;
its trees fell away and it released a rain of flowers.
Furthermore, the peaks of that mountain crumbled on all sides.
Adorned with jewels and gold, they beautify the great mountain; and many trees, struck by her branches,
shine with golden blossoms like clouds charged with lightning.
Those trees there, with their golden blossoms further adorned by the minerals of the mountain and suffused by the rays of the sun, shone brilliantly.
Then that best of birds took his stand upon a peak of that mountain.
Garuḍa devoured both of them, the elephant and the tortoise. Having consumed both that tortoise and the elephant, Tārkṣya,
swift as thought, then soared up from the peak of the mountain summit.
Then, omens foreboding fear appeared among the gods.
Indra’s beloved thunderbolt blazed forth, filled with distress. A celestial meteor, accompanied by smoke and flames, fell from the sky.
Likewise, from all sides, the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas,
Sādhyas, Maruts, and whatever other hosts of deities there were,
each rushed toward their respective weapons as they encountered one another.
Never before had such a thing occurred even in the battle between the gods and the asuras;
winds blew with thunderous crashes, meteors fell on every side,
and even the cloudless sky roared with a great sound.
Even he who is the god of the gods rained down blood at that time;
the garlands of the gods withered, and their splendors indeed faded away. Fierce clouds of ill omen poured down copious amounts of blood.
The dust rising from their crowns overwhelmed them;
then Śatakratu, agitated by fear along with the gods and beholding these terrible portents, spoke thus to Bṛhaspati:
"O Blessed One, for what reason have these terrible portents arisen?
For I see no enemy who could overcome us in battle.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Indra, Lord of the Gods, O Śatakratu, due to your transgression and negligence,
a wondrous being has arisen through the ascetic power of the Vālakhilyas—
a son of the sage Kaśyapa and Vinatā, a traveler of the skies."
The powerful one, capable of assuming any form at will, has arrived to seize the Soma;
this bird, the best among the strong, is able to carry off the Soma.
I consider everything possible in him; he would accomplish even what is impossible.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words, Śakra spoke to the guardians of the nectar:
"A bird of great heroism and strength has prepared himself here to seize the Soma."
I am awakening you so that he may not carry it away by force;
taking up the weapons of Varuṇa,
all of you, at my word, must surround the nectar here.
"O heroic gods, protect him!
For his strength is incomparable," Bṛhaspati said to me.
Having heard those words, the gods were struck with wonder and exerted themselves with great effort.
Surrounding the nectar, Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt and performer of a hundred sacrifices, stood there;
those wise ones wore costly armor,
both golden and variegated, adorned with cat's-eye gems.
And upon their limbs were bright and sturdy shields,
and various weapons of terrible form, many thousands of them, with sharp, keen edges and points, all raised aloft.
Some were emitting sparks and flames along with smoke on all sides;
others were adorned, while still others blazed intensely.
Their tips and edges were sharp and keen, capable of cutting through everything like a thunderbolt.
They took up wheels, iron clubs, tridents, and battle-axes;
various sharp spears and stainless swords; maces of terrifying appearance, all assuming the very forms of their own bodies.
Adorned with divine ornaments and wielding those radiant weapons,
those hosts of gods stood resplendent, free from all taint,
possessing incomparable strength, heroism, and splendor.
The gods, who shatter the cities of the asuras, possess minds steadfast in the protection of the nectar of immortality;
they shine with bodies kindled by fire.
Thus the excellent battlefield, occupied by the gods and crowded with hundreds of thousands of iron clubs,
appeared as if it were falling away into the midst of the sky.
It shone, illuminated by the rays of the sun.
Śaunaka said:
"O son of Sūta, what was the offense of Mahendra, and what was his transgression?"
How was Garuḍa born from the ascetic penance of the Vālakhilyas?
And how did he become the son of the twice-born Kaśyapa and the king of birds? How did he become invincible to all beings and incapable of being slain?
"And how did he become one who acts at will, possessed of the power of desire, and a traveler through the sky?
I wish to hear this, if it is recited in the Purāṇas.
Sūta said:
This subject which you ask me about is the domain of the Purāṇa.
Listen, O twice-born one, as I tell you all of this in brief:
concerning Prajāpati Kaśyapa when he was performing sacrifice, desiring a son.
The sages, gods, and gandharvas indeed granted their assistance. There, Śakra was appointed by Kaśyapa to bring the sacrificial fuel,
along with the Vālakhilya munis and other hosts of deities.

But Śakra, the lord, lifted up a load of fuel as massive as a mountain, commensurate with his own prowess, and brought it along as if without any great effort. Then he saw the rishis, who were so small that their bellies and finger-joints were no larger than a thumb.

On the road, they saw those whose wealth was their asceticism— emaciated, abstaining from food, and of feeble strength— carrying a single palāśa stalk between them, appearing as if dissolved into their own limbs, sinking in a puddle of water within a cow’s footprint.

Puraṃdara, filled with pride and intoxicated by his own prowess, laughed at them all and quickly passed them by, leaping over and disregarding them. Then they were overcome with rage and became exceedingly indignant.

Then they began that great undertaking, which inspired fear even in Śakra. Those sages of great austerity offered oblations into the sacrificial fire according to the prescribed rites; hear now the purpose for which those Brahmins used various mantras.
Possessing the vigor of desire and moving at will, he struck fear into the king of the gods;
for those of firm vows thought that another Indra might become the lord of all the deities.
In both valor and prowess, he was a hundred times superior to Indra, possessing the speed of thought.
"By the fruit of our asceticism, let him today become fierce!
Having understood this, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, deeply distressed,
went for refuge to Kaśyapa, who was firm in his vows.
Having heard those words of the king of the gods, Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures (prajāpati),
then approached the Vālakhilyas and asked about the success of their ritual performance. Kaśyapa.
"O Vālakhilyas,
with what purpose has this sacrificial rite been undertaken by you?
Tell me exactly as it is, for I have a great curiosity to hear it."

O Kāśyapa, he undertook that undertaking according to the prescribed rule for the purpose of thwarting him— the foolish Indra of the gods, whose intellect was unrefined, who was intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty, and who had cast aside all righteous conduct.
"So be it," they replied to him, being speakers of truth.
To them, Kaśyapa, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), spoke these words with conciliation:
"This Indra has been appointed over the three worlds by the command of Brahmā."
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, you too must exert yourselves for the sake of Indra. O most excellent beings, you ought not to make the word of Brahmā false;
nor is this resolve of mine, which I intend to carry out, false for you."
"Let this one, possessed of exceeding strength and courage, be the Indra of the winged creatures;
let a favor also be granted to the King of the Gods who makes this request.
Thus addressed by Kaśyapa, the Vālakhilyas, whose wealth was their asceticism, [consented].
Having honored Prajāpati, the best of sages, they replied:
"O Prajāpati, this undertaking of all of us is for the sake of Indra;
