and this undertaking of yours is likewise desired for the sake of offspring."
"Please accept this fruitful deed of mine,
and act herein in such a way that you perceive what is for your own welfare.
At that very moment, however, the auspicious goddess Dākṣāyaṇī appeared.
The auspicious and illustrious Vinatā, desiring sons,
having performed austerities and being devoted to her vows, bathed and purified herself for the *puṃsavana* rite;
she approached her husband, and Kaśyapa then spoke to her.
"O Goddess, this undertaking of yours shall be fruitful;
you will give birth to two sons, heroes who will be lords of the three worlds. Through the ascetic power of the Vālakhilyas, they shall likewise be born from my own resolve."
"Your two sons shall be highly fortunate and honored by the world. Then the Blessed One, the son of Marīci, spoke to her once again: "Let this embryo of great promise be maintained with vigilance."
"One among all winged creatures shall exercise the sovereignty of Indra;
he shall be a hero honored by the world, a bird of irresistible power.
Then Prajāpati, being well-pleased, spoke to Śatakratu.
"These two birds shall become your brothers as your companions;
no harm shall come to you from them, O Purandara. Let your distress depart, O Śakra; you yourself shall become Indra."
"Furthermore, you must never again thus revile those who discourse on Brahman; out of pride, you must not treat with contempt those whose speech is poison and who are prone to great wrath.
Having been addressed in this way, Indra departed for Triviṣṭapa, free from all doubt.
Vinatā, her purpose accomplished, was then filled with joy;
she gave birth to two sons, Aruṇa and Garuḍa.
Of these two, Aruṇa was the one who preceded the Sun.
Among the winged creatures, Garuḍa was consecrated as their Indra.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, hear now of his very great deed.
Sūta said:
Then, O best of the twice-born, when that [host] had thus risen up,
Garuḍa, the king of birds, swiftly arrived before the gods. Seeing him of such exceeding strength, they trembled on all sides.
They struck one another with all kinds of weapons;
there stood the protector of Soma, the son of Bhuvana, of immeasurable soul, possessed of great heroism, and radiant like lightning and fire.
Wounded by that lord of birds with his wings, beak, and talons,
and having fought an incomparable battle for a moment, he was slain in combat; meanwhile,
the sky-ranger raised a vast cloud of dust with the wind of his wings.
Having rendered the worlds devoid of light, he scattered that dust over the gods. Covered by that dust, the gods fell into a state of delusion;
shrouded by the dust, the guardians of the nectar could not see him.
Thus did Garuḍa agitate the abode of the three heavens;
with blows from his wings and beak, he tore apart the gods.
Then the thousand-eyed god quickly urged Vāyu.
"O Māruta, scatter this rain of dust; this is your task.
Then the powerful Vāyu swiftly blew away that dust. When the darkness had vanished, the gods assailed Śakuni.
The powerful bird, whose roar was like that of a great cloud, cried out loudly;
being struck by the hosts of gods, he, the king of birds and slayer of enemy heroes, possessed of great valor, flew up, terrifying all living beings.
Having leapt up and stationed himself in the sky above the gods, he stood there;
then all the armored deities, together with Vāsava, showered him from every side with various weapons— spears, iron clubs, pikes, and maces.
Being struck from all sides by flaming discuses with razor-sharp edges resembling the sun, and by the discharge of various weapons,
the king of birds did not waver, even while engaging in a most tumultuous battle.
Roaring as it were in the sky like the powerful Vainateya,
he scattered the gods on all sides with his two wings and his breast.
Thus scattered and tormented by Garuḍa, those gods then fled away.

Wounded by the tips of his claws, they bled profusely. Oppressed by the lord of birds, the Sādhyas departed toward the east along with the Gandharvas, and the Vasus went to the southern quarter together with the Rudras.
The Ādityas and the Nāsatyas looked again and again toward the western quarter and the northern quarter as they fought the one of great energy,
along with the heroic Aśvakranda and the bird Renuka.
By the heroic Balāka, by Ghasa and Praghasa,
by the heroic Krathana, and by Tapan the sky-ranger;
by the heroic Suparṇa and by Śvasana, the king of birds.
He engaged in combat with Ulūka, Śvasana, the bird Nimeṣa, Praruja, and Pralīha;
the son of Vinatā tore them apart with his wings, claws, and the tips of his beak.
At the end of the age, like the mighty Pinākin when enraged, he—
possessing great heroism and great energy— wounded them in many ways;
resembling dense clouds, they shone as they rained down torrents of blood.
Having rendered them all lifeless, that best of birds moved forward for the sake of the nectar and beheld a fire on all sides,
enveloping the entire sky with its great flames and radiant rays.
Like the fierce sun with its sharp rays, as if burning, impelled by the wind,
touching the sky with its flames, and terrifying to all living beings—
then, with ninety times ninety mouths;
Having acted thus, the powerful and high-souled bird Garuḍa made a thousand mouths for the sake of destroying the fire that was joined with the river.
With those great splendors and his armies,
the Great-Souled One extinguished that blazing fire by drinking up the rivers with those very mouths.
Having returned with great speed,
that scorcher of enemies, the bird, again covered the blazing fire with rivers by means of his wings.
Then, desiring to enter the fire, he extinguished it and assumed another, smaller form.
Sūta said:
Having become like Jāmbūnada gold, blazing with a mass of rays,
the bird entered by force like the surge of water into the ocean.
Near the nectar, he beheld a discus with edges as sharp as razors.

That extremely terrible machine, well-constructed by the gods, was made of iron with sharp edges, revolving incessantly, possessing the fierce brilliance of a blazing sun, and intended for the cutting down of those who would seize the Soma.
Seeing that opening, the sky-goer turned back;
contracting his limbs in an instant, he rushed through the space between the spokes.
And there, beneath the wheel, were two [beings] possessing a splendor like blazing fire.

He beheld two supreme serpents for the protection of the nectar— two beings with tongues like lightning, most terrible, with flaming mouths and blazing eyes, possessing venom in their gaze, of great prowess, eternally wrathful, and full of speed.
Seeing those two, whose eyes were always bloodshot and whose glances were ever unblinking, the son of Vinatā was suddenly overcome with distress:
"How are these two of great prowess, who feed upon tigers, to be conquered?"

Having reflected thus, Garuḍa quickly deprived those two of their vision; whichever of them even one looked upon would instantly be reduced to ashes. Suparṇa then swiftly covered their eyes with dust.
Not seeing their forms, he pursued them both from every side;
then Vainateya, moving through the air, alighted upon their bodies and swiftly tore them asunder in the middle, whereupon he rushed toward Soma.
Then the powerful and heroic Vainateya, having uprooted that nectar and shattered the machine, flew upward with great speed;
even before drinking the nectar, the heroic bird swiftly seized it.
The bird went on without weariness, obscuring the radiance of the sun;
then, in the sky, he was met by Viṣṇu, the son of Vinatā,
for Nārāyaṇa was pleased with him because of that act of selflessness.
The imperishable God said to that sky-traveler, "I am the giver of boons. He, moving through the atmosphere, chose [this boon]: "May I remain above you.
And he spoke these words once more to Nārāyaṇa.
"May I be free from old age and free from death, even without the nectar.
"So be it," Viṣṇu said to that son of Vinatā. Having accepted those two boons, Garuḍa spoke to Viṣṇu.

"I shall grant you a boon as well; let the Blessed One choose one too. Kṛṣṇa chose the mighty Garuḍa as his vehicle, and the Blessed One made him his banner, saying to him, "You shall remain stationed above this."
Having said "So be it" to that god Nārāyaṇa, the bird,
possessing great speed, departed with force and velocity, as if competing with the wind.
The bird replied "So be it" to the eternal Lord.
At that very moment, however, the Lord Indra, whose vehicle is the green horse,
pursued the bird and struck the enemy of the gods— the one who was forcibly carrying away the nectar— with his thunderbolt upon his body.
To Indra in that cry of distress, Garuḍa, the best of winged creatures,
spoke while laughing with gentle words, even though he was struck by the thunderbolt:
"I shall show honor to the sage from whose bones the thunderbolt was produced."
"O Śatakratu, I shall create both for the thunderbolt and for you;
I shall cast off a single feather such that you shall not find its end.
From the tip of that [feather], a peacock was born."
In the middle is Dvivaktrā, the queen of the serpent lords;
at the root is Śatru, the mongoose of the serpents. These three are indeed remembered as the removers of snake venom.
"Indeed, I have never felt pain from the falling of a thunderbolt.
Having spoken thus, the king of birds then released the leaf. Beholding that unsurpassed leaf which had been released by him, [he took it].
Having spoken thus, Garuḍa shed a single feather;
there, all beings, filled with wonder upon beholding that beautiful feather, then said, "May he become Suparṇa."
Having divided the vajra into three parts, it returned indeed to its own place.
Seeing that wonder, the thousand-eyed Purandara,
thinking "This is a great being moving through the sky," spoke.
"I wish to know your strength, which is supreme and unsurpassed;
and I desire eternal friendship with you, O best of birds.
Thus addressed, Garuḍa replied to the Lord of Śacī.
Garuḍa said:
"O God, O Purandara, let there be friendship between you and me as you desire;
however, know that my strength is great and indeed unbearable."

"O best of gods, O Śatakratu, while it is true that the virtuous do not approve of praising one's own power, such self-praise without cause immediately incurs reproach; and even the proclamation of one's own virtues [is likewise censured]."
O Lord of the Earth, when questioned by another, one should speak; but one should not speak out of mere friendship. However, O friend, being asked by you as a friend, I shall speak.

For one should not speak words joined with self-praise without a cause. O Śakra, [I shall lift up] this earth, together with its mountains, forests, and oceans, and you yourself hanging here, with a single feather-vein.
I could carry all the worlds combined—both stationary and moving—without fatigue; know this to be my great strength.
O Lord of Śacī, [I can carry] the eight earths, the nine heavens, and the three oceans.
"If you so desire, I could carry thousands of mountains.
Sūta said:
Having spoken these words, the hero, the best among the illustrious, [the wearer of] the diadem (Arjuna) [replied].
Śaunaka said: The lord Śakra, the king of the gods and benefactor of all beings, spoke thus:
"It is exactly as you have said; everything is possible in you."
"Accept now from me this supreme and eternal friendship.
You have no need for Soma; let my Soma be given to you.
For those to whom you might give this [Soma] would surely cause us harm."
Garuḍa said:
"I am carrying this Soma for a specific reason;
I will not give the Soma to anyone at all to take."
"O Thousand-eyed One, wherever I myself might cast this down,
you should then quickly take it up and carry it away, O Lord of the Thirty-three Gods.
Śakra said:
"O bird, I am pleased by these words that you have spoken here;
O best of birds, accept from me whatever boon you desire.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, he replied as follows, recollecting the sons of Kadrū and remembering the deceitful trickery his mother had employed for the sake of slavery:
"Though I am the lord of all, I shall nevertheless fulfill your request."
"O Śakra, may these mighty serpents become my food. Having said, "So be it," the slayer of the Dānavas then followed him—
the high-souled God of gods, Hari, the Lord of yogins.
He indeed approved all that had been said by Garuḍa;
then the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of the thirty-three gods, spoke these words once more to him:
"I shall take away the Soma once it has been set down."
Then Suparṇa Garuḍa quickly went to his mother Vinatā.
Bowing low in humility, he spoke these words:
"O Mother of auspicious vows, this nectar has been brought by me from the abode of the gods; command me, what shall I do with it?"
"I am well-pleased with this deed of yours, my son;
may you be undecaying, immortal, and dearly beloved by the gods.
Then, being exceedingly joyful, he spoke these words to all the serpents:
"I have brought this nectar; I shall place it upon the *kuśa* grass for you. O serpents, having bathed and performed the auspicious rites, you may then consume it.
This is the very word that was spoken by you all while seated at that time."
"From this day forward, let this mother of mine be my slave;
these words of yours have been carried out by me exactly as spoken. Then, having replied to him, "So be it," the serpents went to bathe.
Śakra, having seized the nectar, returned once more to the third heaven. Then the serpents, seeking the soma, arrived at that place;
they had bathed, performed their prayers, and were joyful, having completed the auspicious rites.
Where this nectar was placed upon a bed of *kuśa* grass,
those who harbored mutual hatred during the rite of consuming the *soma* rushed forward, each crying out, "I first! I first!"
Realizing that it had been stolen and that it was merely a deceptive illusion,
and thinking, "This is the place where Soma stood," the serpents then licked the darbha grass.
By that act, the tongues of the serpents were split in two.
And because they were touched by the nectar, those *darbha* grasses then became purifiers. Thus was that nectar taken away and brought back by him;
and the double-tongued serpents were [subdued] by the high-souled Garuḍa.
The Nāgas, having been deceived and having then abandoned Vinatā,
fell into intense despair due to the power of Garuḍa, O Lord. Thereupon,
Suparṇa was exceedingly delighted.
Having dwelt there in that forest with his mother,
he who feeds on serpents, who is highly honored by birds,
and whose fame is undiminished, brought joy to Vinatā.
The man who always hears this story,
or recites it in an assembly of the foremost among the twice-born,
shall undoubtedly go to heaven as a partaker of merit.
By the glorification of the Great-Souled Lord of Birds,
there shall be no danger arising from fire, nor from thieves or kings,
nor from hunger, serpents, vetālas, or piśācas.
In whatever house there may be fear, even if this story were merely written in a book, Garuḍa would remain there;
and that man who remembers it constantly and without sloth—
Then one should worship the form of Garuḍa in the house,
always reciting the mantra "Oṃ Pakṣirāja"; by this,
serpents quickly come under his control.
Śaunaka said:
"O son of a Sūta, you have related the cause of the curse upon the serpents by their mother and also that concerning Vinatā."
01.031.002 The granting of boons by the husband to Kadrū and Vinatā,
as well as the names of those two birds, the sons of Vinatā, have been declared by you. 01.031.003 But you do not recite the names of the serpents, O son of a Sūta.
"O one rich in asceticism, we wish to hear the names of the serpents according to their principal ones, for their names are numerous.
Sūta said:
"O one rich in asceticism, because the names of the serpents are so many..."
I shall not mention them all; listen rather to me regarding the principal ones.
Śeṣa was born first, and Vāsuki immediately after him;
then Airāvata, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya.
Kāliya, Maṇināga, and the Nāga Āpūraṇa;
likewise the Nāga Piñjaraka, Elāpatra, and Vāmana; as well as the two Nāgas Nīla and Anīla, and Kalmāṣa and Śabala.
Āryaka, Ādika, the Nāga Śalapotaka, Sumanomukha, Dadhimukha, as well as Vimalapiṇḍaka,
Āpta, Koṭanaka, Śaṅkha, and Vālaśikha.
Niṣṭhyūnaka, Hemaguha, Nahuṣa, Piṅgala, Bāhyakarṇa, Hastipada, Mudgarapiṇḍaka,
as well as Kambala and Aśvatara, and the nāga Kālīyaka.
The two nāgas known as Vṛtta and Saṃvartaka, and the two called Padma; the nāga Śaṅkhanaka, and likewise another, Sphaṇḍaka;
the great nāga Kṣemaka, and the nāga Piṇḍāraka.
Through his contempt for the Brahmin, Śakra caused the mother’s serpents to fall into calamity;
yet Suparṇa, out of affection for both, remained even above Hari.
Karavīra, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, Eḷaka, and Bilvapāṇḍuka [were the names of those serpents].
Mūṣakāda, Śaṅkhaśiras, Pūrṇadaṃṣṭra, Haridraka, Aparājita, Jyotika, the serpent Śrīvaḥ,
as well as Kauravya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Puṣkara, and Śalyaka.
Viraja, Subāhu, the vigorous Śālipiṇḍa,
Hastibhadra, Piṭharaka, Mukhara, Koṇavāsana,
Kuñjara, Kurara, as well as Nāga and Prabhākara.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Tittiri, and likewise Halika; Sumukha, Vimukha, and also Vimukha and Asimukha;
the great nāga Kardama and the nāga Bahumūlaka.
Karkara and Akarkara, as well as Kuṇḍodara and Mahodara—
these, O best of the twice-born, are the nāgas who have been proclaimed by way of their principal names;
others have not been mentioned because of the vastness of their names.
O best of the twice-born, considering that their progeny and the continuation of that progeny are innumerable, I do not name them;
for here there are many thousands, millions, and billions.
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, it is impossible even to count the number of serpents.
Śaunaka said:
"O dear one, these serpents were indeed born powerful and difficult to approach."
Having understood that curse, what did they do next?
O son of a Sūta, what counsel did those serpents have,
and what actions did those best of snakes perform as a result of the curse?
"And what did Vāsuki, the lord of the *nāgas* and possessor of great wisdom, do?
Sūta said:
"But among them, the illustrious and highly renowned Lord Śeṣa abandoned Kadrū."
Subsisting on air and firm in his vows, he undertook extensive austerities;
having reached Gandhamādana and Badarī, he was devoted to penance at Gokarṇa,
in the Puṣkara forest, and likewise on the slopes of the Himavat.
In those various meritorious sacred fords and shrines,
he was constantly devoted to solitude, self-restrained, and ever-victorious over his senses;
enduring cold, wind, and heat, he had abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Having fixed his mind on the Dharma during the three daily ablutions,
the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) beheld that lord performing severe austerities,
his flesh, skin, and sinews withered away, wearing matted hair and bark garments.
The Grandfather spoke to Śeṣa, who was performing austerities and was firm in truth:
"What is this that you are doing, Śeṣa? Indeed, bring about the welfare of all creatures.
For you, O sinless one, are scorching those creatures with your intense austerity."
"Tell me freely, Śeṣa, whatever has long resided in your heart.
Śeṣa said:
"Indeed, all my uterine brothers are dull-witted."
I do not wish to dwell with them; therefore, may you grant me your permission. They are constantly jealous of one another like enemies;
therefore, I shall undertake ascetic penance so that I may not see them again.
They constantly cannot endure Vinatā and her son;
furthermore, O Grandfather, our other brother Vainateya is there,
and they hate him exceedingly, though he is possessed of great strength.
"By virtue of the boon granted by my high-souled father Kaśyapa,
I shall now apply myself to asceticism and cast off this body,
so that even in the state after death, there may be no further union with them."
To Śeṣa, who was speaking thus, the Grandfather spoke.
Brahmā said:
"I know, O Śeṣa, the conduct of all your brothers."
"O serpent, there will indeed be great danger for your brothers due to their mother's transgression;
however, a remedy for this has already been provided previously.
You should not grieve for all your brothers."
"O mighty one, because you have been addressed by your mother with that most terrible curse,
choose from me whatever boon you desire;
for I wish to grant you a boon today, as my affection for you is supreme."
"By good fortune, O best of serpents, your mind has been fixed upon dharma;
may your intellect become even more firmly established in dharma.
Śeṣa said:
"O Great-Grandfather, this alone is the boon I desire today:
O Lord, may my intellect delight in dharma, in tranquility, and in austerity.
Brahmā said:
"I am pleased with this self-restraint and tranquility of yours, Śeṣa. However, you must carry out these words at my command for the welfare of all creatures:
[protect] this earth, which is filled with mountains and forests."
O Śeṣa, you must properly support this entire earth, including its oceans and its cities of commerce,
as it trembles; remain so that it may become as immovable as a mountain.
"I grant you another boon indeed, O best of serpents:
you shall support this entire earth upon your head.
Śeṣa said:
Just as the god who grants boons, Prajāpati— the lord of the earth, the lord of beings, and the lord of the world— has said,
so shall I support the earth, remaining immovable.
"O Prajāpati, place it upon my head.
Brahmā said:
"Go down to the earth, O best of serpents."
She herself will provide you an opening.
O Śeṣa, by supporting this earth, you will indeed perform a great service that is dear to me.
Sūta said:
Having agreed, saying "So be it," that lord, the eldest of the foremost of serpents, entered the opening and remained within the earth.
Bearing this goddess Earth upon his head,
she who encompasses the ocean on all sides as her rim;
thus spoke Brahmā.
"You are Śeṣa, O best of nāgas, a god of Dharma,
since you alone, possessing infinite coils, sustain this entire earth by embracing it."
"Just as I am, so is the slayer of Bala.
Sūta said:
"In this manner, the powerful Naga Ananta dwells beneath the earth."
Solely by the command of Brahmā, the all-pervading Lord, the foremost of the immortals, alone sustained the earth;
and then the Grandfather bestowed Suparṇa Vainateya as a companion upon Ananta.
When Ananta had departed, that mighty Vāsuki was consecrated by the Nāgas, just as Vāsava is by the deities.
Sūta said:
Having heard that curse from his mother, Vāsuki, the best of serpents, reflected: "How might this curse not come to pass?
Thereupon, he consulted with all his brothers.
"Those led by Airāvata were devoted to righteousness.
Vāsuki said:
"O sinless ones, this curse has been pronounced exactly as you know it."
"O serpents, let us deliberate and strive for the sake of liberation from that curse;
for while a counteraction exists for all other curses,
there is no liberation for those cursed by their own mother."
But even after propitiating Brahmā, the Lord of the World, those best of serpents did not obtain a boon from Śeṣa for the sake of release from their mother’s curse,
standing as they were before the Imperishable, the Immeasurable, and the Truthful One.
"Upon hearing that I have been cursed, a trembling arises in my heart.
Surely this utterance of total destruction for us is a most terrible curse unleashed by our ill-behaved mother."
For that imperishable god did not forbid her as she was cursing him;
therefore, let us deliberate here upon the welfare of the serpents,
so that it may come to pass for all of us, lest this time should pass us by.
For all of us are indeed wise and discerning;
even as we deliberate, we perceive a means for our liberation,
just as the gods of old perceived the lost fire hidden deep within a cave.
"So that the sacrifice might not take place, or else that it might fail,
for the purpose of destroying the serpents of Janamejaya.
Sūta said:
Having said, "So be it," all those assembled sons of Kadrū,
who were experts in counsel and intellect, made a covenant there,
O best of the twice-born, while those serpents were seated.
Elāpatra, the most eminent among those skilled in mantras and sciences by virtue of his powers, spoke to them.
Some of the *nāgas* there said, "Becoming bulls among the twice-born (*dvijarṣabha*),
let us beg Janamejaya, saying, 'May this sacrifice of yours not take place.'"
But other nāgas there, who considered themselves wise, said:
"We shall all become his highly esteemed ministers;
he will consult us for the determination of policy in all matters."
In this matter, we shall state our intention regarding how the sacrifice may be brought to an end.
Once that king—the best among the wise—has understood our well-considered view, he will clearly ask us for the sake of the sacrifice; and we shall say, "No."
Demonstrating many dreadful faults both in this world and after death through various arguments and reasons, so that such a sacrifice might not take place;
or else, [the words of] whichever officiating priest shall be present at that sacrifice—
"Go to that man who knows the ritual for the snake-sacrifice and is devoted to the king's business and welfare; let some serpent bite him, and he will die.
When that performer of the sacrifice is slain, the sacrifice will not take place."

"And those others who are experts in the snake-sacrifice and shall serve as its officiating priests—all of them we shall bite; thus our purpose will be accomplished. Thereupon, other virtuous serpents deliberated.
This lack of wisdom on your part—that the killing of a Brahmin is not right—is not at all auspicious.
For peace in times of calamity is rooted in the true Dharma;
indeed, the preeminence of unrighteousness would destroy the entire world.

But other Nāgas said, "We shall extinguish the kindled Jātavedas with rain, having become clouds accompanied by lightning. Others, the best of serpents, said, "Or we shall go at night and [destroy] the sacrificial ladles and vessels."
"Let them swiftly seize those who are heedless; thus there shall be an obstacle.
Or let the serpents in that sacrifice, by the hundreds and thousands, bite all the people; thus there will be terror."
"Or rather, let the serpents defile the prepared food with their own urine and excrement, which destroy all that is fit for consumption.
Others there, however, said, "We shall be his officiating priests."
"We shall cause an obstacle to the sacrifice; let the sacrificial fee be given! [Thinking thus, they approached him. Having come under our control, he will do as we desire.
But others there said, "The king is sporting in the water."
"Let us bring him home and bind him; in this way, his intention will not be fulfilled.
But others there, serpents who were doers of good deeds, said:
"Seize him quickly and bite him; in this way, it will be accomplished."
When he is dead, the root of all misfortunes will be severed. This is indeed the final decision, agreed upon by everyone;
O King, whatever you deem appropriate, let it be carried out quickly.
Having spoken thus, they gazed intently at Vāsuki, the lord of the serpents.
And Vāsuki, having reflected, said to those snakes:
"O serpents, this resolve of yours is not considered by me to be final."
"My own opinion is that it does not please any of you snakes at all.
However, what should be arranged here that would be for your benefit?
I believe that propitiating the high-souled Kaśyapa is the best course."
"O serpents, out of affection for my circle of kinsmen and for myself,
my mind knows not what to do with your words; indeed,
I must act in such a way that it may be for your welfare."
"Because of this, I am greatly tormented by the virtues and vices residing within me.
Sūta said:
"Having heard the words of all of them, both in this way and that,"
Having heard the words of Vāsuki, Elāpatra spoke this:
"O best of serpents, this very intention was already shown by me previously; if it is your thought that [the sacrifice] should be abandoned, then let it be so for you as well, O Lord."
"O serpents, let my memory return to me as it pleases; listen, for I shall relate it to you exactly as it happened.
That sacrifice shall no longer be, nor shall there be such a king."
Janamejaya, the son of Pāṇḍu, from whom our great fear arises—
O King, whatever man here is struck down by fate resorts to fate alone; there is no other refuge in that matter.
"O best of serpents, this fear of ours is indeed divine. We must take refuge in destiny alone in this matter; listen to my words.
When the curse was uttered, I heard those words at that time."

O best of serpents, O lords of snakes, having climbed onto his mother’s lap out of fear, the gods cried out, "They are fierce! They are fierce! O Lord, this was for the well-being of the serpents who were scorched by the fire of the pain of that curse.
Overcome by supreme compassion and seeking [a solution], the gods,
afflicted with grief, approached the Grandfather, O one of great splendor;
the gods said:
"O Grandfather, who indeed, having obtained beloved sons, would curse them in this manner—
save for Kadrū of fierce nature, O God of gods, in your presence?
And the words 'So be it' were spoken by you as well, O Grandfather."
"We wish to know the reason why we were not prevented.
Brahmā said:
"There are many serpents who are fierce, of terrible prowess, and full of virulent poison."
Desiring the welfare of all creatures, I did not restrain them at that time.
Those who are venomous, base, evil-doing, and full of virulent poison—
their destruction shall come to pass, but not that of those who walk in righteousness.

And learn that at that time, when the Tathāgata has appeared, there will be a wise and great seer born in the Yāyāvara lineage, by whose cause those serpents shall be liberated from their great terror.
There will be born a son of Jaratkaru, known as Jaratkaru, who is radiant and has his senses subdued.
From that Jaratkaru shall arise a son of great asceticism named Astika,
who at that time shall halt that sacrifice.
01.034.013 Therein shall those serpents who are righteous be liberated.
01.034.014 The gods said:
01.034.014a "O Lord, that Jaratkaru, the foremost of sages, is a man of great asceticism."
"In whose womb will that powerful and high-souled one procreate a son?
Brahmā said:
"A very beautiful maiden was born as the sister of Vāsuki."
Vāsuki, the best of serpents, will give that maiden to him;
and that most excellent of the twice-born shall beget upon her a son who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, bearing the same name as she.
"O gods, that powerful one shall beget a heroic son.
Jaratkāru is indeed the sister of Vāsuki, the king of serpents;
from her he shall have a son who will liberate the Nāgas from their curse."
Elāpatra said:
"So be it," the gods then said to the Grandfather;
having spoken thus, the gods departed, as did that god, the Grandfather.
"O Vāsuki, seeing things in this way, I urge you to bestow upon him your sister, known as Jaratkāru,
who is begging like a mendicant for the sake of pacifying the fear of the Nāgas."
"O sage of excellent vows, this liberation has been heard by me.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, having heard the words of Elāpatra, the Nāgas..."
All, with delighted minds, honored them, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
From that time forward, Vāsuki protected that maiden, his sister Jaratkāru, and attained supreme joy.
Then, as it were, not a very long time passed;
thereafter, all the gods and asuras churned the abode of Varuṇa.
There, the serpent Vāsuki, the best among the strong, became the churning rope.
Having completed that rite,
the gods, together with Vāsuki, approached the Grandfather and said to him:
"O Blessed One, this Vāsuki is suffering greatly, terrified of the curse."
"O Lord, you ought to extract this mental dart from him—
a dart born of his mother's curse— for he desires the welfare of his kinsmen.
Indeed, this king of serpents has always been beneficial to us and a doer of what is pleasing."
"O Lord of Gods, show favor; appease the fever of his mind.
Brahmā said:
"O immortals, these very words were indeed granted by me through my own mind."
"O gods, that which was previously spoken to me by the Naga Elapatra cannot be made otherwise by me: this curse of my mother,
for the mother is the weightiest of all embodied beings."
"Let this lord of serpents act accordingly upon these words, as the time has come;
those who are wicked shall perish, but not those who practice dharma.
That twice-born Jaratkāru has been born, devoted to fierce asceticism."
Let him give his sister Jaratkāru to him at the proper time,
according to those words spoken by the serpent Elāpatra; for what was said for the benefit of the *pannagas* by the gods shall be so, and not otherwise.
Sūta said:
Having then heard these words of the Grandfather,
Vāsuki, the lord of the Nāgas, deluded by the curse, gave instructions to all the serpents.
Then, lifting up his sister toward the seer Jaratkaru, he said,
"O Jaratkaru, [I am] providing many serpents who are ever-vigilant;
when the lord Jaratkaru desires to choose a wife, [let him take one]."
"Having arrived quickly, you must inform me; that will be for our welfare.
Śaunaka said:
"O son of a Sūta, as for what was mentioned by you regarding the name Jaratkāru—"
"I desire to hear from that high-souled sage the reason why this name Jaratkāru is celebrated on earth; you ought to explain the etymology of Jaratkāru to me exactly as it is."
Having heard those words of his, that one of great splendor spoke.
Sūta said:
"They say that *jarā* (old age) is indeed decay, a terrible thing known by the name of *kāru*."
The wise one gradually withered away his body through intense austerity; therefore,
O Brahmin, he is called Jaratkāru, and likewise [the sister] of Vāsuki.
Thus addressed, the righteous Śaunaka then laughed aloud;
addressing Ugraśravas, he said,
"It is well spoken," and Śaunaka spoke.
"I have indeed heard all that was previously spoken; however, I wish to know how Āstīka was born. Having heard those words of his, the Sūta spoke according to the scriptures.
Sūta said: Having instructed all the serpents, Vāsuki, being well-composed,
then raised up his sister toward the ṛṣi Jaratkāru.
Then, after a long time, that wise sage of rigid vows, devoted to asceticism, did not desire a wife; he remained chaste,
intent upon his penance.
Possessed of sacred study and free from fear and fatigue,
that high-souled one wandered over the entire earth,
nor did he desire a wife even in his mind.
Then, when some other time had arrived,
there was a king renowned as Parīkṣit, the sustainer of the Kuru lineage,
who was like the long-armed Pāṇḍu, the foremost of archers on earth.
In former times, his great-grandfather was devoted to hunting; likewise, Parikṣit, the son of Abhimanyu, became famous in the world for piercing deer,
boars, hyenas, and buffaloes.
The lord of the earth roamed about, gathering various other forest products.
Once, having pierced a deer with a straight-knotted arrow,
he took his bow upon his back and pursued it into the dense forest.
For just as the Lord Rudra, having pierced the sacrificial deer in the sky,
pursued it with bow in hand, searching for it here and there;
yet the deer pierced by him did not indeed depart alive from the forest.
"That deer which was wounded and then lost by King Parikṣit was surely a premonitory sign regarding his departure to heaven;
for that lord of the earth was carried far away by that deer."
Exhausted and afflicted by thirst, he approached a sage in the forest who was sitting among the grazing cattle,
consuming the abundant froth of the milk as it issued from the mouths of the calves.
Rushing toward that sage of rigid vows with speed, the king,
overcome by hunger and fatigue, raised his bow and asked him:
"O Brahmana, I am King Parikshit, the son of Abhimanyu."
"A deer pierced by me has vanished; have you perhaps seen it?
The sage, established in a vow of silence, said nothing at all to him.
Enraged, the king fastened a dead snake upon his shoulder.
Lifting him up with the tip of his bow, he gazed at him,
yet he said nothing to him, whether good or bad.
The king, casting off his anger and feeling distressed, [beheld] him who had thus come.
Having seen him, the sage departed for the city, yet he remained there just as before;
for that great muni, whose nature was forbearance, did not provoke or overcome that tiger among kings, who was devoted to his own duty, even though he had been insulted.
For that tiger among kings did not know him to be so devoted to dharma; therefore, O best of the Bharatas, he insulted him. His son was young, possessed of fierce energy, and a great ascetic.

Named Śṛṅgin, he was possessed of great wrath, difficult to appease, and observed a strict vow. At every appropriate time, being well-restrained, he would attend upon the supreme lord Brahmā, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Permitted by that Brahmā, he returned home;
there, while playing and laughing, a friend said to him:
"The son of the Ṛṣi is exceedingly impetuous and irascible, truly like poison."
O best of the twice-born, having heard what was spoken by the son of the seer, Kṛśa, for the sake of a joke regarding his father, he gave way to anger:
"Your father is as full of splendor as he is an ascetic."

"You carry a corpse upon your shoulder; O horned one, do not be arrogant. While the sons of the sages are speaking, do not utter a single word against us—against those like us who are perfected, knowers of Brahman, and practitioners of austerity."
Where is your pride as a man, and where are those words born of arrogance, you who would look upon your father as a corpse-bearer? And that deed of yours was not at all worthy of yourself, O son.
"O best of sages, that which has been done by you has caused me extreme suffering.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, the radiant Śṛṅgin was filled with anger.
Hearing that his father had died while carrying water, he was consumed with grief.
Seeing him so emaciated, [the sage] uttered kind words and asked: "How is it that my father, who used to carry water for me, has died today?"
With undistracted mind, he constantly gratified the god Viṣṇu;
subsisting always on forest food, the sage remained steadfast in the vow of silence.
Such was that radiant one, who today has become my bearer of death.
Kṛśa said:
"O dear one, while King Parikṣit was wandering about on a hunt today,
a snake was placed by him upon the shoulder of your father, and he died."
Śṛṅgin said:
"O Kṛśa, tell me truly what wrong my father did to that evil-minded king; behold the power of my asceticism!"
Kṛśa said:
That king Parikṣit, the son of Abhimanyu, having gone out on a hunt,
pursued a deer alone after piercing it with a feathered arrow.

While wandering in that great forest, the king did not see the deer; however, upon seeing your father standing there like a pillar, though he remained silent, the king— afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue— questioned him.
Again and again he asked your father about the lost deer;
yet, being committed to a vow of silence, he did not speak to him at all.
Then the king placed a snake upon his shoulder with the tip of his bow.
"O Śṛṅgin, your father remains there today, likewise restrained by his vows. That king has also returned to his own city, named after the elephant.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the son of the sage stood as if transfixed, gazing toward heaven;
with eyes bloodshot from anger and as if blazing with fury,
he was overcome by wrath and then cursed the king.
Having touched water for purification, the radiant Śṛṅgin, impelled by the force of his anger,
said:
"He who [acted] thus toward my aged father while he was in such a state of distress..."
Upon the shoulder of the king, that sinful monarch, Takṣaka—
the best of serpents, a venomous snake of fierce splendor— discharged a dead serpent, being impelled by the power of my words and filled with extreme rage toward that wicked man.
Within seven nights from now, the leader shall go toward the abode of Yama—
the scorner of the twice-born and the bringer of infamy to the Kurus;
otherwise, even Takṣaka himself shall depart for the mansion of Yama.
Sūta said:
Having thus cursed the king, the enraged Śṛṅgin approached his father,
who was sitting in that very pasture, carrying a corpse-serpent.
Beholding his father with that dead serpent upon his shoulder,
Śṛṅgin was once again overcome with rage;
shedding tears from grief, he spoke thus to his father:
"O dear one, having heard of this insult to you by that evil-minded King Parīkṣit,
I cursed that monarch in my wrath, saying:
'May that lowest of the Kuru lineage deserve a terrible curse such as this.'"
"On the seventh day, Takṣaka, the best of serpents, will lead that wicked man to the most dreadful abode of Vaivasvata. To him,
who was thus filled with wrath, his father spoke, O Brahmin:
"Dear son, you have not done what is pleasing to me; this is not the dharma of ascetics.
An ascetic who is unable to conquer desire, anger, and likewise greed—being one whose wisdom is unrefined—he certainly goes to hell."
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to one’s own ruin—
namely, lust, anger, and greed— one should therefore abandon these three.
For he who, having taken up the life of renunciation, does not become a master of his senses [is lost].
For thousands of millions of years, he will certainly go to hell.
We dwell within the realm of that lord of men;
since we have been protected by him in accordance with justice, I do not approve of his sin.
"O son, a king who conducts himself in every way must always be forgiven by those such as us; for there is no doubt that dharma, when violated, destroys.
If the king did not provide protection, we would surely suffer the greatest affliction."
"O son, we would not be able to practice dharma at our ease if we were being guarded by kings who look to the scriptures, my dear. Protected by them,
we practice extensive dharma, and according to the law, they have a share in that merit."
Indeed, a king who conducts himself in every way must certainly be forgiven;
Parīkṣit, moreover, especially so, just as his great-grandfather was.
Just as a king must protect his subjects, so does he protect us.
Therefore, having been hungry and exhausted today,
this ascetic undoubtedly committed this act without knowing of this vow;
for in a kingdom without a king, evils indeed always arise.
When the world is constantly rebellious, the king indeed governs it with punishment; from that punishment arises great fear, and then peace is produced.
One who is not agitated practices the Dharma; one who is not agitated performs their duties.
By the king, Dharma is established; from Dharma, heaven is established.
All sacrificial rites depend on the king; from sacrifice, the gods are established. From the gods, rain proceeds; from rain, it is taught that medicinal herbs arise.

Constantly maintaining what is beneficial for human beings from medicinal herbs, he who is the sustainer of men and the king who establishes the kingdom is equal to ten Vedic scholars; thus Manu has declared.
Therefore, this evil deed was committed by you out of childishness and impulsiveness.
For a king, my son, does not deserve a curse from us in any way;
yet, by casting a curse out of anger, you have suffered an unsurpassed loss of ascetic merit.
O dear one, since you have purified yourself through acceptance [of this knowledge] just as a brahmin is purified by receiving gifts,
I therefore speak to you so that no curse may befall Parikṣit, O illustrious one of firm vows; act accordingly.
Śṛṅgin said:
"O dear one, whether this was an act of rashness, or an evil deed committed,
or whether it was pleasing or displeasing to you, the word spoken by me has not been uttered in vain."
"O father, this shall not be otherwise; this I tell you. I do not speak falsely even in jest, so how much less when pronouncing a curse?
Śamīka said:
"I know you, my son, to be of fierce power and likewise truthful in speech;
for never before have you spoken an untruth, so this shall not prove false. Indeed, even when he has reached maturity, a son must always be instructed by his father."
Just as one might become endowed with virtues and attain great fame,
how much more so for you, O Lord, who have been purified by asceticism even from childhood?
For the anger of high-souled and powerful men increases all the more.
These worlds would perish, yet forgiveness is the remedy for this. Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, I see that you must speak;
considering both your status as my son and your youth, as well as your rashness.
Therefore, becoming endowed with tranquility and subsisting on forest food, wander about having abandoned this anger; in this way you will not abandon the Dharma.
For anger carries away the Dharma of ascetics that has been accumulated through great hardship.
Therefore, for those devoid of Dharma, no desirable destination exists.
Blessed are those here who possess pure minds and are constantly devoted to Dharma—
men of virtuous and auspicious deeds who desire their own welfare.
For tranquility alone brings about success for those ascetics who are patient;
this world belongs to the patient, and the next world belongs to the patient. Therefore, you should always conduct yourself with a disposition of patience, having conquered your senses.

"Through forgiveness, you shall attain the worlds that are immediately adjacent to those of Brahmā. But as for me, O father, having established myself in tranquility, I shall today do whatever is possible to be done; indeed, I shall now send word to the king."
Then, having summoned his disciple Gauramukha, who was virtuous and endowed with good qualities, he said:
"Go to the king and let this account be told:
'You have been cursed by my son, a mere child of unrefined intellect.'"
"O King, having witnessed this insult from you, I have become indignant.
The charioteer said: Having thus instructed his disciple, that one of noble vows sent him forth.
Filled with compassion for King Parikṣit, that great ascetic,
having inquired after his welfare and delivered his message regarding the matter at hand,
[dismissed] his disciple named Gauramukha, who was virtuous and composed.
Having approached the king, the enhancer of the Kurus, he quickly entered the monarch’s palace after first being announced by the gatekeepers. Then,
that twice-born Gauramukha was honored by the lord of men.
Having fully recovered from his fatigue, he related everything in its entirety to the king—
in the presence of the ministers— the terrible words spoken by Śamīka exactly as they had been said:
"O Indra among kings, there dwells in your territory a man named Śamīka."

O tiger among men, best of the Bharatas, you have deprived that sage— who was supremely righteous, self-controlled, tranquil, and a great ascetic— of his life by striking him with the tip of your bow as he rested upon his shoulder.
Your father endured that deed, but his son did not forgive it; by him you have been cursed today, O king of kings, without your father's knowledge:
"In seven nights, Takṣaka shall indeed become your death."
"There, provide protection," he said again and again;
yet that could not be made otherwise by anyone at all,
for he was unable to restrain his son who was possessed by such wrath.
"Therefore, O King, I have been sent by him who desires your welfare.
Having heard these terrible words, that king, the joy of the Kurus,
a monarch of great asceticism, was consumed with remorse for having committed that sin.
Having heard that the best of sages was then observing a vow of silence,
the king’s mind became once again tormented by grief;
for he perceived the compassionate nature of Śamīka.
Having committed that offense against the sage, he was tormented even more;
for the king, who resembled an immortal, did not grieve so much upon hearing of his own death as he did after performing that deed here.
Then the king dispatched Gauramukha once more,
saying, "May the Blessed One show me further favor.
Having heard these words of the king, the sage Gauramukha then [departed].
Having taken leave of him, he departed swiftly for the hermitage of his preceptor.
As soon as he had gone, King Gauramukha,
with an agitated mind, took counsel together with his ministers.
Having deliberated with his ministers, he who was conversant with the principles of counsel had a single-pillared palace constructed that was well-protected;
and he established there a guard as well as physicians and medicinal herbs.
He settled Brahmins who had mastered the mantras everywhere; remaining there, he, the knower of dharma, protected by his ministers on all sides, performed all the affairs of state.
No one at all could approach that best of kings once he had ascended [the throne];
even the wind blowing there was turned back at the entrance.
But when that seventh day arrived, O best of the twice-born...
The wise Kāśyapa arrived to treat that king,
for he had heard that today Takṣaka, the best of serpents, would send that most excellent of kings to the abode of Yama.
"Thinking, 'I shall make him free from fever after he has been bitten by the lord of serpents;
therein both my purpose and my merit will be fulfilled,' the lord of snakes Takṣaka saw Kāśyapa on the road."
As he was traveling with a focused mind, the lord of serpents, having assumed the form of a twice-born man advanced in years, spoke to that bull among sages, Kāśyapa:
"Where are you going in such haste, and what task do you wish to accomplish?"
Kāśyapa said:
"Today Takṣaka, the best of serpents, shall consume by his fiery energy King Parīkṣit, the subduer of enemies born of the Kuru lineage."

O gentle one, I am going quickly to immediately relieve of his fever that king of immeasurable splendor, the perpetuator of the Pāṇḍava lineage, who has been bitten by that lord of serpents whose radiance is equal to fire.
"I am a Brahmin, honored by the world, who has mastered the science of poisons; by the glance of my preceptor, I am capable of destroying poison. Takṣaka said:
"O Brahmin, I am that Takṣaka; I shall burn that lord of the earth.
Turn back, for you are not capable of treating one bitten by me.
Kāśyapa said:
"O Naga, relying on the power of my knowledge, it was my intention that I would render that king free from fever once he had been bitten by you. Takshaka said:
"If you are able to provide any remedy for what has been bitten by me here,
then, O Kāśyapa, revive this tree bitten by me;
demonstrate whatever supreme power of mantras you possess and exert yourself."
"O best of the twice-born, I shall burn this banyan tree while you look on.
Having been addressed thus by Takṣaka, Kāśyapa spoke again.
Kāśyapa said:
"O lord of serpents,
O snake, I shall restore to life this tree which you consider to have been bitten by you."
"Behold today the power of my mantra; O serpent, [surround] the banyan tree!
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the high-souled Kāśyapa, that lord of serpents...
The best of serpents approached and bit the banyan tree.
O one of great luster, as soon as that tree was bitten by him,
it blazed up on all sides, pervaded by the venom of the poisonous snake.
Having burned that mountain, the Naga spoke again to Kāśyapa:
"O best of the twice-born, exert your effort; restore this lord of the forest to life.
Then [he saw] the tree reduced to ashes by the splendor of the king of the Pannagas.
Having gathered all the ashes, Kāśyapa spoke these words:
"O Lord of Serpents, behold the power of my knowledge regarding this tree;
O serpent, I shall restore it to life while you look on."

Then that venerable and learned Kāśyapa, the best of the twice-born, restored to life by means of his magic power the tree that had been reduced to a heap of ashes. He then caused it to sprout, provided with two leaves.
Seeing that tree— leafy, branched, and possessed of spreading boughs— still alive, the high-souled Kāśyapa said to Takṣaka,
"O Brahmin, this is truly marvelous in you."
"O best of Brahmins, since this poison would destroy me or one like me,
for what purpose do you go there, O rich in asceticism? What desired fruit do you seek to obtain from that best of kings?"
I myself shall grant that to you, even though it is difficult to obtain; yet, O Brahmin, if the lord of men is overcome by a brahmin’s curse and his life is exhausted,
your success despite your efforts would be uncertain.
"Then your blazing fame, renowned throughout the three worlds,
would vanish from here like the sun when its rays have faded.
Kāśyapa said:

"I am going there seeking wealth; O serpent, grant that to me, and then I shall return from my home, O best of serpents. Having indeed taken this [wealth] which you have given, I shall depart, O serpent."
Takṣaka said:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall give you today even more wealth than that which you seek from the king; turn back."
"Your king shall not seize even a fraction of that wealth of yours;
these elephants shall carry it away—the vast amount of gold given by me.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Takṣaka, the wise Kāśyapa, the best of the twice-born and possessed of great splendor, reflected upon the king;
that radiant one, endowed with divine knowledge, then understood the state of that monarch.
Seeing that the life of the son of Pāṇḍu was exhausted, Kāśyapa turned back and said:
"O best of serpents, give me ten *koṭis* of wealth;
I will not go to the king—what use have I for that prince?"
Thus addressed by him, Takṣaka gave him twenty crores of wealth;
having obtained that wealth as he desired from Takṣaka, the best of sages departed from there at his pleasure.
When that great-souled Kāśyapa had departed at that time,
Takṣaka quickly went to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
Then, as he was traveling, Takṣaka heard of the lord of the world.
While he was being diligently protected by mantras, antidotes, and poisons that neutralize venom,
the king then reflected through the application of his illusory power (*māyā-yoga*):
"By what means might I deceive him?"
Then, in the form of an ascetic, that serpent Takṣaka dispatched other serpents to the king, taking with them fruits, leaves, and water. Takṣaka said:
"Go, all of you, with focused minds, to the king on account of this business,
so that you may cause the monarch to accept what is called 'fruit, leaf, and water'.
Sūta said:
Commanded by Takṣaka, those serpents did exactly so;
they presented the king with darbha grass, water, and fruits.
And that powerful lord of kings accepted all of it.
"Having performed their business, you may depart," he said to them.
When those nāgas, disguised in the form of ascetics, had gone,
that lord of men spoke to his ministers and friends.
"May you all indeed eat these delicious fruits in their entirety, brought here by the ascetics along with me.
Then the king, together with his ministers, desired to take the fruits.
Indeed, acting in accordance with that injunction from the words of the seer,
the Naga himself ate whatever fruit had been taken by the king; however, within that very fruit, there was a tiny worm.
O Śaunaka, he was short-statured, with dark eyes and copper-colored skin;
having seized him, that best of kings spoke thus to his ministers:
"The sun is setting; today I have no fear from poison."
"Let that sage be a speaker of truth; let this worm bite me, having indeed become one named Takṣaka, so that [the curse] may be thus avoided.
And those ministers, impelled by time, followed his lead.
Having spoken thus, that lord of kings,
desiring to die and deprived of his senses, quickly placed Kṛmika around his neck and laughed; even as he was laughing, he was completely encircled by the coils of Takṣaka.
Emerging from that fruit, Takṣaka, the lord of serpents, having coiled himself around the king and uttered a great roar, bit the protector of the earth— exactly as had been reported to the king.
Sūta said:
Seeing him thus encircled by the serpent, all the ministers,
their faces pale, wept, overcome with intense grief.
Upon hearing that roar, those ministers fled;
and they beheld a wondrous serpent moving through the sky,
possessing the luster of a lotus and appearing to part the very heavens like a hairline.
Deeply overcome by grief, they [sought] Takṣaka, the best of serpents. Then those hooded snakes saw that house enveloped by fire and blazing with the poison of the serpent.
Out of fear, they fled in all directions;
and it fell like something struck by a thunderbolt.
Then, when the king had been slain by the power of Takṣaka, [the people were overcome].
Then the twice-born royal chaplain, having performed all the funeral rites for the next world while remaining pure,
as did the ministers of that king.
All the city-dwellers, having assembled together, installed his infant son as king;
he whom they call the slayer of enemies was made their monarch.
The people [called] Janamejaya, the hero of the Kurus;
that best of kings, though still a child, possessed a noble mind, and at that time he was together with those ministers and priests.
The eldest of the Kuru bulls ruled the kingdom just as his heroic great-grandfather had done;
then [he installed] the king, the scorcher of his enemies.
Having deliberated upon this, those ministers of the king approached Suvarṇavarman, the lord of Kāśī,
and proceeded to request his daughter Vapuṣṭamā as a bride.
Then that king, having examined her according to dharma, gave Vapuṣṭamā to the hero of the Kurus; and he too,
having obtained her, was filled with joy.
And he never set his mind upon any other woman; with a serene heart, the heroic one wandered through blooming lakes and forests.
Thus that best of kings sported, just as Purūravas did in ancient times after obtaining Urvaśī;
and Vapuṣṭamā likewise then [regarded] her excellent husband.
Having obtained a king of such renowned form,
that beautiful woman of the inner apartments truly delighted him with her affection during their times of recreation.
Sūta said:
At that very time, the great ascetic Jaratkāru,
a sage who made his home wherever evening found him, was wandering over the entire earth.
Practicing a consecration difficult for those of unrefined souls to perform, the one of great splendor wandered about,
bathing in sacred fords and holy places;
subsisting on air and taking no food, the sage withered away day by day.

He saw his ancestors hanging head-downwards in a pit, clinging to a clump of *vīraṇa* grass from which only a single fiber remained; and he saw a rat dwelling in a hole slowly gnawing away at that very fiber.
Approaching those who were without food, emaciated, miserable, distressed in a pit, and seeking protection,
he— himself appearing wretched— addressed those wretched ones:
"Who are you that hang there, clinging to this clump of *vīraṇa* grass?"
The weak grass-stalk has been gnawed at its roots by a hole-dwelling mouse;
even that single root which remains here,
this mouse is gradually devouring with his sharp teeth.
Because only a small portion remains, even this will soon be severed; therefore, you shall fall headlong into this pit. Upon seeing you thus facing downward, grief has arisen within me.
"Having fallen into this painful calamity, what dear service may I do for you?
Speak without delay whether you wish to overcome this misfortune by one-fourth, one-third, or even one-half of this ascetic merit."
"Alternatively, may you all cross over this [ocean] through complete austerity; let my wish be fulfilled in this way.
The ancestors said:
"You are a powerful celibate who desires to protect us here;
yet, O foremost of Brahmins, this cannot be warded off by asceticism alone.
We have, O dear one, the fruit of our asceticism, O best of speakers."

"O Brahmin, through the destruction of our lineage, we shall fall into an impure hell; for the Grandfather has declared that the lineage is indeed the supreme dharma. O dear one, let it not perish here, for knowledge does not manifest to us."
By what means do we not recognize you, whose prowess is renowned in the world? You are prosperous and highly fortunate, yet you [look upon] us who are pitiable and deeply afflicted;
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, why is this so toward us, who are pitiable and deeply afflicted?

"O twice-born one, approach me out of compassion and listen: we are indeed the Yāyāvaras, sages of rigid vows. O Lord, we have fallen from that meritorious world here due to the extinction of our lineage."
Our ascetic merit has perished, for indeed we have no thread remaining. Yet there is one thread left for us today; even that is as if it does not exist.
He was truly the friend of the unfortunate in our lineage.
Known as Jaratkāru, he was a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
self-controlled, high-souled, observant of excellent vows, and a great ascetic.
It was by him that we were brought to this hardship through his greed for the fruits of penance.
"He has no wife, nor son, nor any kinsman whatsoever. Therefore, we hang in this pit like those who have lost their senses and are without a protector.
Having seen us, he must be told by you [to come] for our sake as one who possesses a protector."

"Your ancestors hang in the pit, wretched and with faces turned downward; 'O Lord, please take a wife' and 'Beget offspring,' they cry out. Yet that supreme fruit is not attained even through gifts of woolen blankets."
And that which is obtained in measureless quantity upon obtaining a lineage of wives—
O dear one, all men are indeed born as a cleansing;
for those born of noble caste must support their ancestors, gods, sages, and men.
Otherwise, they would have to be restrained by the inhabitants of heaven.
My dear son, you who know the dharma, understand this correctly; why do you not see it?
For you alone remain as the sole thread of our lineage, O one whose wealth is asceticism.
"O Brahmin, as for this clump of *vīraṇa* grass upon which you see us leaning,
this was the ancestral pillar of our lineage, the increaser of its own kin. And those roots of this plant that you see here, O Brahmin— "
"O dear one, these threads of ours have been consumed by Time;
but this root which you see here, O Brahmin, is half-eaten. We all hang from it, while he alone remains established in austerity."
"O Brahmin, this rat that you see is Time, possessed of great power;
he is gradually wearing away that dull-witted Jaratkaru, who is devoted to asceticism, by gnawing at him— he who is greedy for penance, slow-minded, and lacking in discernment."
"O best of beings, that ascetic merit of ours will certainly not save us—
us who are severed at the root, fallen, our minds destroyed by Time,
and established in hell like evildoers."
When we have fallen here along with our ancestors,
even he will then go to hell, cut down by time.
Whether it be austerity, or sacrifice, or whatever else is a great purifier— [all these shall avail him nothing].
"O dear one, all that does not lead to equality; such is the opinion of the virtuous.
Therefore, O dear one, having seen him, you should speak to the ascetic Jaratkāru, and you must relate this to him exactly as it was seen, without omission."

"O Brahman, you must speak on our behalf for the sake of our protection— just as one would act for the benefit of kinsmen here, and just as one would for his own family— so that he may take a wife and procreate sons."
"O best of beings, who are you that grieves for us as if we were your kinsmen? We all wish to hear: who are you standing here?
Sūta said:
Having heard this, Jaratkāru, overcome by pain and grief,
spoke to his ancestors in sorrow with a voice choked with tears.
Jaratkāru said:

"O venerable ones, you were indeed my ancestors and grandfathers in former times. Tell me what must be done by me out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you. I am that very Jaratkāru, your sinful son."
"01.042.002c Therefore, mete out punishment for this evil deed of mine, who am undisciplined.
The fathers said:
"01.042.003a Son, by good fortune you have arrived at this place by chance."
"And for what purpose, O Brahmin, have you not taken a wife?
For the sake of dharma, artha, and kāma, [those who do] abandon happiness,
wander for alms, and wear rags bound to their bodies."
Those men who have abandoned their wives and wander the earth with throats parched by hunger— O giver of honor,
the worlds in heaven cannot be attained by them even through hundreds of sacrifices.
"Or even those worlds which men with sons have attained through various austerities.
Jaratkāru said:
"O ancestors, this purpose has been constantly revolving in my heart."
"O one whose vital energy is drawn upward, my mind was resolved that I would indeed attain a body in the hereafter and would certainly not take a wife; yet,
having seen you hanging there like birds, [I have changed my mind]."
"O grandfathers, my mind has been turned away from the life of celibacy by me.
I shall do what is pleasing to you as you desire; I will marry, there is no doubt about this—provided that I should ever obtain a maiden who bears the same name as mine."

Whatever woman there may be who, like a mendicant, offers herself of her own accord, I shall accept her; and I shall not support any woman whom I myself must maintain. Such a marriage I would enter into, were I to obtain one.
"O Grandfathers, I shall not act otherwise; this is the truth. Therein shall a being be born for the sake of your deliverance. O Pitṛs, may you remain eternal and immutable."
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to the ancestors, the sage wandered the earth,
yet he did not obtain a wife, O Śaunaka, because people thought, "He is old."
When he had become despondent and was thus urged by his ancestors,
he went to the forest and, being deeply afflicted with grief, cried out loudly.
Having gone to the forest, that wise man, out of a desire for the welfare of his ancestors, [continued his search].
He spoke these three words softly regarding the maiden:
"Whatever beings exist here, whether stationary or moving, and whatever are hidden— let them hear my words."
"My ancestors, afflicted with grief, urge me— who am engaged in fierce asceticism— to settle down; desiring to do what is pleasing to them,
I wander as a beggar for maidens across the entire earth in search of a wife."
"May those beings whose daughters have been proclaimed by me here— who are poor, of a miserable disposition, and appointed by their fathers—
grant their daughters to me as I wander in every direction."
"Give me that maiden of mine who bears my name, who may be offered like alms, and whom I myself shall maintain. Then those serpents who were indeed intent upon Jaratkāru [spoke].
Taking that news, they reported it to Vāsuki. Having heard them, that lord of the Nāgas, the serpent, took the well-adorned maiden and went to the forest into his presence.
There, O Brahmin, the lord of the nāgas, Vāsuki, offered that maiden to that high-souled one like alms; however, he did not accept her,
thinking that she was nameless and that her maintenance had not been considered.
Although he was established in the state of liberation, he became subject to the duality of possession;
then, O descendant of Bhṛgu, he asked for the maiden’s name,
saying, "Vāsuki, I shall not provide her maintenance."
Ruru said:
"O lord of serpents, for what reason was that lotus-eyed sister given by you to a supreme brahmin of perfected self who was indeed unknown?"
Pramati said;
Sūta said:
Vāsuki then spoke these words to the seer Jaratkāru.
"O best of the twice-born, this maiden of mine is your namesake and my sister, endowed with ascetic power. I shall support your wife;
please accept her, O ascetic rich in penance, and I will protect her with all my might."
The sage said:
"O best of supreme sages, she is being protected by me for your sake;
I shall certainly not support her myself, for this is the vow I have made."
"One should not do what is displeasing, and once it has been done, I shall abandon her. Having thus promised to support his sister,
Jaratkaru then went to the abode of the serpent.
There, the best among those who know the mantras, aged in asceticism and firm in his great vows,
that righteous-souled one took her hand in marriage according to the prescribed rites and mantras. Then he entered the bright bedchamber approved by the lord of the serpents.
Being praised by the great seers, he departed taking his wife with him.
There, a bed had been prepared, covered with exquisite rugs;
there Jaratkaru dwelt together with his wife.
There, that best of men made an agreement with his wife:
"You must never do anything displeasing to me, nor ever speak such words. For if you do something unpleasant, I shall abandon you and my residence in your house."
"Accept these words that have been uttered by me. Then that sister of the lord of the nāgas, deeply agitated and overcome with great sorrow, spoke these words to him: "So be it."

In that same manner, the illustrious lady, desiring her husband's welfare, attended upon him who was of a difficult disposition by employing the stratagems of the "white crow" and other such means. Then,
on one occasion, having bathed after her menses, she approached her brother Vāsuki at the proper time.
She approached that great sage, her husband, according to the prescribed rites. There, a fetus was formed within her, resembling a blazing fire,
endowed with extreme ascetic power and possessing a splendor equal to Vaiśvānara.
Just as the moon waxes during the bright fortnight, so too did he [grow].
Then, after a few days had passed, Jaratkāru, the great ascetic,
placed her head upon his lap and fell asleep like one who was utterly exhausted.

While that best of Brahmins was asleep, O Brahmin, the sun went down behind the mountain at the close of day; then that high-minded sister of Vāsuki, fearing a transgression of dharma, began to reflect.

"What would be the better deed for me: waking my husband, or not? For he is a righteous soul of a difficult temperament; how can I avoid offending him? Would it be an act of anger on the part of one whose nature is dharma, or rather a violation of dharma?"
"In this matter, the loss of dharma would surely be more grievous," he thought;
"if I rouse him, he will certainly become angry,
and there will surely be a loss of dharma for him in the neglect of his twilight devotions."
Having thus resolved in her mind, O serpent, Jaratkaru,
who was sweet of speech, then addressed these gentle words to that rishi of blazing asceticism as he lay there like a fire:
"Arise, O illustrious one! The sun is setting. Having touched water and restrained your vows, O Blessed One, perform the twilight worship.
This moment, when the *agnihotra* has been kindled, is both beautiful and formidable."
"O Lord, this twilight is now setting in the western direction.
Thus addressed, the blessed Jaratkaru, a man of great asceticism,
spoke these words with his lips quivering:
"O serpent, this insult has been offered by you to me;
I shall no longer dwell near you, but will depart as I came.
For there is no heat from fire while I am asleep, O lady of beautiful thighs."
"It is my heart's desire that he should depart at the proper time; for who would wish to dwell here once they have been insulted,
much less one of virtuous character like me or someone such as I?"
"Because of this slight, the day has reached its end.
Thus addressed by her husband, Jaratkaru, whose heart was trembling,
spoke there in the dwelling of Vāsuki to her sister.
"I did not wake you out of disrespect;
rather, O Brahmin, I did this so that there would be no lapse in your religious duty.
When he had spoken thus to his wife, the great ascetic Jaratkāru said:
Overcome with anger and desiring to abandon the serpent-woman, the sage said:
"My speech has never uttered a falsehood; O serpent-woman, I shall depart.
For this was the agreement previously made between you and me in private."
"I have lived happily, O blessed lady; you should say to your brother, 'O auspicious one, when I have departed from here, that Blessed One has gone,' O timid one.
And you too, now that I have gone forth, ought not to grieve."
Thus addressed,
Jaratkāru— she of faultless limbs, who was then devoted to anxiety and grief— replied to her husband Jaratkāru with a voice faltering with tears and a parched face.
Then the woman of noble form, her eyes filled with tears, joined her palms in reverence; and though her heart was trembling, that fair-thighed woman summoned her fortitude and said:
"O knower of dharma, you ought not to abandon me, for I am innocent."

O best of the twice-born, she stands firm in dharma, and I too stand firm in dharma; she is always devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial. As for the reason why I am giving her to you, O foremost of brahmins, it is that my brother, out of a desire for the welfare of our kinsmen, intends her for the sake of offspring.
"O best of beings, what will Vāsuki say to me, a dull-witted woman who has failed to obtain [an offspring]? For my kinsmen, who are overwhelmed by their mother’s curse,
desire a child from you, yet such a thing is not yet seen."
"O twice-born one, through the gain of offspring from you, may there be well-being for my kinsmen. Let this union of mine with you not be in vain.
Desiring the welfare of my relatives, O Blessed One, I propitiate you."
"O best of beings, having placed this embryo of unmanifest form within me, how can you,
being a high-souled one, wish to depart, abandoning me who am innocent?
Thus addressed, the sage spoke these words to his wife.
"O Jaratkāru, rich in asceticism, what you have said is fitting;
O blessed lady, this embryo of yours shall indeed be like Vaiśvānara—
a rishi of supreme righteousness whose soul is fixed on dharma and who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas."
Having spoken thus, that righteous-souled great ṛṣi Jaratkāru,
having made his resolve, departed once more for fierce asceticism.
Sūta said:
As soon as her husband had departed, Jaratkāru,
O ascetic, quickly went to her brother and informed him of everything exactly as it had happened.
Then that best of serpents, having heard that most grievous and unpleasant news, [was overcome with sorrow].
Then, even more distressed than his wretched sister, he himself said:
"O blessed lady, you know what must be done and the reason for bestowing [the boon],
so that through it a son might be born to you for the welfare of the serpents."
"That heroic one will surely deliver us from the snake-sacrifice," so my grandfather previously told me along with the gods. "O blessed lady, does that best of sages still have an embryo within you?"
I do not desire that the marriage of that wise man be fruitless.
Although it is not proper for me to ask you such a thing as this,
I have urged you because of the great importance of the matter.
"Knowing that your husband is an ascetic of extreme austerity and his state of being difficult to please,
I shall not follow him, for he might at some point curse me.
O blessed lady, tell me everything regarding your husband's conduct."

"O blessed lady, extract this terrible dart that has long remained in my heart. Having been addressed with these words by Jaratkāru, she replied, consoling the afflicted Vāsuki, the lord of the serpents.
Questioned by me for the sake of offspring, that great-souled one of mighty asceticism replied,
"It is so," pointing toward my womb; and having departed,
he has once again become my brother, his mind tormented by grief.

"O serpent, I do not recall him ever having spoken falsely even in jest; how much less, O King, would he speak so when it concerns the ultimate goal? You should not feel any distress regarding this matter."
"For a son shall be born to you, possessing a radiance equal to the blazing sun.
Having said this to me, O brother, my husband has gone to the forest of asceticism. Therefore, let this great sorrow that dwells in your mind depart.
Having heard this, Vāsuki, the lord of the nāgas, with supreme joy accepted his sister’s words, saying,
"So be it," and honored her with kind words, respect, gifts of wealth, and appropriate hospitality.
The best of serpents honored his uterine sister.
Then that embryo, possessed of great splendor and radiant as the sun, grew,
O best of the twice-born, like the moon risen in the sky during the bright fortnight.

O Brahmin, in due time that sister of the serpent gave birth to a son who shone like the offspring of a god and who dispelled the fear of his father and mother. And he grew up right there in the abode of the king of the Nāgas.
He studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches from Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu; even as a child, he was devoted to his vows and endowed with the qualities of intelligence and goodness,
and his name became renowned throughout the worlds as Āstīka.

Because his father departed for the forest while he was still in the womb, having said "He exists" (asti), he became renowned by the name Astīka. While still a child staying there, that one of immeasurable intelligence wandered about.
In the house of the king of serpents, he was protected with great care,
like the blessed Lord of the Gods, the trident-bearing Hiraṇyada;
as he grew, he brought joy to all those serpents.
01.045.001 Śaunaka said:
Having heard the words of Sūta, the astonished Śaunaka spoke regarding that which King Janamejaya had then asked of his ministers.
"Tell me again in detail that account of my father’s journey to heaven.
Sūta said:
"Listen, O Brāhmaṇa, to how the ministers were questioned by the king at that time."
01.045.002c They all related that death of Parīkṣit. 01.045.003 Janamejaya said:
01.045.003a "But you know exactly how my father met his end."
Having heard from you the entire account of my father’s life and how that highly illustrious man met his end in due time,
I shall surely follow what is auspicious and never what is contrary.
Sūta said:
Then the ministers, who were wise and learned in all duties, being questioned by that high-souled one, spoke these words to King Janamejaya.
Listen, O King, to what you ask concerning the conduct of your high-souled father,
that lord of kings, and how he reached his final end—
he who was righteous, great-souled, and the protector of his subjects.

Listen to how that great-souled one lived here as he did; hear that. Having established the four social orders in their respective duties, the king—who knew the dharma—protected them according to dharma, like Dharma himself in embodied form.
The illustrious one of incomparable prowess protected the goddess Earth;
he had no enemies, nor did he bear malice toward anyone.
Equal toward all beings, he was like Prajāpati himself.
O King, the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras remained well-disposed toward their own duties,
being properly guided by that king;
he also supported widows, the helpless, the miserable, and the infirm.
He was pleasing to behold for all beings, like a second Soma;
he delighted and nourished his people, being illustrious, truthful in speech, and firm in prowess.
Furthermore, that king became a disciple of Śāradvata in the science of archery.
O Janamejaya, your father was dear to Govinda and possessed great fame; he was beloved by the entire world. He was born in Uttara when the Kuru lineage had been greatly diminished.
By him was born the powerful Parikṣit, the son of Saubhadra.
