That king was skilled in the duties, purposes, and principles of royalty; he was endowed with all virtues, had his senses subdued, possessed self-mastery, was wise, and attended upon the elders.

Your father, a master of the sixfold group [of sense objects], possessed of great intelligence, and supreme in his knowledge of policy and dharma, protected these subjects for sixty years; thereafter,
he attained that state from which there is no returning for anyone.
Then, having met his end through a serpent that could not be avoided,
you, O best of men, attained [the kingdom] through righteousness—
this kingdom which has come down through the Kuru lineage for a thousand years.
"Even as a child, you were noble-born and a protector of all beings.
Janamejaya said:
"In this lineage, there has never been a king [who was not so]."
He who does not act for the welfare of his subjects nor is dear to them— especially when he has observed the great conduct of his ancestors, who were devoted to righteous behavior.
"How did my father, who was such as he was, meet his end? Tell me exactly; I wish to hear the truth. Sūta said:
That king, Pṛthivīpāla, the best among all wielders of weapons—
thus urged by the king, all those ministers, who were devoted to the welfare and pleasure of their sovereign, spoke to the lord of men exactly as it had occurred.
O King, your father was always devoted to hunting,
just like the illustrious Pāṇḍu, that foremost of archers in battle;
he entrusted all royal duties to us without exception.
Once, while wandering in the forest, he pierced a deer with a feathered arrow;
having struck it, he pursued that deer swiftly into the dense woods,
on foot, with his sword girt and carrying his bow and quiver.
Your father, sixty years of age, advanced in years, and overcome by decrepitude, though still possessed of vigor, could not find the lost deer in the dense forest; exhausted and hungry,
he beheld a sage nearby in the great wilderness.
That lord of kings questioned the sage who was observing a vow of silence;
yet that sage said nothing at all to him, even though he was being questioned.
Then the king, afflicted by hunger and fatigue, [beheld] that sage standing like a pillar.
Though he was peaceful and observing a vow of silence, [the king] instantly fell under the sway of wrath.
Indeed, the king did not realize that the sage was observing a vow of silence;
thus, your father, possessed by anger, insulted him.
O best of the Bharatas, having lifted a dead snake from the surface of the earth with the tip of his bow, he placed it upon the shoulder of that pure-souled man;
yet that wise one said nothing to him, whether good or ill.
He remained standing just as he was, without becoming angry, carrying the serpent upon his shoulder.
Then the ministers said:
"O Indra among kings, that king [remained] with the serpent upon his shoulder."

Emaciated by hunger, the sage returned once more to his own city. That rishi had a son born of a cow, who was highly illustrious, possessed of great splendor, fierce valor, and an exceedingly irascible nature; his name was Śṛṅgin.
Approaching Brahmā, that sage paid him homage;
having received permission, Śṛṅgin went there and heard from his friend how his father had been thus insulted by your father.
O Janamejaya, tiger among the Kurus, your father once carried upon his shoulder a dead snake that had fastened itself there, though he had done it no harm;
O King, he was then a most eminent sage and an ascetic of great fervor.

He had conquered his senses and was pure, established in wondrous deeds; his soul was illuminated by austerity, and he was likewise restrained in his own limbs. He was of auspicious conduct and auspicious speech, steadfast, and free from greed.
"He is noble-minded, free from malice, aged, established in the vow of silence,
and a refuge for all beings— yet he has been mistreated by your father.
Upon hearing this, he was filled with rage and cursed your father.
The son of the seer, possessed of great splendor, though but a child, was superior even to the elders;
touching water quickly, he spoke these words out of anger,
as if blazing with his own energy, directed toward your father.
"He who has cast a dead snake upon my innocent elder—
him the enraged Naga Takṣaka shall destroy with his fiery power;
that serpent of sharp venom, impelled by the force of my word."
"Within seven nights from now, behold the power of my asceticism over evil!
Having spoken thus, he went to where his father was;
and having seen his father, he reported that curse to him.
And that tiger among sages sent to your father a disciple named Gauramukha, who was virtuous and endowed with excellent qualities. Having rested, he related everything to the king in its entirety.
"You have been cursed by my son; be on your guard, O lord of the earth!
Takṣaka, O great king, will destroy you with his fiery power.
Having heard those terrible words, your father, Janamejaya—
He remained on guard, terrified of Takṣaka, the best of serpents;
then, when that seventh day had arrived,
the Brahman-seer Kāśyapa desired to go into the presence of the king.
Then Takṣaka, the lord of the Nāgas, beheld Kāśyapa.
As he proceeded in haste, that king of the serpents said to Kāśyapa:
"Where are you going so quickly, and what task do you wish to accomplish?"
Kāśyapa said:
"O twice-born one, it is said that in that very place where the king named Parikṣit, the best of the Kurus,
shall be consumed by the serpent Takṣaka."
"I shall go there quickly to immediately render him free from fever;
once he has been protected by me, even a serpent shall not overcome him.
Takṣaka said:
"Why do you wish to revive him who has been bitten by me?
O Brahmin, I am that Takṣaka; behold my wondrous power!
You are not capable of reviving that king once he has been bitten by me."
Having said this, Takṣaka thereupon bit that lord of the forest; as soon as he was bitten by the serpent, the tree was reduced to ashes. Then, O King, Kāśyapa restored that tree to life.
Then Takṣaka tempted him, saying, "State your desire. Being thus addressed, Kāśyapa spoke again to Takṣaka:
"State your desire; I shall grant it to you today. You may go to your own abode."
The ministers said: "When he said,
'I am going there desiring wealth,' he addressed that high-souled one with gentle words, showing him respect."
"O sinless one, take from me alone as much wealth as you desire, even more than that which you seek from the king; therefore, turn back.
Thus addressed by the naga, Kāśyapa, the best of bipeds, [consented].

Having obtained from Takṣaka as much wealth as he desired, the brahmin returned. When that brahmin had departed, O best of kings, Takṣaka approached your righteous father, the monarch, by means of a disguise.
O tiger among men, you were consecrated for victory because you consumed even him who was stationed within the palace with the fire of poison;
this has been seen and heard by me exactly as it happened, O best of kings.
We have related all of this to you in its entirety, most terrible as it is.
O best of kings, having heard of this defeat of the monarch,
do what must be done next for this seer Uttaṅka.
Sauti said:
Janamejaya said:
At that very time, however, King Janamejaya—
The subduer of enemies spoke these words to all his ministers:
"Now, by whom was that which occurred regarding the tree reported?
It was a marvel to the world, for it had then been reduced to a heap of ashes."

"That very tree which Kāśyapa restored to life was surely rendered poisonless by his mantras; it could not have perished because of Kāśyapa. Thus did that evil-souled one, the lowest of serpents, reflect in his mind.
"If, having been bitten by me, the Brahmin revives the king,
Takṣaka, his venom neutralized, will become an object of ridicule in the world.
Having reflected thus, he certainly brought satisfaction to the twice-born one.
"For by some means, I shall surely bring about the torment for him to whom I shall give [this].
Janamejaya said:
"I wish to hear this regarding what happened in the lonely forest."
"Who has seen or heard that conversation between the lord of the serpents and Kāśyapa at that time, such that it has now reached your ears?
Having heard it, I shall then form a plan for the destruction of the serpents."
The ministers said:
"Listen, O King, to how this was previously told to us by that lord of birds regarding the meeting on the road between the best of the twice-born and the lord of the serpents."
O King, on that tree, a certain man who was previously climbing the lord of the forest with its dry branches for the sake of firewood remained there,
unaware of the serpent and the bird dwelling in that tree.

But at that moment, O Indra among kings, that tree was reduced to ashes by him; yet, through the power of the twice-born one, the lord of trees was restored to life. Having returned, O best of monarchs, he reported this in this city.
All that occurred between Takṣaka and the brahmin has been related to you exactly as it happened and exactly as I heard it, O King. Having heard this, O tiger among kings, do as you desire.
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of his ministers, King Janamejaya,
afflicted by grief, was consumed with remorse and wrung his hands together.
Then the lotus-eyed king repeatedly exhaled long,
hot sighs and shed tears continuously from his eyes;
and the protector of the earth, overcome by pain and grief, spoke:
Shedding his unbearable tears and touching water according to the prescribed rite,
the king meditated for a moment; then, having reached a resolution in his mind,
the indignant monarch spoke these words to all his ministers:
"Having heard these words of yours regarding my father’s departure to heaven,
listen now to this firm resolve of mine:
I consider that immediately thereafter, [revenge] must be taken against the evil-minded Takṣaka."
"I must surely take revenge upon him by whom my father was harmed.
For, having acted upon the words of the seer Śṛṅgin and having burned the king,
he displayed such wickedness as to turn Kāśyapa back."
If that wicked man had gone, surely my father would still be alive. What would have been lost to him if that king had lived,
through the grace of Kāśyapa and the sound policy of his ministers?
But out of delusion, he [Takṣaka] prevented Kāśyapa, the best of the twice-born,
who had arrived desiring to restore the unconquered king to life;
for this was a great transgression on the part of the evil-minded Takṣaka.
"Thinking, 'May he not cause the king to live,' he gave wealth to the twice-born; now,
doing what is pleasing to Uttaṅka and a great favor to myself,
as well as to all of you, I shall go to pay honor to my father."
"I shall perform a snake-sacrifice that will bring about the destruction of the Nāgas.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the illustrious king was then approved by his ministers.

Then that king, the tiger among the Bharatas, the son of Parikṣit, made a solemn vow for a snake sacrifice, O Brahmin. Having summoned his domestic priest and the officiating priests, the lord of the earth spoke.
Endowed with eloquence, he spoke these words which were full of purpose:
"O sirs, tell me how I may retaliate against that evil-minded Takṣaka, who has harmed my father."
Do you know that deed by which I shall cause Takṣaka,
the serpent, along with his kinsmen, to enter a blazing fire,
just as my father was previously consumed by the fire of his own poison?
"In the same way, I also desire to consume that sinful serpent.
The officiating priests said:
"O King, there exists a great sacrificial session (*sattra*) for your sake, ordained by the gods."
"O King, it is told in the Purāṇa that there was a sacrifice known as the Sarpasattra;
O lord of men, no one other than you is the performer of that sacrifice—
thus say the experts in the Purāṇas, and we possess that ritual."
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, O best of men, that royal sage considered Takṣaka the serpent to have entered the blazing mouth of the sacrificial fire.
Then the king, who was skilled in mantras, spoke to those brahmins:
"I shall perform that sacrificial session; let the necessary materials be gathered for me.
O best of the twice-born, thereupon those officiating priests [prepared them] according to the scriptures.

Those who were experts in knowledge and had reached the highest state through their intellect measured out that site for the purpose of constructing a sacrificial ground, according to the rules. It was a desirable place,
endowed with supreme prosperity, and frequented by hosts of twice-born brahmins.
Having constructed a desired sacrificial ground according to the rules— a place rich in abundant wealth and grain and well-established by officiating priests—
they then initiated the king for the performance of the snake-sacrifice.
And this had previously occurred there during the snake sacrifice:
a great omen had arisen that was to cause an obstacle to the sacrifice. While that sacrificial ground was being prepared, he spoke these words:
Then the master builder, endowed with wisdom and expert in the science of architecture, spoke; as did the architect, the charioteer, and the reciter of the Purāṇas:
"In whatever place and at whatever time this measurement was undertaken..."
"Making the Brahmin the cause, this sacrifice shall not be concluded.
Having heard this, the king, before the time for initiation, said to the Kshattri:
"Let no one enter here who is unknown to me."

Then the ritual for the snake-sacrifice proceeded according to the prescribed rules, and the officiating priests moved about their respective duties in accordance with the injunctions. Having donned black garments, their eyes were reddened by the smoke.
They offered oblations with mantras into the kindled Jātavedas,
causing the minds of all the serpents to tremble;
they then sacrificed all the snakes there into the mouth of the fire.
Then the serpents rushed toward the blazing fire,
writhing piteously and calling out to one another;
quivering and gasping, others likewise coiled themselves around it.
With their tails and heads, they fell violently toward Citrabhānu;
white, black, and blue, both old and young,
crying out with terrifying sounds, they fell into the blazing fire.
O best of those who possess the sacred fire, they fall incessantly with great speed into the fire for a distance of only one *krośa* or one *yojana* from Gokarṇa;
thus, hundreds of thousands, millions (*prayuta*), and billions (*arbuda*) [fall].
O best of the twice-born, the serpents there were helpless and destroyed;
some were like Indurās, others like the trunks of elephants—
great-bodied and possessed of great strength, like elephants in rut.
Many snakes of various sizes and diverse colors, fierce with potent venom, terrible as iron clubs, and possessed of great strength—
biting serpents tormented by the punishment of their mother’s words— fell into the fire.
Śaunaka said:
At that time, during the snake sacrifice of the wise Pāṇḍava king Janamejaya, who were the supreme ṛṣis who served as the officiating priests?
Who were the members of the assembly at that most dreadful snake-sacrifice,
which produced extreme despair and was a source of great terror for the serpents?
O dear one, you ought to recount all of this in detail.
"O son of a Sūta, they should be known as those who are experts in the ritual procedures for the snake-sacrifice (sarpasatra).
Sūta said:
"Indeed, I shall now recount to you the names of these wise men."
Those who were then the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) for that king—
among them, the Hotṛ priest was the Brahmin Caṇḍabhārgava,
born in the lineage of Cyavana, renowned and the best among those who know the Vedas.
The Udgātṛ was the aged and learned Brāhmaṇa Kautsa, the son of Ṛji; Śārṅgarava was the Brahman priest, and Bodhapiṅgala was the Adhvaryu. Uttanka, the best of Brāhmaṇas, was indeed the leader there.
There, out of hatred for the earrings, he burned the serpents on all sides. Vyāsa was the presiding priest (*sadasya*), accompanied by his sons and disciples:
Uddālaka, Śamaṭhaka, and Śvetaketu as the fifth.
Asita, Devala, Nārada, and likewise Parvata;
Ātreya, Kuṇḍajaṭhara, and the twice-born Kuṭighaṭa;
Vātsya, Śrutaśravas, and the aged one who was devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas.
Kahoḍa, Devaśarman, Maudgalya, and Śamasaubhara—
these and many other Brāhmaṇas of rigid vows were the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*) at that sacrificial session of the son of Parikṣit.
Then, while the officiating priests were offering oblations during that great serpent-sacrifice,
terrible snakes, bringing fear to all living beings, began to fall there. Streams of fat and marrow began to flow from the serpents.
Then a tumultuous stench arose from those being incessantly burned; likewise,
the sound of the falling and stationary nāgas was heard constantly as they were being violently cooked by the fire.
But Takṣaka, that lord of the Nāgas, agitated by fear and seeking refuge, went to the abode of Purandara, the bull among the gods;
he departed as soon as he heard that King Janamejaya had been initiated for the sacrifice.
Then, having related everything exactly as it had happened, that best of serpents, terrified after having committed an offense, sought refuge with Purandara.
Indra, well-pleased, said to him: "O Takṣaka, there is no fear for you here."
"O Lord of Nagas, you shall have no fear whatsoever from that snake-sacrifice. I have already propitiated the Grandfather (Brahmā) on your behalf;
therefore, you have no cause for fear. Let the fever of your mind depart."
Thus consoled by him, that best of serpents dwelt there in the palace of Śakra, joyful and at ease;
yet he remained deeply distressed as the nāgas continued to fall incessantly into the fire.

With only a small remnant of his retinue remaining, Vāsuki was consumed by anguish; a terrible despondency overcame Vāsuki, the lord of the serpents. With his heart reeling, he spoke these words to his sister:
"O blessed lady, my limbs burn and the quarters of the sky no longer appear clear to me.
I feel as if I am sinking due to delusion, and my mind seems to reel.
My vision wanders excessively, and my heart feels as if it is being torn apart."

Today, against my will, I shall fall into that blazing fire; for this sacrifice of the son of Parikṣit proceeds with the intent to destroy me. Clearly, I too must go to the abode of the King of the Ancestors.
"O sister, that time has now arrived for which you were given to Jaratkaru by me in the past; save us along with our kinsmen!
For it is said, O best of serpent-women, that Āstīka will stop that sacrifice as it proceeds."

"The Grandfather himself has previously declared that he will reject me. Therefore, O child, speak today for the sake of the liberation of myself and my attendants to your own son, the prince who is esteemed by the elders and most learned in the Vedas."
Sūta said:
Then, having summoned her son, the serpent-woman Jaratkaru spoke these words at the command of Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas.
"O son, I was given to your father by your brother for a specific purpose;
that time has now arrived, so act accordingly.
Āstīka said:
"For what reason were you given to my father by my maternal uncle? Tell me that in truth; having heard it, I shall act accordingly.
Sūta said:
Then Jaratkaru, the sister of the Naga king, unflinching and desiring the welfare of her kinsmen, told him:
"It is heard that Kadrū is the mother of all the snakes without exception."
"Listen, my sons, to that for which she was cursed by me in my anger: because Ucchaiḥśravas, the king of horses, was not made subject to me as a slave in the wager on account of Vinatā."
"At the sacrifice of Janamejaya, the one whose chariot is drawn by the wind (Agni) shall consume you;
having met your death there, you will go to the world of the departed.
And the Grandfather of the World himself spoke thus to her as she was pronouncing this curse.
"So be it," he replied, and he gave his assent to those words. And Vāsuki, having heard that speech of the Grandfather at that time,
O dear one, sought refuge with the gods once the nectar had been churned.
01.049.010a And all the gods, having attained the unsurpassed nectar (*amṛta*) and having achieved their purpose,
approached Prajāpati, placing my brother at their head.
01.049.011a All those gods propitiated him, the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*).
"May this curse not come to pass together with King Vāsuki.
"This Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, is distressed on account of his kinsmen;
O Blessed One, may this imprecation from his mother not take effect."
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, let this be ordained accordingly.
Brahmā said:
"Jaratkāru shall obtain as his wife a woman named Jaratkāru."
"Born there, a twice-born man shall liberate the serpents from their curse.
Jaratkāru said:
"Having heard these words, Vāsuki, the lord of the *pannagas*, [spoke]."

O one who resembles an immortal, my father, that great-souled one, gave me to you long ago, even before the time had arrived; there you were born from me. Now that time has come; you ought to protect us from this danger.
"Therefore, you ought to save my brother from that fire.
Let our union with you, the wise one, not be in vain—that I was given by my father for the sake of his liberation. Or how do you, my son, consider this?"
Sūta said: Having been thus addressed, Astīka then replied "So be it" to his mother,
and spoke as if restoring Vāsuki, who was tormented by grief, back to life.
"O Vāsuki, best of serpents, I shall release you from that curse, O being of great power; I tell you this truly. Be at ease in mind, O Nāga, for no fear exists for you."
"O gentle one, I shall strive in such a way that there will be welfare;
my speech has never uttered an untruth even in jest, so how could it be otherwise?
Having gone to that best of kings, Janamejaya, who is consecrated for the sacrifice..."
"O uncle, O best of beings, today I shall gratify you with words endowed with auspiciousness, so that the king's sacrifice shall be brought to completion. Therefore,
O great-minded lord of nāgas, place your full confidence in me."
"Your mind can never be otherwise toward me.
Vāsuki said:
"O Āstīka, my heart reels and it seems to break asunder."
"Oppressed by the Brahman’s staff, I do not even know the directions.
Āstīka said:
"O best of serpents, you should not feel any distress whatsoever."
I shall destroy the fear arising from the blazing fire;
I shall destroy that most terrible Brahma-staff, which possesses a splendor equal to the fire of time. Do not feel any fear at all on my account.
Sūta said:
Then, having removed the terrible mental fever from Vāsuki and having transferred it to his own limbs, he departed with great haste.
For the sake of the liberation of the lords of the serpents, Āstīka, the best of the twice-born, went to that sacrifice of Janamejaya, which was endowed with every excellence;

In that interval, they there fell into a very deep swoon;
seeing those sages unconscious, he became distressed.
Then the Brahmins present in the assembly spoke to Janamejaya.
"Fie, fie upon your conduct, O King! You have slain Brāhmaṇas.
Indeed, eighteen acts of Brahman-murder have been committed by you, O lord of men. Wander through many sacred fords; thereafter you shall attain purification."
In that interval, an incorporeal voice spoke there,
as if restoring to life the king who was distressed and overcome by anxiety,
saying: "For the sake of liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin, having fashioned a garment of bark, put it on."
Having donned that garment measuring eighteen cubits,
listen here to the story of the Pāṇḍavas, which consists of eighteen sections;
then you shall attain purity through the Bhārata.

Having heard those words and being approved by the sages, the king, having clothed himself in that garment prescribed for him, bowed low with humility and questioned Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, concerning the history of his ancestors.
I shall describe that; listen, O lords of sages!
Listen, O King, to how the division between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas arose, born of the gambling match for the sake of the kingdom, as well as their exile in the forest.

O bull of the Bharatas, since you ask, I shall relate to you how that battle occurred which brought about the destruction of the earth. When their father had died, those heroes returned from the forest to their own palace.

In no long time, those wise ones became proficient in both the Veda and the bow. Seeing the Pāṇḍavas endowed with such beauty, heroism, and vigor, esteemed by the citizens, and bearing prosperity and fame, the Kurus could not endure them.
Then the cruel Duryodhana, along with Karṇa and the son of Subala,
inflicted upon them various forms of restraint and exile.
Then the cruel Duryodhana, remaining steadfast in the counsel of Karṇa, [acted].
For the sake of the kingdom, he oppressed the Pāṇḍavas by various means. Then the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra gave poison to Bhīma;
however, the heroic Vṛkodara digested it along with his food.
Having bound Vṛkodara once more at Pramāṇakoṭi and cast Bhīma into the waters of the Gaṅgā, he returned to the city. When the son of Kuntī awoke, he then tore asunder his bonds.
O great king, Bhīmasena rose up, free from pain;
yet they bit him, who was as if asleep, with venomous black serpents on every part of his body, and still that slayer of enemies did not die.
By means of many petty stratagems, both covert and overt,
he oppressed the Pāṇḍavas, yet he achieved nothing at all. Despite those various injuries inflicted upon them, the high-minded one [remained steadfast].
Vidura remained vigilant in both liberating them and warding off obstacles;
just as Śakra brings happiness to the world of living beings while residing in heaven,
so too did Vidura constantly bring happiness to the Pāṇḍavas.
But when, through various means— both concealed and overt— he was unable to destroy them, as they were protected by the destiny of their lot,
he then consulted with his ministers, Vṛṣa, Duḥśāsana, and others.
Having obtained Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s permission, he directed them to a house made of lac;
there he caused those Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess to dwell,
and then he set it on fire while they were unsuspecting.
Then, at the very word of Vidura, a female digger was provided;
she liberated them by means of yoga, and once freed, they fled in fear.
Indeed, Hiḍimbī reached the place where Bhīma was, and there Ghaṭotkaca was born.

Then, in that terrible great forest, Bhīmasena of fearsome prowess, filled with rage, slew the Rākṣasa named Hiḍimba on the earth. Thereafter, those heroes, having made their arrangements, then proceeded toward Ekacakrā.
Assuming the forms of Brahmins along with their mother,
those subduers of enemies killed the mighty crane there for the sake of the Brahmins;
then, accompanied by the Brahmins, they went to the city of the Pañcālas.
Desiring to please them, the son of Ambikā, the king, then sent those Pāṇḍavas into exile out of a desire to enjoy the kingdom himself;
they departed together from the city named after the elephant.
And at their departure, the steward Vidura became the minister for those high-souled ones;
by him they were released from the house of lac and fled to the forest at nightfall.
Then the sons of Kuntī reached the city of Vāraṇāvata.
Those high-souled subduers of enemies lived there together with their mother;
commanded by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they dwelt for a year in a house made of lac, remaining vigilant while being protected from Purocana.
Having had a tunnel constructed as urged by Vidura, those subduers of enemies,
having set fire to the house of lac and burnt Purocana,
fled in great agitation along with their mother.

They beheld the terrible Rākṣasa Hiḍimba at a forest waterfall; and having slain that lord of Rākṣasas, the sons of Pṛthā, terrified by the awakening of their fear and afflicted by the dread of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, fled away in the night.
Then, having gone to Ekacakrā, the Pāṇḍavas, firm in their vows,
became celibate students (*brahmacārin*) perfected in the study of the Vedas. There, those bulls among men dwelt for some time with self-restraint.
Together with Mādrī, in the house of a Brāhmaṇa at Ekacakrā, Vṛkodara encountered there a hungry man-eater,
the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, who was of great strength and named Baka.

And that tiger among men, the heroic Pāṇḍava, having slain him with the strength of his arms and by his own prowess, consoled the citizens. Then they heard that Kṛṣṇā was holding her *svayaṃvara* among the Pañcālas.
Having heard this, they went forth and found her;
having obtained Draupadī there and having dwelt for a full year,
those subduers of enemies returned to Hastināpura, now known [to all].

They were addressed by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and by the son of Śāntanu: "O dear ones, how may there be no conflict between you and your brothers? "We have considered that your dwelling shall be at Khāṇḍavaprastha."
"Therefore, with your anger appeased, go to Khāṇḍavaprastha for a dwelling— a place endowed with many people and well-laid-out great highways.
At their word, they departed together with all their friends and kinsmen.
Taking all kinds of jewels, they dwelt there in the city of Khāṇḍavaprastha for many groups of years, O King,
bringing other rulers of the earth under their control through the prowess of their weapons.
Thus, those who were devoted to righteousness, dedicated to the vow of truth,
vigilant, alert, and patient, then scorched their enemies; meanwhile,
the mighty Bhīmasena conquered the eastern quarter.
The heroic Arjuna conquered the north, Nakula likewise the west,
and Sahadeva, the slayer of enemy heroes, conquered the south.
In this manner, they all brought this entire earth under their control.
With the five [Pāṇḍavas] who resembled the sun, and with the sun itself shining brightly,
the earth gleamed as if there were six suns, owing to those Pāṇḍavas of true prowess. Then, for some reason, the Dharma King Yudhiṣṭhira—
Having indeed dwelt in the forest for twelve years,
that radiant one of true prowess sent his brother Dhanañjaya forth from the forest.

Even more dear than his own life was Arjuna, that tiger among men, steadfast in soul and endowed with all virtues— dearer to him through his fortitude, his righteousness, his truthfulness, and his victory.
Arjuna never transgressed against his eldest brother at any time;
he indeed dwelt in the forest for a full year and one month,
and having obtained a Naga maiden, he undertook a pilgrimage to the sacred fords.
Then, having obtained the daughter of Pāṇḍya and dwelling together with those two,
he once went to Dhṛṣīkeśa at Dvāravatī;
there Bībhatsu obtained a lotus-eyed wife.
Subhadrā, the sister of Vāsudeva, who spoke so auspiciously,
was joined in marriage with Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava; she was as delighted by that union as Śacī is with Mahendra, or as the Goddess Śrī is with Kṛṣṇa.
And the son of Kuntī, Bībhatsu, together with Vāsudeva, O best of kings, gratified the consumer of oblations (Agni) in the Khaṇḍava forest; for indeed,
when accompanied by Keśava, no task was too great a burden for Pārtha.
Just as Viṣṇu, aided by his resolve, assists in the slaying of enemies,
Agni likewise gave to Pārtha the supreme bow Gāṇḍīva,
two quivers with inexhaustible arrows, and a chariot marked with the sign of the monkey.
There, Bībhatsu liberated the great asura Maya;
he constructed a celestial assembly hall adorned with every kind of jewel.
In that hall, the dull-witted and evil-minded Duryodhana conceived a greedy desire.
Then, having deceived Yudhiṣṭhira with dice by means of Saubala,
he sent him forth to the forest for twelve years— seven and five—
and likewise the thirteenth year to be spent incognito within the kingdom.
Then, in the fourteenth year, while they were begging for their own wealth, O Great King, they did not obtain it; thereupon, war broke out.
Then, having utterly destroyed them and slain King Duryodhana, they [prevailed].

After Dhṛtarāṣṭra had gone to heaven and Vidura had met his death, the Pāṇḍavas obtained a kingdom that was for the most part devastated, having performed many various sacrifices, such as the horse sacrifice and others.
Having caused the wives of kings of immeasurable splendor to attain heaven,
and having protected the wives of Kṛṣṇa when the descendant of Vṛṣṇi had reached his final abode,
they performed the Great Departure and went to the unsurpassed heaven.
"O best among victors, such was this event of old concerning those of untainted deeds: their division, the destruction of their kingdom, and their victory. Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have indeed related all of this in brief—
the narrative of the Mahābhārata, the great history of the Kurus.
O sinless one, as you relate this story of manifold meanings, [it is as if] you yourself are speaking it."
"An intense curiosity has arisen in me regarding this detailed account.
Therefore, you ought to relate it to me once more in full detail;
for I am not yet satiated by hearing the great deeds of my ancestors."
That cannot be a small cause, for those who know the Dharma— wherein the Pāṇḍavas slew those who were in every way unslayable— are praised by men.
For what reason did those tigers among men, though capable and [themselves] innocent, [act thus]?
How did Vṛkodara,
the scorcher of foes, who possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants and mighty arms, endure the afflictions inflicted by those evil-minded ones while his brothers were being tormented?
O best of the twice-born, although he was being tormented, he indeed restrained his anger. But how was it that Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, while being oppressed by those evil-minded ones,
though she was capable, did not consume the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with her terrible gaze?
How was it that Draupadī was not able to consume the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
And how was it that the two sons of Mādrī, the Pārthas,
followed that tiger among men as he was being deceived by those evil-minded ones during the transgression at the game of dice?

How did Yudhiṣṭhira, the best among the upholders of dharma, the son of Dharma who knows the law, endure such supreme suffering though he was undeserving of it? And how did the Pāṇḍava, with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, withstand those vast armies?
"Shooting alone, Dhanañjaya led them all to the world of the ancestors.
O one rich in asceticism, tell me all this exactly as it happened—
everything that those great car-warriors did at each stage."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Wait a moment, O Great King; this extensive sequence of the meritorious narrative, as uttered by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, must be told."
I shall proclaim the entire doctrine of the great-souled Maharṣi Vyāsa, who is honored in all the worlds and possesses immeasurable splendor;
for this consists of one hundred thousand verses concerning meritorious deeds.
This supreme *Bhārata*, which is to be known and heard along with its sub-narratives (*upākhyāna*), has been explained here by the son of Satyavatī, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
However, O lord of men, I shall relate all of this in brief.
Two thousand chapters and one hundred sections;
nine thousand and ten hundred verses—
this was then compiled by the great seer into eighteen books.
The wise man who causes this to be heard, and the person who hears it,
shall go to the abode of Brahmā and attain equality with the gods.
For this is equal to the Vedas, purifying, and supreme.

This Purāṇa, praised by the seers, is the most excellent among those worthy of being heard. In this highly meritorious history (itihāsa), both worldly prosperity and dharma are taught in their entirety, as is the wisdom of final liberation.
A learned man who causes those who are noble, generous, truthful, and non-nihilistic to hear this Veda of Kṛṣṇa attains its purpose;
he would undoubtedly cast off even the sin committed by killing an embryo.
Having heard this history, even a most cruel person is liberated from all sins, just as the moon is released from Rāhu;
at that very moment he becomes self-controlled and attains eternal peace.
This history named *Jaya* should be heard by one who desires victory;
he shall conquer the entire earth and also defeat his enemies. A pregnant woman gives birth to a son, and a maiden obtains a virtuous husband.
This is the most excellent *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child); this is a great means of securing well-being (*svastyayana*).
It should be heard repeatedly by both the queen and the crown prince;
it causes one to give birth to a heroic son or a daughter destined to share in the kingdom.
"This is the science of polity (*artha-śāstra*), this is the supreme science of dharma (*dharma-śāstra*),
and this is declared to be the science of liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) by Vyāsa of immeasurable intellect. They recite it now, and others likewise shall recite it in the future."
Sons who are obedient exist, as do servants who act for one's pleasure;
however, a man who constantly hears this [teaching] quickly casts off all evil committed by body, speech, and mind.
For those who listen without malice to this great birth of the Bharatas, there is no fear of disease; how much less could there be fear of the next world?
It is auspicious, conducive to fame, bestowing long life, leading to heaven, and likewise meritorious.
This was composed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, desiring to perform a meritorious act,
in order to spread the fame throughout the world of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas and of other Kṣatriyas of immense wealth and splendor.
For that man in this world who causes these meritorious and pure Brahmins— whose deeds are renowned in the world and whose knowledge is as bright as all branches of learning—
to hear this, his merit shall be great and his dharma eternal.
Constantly reciting the celebrated lineage of the Kurus, one who is pure attains a vast progeny and becomes most worthy of honor in the world—
he who, a Brahmin restrained by his vows, studies the meritorious Bhārata.
By reciting the Bhārata for four months of the rainy season, one is liberated from all sins; he who reads it should be known as one who has mastered the Vedas.
Therein dwell the gods, the Brahman-sages, and likewise the meritorious royal sages.
Therein the sinless ones are glorified, and likewise Keśava is glorified;
there the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of the gods, is glorified, as is the Goddess. Therein also occurs the birth of Kārttikeya, who is the progenitor of many.
In this work, the greatness of the Brahmins and of cows is celebrated;
this compendium of all the Vedas should be heard by those whose minds are intent on dharma.
It is like the blessed ocean and like the Himavat mountain.
In both [epics], there are two treasures of jewels; likewise, the Bhārata is so called.
The wise man who causes this to be heard by Brahmins here on the festival days (parvan), having shaken off all evil and conquered heaven, attains union with Brahman.
And whoever should cause even a single foot of this [text] to be heard by Brahmins at a *śrāddha* ceremony,
that *śrāddha* shall become inexhaustible and reach even the ancestors.
Whatever sin a man commits during the day while acting out of ignorance, [it is all removed].

Upon merely hearing this narrative known as the Mahābhārata, it is completely dissolved. Whatever sin is committed in a single day by the senses or even by the mind— whether a man performs it knowingly or unknowingly— it is all destroyed.
Because it concerns the great birth of the Bharatas, it is called the Mahābhārata;
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins. Since this most wonderful history (itihāsa) belongs to the Bharatas, it is so named.
For when recited, it shall liberate mortals from even great sin. After three years, having achieved his purpose, the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana—
ever industrious and pure— began the Mahābhārata from the beginning with great capability.
This was composed by the great seer while established in ascetic discipline and self-restraint;
therefore, this meritorious and supreme narrative of the Bhārata, spoken by Kṛṣṇa, should be heard by Brāhmaṇas who are likewise joined with self-restraint.

Those Brahmins who shall cause [this] to be heard and those men who shall listen— whether they are engaged in any state whatsoever— they are not to be grieved for on account of what they have done or left undone.
Indeed, this should be heard by every man who desires dharma.

By means of this entire history (itihāsa), one shall thereafter attain perfection; a human being does not obtain such satisfaction even by reaching the path to heaven as that which one enjoys merely by hearing this highly meritorious history.
A faithful man of virtuous character who hears this wonder, or causes it to be heard,
obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Just as the Blessed Ocean, and just as Mount Meru, the great mountain...
Both are renowned as treasures of jewels, and likewise the Bhārata is so called.
For this is equal to the Vedas, pure, and most excellent;
it is worthy of being heard, pleasant to the ear, purifying, and increases one's virtuous conduct.

O son of Parikṣit, listen to this entire divine narrative, which brings joy, merit, and victory, as it is told by me. For three years, the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana remained constantly engaged, rising at dawn.
He has composed this supreme narrative, the Mahābhārata. The king who listens to it in its entirety enjoys the whole earth;
a pregnant woman gives birth to a son, and a maiden is quickly given in marriage.
Merchants shall have successful voyages, and heroes shall achieve victory.

One should constantly cause those who are believers to hear [this], as well as Brāhmaṇas who are free from malice, Kṣatriyas who have completed their Vedic studies and vows, and those established in triumph.
One should cause the Vaiśyas who are devoted to their own duties and those dependent on the Kṣatriya to hear [the teachings].
O Bhārata, this dharma was observed of old among all the social orders;
O King, hearing it from a Brāhmaṇa is specifically ordained.

If one should recite this constantly again and again, one shall go to the supreme goal. Whether one grasps a single verse, or even half a verse, or should constantly recite even a single quarter-verse, one shall never be destitute.
In this [epic], there is the birth of many high-souled royal sages;
here are the appropriate words of counsel and the dharma seen from many perspectives; here are the diverse battles of kings, and here alone is their prosperity.

O dear one, here [in this work] the discourses of the ṛṣis, as well as those of the Gandharvas and Rākṣasas, have been set forth in detail after encountering various [traditions]. Furthermore, the names of the meritorious *tīrthas* and their very sight have been proclaimed.
The glorification of forests, mountains, rivers, and the ocean; of regions and divine cities of antiquity;
as well as the foremost of rituals and superhuman prowess.
In this Bhārata, the supreme seer has set forth the practice of honoring guests,
the training of chariots, horses, and lordly elephants, skill in warfare,
and many varieties of speech— all of these are contained herein.

Just as the ocean is exceedingly vast, and as the Himavat mountain is renowned as a mine of jewels, so too is the Mahābhārata called [a mine of jewels]. Just as one would experience no lack of joy upon reaching heaven, [so it is with this work].
Likewise, upon hearing this meritorious narrative, joy indeed arises;
and if women and Śūdras should listen, placing the best of the twice-born at their head,
they obtain the fruits exactly as described, without exception.
O King, for the prosperity of your lineage, for long life, and for victory,
listen as I recite this entire ancient history. Furthermore,
whoever should cause even a single quarter-verse of this to be heard by the Brahmins at a funeral rite for the ancestors, [attains great merit].

For him who causes this to be heard by the learned and the man who hears this, there shall be inexhaustible food and drink that attends upon his ancestors. Having reached the abode of Brahmā, he shall attain equality with the gods.
Whatever sin a Brahmin commits by day while acting through his senses,
he is released from it by reciting the *Mahābhārata* at the evening twilight; likewise,
whatever sin a Brahmin commits by night while acting through his senses, [he is released from it].

By reciting the *Mahābhārata*, one is liberated from the sins of the previous day; the great birth of the descendants of Bharata is called the *Mahābhārata*. He who knows its etymology is liberated from all evils.
The highly fortunate Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana declared that, being ever-risen and always a yogin, he composed the Mahābhārata from the beginning in three years—
concerning dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, O bull of the Bharatas.
What exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere else.
For this has been proclaimed by the Brahmins in the world, and among the Brahmins here:
[it concerns] giving, enjoying, as well as hearing, and fighting with enemies.
Does that man know anything at all, O Bhārata, who has not heard this?
O King, he who bestows this Bhārata upon a reciter has,
by that act, given away the entire earth girdled by the oceans.
"These eighteen sections were indeed narrated by Vyāsa;
whoever should give even one of them, by him everything has been accomplished.
Vaiśampāyana said:
There was once a lord of the earth named Rājoparicara, a king ever devoted to righteousness and firm in his vows. Once, he set out for a hunt;
that Vasu, the joy of the Pauravas, entered the delightful realm of Cedi.
Following Indra’s instruction, the lord of the earth accepted that which was worthy of being received.
While he dwelt in the hermitage, having laid down his weapons and devoted himself to asceticism,
the god who wields the thunderbolt himself appeared in person before the monarch.
"Considering that this king is worthy of the status of Indra through his asceticism,
'O Great King, you are our refuge,' the wielder of the thunderbolt said repeatedly.
With soothing words, he directly turned that king away from his asceticism."
Indra said:
"I am the protector of the gods; you, indeed, must protect human beings, O lord of the earth, so that this dharma may not become confused upon the earth."

Protect that [dharma], for when dharma is upheld, it sustains the entire world. Guard the worldly dharma with constant diligence and concentration; thus, endowed with dharma, you shall attain the eternal, meritorious worlds.
"O lord of men, you who dwell upon the earth have become my dear friend, dwelling with me in heaven; therefore, inhabit that region of the earth which is like a udder—
pastoral, auspicious, very stable, and rich in wealth and grain."
Easy to protect and pleasant, endowed with the excellent qualities of the soil,
this land indeed surpasses all others in its wealth of riches, gems, and the like;
the earth is full of treasures— dwell among the Cedis, O King of Cedi!
The people of the land are virtuous in character, contented, and upright;
there is no false speech here even in jest, much less otherwise. Furthermore, men who delight in the welfare of their elders are not divided by their fathers.
They yoke even emaciated oxen to the pole and provide them with fodder;
O giver of honor, among the Cedis all social classes always abide by their own duties.
There is nothing that exists within the three worlds that is unknown to you.

A great, divine crystal chariot, fit for the enjoyment of gods, shall appear for you in the sky; this celestial vehicle, granted by me, shall attend you as you travel through the air. You alone among all mortals shall be seated upon this most excellent of chariots.
You shall indeed move about as one standing above, like a god in embodied form.
I give you this Vaijayantī garland of unfading lotuses,
which shall keep you unscarred by weapons in battle.
"O lord of men, this very thing shall become your insignia here on earth,
renowned as the *indramālā*, auspicious, peerless, and great.
Having thus consoled the king, he turned him back from his asceticism.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The slayer of Vṛtra gave him a bamboo staff,
intended as a gift for his desires and a protector of the disciplined.
Having accomplished the task for the denizens of heaven, he departed together with the deities.
Then the king of the Cedis, adorned with Indra’s ornaments,
mounted that celestial chariot given by Indra and set out for his city.
Then, after one year had passed, the lord of the earth caused that [image] to be brought into the city upon the ground for the sake of Śakra’s worship; at that time,
he held a festival superior to all others.
O Great King, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
O Great King, on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, there was a great festival.
From that time until the present day, the best of kings have performed sacrifices with the sacrificial post (*yaṣṭi*).
O King, the entry was performed just as it had been initiated by him;
on the following day, the raising of the [palanquin] was likewise carried out by the kings for her,
who was adorned with baskets, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Furthermore, it is duly encircled with garlands of flowers;
having raised [the image] to a height of thirty-two *kiṣkus*,
it is placed upon a pedestal twelve *aratnis* high.
Having draped the supreme banner with garments of great kingship, and having honored it with clothes, food, and drink by the preeminent Brahmins,
the banner is then raised after the ritual for declaring an auspicious day has been performed.
With conchs, kettledrums, and clay drums;
twenty-four finger-breadths are known as one *hasta*, which is called a *kiṣku*;
[the city] is thirty-two *kiṣkus* in length.
On a pedestal twelve *ratni*s high, adorned with jewels,
there stands a banner decorated with cloths of five colors and garlands;
here the Blessed One Śaṅkara is worshipped in the form of Hāsya.
The yakṣas, headed by Māṇibhadra, are worshipped together with the deities;
having given various kinds of gifts to those in need by means of their kinsmen,
and having likewise adorned themselves with garlands of flowers and various garments.
Having played with all those who were observing vows and carrying water at the king’s command,
and having honored the king after engaging in humorous conversation,
all the city-dwellers likewise enjoyed themselves together with the people from the countryside.
Charioteers and bards, along with actors and dancers, performed;
and out of joy, O tiger among men, they all celebrated a great festival.
Accompanied by his harem and his ministers, he was adorned with every ornament.
Having put on garments dyed with great kingly yellow, the King of Cedi likewise,
smeared with vermilion, rejoiced then together with his wife.
In this manner, all the people of the countryside then celebrated the festival of Indra.
Just as Vasu, the lord of Cedi, joyfully performed the sacrifice for Indra,
so did the lord of Cedi shine there like the lord of the gods in heaven,
having himself taken [the sacrificial vessels] out of affection for the high-souled Vasu.
Having seen this auspicious worship performed by the gods, Mahendra,
mounting his chariot drawn by bay horses and traveling through the atmosphere,
arrived together with Śacī and surrounded by hosts of apsarases.
The powerful Lord, being well-pleased, spoke to Vasu, the chief of kings:
"Those men and kings who shall honor my festival with joy, even as King [Rukmī], the lord of Cedi, has done."
Prosperity and victory shall belong to them and their kingdoms;
likewise, the countryside shall become flourishing and joyful. O King, the crops shall be free from calamities in many ways.
Neither Rākṣasas nor Piśācas shall harm him in any way. Thus, O lord of men, was the great king Vasu honored with affection by that high-souled Mahendra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Having done this, Mahendra went to his own abode. Those men who always cause a festival to be held for Śakra become truly purified through gifts such as the donation of land.
Then, having been honored by Maghavan with the great sacrifice of the granting of boons as well as the festival of Indra, Vasu, the lord of Cedi,
ruled this earth from Cedi in accordance with righteousness.
Out of devotion to Indra, the lord of the earth, Vasu, performed a great sacrifice to Indra.
He had five sons of immense heroism and immeasurable power,
and as a sovereign emperor, he consecrated his sons in various kingdoms.
The renowned Bṛhadratha, the king of Magadha and a great chariot-warrior; Pratyagraha and Kuśāmba, whom they call Maṇivāhana;
Macchilla and Yadu, and the unconquered Rājanya.
O King, these were the sons of that royal sage of great splendor; they established countries and cities after their own names. These five Vāsava kings each founded eternal lineages.
While that high-souled king was dwelling in Indra’s palace, made of crystal and situated in the sky, the Gandharvas and Apsaras waited upon him;
thus he became renowned by the name Uparicara.
The mountain Kolāhala, possessed of consciousness, reportedly obstructed the Śuktimatī river that flowed past his city out of lust.
But Vasu struck that mountain Kolāhala with his foot.
Through that opening created by the blow, the river flowed out;
in that river, Parvata himself begat a pair of twins.
Delighted by that deliverance, the river announced it to the king.
"The maiden shall become the queen, and Pauṣya shall be the commander-in-chief.
Having heard the words of Śuktimatī and having seen those two,
that best of royal sages [chose] the man who was present there.
Vasu, the bestower of wealth and subduer of enemies, appointed him as his general;
the king, however, made his beloved daughter Girikā his wife.
Then Girikā, the wife of Vasu, at the proper time, out of desire, informed him [of her condition].
When the time of her season had arrived, she bathed and, being pure for the *puṃsavana* rite,
on that very day the ancestors said to him, "Slay the deer," being well-pleased with that best of kings, the foremost among the wise.
Not transgressing that command of his ancestors, the king,
though filled with desire, went hunting while constantly thinking only of Girijā,
who was endowed with exceeding beauty like another Śrī herself manifest before his eyes.
With *aśoka*, *campaka*, *cūta*, *tilaka*, and *atimuktaka* trees;
with *puṃnāga*, *karṇikāra*, *bakuḷa*, and divine trees; as well as with *panasa*, coconut palms, *candana*, and *arjuna* trees.

Seeing that forest, which in the springtime resembled Caitraratha, endowed with these and other great trees, auspicious and laden with sweet fruits, filled with the warbling of cuckoos and the humming of intoxicated bees.
Then, his soul overwhelmed by passion, he did not see Girikā;
tormented by desire, as he was wandering at will, he beheld [a tree] with its tips of branches covered in flowers and adorned with young shoots.
At that time, O King, the monarch sat comfortably upon a branch beneath a tree that was lovely and covered with clusters of *aśoka* blossoms;
the delightful fragrance of the flowers was mingled with the scent of honey.
Driven by the wind, he smelled it and was filled with joy;
as he thought of his wife, the fire of passion grew within him. As he moved through the beautiful forest, his semen was discharged.
The lord of the earth caught that semen right there as soon as it was spilled; indeed,
the lord of the earth caught it with a tree leaf, thinking, "May my semen not be spilled in vain."
"Lest this semen be wasted in vain," the king thus provided protection for his seed with a ring; he also bound it with copper-colored clusters of *aśoka* flowers and tender sprouts.
"This semen of mine has been discharged in vain; it would be a very great loss.
Yet, let not the fertile season of my wife be fruitless," the lord thought thus, reflecting again and again.
Having realized that the seed was not in vain, that best of kings,
observing the proper time for the queen’s conception,
consecrated that seed with mantras and dispatched the swift messenger standing nearby.
Knowing the subtle truth of the nature of things, he understood the hawk's intent and then said to him:
"O gentle one, for the sake of my pleasure, take this semen to my house;
give it quickly to Girikā, for today is indeed her fertile season."
Then, seizing it, that powerful hawk, having swiftly flown up and exerting the utmost speed,
sped away through the air. Then another hawk saw that hawk approaching.
Upon seeing him, he immediately rushed toward him, suspecting him to be meat;
then the two of them engaged in a battle with their beaks in the sky,
and as they fought, their semen fell into the waters of the Yamunā.
There, a most excellent Apsaras known as Ādrikā, having fallen into the state of a fish due to a Brahmin’s curse, became a dweller of the Yamunā. Then,
that seed of Vāsava, fallen from the talons of a hawk—

Approaching with speed, she seized it while still possessing her mountain-like form and taking the shape of a fish. Then, O best of the Bharatas, when the tenth month had arrived, fishermen caught that fish.
They extracted from her womb a human being, both female and male;
considering it a marvel, they reported it to the king,
saying, "O King, these two humans have been born within the body of a fish."
Of those two, King Uparicara then took the male;
he became the righteous king named Matsya, true to his promise.
And that Apsaras was instantly released from her curse.
"O auspicious one, as was previously declared by the Blessed One— that you, though born of animal birth,
would give birth to two humans and thereby obtain release from your curse—
she then gave birth to those two and was subsequently butchered by a fisherman."
Having cast off her fish-form and attained a divine form,
that excellent Apsaras then departed upon the path of the Siddhas, Rishis, and Cāraṇas.
As for the girl who was her daughter, she was a fish-woman (matsyā) and possessed the scent of a fish.
Then the king gave her to the fisherman, saying, "Let this woman be yours," for she was endowed with beauty and character, and possessed of all excellent qualities;
yet she was named Satyavatī because of her reliance on the fisherman.
For some time, that woman of pure smiles remained smelling of fish;
then, while she was rowing that boat upon the water for the sake of serving her father,
Parāśara, wandering on his pilgrimage, beheld her.

"O auspicious lady, grant me union with you, who are exceedingly endowed with beauty and desired even by the *siddhas*," he said. And as soon as that wise man saw her, he fell in love with that woman of lovely appearance.
The wise bull among sages, Śakti’s son, being occupied with his task, reflected upon her origin; having understood that she was the daughter of Vāsava, he spoke to Matsyagandhā.

"O beautiful lady, tell me, where is the helmsman by whom this boat is to be steered? O twice-born one, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to him, I am steering the boat belonging to a fisherman who is childless; it is filled with a thousand people."
Parāśara said:
"Excellent, O daughter of Vasu! Why do you delay, O auspicious one?
Let the jar be carried forth; it shall be equal to half of a thousand [pounds], O blessed lady."
"I shall remain as the last; let the boat be taken away without delay.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having said "So be it," Matsyagandhā began rowing the boat upon the water.
Seeing the sage looking at her, Matsyagandhā then spoke these words:
"People call me Matsyagandhā, the daughter of the king of fishermen."
Parāśara said:
"How will you know the birth of her who is tormented by grief? Tell me;
for by means of divine knowledge, your very form has been seen as soon as it was beheld."
O son of Vasava, listen as I speak for the sake of securing your affection:
there are ancestors known as the Barhiṣads who drink the Soma;
you are their mind-born daughter, renowned by the name Acchodā.

That divine lake named Acchoda from which you have emerged has never before been seen by you; for your ancestors were produced from your mind alone, and thus you did not recognize them as your own fathers.
But she chose another father, bypassing those ancestors of her own,
the lord of the earth known by the name Vasu, the son of Manu,
who was stationed in a celestial chariot in the sky together with the Apsaras Adrikā.
Through that mental transgression, she who acted according to her own desires,
having solicited another from her father, fell away from her yoga;
as she was falling, she saw three celestial chariots nearby.
There she saw her own ancestors, as minute as *trasareṇu* atoms—
extremely subtle and indistinct, as if placed limb within limb.
Distressed, falling with her face cast downward, she cried out to them, "Save me!"
Addressed by them, she said, "Do not fear," and because of that, she was established in heaven. Then, with a piteous voice, she propitiated her own ancestors.
Her ancestors spoke to that maiden, who had fallen from her sovereignty due to her transgression:
"O lady of pure smiles, you fall through your own fault, having been deprived of your sovereignty.
By those very bodies with which the deities undertake actions here in this world,
by those same bodies the deities obtain the fruit of those actions."
For humans, however, the rule is that good and evil deeds bear fruit through another body;
actions ripen immediately in the state of divinity, but after death in the human state.
Therefore, daughter, you fall [now], but after death you shall obtain the fruit.

"Deprived of her father, you, O maiden, have indeed come from Vasu; born from the womb of a fish, you shall become the daughter of a king. Adrikā took the form of a fish at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā."
"You shall give birth to a son who will be the heir of Parāśara;
he, a brahmin seer, will divide the single Veda into four parts,
and he will increase the fame of Śantanu, the son of Mahābhiṣak."
Having begotten these sons— the heroic Jyeṣṭha, Citrāṅgada, and the renowned Citravīra— you shall return once more; however,
due to your transgression against your ancestors, you shall obtain a contemptible birth.
"You shall indeed become the daughter of this very king Adrika;
in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will be born from the womb of a fish. Having been addressed thus by them in the past, you were born as the auspicious Satyavatī.
The excellent Apsaras known as Adrikā, having fallen into the state of a fish due to a Brahmin’s curse,
went to heaven after giving birth to you;
for it was by the king's prowess that you were born from her as that maiden.
"Therefore, O son of Vāsava—blessings be upon you—I beg for a son who shall perpetuate our lineage.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Her entire body was filled with wonder as she attained the recollection of her past lives.
She said, "O Blessed One, behold the sages standing on both banks;
while we are visible to them, how indeed can our union take place?
Thus addressed by her, the powerful Lord created a mist.
By that [mist], the entire region became as if shrouded in darkness.
Having seen that mist created by the supreme seer,
the wise maiden, both astonished and bashful, spoke.
"Know me, O Blessed One, to be a maiden who is always subject to her father's will. O sinless one, through union with you, my maidenhood would be defiled;
and once my maidenhood is defiled, O best of the twice-born, how shall I be able [to live]?"
"O wise one, I do not venture to go home, nor can I bear to remain in this house.
Having reflected upon this, O Blessed One, please ordain what must follow.
To her who had spoken thus, that best of sages was filled with joy.
"Having done what is pleasing to me, you shall remain a maiden," he said.
"Choose a boon, O timid one, whatever you desire, O beautiful lady; for never before has my favor been in vain, O lady of pure smiles."

Thus addressed, she chose as her boon the supreme fragrance of her limbs; and the Lord, the Master, granted her that which was desired by her heart. Then, having obtained the boon, she was delighted, adorned with the qualities of womanhood.
With her face bowed in modesty, she approached the presence of the Sage;
she entered into union with that seer of wondrous deeds,
and thus her name became celebrated on earth as Gandhavatī.
Men on earth could smell her fragrance from a distance of a yojana;
therefore, she became renowned by the name Yojanagandhā.
Then, in a delightful forest region, there was a place covered with divine carpets.
Having assumed the heroic posture (vīrāsana), the yogin became intent on meditation in a beautiful chamber of white silk, upon a couch covered with a fine spread;
at that time, the maiden remained silent, blazing with the splendor of yoga.

Having seen her, and having composed himself and reflected upon it again and again, the sage pondered: "What would be a meritorious deed? The conduct of the disciplined is traditionally known as 'the conduct of the disciplined' (śiṣṭācāra)."
Brahmins who know the *śruti* and *smṛti*, who understand *dharma*, and who possess wisdom, are traditionally regarded as such.

Dharma has been ordained by those twice-born ones who know *dharma* in two ways: that which is based on the *śruti* and that which is based on the *smṛti*. Indeed, charity, the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), and ritual worship are the characteristics of the *śrauta* [dharma].
The conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramācāra), joined with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), is based on tradition (smārta).

Regarding the word *dharma*, the verbal root is taught in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) as well as in the sense of "greatness" (*mahattva*). Among these, that which results in a desired fruit is designated as *dharma* by the teachers.
And because one would partake of undesirable results, unrighteousness (adharma) would prevail through them;
therefore, for the sake of obtaining desirable results, one should practice only dharma. The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, and Prājāpatya [forms of marriage] are righteous.
For Brāhmaṇas, however, the Gāndharva form of marriage is not at all righteous.
For those born of the other three castes, the Gāndharva, Āsura, and Rākṣasa forms are permitted.
The Paiśāca form must never be performed; the Paiśāca is the eighth and most base.
One should not marry a girl who is indignant, deformed, or born of her mother’s own family; nor one who is aged, a renunciant, barren, fallen, or menstruating;
nor one born into a family afflicted by epilepsy, or one who is tawny-eyed, leprous, or scarred.
"One should not approach a woman who has not bathed"— this is the instruction of the Dharma.
The father, grandfather, brother, mother, maternal uncle,
as well as the preceptor and the officiating priest, are the most authoritative in the giving away of a maiden.
"One should enjoy what is given by these [relations], and one should not take what is not given"—
thus have the seers, most learned in the Dharma, declared regarding marriage.
For this woman, there is no father, no brother, no mother, and no maternal uncle.
I do not touch her by chance through the Gāndharva form of marriage;
for the Gāndharva rite, being devoid of formal ritual, should not be performed except in times of distress.
If a son is born of her, he shall become a seer (ṛṣi) known as Vedavyāsa.
"How can a Brahmin devoid of ritual action become a seer of noble intellect?"—
while the Great Seer of purified soul was thus reflecting on this state of being,
the Pitṛs of Barhiṣ then appeared before him, having perceived his thought.
At that moment, Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā,
also arrived. Having first said "Welcome" to the hosts of ancestors, Vasiṣṭha replied:
"O Vāsavi, if you desire a son, accept without delay this daughter of our mind, born from our curse."—
Vaiśampāyana.
Having heard the words of the ancestors, Vasiṣṭha replied:
"The word of the great seers is true; I have also heard it in the Purāṇas that Parāśara, a celibate student, shall be the sustainer of my lineage for the sake of progeny."
While Vasiṣṭha was thus conversing with the ancestors,
the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest arrived there,
desiring to witness the marriage of the wise son of Śakti.
The highly blessed Arundhatī, together with Adṛśyantī,
entered the divine leaf-hut fashioned by Viśvakarman; and she prepared the marriage requisites in their proper order.

Arundhatī, taking the hand of her daughter-in-law Satyavatī with her own hand and seating her upon an auspicious throne, caused her to perform the rites of Indrāṇī during the fortnight of the waxing moon on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, under the constellation presided over by Soma.

When the thirteenth lunar day was auspiciously joined with a favorable planet and the hour known as Maitra had arrived, Vasiṣṭha, together with the sages, declared, "This is the time for the wedding," and proceeded to an island in the Yamunā accompanied by his disciples and the wives of the sages.
Having smeared a square sacrificial mound with cow dung,
it was adorned on all sides with unbroken grains, fruits, flowers, svastikas, fresh sprouts, and jars filled with water.
Then, having seated that best of sages upon a grass mat in its center, they bathed the great sage with a paste of *siddhārtha* and barley, as well as with all medicinal herbs,
and dressed him in white garments.
Having had the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) recited and being honored with unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
anointed with perfumes, wearing garlands, and carrying his goad, he then proceeds on foot to the bride’s house,
where he is honored by the bride’s kinsmen.
Having beheld the bride— bathed, clad in unwashed garments, anointed with perfumes, radiant with garlands, adorned with auspicious rites, and holding a bow in her hand—
the one who knew the proper time and understood all duties spoke these words at that opportune moment.
"Acceptance depends on the giver; such was heard by me in the past," said Vaiśampāyana. "We shall do exactly as our fathers say."
Having heard those words of the speaker of truth, which were most righteous and conducive to fame, all the ancestors— free from attachment and devoid of possessions—
summoned Vasu, who was supremely devoted to dharma, and spoke these words to him.
Your daughter, born specifically from the womb of a fish,
you ought to give according to dharma to the sage Parāśara as Vasu.
"It is true that she is my daughter; however, it was by the wise King of the Fishermen that she was won.
As for me, O protector of subjects, I am the master in the matter of bestowing daughters upon those who seek offspring.
Thus spoke the fathers.

We are all free from desire, unattached, and without possessions. A connection formed by the giving of a daughter is said to be a bond of obligation. The human realm is the field of action, while heaven is the field of enjoyment.
In this world, those who have performed meritorious deeds go to the heavenly realm; of this there is no doubt.
In this world, those who have committed evil deeds, being pitiless, go to hell. When the "bondage of the sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā-bandha) is mentioned, both merit and demerit are implied.
Bound by the fetters of sacrificial fees, those yogins fall;
therefore, O lord of the people, grant alms to this virtuous woman who, having fallen from yoga, has become your daughter through her mental conception.
Having spoken thus, all the ancestors then vanished in an instant;
they summoned Yājñavalkya, appointing him as the preceptor for the marriage ceremony.
And having summoned Vasu, Vasiṣṭha, together with the sages,
caused Vasu to perform the marriage ceremony according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas.
"O Parāśara of great wisdom, I shall give my daughter to you;
accept her—may prosperity be yours—and take her hand with your hand.
—Vaiśampāyana.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha and remaining steadfast in the opinion of Yājñavalkya,
he performed the auspicious rites of the marriage-thread and touched hand to hand;
then, having offered oblations into the fire with mantras and abundant clarified butter as the sacrificial offering, he proceeded.
Having circumambulated the fire three times and worshipped the consumer of oblations,
and having gratified the great sages, Yājñavalkya and the others, with sacrificial fees,
he quickly saluted them for permission and then performed a circumambulation.
When Parāśara had performed the marriage, the gods, together with the hosts of ṛṣis,
were delighted and departed in an instant, saying, "May he become Vedavyāsa.
The venerable Parāśara also went to his own dwelling.
Thus Satyavatī, delighted at having obtained this unsurpassed boon,
was united with Parāśara and immediately gave birth to a child;
that powerful son of Parāśara was born on an island in the Yamunā.

As soon as he was born, he grew; then, when he was seven years old, Vyāsa bathed, saluted his father, and stood there with a concentrated mind. Having uttered the words "May it be well," [his father] gave him an excellent water-pot.
Having taken the water-pot, Vyāsa stood by his side with a concentrated mind.
Then, out of fear of the fisherman, that wife bathed and became a maiden;
she saluted the feet of the sage and took her son by the hand.
As soon as he was touched, he rebuked his mother and spoke these words: "O Mother, you have become pure through contact with my father. Vaiśampāyana said:
"O blameless one, today the daughter of the fisherman shall not touch me.
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, that woman, her face filled with tears,
then fell at the feet of the sage out of her human nature.
The Blessed One, possessed of great grace and knowing the Dharma, spoke to his son:
"Do not act in such a manner; for this is not considered righteous by us. Neither mother nor father are to be reviled, especially when they have been benefactors in the past."
Because she bears him and endures suffering, the mother is more venerable than the father.
Just as grain arises from the union of seed and field in the world,
so too is a son born from the union of man and woman.
Sages who have mastered the Vedas are born even from the wombs of deer, birds, and likewise from Apsarases, as well as from the womb of a Śūdra;
such as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the son of a deer, and Kaṇva, the son of Barhiṣmat.
Both Agastya and Vasiṣṭha were begotten by him upon Urvaśī; Somaśravas was born of a female serpent, while the two Aśvins were born from the Aśvinīs.
In ancient times, Skanda was born from the spilled semen in a thicket of Śara reeds.
In this very same way is the origin of the gods and the sages;
for the worldly discourse regarding their emergence should never be subjected to critical scrutiny by the wise.
And in the Purāṇa, he was proclaimed by the Self-existent One himself as Vedavyāsa.
"You alone are the leader of the great sages and of men;
therefore, O son, Vāsavi, who practices yoga, should not be blamed. For my sake, O one of great wisdom, you ought to speak with affection."
The great sage Vaiśampāyana, a portion of Viṣṇu born for the welfare of all creatures,
said out of affection to his own mother: "O you whose wealth is asceticism, speak."
Having received the command of his preceptor, Vyāsa was then filled with joy;
reflecting upon the ways of the world, he then entered his mother’s lap. Indeed, in all the worlds, there is no happiness whatsoever that exceeds the touch of a son.
Embracing Vyāsa, whose eyes were like lotus petals,
Vāsavī wept, drenching him with a torrent of breast milk; then, smelling her son upon the crown of his head, she spoke.
"For those who desire offspring, there is nothing in this world superior to the gain of a son;
I consider that which is so difficult to attain has been acquired by me through great asceticism and, O dear one, through the power of great yoga."
"O you of great wisdom, I have indeed found you as the immortals find the nectar of immortality. Therefore, O son of a seer, it does not behove you to abandon me now.
— Vaiśampāyana.
Having been addressed thus, Vyāsa then spoke to his mother out of affection:
"O daughter of a king, you shall be satisfied with this much alone: that I have been touched by you, embraced, and repeatedly smelled upon the head."

Having attended upon his mother, he set his mind once more upon asceticism; and he said, "I shall appear when I am remembered for specific tasks. Then, having given leave to the maiden, [he added], "May she become a maiden again."
The venerable Parāśara also went together with his son;
having reached the holy hermitage of Adṛśyantī, Parāśara performed the birth rites and other sacraments according to the Dharma.
O Bhārata, having been initiated by Yājñavalkya, Vyāsa studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches through the syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures; then,
having given the teacher’s fee, he began to practice austerity.
Thus Dvaipāyana was born to Satyavatī from Parāśara;
because he was placed upon an island (*dvīpa*) while still an infant, he became known as Dvaipāyana. Being wise, he [knew] that Dharma recedes foot by foot in age after age.
Having observed the lifespan and strength of mortals according to the sequence of the ages,
and likewise out of a desire to bestow grace upon Brahmā and the Brahmins,
that learned great seer then summoned his disciples in accordance with dharma.
Because he divided the Vedas, he is remembered as Vyāsa;
he taught the Vedas, with the Mahābhārata as the fifth,
to Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and his own son Śuka.
The supreme Lord, the bestower of boons, [bestowed them] upon Vaiśampāyana;
by them, the compilations (*saṃhitā*) of the *Bhārata* were made manifest separately.
Then Satyavatī, delighted, went to her own dwelling.
From a distance of one yojana on this earth, men can smell its fragrance;
and the King of the Dāśas, smelling that fragrance, experienced great joy.
"01,057.075d@039_0004 They call you 'Fish-Smelling' (Matsyagandhā); how, O girl, can there be fragrance?
01,057.075d@039_0005 Having cast off the fish-smell, by whom was this fragrance bestowed? Satyavatī [replied].
The son of Śakti, renowned as the highly wise Parāśara,
having seen my extreme loathsomeness as I was rowing the boat,
cast off his own fishy odor and bestowed upon me a fragrance that reached for a league.
Seeing the grace of the seer, the people attained great joy.
"In this way, I have obtained the fragrance; you ought not to be angry," said Vaiśampāyana.
The King of the Daśārhas praised those words and rejoiced. Having heard this supreme, purifying, and meritorious history originating from Vyāsa, people become endowed with progeny.
Likewise, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, of immeasurable splendor, great heroism, and great fame, was born of Gaṅgā through the seed of the Vasus;
he was a venerable rishi, a learned brahmin, and a knower of the meaning of the Vedas.

In former times, the ancient seer known as Aṇīmāṇḍavya, who was highly renowned and not a thief, was impaled upon a stake under suspicion of being a thief. Having summoned Dharma, that great seer spoke these words in the past.
"O Dharma, I remember that single sin: out of childishness, I pierced a small bird with a blade of grass. I do not recall any other evil deed.
Why, then, has my asceticism—which is equal to a thousandfold—failed to conquer this [sin] here?"
"Since the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is weightier than the killing of any other living being,
