you shall therefore be born from a Śūdra womb because of this sin. By that curse, Dharma was also born from a Śūdra womb.
The wise and righteous Vidura was born as a sinless body; and Saṃjaya, who was like a sage, was born as a Sūta from Gavalgaṇa.
And from the Sun-god, the great chariot-warrior Karṇa was born of Kuntī’s maidenhood.
Wearing his innate armor, his face illuminated by earrings,
Viṣṇu— honored by the worlds— manifested from Vasudeva and Devakī for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds, he of great renown.

The God who is without beginning or end is the creator and the Lord of the universe. He is the origin of all origins; he is the uncreated creator and the sovereign Lord. He is the unmanifest, imperishable Brahman, the primary cause (pradhāna) whose nature is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
The self, which is indeed imperishable, the primordial nature, the supreme source, the Puruṣa who is the architect of the universe, the union with pure being, the eternal and indestructible,
the infinite and immovable God, the Haṃsa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
They call him the Ordainer, undecaying and eternal, the supreme and immutable;
he is absolute liberation, devoid of qualities, the universe itself, without beginning, unborn, and imperishable.
He is the all-pervading Puruṣa, the creator, the grandfather of all beings.
For the sake of increasing the Dharma, he was born among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis—
those two of great heroism, skilled in weapons and proficient in all arms.
Whatever one attains, whatever one takes up, and whatever sense-objects one experiences;
And because that which is his constant state is called the "Self" (ātman),
Sātyaki and Kṛtavarman— both devoted to Nārāyaṇa and experts in weapons— were born respectively from Satyaka and Hṛdika.
Hṛdika, Kṛtavarman, and Yuyudhāna Sātyaki;
and from the spilled seed of Bharadvāja, which grew within a wooden vessel (*droṇī*),
Droṇa was born from that great seer of fierce asceticism.
From Gautama Śaradvat, a couple was born from a clump of reeds:
Kṛpa of great strength and the mother of Aśvatthāman.
Then Aśvatthāman, the best among those who wield weapons, was born from Droṇa.
He was created by the Great-Souled Creator for the destruction of Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
likewise, Dhṛṣṭadyumna himself, possessing a splendor equal to fire itself,
was born from the sacrificial fire while the ritual was being performed.
The heroic and powerful [Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana] was born from the sacrificial altar along with his bow for the destruction of Droṇa;
likewise, the radiant and auspicious Kṛṣṇā was also born there,
shining with a beautiful form and possessing supreme beauty.

From him was born Nagnajit, the disciple of Prahrāda, and also Subala. Due to his provocation of the gods, his offspring were born as destroyers of righteousness. Likewise, there was Śakuni, the son of Subala and king of the Gāndhāras.
Both Duryodhana’s mother and [Gāndhārī] were born as those who understood worldly affairs. From Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana was born Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
in the wife of Vicitravīrya, and likewise the mighty Pāṇḍu.
Skilled in both dharma and artha, wise, intelligent, and cleansed of all taints,
Vidura was born from Dvaipāyana in a Śūdra womb. To Pāṇḍu, however, five sons were born individually, each equal to a god.
Among those two women, Yudhiṣṭhira was the eldest by virtue of his qualities. Yudhiṣṭhira was born from Dharma; Vṛkodara was born from Marut;
and the illustrious Dhanañjaya, the best among all wielders of weapons, was born from Indra.
Both Nakula and Sahadeva were born from the Aśvins, endowed with beauty and devoted to the service of their elders;
likewise, a hundred sons were born to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Duryodhana and the others, as well as Yuyutsu and Karṇa,
O Bhārata, and then Duḥśāsana, Duḥsaha,
Durmarṣaṇa, Vikarṇa, Citrasena, and Vivimśati.
Jaya, Satyavrata, Purumitra, O Bhārata,
and Yuyutsu, the son of a Vaiśya woman— these eleven were great car-warriors (*mahāratha*s).
Abhimanyu was born to Subhadrā from Arjuna.
The nephew of Vāsudeva and grandson of the high-souled Pāṇḍu,
five sons were born to him from Kṛṣṇā; even more than the five Pāṇḍavas,
these princes were endowed with beauty and were experts in all weapons.
Prativindhya was born from Yudhiṣṭhira, Sutasoma from Vṛkodara,
Śrutakīrti from Arjuna, and Śatānīka from the son of Nakula;
likewise, the powerful Śrutasena was born from Sahadeva.
And from Bhīma and Hiḍimbā was born Ghaṭotkaca in the forest.
Śikhaṇḍin was born to Drupada as a daughter who attained manhood,
whom the Yakṣa Sthūṇa had turned into a male out of a desire to do her a favor.
Then, in that conflict of the Kurus, many hundreds of thousands of kings gathered together, intending to fight in the battle. Their names were all immeasurable in every respect.
"It is not possible to enumerate them even in tens of thousands of years;
however, these principal ones have been recited, by whom this narrative was expanded.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, I wish to hear correctly about those who have been mentioned and those others who have not been mentioned, as well as other radiant kings—
for what purpose were these god-like great chariot-warriors born here?"
"O highly fortunate one, you ought to explain this to me correctly as it exists on earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, we have heard that this is indeed a secret of the gods."
I shall relate that to you after bowing to the Self-Existent One.
In ancient times, having cleared the earth of the Kṣatriya caste twenty-one times,
the son of Jamadagni performed austerities on Mahendra, the best of mountains.

Then, O King, when the world had been rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas by the descendant of Bhṛgu, the Kṣatriya women who desired offspring approached the Brāhmaṇas. Those Brāhmaṇas of rigid vows united with them.
O tiger among men, at every proper season— and never out of season—
those thousands of Kṣatriya women conceived from them;
and then, O King, they gave birth to Kṣatriyas esteemed for their prowess.

And [he begot] sons and daughters for the further increase of the kṣatriya power. Thus, O King, that kṣatriya race which had perished was raised up by ascetic brahmins through kṣatriya women, exactly as it was proclaimed by the Self-existent One himself.
O Lord of the Earth, when all the social orders have perished,
it is the Brāhmaṇas alone who, in age after age, perpetually restore them; they cause what has been born to prosper through righteousness and endow it with very long life.
Then, O protector of the earth, because they maintained their own duty (*svadharma*), the four castes (*varṇas*) all became those for whom the Brāhmaṇas were foremost. At that time,
men approached women only during their fertile period (*ṛtu*), neither out of lust nor outside of that period.
In that same way, O bull of the Bharatas, other beings— even those born of animal wombs— approached their mates only during the proper season;
then they flourished through righteousness, living for hundreds and thousands of years.
O protector of the earth, those subjects were entirely devoted to the vows of dharma;

all the men were completely liberated from both mental anxieties and physical diseases. Then, they [ruled] this earth, which has the ocean for its boundary and whose entirety is traversed by lordly elephants.
He presided once more over the Kṣatriya power, including its mountains, forests, and groves. While he was again ruling this earth according to dharma,
the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, attained the highest joy.

Having cast aside the defects arising from desire and anger, the lords of men protected their subjects by administering punishment to those deserving of it in accordance with dharma. While the kṣatriyas were thus devoted to dharma, the thousand-eyed Śatakratu [Indra] [remained satisfied].
In pleasant regions and at the proper time, the rain fell, nourishing all creatures.
O lord of men, no child died then,
nor did anyone know a woman before reaching youth.
O bull of the Bharatas, by these noble women, who were like daughters,
this earth was filled to its ocean-boundaries;
and the Kṣatriyas performed great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
At that time, O King, the Brahmins studied the Vedas along with their limbs and Upaniṣads; they did not sell the Veda,
nor did they ever utter the Vedas in the presence of Śūdras.

In this world on earth, the Vaiśyas practiced agriculture with oxen; they did not yoke a cow to the burden, and they sustained even those whose limbs were emaciated. Likewise, men did not milk calves that were still drinking froth.
At that time, O tiger among men, merchants did not sell their wares using false measures;
and men, devoted to dharma and perceiving only dharma, performed their duties in accordance with righteousness.
O lord of men, all the social classes were devoted to their own respective duties;
they followed only the Dharma and perceived no wrongdoing. All the subjects remained perfectly established in their own tasks.
Thus, O tiger among men, at that time dharma did not diminish anywhere.
Cows and women gave birth in their proper seasons, O bull of the Bharatas,
and trees bore flowers and fruits according to the seasons.
O King, while the Kṛta Yuga was thus proceeding perfectly,
the entire earth became densely filled with many living beings.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, when the world of humans had flourished, [the following occurred].
O bull among men, the Asuras were born in the wombs of kings;
for at that time, the Daityas, having been repeatedly defeated in battle by the Ādityas and cast down from their sovereignty, were reborn here upon the earth.
O Lord, O Indra among kings, desiring divinity here among humans, those wise Asuras were born upon this earth among various beings—
among cows, horses, donkeys, camels, and buffaloes.
O protector of the earth, because of those born here among flesh-eating spirits, elephants, and deer—
both those already born and those currently being born—
this earth was unable to support herself by her own power.
Then, certain sons of Diti and Danu, endowed with great strength, were born as rulers of the earth; fallen from that world to this one,
they were heroic and arrogant, assuming various forms upon the earth.
These subduers of enemies traversed this earth bounded by the ocean,
oppressing the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
and by their might they oppressed all other living beings as well.
Terrifying and striking down various hosts of beings, O King, they roamed everywhere across the earth by the hundreds of thousands,
assailing the great seers dwelling in their hermitages here and there.
O protector of the earth, this world, oppressed by those great asuras who were intoxicated with the pride of their prowess and the strength of their arrogance,
and who were thus swollen with power and force,
approached Brahmā.

O King, neither the wind, nor the serpents, nor the mountains were then able to support this earth when it was forcibly overwhelmed by the Dānavas. Thereupon, O protector of the earth, the world, afflicted by the burden and oppressed by fear—

She went for refuge to the god who is the grandfather of all beings. She beheld the imperishable god Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, surrounded by highly fortunate gods, twice-born brahmins, and great seers.
Being praised with joy by Gandharvas and Apsarases who were intent on the duties of bards, she approached and paid homage to him;
then the Earth, seeking refuge, made this petition to him.
O Bhārata, in the presence of all the world-protectors,
that task for the earth— which pertains to the Self of Pradhāna—
was already known beforehand to the Self-existent Parameṣṭhin, O King.
"O Bhārata, why indeed would the Creator not be fully aware of everything that is in the minds of the gods, the asuras, and all the worlds without exception? To him,
O great king, the powerful lord of the earth spoke regarding the Earth.
The source of all beings, the Lord, Śambhu, the Lord of Creatures— O Vasundharā, for whatever purpose you have come into my presence,
for that purpose I shall employ all the dwellers of heaven.
"Arise, go to your own place, O Earth!
Having spoken thus and dismissed the Earth, O King, that god Brahmā,
the creator of beings, himself then gave instructions to all the deities.

"In order to remove the burden of this earth, he said, 'Be born upon this very earth, each in separate portions, for the sake of opposition. And in that same manner, having assembled the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,"
The Blessed One spoke these supreme words to them all:
"Be born among humans through your own portions, according to your desire.
Then Śakra and all the others, having heard the words of the Preceptor of the Gods, [acted accordingly].
Then they accepted his words, which were true, meaningful, and beneficial.
Having made their preparations to depart for the earth with all their respective portions,
they approached Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa, the slayer of enemies.
He who holds the discus and mace in his hands, who is clothed in yellow garments and possesses a dark luster;
he whose navel is a lotus, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, with large, beautiful, and curved eyes;
the Lord of the Lords of Creatures, the God, the Sovereign of the Suras, endowed with great strength.
Marked with the Śrīvatsa, Hṛṣīkeśa, worshipped by all the deities—
that Hari, the best of gods— also took birth among humans.
To that Supreme Person, Indra spoke for the sake of purifying the earth.
"Descend with a portion [of yourself]," and Hari said "So be it" to him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Indra entered into an agreement with Nārāyaṇa.
Having personally commanded all the inhabitants of heaven to descend to earth from the celestial realm together with the gods by their respective portions,
Śakra himself departed once more from that abode of Nārāyaṇa.
For the destruction of the enemies of the immortals and for the welfare of all the worlds,
those celestial dwellers descended from heaven to this earth in succession.
Then, they were born into the lineages of the Brahman-sages and the families of the royal seers.
O tiger among kings, the denizens of heaven were born according to their desire;
they likewise slew Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas,
as well as many other man-eating creatures in great numbers.
O best of the Bharatas, neither the Dānavas, nor the Rākṣasas, nor the Gandharvas, nor the Pannagas could slay them, even in their childhood, for they were established in strength. Janamejaya said:
And those who were the leaders of the Dānavas, as well as of the Bhujagas and Rākṣasas;
likewise of the hosts of Devas and Dānavas, and of the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
and of all human beings, as well as of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
"I wish to hear in truth the entire account of their origins from the beginning, as well as that of all living beings in every respect; for you are all-knowing.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Come now, having paid homage to the Self-Existent One, I shall fully describe to you the origin and dissolution of the worlds beginning with the gods,
as well as the origin and dissolution of all living beings in every respect.
Six great sages are known as the mind-born sons of Brahmā:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, and from Kaśyapa these creatures [descended].
Thirteen highly fortunate daughters of Dakṣa were born:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, Muni,
Krodhā, Prāvā, Ariṣṭā, Vinatā, and Kapilā.
And Kadrū, O tiger among men, was also a daughter of Dakṣa, O Bhārata. The sons and grandsons of these women, endowed with great prowess, were infinite in number.
From Aditi were born the twelve Ādityas, the lords of the world.
O King, O Bhārata, I shall proclaim to you by name those who were born from them:
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Śakra, Varuṇa, and Aṃśa;
as well as Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Savitṛ as the tenth.
Likewise, Tvaṣṭṛ is the eleventh, and Viṣṇu is called the twelfth;
he was the youngest-born of all the Ādityas and was superior in qualities. Diti is remembered to have had only one son, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
These five sons of that high-souled one were renowned by name:
Prahrāda was the eldest of them, followed by Saṃhrāda;
Anuhrāda was the third, and after him came Śibi and Bāṣkala.
O Bhārata, Prahrāda had three sons who were famous everywhere:
Virocana, Kumbha, and Nikumbha—these are the renowned ones.
The son of Virocana was the powerful Bali alone.
And the celebrated son of Bala was the great Asura named Bāṇa,
the illustrious follower of Rudra whom they know as Mahākāla. O Bhārata, forty sons of Danu are renowned everywhere.
The first-born among them was the king Vipracitti of great renown;
also well-known were Śambara, Namuci, Puloman,
Asiloman, Keśin, and the Dānava Durjaya.
Ayaḥśiras, Aśvaśiras, and the powerful Ayaḥśaṅku; likewise Gaganamūrdhan, Vegavān, and he who is Ketumān;
Svarbhānu, Aśva, Aśvapati, Vṛṣaparvan, and Añjaka.
Aśvagrīva, Sūkṣma, and the great asura Tuhuṇḍa; Isṛpa, Ekacakra, Virūpākṣa, Harāhara, Nicandra, Nikumbha, Kupatha, and likewise Kāpatha.
Śarabha and Śalabha, as well as Sūrya and Candramas—
these are the Dānavas celebrated as being renowned in the lineage of Danu.
However, there are indeed two others who are considered to be the Sūrya and Candramas of the gods.
Furthermore, O Great King, there were two others among the leaders of the Dānavas, namely Sūrya and Candramas;
these ten foremost Dānavas, sons of Danu, are celebrated in this lineage as beings of great courage and immense strength.
Ekākṣa, Mṛtapā, Vīra, Pralamba, Naraka,
Vātāpi, Śatrutapana, the great asura Śaṭha,
Gaviṣṭha, Danāyu, and the Dānava Dīrghajihva.
O Bhārata, their sons and grandsons are remembered as being innumerable.
Siṃhikā gave birth to a son, Rāhu, the oppressor of the moon and sun,
as well as Sucandra, Candrahantṛ, and Candravimardana.
The endless host of sons and grandsons of that cruel woman, who were of a cruel nature, was known as the *Krodhavaśa* group; they were performers of cruel deeds and crushers of their enemies.
Furthermore, the sons of Anāyuṣ were four bulls among the Asuras.
Vikṣara, Balavīra, and the great asura Vṛtra—
these were the celebrated sons of Kālā, who were like Death itself in their striking power. Renowned on earth for their great heroism, they were the subduers of enemies among the Dānavas.
Vināśana, Krodha, Hantṛ, another Krodha,
and likewise another, Krodhaśatru— these are renowned as the Kāleyas. Śukra, the son of a seer, was the preceptor of the Asuras.
The four sons of Uśanas are well known as the officiating priests for the Asuras:
Tvaṣṭṛ, Avara, Atri, and two others who perform rites with mantras;
they are equal to the sun in splendor and are the originators of the world of Brahmā.
"Thus has this origin of the lineages of the powerful Asuras and Suras been told to you, as heard by me from the Purāṇa. However,
it is not possible to describe their offspring in their entirety."
O protector of the earth, it is impossible to enumerate their infinite qualities. Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, as well as Garuḍa and Aruṇa,
Āruṇi and Vāruṇi— these are known as the Vainateyas.
Śeṣa, Ananta, Vāsuki, and the serpent Takṣaka; Kūrma, Kulika, and the other mighty sons of Kadrū;
as well as Bhīmasena, Ugrasena, Suparṇa, and Varuṇa.
Gopati, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Sūryavarcas as the seventh; Anetra, Varhaparṇa, and likewise he who was the lord of Kāśī;
Patravat, Arkaparṇa, and the renowned Prayuta.
Bhīma, Citraratha, and the renowned Sarvavid Vaśin; likewise, O King, Śāliśiras as the fourteenth, Pradyumna as the fifteenth,
and Kali as the sixteenth, and Nārada as the seventeenth.
Thus have these divine Gandharvas, the Mauneyas, been fully described.
Now, O Bhārata, I shall proclaim other beings:
Anavadyā, Anuvaśā, Anūnā, Aruṇā, and Priyā.
From Prāvā was born Anūpā, Subhagā, and Bhāsī;
Siddha, Pūrṇa, Barhī, the highly renowned Pūrṇāśa,
Brahmacārī, Ratiguṇa, and Suparṇa as the seventh.
Viśvāvasu, Bhānu, and Sucandra as the tenth—
these are proclaimed as the Devagandharvas known as the Prāveyas. Now, hear this lineage of the Apsarases, renowned for its auspicious characteristics.
In former times, the highly fortunate goddess Menakā gave birth to them from the divine ṛṣi:
Sahajanyā, Pārṣṇī,
Puñjikasthalā, Ghṛtasthalā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, and likewise Urvaśī.
Alambusā, Miśrakeśī, Vidyutparṇā, Tulānaghā,
Aruṇā, Rakṣitā, Rambhā— who is likewise charming— and Asitā, Subāhu, Suvratā, and Subhujā.
Supriya, Atibāhu, the renowned Hāhā and Hūhū,
and Tumburu— these four are remembered as the most excellent of the Gandharvas. Furthermore, Jānibāhu is renowned, as are Hāhā and Hūhū.
The nectar of immortality, the Brahmins, the cows, and likewise the Gandharvas and Apsarases—
these are proclaimed in the Purāṇa as the offspring of Kapilā.
Thus, the origin of all beings has been recounted by me to you.
Just as the number of Gandharvas and Apsarases has been correctly enumerated,
so too have those of the Bhujangas, Suparṇas, Rudras, and Maruts,
as well as of cows and glorious Brahmins of meritorious deeds.

It bestows long life, merit, and wealth, and brings delight to the ear; it should be constantly heard and recited by one free from malice. Furthermore, whoever should read this lineage with regularity—
In the presence of great-souled ones and the gods of the Brahmins,
he obtains abundant offspring,
as well as prosperity, fame, and a beautiful state after death.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Six great sages are known as the mind-born sons of Brahmā;
eleven sons of Sthāṇu are celebrated as the supreme mind-born ones.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and the highly illustrious Nirṛti;
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Paraṃtapa; Dahana, Īśvara, and the immensely radiant Kapālin.
Sthāṇu and the blessed Bhava are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu—
these six are the powerful great sages who are the sons of Brahmā.
Three sons of Aṅgiras are renowned throughout the world:
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, and Saṃvarta, all firm in their vows.
O lord of men, it is heard that Atri had many sons.
All the great ṛṣis, who were knowers of the Vedas, perfected beings, and tranquil in soul,
as well as the Rākṣasas, Vānaras, Kiṃnaras,
and Yakṣas, O tiger among men, were the sons of that wise Pulastya.
O King, the deer, lions, tigers, and kimpuruṣas are known as the sons of Pulaha; likewise, the śarabhas, lions,
kimpuruṣas, tigers, bears, and hyenas are also proclaimed to be his offspring.
From Kratu were born sons equal to him in wisdom, who moved together with the sun-birds (Pataṅga),
renowned throughout the three worlds and devoted to the vow of truth. But the blessed sage Dakṣa was born from the right thumb.
O protector of the earth, from the thumb of Brahmā was born a son, the best among those who possess sons; he was the wife of that high-souled one. From her, that very sage begot fifty daughters.
All those girls, possessing faultless limbs and lotus-like eyes,
were appointed as *putrikās* by Prajāpati, who had lost his sons.
He gave ten of them to Dharma and twenty-seven to Indu.
O King, by divine ordinance, thirteen lawful wives were given to Kaśyapa; hear from me their names as they are proclaimed:
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, and likewise Kriyā.
Intellect, modesty, and understanding—these ten are the wives of Dharma.
These gates of Dharma were ordained by the Self-Existent One.
Twenty-seven wives of Soma are renowned in the world.
The wives of Soma, devoted to auspicious vows, are engaged in the regulation of time;
all of them, conjoined with the lunar mansions, are established in the maintenance of the world's course.
The Grandsire is the divine sage, and his son is Prajāpati.
He had eight sons who were the Vasus; I shall describe them in detail:
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Aha, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are remembered as the eight Vasus.
Dhara was the son of Dhūmrā, as were Brahmavidya and Dhruva; Candramas was the son of Manasvinī, and Śvasana was the son of Śvasā; Ahar was the son of Ratā, and Hutāśana was the son of Śāṇḍilī.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are remembered as the two sons of Prabhātā.
Dharā’s sons were Draviṇa and Hutahavyavaha. Āpa’s sons were Vaitaṇḍya, Śrama, Śrānta, and Muni.
The lord Kāla, the destroyer of the worlds, was the son of Dhruva. Soma’s son was Varcas, by whom Varcasvin is born;
[Soma’s other sons were] Śiśira, Prāṇa, and likewise Ramaṇa, born of Manoharā.
Jyotis, Śrama, Śānta, and likewise Muni are remembered as the sons of Ahna. The illustrious Kumāra, whose abode is the forest of reeds (Śaravaṇa), is the son of Agni;
his younger brothers are Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameśa.
And because he was born under the constellation Kṛttikā, he is remembered as Kārttikeya. Śivā was the wife of Anila; her son was Purojava.
The highly fortunate Viśvakarman was his son, and Manojava was his son.
Avijñātagati was indeed one of the two sons of Anila;
they know Pratyūṣa’s son to be the ṛṣi named Devala. Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise.
Śaṅkha and Likhita were both experts in all the scriptures;
the sister of Bṛhaspati was an excellent woman who observed celibacy,
and having attained perfection through yoga, she wanders throughout the entire world unattached.
She was the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus,
and she gave birth to Viśvakarman, the foremost among all masters of the arts. The highly fortunate Viśvakarman was born as the lord of craftsmen.
He is the creator of thousands of crafts and the carpenter of the thirty gods;
he is the maker of all ornaments and the best among artisans,
who indeed fashioned the celestial chariots of the deities.
Men subsist upon the craft of that great-souled one,
whom they constantly worship as the imperishable Viśvakarman; then,
having pierced the right breast of Brahmā, he appeared in human form.
The Blessed Dharma has emerged, bringing happiness to the entire world.
He has three excellent sons who captivate the hearts of all beings: Śama, Kāma, and Harṣa, who sustain the world through their splendor.
Rati was the wife of Kāma, and Prāpti was the wife of Śama;
Nandī was the wife of Harṣa, upon whom the worlds are established. Marīci’s son was Kaśyapa, and from Kaśyapa came the gods and the asuras.
O tiger among kings, he was the source of the worlds; from him they were born.
Now, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, the wife of Savitṛ, assuming the form of a mare, that highly blessed lady gave birth to both the Aśvins in the mid-air.

O lord of men, there are exactly twelve sons of Aditi, headed by Śakra; among them, Viṣṇu is the youngest, upon whom the worlds are established. These are the thirty-three gods; of them, I shall [speak] to you.
I shall now fully declare the lineage according to its branches, families, and groups:
the other group of the Rudras, as well as that of the Sādhyas and the Maruts;
one should know the Bhārgavas to belong to the Vasus, and likewise the Viśvedevas.
Vainateya, Garuḍa, the powerful Aruṇa,
and the lord Bṛhaspati are likewise counted among the Ādityas.
Know that from the Aśvins come the Guhyakas, as well as all medicinal herbs and animals.
O King, this host of gods has been recited to you in their proper order;
by reciting this, a human being is liberated from all sins. Having pierced the heart of Brahmā, the blessed Bhṛgu emerged.
The son of Bhṛgu, the wise and learned Śukra, the planet who is the son of Kavi,
having been appointed by the Self-Existent One for the sake of sustaining life in the three worlds— regarding rain and drought, fear and security— roams throughout the universe.
The great-minded Yogācārya became the preceptor of the Daityas; he was also the wise teacher of the gods, a celibate observer of strict vows.
First of all, Śaṇḍa and Mārka appeared, renowned for their fierce splendor.
When that descendant of Bhṛgu had been appointed by the Lord for the sake of security and prosperity,
Bhṛgu begot another irreproachable son—
Cyavana, who was radiant in asceticism, righteous-souled, and wise.
O Bhārata, he who had fallen from his mother’s womb out of anger for the sake of liberation was that high-souled one; Sukanyā was indeed the wife of that great-souled one,
while Āruṣī, the daughter of Manu, was the wife of that wise sage.
The highly illustrious Aurva was born from her by bursting through her thigh;
he was a man of great asceticism and great splendor, endowed with all virtues even as a child. Ricīka was his son, and from him Jamadagni was born.
The high-souled Jamadagni had four sons;
among them, Rāma was the youngest, yet he was endowed with qualities that were not inferior.
Skilled in all weapons and missiles, self-controlled, he was the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas.
Aurva had a hundred sons, headed by Jamadagni;
from them were born thousands of sons, who constituted the expansion of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Furthermore, Brahmā had two other sons, the characteristics of whom persist to this day.
In this world, Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ abide together with Manu;
their sister is the auspicious goddess Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus. Her mind-born sons are the horses that travel through the sky.

The eldest wife of Varuṇa, the goddess Śukrā, gave birth to her son Bala and to Surā, who brings joy to the gods. Know that because of their mutual devouring of one another, those creatures who desired food [fell into ruin].
Therein was born Adharma, the destroyer of all beings. His wife was Nirṛti, from whom the Rākṣasas originated;
she had three terrible sons who were always devoted to evil deeds.
Fear itself, Great Fear, Death, and likewise the Ender of Beings— He has no wife, nor any son, for He is the Finisher.
[She gave birth to] Kākī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī.
The goddess Tāmrā gave birth to these five daughters, world-renowned:
Bhāsī, Krauñcī, Śukī, and likewise Dhṛtarāṣṭrī as the fourth; they were the wives of Garuḍa. Learn from me now of their offspring.
Kākī gave birth to owls, and Śyenī gave birth to hawks;
Bhāsī gave birth to Bhasas and vultures, O lord of men;
and Dhṛtarāṣṭrī gave birth to swans and all kinds of Kalahaṃsas.
That beautiful woman gave birth to ruddy geese— blessings be upon you— and the high-minded Śukī, O knower of dharma, gave birth to parrots;
she was endowed with auspicious qualities and honored by every mark of excellence.
She gave birth to nine female offspring of the Krodhavaśā class, born from her own self: Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Harī, Bhadramanā,
Mātaṅgī, Śārdūlī, Śvetā, and Surabhī.
She was endowed with all auspicious marks, delightful, and illustrious. O son of the best of men, all deer were the offspring of Mṛgī,
while bears, sṛmaras, and camaras were the offspring of Mṛgamandā.
Then Bhadramanā gave birth to a son, the nāga Airāvata;
his son was the divine nāga Airāvata, the great elephant.
And from Haryā were born offspring who were monkeys and swift-moving apes.
"May you be blessed; they say the golāṅgūlas are the sons of Haryā.
Then, O Bhārata, Śārdūlī gave birth to lions and tigers, and all the leopards as well, O highly fortunate one; of this there is no doubt."
O lord of men, the Mātaṅgas were the offspring of Mātaṅgī;
Śvetā, however, gave birth to the swift-moving elephant of the quarter known as Śveta.
Likewise, O King, Surabhi indeed gave birth to two daughters.
"May you be blessed; Rohiṇī and the illustrious Gandharvī, as well as Vimalā and Amalā—may you be blessed, O Bhārata. From Rohiṇī were born cows, and from Gandharvī were born horses as sons."
O King, Surasā gave birth to the Nāgas, and Kadrū to the Pannagas. From Irā were born three lotus-eyed daughters,
who became the mothers of forest trees, common trees, and creeping plants.

Two types of climbing plants (*latā*) are mentioned, and they are known as creepers (*vīrudh*). Those who forcibly take their flowers and fruits separately should be known as *sutā*; them alone they call *vanaspati*.
They know that from flowers come fruit-bearing trees, and from roots, sprouts; likewise, creepers, shrubs, climbing vines, species of bast-fiber plants,
and grasses— these are the lineages of her offspring, and therein the family tree comes to its end.
Anala also gave birth to seven trees that bear fruit as edible balls (*piṇḍaphala*).
Śukī was the daughter of Anala, while Surasā was the daughter of Kadrū. Śyenī, however, was the wife of Aruṇa; they had two sons who were both heroic and possessed of great strength.
She gave birth to Saṃpāti and likewise to Jaṭāyu;
Kadrū gave birth to the serpent Ananta, the supporter of the earth.
Vinatā, however, had two sons who were renowned as Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
Thus, O lord of men, best among the wise, I have correctly proclaimed this origin of all great beings;
having heard this properly, a person becomes purified of sin.
He attains omniscience and finds the supreme goal.
Janamejaya said:
"Of the gods, the Dānavas, the Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas..."
O Blessed One, I desire to hear in truth about the great-souled ones among human beings, as well as lions, tigers, deer, serpents, birds, and all other living beings.
"The birth and deeds of these beings, in their proper sequence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Indra among men, those dwellers of heaven who were born among human beings—"
First, I shall describe to you in their entirety those who were Dānavas.
He who was known as Vipracitti, the bull among the Dānavas,
became known as Jarāsaṃdha, the bull among men.
O King, he who is known as Hiraṇyakaśipu, the son of Diti,
was born in the world of men as Śiśupāla, that bull among men. And he who was the younger brother of Prahlāda, renowned as Saṃhrāda, [was likewise born there].
He was born as the bull among the Bāhlīkas, renowned as Śalya. As for the energetic Anuhrāda, who was known as the youngest-born,
he became the lord of men celebrated as Dhṛṣṭaketu.
O King, he who was celebrated among the Daityas by the name Śibi became the monarch on earth renowned as Druma.
And he who was the best of Asuras among them, named Bāṣkala, [became the king known as Bāhlīka].
He was the lord of men known as Bhagadatta. There were also Ayaḥśiras, Aśvaśiras, the heroic Ayaḥśaṅku, as well as Gaganamūrdhan, and Vegavat was the fifth among them.

O King, these five powerful and great Asuras were born as high-souled and most excellent bulls among monarchs among the Kekayas. One of them was renowned as Ketumān, who was possessed of great majesty.
He became the king on earth known as Amitaujas;
and that illustrious great Asura who was known as Svarbhānu became the lord of men known as Ugrasena,
a ruler of fierce deeds.

The illustrious great asura who was known as Aśva became the king named Aśoka, possessed of great heroism and prowess. O King, he who was the younger brother of that [asura] is remembered as Aśvapati.
That son of Diti became King Hārdikya, a bull among men;
that illustrious great Asura who was known as Vṛṣaparvan became the king on earth known as Dīrghaprajña.
O King, he who was the younger brother of Vṛṣaparvan, Ajaka,
became a king on earth renowned as Malla. And that powerful great Asura known as Aśvagrīva—
He became the king on earth known as Rocamāna. O King, he who was celebrated as the wise and illustrious Sūkṣma became the ruler of the earth renowned as Bṛhanta.
The foremost of the Asuras who was known as Tuhuṇḍa became the lord of men celebrated as Senābindu. Among those Asuras, he who was the most powerful, named Isṛpa—
There was a king on earth named Pāpajit, renowned for his prowess;
he who had been the great asura known as Ekacakra became the celebrated Prativindhya upon the earth.
The Daitya Virūpākṣa, that great Asura who fought with diverse tactics,
became on earth the king renowned as Citravarma.
And Hara, the heroic and best of Dānavas, who was the destroyer of his enemies, [became the king known as Arihara].
Known as Suvāstu, that bull among men was born;
he was the highly energetic Ahas, the destroyer of the enemy faction,
who became the king named Bāhlīka, renowned upon the earth.
The best of asuras, who was Nicandra and Candravaktra,
became that illustrious king known as Muñjakeśa.
And Nikumbha, unconquered in battle, was born as the highly intelligent Mahāmati.
On earth, the best of kings was known as Devādhipa;
that great Asura among the Daityas named Śarabha became the royal sage (rājarṣi) named Paurava here among men.
O King, the illustrious and very powerful great Asura Kāpatha was born on earth as the renowned monarch Supārśva;
and the great Asura Kratha, O King, was born on earth as the royal sage Rājarṣi.
The one among those Asuras who was known as Pārvateya, resembling a mountain of gold,
became the second,
namely Prahrāda Bāhlīka, who was a lord of men.
The son of Diti named Candra, who was like the lord of stars in the world,
became famous as Candravarman, the king of the Kambojas. Furthermore, he who was the preeminent among the Danavas, known as Arka, [became the ruler of the Kalingas].
O best of kings, know that the royal sage named Ṛṣika was formerly the most excellent of Asuras known as Mṛtapā;
he was the king of Paścimānūpaka.
The great Asura Gaviṣṭha, who was renowned for his great splendor,
became the king on earth known as Drumasena.
And the illustrious great Asura who was celebrated as Mayūra, [became the king known as Citraratha].
He became the lord of the earth, renowned as Viśva; and he who was his younger brother, known as Suparṇa,
became the king on earth celebrated as Kālakīrti.
The foremost asura among them who was celebrated as Candrahanta became the royal sage named Śunaka, a lord of men. And the great asura who was called Vināśana of the Moon [became...]
O lord of men, that royal sage known as Dīrghajihva, who was described as a bull among the Dānavas, became the ruler of the earth celebrated on this world as Kāśirāja. He was the king named Jānaki.
The lioness gave birth to that *graha* who is the crusher of the moon and sun;
he became the king of men widely known as Krātha.
Among the four sons of Anāyuṣ, the Asura was the most eminent.
The energetic one named Vikṣara became King Vasumitra;
the second great Asura, who was the first after Vikṣara,
became the king renowned as Pāṃsurāṣṭrādhipa.
He who was the best of the Asuras, known as Balavīra,
became the lord of men named Pauṇḍramatsyaka.
And he who was the great Asura widely renowned as Vṛtra, O King, [became Śālva].
There was a royal sage named Maṇimān who became a lord of men;
his younger brother, the asura known as Krodhahantṛ,
became the king on earth celebrated as Daṇḍa.
He who was celebrated as Krodhavardhana became the lord of men known as Daṇḍadhāra. As for the sons of Kālakāya, eight among them were lords of men.
O tiger among kings, they were born with prowess equal to that of tigers.
Among them, the illustrious Jayatsena became the king in Magadha;
he was the foremost of those eight great Asuras known as the Kāleyas.
The second among them,
O King, was the illustrious Aparājita, who resembled Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra;
the third, however, was a great Asura with mighty arms.
The lord of the Niṣādas was born on earth, possessed of terrible prowess. He who was proclaimed as the fourth among them became renowned on earth as Śreṇimān, the best of royal sages.
The fifth among them was the preeminent great asura,
who became renowned here as Mahaujas, the scorcher of his foes. The sixth among them was indeed the wise great asura.
The best of royal sages (rājarṣi) on earth, renowned as Abhīru,
was the seventh among them; he who was the preeminent great Asura became King Samudrasena from that very group.
O King, the eighth among those Kāleyas was named Bṛhat, a scorcher of foes who was renowned throughout the earth as far as the ocean’s edge, a knower of the truth of dharma and artha,
righteous-souled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Then there was the one of great strength known as Kupatha among the Dānavas;
he was renowned as Pārvatīya, resembling a mountain of gold.
And the illustrious great Asura Krathana, O King, was possessed of great heroism.
A lord of the earth renowned as Supārśva was born upon this world;
he was the illustrious and great Asura Sūrya among the Asuras, O King,
who became the Bāhlīka king named Darada, the foremost of all rulers of the earth.
O King, from that host known as Krodhavaśa which was proclaimed by you,
there were born here upon the earth these heroic lords of men:
Nandika, Karṇaveṣṭa, Siddhārtha, and likewise Kīṭaka.
Suvīra, Subāhu, Mahāvīra, and Bāhlika; Krodha, Vicitya, Surasa, the illustrious Nīla the king of the earth,
Vīradhāman, and Bhūmipāla by name, O descendant of Kuru.
There was one named Dantavaktra, and another known by the name Durjaya;
also Rukmin, that tiger among kings, and King Janamejaya;
as well as Āṣāḍha, Vāyuvega, and Bhūritejas.
Ekalavya, Sumitra, Vāṭadhāna, and Gomukha;
the Kārūṣaka kings, as well as Kṣemadhūrti; Śrutāyu, Uddhava, and likewise Bṛhatsena.
Kṣemo-gratīrtha, Kuhara, and the lord of men among the Kaliṅgas, as well as the wise Manuṣyendra and the renowned Īśvara—
thus did this multitude of kings arise on earth from the Krodhavaśa host.
O Great King, in former times there was one born of great fame and great strength,
known as Kālanemi, a Dānava of immense power;
he is the mighty son of Ugrasena, renowned as Kaṃsa.
He who was formerly named Devaka, equal in splendor to the king of the gods,
was born on earth as a preeminent lord of the Gandharvas, a ruler of men; know him, O Bhārata, to be the son of the celestial seer Bṛhaspati of great renown.
From Aṃśa was born Droṇa, the son of Bharadvāja, not born from a womb;
O tiger among kings, he who was the foremost of all bowmen and the knower of all weapons,
possessed of great fame and great splendor, was thus born here among men.
Those who know the Vedas recognize him as the foremost among those learned in the science of archery and the Vedas— the performer of Indra’s deeds, Droṇa, the enhancer of his own lineage— who,
O Bhārata, was born from Mahādeva and Antaka through desire and wrath.
To those who had attained oneness was born the hero, the scorcher of foes,
the immensely powerful Aśvatthāman, the destroyer of the enemy host—
a valiant man with eyes like lotus petals, O lord of men, who dwelt upon the earth.
Eight Vasus were born as the sons of Śantanu from Gaṅgā,
due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha and the command of Vāsava.
Among them, the youngest was Bhīṣma, who brought fearlessness to the Kurus.
Intelligent, learned in the Vedas, eloquent, and the destroyer of the enemy faction—
he who was the best among all knowers of everything— fought with the high-souled Bhārgava Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, who possessed great splendor.

O King, know that the one who was the Brahman-sage named Kṛpa on earth was born from the host of the Rudras, possessed of exceeding prowess. And he who was the king named Śakuni, a great chariot-warrior in the world—
Know him, O King, as Dvāpara incarnate, the crusher of enemies. He who is Sātyaki, the upholder of truth and the sustainer of the Vṛṣṇi clan,
was born from a portion of the Maruts, the gods who crush their foes.
And Drupada, the royal seer, likewise emerged from that very host;
O King, he became the foremost of all wielders of weapons in this world of men.
And know, O ruler of men, that Kṛtavarman also arose from there.
Know that he was born as one beyond all need for remedial action, the most excellent among the bulls of the Kṣatriyas;
know him to have been born from the host of the Maruts, a crusher of enemies,
the royal sage named Virāṭa, who scorches the kingdoms of his foes.
The son of Ariṣṭā, renowned as Haṃsa,
was born as the lord of the Gandharvas, increasing the Kuru lineage;
he was also known as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, born from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Long-armed, of great majesty, and possessing the eye of wisdom,
that lord of men was born blind due to his mother’s fault and the sage’s anger;
his younger brother, however, was a being of great essence and great strength.

He was renowned as Pāṇḍu, pure and devoted to truth and righteousness. O highly fortunate one, that hero, the best among all wielders of weapons, was born from the host of the Maruts; he was your great-grandfather.

Know that Vidura, the most excellent among those who possess sons and the foremost among the wise in this world, was born as the highly fortunate son of Atri. And from a portion of Kali was born King Duryodhana upon the earth.
Of evil intellect and wicked mind, the bringer of infamy to the Kurus—
he who was hated by the entire world, that man of strife,
that lowest of men, who caused the whole earth to be slaughtered.
By whom great enmity was kindled, which brought about the end of beings—
by him were born here among men all the brothers of Paulastya,
a hundred in number beginning with Duḥśāsana, all of whom were performers of cruel deeds.
Durmukha, Duḥsaha, and those others who have not been mentioned by name—these were the companions of Duryodhana, O bull of the Bharatas; they were all descendants of Pulastya. Janamejaya said:
The son of the Vaiśya woman was Yuyutsu, and he was the one hundred and first among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O Lord, [tell me] their order of seniority and their names.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Recite the names of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons in their proper order:
O King, Duryodhana, Yuyutsu, Duḥśāsana,
as well as Duḥsaha, Duḥśala, and another, Durmukha.
Viviṃśati, Vikarṇa, Jalasaṃdha, Sulocana, Vinda and Anuvinda, Durdharṣa, Subāhu, Duṣpradharṣaṇa,
Durmarṣaṇa, Durmukha, Duṣkarṇa, and Karṇa himself.
Citra and Upacitra, Citrākṣa, and Cārucitrāṅgada;
Durmada, Duṣpraharṣa, Vivitsu, Vikaṭa, and Sama;
Ūrṇanābha, Sunābha, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka.
The commander-in-chief Suṣeṇa, Kuṇḍodara, Mahodara, Citrabāhu, Citravarman, Suvarman, Durvimocana, Ayobāhu,
Mahābāhu, Citracāpa, and Sukuṇḍala.
Bhīmavega, Bhīmabala, Balākī, Balavardhana, Ugrāyudha, Bhīmaśara, Kanakāyu, Dṛḍhāyudha,
Dṛḍhavarman, Dṛḍhakṣatra, Somakīrti, and Anudara.
Jarāsandha, Dṛḍhasandha, Satyasandha, Sahasravāk, Ugraśravas, Ugrasena, Senānī, Duṣparājaya,
Aparājita, Paṇḍitaka, Viśālākṣa, and Durādhara.
Dṛḍhahasta, Suhasta, Vātavega, Suvarcas,
Ādityaketu, Bahvāśin, Nāgadanta, Ugrayāyin, Kavacin, Niṣaṅgin, Pāśin, Daṇḍadhāra, and Dhanurgraha.
Ugra, Bhīmaratha, Vīra, Vīrabāhu, Alolupa, Abhaya, Raudrakarman, as well as Dṛḍharatha,
Anādhṛṣya, Kuṇḍabhedin, Virāvin, and Dīrghalocana.
Dīrghabāhu, Mahābāhu, Vyūḍhoru, Kanakadhvaja, Kuṇḍāśin, and Virajas; and Duḥśalā, who was more than a hundred [in number];
and Yuyutsu, the son of a Vaiśya woman, who was also more than a hundred [in number] among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O King, these one hundred and one sons and one daughter have been proclaimed;
they are known according to the sequence of their names and their order of seniority.
All of them are heroic Atirathas, all of them experts in battle.

All were knowers of the Vedas and masters of the science of statecraft; all were distinguished by their learning and noble birth in the sciences of social conduct, O Lord of the Earth, and wives were chosen for each of them according to their merit.
And at that time, the Kaurava, with the approval of Saubala, gave Duḥśalā in marriage to Jayadratha, the king of Sindhu.
Know, O King, that King Yudhiṣṭhira was a portion of Dharma.
Bhīmasena was born from Vāta, and Arjuna from the King of the Gods;
likewise, Nakula and Sahadeva were portions of the Aśvins— beings of incomparable beauty on earth who captivated the hearts of all the world.
The powerful son of Soma, renowned as Suvarcas,
became Abhimanyu of great fame, the son of Arjuna.
O King, at the time of his incarnation, Soma spoke these words to the gods:
"I would not give up my dear son, even though he is more beloved than life itself.
Let this agreement be made; it cannot be transgressed.
For the work of the gods is our task—the destruction of the asuras upon the earth."
There this Varcas shall go; he will not remain with me for long. But there shall be a son of Indra who will have Nārāyaṇa as his friend; he, the powerful son of Pāṇḍu, shall be renowned as Arjuna.
He shall have a son who, though a child, will be a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) on earth. O best of immortals, he will remain there for sixteen years;
during his sixteenth year, that battle shall take place.
Wherein your portions shall perform the deed that slays the Dānavas;
yet that battle has been deprived of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Having formed the *cakravyūha* array, the Asuras will fight.
"My son will cause all his enemies to turn their faces away from him; though but a boy, having entered that impenetrable array,
he will move through it and slaughter the heroic great chariot-warriors."
The mighty-armed one shall lead a fourth part of all his enemies toward the city of the King of the Dead within half a day;
then, having encountered many heroic great-chariot warriors in battle, [he will encounter] them.
At the end of the day, the mighty-armed one will once again come together with me;
he shall indeed procreate a single heroic son who will perpetuate the lineage. He shall restore the Bharata dynasty which has been lost.

Having heard these words of Soma, all the inhabitants of heaven replied together, "So be it," and they honored the Lord of the Stars. Thus, O King, has the birth of your father’s father been recounted to you.

Know that the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna is a portion of Agni; and know, O King, that Śikhaṇḍin was formerly a woman who became a Rākṣasa. And as for those five sons of Draupadī who were born, O bull of the Bharatas—
O King, O bull of the Bharatas, know those to be the hosts of the Viśvedevas.
From Bhīmasena was born the lord of the Rākṣasas from the Guhyakas;
for he was created by the Great-souled One for the purpose of protecting Jaya.
O Lord of the Earth, know that after giving the portion due to all the deities, [these were born]:
Prativindhya, Sutasoma, and another, Śrutakīrti; then Nakula’s son Śatānīka, and the heroic Śrutasena.
There was one named Śūra, the best of the Yadus and the father of Vasudeva.
He had a daughter named Pṛthā, whose beauty was peerless on earth.
That heroic man [gave her] to his paternal aunt’s son, who was childless.
Having previously promised his first-born child,
Śūra then gave that daughter— who was indeed born as the first-born— to Kuntibhoja out of a desire to show him favor.
Appointed by her father to honor Brahmins and guests in his house,
she attended upon a fierce and formidable Brahmin of rigid vows,
who was known as Durvāsas and whose resolve in dharma was hidden from view.
With all her efforts, she gratified that fierce one who had purified his soul;
being pleased, he explained to her the ritual of *abhicāra* according to the prescribed rules.
And the Blessed One said to her: "I am pleased with you, O fortunate lady."
"Whichever deity you shall invoke with this mantra, O Goddess, by the grace of that very deity you will give birth to sons. Having been addressed thus, the young woman was then filled with curiosity.
While still a maiden, the illustrious Kanyā invoked the god Arka;
the radiant Tapanas then placed his seed within her.
And from her he begot a son, the best among all wielders of weapons.
Adorned with earrings and armor, a divine child endowed with splendor,
equal to the sun in brilliance, and with all his limbs beautifully decorated,
she then indeed concealed him who had been born out of fear of her kinsmen.
Kuntī cast that illustrious boy into the water.
When that embryo had been cast into the water, the highly renowned husband of Rādhā,
Adhiratha, then adopted him as his son for Rādhā.
Both husband and wife gave that boy the name Vasuṣeṇa, which became renowned in all directions. As he grew up, he became powerful and the most excellent in all weapons.
Then, until his back was scorched by the sun, that best of those who recite prayers continued his *japa*.
While that wise man of true prowess remained engaged in recitation,
there was nothing that could not be given away by that high-souled one to the Brahmins.
Indra, the creator of beings, having become a Brahmin, requested from that hero his earrings and armor along with his son for the sake of his own son;
and Karna, having cut them off, gave him those earrings and that armor.
Śakra, filled with wonder, gave him his own power and spoke these words:
"O invincible one, whomever you shall hurl this power against— whether among gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, or rākṣasas— that one alone shall cease to exist."
Formerly, his name was renowned as Vasuṣeṇa; thereafter, he became Karṇa Vaikartana because of that deed. And Karṇa, who was born already clad in armor, was a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha).
The first son of Pṛthā was widely known as Karṇa; that hero, O best of kings, grew up in the family of a charioteer. He was the foremost among men and the most excellent of all archers.
Know that he who was the counselor and minister of Duryodhana, equal to Śakuni, was the unsurpassed portion of the god Divākara. And he who was named Nārāyaṇa, the eternal God of gods—
The master of all beings, the destroyer, and the unconquered—
of him, the powerful Vāsudeva was a portion among men;
and of the serpent Śeṣa, the exceedingly strong Baladeva was a portion.
"O King, know that Sanatkumāra is Pradyumna of great splendor.
In this way, O lord of men, many other portions of the celestial dwellers were born in the lineage of Vasudeva, increasing the glory of the family."
O King, that host of Apsarases which was indeed proclaimed by me—
that portion of them was born upon the earth by the command of Vāsava.
These, O lord of men, were sixteen thousand of those goddesses.
In the world of men, they became the consorts of Nārāyaṇa;
and a portion of Śrī herself was born upon the surface of the earth for the sake of delight,
in the family of Bhīṣmaka, as a virtuous woman known by the name of Rukmiṇī.
Then the blameless Draupadī was born from a portion of Śacī;
she was an irreproachable maiden born from the middle of the sacrificial altar in the lineage of Drupada. She was neither too short nor too tall, and she possessed the fragrance of a blue lotus.
With eyes as long as lotuses, beautiful hips, and long black hair,
she was endowed with every auspicious mark and resembled a lapis lazuli gem;
in private, she captivated the hearts of the five lords of men.
The two goddesses Siddhi and Dhṛti were the mothers of five;
they were born as Kuntī and Mādrī, while Mati was the daughter of Subala.
Thus [ends the account] of the gods, Asuras, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
O King, the partial incarnations of the Rākṣasas have been proclaimed—
those kings born upon the earth who were intoxicated with the pride of battle,
as well as those great-souled ones born in the vast lineage of the Yadus.
And those kings of great splendor who were born in various families—
whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas— I have proclaimed them all to you.
These, O best of kings, are the principal ones that I have described to you.
This account of the partial incarnations (aṃśāvataraṇa) should be heard by one free from malice; it brings merit, fame, progeny, long life, and victory.
Having heard this account of the partial incarnations of the gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas...
The wise man who understands the origin and dissolution [of all things] does not despair in times of distress.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, from you I have heard this account of the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas."
The partial incarnations of the Gandharvas and Apsarases are likewise correctly described;
and the deeds of the royal sages, encompassing virtue, wealth, and pleasure, have been proclaimed.
Listen now to this purifying account of those wise ones as it is being recited by me.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear in detail here the birth and deeds of the high-souled Bharata; you should relate them to me."
"But, O Brahmin, I desire to hear this lineage of the Kurus from the beginning as it is being told by you in the presence of these hosts of brahmin-sages.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O best of the Bharatas, the heroic one named Duḥṣanta was the founder of the Paurava lineage; he was the protector of the earth bounded by its four oceans. That lord of men enjoyed the entire fourth part of the world.
That conqueror in assembly, the crusher of enemies, enjoys even those regions bounded by the ocean, including all the lands of the Mlecchas and forest-dwellers,
extending to the jewel-bearing seas and filled with people of the four castes.

While that king was ruling, there was no one who caused the intermixture of castes, no one who practiced agriculture, and no one who committed evil deeds. Devoting themselves to lawful pleasures, they pursued both dharma and worldly prosperity.
O tiger among men, when that lord of the realm was ruling,
O dear one, there was no fear of thieves among the people, nor even the slightest fear of hunger;
and while he was the lord of the realm, there was also no fear of disease.
The social classes took delight in their own duties, free from desire for the work of the gods;
relying upon that protector of the earth, they lived without fear from any quarter. The rain-cloud poured forth at the proper time, and the crops were laden with fruit.
At that time, the earth was enriched with all kinds of jewels;
the Brahmins were devoted to their own duties, and no falsehood was found among them.
And he [the prince] was a youth of marvelous and great prowess, with a body as firm as a diamond.

Lifting up Mount Mandara with his two arms, he could carry it away along with its forests and groves. Furthermore, he was thoroughly proficient in the use of the bow, in mace-fighting, in striking with sword-hilts, on the back of an elephant, and on the back of a horse.
In strength he was equal to Viṣṇu, and in splendor like the sun;
in imperturbability he was like the ocean, and in endurance like the earth. That protector of the earth was highly esteemed, and his cities and kingdom were tranquil.
Dwelling among people who were even more devoted to righteousness,
Janamejaya said:
"O high-minded one, I wish to hear of the birth and the life of Bharata."
I wish to hear in truth the origin of Śakuntalā,
and how she was obtained by the heroic Duṣyanta;
O Blessed One, I desire to hear that account in detail regarding that lion among men.
"O knower of truth, O best among the wise, I wish to hear all of this.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Once, that mighty-armed one, possessing abundant forces and vehicles..."
Surrounded by hundreds of horses and elephants,
and encircled by hundreds of warriors bearing swords and spears, with maces and clubs in their hands, and with darts and lances in their grasp, he went forth into the dense forest.
With the lion-roars of the warriors, the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, the rattling of chariot wheels, and the trumpeting of excellent elephants;
and likewise with those bearing various weapons and wearing various garbs.
Mixed with the sounds of neighing, the cries of *kṣveḍita*, and the slapping of arms,
there arose a tumultuous roar of joy as that king proceeded.
Standing upon the pinnacles of the finest palaces, they beheld him with supreme royal splendor.
There the women beheld that hero, the enhancer of his own fame,
who was like Śakra, the slayer of enemies, and the repeller of the elephants of his foes;
he was surrounded by a most beautiful fourfold army.
Seeing him there with weapon in hand, the throngs of women thought:
"This is that tiger among men of wondrous prowess in battle,
by whose strength of arm hosts of enemies are no more."
Speaking thus with words of love, those women praised the lord of men and showered flowers upon his head; and there,
in every direction, he was being extolled by the foremost of brahmins.
He went forth to the forest with supreme joy, desiring to hunt deer. As he departed, seated upon the back of a rutting elephant and resembling the king of the gods,
the twice-born, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras followed after him.
They watched him as he grew in stature with blessings and cries of victory;
then the citizens and the people of the countryside followed him for a great distance,
but afterwards they turned back, having been granted leave by the king.

Then, with a chariot resembling a garuḍa, the lord of the earth filled the earth and likewise the triple heaven with his roar. As he proceeded, the wise king beheld a forest resembling the Nandana grove.
It was thickly covered with *bilva*, *arka*, and *khadira* trees, crowded with *kapittha* and *dhava* trees;
it was rugged with mountain ridges and strewn with rocks,
devoid of water and human beings, and extended for many yojanas.
Surrounded by herds of fierce deer and other forest-dwelling creatures, that tiger among men, Duḥṣanta, together with his servants, army,
and mounts, agitated that forest while slaughtering various kinds of wild animals.
Having come within the range of his arrows, Duḥṣanta struck down many groups of tigers there and pierced them with his shafts;
that bull among men also split some who were at a distance with his arrows.
He cut down others who had come close with his sword;
that best among the powerful struck down some of the deer with his spear. Knowing the true principles of the circle of the mace, he of immeasurable prowess moved about.
With iron clubs, swords, maces, bludgeons, and arrows,
he roamed about slaughtering the wild beasts and birds there;
accompanied by the king of wondrous prowess and by warriors who delighted in battle.
As the great forest was being agitated, the large deer abandoned it;
there, with their herds scattered and their leaders slain,
the deer troops cried out here and there out of desperation.
Having reached even a dried-up river, emaciated by their despair for water and with hearts exhausted by exertion, they fell down unconscious;
overcome by hunger and thirst and utterly fatigued, they collapsed upon the ground.
Some there, O tiger among men, were eaten by those who were hungry;
others, having kindled and ignited fires, then roasted and ate the meat according to the prescribed rites while dwelling in the forest.
There, some intoxicated and powerful elephants, wounded by weapons,
fled with great speed in their fear,
contracting their trunks and discharging dung and urine while shedding much blood.
There, the excellent wild elephants trampled many men;
that forest, covered by the cloud of his army with its showers of arrows,
shone as it was strewn with buffaloes and great deer slain by the king.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having slain thousands of deer with his vast array of mounts,
he [approached] that mountain which resembled a dense cloud and was frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
He gazed upon a forest two yojanas from the city;
pursuing wild deer, he was oppressed by exhaustion,
and while pursuing the deer, he urged his horses forward with speed.

In pursuit of deer, the king entered another forest alone, endowed with supreme strength yet afflicted by hunger and thirst. Having reached the edge of the forest, he came upon a vast, barren wasteland.
Having passed that [place] as well, which was endowed with the highest hermitages,
which produced delight in the mind, was exceedingly beautiful to behold,
and was filled with cool breezes, the king went to another great forest.
It was strewn with flowering trees and possessed exceedingly pleasant grassy meadows; it was vast and resounded with the sweet cries of birds,
as well as with the warbling of male cuckoos and the humming of swarms of crickets.
It was covered with trees possessing fully grown branches and pleasant shade, with creepers swaying from the humming of bees, and endowed with supreme splendor;
there was not a single tree there that lacked flowers, lacked fruit, or was thorny.
That forest was indeed not crowded even with six-legged insects;
it resounded with the songs of birds and was exceedingly adorned with flowers.
With trees bearing blossoms of every season, its grassy meadows were most pleasant.
The great archer entered that most excellent and enchanting forest.
There, trees adorned with blossoms, shaken by the wind,
repeatedly released a wondrous rain of flowers.
Then, touching the heavens and resounded by birds of sweet voice,
the trees there shone, clothed in garments of variegated blossoms. Upon their sprouts, which were bent down by the weight of flowers, [the birds perched].
The birds, accompanied by bees, utter soft cries;
and there are many regions adorned with heaps of flowers,
enclosed by bowers of creepers, which increase the joy of the mind.
Beholding this, the one of great splendor then became joyful;
that forest shone with those trees, their branches entwined with one another and covered in flowers, resembling the banners of Mahendra.
The forest was intensely frequented by hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, by groups of Gandharvas and Apsarases, and by intoxicated elephants and Kiṃnaras; there,
a breeze blew, pleasantly cool, fragrant, and carrying the pollen of flowers.
Wandering through the forest, he approached the trees as if out of a desire for sport;
thus the king beheld that lovely grove, endowed with such qualities,
situated on a riverbank and resembling a raised banner.
Beholding that forest filled with most joyful birds,
he saw a delightful and enchanting, preeminent hermitage,
crowded with various trees and with sacrificial fires blazing brightly.
Then the illustrious one paid homage to that incomparable hermitage,
which was surrounded by the Vālakhilya ascetics and filled with hosts of sages,
and which was provided with many fire-sanctuaries and strewn with carpets of flowers.
O King, it was exceedingly resplendent with great thickets and large boulders;
it lay along the sacred river Mālinī, whose waters are pleasant,
which is crowded with flocks of various birds, and which is as delightful as a grove for ascetic penance.
There, beholding both fierce beasts and gentle animals, he attained great joy; and that illustrious great chariot-warrior reached the hermitage,
which resembled the world of the gods and was enchanting from every side.
He beheld a river of holy waters embracing the hermitage,
standing there like a mother to all living beings;
its sandy banks were filled with *cakravāka* birds, and it flowed with foam of flowers.
It was inhabited by hosts of kinnaras, frequented by monkeys and bears,
resounded with sacred recitations, adorned with sandy banks,
and frequented by rutting elephants, tigers, and lordly serpents.
On its bank was the preeminent, meritorious hermitage of the great-souled Blessed Kāśyapa, frequented by hosts of great seers;
having seen the river connected to the hermitage and likewise the site of the hermitage itself.
Then that king set his mind upon entering [the city],
which was adorned by the river Mālinī with its islands and beautiful banks,
appearing like the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa graced by the Gaṅgā.
Resounding with the cries of intoxicated peacocks, he entered that great forest.
Having approached that place, which resembled Caitraratha and was exceedingly endowed with excellence, the lord of men found it indescribable in its splendor.
Then, desiring to see the great seer Kaśyapa, that treasury of asceticism,
he halted his army— crowded with chariots, thronged with horses,
and filled with multitudes of foot soldiers— at the entrance of the forest and spoke these words.
"I shall go to see the stainless sage, Kāśyapa, whose wealth is his asceticism; please remain here until my return. Having reached that forest, which resembled the Nandana grove, the lord of men—
The king abandoned hunger and thirst and attained abundant joy;
having removed the royal insignia along with his ministers, that lord of men,
accompanied by his domestic priest, went to the supreme hermitage.
Desiring to see that sage there, who was an inexhaustible mass of ascetic power,
he beheld the hermitage which resembled the world of Brahmā,
resounding with the humming of bees and filled with various flocks of birds.
Likewise, with the Sāman chants uttered by those learned in the Sāma-veda, and with those chants of the Ṛg and Sāma combined with the Atharvaśiras,
he was addressed by those immeasurable [verses].
At that time, the king heard [the sound], and his eyes wide with wonder, he stood there;
meanwhile, the Rigvedic verses were being recited by the foremost of the Bahvṛcas according to the *pada* and *krama* methods.

That tiger among men heard the *yajus* mantras being recited many times during the performed rites— mantras that clarify the elements of the sacrifice, are uttered with pure intonations, and are pronounced by those who know the distinctions between the matted locks and the phonemes.

By those learned in the science of sacrifice and its auxiliary branches, by those reciting the *krama-pāṭha* and other methods of Vedic recitation, and by sages of fixed vows chanting the sweet melodies of the *Sāmaveda*— with the songs of the *Bhāruṇḍa-sāman* and the hymns arising from the *Atharvaśiras*.
That hermitage then shone with those of immeasurable soul who were well-restrained;
they, the foremost among those learned in the Atharvaveda and honored by the assemblies of sacrificial priests, recited the Saṃhitā together with its word-for-word analysis and the Krama-pāṭha.
Resounding with other twice-born ones who spoke while applying the refinements of phonetics (*śabdasaṃskāra*),
that glorious hermitage shone like the world of Brahmā;
it was filled with those learned in the rituals of sacrifice and experts in the sequential training of phonology (*kramaśikṣā*).
[He was surrounded] by those perfected in the knowledge of the true meaning of logic, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas,
who were experts in the collection and synthesis of various statements,
who understood specific ritual duties, and who were devoted solely to the dharma of liberation.

[They were] those who had attained mastery in the knowledge of formal positions, refutations, and established tenets, as well as the ultimate truth; who were experts in grammar, prosody, and etymology, and proficient in the knowledge of time;
and who understood substances, actions, and qualities, as well as cause and effect.
He heard the sound uttered by those skilled in sophistry, debate, and cavil, who rely on the treatises of Vyāsa; by leaders in various sciences,
and by the foremost of the Lokāyatikas, it was echoed from all sides.

In various places, the slayer of enemy heroes beheld the foremost of Brahmins— self-controlled, firm in their vows, perfected masters devoted to silent recitation and burnt offerings; and the lord of the earth saw their diverse seats strewn with flowers.
Seeing those [offerings] presented with great effort, he was filled with wonder;
and beholding the worship performed by the twice-born at the temples of the gods,
that best of kings considered himself to be dwelling in the world of Brahmā.

Beholding that auspicious and preeminent hermitage protected by the ascetic power of Kāśyapa, filled with hosts of those whose wealth is penance, he was not yet satiated. He [beheld] the abode of Kāśyapa, [inhabited] by those of great vows.
Surrounded on all sides by ṛṣis whose wealth was their asceticism,
the slayer of enemies entered that secluded, exceedingly charming, and auspicious place together with his ministers and family priest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having dismissed those ministers, the mighty-armed one went alone;
he did not see that rishi of rigid vows in that hermitage.

Not seeing that seer and finding the hermitage empty, he cried out "Is anyone here? in a loud voice, as if making the forest resound. Then, hearing his voice, a maiden appeared, like the goddess Śrī incarnate in form.

She emerged from that hermitage wearing the garb of an ascetic. Then, she— beautiful, endowed with youth, possessed of virtuous character and conduct, and auspicious— honored the Lord who had arrived as a guest, worthy of worship and observing excellent vows.
O Janamejaya, she spoke clearly with sweet words to him, who had long lotus-like eyes, a broad chest, a well-knit body, lion-like shoulders, long arms, and was honored by all auspicious marks.
As soon as that dark-eyed woman saw King Duḥṣanta,
she quickly said, "Welcome to you," and having honored him,
she indeed worshipped him with a seat, water for his feet, and the arghya offering.
She inquired after the health and well-being of the king, the lord of men.
Having honored him as was fitting and having thus asked after his welfare,
she then spoke as if smiling, "What task may be performed?"
"By coming to this hermitage, what purpose do you wish to accomplish?
Who are you that have arrived here today at the auspicious hermitage of the great seer?
Then the king spoke to that sweet-speaking maiden.
Having seen her, whose every limb was faultless, and having honored her appropriately,
Duḥṣanta said:
"I am the son of the royal seer Ilila, the lord of the earth."
"O lotus-eyed one, my name is Duḥṣanta; this is the truth.
Welcome to you, O Great King! Please accept our fruits, roots, and water, and enjoy them. And what may I do for you?"
"I have come, O illustrious lady, to attend upon the seer Kaṇva. Where has the blessed one gone, O auspicious one? Tell me that, O beautiful one.
"O best of the twice-born, salutations to you, O auspicious one! The powerful seer Kaṇva—"
Śakuntalā said:
"My venerable father has gone from the hermitage to gather fruits.
Wait for a moment; you shall see him when he returns here."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Not seeing that sage, and having been addressed by her in that manner,
the king beheld her— she of the beautiful hips, radiant and sweetly smiling.
Radiant in her form, through asceticism, and through self-restraint, and endowed with beauty and youth—thus spoke the lord of the earth:
"Who are you? Whose are you, O fair-hipped one? And for what purpose have you come to the forest?"
"O beautiful one, from where do you come, endowed with such qualities?
O auspicious lady, by the mere sight of you, my mind has been stolen away. I wish to know you; therefore, tell me, O beautiful one."
I stand here, O lady of boundless beauty, desiring to say something;
listen to my words, O elephant-nosed one, you who are radiant like an intoxicated woman. I am born specifically in the lineage of Pūru, a royal seer.
"O fair-hipped one of excellent complexion, Duḥṣanta chooses you today;
my mind never turns toward anyone other than a Kṣatriya woman— not toward the daughters of sages, nor toward others of inferior or different castes."
"Know me, O sweet-voiced one, to be one whose soul is thus resolved.
My heart is set upon you; for you are a Kṣatriya woman—tell me, who are you? For my mind, O timid one, does not find pleasure in approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman."
"O lady with long-cornered eyes, I worship you; you ought to favor me, your devotee. O large-eyed one, enjoy the kingdom; do not let your mind be otherwise.
Thus was the maiden addressed at that time by the king in his hermitage.
Laughing, she spoke these words in very sweet syllables:
"O venerable Duḥṣanta, I am considered the daughter of the illustrious Kaṇva.
Then the king spoke to that lotus-eyed maiden.
"O Indra among kings, I am not my own mistress; Kāśyapa is my father and my guru. He is an ascetic, steadfast, a knower of dharma, and illustrious.
Seek him for your purpose; you ought not to do what is improper."
Duḥṣanta said:
"The illustrious and worshipful one, whose vital energy is drawn upward, is honored by the world;
for even Dharma might waver from its course, but he of firm vows shall not waver."
"How have you, O woman of excellent complexion, become his daughter?
I have a great doubt in this matter; you ought to dispel it for me here.
Śakuntalā said:
Just as this tradition has come down to me, and just as it was in the past,
so too that fool, being one thing, speaks of himself as something else among the virtuous; covered by evil, he is therefore a thief of his own self.
"Listen, O King, to the truth of how I am the daughter of a sage.
A certain ṛṣi came here and questioned me regarding my birth:
'Since you are one whose vital seed is drawn upward (a celibate), from where does this Śakuntalā come?'"
"How was a daughter born to you from [your wife]? Tell me that, O Kāśyapa.
To him the Blessed One spoke; listen, O King, to how that came to pass.
It is said that in ancient times Viśvāmitra was performing great ascetic penance.
He caused Śakra, the lord of the hosts of gods, to suffer intensely, [thinking]:
"This one, whose prowess is kindled by asceticism, might displace me from my station.
Fearing him, Purandara spoke thus to Menakā:
"O Menakā, you are distinguished among the Apsarases by your divine qualities.
O auspicious lady, do what is for my welfare; listen to that which I shall tell you.
This Viśvāmitra, who resembles the sun, is a man of great ascetic power."

As he performs this terrible asceticism, my mind trembles. O Menakā, O slender-waisted one, Viśvāmitra— who has undertaken such extremely formidable penance and devotion to celibacy— is now a burden for you.
He is self-disciplined, extremely difficult to overcome, and engaged in fierce asceticism.
He might dislodge me from my position; therefore, go to him and entice him. Create an obstacle to his penance and do what is most pleasing to me.
"O lady of beautiful hips, entice him with your beauty, youth, sweetness, gestures, smiles, and speech, and cause him to turn back from his asceticism.
Menakā said:
That Blessed One is always possessed of great splendor and great ascetic power;
he is also prone to anger, for even the Blessed One knows this of that high-souled one— his brilliance, his austerity, and his wrath.
How could I not tremble before him who made even you tremble—
he who separated the illustrious Vasiṣṭha from his beloved sons,
and who, though born in the Kṣatriya order, formerly became a Brāhmaṇa by force?
He who, for the sake of purification, made the river difficult to cross with its many waters— that most meritorious stream which people in the world know as the Kauśikī—
there, in former times, during that difficult period, he sustained the high-souled one.
The righteous royal sage Mataṅga, having become a hunter,
returned to his hermitage after the famine had passed;
then that powerful lord gave the river its name, "Pārā."
It was there that he, with a well-pleased mind, himself officiated as the priest for Mataṅga;
it was out of fear of him, O Lord of the Gods, that you went to drink the Soma juice.
Furthermore, when enraged, he surpassed the lineages of the stars by means of his abundance of stellar splendor.
He who created the constellations beginning with Śravaṇā,
and who granted refuge even to Triśaṅku when he was struck down by his preceptor’s curse—
how will that royal sage Kauśika be released from the curse of the Brahman-sage?
Then, disregarding the gods, that part of the sacrifice was destroyed;
however, the Lord of great splendor created other components of the sacrifice,
and that one of great ascetic power then led Triśaṅku to heaven.
"I am greatly terrified of him whose deeds are these.
O Lord, command me so that he, when enraged, may not consume me;
for with his splendor he could burn the worlds and shake the earth with his foot."
He could contract Mount Mahāmeru and likewise swiftly cause it to revolve;
he could dry up the great ocean and crush the great mountain.
How could a young girl like me touch one such as him, endowed with ascetic power and blazing like a fire, who has conquered his senses—
he whose mouth is a flaming sacrificial fire and whose eyes have the sun and moon for their pupils?
O best of gods, how could one such as I touch Kālajihva?
