Yama, Soma, the great ṛṣis, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and all the Vālakhilyas [are likewise unable].
Even these tremble before his power;
why then should one like me not tremble?
And having been addressed by you in this way, how could I [approach] his presence?
"O Lord of the Gods, I shall not go to the rishi;
however, O King of the Devas, devise a protection for me so that I may move about protected for your sake."
"O God, let the Wind-god reveal my dwelling there as I sport;
and let there be passion for me in that place."
Through the grace of the gods, may a fragrant breeze blow from the forest as your companion;
at that time, while you are tempting that rishi.
Having said, "So be it," and that having been performed, she then departed for the hermitage of Kauśika.
Śakuntalā said:
Thus addressed by her, Śakra gave instructions to the Wind-god (Sadāgati).
Then, at that time, Menakā set forth together with the Wind.
Thereupon, the woman of excellent hips beheld him whose sins had been consumed by ascetic penance.
While Viśvāmitra was performing austerities in the hermitage, the timid Menakā approached him,
paid her respects, and then began to sport in his presence; meanwhile,
the wind blew away her garment, which was as bright as the moon.
She quickly descended to the ground, clutching her garment; the woman of excellent complexion, as if smiling yet bashful, faced the wind even as that seer,
whose splendor was equal to fire, looked on.
Then Viśvāmitra, the best of sages, beheld Menakā— then in an awkward position, blameless, clinging to her garment, and agitated— with her age and beauty indescribable, as she stood exposed.
Having seen her beauty and virtues, that bull among brahmins then fell under the sway of desire and felt an inclination toward union with her;
he invited her, and she, being blameless, desired him as well.
There, both of them dwelt in the forest for a very long time,
sporting according to their desire as if it were but a single day; thus,
they did not perceive that thousands of years had passed.
The sage, though always endowed with patience, had not conquered desire and anger;
that seer brought about the destruction of his long-accumulated ascetic merit,
and through that very depletion of his ascetic power, the sage fell into delusion.
Overcome by delusion and possessed by anger, the sage, while devouring roots and fruits,
made a splashing sound with his feet as he entered his hut on the inner island; Menakā, desiring to depart, heard that sound of water.
"By means of his ascetic power, he possesses such radiant vigor that he comes and goes through the sky;
today I have recognized him by whatever sign of the exhaustion of his asceticism.
Alas, I shall depart! Having said this, Menakā, having bathed after her menses, [prepared to leave].
Overcome by desire for her, she approached the sage;

Constantly wearing pure rags or bark garments that are not required for his status,

Half-nālīkas, nārācas, śaktis, tomara-spears, and mallets fell upon my body, my feet, thighs, and head; yet,

was protected by excellent gates and watchtowers, as well as hundreds of upper chambers, and secured by hundreds of *śataghnī* weapons and mechanical engines, making it difficult for others to approach.
It was crowded with mansions and palaces, adorned with various kinds of merchandise, filled with delightful pavilions and assembly halls, and graced by water-stations and a great,
well-laid-out royal highway.
It was adorned with gateways shaped like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa,
beautified by auspicious arches, portals,
and turrets, and possessed a great girdle of *sāla* trees together with gardens and mango groves.

It was surrounded by all kinds of lotus ponds and gardens, filled with people belonging to the various castes and stages of life who remained steadfast in their own duties, constantly engaged in festivals,
abundant in wealth and grain, contented, and honored with jewels.
[He was surrounded] by learned men constantly devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice, engaged in ritual acts, who avoided forbidden deeds, were habituated to giving, intent on compassion,
fearful of unrighteousness, and all desiring to conquer the heavenly world.
Filled with such people, it was like another realm of Indra.
In the center of that city stood the royal palace,
resembling the abode of Indra and replete with stores of wealth.
In its center was a divine assembly hall, variegated with various jewels;
in that hall sat the royal seer, adorned with every ornament,
surrounded by brahmins, kshatriyas, and ministers.
While being praised by *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards, that lord of kings—
having been approached by those seeking his favor and having attended to their business— sat at ease once they had departed;
at that time, O great seers, the king was seated in comfort.
Hearing the cry of the birds, those who understood omens observed:
"O Śakuntalā, these omens are auspicious for us;
they declare the certain accomplishment of our purpose—you shall become a queen."
On this very day, however, the son shall become the crown prince.
With the gates of Vardhamānapura resounding with the blare of trumpets,
those great seers entered, placing Śakuntalā at their head.
As the prince entered, the spectators praised him;
even as he entered the gate of the city of Vardhamāna, the descendant of Puru,
filled with joy, considered himself to be in the realm of Indra.
Then, O Bhārata, all the citizens, having summoned one another, became desirous of seeing the prince;
he shone before the people like a deity, appearing as if the Goddess Śrī herself had arrived.
"Like Paulomī coming here from Indra’s world with Jayanta," saying this,
they all addressed the great ṛṣis,
greeting those great ṛṣis who possessed the splendor of gods.
"Today our birth has become fruitful, and therefore we have achieved our purpose,
since we behold such great seers possessing the splendor of the sun.
Having spoken thus, some followed the descendant of Puru together.
Like Kumāra, the son of Haimavatī, with eyes like lotuses—
those fools who, desiring to see Śakuntalā, said that they did not wish to see the ascetics covered in black antelope skins.
The deformed ones among the city-dwellers appear like *piśācas*;
even without the twilight hour, those *piśācas* enter the supreme city—
wretched, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and clothed in bark and skins.
Seeing them reduced to skin and bone, devoid of flesh, and covered with a network of veins;
seeing them with tawny eyes, tawny matted hair, long teeth, and no bellies;
seeing them headless and with hands raised upward—the citizens will flee in terror.
Having heard these words spoken by them, the great seers called out to one another and spoke these words:
"The speech uttered by the Blessed One has not been carried out by the speaker of truth."
"The command is that he must not enter the city here. What is the reason? Why should we enter a city filled with wicked people?
And what purpose would there be for a sage who has abandoned all attachments in a city?"
"Therefore, we shall go to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Having spoken thus, the hosts of sages returned the way they had come.
Seeing that the hosts of sages had departed, he took his son by the hand.
Just as children grieve at being separated from their mother and father,
so too did that beautiful woman, her limbs overwhelmed with sorrow, take hold of fortitude while she was in distress as those brahmins departed by way of the royal road.
Accompanied by her son as her sole companion, she proceeded slowly and slowly along the royal highway, beholding for the first time the mansions,
palaces, and shrines, as well as the variously adorned celestial assembly halls.
Overcome with curiosity, he was filled with wonder upon seeing her;
everyone, having seen her, spoke of her as being like the goddess Śrī deprived of her lotus,
yet resembling a female swan in her gait and equal to a cuckoo in her voice.
With a face like the moon, in splendor equal to the goddess Padmālayā,
with a smile like the kunda flower and skin like the interior of a lotus;
she whose large eyes were like lotus petals and who possessed the luster of refined gold.
Her waist was slender as a lotus stalk, and she possessed beautiful hair and firm breasts.
Her hips were indeed very broad, her thighs resembled the trunks of elephants,
and her feet— with their red, elevated nails— were well-set upon the ground.
"Endowed with such a form, she has come here from the heavenly world"—
thus did all the people in the city of Duḥṣanta think;
again and again they spoke of the virtues of Śakuntalā.
He has the eyes of a lion, the fangs of a lion, the shoulders of a lion, and mighty arms;
he has the chest of a lion, the strength of a lion, and moves with the stride of a lion.
He is large, with broad shoulders and a broad chest, and his head is shaped like a parasol.
The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are red; his face is red, and his voice is like the sound of a drum.
He is endowed with the marks of a king, and royal splendor is seen in him—both in his appearance, his form, his body, and his majesty.
"Whose son indeed will he be, for he is equal to Duḥṣanta?
Speaking thus, all those thousands of women praised him; all the living beings spoke words of reasoned praise.
Like affectionate kinsmen, they followed Śakuntalā with love. Having heard those words of the citizens, Śakuntalā became silent;
having reached the door of the palace, the princess stood there trembling.
Overwhelmed by shame before the king in the presence of the monarch, her limbs trembling, she suddenly reflected on account of the gravity of the matter:
"What indeed shall I say to Duḥṣanta because of me, even though I am pitiless?"
Having spoken thus, the wretched Śakuntalā, lost in thought,
approached the king; once recognized, she was ushered in together with her son, who possessed the splendor of the rising sun.
Having made their report, they all returned once more to the hermitage; there,
Śakuntalā, having attained supreme joy, bowed her head before the king, who sat upon his throne with a splendor like that of Mahendra.
Having honored him according to custom, Śakuntalā said to him:
"Salute the king, your father of firm vows."
Having spoken thus to her son, she stood there with her face bowed in shame;
embracing a pillar, she said to the king, "Be gracious! Then Śākuntala, having saluted the king with palms joined in reverence, [spoke].
With eyes wide open in joy, he gazed upon the king;
then Duḥṣanta, reflecting with a mind fixed on dharma, said:
"O woman of excellent complexion, tell me, what is the purpose of your visit?"
"I shall do so, without a doubt, especially for one who has a son. Be gracious, O Great King; I shall speak, O Supreme among Men.
Let this son of yours, O King, be consecrated to the position of crown prince."
"O King, this son of yours, who is like a god, was begotten by you upon me;
O best of men, abide by the agreement made with him according to the stipulated time,
just as that agreement was previously made by you at our union."
"O illustrious one, remember that hermitage of Kaṇva.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Bhārata, while he was thus attached to the enjoyment of other women..."
Śakuntalā, together with her son, vanished from his mind. Holding her in his heart— her with her son and her smile—
he then embraced her mentally and attained long-lasting happiness.
Upon hearing those words of hers, the king, though he remembered her, said:
"I do not remember you; who are you, O wicked ascetic? Furthermore, it is my firm resolve that I shall never engage in sexual intercourse in vain."
"O auspicious lady, I do not recall ever having had a union with you;
I have no memory of any connection with you regarding dharma, pleasure, or wealth.
Go, stay, or do whatever you desire."
Thus addressed, that high-minded woman of beautiful hips stood as if ashamed,
and as if deprived of consciousness by her grief, she remained motionless like a pillar.
Her eyes were copper-red with agitation and indignation, and her lips were quivering.
Glaring askance at the king as if burning him with her side-long glances,
she concealed her outward expression while being impelled by inner wrath;
yet, she maintained the splendor accumulated through her ascetic penance.
Having reflected for a moment, filled with grief and indignation,
she looked at her husband and, enraged, spoke these words:
"O Great King, even though you know [the truth], why do you speak thus?"
"I do not know"—saying this without attachment, like any other ordinary person;
yet here your heart knows the truth as well as the falsehood. O auspicious one, you are indeed a witness; do not despise yourself.
"What sin is not committed by that thief who robs himself, who represents himself as one thing when he is otherwise?
And yet you think, 'I am alone'."
You do not know the ancient sage dwelling in the heart,
who is the knower of evil deeds; it is in his presence that you commit sin.
For Dharma alone is the cause of welfare for all virtuous people;
it is never devoid of falsehood and shall not bring about suffering. Having committed an evil deed, one thinks, "No one knows me."
The gods, the ancestors, and the inner person within know him;
as do the sun and the moon, wind and fire,
heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama.
Day and night, as well as both twilights,
and Dharma know the conduct of a man; Yama, the son of Vivasvat, makes him pay for his evil deeds.
The Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), who dwells in the heart as the witness of one's actions, is pleased with that person; but when He is not pleased with a wicked-souled man,
Yama delivers that evildoer for his misdeeds.
One who disregards oneself and acts otherwise [than what is right]—
for him, even the gods are not superior, he for whom one's own self is not the cause [of action].
Do not thus despise me, a devoted wife, thinking that I have come here of my own accord.
"You do not honor me, who am worthy of the guest-offering (*arghya*), though I, your own wife, have come before you. For what reason do you look upon me in this assembly as if I were a common woman?
Indeed, I am not crying out here in an empty place; why do you not hear me?"
"O Duḥṣanta, if you do not do as I, who am entreating you, say, then your head shall split into a hundred pieces this very day. For it is by entering his wife that a husband is born again from her."
The ancient seers knew the nature of a wife to be this:
that offspring is born from a man who possesses sacred scripture (āgama),
and through that lineage, it delivers his deceased ancestors.

Furthermore, because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put, he was called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself. Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a son one attains immortality.
Then, through a son’s son, the great-grandfathers rejoice.
She is a wife who is skillful in the home; she is a wife who bears offspring;
she is a wife whose life is her husband; she is a wife who is devoted to her husband.
A wife is half of a man; a wife is the best of friends.
She is declared by the wise to be his very body. A wife is the most excellent [treasure] in the world.
A wife is the root of the three goals of life; a wife is the friend of one who is about to die.
Those who have wives perform sacred rites; those who have wives are householders. Those who have wives rejoice; those who have wives are endowed with prosperity.
Even Brahmā, the preceptor of gods and asuras, first brought forth his power;
having quickly entered his own primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he then became the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
For a wife must always be supported and protected by her husband.
In the successful attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma, the wife is the companion of the husband;
when both husband and wife are subject to each other's will, then there is the union of all three— dharma, artha, and kāma.
"O Lord, how can there be dharma without a wife, or how can a man attain desire or wealth? For these three goals are established in her;
and likewise, without a husband, a wife cannot accomplish dharma and the other aims."

This triad of goals, when relied upon by a husband and wife together, is not capable of performing the worship of the gods, guests, and dependents, nor the honoring of visitors; this cannot be accomplished by men in any way whatsoever without a wife.
Even wealth acquired by men and brought to their own home goes to ruin without a wife, or through the acquisition of a bad wife; yet,
it is clearly observed that he has no desire for such [wealth].
In secluded places, these women become sweet-spoken friends;
in matters of dharma, they become fathers; and for one who is distressed, they become mothers.
Even in the wilderness, they are indeed the resting place for a man traveling on a journey.

He who has a wife is trustworthy; therefore, a wife is one's ultimate refuge. Even when the deceased is wandering alone through treacherous places, it is only the wife who is devoted to her husband that follows him constantly.
First, the wife established in virtue awaits her husband after death;
and when the husband has died first, the virtuous woman follows him afterwards.
For this reason, O King, the taking of the hand (marriage) is desired.
Whatever a husband obtains from his wife in this world and in the next—
for the sake of nourishing his body and as provisions for his journey when he has gone to heaven—
the wise declare that the son is indeed one's own self begotten by oneself.
Therefore, a man should look upon his wife as he would a mother, and upon the mother of his son as his own mother;
for the inner self of everyone is always called "son.
One's destination, form, activity, movements, and physical characteristics [are derived from it].
Whatever qualities are seen in fathers are present in their sons; their virtues, conduct, and behavior arise from association and from what is auspicious or inauspicious.
A son begotten upon a wife is like one's own face reflected in a mirror.
The progenitor rejoices at seeing her, like a doer of merit who has attained heaven;
yet those women who assume the form of devoted wives, by accepting the seed of another,
destroy their family and go to a terrible hell for the sake of their husbands.
Sons begotten by another upon one's own wife according to one’s will are considered "my sons," yet even those sons are enemies; they hate, they act in opposition, and they do not obey one's word.
O King, even a father does not feel such hatred toward his own offspring as he does toward those others;
likewise, a son does not hate his progenitor, nor does the progenitor hate his son. Therefore, the son is indeed one's own self.
Men burning with mental sorrows and afflicted by diseases find refreshment in their own wives, like those oppressed by the heat in cool waters;
yet other men, emaciated by exile, wretched, and clad in soiled garments, [seek solace elsewhere].
Even they, though poor, find contentment in their own wives as if they had gained great wealth;
even when greatly provoked by women, a wise man should not speak unpleasantly to them,
considering that pleasure, affection, and dharma depend upon them.
"She is the half of oneself," so says the Śruti; she protects one's wealth, progeny, body, worldly affairs, dharma, heaven, the sages, and the ancestors.
Women are the eternal, sacred field for the birth of oneself.
What power do even the ṛṣis have to create a woman other than from [their own] offspring?
What power do even the gods have to bring about their own birth?
Even for a wise man, the creation of women is established throughout the worlds.
Some sages were even born from *caṇḍālī*s;
when a son, covered in the dust of the earth,
runs forward and embraces his father’s limbs, what indeed could be greater than that?
Why do you disregard this son of yours, who has come to you of his own accord and gazes at you with longing? Even ants do not break their own eggs when they carry them.
How could you, being a knower of dharma, not cherish your own son? Crows may even raise cuckoo eggs as their own; why then would you, who are all-knowing, not regard such a son as your own?
They say that sandalwood produced from the Malaya mountains is indeed exceedingly cool;
yet the embrace of a child would be even more cooling than that sandalwood.
Neither the touch of garments, nor of women, nor of water provides such pleasure.
Just as the touch of a son being embraced while he is still an infant is a source of happiness,
so too is the Brahmin the best among bipeds, the cow the most excellent among quadrupeds,
the teacher the foremost among those who are venerable, and the son the best among all things that can be touched.
"Let this handsome son embrace and touch you.
For one without a son, the world is empty; what is the use of a house for one without a son?
Through a son, one conquers the worlds—this is the eternal Vedic revelation."
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no happiness equal to that for a son;
there is no joy equal to that for a son; there is no refuge equal to that for a son.
This world speaks falsely, saying that sandalwood is indeed cool.
The embrace of a son's body is cooler even than sandalwood;
there is no touch in this world more blissful than the touch of a son. O subduer of enemies, three full years having passed, I have given birth.
"O Indra among kings, O Paurava, by my command this youth now awaits your summons; he shall perform for you one hundred horse-sacrifices, which will destroy your grief."
"O you of immeasurable sacrificial fees, perform other rites such as the Rājasūya"—
thus did a voice in the intermediate space address me at my birth long ago. Indeed, out of affection, they placed me upon their lap and went to another village.
Having smelled his son on the head, [he said:
"In this way, others too [are honored] by their son... Having smelled their sons on the head, men rejoice.
Even in the Vedas, the twice-born recite this mantra regarding the ritual for sons, which is likewise known to you:
"From limb by limb you are born; from the heart you arise."
"You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns!
With this mantra, the ancestors kiss him on the head.
"For my prosperity depends upon you, as does my inexhaustible lineage."
"Therefore, my child, live a very happy life for a hundred autumns.
It is observed that there is a saying: 'Having been one, he has become two.
This other person has been produced from your own limbs, as one man from another."
"Behold my son, like a second self, as if in a pure lake;
behold Soma within yourself, as if in a pure lake. For just as the Āhavanīya fire is carried forth from the Gārhapatya fire,"

"Thus, this one was born from you; though being one, you have been made twofold. For while you were pursuing a deer during a hunt, O King, I was encountered by you as a maiden in my father’s hermitage."
Urvaśī, Pūrvacitti, Sahajanyā, Menakā,
Viśvācī, and Ghṛtācī— these six are the foremost among the Apsarases. Among them, the excellent Apsaras named Menakā, who was born of Brahmā, chose me.
Having descended from heaven to the world of mortals, he begot [Kuśa] from Viśvāmitra—
a glorious seer devoted to dharma, like another Vaiśvānara.
Born of Brahman, named Kuśa, he was the grandfather of Viśvāmitra.
Kuśa’s son was the powerful Kuśanābha, who was righteous;
his son was King Gādhi, and Viśvāmitra was born of Gādhi. Such was my father, O King, and my mother was the Apsaras Menakā.

On the slopes of the Himalayas, the Apsaras Menakā gave birth to me; having abandoned me there like the offspring of another, that unfaithful woman departed. At that time, those meritorious birds gathered together in accordance with dharma.
And because I was protected by those wings, I am therefore Śakuntalā.
Then I was seen by the high-souled seer Kāśyapa,
who saw that the birds had gone for the sake of water for the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
They presented me to the compassionate sage as if I were his own entrusted charge;
but Kaṇva, beholding me, was delighted and said, "The fire-eaters are laughing," and taking me like a sacrificial ladle, he returned to his own hermitage.
O King, she was indeed honored by that great seer out of compassion;
and for that very reason, O King, I too, a woman of excellent complexion, have been raised like his own daughter by him, O monarch,
as the daughter of Viśvāmitra and nurtured by the sage.
And you saw me, O King, while I was still in my youth,
a maiden in a leaf-hut within a hermitage in the lonely forest— impelled by the Creator, left alone by my father, and dwelling there in solitude.
With truthful and pleasant words, you urged me toward the goal of offspring;
you dwelt in the hermitage, resolved upon dharma, kama, and artha,
and you took my hand according to the Gandharva rite of marriage.
Having placed my family, my virtue, my own truthfulness,
and my duty before me, I have today come to you for refuge;
therefore, it does not behove you to make the word "so be it," which you previously promised, false.
Having cast aside your own duty, you, the Lord of the World, ought not to abandon me, who am innocent and have come to you for refuge; what evil deed did I commit in a previous birth?

"O tiger among kings, since I was abandoned by my kinsmen in childhood and have now been separated from you, I am one whose past karma has reached its end. Even if I am forsaken by you, I shall go to the hermitage as I please."
"You ought not to abandon this child, your own son, by yourself.
Duṣyanta said:
"O Śakuntalā, I do not recognize this son born of you."
Women are speakers of untruth; who will believe your words? Your mother Menakā was merciless and unchaste, by whom you were cast away upon the ridge of the Himavat like a withered garland.
And that pitiless father of yours,
Viśvāmitra, born of the Kṣatriya lineage, greedy for the status of a Brāhmaṇa and devoted to his own desires,
begot me from a celestial woman according to his wish.
"O unchaste woman, alas! I know your despicable birth as described by people:
Menakā, the foremost of the Apsarases, is your mother, and a great seer is your father. Why do you, their offspring, call yourself a harlot?"

Your birth is indeed lowly, yet you prattle on about being of noble lineage; having been abandoned after being born, you were nurtured by others like a cuckoo. Your father Kaṇva, who raised you, was a man of evil intent, like a portent of misfortune.
"This speech which you utter, O female ascetic, is not to be believed; since you speak thus in the presence of the king, go wherever you wish. [Take] gold, gems, pearls, garments, and ornaments."
"O female ascetic, whatever you desire here for the sake of enjoyment, let it be accepted.
Are you not ashamed to utter such an incredible statement?
Especially in my presence, O wicked ascetic, begone!"
Where is that great ṛṣi who is always so fierce, and where is Menakā along with the apsarases?
And where are you, so wretched, wearing the garb of an ascetic? Moreover, this son of yours is of immense stature; though but a child, he is powerful.
"How is it that in so short a time you have grown like the trunk of a *śāla* tree?
Your birth is of the lowest kind, yet you appear to me as a harlot;
for you were born by chance from Menakā out of lustful passion."
"O female ascetic, all that you say is beyond my perception. All women in the world are fickle; all are devoted to their desires;
all women are dependent on others; and all are agitated by anger."
"All women have spoken falsely; you ought not to speak thus to Kaṇva.
I do not recognize you; you may go wherever you please.
Śakuntalā said:
O King, you see the faults of others even when they are the size of mustard seeds, yet though you see your own faults as large as bilva fruits, you do not perceive them.
Menakā dwells among the gods alone, and the gods dwell after Menakā.
"O Duṣyanta, my birth alone surpasses yours;
you roam upon the earth, O King, while I move through the atmosphere. Behold the difference between us, like that between Mount Meru and a mustard seed."
"I travel to the palaces of Mahendra, Kubera, Yama, and Varuṇa; behold my power, O King!
Long ago, O best of men, a son was begotten by me upon Urvaśī."
"O Great King, Āyu was indeed your great-grandfather;
and many great seers and kṣatriyas, O scorcher of foes, have been born [of such unions].
No fault of the mother is found in the case of apsarases or of does."

O sinless one, this report which I shall relate to you is true; it is for the sake of illustration and not out of malice, so you should forgive me upon hearing it. Elephants in rut rejoice at the falling of dust.
As long as a deformed man does not see his own face in a mirror,
he considers himself more handsome than others;
but when he beholds his distorted face in the mirror, [he realizes the truth].
He recognizes only this other [world] and not his own self, nor any other person.
Being excessively endowed with physical beauty, he holds nothing in contempt.
Speaking excessively and using harsh words, he becomes a harasser in this world.
For a fool, hearing the auspicious and inauspicious words of men who are speaking,
takes up the inauspicious speech just as a pig takes up excrement;
but a wise man, hearing the auspicious and inauspicious words of men who are speaking, [takes up the auspicious].
A virtuous person accepts excellent speech just as a swan extracts milk from water; whereas a base person, due to his own corrupt nature, being ignorant and of unrefined intellect,
perceives even the qualities of others to be like his own actions.

But base people, being scorched by the intense fire of another's fame, are unable to attain that same state; therefore, they engage in slander. For just as a virtuous person is deeply pained when censuring others, so too do the base feel such burning distress.
Likewise, the wicked man becomes delighted when he slanders others;
for in this world, fools especially take pleasure in defamation,
whereas the virtuous never take pleasure in it.

Just as virtuous people find peace by honoring their elders, so does a fool find satisfaction by reviling the good. Those fools who perceive only faults live happily, for they are ignorant of virtues.

Where the virtuous are censured by others, they in turn call those others "virtuous" in that same manner; therefore, nothing else in the world is found to be more laughable than when a wicked man himself calls a good man "wicked."
From the terrible affliction of the world, one undoubtedly incurs suffering,
like from a man fallen from truth and righteousness who is as enraged as a venomous serpent; even an atheist trembles before such a person, how much more so a believer?

The gods destroy the prosperity of one who, having himself begotten a son like unto himself, treats him with contempt; such a person does not attain the higher worlds. [This applies even] toward one who is unworthy, untruthful, impure, an atheist, or a doer of evil deeds.
In one of evil conduct, strife shall abound; there is no strife among those who practice dharma. For the ancestors have declared that a son is the foundation of the family lineage;
since he is the highest of all dharmas, one should not abandon a son.

Manu has declared that sons are of five kinds: those born of one’s own wife, those received [as gifts], those purchased, those reared, and those begotten on other women. Among these, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs.
"Bringing about the fame of dharma for men and increasing the joy of the mind,
sons born as rafts of dharma rescue their ancestors from hell.
Therefore, O tiger among kings, you ought not to abandon your son."
Therefore, O lord of the earth, protect both your son and the truth;
for while protecting both, you ought not to speak an untruth. O lord of the earth, by thus protecting yourself, as well as truth and righteousness, you fulfill your duty.
"O lion among men, you ought not to bear this deception here.
A large tank is better than a hundred wells; a sacrifice is better than a hundred tanks; a sacrificial rite is better than a hundred lakes; and a virtuous son is better than a sacrifice."

A son is better than a hundred sacrifices; truth is better than a hundred sons. When a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale, truth indeed outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices.
O King, the mastery of all the Vedas and the bathing in all the sacred fords may or may not be equal to speaking the truth;
yet there is no dharma higher than truth, and nothing exists that is superior to truth.
"O King, nothing indeed is found in this world more intense than untruth;
truth is the supreme Brahman, and truth is the highest covenant. Do not abandon your covenant, O King; let truth be united with you."
O lord of men, there is no sin greater in this world than that which a person does not recognize as evil after having committed it;
for your heart alone knows the truth and the falsehood of such an act.
Therefore, you ought to make him a virtuous witness according to dharma—
he who does not act out of desire, nor out of anger, nor out of delusion,
whether toward an enemy or a friend; he is indeed the supreme person.
"If you have such an attachment to falsehood, or if you do not believe me yourself, then alas, I depart; there can be no association with one such as you.
For one who suspects [my motives], the intellect that illuminates the means of knowledge serves only to reveal my true nature."
If his gait, voice, mindfulness, strength, conduct, learning, and prowess;
his boldness, natural disposition, and the whorls of his body hair; and his lines of hair are all symmetrical—if these qualities belong to him, he is undoubtedly the son.
O lord of the people, this image drawn from your body by its likeness—
do not, O King, let it be in vain as it calls out "Father!
Even without the milk of a donkey, my son shall drink his milk.
"O Duḥṣanta, even without you, my son shall protect this earth, which is bounded by the four oceans and adorned with the king of mountains as its crest-jewel.
Having been addressed thus by Mahendra, it shall not be otherwise."
"Though many, such as the messengers of the gods, are said to be considered witnesses, do they not speak the truth, or rather, do they perhaps speak falsehood?
I am an unworthy witness; unfortunate as I am, I shall go back the way I came."
01,069.028 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken these words, Śakuntalā departed;
at that moment, a smoke-ensnared fire arising from her anger was seen upon her head.
Having restrained the fire of his anger, which was born within his own body, she of faultless limbs set out for the forest with her son. Then,
a bodiless voice spoke to Duḥṣanta from the sky:
Then, surrounded by officiating priests, family chaplains, teachers, and ministers, [the king said]:
"A mother is but a leather bag; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very one by whom he was begotten.
Support your son, Duḥṣanta; do not despise Śakuntalā."
Śakuntalā has spoken the truth:
for a son is born directly from every limb [of the father];
and since a son is indeed one's own self, by that very fact you are my son, O Paurava.
"Indeed, having begotten this son yourself, protect him; wait for no other woman. For women, O Duḥṣanta, are an incomparable purifier according to the Dharma."
For month after month, their menstrual flow indeed carries away their misdeeds;
therefore, all beings cried out to him from every side:
"This [impurity] has been deposited upon your body!"
"O god among men, the son, the bearer of seed, leads [the father] out from the abode of Yama;
and you are the progenitor of this child—Śakuntalā has spoken the truth. For the husband enters the wife, and he is born again from her."
For this is the nature of things:
a wife gives birth to a son who is her own body divided in two.
Therefore, O King Duḥṣanta, cherish the son of Śakuntalā as your own.
"This is an unnatural thing; who would abandon a living son? O Paurava, support the high-souled Śākuntala, the son of Duḥṣanta!
Since he must be supported by you even at our word."
"Therefore, let this son of yours be named Bharata.
Having spoken thus, O Vaiśampāyana, the gods and the sages rich in asceticism [departed].
"Because she is devoted to her husband," they cried out with joy and rained down a shower of flowers.
Hearing those words spoken by the dwellers of heaven, the Paurava king rose from his throne and bowed down to the gods.
Greatly delighted, he spoke these words to his family priest and ministers:
"May you all hear this speech of the messenger of the gods;
may you also hear the speech of the deities and the great seers."
I too know him to be my own son in this very way. If I were to accept this son merely on the strength of his word, there would indeed be suspicion among the people; thus he would not be proven pure.
O Bhārata, having then purified him with the assistance of a divine messenger, the king,
thrilled and exceedingly joyful, accepted that son.
Thereupon, the king performed for him all the ancestral rites in their entirety.
Filled with joy and affection for his son, he caused [the rites] to be performed; having smelled the crown of his head, he embraced him with love,
while being honored by the brahmins and praised by the bards.
The king experienced supreme joy born from the touch of his son;
and that knower of dharma honored his wife according to the law.
Then the king spoke these words to her with words of consolation:
"This relationship with you was indeed established out of sight of the world; previously, this connection between us was hidden from the people,
but today it has been established once more, made manifest before the eyes of the world."
Therefore, for that reason, I have spoken this today;
therefore, O Queen, I have investigated this for the sake of your purification. Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are indeed of various kinds.
"O Goddess, people will worship you, devoted to your husband, without any doubt; moreover, the world perceives my association with you as being due to my female nature.
Furthermore, this son has been chosen for the kingdom by me; therefore, I have reflected upon this."

O beloved, O large-eyed one, O auspicious lady, whatever unpleasant words were spoken by you to me when you were excessively provoked— though they were untruthful, disagreeable, harshly uttered, or even ill-intended— that has been forgiven by me.
"O large-eyed one, you too must likewise forgive my harsh words;
women who possess the virtue of devotion to their husbands must forgive what is done by their lords.
Having spoken thus to his beloved queen, the royal seer Duḥṣanta—
O Bhārata, having brought that woman of blameless gait into the inner apartments, he honored her with garments, food, and drink.
Having approached his mother, he spoke to Rathantaryā:
"O beautiful one, my son, born in the forest, has become the destroyer of your grief;
today I am released from my debt to you by means of your grandson."
"This daughter of Viśvāmitra was raised by Kaṇva;
O illustrious lady, she is your daughter-in-law—be gracious toward Śakuntalā.
Hearing her son’s words, she embraced her grandson.
There, Rathantari embraced Śakuntalā, who had fallen at her feet,
with both arms and shed tears out of joy;
she spoke these truthful words, "I perceive [your] marks."
"O large-eyed one, your son shall become a universal monarch;
O large-eyed one, your husband shall be a conqueror of the three worlds. O woman of excellent complexion, may you attain divine enjoyments."

Having been addressed thus, Rathantaryā attained supreme joy. Then the king, having made Śakuntalā his chief queen and adorned her with all ornaments, performed the rites according to the injunctions of the scriptures.
Having bestowed wealth upon the brahmins and his soldiers,
King Duṣyanta then installed his son Śākuntaleya,
naming him Bharata, as the heir apparent (yauvarāja).

Then, after that king had ruled the kingdom for a long time and had passed away according to the law of time, Bharata obtained the sovereignty. Having entrusted the burden of rule to Bharata, the king felt his purpose was fulfilled.
Then, having ruled the kingdom for a full hundred years and having performed various acts of charity, that king Duḥṣanta ascended to the heavenly world;
his son Bharata, the descendant of Duḥṣanta, obtained the kingdom in accordance with what is right.

The celebrated, radiant, divine, invincible, and great wheel of that high-souled one rolled forth, making the worlds resound. Having conquered the rulers of the earth, he brought them under his control.
He practiced the dharma of the virtuous and attained unsurpassed fame.
That king was a powerful universal monarch, a sovereign of the whole earth,
and he performed many sacrifices just as Śakra, the lord of the Maruts, does.
Kaṇva officiated at his sacrifice, which was performed with great skill and abundant sacrificial fees;
that illustrious king obtained the horse-sacrifice known as Govitata,
in which Bharata gave a thousand padmas to Kaṇva.
From Bharata came the fame known as Bhāratī, by which this lineage became the Bhārata clan;
both those who followed and those who preceded him are renowned as the Bhāratas,
for in the lineage of Bharata were born beings equal to gods and possessed of great majesty.
There were many excellent kings who were equal to Brahmā,
whose names are immeasurable in every respect; of them,
O Bhārata, I shall proclaim the principal ones.
O King, he who constantly hears this unsurpassed *Śākuntala*, concerning those highly fortunate ones who were like gods and devoted to truth and uprightness,
will certainly become possessed of sons, just like Duḥṣanta.
Therefore, this indeed should be heard and should be recited with effort;
for men, there shall be prosperity and pure fame, just as were the words of Dvaipāyana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In the lineage of Prajāpati Dakṣa, of Manu Vaivasvata,
and in the lineages of Bharata, Kuru, Pūru, and Ajamīḍha—
this entire genealogy of the Yādavas and the Pauravas [is told].
In the same way, O sinless one, I shall recite for you that great, meritorious, auspicious benediction of the Bharatas, which bestows wealth, fame, and long life—
all of whom were risen with splendors equal to those of the great ṛṣis.
The ten sons of Pracetas, who were of great power and were formerly consumed by the fire born of the clouds, are remembered as the virtuous beings of an earlier age.
From them was born Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas; and from Dakṣa, these creatures [were produced].
O tiger among men, he was indeed the grandfather of the worlds; for the sage Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, having united with Vīriṇī,
begot a thousand sons who were like himself and firm in their vows.

Nārada taught the unsurpassed knowledge of Sāṃkhya for the sake of liberation to the thousand sons of Dakṣa who had assembled there; he engaged them in activities directed toward knowledge that reaches to the ends of the quarters, for the purpose of their destruction [of rebirth].
Then, O Janamejaya, Prajāpati Dakṣa, desiring to create offspring, produced fifty daughters. He gave ten of them to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa.
Appointed to guide Time for twenty-seven Indus, Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, begot the Ādityas upon her who was the most excellent among the thirteen wives of Dakṣa.
01.070.009e Indra and the other gods endowed with heroic power, as well as Vivasvat; 01.070.010a from Vivasvat was born the son Yama Vaivasvata, the lord;
01.070.010c and from Yama, O King, Mārtaṇḍa was also born as a son.
To Mārtaṇḍa was born a son, the wise and powerful Manu;
and Yama was also born as his son, the renowned and powerful younger brother. That wise Manu was righteous-souled, in whom the lineage was firmly established.
From that, this lineage of Manu became renowned as the Mānavas;
from that Manu were born the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others, who are thus called Mānavas.
At that time, O King, the Brāhmaṇa order was united with the Kṣatriya order.
The Brāhmaṇas and Mānavas preserved the Veda with its auxiliary branches for them: Vena, Dhṛṣṇu, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Ikṣvāku,
Karūṣa, Śaryāti, and likewise Ilā as the eighth.
They say that the sons of Manu, who were devoted to the duties of the Kṣatriyas, had Pṛṣadhra as the ninth and Nābhāga-Ariṣṭa as the tenth; these sons of Manu were possessed of great strength.
Furthermore, there were fifty other sons of Manu on earth.
We have heard that they all perished due to their mutual dissension;
thereafter, the wise Purūravas was born of Ilā,
for we have heard that she was indeed both his mother and his father.
Purūravas, though he was a man of great renown, conquered thirteen islands of the ocean while surrounded by non-human beings;
yet we have heard that he was never satisfied with the jewels, for he was free from greed.
Intoxicated by his own prowess, Purūravas engaged in conflict with the brahmins;
and even as they cried out in protest, he seized their jewels.
O King, Sanatkumāra, having arrived there from the world of Brahmā, [confronted him].
He then showed it [to him], but he did not accept it. Thereupon,
cursed by the enraged great seers,
the lord of men, possessed by greed and intoxicated by pride, lost his senses and perished instantly.
For that Virāṭ, residing in the world of the Gandharvas together with Urvaśī, brought forth the sacrificial fires according to the rules, duly established in their threefold form.
Then, six sons were born to Āyu from Ilā: Dhīmān and Amāvasu.
Dṛḍhāyu, Vanāyu, and Śrutāyu were the sons of Urvaśī. Nahuṣa, Vṛddhaśarmā, Raji, Rambha, and Anenas—
these are said to be the sons of Āyu born of Svarbhānavī.
The son of Āyu was Nahuṣa, wise and of true prowess;
that lord of the earth ruled a vast kingdom with righteousness.
He [honored] the ancestors, the gods, the sages, the brahmins, the gandharvas, the serpents, and the rākṣasas.

Nahuṣa protected the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and the common people. Having slain the hosts of Dasyus, that powerful king compelled the sages to pay tribute and made them carry him on their backs like beasts of burden.
Having surpassed the inhabitants of heaven through his splendor, ascetic power, valor, and might, he caused himself to be made the Indra;
yet Nahuṣa, though distinguished, was immediately cursed and became a python.
Nahuṣa begot six sons upon Priyavāsas: Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Pāñca, and Uddhava.
But Yati, having applied himself to yoga, became a sage who had become one with Brahman.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was a sovereign emperor whose prowess was truth;
he protected the earth and performed various sacrifices.
With great devotion, he always worshipped the ancestors and the gods beyond his own capacity.
The unconquered Yayāti showed favor to all his subjects.
His sons, great archers endowed with every virtue,
were born, O Great King, of Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā.
From Devayānī were born Yadu and Turvasu;
from Śarmiṣṭhā were born Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru. O King, he (Pūru) protected his subjects with righteousness for eternal years.
01.070.033c The son of Nahuṣa underwent most terrible old age, which destroys one's beauty. 01.070.034a Overcome by old age, that king spoke these words to his sons—
Yadu, Pūru, Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu, O Bhārata.
"Moving through my youth, enjoying desires with young women, I wish to sport; O sons, give me your assistance!
To him, his eldest son Yadu, the son of Devayānī, replied:
"What service can be done for you by us, or by our youth?
Yayāti said to him: "Please accept my old age;
with your youth, I shall enjoy the objects of the senses."
"O sons, because I have performed long sacrificial sessions (*dīrghasattra*) and because of the curse of the sage Uśanas, my purpose for desire has been frustrated; therefore, I suffer.
Let one of you rule the kingdom with my body."
"May I, as a youth with a fresh body, obtain my desires.
Yadu and the others did not accept his old age;
then Pūru, the youngest, whose prowess was truth, spoke to him.

"O King, while you remain within the domain of youth with this fresh body, I shall assume old age and abide in your kingdom by your command. Thus addressed, that royal sage, relying on the power of his asceticism, [consented].
He then transferred his old age to his high-souled son;
having thus assumed youth through the Pūru-lineage’s vital energy,
the king [Pūru] ruled the kingdom with the vitality of Yayāti.

Then, at the end of a thousand years, that unconquered Yayāti, a tiger among kings whose prowess was equal to a tiger's, remained [in that state]. And Yayāti, having sported with his two wives for a long time, [departed].
Accompanied by Viśvācī, he took his pleasure again in the Caitraratha forest;
yet that highly illustrious one did not find satisfaction in desires at that time.
O King, having understood this in his mind, he then sang this verse:

Desire for sensual pleasures is never extinguished by the enjoyment of those pleasures; rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. Even the entire earth filled with jewels, gold, livestock, and women—
Realizing that all this is not enough for even one person, one should seek tranquility. When one never commits evil toward any living being,
whether by deed, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
"When one does not fear, and when others do not fear him;
when one neither desires nor hates—then he attains Brahman.
Having considered this, O King, the man of great wisdom [perceives] the worthlessness of sensual pleasures.
Having composed his mind through his intellect, he accepted old age from his son;
and having bestowed youth upon him and consecrated Pūru in the kingdom, the king,
still unsatiated with desires, spoke to his son Pūru.
"By you I am possessed of an heir; you are my son who shall continue my lineage. Your line shall attain fame in the world as the Paurava dynasty.
Then that tiger among kings, having consecrated Pūru upon the throne, [departed].
Having performed austerities well on the peak of Bhṛgu,
that great ascetic eventually met the law of time after a long period; having completed his fast unto death, he attained heaven together with his wife.
Janamejaya said:
Our ancestor Yayāti, who was the tenth from Prajāpati—
how did he obtain the daughter of Śukra, who is so exceedingly difficult to attain?

O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear this in detail: how was it that the dharma born of the intermixture of castes did not touch him at that time? We have also heard of his movement through old age into other bodies.
"And tell me in due order, separately, those who founded the lineage of Puru.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"There was a royal seer named Yayāti, equal in splendor to the king of the gods."
Śukra and Vṛṣaparvan welcomed him just as in former times. O Janamejaya, since you ask, I shall relate to you that union between Devayānī and Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
A rivalry arose between the gods and the asuras concerning sovereignty over the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. Then,
desiring victory, the gods chose the sage Aṅgiras.
The office of family priest was for the sake of performing sacrifices, while the office of Kāvya belonged to Uśanas;
both of those Brāhmaṇas were constantly and intensely vying with one another.
There, the gods slew those Dānavas who had encountered them in battle.
Then Kāvya, relying on the power of his knowledge, brought them back to life once more;
having risen again, they then fought the gods.
As for those gods whom the asuras had slain at the front of the battle, [Kāvya restored them as well].
The noble-minded Bṛhaspati did not restore them to life,
for he did not know that science which the powerful son of Kavi knew— the science of reviving the dead; consequently, the gods fell into great despondency.
Then those gods, agitated by fear of Kāvya Uśanas, approached Kaca, the eldest son of Bṛhaspati, and said:
"Favor us who favor you; grant us your supreme assistance."

"Retrieve quickly that knowledge which resides in the Brāhmaṇa Śukra of immeasurable splendor; you shall become a sharer in our portion. That twice-born one can be seen by you in the presence of Vṛṣaparvan."

There he protects the Dānavas, but he does not protect those who are not Dānavas. You, being of youthful age, are capable of propitiating that sage and his beloved daughter Devayānī, the offspring of that high-souled one.
No one else exists who is capable of propitiating him as you are,
through your character, courtesy, sweetness, conduct, and self-restraint;
for when Devayānī is pleased, you will certainly obtain that knowledge.
Having said, "So be it," Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, then departed,
honored by the gods, toward Vṛṣaparvan. O King, having been dispatched by the gods, Kaca went there in haste.
Having seen Śukra in the city of the lord of the Asuras, he spoke these words:
"May your honor accept me as a disciple— me, the grandson of the seer Aṅgiras and the son of Bṛhaspati himself, known by the name Kaca."
"I shall practice the life of a religious student under you, my supreme guru;
O Brahmin, grant me permission for a thousand years.
Śukra said:
"O Kaca, a very welcome to you! I accept your words. I shall honor you, who are worthy of honor; may Bṛhaspati be honored.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Kaca, having replied "So be it," undertook that vow which had been personally prescribed by Śukra Uśanas, the son of Kavi. He accepted the duration of the vow exactly as it had been stated.
O descendant of Bharata, seeking to please his preceptor as well as Devayānī,
that youth, being at the very dawn of his prime,
constantly sought to gratify her by singing, dancing, and playing musical instruments.
Constantly attending upon the maiden Devayānī, who had reached the bloom of youth,
he gratified her with flowers, fruits, and various services, O Bhārata.
Thereafter, protecting a thousand cows for his teacher, he gathered forest produce.
Then Devayānī, too, following that brahmin who was observing his vows and restraints,
attended upon him in private as he sang—
him who was pure, a giver, and one who spoke kindly.
Women desire a man who is handsome and adorned with garlands;
thus Kaca practiced his vow for five hundred years.
Then, having learned of him, the Dānavas went there to seize Kaca.

Seeing him alone in the forest tending the cows, they, filled with indignation out of hatred for Bṛhaspati and for the sake of protecting their own learning, killed him; having slain him, they cut him into pieces as small as sesame seeds and gave him to the jackals.
Then those cows, without their cowherd, returned to their own pen. Seeing that the cows had returned from the forest deprived of Kaca,
O Bhārata, Devayānī then spoke these words at that time:
"O Lord, your Agnihotra sacrifice has not been offered and the sun has set;
the cows have returned without their herdsman, and Kaca is not to be seen, my son.
Clearly, Kaca, my son, must be either slain or dead."
"I tell you truly: I cannot live without that Kaca.
Śukra said:
"By the mere sound of 'Come here!', I restore the dead to life."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having employed the Saṃjīvanī lore, he called out for Kaca.
Thus summoned by the lore, Kaca appeared unharmed.
When asked, "Why have you been delayed? Kaca said to that daughter of Bhṛgu:
"O beautiful lady, [I was gathering] sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and other such items, as well as a load of wood."
Exhausted by the burden of my labor, I took hold [of the reins] and rested beneath a banyan tree;
all the cows together likewise sought refuge in the shade of the tree.
Seeing me there, the asuras questioned me, "Who are you?"
"I am Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, renowned by that name.
As soon as he had spoken these words, the Dānavas killed me, ground me into a paste,
gave me to the jackals, and went happily to their own abode.
"Summoned by the high-souled Bhārgava through his supernatural power, O blessed lady,
I have somehow returned here to your presence with my life restored.
When questioned by the Brahmin girl, he declared, 'I was slain.'"
Having repeatedly torn through the bodies of the wolves, he emerged; then,
at the request of Devayānī, that brahmin went again to the forest to gather flowers as he pleased, and the Dānavas saw him there.
Having ground it once more and mixed it with the waters of the ocean,
the maiden reported it to her father after a long time had passed. Then,
summoned again by the Brahmin through his supernatural power, the one born from the body of the Guru appeared.
Returning once more, he reported that event exactly as it had occurred:
"Having split open the bodies of the fish and the others, he emerged.
Later, on another occasion, Devayānī gathered forest produce there."
Having been thus addressed, he went to that forest; however, the Dānavas saw him again.
Then, having slain that second one, burnt him, and reduced him to powder, they collected it, filled it with wine, and stirred it together.

At that time, the Asuras offered the *surā* liquor to a Brāhmaṇa; then Kaca, the descendant of Bhṛgu, drank it along with the *surā*, together with the ashes. At the time of evening, the cows returned home without their herdsman.
Then Devayānī spoke these words once more to her father.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard his daughter’s words, Kāvya summoned Kaca with a mantra.
"O King, having known Kaca to be outside and not knowing he was within your own belly, Kaca—
your son who used to fetch flowers and perform errands— is no longer seen.
Śukra said:
"Though being raised up by the science (*vidyā*), he does not return; what can I do? O daughter, Bṛhaspati’s son Kaca has gone the way of the dead.
Even though restored to life by the science, he is thus destroyed; what can I do?"
"Do not grieve thus, do not weep, Devayānī; one such as you should not mourn for a mortal,
you for whom both the Veda and the Brahmins [are the refuge]."
The gods together with Indra, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, all the Suras, and the entire world—
everyone bows down before this transformation that has appeared.
"That twice-born man cannot be brought back to life;
even if he were restored to life, he would surely be slain once again.
Devayānī said:
He whose grandfather was Aṅgiras, the eldest,
and whose father was Bṛhaspati, rich in asceticism— that son of the Ṛṣi, or even his grandson.
How may I not grieve, how may I not weep?
He was a celibate student, rich in asceticism,
ever-diligent, and indeed skilled in his duties.
"I shall follow the path of Kaca; I will not eat, for dear to me, O father, is the handsome Kaca.
Śukra said:
"Without doubt, the Asuras hate me,
for they are destroying my sinless disciple; these fierce ones desire to make him a non-Brahmin."
"Since they have thus addressed me regarding the dānavas,
may there indeed be an end to this evil here;
for whom would the slaughter of a brahmin not consume, even Indra himself?"
01,071.040 Vaiśampāyana said:
Urged by Devayānī, the great seer Kāvya, filled with indignation,
summoned Kaśyapa’s son Kaca once again.
O King, that great seer Kāvya, being thus tormented by Devayānī, was overcome with agitation; and Kaca,
too, who possessed supreme majesty, [was likewise affected].
The high-souled one, having attained wisdom through the power of knowledge—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the powerful lord caused [the sacrifice] to be performed for the sake of Devayānī.
Terrified of his teacher and summoned by the spell,
Kaca slowly uttered a voice from within the belly.
"Be gracious to me, O Blessed One! I am Kaca, and I offer my salutations.
May you consider me as highly as your own son.
He said to him: "By what path have you been brought here?"
"You dwell within my belly; speak, O Brahmin!
For at this very moment, having destroyed the Asuras, I shall go to the gods today, O Brahmin."
Kaca said:
"By your grace, memory does not desert me;
I remember everything, exactly as it occurred."
"However, there shall be no depletion of my ascetic merit;
therefore, I endure this terrible suffering.
I have been given to you by the Asuras for the sake of the Suras."
Having slain, burnt, and ground to powder both the Brahma-illusion and the Asura-illusion, O Kāvya,
how could they possibly prevail while you stand firm?
Śukra said:
"What dear thing may I do for you today, my child?
By the death of Kaca, my life shall be saved."
"Kaca could not be seen within me unless my belly were torn open," Devayānī said.
Two sorrows, like fires, would consume me:
the destruction of Kaca and your own injury.
Upon the destruction of Kaca, I find no peace.
"I am not able to live if you are harmed.
Śukra said:
"O son of Bṛhaspati, you have attained perfection."
Since Devayānī honors you as her devotee,
may you obtain this life-restoring knowledge;
otherwise, you shall be Indra today in the form of Kaca.

"No one else, while still alive, shall emerge from my womb again, with the sole exception of a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, acquire this knowledge. Having become my son, cherish me, for I have been cherished by you."
Having departed from this body, my dear,
you should exercise a righteous regard;
having acquired knowledge from your teacher, you shall be truly learned.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having acquired the knowledge from his preceptor,
the brahmin emerged by bursting open the [preceptor's] belly.
Kaca, handsome and eloquent,
was like the moon at the end of the bright fortnight on the day of the full moon;
and having seen that heap of Brahman fallen there, [he was struck with wonder].
Having attained that perfected science and offered his salutations, Kaca also raised the dead man back to life;
then Kaca spoke thus to his preceptor.
I consider him to be both my father and my mother, who would pour the nectar of knowledge into my two ears, just as he has done for me who was ignorant.
Knowing what he has done, one should not bear malice toward him who is the giver of the unsurpassed Truth (*ṛta*), the bestower of the highest gift,
and the storehouse of treasures that extend through the four lineages.
"Those who do not honor their venerable teacher go to sinful worlds that offer no refuge.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the beings were listening, Kāvya spoke these words: "The ancient mass of Brahman has arisen;
having been deceived by the drinking of liquor,"
And having seen the utter destruction of consciousness, as well as that most terrible sight, and Kaca likewise so handsome,
then drunk and deluded by wine;
Then the high-souled Uśanas Kāvya,
rising up in anger and desiring to act for the welfare of the gods,
himself spoke these words:
From this day forward, whatever Brahmin here, having conceived a doubt regarding the drinking of liquor,
should drink it out of delusion— that person of dull intellect— [shall incur the penalty].
He would be one whose dharma has departed, a slayer of a Brahmin indeed;
he would be censured in this world and in the next.
And by me, this boundary of the declaration of the law for Brahmins [has been established].
Let the virtuous Brahmins who have heard the teachings of their gurus, the gods, and all the worlds indeed listen to the boundary that has been established throughout the entire world.
"The sin of that Brāhmaṇa who,
out of delusion, shall drink liquor would be equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, and he shall also go to hell.
Having said this, that noble-souled one—
That immeasurable treasury of those who are treasuries of asceticism,
having summoned those Dānavas whose intellects were deluded by fate, spoke these words to them:
"I tell you, O Dānavas, you are fools!
Kaca has succeeded and will dwell in my presence,
having acquired the highly significant science of the Saṃjīvanī."
Equal in power to Brahmā, he has become one with Brahman;
Kaca, who performed difficult deeds for the sake of the gods,
shall not have his fame fade away, and he shall be worthy of the sacrificial offerings.
Having spoken these words, that descendant of Bhṛgu fell silent;
the Dānavas, overcome with wonder, departed for their own abodes.
Having resided in the presence of his preceptor for a thousand years, he—
Having been granted permission, Kaca desired to go to the abode of the gods.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that time, he whose vow was completed was dismissed by his preceptor.
As he was setting out for the abode of the gods, Devayānī said this to him:
"O grandson of the seer Aṅgiras, you shine by virtue of your conduct, your noble lineage, your learning, your asceticism, and your self-restraint."
Just as the highly illustrious seer Aṅgiras is honored by my father,
so too is Bṛhaspati even more honored and worthy of worship by me.
Knowing this, O one rich in asceticism, understand what I am about to say.
"Just as I have conducted myself toward you while remaining steadfast in my vows and endowed with self-restraint, so too,
O you who have completed your studies, it behoves you to accept me, your devotee. Take my hand according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the sacred mantras."
Kaca said:
"O lady of faultless limbs, just as the Blessed One, your father, is worthy of worship and honor for me,
so too are you even more worthy of my worship."

"O blessed lady, you are dearer than my own life to the high-souled Bhārgava; according to dharma, you are always worthy of my worship as the daughter of my guru. By virtue of the conduct due to a guru, you are even more venerable to me than my own teacher."
"O auspicious one of pure smiles, you ought not to speak to me in such a manner.
O Devayānī, just as my father Śukra is eternally venerable to me as a guru, so too are you; you ought not to speak to me thus."
Devayānī said:
"O best of the twice-born, you are indeed the son of my father's preceptor; you are not the son of my father. Therefore, you are both to be honored and worshipped by me as well."
And while you, Kaca, were being struck down again and again by the Asuras,
from that time forward, you yourself remember the affection I felt for you;
you know my friendship, my passion, and my supreme devotion.
"O knower of dharma, you ought not to abandon me, your devoted and innocent servant.
Kaca said:
"O lady of auspicious vows, you are enjoining me to a task that is improper for me to perform."
"Be gracious to me, O fair-browed one; you are more venerable than my preceptor, O auspicious lady.
Wherever you have dwelt, O large-eyed one with a face like the moon, there I too have dwelt, O blessed and radiant woman—within the womb of Kāvya."
"O fair-faced one, you are my sister by dharma; do not speak thus. O blessed lady, I have lived here happily, and no resentment remains within me.
I take my leave of you; I shall depart. May you wish me well on my path."
"Without contradicting dharma, I am to be remembered by you in other conversations; remaining ever vigilant and alert, serve my guru.
Devayānī said:
"A maiden who has reached her youth, being appointed to a religious duty— if, when urged for the sake of dharma and desire, you reject me,
then, O Kaca, this knowledge of yours shall not attain perfection."
Kaca said:
"I refuse you because she is my preceptor’s daughter, not out of any fault on her part. Since I have been permitted by my preceptor, curse me as you wish."
"O Devayānī, since I was speaking the dharma of the seers when you cursed me— and as I am not deserving of that curse, for it was done out of passion today and not according to dharma—
therefore, your desire shall not be fulfilled."
"No son of a seer shall ever take your hand;
your knowledge shall not bear fruit, just as you have told me.
However, for whomever I shall teach it, for him that knowledge will bear fruit."
01,072.021 Vaiśampāyana said: Having thus spoken to Devayānī, Kaca, that best of the twice-born and most excellent of brahmins,
then went quickly to the abode of the lord of the thirty gods.
Seeing him arrive, the gods, led by Indra, honored Bṛhaspati and, filled with joy, spoke thus to Kaca:
"Since you have performed this most wonderful deed for our benefit..."
"Your fame shall not perish, and you shall become a sharer in our portion.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Kaca had returned having acquired the knowledge, the dwellers of heaven were filled with joy.
O bull of the Bharatas, having learned that science from Kaca, they all felt their purpose was fulfilled;
then, having come together, they said to Śatakratu:
"O Purandara, now is the time for your prowess; slay the enemies!"
Thus addressed by the assembled gods, Maghavan then said,
"So be it," and set forth; he beheld women in the forest,
which was like the Caitraratha grove, as they were sporting there.
Becoming like the wind, he mixed up all their garments. Then,
having emerged from the water together, those maidens each took up the clothes that were nearest to them, one after another.
There, Śarmiṣṭhā,
the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, unknowingly took Devayānī’s garment;
thus, a mutual conflict arose between the two of them there.
01.073.007c And because of that, O Indra among kings, between Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā—
01.073.008 Devayānī said: 01.073.008a "Why do you take my garment, O Asura woman, having become my pupil?"
"Since you are devoid of proper conduct, no good will come to you.
Śarmiṣṭhā said:
"Whether sitting or lying down, your father [is subordinate] to my father."
Standing lowly and with humility, you praise and worship me constantly;
for you are the daughter of one who begs, praises,
and accepts gifts, whereas I am the son of one who is praised and gives without accepting.
Shake it! Shake it off! Be hostile and be angry, O beggar! You who are weaponless, you empty one, you agitate against the one who possesses weapons, O mendicant!
Shaking it, shaking it off, O beggar, [you seek] the offering to the gods and the offering to the ancestors.
"You shall find no one to fight you back, for I do not count you at all.
O beggar woman, if from this moment on you speak such opposition, I shall have my maidservants drag you away and cast you out, further and further."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen Devayānī in that state of exaltation, clinging to his garment,
he— having been overcome by that divine calamity— seized her with anger by the waist.
Then Śarmiṣṭhā threw her into a well and returned to her own city;
she then departed for her city while the well was concealed by grass and creepers. Having concluded that she was dead, the evil-minded Śarmiṣṭhā went away.

Without looking back, she went to her quarters, overcome by the force of her anger; having entered her own home, she remained composed, adhering to the demonic way of life. Then Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, arrived at that place.
With his draft animals exhausted and his horses weary, that son of Nahuṣa, seeking game and parched with thirst,
beheld a waterless well;
and there he saw the maiden, radiant like a flame of fire.
Seeing her, endowed with beauty, adorned with all ornaments,
and possessed of every auspicious mark, that lord of men questioned her;
having seen that maiden of celestial complexion, he questioned her.
Having consoled her with most beautiful and gentle words, that best of kings asked:
"Who are you, with copper-colored nails, dark-complexioned, and wearing polished jewel-earrings?
Why do you meditate so deeply, and why do you sigh in such distress?"
"And how have you fallen into this well covered with creepers and grass?
Whose daughter are you? Tell me everything, O slender-waisted one.
Devayānī replied:
"I am the daughter of that Śukra who, by means of his secret knowledge (*vidyā*), raises up the Daityas slain by the gods; surely he does not know me,
Yayāti."
Devayānī said:
"You who are endowed with beauty, heroism, and strength—tell me, who are you?
Tell me why you have come here; I wish to hear the truth of it."
"I am Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa; however, I am weary today from my pursuit of deer.
Having come here somewhere, O blessed lady, I have seen you here.
This is my right hand, O King, with its copper-colored nails and fingers."
"Uplift me by taking hold of me, for you are considered by me to be of noble birth.
Indeed, I know you to be self-restrained, heroic, and illustrious;
therefore, you ought to rescue me from falling into this well."
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
recognizing her as a Brahmin woman, the son of Nahuṣa took her by the right hand and drew her up from the pit.
Having swiftly lifted her out of that well, O lord of men,
Yayāti [rescued] Devayānī.
"Go, blessed lady, wherever you wish; no fear exists for you.
When addressed thus, Devayānī replied to the king:
"Take me with you and go quickly; you are dear to me."
"Since I have taken your hand, you shall therefore become my wife.
When he had spoken thus, the king, born of the Kṣatriya lineage, replied:
"O blessed lady, you are a Brāhmaṇī; therefore, you do not deserve union with me."
"You are indeed the daughter of Kāvya, the teacher of all the worlds;
for that reason, too, I have fear today. Therefore, O auspicious lady, you ought not to refuse me now at my word, O ruler of men."
"I choose you alone; you shall know this later, so go now.
Having thus addressed the fair-hipped Devayānī, Yayāti departed for his own city. When that son of Nahuṣa had gone, the blameless Devayānī also [departed].
In one place, the nurse, distressed and weeping, stood leaning against a tree. Then,
as his daughter delayed for a long time, Bhārgava said:
"O nurse, bring Devayānī of the radiant smile here quickly! As soon as this was said, the nurse went in haste to fetch her,
searching for her footsteps wherever she had gone with her friends.
She saw her standing there, thus dejected, afflicted by fatigue, and weeping.
"What is this that has happened to you, blessed lady? Speak quickly; your father is calling.
Thus addressed, Śarmiṣṭhā spoke to that nursemaid about the wrong she had committed.
Remembering her, he, overwhelmed with affection for his daughter,
spoke to that nurse who was bathing her full, high breasts with tears,
as she sat at the foot of a tree in that forest like a goddess.
