01,073.024 Devayānī said:
01,073.024a "O Ghūrṇikā, go quickly and tell my father everything."
"I shall not now enter the city of Vṛṣaparvan.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having gone quickly indeed to the palace of the Asura Ghūrṇika,"
Seeing the poem, her mind overcome with agitation, Ghūrṇikā spoke these words; having gone quickly, she entered that best of cities and,
approaching the most eminent of the twice-born, addressed him with this speech.
"O one of great wisdom, I tell you that Devayānī has been struck down in the forest by Śarmiṣṭhā,
the highly fortunate daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Upon hearing that his daughter had been struck down there by Śarmiṣṭhā, Kāvya [Śukra]—
Hurrying along the path, he departed from that best of cities;
driven by haste and sorrow, he went forth searching for his daughter in the forest.
Then, having seen his daughter Devayānī in the forest, the son of Kavi [Kāvya]—
Embracing him with both arms, he spoke these words in distress:
"All people experience suffering and happiness as the result of their own faults.
I believe there must have been some misdeed on your part for which this atonement has now been made."
Devayānī said:
"Whether there be atonement for me or not, listen attentively to what I have been told by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan."
"Is this indeed true? She said, 'You are the singer for the Daityas. For thus did Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, speak to me;
thus did Śarmiṣṭhā, your disciple, O great sage, speak to me."
With eyes intensely red with anger, she spoke these words, sharp and harsh:
"For you are the daughter of one who praises, begs, and accepts;
whereas I am the daughter of one who is praised, gives, and does not accept."
"Thus spoke Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan,
her eyes bloodshot with anger and filled with pride, again and again:
'O father, if I am the daughter of one who praises and accepts [gifts]...'"
"I shall appease Śarmiṣṭhā," so indeed was I told by my friend.
Yet, even though I spoke thus, she became violently enraged; seizing me in the lonely forest, she threw me into a well, and having thrown me in, she went home.
Thinking me, who was immortal, to be dead in a well utterly devoid of water,
and seeing that I had not returned, she went to her own home filled with joy.
Śukra said:
"O blessed one, you are not the daughter of one who praises nor of one who receives praise;
Devayānī, you are the daughter of one who is praised though he offers no praise. Vṛṣaparvan knows this as well as King Śakra, the son of Nahuṣa."
Inconceivable is Brahman, free from duality; for such is my divine power.
Neither I nor others know it;
even as I sing of it here, I do not truly know it.
There is neither one who praises nor one who worships me;
for my knowledge is free from dualities.
O auspicious lady, in truth, there is no wretchedness, deceit, or crookedness in me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Whatever exists everywhere, whether on earth or in heaven, I am eternally the master of it; so was I told by the Self-born One when he was pleased."
"Out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures, I release the waters;
I nourish all medicinal herbs—this I tell you as the truth.
[Thus she spoke to him] who was thus fallen into despondency and deeply oppressed by grief.
With sweet and gentle words, her father consoled her.
Śukra said:
"The man who always endures the insults of others..."
O Devayani, understand this: by him all this has been conquered—he who restrains rising anger like a horse.
He is called a driver by the virtuous, not he who merely hangs onto the reins.
O Devayānī, know that he who casts away arisen anger through non-anger has conquered all this;
he who here casts away arisen anger through forgiveness.

He who, like a snake shedding its worn-out skin, casts off anger and endures insults, and who, though himself tormented, does not inflict harm upon others— he is truly called a man; he is a firm vessel for prosperity.
He who might sacrifice without weariness month after month for a hundred years, and he who does not become angry with anyone—the one who is free from anger is superior to both.
Therefore, freedom from anger is supreme; desire and anger are not to be honored.
For one who is angry, acts of charity, sacrifice, and austerity are indeed fruitless.
Therefore, when free from anger, sacrifice, austerity, and charity yield great fruit.
Such a person is neither purified, nor an ascetic, nor a performer of sacrifice, nor a doer of dharma.
He who falls under the sway of anger will lose both worlds;
his sons, servants, friends, allies, wife, and even his merit and truthfulness will certainly depart from him, for he is of a wrathful nature.
"What enmity young men and young women might harbor in their ignorance, a wise man should not imitate that; they do not understand strength and weakness.
Devayānī said:
"O father, though I am but a girl, I know the distinction between these duties; I know how to remain free from anger even when reviled, and I also know the relative strength and weakness of each.
Yet, by failing to follow my own proper conduct and abandoning dharma in its true essence,"

One who desires prosperity must not tolerate a disciple who behaves like one who is not a disciple; nor should one tolerate a teacher who, having abandoned his proper conduct toward a disciple, has gone astray. Therefore, dwelling among those of confused conduct does not please me.

But those base people, being scorched by the intense fire of another's excellence and unable to attain that same state, then engage in slander. For those men who revile others on account of their conduct or their noble lineage—

A wise person seeking his own welfare should not dwell among those of evil intent. However, one should reside with those virtuous people who recognize him for his conduct and noble birth; that is said to be the best kind of dwelling.
Men who are always well-restrained, even if they are destitute of wealth; or those of evil conduct and sinful deeds, even if they are wealthy Cāṇḍālas— indeed,
there are no Cāṇḍālas by birth alone, except as determined by their own actions.
Attached to wealth, noble birth, and learning, they possess the nature of outcasts;
without cause they harbor enmity and utter slander.
There is no dwelling for him there; by associating with sinners, he would fall into sinfulness.
"Wherever a man becomes attached, whether to good deeds or evil deeds, there his pleasure will surely be fixed; therefore, I do not approve of those [pleasures].
These were the most terrible and ill-spoken words of Vṛṣaparvan’s daughter."
Indeed, I consider nothing in the three worlds to be more difficult than this:
to strike at the vital points of a man without hesitation,
while his friends and kinsmen offer no resistance.
He who, being destitute of fortune, gazes upon the blazing prosperity of his rival,
churns my heart like one desiring fire churns the fire-drill;
the wise know that for such a person, death is better.
One who associates with the base gradually incurs contempt;
harsh words issue from the mouth,
struck by which one grieves day and night.
A wise person should not discharge at others those [words] which strike the vital spots of another;
for even slowly, suffering born of weapons, poison, and fire [arises].
A wound inflicted by speech does not heal; indeed,
a forest struck down by an axe may grow back slowly,
but a loathsome wound caused by harsh words never heals.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śukra, the son of Kavi and best of the Bhṛgus, having approached in great anger and entered the inner apartments, was saluted by Vṛṣaparvan.
Having entered, Śukra, with his lips bitten in rage, spoke thus without hesitation to Vṛṣaparvan as he sat upon his throne:
"O King, unrighteousness practiced does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow."
For when an evil deed is slowly revolved, it cuts away the very roots of the doer—
whether among his sons or his grandsons— if he does not perceive it within himself;
for sin surely bears fruit, like food that has been eaten by a teacher ripening in his own belly.
O King, because you then had that Brahmin Kaca, the descendant of Aṅgiras— though he was studying, patient, self-controlled,
free from evil intent, a knower of dharma, obedient, and devoted to my household— put to death; [for that reason...]
O Lord, Devayānī was addressed with many cruel words by Śarmiṣṭhā;
having been mistreated, the high-minded woman was thrown into a well out of rage. Without her, how could he possibly find rest?
"O King, because of this, I shall dwell here; therefore, I renounce your realm.
O Vṛṣaparvan, understand this: because of the killing of that man who deserved not to be slain, and because of the killing of my daughter, I shall abandon you along with all your kinsmen."
"Do not grieve, O Vṛṣaparvan; do not be angry, O lord of the people.
O King, I shall not be able to remain in your domain together with you."—Vṛṣaparvan.
Her path is my path; what is dear to her is dear to me.
O Brahmin, whether I cause Devayānī to be killed by Śarmiṣṭhā or whether I myself instruct her [to do so], by that act I shall go to an evil destination.
"O Daitya, alas, you recognize me as one who speaks falsely,
since you do not restrain this fault of yours but instead neglect it.
Vṛṣaparvan said:
"O Bhārgava, I know neither unrighteousness nor falsehood in you;
in you both dharma and truth reside. Therefore, may your lordship be gracious toward us. O Bhārgava, if you depart from here after abandoning us..."
"We shall enter the ocean; there is no other refuge.
[Just as] previously, together with my kinsmen, [we entered] Pātāla or even the fire."
"If you should go to the gods, O lord of the house, abandoning me,
then I shall renounce everything and enter the fire.
Śukra said:
"Enter the ocean, O Asuras, or flee in all directions!
I am not able to endure anything unpleasant to my daughter, for she is dear to me. Let Devayānī be propitiated, for my very life depends upon her."
"Devayānī is pleased, and nothing else is dearer to me. I am the provider of your security and well-being, just as Bṛhaspati is to Indra.
Thus spoke Vṛṣaparvan.
"O Bhārgava, whatever wealth belongs to the lords of the Asuras—
whether elephants, cattle, or horses on this earth— you and I are the masters of it all.
Śukra said:
"O great Asura, whatever wealth belongs to the lords of the Daityas, I am its master; if that is so, let Devayānī be propitiated by you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Śukra went quickly with that king and said to her,
"O blessed lady, your word has been accepted.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the great poet Vṛṣaparvan said, "So be it.
Having gone into the presence of Devayānī, the descendant of Bhṛgu (Śukra) spoke of that matter.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Śukra, Vṛṣaparvan, together with his kinsmen, said,
"Be gracious, Devayānī," and fell at her feet upon the ground.
Devayānī said:
"O Bhārgava, if you, my dear, are the master of the king's wealth, I do not know that; let the king himself tell me. Vṛṣaparvan said:
"O auspicious one, both you and your father are to be constantly praised and honored by me. O Devayānī of pure smiles, whatever desire you long for,
I shall grant it to you, even if it be difficult to obtain."
Devayānī said:
"I desire Śarmiṣṭhā as my slave along with a thousand maidens;
let her follow me wherever my father gives her to me."
Vṛṣaparvan said:
"Rise, O charioteer! Bring Śarmiṣṭhā here quickly.
Let Devayānī fulfill whatever desire she wishes for."
One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of a family; one should sacrifice a family for the sake of a village;
one should sacrifice a village for the sake of a country; and one should sacrifice the whole earth for the sake of the self.

Then the nurse went there and spoke these words to Śarmiṣṭhā:
"Arise, blessed Śarmiṣṭhā; bring happiness to your kinsmen!
The Brahmin, urged by Devayānī, is abandoning his pupils."
"O sinless one, whatever desire she wishes for must be fulfilled by you today.
Śarmiṣṭhā said:
"Whatever desire she wishes for, I shall fulfill it today."
"If Śukra were to summon me for the sake of Devayānī in this way,
let it not be that Śukra and Devayānī depart from me because of my actions.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, surrounded by a thousand maidens in a palanquin,
she quickly departed from that best of cities at her father’s command.
Śarmiṣṭhā said:

"With a thousand maidens, I shall be your slave and attendant. Even if you employ me as a Caṇḍāla today, I will bear that upon my head. Or I shall touch even a Guru; this is the supreme duty of female slaves."
"I shall follow you there, wherever your father gives you.
Devayānī said:

"How can you, the daughter of one who is thus being praised, become a slave?
Śarmiṣṭhā replied:

"Having gathered everything together, it must be done; this is the eternal law (*sanātana-dharma*).
Having done so, O beautiful one, I shall do whatever you tell me.
Therefore, I will follow you wherever your father gives you away."

"I shall enter the city, my dear, for I am satisfied, O best of the twice-born;
your knowledge is unfailing and you possess the power of sacred lore.
Thus addressed by his daughter, that highly illustrious and foremost of the twice-born—
He entered the city joyfully, honored by all the Dānavas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, after a long time, O best of kings, Devayānī—"
That woman of excellent complexion went out to that very forest for the sake of sport,
accompanied at that time by Śarmiṣṭhā and those thousand handmaidens;
having reached that same region, she wandered about according to her pleasure.
Accompanied by all those friends, she was exceedingly joyful;
they all played with delight, drinking honey-sweet wine,
eating various kinds of foods, and biting into fruits.
And again, King Nahuṣa’s son, seeking game,
arrived by chance at that very place, exhausted by fatigue and desiring water;
there he beheld Devayānī, Śarmiṣṭhā, and those other women.
He saw Devayānī, who possessed a pure smile, seated upon an excellent, divine throne adorned with every kind of jewel; she was drinking and sporting, adorned with celestial ornaments.
Among those women, he saw that excellent lady of incomparable beauty,
adorned with golden ornaments, seated slightly lower than her throne;
and also Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the lord of the Asuras, who possessed a lovely smile.
O Bhārata, seeing Yayāti being attended by Śarmiṣṭhā with such services as massaging his feet, the women— some singing, some dancing, and some playing instruments—
stood with their heads bowed in shame.
Yayāti said:
"I ask you both about the lineages and the names of these two maidens who are surrounded by two thousand girls."
Devayānī said:
"I shall tell you; take my word to heart, O lord of men.
Know me to be the daughter of him whose name is Śukra, the preceptor of the Asuras."
"And this friend of mine, Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, the lord of the Dānavas, is my slave; wherever I go, she shall go with me.
Yayāti said:
"How is it that this maiden, your friend and handmaid, possesses such excellent complexion? O fair-browed one, she is the daughter of the Lord of Asuras; indeed, my curiosity is great.
She is neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Kinnarī."
Never before have I seen such a woman upon this earth— possessing long,
lotus-like eyes, adorned with every auspicious mark,
and endowed with beautiful brows; was she struck down by fate, or perhaps by her own ascetic penance?
Otherwise, this woman of faultless limbs shall not become a slave here;
your own form could not possibly be equal to her beauty. Alas! It was due to her past misconduct that she has become your slave.
Devayānī said:
"O tiger among men, everyone indeed follows destiny.
Considering that all is ordained by destiny, do not utter such strange words."
"Your appearance and attire are like those of a king, yet you bear the speech of a Brahmin.
What is your name, from where do you come, and whose son are you? Tell me.
Yayāti replied:
"Through my practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the entirety of the Veda has entered the path of my hearing. I am a king and a prince, renowned as Yayāti," said Devayānī.
"For what purpose, O King, have you come to this region?
Do you wish to seize some aquatic creature, or perhaps out of a desire for game?
Yayāti replied:
"O blessed lady, desiring deer, I have come here for the sake of water;
furthermore, I have been pursued by many, so you ought to grant me permission.
Devayānī said:
"With two thousand maidens and my servant Śarmiṣṭhā, I am at your disposal; may you be blessed. Become my friend and my husband.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having beheld the daughter of the lord of the Asuras, his mind became attached to her;
thinking, "Śarmiṣṭhā is my queen," he spoke these words.
Yayāti said:
"Know me to be the son of Uśanas; may prosperity be yours, O blessed lady. I am not worthy of you, O beautiful one.
For kings, O Devayānī, are ineligible for marriage with your father. Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa is entitled to marry from all four castes."
Kṣatriyas and others who act in descending order, rather than ascending,
and whatever a man does out of desire, anger, or greed— Devayānī, know this well— he will certainly go to hell.
The wife of another, one's own elder sister, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), an outcaste (*patitā*), a daughter-in-law,
and others who are mendicants or unwell— these are declared by the wise to be women who must not be approached.
Devayānī said:
The Kṣatriya power is united with the Brahmanical power, and the Kṣatriya is joined with the Brahman;
there is no difference between the two, for they are most closely related.
You are both a seer and the son of a seer, O son of Nahuṣa; take me as your wife.
Yayāti said:
"O beautiful lady, although all four castes originate from a single body, they have distinct duties and distinct purifications; among them, however, the Brāhmaṇa is the best."
Devayānī said:
"O son of Nahuṣa, this rite of joining hands has never before been practiced by men;
since you took my hand first, I therefore choose you."
"How indeed might another man touch the hand of me, a high-minded woman,
once it has been grasped by you— the son of a seer, or by the seer himself?
Yayāti said:
"A wise man who understands should consider a learned brahmin more difficult to overcome than an enraged venomous serpent or a fire blazing in all directions.
Devayānī said:
"O bull among men, how is it that you say a Brahmin is more difficult to overcome than a venomous serpent or a fire blazing in every direction?
Yayāti replied:
A venomous serpent kills one person, and by a weapon only one is slain;
but a brahmin, when provoked to anger, destroys entire kingdoms and even cities.
Nowhere indeed does a serpent kill [everyone], nor does a weapon cut down others [in such a manner].

Fire burns by chance, but a twice-born man slays with his mind; therefore, O timid one, I consider a Brahmin to be most invincible. For this reason, O blessed lady, I will not marry you unless you have been given away by your father.
Devayānī said:
"O King, marry me, for I have been given by my father; indeed, you were chosen by me. There is no fear in accepting what has been given without a request."
"Wait a moment, O King; I shall send word to my father.
Go quickly, Dhātrikā, and bring Brahmakalpa here. Quickly announce that the son of Nahuṣa has been chosen at the *svayaṃvara*."
01.076.027 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the nurse, having been quickly dispatched by Devayānī to her father,
reported everything to him exactly as it had happened.
And as soon as he heard this, Śukra Bhārgava showed himself to the king;
thus says Vaiśampāyana.
Then the nurse went quickly toward Śukra;
having seen him, she saluted him according to custom and spoke these words:
"The son of Nahuṣa, the lord of the earth, has been chosen as the husband by Devayānī."
"O Brahmin, devoted to truth, grant me your permission today.
Go, go ahead, my dear; I shall follow along with you.
Having consulted with the infallible King, I will carry out her command."
Then Śukra appeared, blazing as if with splendor,
a Brāhmaṇa who illuminated all beings like a mass of radiance.
Upon seeing that Śukra had arrived, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, [stood before him].
Standing with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, she paid homage to the Brahmin Kāvya.
Devayānī said:
"O father, this king, the son of Nahuṣa, took my hand when I was in a state of distress."
"01,076.029b No other man has previously taken me; by that [act], I have been made fearless.
01,076.029c Homage to you! Give me to him; I choose no other husband in the world.
01,076.030 Śukra said:
"One thing is the law, another is what is pleasing; you have chosen the son of Nahuṣa as your husband.
Because of Kaca’s curse, nothing else could have happened previously for you.
O hero, you have been chosen as husband by this daughter of mine, whom I hold so dear."
"There is great fault in taking [a woman] by force, due to the mixing of castes with a Brahmin woman.
Accept this queen given by me, O son of Nahuṣa.
Yayāti said:
"O Bhārgava, O Brahmin, so that no great unrighteousness born of the intermixture of castes may touch me here, I choose you. Śukra said:
"I release you from unrighteousness; choose whatever you desire.
Do not falter in this marriage; I shall drive away your sin. Marry the slender-waisted Devayānī according to dharma."
"You shall attain incomparable joy together with her. Moreover, O King, this maiden Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, must always be honored by you; do not summon her to your bed."
"This maiden Śarmiṣṭhā is the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan;
you should honor her, but do not summon her to your bed. Do not call her in private, nor should you touch her."
"Take her as your wife; may prosperity be yours, and you shall obtain whatever you desire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then Devayānī was chosen by him through the Gāndharva form of marriage."
Thus addressed, O King, Yayāti circumambulated Śukra and,
according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures, performed the auspicious marriage ceremony;
having received from Śukra great wealth as well as the excellent Devayānī.
Accompanied by two thousand maidens as well as Śarmiṣṭhā,
that best of kings was honored by Śukra and the Daityas;
having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites, he then circumambulated [the fire].
Having been granted leave by the high-souled one, he went to his own city, joyful.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached his own city, which was like the city of Mahendra, Yayāti—
Having entered the inner apartments, he settled Devayānī there;
and with Devayānī’s consent, having built a house near the Aśoka grove, he settled that daughter of Vṛṣaparvan there.

Accompanied by Devayānī, that king, the son of Nahuṣa, provided Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the Asura, who was attended by a thousand maidservants, with garments, food, and drink, honoring her with great respect.
Endowed with supreme joy, he rejoiced for eternal years.
Devayānī arrived in the vicinity of the Aśoka grove;
having played there with Śarmiṣṭhā in that delightful and charming place, she remained.
Having pointed her out right there, he went home together with the king.
In this very way, for a long time, he rejoiced with great affection;
he sported for many years, exceedingly delighted like a god.
When her season had arrived, the beautiful woman Devayānī first conceived and gave birth to a son. After a thousand years had passed, Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, [conceived].
Having reached her youth, she reflected upon her season.
Then Śarmiṣṭhā, having bathed and purified herself, adorned with all her ornaments and leaning against an aśoka branch covered with clusters of full-blown flowers, [waited].
Beholding her own face in a mirror, longing for the sight of her husband and overwhelmed by grief and delusion, she spoke these words:
"O Ashoka, dispel the sorrow of one whose mind is struck down by grief!"
"Quickly give me a name that reflects you, for I am longing for the sight of my beloved.
When she had spoken thus, Śarmiṣṭhā replied once more:
"The time of my season has arrived, yet I have not chosen a husband."
"What has been gained? What indeed must be done? Or what, having been done, would be truly accomplished? Devayānī has borne children, while I have reached my youth in vain.
Devayānī is a performer of meritorious deeds, for her husband is the son of Nahuṣa."
Just as she chose him as her husband, so do I choose him.
It is my firm conviction that the king must grant me the fruit of a son;
even now, may that righteous-souled one come into my sight in private.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having bound the king by the hair, I entreated him for a husband worthy of me,
as I looked again and again with joy at Devayānī’s son within the house.
While sporting in her inner apartments, he remained there for a moment;
then, at that time, the king, having gone out by chance,
arrived near the Aśoka grove and stood there, having encountered Śarmiṣṭhā.
Seeing him alone in that secluded place, the sweetly smiling Śarmiṣṭhā went forward to meet him,
joined her palms in reverence, and spoke these words to the king:
"Are you Soma, Indra, Viṣṇu, Yama, or Varuṇa?"
"O son of Nahuṣa, who in your lineage would dare to touch a woman? For you, O King, always know me by my beauty, noble birth, and character.
Therefore, I entreat you; having propitiated you, grant me my season, O lord of men."
Yayāti said:
"I know you to be a Daitya maiden, endowed with virtue and irreproachable;
in your beauty, I do not see even a point the size of a needle's tip that is blameworthy."
"O most excellent lady, from that time forward, whenever I have seen you, I have remembered [him] incessantly.
When I had brought Devayānī away, Uśanas Kāvya said to her:
"This daughter of Vṛṣaparvan must not be summoned by you to your bed."
"Having done what was pleasing to Devayānī, you must also support Śarmiṣṭhā.
Śarmiṣṭhā said:
"A word spoken in jest does no harm;"
O King, they say that five kinds of untruths are not sinful: [speaking falsely] regarding women, at the time of marriage, when life is at stake, and when all one's wealth is being seized.
O King, when questioned regarding testimony, those who speak otherwise than the truth speak falsely; however,
when they are focused on a single purpose, they speak with consistency.
Falsehood destroys one who speaks untruth;
yet there is no falsehood in lies told to women, in jest, or at a wedding.
In cases involving the protection of one's own life or wealth, such speech indeed attains the status of being supreme.
The wise ones who know the truth regarding the subtle meaning of the Dharma have spoken thus.
Yayāti said:
"O auspicious lady, it is exactly as you say; for this is indeed my own desire."
Those words of the brahmin revolve within my heart:
"The king is the authority for all beings; he would perish by speaking falsely.
Even though I have fallen into a crisis of necessity, I cannot bring myself to speak untruth.
Śarmiṣṭhā said:
"O King, these two are considered equal: he who is a husband and he who is the husband of a friend.
They say that a marriage is equal; you have been chosen by my friend as her husband."
Yayāti said:
"It is my established vow that I must give to those who ask. Since you ask me for a boon, tell me what I may do for you."
"Whether it be wealth, or desire, or even a kingdom, O lady of pure smiles," Śarmiṣṭhā said,
"save me from unrighteousness, O King, and establish me in righteousness."

"Desiring a son, I choose no other; there is nothing superior to a son. Through you, may I become a mother of offspring and practice the highest dharma in this world. Women were created by the Self-Existent One for the sake of sons and for the sake of supporting their husbands."

A maiden who has no husband, and she who remains childless—her birth in this world is in vain, and no higher destination exists for her. O King, there are only three who possess no property of their own: a wife, a slave, and likewise a son.
Whatever they acquire for you, that wealth belongs to him [your husband].
I was given along with Devayānī by the great seer Kāvya;
you ought not to make false the words "she is to be honored and supported."
O King, you give gold, jewels, pearls, garments, and ornaments, as well as cattle, villages, and other such things, to those who ask;
this is called external giving, not that which relies upon the body.
Giving away one's children is difficult, and giving away oneself is difficult;
O worthy one, by the gift of one’s body, all that becomes given. Whatever anyone desires, that very thing I give to him.
"O King, having spoken thus, you have caused a proclamation to be made three times a day throughout the city.
O Indra among kings, what you have said is false, and your proclamation was indeed in vain. Therefore, O Indra among kings, make that true, just as Vaiśravaṇa does."
"I am Devayānī’s maidservant, and as a Bhārgava woman, I am under your control. Both she and I, O King, must be supported by you; therefore, accept me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the king recognized this as the truth; yet,
out of fear of Śukra and Devayānī, and also out of dread of violating dharma, he honored Śarmiṣṭhā and established her in the right.
Surrounded by officiating priests, family chaplains, teachers, and ministers,
he performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites and gave sacrificial fees to the Brahmins at an auspicious conjunction of stars and a moment honored by the twice-born.
Having met with Śarmiṣṭhā and having obtained her desire,
they honored one another and departed as they had come.
During that encounter, the fair-browed Śarmiṣṭhā, who possessed a lovely smile—
She conceived her first pregnancy from that best of kings; and then, O King,
at the proper time, the lotus-eyed lady gave birth to a prince who shone like a celestial child and possessed eyes resembling lotuses.
01,078.001 Vaiśampāyana said: 01,078.001 Yayāti;
01,078.001 Vaiśampāyana.
During that conjunction of the constellations, when the moon was situated in an auspicious asterism in the bright fortnight,
that sovereign king rejoiced together with Śarmiṣṭhā; for to him,
Śarmiṣṭhā became like the foremost prosperity of his subjects, even as a daughter-in-law.
Devayānī, who was indeed as fierce in appearance as a female serpent, became mine;
just as rain is to crops and nectar is to the gods,
so too did Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, come into being for me.
Having thus reflected in his mind, he avoided Devayānī. But upon hearing that a son had been born, O Bhārata, the sweetly-smiling Devayānī, afflicted with grief, thought about Śarmiṣṭhā.
Having approached Śarmiṣṭhā, Devayānī said this:
"O fair-browed one, what is this transgression that you, driven by lust, have committed?
Śarmiṣṭhā replied:
A certain rishi arrived, a righteous soul who had mastered the Vedas;
he was a granter of boons, and I requested of him a desire consistent with dharma— for the sake of offspring, O lady of lovely smiles, I chose him indeed.
"O lady of pure smiles, I do not pursue desire through unrighteous means;
therefore, I tell you the truth: this child is my offspring from that seer.
Devayānī said:
"O timid one, it is well if this is true; then let that twice-born man be known.
I wish to know that brahmin by his lineage, name, and ancestry.
Śarmiṣṭhā replied:
"O lady of pure smiles, seeing him blazing with vital power and splendor like the sun, I had no strength to question him. Devayānī said:
"O Śarmiṣṭhā, if this is so, no resentment remains within me,
provided that you have obtained offspring from the eldest and most excellent of the twice-born.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus spoken to one another and laughed together,
the daughter of Bhṛgu went to her own quarters, convinced that what had been said was the truth.
King Yayāti, however, begot two sons upon Devayānī.
Yadu and Turvasu were like two other Śakra and Viṣṇu.
At that time, the royal sage Yayāti, lord of the earth,
[drank] wine mixed with honey-juice, which increases intoxication.
She made the daughter of Śukra drink wine that was reddish-yellow;
and having drunk the liquor again and again, Devayānī became intoxicated.
She wept, sang, and danced repeatedly.
The queen, speaking at great length, said this to the king:
"Your appearance and attire are like those of a king; for what purpose have you come here?
For what business have you arrived in this desolate and dense forest?"
"O best of the twice-born, King Yayāti of fierce appearance is coming! If you desire your own welfare, O brāhmaṇa, flee from here!
To Devayānī, who was thus lamenting, the son of Nahuṣa [spoke].
He rebuked her with words— she who was sinless yet increased his own sin.
Then he commanded the eunuchs, the mute, the lame, the elderly,
and the impotent to guard and nourish Devayānī.
Then the wise King Nahuṣa, having obtained Śarmiṣṭhā, took delight with her for a very long time.
And from that royal sage, Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, [gave birth].

He begot three sons—Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru. When the king became devoted to Śarmiṣṭhā, his lineage was established through her; having made Madirā helpless, he took pleasure with Śarmiṣṭhā day after day.
Then, O King, at a certain time, Devayānī of the pure smile went out into the great forest accompanied by Yayāti. And there she beheld youths of celestial form.
While they were playing with great confidence, she, filled with wonder, said this:
"O King, whose children are these, auspicious as the sons of gods? In their splendor and in their form, they appear to me to be just like yours."
Having thus questioned the king, he then questioned the princes;
[he saw] one who was looking at the surface of the earth,
and having understood that the curse had been brought about by him...
At that time, having heard those words of theirs, their nurse spoke:
"O princes, why do you not speak to your father, that bull among the twice-born?
O sons, what is the name and lineage of your brahmin father?"
"Tell me quickly and in truth: who is he, and where does he dwell?
Speak to me exactly as it is, for I desire to hear of him.
Thus addressed by Devayānī of the slender waist, those princes replied.
With their index fingers, they pointed out that very best of kings;
the children also told him of Śarmiṣṭhā and their mother, saying,
"Our father is both a seer and a brahmin, a twice-born man."
"Śarmiṣṭhā would not speak a falsehood; Devayānī, please forgive her. When questioned by her in private, the children spoke the truth.
Having said this, they all together approached the king.
The king did not approve of them in the presence of Devayānī;
then those boys, weeping, went toward Śarmiṣṭhā,
and from no great distance away, she stood before the king with her face cast down.
Having seen the affection of those children toward the king,
and having understood it according to the truth, the queen spoke thus to Śarmiṣṭhā.
Upon hearing of those children, the king, as if filled with shame, [remained silent].
Unable to reply, the king became silent; then,
seizing Śarmiṣṭhā by the hand in anger,
Devayānī spoke again.
"Someone is approaching me who is a seer," she said.
"O beautiful lady, you are surely inciting me toward Yayāti;
I had already spoken of this before, yet you have committed a transgression."
"Since you are dependent on me, why have you done what is displeasing to me? Having resorted to that very conduct of an Asura, do you not fear [me]?
Śarmiṣṭhā said:
"What was said, 'He is a seer,' is indeed true, O lady of the lovely smile;
yet, as you conduct yourself both according to logic and according to dharma, I do not fear you.
When the king was chosen by you, he was already chosen by me."
"For according to dharma, O beautiful lady, a husband is indeed the protector of his wife's friends.
You are worthy of my worship and respect, being my elder, most excellent, and a Brahmin woman. Yet the royal sage is even more worthy of my worship than you; do you not know that?"
"Both auspicious gifts were bestowed upon me by your father, my preceptor;
therefore, he is both my husband and my venerable one, and he sustains me here as one who is to be supported.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard her words, Devayānī then spoke this:
"O King, I will not dwell here today; you have done me a displeasure.
Enjoy yourself here as you wish with Queen Śarmiṣṭhā."
Then Devayānī blazed up violently with anger,
as if burning the ashamed Śarmiṣṭhā upon beholding her;
and the dark-eyed woman cast off all her ornaments.
Seeing that dark-complexioned woman rise up suddenly with tearful eyes and hasten toward the presence of Kāvya,
the king was then distressed; agitated, he followed behind her, offering words of consolation.
She turned back, her eyes reddened with anger, yet that lovely-eyed woman said nothing at all to the king;
in no long time, she arrived in the presence of Kāvya Uśanas.
Upon seeing her father, she saluted him and stood before him;
immediately thereafter, Yayāti honored Bhārgava.
Devayānī said:
"By unrighteousness, righteousness has been defeated; the order of high and low has been overturned. I have been surpassed by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan;
for she has borne three sons to this King Yayāti."
"O dear one, I tell you this: though I am unfortunate, I have two sons.
O descendant of Bhrigu, this king is renowned as a knower of dharma;
yet he has transgressed the bounds of propriety—this I tell you, O son of Kavi."
Śukra said:
"O great king, since you, though knowing the dharma, have committed an unrighteous act for the sake of what was pleasing to you, therefore invincible old age shall soon overcome you."
Yayāti said:
"O Blessed One, when the daughter of the lord of the Dānavas was indeed soliciting me for the fertile season, I acted in accordance with dharma, my mind being focused on nothing else."

O Brahmin, a man who has been chosen as a husband but does not grant his seed to a woman who solicits him during her fertile season is called a "feticide" (bhrūṇahan) by the exponents of the Veda in this world.
Furthermore, he who, when solicited in private, refuses a desiring woman who is a fit partner for intercourse—
He does not transgress against these principles, and thus he is called a "destroyer of the embryo" by the wise.
My vow is this: whatever anyone asks of me, that must be given.
You have granted her to me, for she desires no other protector here.

"O Brahmin, considering that 'this act of mine was done for the sake of dharma,' please forgive me. O descendant of Bhṛgu, having reflected upon these reasons and being agitated by the fear of unrighteousness, I approached Śarmiṣṭhā.
Śukra said:
"O King, am I not to be consulted by you? You are dependent on me. O son of Nahuṣa, for one who acts falsely regarding his duties, theft occurs."
01,078.036 Vaiśampāyana said: Then Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, having been cursed by the enraged Uśanas,
immediately cast off his former youth and was overtaken by old age.
Yayāti said:
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, I am not yet satiated with youth in the company of Devayānī. O Brahmin, show me your favor; let this old age not enter me."
Śukra said:
"O lord of the earth, I do not speak this falsely; you have indeed attained old age.
However, if you so desire, you may transfer this old age to another."
Yayāti said:
"O Brahmin, let that son who gives me his youth become the sharer of my kingdom, the sharer of my merit, and likewise the sharer of my fame; please grant your consent to this."
Śukra said:
"O son of Nahuṣa, whether it be the eldest or the youngest, whichever of your sons gives you his youth, to him you shall transfer your old age as you desire."
"By meditating upon me with devotion, you shall incur no sin.
Your son shall grant you long life— he who will become the king— and he shall likewise be long-lived, renowned, and possessed of many offspring."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having reached old age and returned to his own city,
Yayāti spoke these words to his eldest and most excellent son, Yadu:
"O dear one, old age, wrinkles, and gray hair have come upon me;
yet, due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, I am not yet satiated with youth.
O Yadu, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age."
"By means of your youth, I shall enjoy the objects of the senses;
but when a full thousand years have passed, I shall give my own youth back to you and receive back my own body along with old age and its evils."
Yadu said:
"O King, there are many defects in old age regarding the consumption of food and drink; therefore, I shall not accept [the kingship]. This is what my mind approves."
With white hair and beard, dejected and made frail by old age,
his body covered in wrinkles, he was unsightly, weak, and emaciated;
unable to perform his duties, he was held in contempt by the young.
Together with those who depend on me for their livelihood, as well as my wife, sons, and friends, I do not desire that old age—
so terrible and destructive of beauty.
"O King, you have many sons who are dearer to you than I am;
therefore, O knower of dharma, choose another to take upon yourself the burden of old age.
Yayāti replied:
"Since you, though born from my heart, do not grant me your own youth,
therefore, my dear son, your progeny shall indeed be excluded from sovereignty.
Thus addressed, the king spoke to Turvaśu:
"O Turvasu, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
O dear son, I shall indeed enjoy the objects of the senses with your youth.
When a full thousand years have passed, I shall give back your youth once more."
"I shall take upon myself my own sin along with old age.
Turvasu said:
"O father, I do not desire old age, which destroys the enjoyment of desires."
[That which] destroys strength and beauty, and annihilates intellect and life-force—
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth."
"O Turvaśa, this dear desire of yours shall never be fulfilled;
therefore, O Turvaśa, your progeny shall go to utter extinction among those of mixed conduct and laws, and those who act in a contrary manner."
O fool, you will become a king among the lowest of flesh-eaters;
you will rule over those addicted to the wives of their gurus, those born of animal wombs, those who follow the ways of cattle, and sinful barbarians.
01,079.014 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus cursed his own son Turvasu,
Yayāti spoke these words to Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā.
"O Druhyu, accept for a thousand years this old age that destroys complexion and form, and give me your own youth;
when the thousand years are complete, I shall return your youth to you."
"And I shall take back my own sin along with old age.
Druhyu said:
"An aged man enjoys neither elephant, nor chariot, nor horse, nor woman."
"His speech becomes faltering; therefore, I do not desire that old age.
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth,"
Therefore, O Druhyu, your cherished desire shall never be fulfilled anywhere—
wherever there is no passage for the foremost of horse-drawn chariots, nor for horses,
nor for elephants, nor for sedan chairs, nor likewise for donkeys.
Where there shall always be crossings by means of goats, cattle, and likewise palanquins, as well as rafts and floats— there you,
along with your lineage, shall obtain the title of "Bhoja," though you are not a king.
"O Anu, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
for one thousand years, I shall live with your youth.
Anu replied:
"An old man eats food at the improper time like a child, just as one who is impure;
he does not offer oblations into the fire at the proper time—I do not desire such old age.
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your own youth,
this defect of old age which you have mentioned shall therefore befall you;
and your offspring, O Anu, shall perish upon reaching their youth."
And you too shall become like Druhyu and Yayāti, intent on leaping into the fire.

Like a child, the aged man takes food at the improper time, just as one who is impure;
he does not offer oblations to the fire at the proper time, nor does he perceive the right moment. He performs no duty; I do not desire such old age.
"O you who were born from my heart, why do you not grant me your own youth?
This defect of old age has been described by you, and therefore you do not accept it.
Furthermore, your offspring, having reached youth, will perish because of it."
"You too shall become one who leaps into the fire.
O Anu, accept this evil along with old age;
for one thousand years, I shall indeed wander about assuming your form."
When a full thousand years have passed, I shall give you back your youth once more, and I shall indeed take back my own self along with old age.
An aged man does not enjoy an elephant, nor a horse, nor even a seat.
One's speech becomes ill-favored; I do not desire such old age, you who, born from my very heart, do not grant me your own youth.
May there never be a road for elephants, horses, chariots, or carriages.
Whether it be elephants, seats, or donkeys, and likewise camels, cattle, or palanquins,
or whatever other vehicle there may be— the god may destroy them here and there.
"O evil-minded one, he who is born from you shall not be king, nor shall he ever be so;
and he shall be rejected by the four [ancestors]. Having thus cursed them each according to his desire, and knowing that Pūru would not transgress [his command], he went into the presence of Pūru.
Having thus cursed his own son who spoke in this manner,
Yayāti then addressed these words to the son of Śarmiṣṭhā, Anu;
and then, having summoned his son Anu, the king spoke these words.
"O Pūru, you are my beloved son; you shall become even more excellent than I. O dear one, old age, wrinkles, and grey hair have come upon me;
yet, due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, I am not yet satiated with youth."
"O Pūru, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
for a certain period of time, I shall indeed enjoy the objects of the senses through your youth.
When a full thousand years have passed, I shall return your youth to you."
"And I shall take upon myself my own sin along with old age.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, Pūru immediately replied to his father.
"O Great King, I shall do as you have told me; I will carry out your word.
For the word of a guru is meritorious for men, leading to heaven and prolonging life. By the grace of his guru, Indra (Śatakratu) ruled over the three worlds."
Having obtained the permission of his guru, he shall attain all his desires. "O King, I shall take upon myself your evil along with your old age;
or as long as you wish to live, I shall bear that [burden] for you."
"Take youth from me and enjoy your desires as you wish;
I shall remain hidden by old age, assuming your form. Having given my youth to you, I will conduct myself exactly as you have told me."
Yayāti said:
"O Pūru, my child, I am pleased with you; being pleased, I grant this to you:
your progeny shall possess all their desires fulfilled within the kingdom."
"He shall attain renown in the world for his righteousness, wealth, and pleasure.
Having spoken thus, Yayāti, the great ascetic, called to mind Kāvya and then transferred his old age into the high-souled Pūru.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Now, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, being endowed with the youth of a Pūru,
possessed such beauty and vigor that he was like a young prince.
Filled with joy, that best of kings enjoyed his beloved sense-objects according to his desire, according to his energy, according to the season, and according to his pleasure— indeed,
as was fitting for him, O lord of kings, in a manner not contrary to dharma.

He gratified the gods with sacrifices, and likewise the ancestors with funeral offerings (śrāddha); he favored the poor with desired boons, and the best of the twice-born with the objects of their hearts' desire;
he honored guests with food and drink, and the Vaiśyas with protection.
By means of compassion toward the Śūdras, by suppression of the Dasyus,
and by righteousness toward all his subjects,
Yayāti protected them properly, like a second Indra in person.
That king, possessing the prowess of a lion, being young and engaged in the objects of the senses,
moved about in supreme happiness without violating the dharma. Having attained auspicious desires, that monarch became both satisfied and weary.
The lord of men, who knew the divisions of time, being powerful and skilled in calculation, recalled a period lasting for a thousand years;
having attained youth, that royal seer remained for a thousand autumns.
Accompanied by Viśvācī, he took delight and shone resplendently in the Nandana grove.
That righteous lord of the earth spent his time in Alakā as well as on the northern peak of Mount Meru;
yet, when that king beheld the passage of time, he [became aware of it].
Thinking that the time was now complete, he then spoke to his son Pūru:
"O subduer of enemies, my son, I have enjoyed the objects of the senses according to my desire, according to my energy, and according to the proper time during my youth."
O virtuous son, your supreme youth is filled with splendor;
yet desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of its objects,
but rather increases further, like a fire fed with sacrificial oblations.

Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon this earth are not sufficient for even one person; therefore, one should abandon craving. That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to relinquish, and which does not age even as one ages—[that craving one should abandon].
For one who abandons that thirst which is a life-ending disease, there is happiness. For a full thousand years my mind was attached to sense objects;
nevertheless, day after day, thirst for these things arose within me.
Therefore, having abandoned her and fixed my mind upon Brahman, I shall wander with the deer, free from dualities and free from the sense of "mine.
O Pūru, I am pleased; may prosperity be yours; take back this youth of your own.
"Take this kingdom as well, for you are my beloved son;
enjoy it for a long life, O long-lived one, for as long as you desire in your youth."
I have bestowed upon you this kingdom together with its lineage; enjoy it for a very long life, endowed with youth for as long as you desire.
Then King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, underwent old age,
while Pūru regained his own youth once more.
[The people saw] the king desiring to consecrate his youngest son, Pūru.
The social orders, headed by the Brahmins, spoke these words:
"O Lord, how can you bypass Yadu— the grandson of Śukra and son of Devayānī,
the eldest— and bestow the kingdom upon Pūru?"
"Yadu is your eldest son, born before Turvasu;
after him were born Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā, then Anu, and Pūru.
How is it that, bypassing the elder sons, the younger one deserves the kingdom?"
"We inform you of this; you must uphold the Dharma.
For a king who transgresses the Dharma brings suffering upon his subjects.
Yayāti said:
"Let all the social orders, headed by the Brahmins, hear my words:
the kingdom must not be given to my eldest son under any circumstances. My command was not obeyed by my eldest, Yadu."

He who is contrary to his father is not considered a son by the virtuous. That son is truly a son who carries out the commands of his mother and father, who is devoted to their welfare, and who behaves toward his parents as a son should.
But a man without a son shall fall from heaven into the suffering of hell;
for "pu" is the name of hell, and they know that hell is indeed suffering (*duḥkha*). Because he protects (*trāṇa*) him, therefore people desire a son both in this world and in the next.
A son who is equal to his father in the worship of ancestral deities and celestial rishis,
and who excels many in virtue, is called the eldest.
He who performs meritorious deeds is the rightful recipient of the eldest’s share, both in this world and in the next.
A son endowed with virtuous qualities is superior; another who is useless is not. Those who know the Dharma say that the performance of duty for the sake of one's ancestors depends upon the son.
One who is mute, blind, deaf, or afflicted with leprosy does not fulfill his own duty.
A son who is a thief and a sinner is not called the eldest, even if he is the eldest. I have been treated with contempt by Yadu, as well as by Turvasu;
and by Druhyu and Anu too, great disrespect has been shown toward me.
Pūru has carried out my word and has been especially honored by me;
he is my youngest heir, by whom my old age was assumed. He has fulfilled for me the origin spoken of in the Vedas, which arose from my heart.
"All this that has been born is his very self; 'the son is the self,' so says the sacred revelation (śruti). My desire has been fulfilled by Pūru, who took the form of a son.
And Śukra Uśanas Kāvya himself granted me this boon."
"The son who follows you shall be the king, the lord of the earth;
or rather, that son among your sons who follows [your will] shall be the heir to the inheritance. Thus I entreat you: let Pūru be consecrated in the kingdom."
The subjects said:
"O Lord, that son who is endowed with virtues and is always devoted to the welfare of his mother and father deserves every auspicious thing, even if he is the youngest."
In the Vedas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Arthaśāstras, it was declared by the sages of old:
"Pūru is worthy of this kingdom, for he is your son who acts for your pleasure.
Because of Śukra’s granting of a boon, it is not possible to speak otherwise.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the satisfied citizens and country-folk,
the son of Nahuṣa then consecrated his own son, Pūru, in his own kingdom.
Having banished his sons Yadu, Turvasu, Druhyu,
and Anu along with their followers to the borderlands, the son of Nahuṣa bestowed the kingdom upon Pūru and consecrated himself for a life in the forest.
O descendant of Bharata, the king went out from the city accompanied by brahmins and ascetics,
as well as Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā;
together with his wives, he performed supreme austerities in the forest.
From Yadu were born the Yādavas; from Turvasu came the sons, the Yavanas; the Bhojas were the sons of Druhyu, while from Anu arose the Mleccha tribes.
From Pūru, however, came the Paurava lineage, in which you yourself were born, O King.
01,080.027c This [kingdom] is for him to rule for a thousand years, he who is self-controlled.

Having joyfully consecrated him in the kingdom, the sage became a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Having lived in the forest in the company of brahmins,
self-controlled and subsisting on fruits and roots, he departed from this world for heaven.
Having gone to that abode of the gods and dwelling there joyfully and at ease,
after no great length of time, he was cast down again by Śakra— namely,
Janamejaya.
Having obtained the company of the virtuous, he went once more to heaven;
and having gone to heaven, O Brahmin, while dwelling in the abode of the gods,
how was he eventually displaced by Śakra after no very long time?
"I have heard that he fell from heaven, neither having reached the surface of the earth nor remaining in the intermediate space; from that very state,

The heroic one, having met in assembly with King Vasumān, Aṣṭaka, Pratardana, and Śibi, spoke. Janamejaya said:
"By what action did that lord of the earth attain heaven again?
I wish to hear all of this in its entirety and according to the truth,
as it is being told by you, O Brahmin, in the presence of this assembly of brahmin-sages."
Yayāti, the lord of the earth, was indeed equal to the king of the gods;
he was the enhancer of the Kuru lineage and possessed a splendor like that of the sun.
Of that high-souled one, whose fame was vast and whose renown was true—
"I wish to hear his life-story in its entirety, both in heaven and here on earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Very well, I shall relate to you the further narrative of Yayāti."
For the sake of merit, both in heaven and here on earth, and for the destruction of all sins,
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, having joyfully consecrated his youngest son Pūru upon the throne, then departed for the forest.
Having settled his sons, led by Yadu, in the border regions,
the king dwelt for a long time in the forest, subsisting on fruits and roots. With his self restrained and his anger conquered, he offered libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Offering oblations into the sacred fires according to the rules prescribed for forest-dwellers,
the powerful lord honored his guests with offerings of forest produce; adopting the practice of gleaning ears of grain and picking up fallen grains, he made his meals from whatever food remained.
For a full thousand years, that king maintained such a practice;
for thirty autumns he subsisted on water alone, with his speech and mind restrained.
Thereafter, he remained unwearied for a year, subsisting only on air.
The king performed austerities in the midst of five fires for one year; he stood on one leg for six months, subsisting only on air. In this very manner, the years passed by in succession.
Then Puṇyakīrti went to heaven, pervading both heaven and earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to heaven, that lord of kings dwelt in the abode of the gods.
Honored by the thirty gods, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and likewise the Vasus,

the highly virtuous Yayāti, a performer of meritorious deeds who had mastered his senses, traveled from the world of the gods to the world of Brahmā while being worshipped by the thirty gods and the Sādhyas.
01.082.002c It is heard that the protector of the earth lived there for a long time.
01.082.003a Once, that best of kings, Yayāti, the descendant of Puru, approached Śakra; 01.082.003b*0855_01 O dear one, having conversed with Śakra on various topics, he [remained].
At the conclusion of their conversation, Śakra questioned that lord of the earth.
Śakra said:
"O King, when that Pūru [was born] with your form..."
Having taken up old age, he then wandered upon the earth after having bestowed the kingdom upon him;
tell me truly here, what was said by you?
Yayāti said:
"The entire territory between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is yours;
you are the king in the center of the earth, while your brothers are the lords of the border regions."
A person should not practice dejection, deceit, or anger; likewise,
one should never engage in crookedness, envy, or enmity under any circumstances.
O Lord of the Gods, a wise man should never show contempt for his mother, nor his father, nor one who is learned, nor one whose wealth is asceticism, nor one who possesses forgiveness.
A man who is capable always forgives; it is the incapable man who cries out in anger.
The wicked man hates the virtuous; the weak man hates the stronger; the ugly man hates the beautiful; the poor man hates the wealthy;
the idle man hates the industrious; and the unrighteous man hates the righteous.

O Śakra, this is a characteristic of confusion: that one who is devoid of qualities should regard as possessing qualities that which is the opposite; O Lord of Devas, among these [beings], whether they be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, such is the mark established.
Those who praise what is praiseworthy are themselves praised as illustrious ones.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, a man should fix his mind upon that which is praiseworthy.
For those who are ignorant of the world are not praiseworthy; they are indeed your brothers, yet they lack wisdom.
By my command, all have indeed become lords of the ends;
for you, O King, are truly called the giver of Dharma, the supreme Dharma. Tell me once again today the excellent account of the world's course.
One who is free from anger is superior to those who are angry;
likewise, one who is patient is superior to one who is impatient.
And humans are superior to non-humans.
In the same way, the wise man is superior to the ignorant one:
when reviled, he should not revile in return; for the anger of one who endures it consumes the reviler and he gains the reviler's merit.
One should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor a speaker of cruel words;
one should not take from another by means of speech through which another would be distressed.
One should not speak that harsh speech which leads to worlds of evil— a man who pierces the vitals with rough words, wounding others with the thorns of his tongue.
One should know him to be the most unfortunate among people,
carrying misfortune fixed upon his face;
yet he should be honored by the virtuous from the very outset.
Thus, one should be protected from behind by the virtuous;
one who follows the conduct of the noble should always endure the insults of the wicked and adopt the behavior of the virtuous.
Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth;
struck by them, one grieves day and night,
for they fall upon the vital points of another.
A wise person should not release these toward others;
for there exists no such means of winning over in the three worlds as friendliness toward all beings, generosity, and sweet speech.
Therefore, one should always speak kindly and never speak harshly;
one should honor those worthy of honor and give, but never beg.
Indra said:
"O King, having completed all your duties,
you have abandoned your home and gone to the forest;
therefore, O son of Nahuṣa, I ask you this."
"With what ascetic power are you equal to Yayāti?
Yayāti replied:
"Neither among gods nor humans, nor among Gandharvas or great seers, am I [equal]."
"O Vāsava, I do not see anyone who is equal to myself in asceticism.
Indra said:
"Since you have disregarded those who are your equals and even your superiors;"
And because you did not recognize the power of the Evil One,
therefore these worlds of yours are finite;
when your merit is exhausted, O King, you shall fall today.
Yayāti said:
"O Śakra, if my worlds have gone to ruin because of my contempt for the gods, sages, gandharvas, and men,"
"O King of the Gods, deprived of the world of the gods, I would rather fall among the virtuous," [he said].
Indra replied:
"O King, you have fallen into the presence of the virtuous,
where one who has lost his standing may regain it once more.
Knowing this, O Yayāti, return [to your former state]."
"They are not to be despised, for they are equal to or even superior [to you].
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, having abandoned those regions frequented by the king of the immortals;"
Beholding Yayāti falling from the meritorious worlds, Aṣṭaka, the best of royal sages and protector of the ordinances of the true dharma, spoke to him.
Who are you, a youth whose form is equal to that of Vāsava,
blazing with your own splendor like fire,
falling from the darkness of the rising clouds?
Just as the sun is the foremost among those who move in the sky,
so too, seeing you falling from the path of the sun—
immeasurable and possessing the splendor of Vaiśvānara and the sun— [he was struck with wonder].
"What indeed is this that falls?"— thus we all wondered,
utterly bewildered upon seeing you stationed in the path of the gods.
O you whose majesty is equal to that of Śakra, Arka, and Viṣṇu,
we have all risen up toward you today, desiring to test the reality of your power.
We did not dare to question you first,
nor do you ask us who we are;
therefore, we ask you, O one of enviable form.
To whom do you belong, and for what reason have you come?
Let your fear depart, and quickly cast off despondency and delusion, O you whose form is equal to that of the Lord of Gods.
For even Śakra, the slayer of Bala, is not able to overcome you when you stand in the presence of the virtuous;
for the virtuous are indeed the refuge of those fallen from happiness.
O you who are like the king of the immortals, those lords of the moving and the unmoving have always been united with the virtuous;
you are firmly established among such worthy beings.
Fire is the master in heating; the earth is the master in receiving seeds;
the sun is the master in illumination; and a guest is the master of the virtuous.
Yayāti said:
"I am Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and the father of Pūru; because of my contempt for all beings,
I have been cast down from the world of the gods, Siddhas, and Ṛṣis."
Falling away and descending with little merit,
I am indeed older than you in years;
therefore, I do not offer you the formal salutation.
"He who is advanced by knowledge, by austerity, or by birth—
he is worthy of honor among the twice-born.
Aṣṭaka said:
O King, if you had said, "He who is old by age is truly venerable," you would not have addressed him at all;
for he was indeed one who was venerable by virtue of his wisdom, even though he was advanced in years.
He alone becomes worthy of worship by the twice-born.
Yayāti said:
"They say that sin is contrary to [righteous] actions."
That conduct exists in those inclined toward evil and leads to a world of sinners;
the virtuous do not follow this,
just as their own selves would speak what is agreeable to them.
"I once possessed vast and great wealth, yet despite my efforts, I could not retain it. Having reflected thus, I am now established in what is truly for my own welfare."
He who lives knows;
he who is wealthy performs great sacrifices with well-conducted rites;
and he whose intellect is disciplined in all branches of knowledge.
Having studied the Vedas and disciplined the body through austerity, a person free from delusion ascends to heaven;
he should never exult over great wealth.
One should study the Vedas, yet one should not be possessed by egoism. In this world of living beings, there are many diverse conditions;
they are dependent on destiny, their efforts rendered fruitless, and their authority lost.
Encountering each of these, the wise man should not be distressed,
for by his own discernment he should realize that destiny is all-powerful;
indeed, whether it be happiness or even suffering for a living being, [it is ordained].
One finds what is dependent on fate, not by one's own power;
therefore, considering destiny to be powerful,
one should never grieve nor ever rejoice.
The wise man should not be distressed by suffering nor rejoice in happiness; he should always conduct himself with equanimity,
considering destiny to be more powerful.
One should neither grieve nor rejoice at any time;
for I have seen this world both here and beyond,
and though enjoyments are obtained from every side, there is no finality.
O Aṣṭakā, I am never bewildered by fear;
I have no mental distress whatsoever.
Just as the Creator ordains me in this world, so do I abide.
Thinking, "I shall certainly become thus," there arose those born from moisture, those born from eggs, those born from sprouts,
reptiles, worms, and then fish in the waters.
Likewise, stones, grass, and wood— all these,
when their destined time has ended, return to their own original nature;
having realized the impermanence of pleasure and pain.
Why should I indulge in the distress of the Aṣṭakā rites? What should I do, and by doing what might I not suffer?
Therefore, being vigilant, I shall avoid such distress.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While King Yayāti was speaking thus,
Aṣṭaka then questioned him once again.
[He saw] his maternal grandfather, endowed with all virtues,
situated there in the heavenly world exactly as he was.
Then Aṣṭaka said:
"O lord of the earth,
tell me truly and in full, O King, which principal worlds were enjoyed by you, for how long, and in what manner."
"You indeed speak of the dharmas like one who knows the field (kṣetrajña).
Yayāti said:
"I was once a king here, a sovereign ruler of the whole earth."
From there, I indeed conquered the great worlds; I dwelt there for just a thousand years,
and from there I have entered the supreme world.
Then he dwelt for a full thousand years in the beautiful city of Puruhūta, which had a thousand gates and extended for a hundred yojanas.
Then I attained the supreme world;
then, having reached that divine, ageless world,
which is difficult to attain even for Prajāpati, the Lord of the World.
There I dwelt for just a thousand years;
from there, I have come to this supreme world,
to the abode of the God of gods.
Having conquered the worlds, I dwelt as I pleased,
being honored by all the thirty gods,
equal in power and splendor to the lords.
Thus, assuming any form at will, I dwelt in the Nandana grove for ten million years,
sporting with the Apsarases amidst fragrant scents.
Beholding the beautiful trees in full bloom,
I remained there, attached to divine pleasures; then, after a vast period of time had passed, [I became] exceedingly [disgusted].
The messenger of the gods, of formidable appearance, spoke aloud with a voice raised three times in a protracted tone: "Perish!
"This much is known to me, O lion among kings."
Then, having fallen from Nandana with my merit exhausted,
O lord of men, I heard the voices of the gods in the sky as they lamented out of compassion for me.
"Alas, what misery! Yayāti, whose merit is exhausted, is falling—though he was a doer of good deeds and possessed of holy fame.
As I was falling, I then spoke to them:
"How indeed might I fall among the virtuous?"—
thus was the sacrificial ground of you all described by them;
having seen it, I have come here in haste.
Perceiving the scent of the sacrificial oblation as a guide from the sacrificial ground—
the smoke trailing like the corner of an eye—
the delighted Aṣṭaka said:
When you, O Lord, who can assume any form at will, dwelt for ten million years in the Nandana grove,
what was the reason, O foremost of the Kṛta Age?
Having abandoned the truth and descended to the earth,
Yayāti said:
"Just as one has kinsmen, friends, and relatives here in this world;"
For when wealth is exhausted, men indeed abandon one;
likewise, when a person's merit is exhausted there,
the hosts of gods together with their lords immediately abandon him.
Aṣṭaka said:
"How do they become exhausted of merit in that state?
My mind is exceedingly bewildered regarding this."
"Of what kind are they, and whose abode do they attain?
Tell me that, for you are considered by me to be a knower of the field (kṣetravid).
Yayāti said:
O god among men, they all fall into this earthly hell, lamenting piteously,
to serve as food for herons, jackals, and crows.
What has diminished undergoes manifold increase;
therefore, a person should avoid that which is wicked and censurable in the world.
"O King, all this has been told to you;
now tell me further, what shall I say to you? Aṣṭaka said:
But when birds, as well as vultures, blue-necked peacocks, and winged insects, tear them apart—
how do they come to be, and how do they arise?
"I do not hear of any other earthly hell.
Yayāti said:
"Above the body, as karma unfolds..."
It is evident that they wander upon the earth;
they fall into this earthly hell and do not look up for many series of years.
Sixty thousand [beings] fall through the sky for eighty full years;
they indeed strike those who are falling down the precipice.
"The terrible, earth-born Rākṣasas with sharp fangs torment you as you fall.
Aṣṭaka said:
"Since they strike you as you fall because of your sin..."
How do the terrible, earth-born Rākṣasas with sharp fangs come to be, how do they manifest,
and in what state do they become when they enter the womb?
Yayāti said:
"The seed, mixed with the essence of flowers and fruits,
follows after it once it has been emitted by the man."
He indeed receives her menstrual blood;
having become an embryo, he enters therein.
The lords of the forest and the medicinal herbs enter as well.
Water, wind, earth, and the atmosphere;
the four-footed and the two-footed— all these,
having become such, become embryos.
Aṣṭaka said: Does the embryo here assume another body,
or does it go by its own will?
Entering this human birth,
I speak to you out of doubt; tell me about the formation of the body, the physical frame, and so forth.
By what means does one obtain the designation "eye" and "ear"?
Being asked, explain all this truth;
for we all consider you, dear father, to be a Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Yayāti said:
"The wind draws up the seed from the womb of the embryo during the season, mingled with the essence of the flower's nectar."
There, having performed his office as a mere constituent element (*tanmātra*),
he gradually develops the embryo here;
being born, his limbs are fully formed.
A person who has reached the culmination of the six types of knowledge perceives sound here with his two ears and beholds every form with his eye.
One perceives odor with the nose, and likewise taste with the tongue;
one perceives touch with the skin and mental states with the mind.
Know this, O Aṣṭakā, as the process of accumulation.
Regarding the body of a great-souled living being,
Aṣṭaka said:
"When that person who has come to rest is cremated..."
Whether it is buried or rubbed away,
having become non-existent and met with destruction,
by what means does it perceive itself beforehand?
Yayāti said:
Having cast off his life-breaths like one who has fallen asleep after groaning, he departs,
placing both his good deeds and his evil deeds before him.
O lion among kings, following the lead of the wind, he leaves one womb and takes up another body;
those who perform meritorious deeds go to a meritorious womb.
Evil-doers go to an evil womb;
they become insects and winged creatures.
O one of great power, I have no further desire to speak.
Four-footed, two-footed, and six-footed beings— such as these come to exist within the womb;
all this has been explained in its entirety.
"But what more do you ask, O lion among kings?
Aṣṭaka said:
"O father, by doing what does one obtain the worlds?"
"By what austerity or by what knowledge does a mortal attain the highest [states]? Being questioned by me, tell me all that correctly, so that one may go in due order to the auspicious worlds."
Yayāti said:
"Austerity, charity, tranquility, self-control, modesty, uprightness, and compassion for all beings— "
The virtuous say that there are exactly seven great gates to the heavenly world for men;
yet those overcome by darkness lose them through pride.
The virtuous say that for a man this is always so:
he who, studying and considering himself wise, destroys the reputation of others by means of his learning.
His worlds become finite,
and that Brahman does not grant him its fruit.
There are four actions that bring about fearlessness:
When performed improperly, they bring fear: the fire-sacrifice of pride, the silence of pride,
study out of pride, and sacrifice out of pride.
One should not take joy when being honored,
nor should one experience distress from being insulted;
for in this world, the virtuous honor the virtuous.
"The wicked do not attain the perception of the virtuous.
"One should give," "one should sacrifice," "one should study"—these are my vows;
they are called the gifts of fearlessness, yet they must always be avoided [by the wicked].
By which the wise perceive the ancient substratum, the mind whose devotion is focused on the Supreme,
that [attainment] is the supreme good, having reached the radiant form.
"May they attain supreme peace both after death and in this world.
Aṣṭaka said:
"How does a householder, while living, reach the gods?"
How does a monk, how does one who performs the duties of a teacher,
or a forest-dweller established on the true path,
experience many [pleasures] in this world?
Yayāti said:
"He who studies when summoned, who does not need to be urged toward his duties for his teacher, who rises before [his teacher] and goes to bed after him."
Gentle, self-controlled, steadfast, and vigilant,
the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) who is devoted to his studies attains perfection. Having acquired wealth in accordance with the Dharma, he should perform sacrifices.
One should always give and feed guests,
never taking from others what has not been given;
this is the ancient secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the householder.
One who lives by his own effort, who has turned away from crookedness,
who gives to others, and who does not harm others—
such a sage attains the highest perfection.
Dwelling in the forest, his conduct and diet restrained, not living by craft and never having a home,
he has conquered his senses and is liberated from everything.
Wandering without a home, light, and of few pursuits, that monk wanders alone through various lands;
he by whom the worlds are conquered even during the night.
Desires are conquered and become sources of happiness; on that very night, the wise man, self-restrained,
should strive to dwell in the forest.
The forest-dweller establishes ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first in the merit of his good deeds.
Having liberated the elements of his own body in the forest,
Aṣṭaka said:
"How many, indeed, are the sages, and how many are the forms of silence?"
"Tell us how they become so; we wish to hear it.
Yayāti said:
"For one who dwells in the forest, the village remains behind his back."
"O lord of men, even while living in a village, that sage would be as one dwelling in the forest.
Aṣṭaka said:
"How indeed, for one dwelling in the forest, does the village become left behind?"
"How can one who dwells in a village have the forest behind him?
Yayāti replied:
"A sage who would be a forest-dweller should not make use of anything belonging to the village."
Likewise, while he dwells in the forest, a village remains behind him;
the sage is without fire, without a fixed abode, and without a lineage or clan,
desiring only as much clothing as is needed for a loincloth.
As long as one maintains the vital breaths, so long should one desire food;
for him who dwells thus in the village, the forest remains behind his back. But he who, having renounced desires, abandoned ritual action, and conquered his senses—
The sage who maintains silence shall attain perfection in this world.
Who would not honor him— whose teeth are cleansed, whose nails are clipped, who is always bathed and adorned, and who, though dark in complexion, abides in pure deeds?
When the sage has been emaciated by austerity, wasted away with his flesh, bones, and blood diminished, and has become free from the pairs of opposites while established in silence, then,
having conquered this world, he conquers the world beyond.
When the sage seeks his food with his mouth like a cow, then his former world is fit for immortality. Aṣṭaka.
Yayāti said:
"The general duty for all is to abandon anger, greed,
malice, intolerance, envy, theft, pride, hypocrisy, and slander."
He who possesses neither anger, nor greed, nor the sense of "mine" is a knower of Dharma.
Whether one is a perpetual student, a celibate, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a sage, how could one incur unrighteousness through eating? Tell me this, as I ask you.
An ascetic (*muni*) should eat eight morsels; one living in the forest (*araṇyavāsin*), sixteen;
a householder (*gṛhastha*), thirty-two; and for a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), there is no limit.
Thus should this cause be understood—the auspicious and inauspicious nature of these eight [rules].
Aṣṭaka said:
"O King, of these two who run as if like the sun and the moon, which one first attains intimacy with the gods?"
Yayāti said:
"The mendicant who dwells even in a village, homeless among householders living according to their desires yet remaining self-restrained— he has already attained that which the other two have not."
If one who has attained a long life should undergo a transformation of character, he should repent for having done that and perform another penance thereafter. Furthermore,
that man who always stands in fear of sinful deeds [is purified].
