Even while constantly practicing what is pleasant, he prospers in ultimate happiness. For they say that which is cruel is unwholesome; yet he who, with a mind intent on his own ruin, pursues such a path.
"O King, even one who is not a horse and is likewise powerless—
that straightforwardness is indeed concentration (samādhi) and that is nobility.
Aṣṭaka said:
"By whom have you been sent as a messenger today, O King—
you who are young, garlanded, handsome, and radiant? From where have you come, and in which direction do you dwell?"
"Or is there perhaps a terrestrial abode?
Yayāti replied:
"This is the earthly hell for one whose merit is exhausted."
As he descended from the sky, scattered across the earth,
I— learned, wise, and noble-minded—
realized that all this world was the result of my own karma.
"Having said this to you, I shall immediately leap down;
the world-protectors and the brahmins are urging me on. Indeed, in the presence of the virtuous, such a fall is ordained."
They were all assembled together and possessed of virtue,
O lord of men, for this boon was indeed obtained by me from Śakra as I was about to fall to the surface of the earth.
Aṣṭaka said:
"I ask you this: do not fall into the abyss, O King, if there are indeed worlds for me here."
"Whether they are situated in the intermediate space or in heaven,
I consider you to be the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) regarding that dharma.
Yayāti said:
As many cattle and horses as are established upon the earth,
along with wild animals and mountains—
just so many worlds are indeed established for you in heaven.
"Know it thus, O lion among kings.
Aṣṭaka said:
"I give those [worlds] to you; do not fall into the abyss."
O King of kings, whatever worlds I possess in heaven,
whether they are situated in the intermediate space or in the celestial realm—
ascend to them quickly, O subduer of enemies!
Yayāti said:
"O chief of kings, one such as I, who is not a Brahmin yet knows the Veda, does not engage in the acceptance of gifts."
O lord of men, just as one should always give to the twice-born, so did I formerly bestow gifts;
never did a miserable man who was not a Brāhmaṇa live [upon my bounty].
And as for that Brahmin woman, the wife of a hero— if I were to do what has never been done before, seeking to know what in that situation would be right, what indeed would be good?
Pratardana said:
"O you of desirable form, I, Pratardana, ask you whether there are worlds for me."
"Whether they are stationed in the intermediate space or in heaven,
I consider you to be the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) regarding that dharma.
Yayāti said:
O lord of men, there are many worlds for you;
in each one, for seven times seven days,
they shall be free from sorrow, dripping with honey and mixed with clarified butter.
"They wait, not having reached their end.
Pratardana said:
"I give those [rewards] to you; do not fall into the abyss!"
"Whatever worlds are mine, let them indeed be yours— whether they rest in the intermediate space or in heaven;
ascend to them quickly, free from delusion."
Yayāti said:
"O King, being a king himself, one who possesses equal splendor should not desire the merit or the security and well-being of another."
Even when encountering calamity through the decree of fate, a wise king should never practice cruelty;
rather, mindful of the path of dharma that brings renown, he should act with righteousness.
A king who regards righteousness should act accordingly;
one like me, possessing a sense of dharma and knowing the truth, would never act so miserably as you have described.

Having thoroughly and correctly determined what is dharma and what is adharma, he who acts with vigilance regarding what ought and ought not to be done is indeed wise, true to his word, and self-disciplined.
The king shall be like a guardian of the world by his majesty;
whenever there is doubt regarding a matter of dharma or for the sake of desire, they find the correct resolution therein.
In that matter, the first task to be performed is the task of Dharma— that which is Dharma does not conflict with Artha and Kāma. I shall perform what has never been done before by others.
While King Yayāti was speaking thus, seeking to know what was truly beneficial in that matter,
Vasumān, the best of kings, addressed him.
Vasumān said:
"O son of Raudrāśva, I ask you, Vasumān:
does there exist for me a world in heaven, O lord of men?"
"If you, O great-souled one, are renowned throughout the intermediate space,
I consider you to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of that dharma.
Yayāti said:
Whatever is the intermediate space, the earth, and the directions;
whatever shines with brilliance and is radiant—
so many worlds indeed exist established in heaven.
"They wait, having no end.
Vasumān said:
"I give those [worlds] to you; do not fall into the abyss."
"Whatever worlds are mine, let them indeed be yours! O King, buy these [worlds] even for a blade of grass,
if the acceptance of a gift is rightly considered by you to be utterly corrupt."
Yayāti said:
"I do not recall ever making a false sale; I suspect that I might have taken something in vain from a child."
"I would not do anything that has not been done before by others;
desiring to know what is truly beneficial in this matter," Vasumān said.
"O King, enter those worlds granted by me, if you do not desire to purchase them;
O lord of men, I shall certainly not go to them."
"May all the worlds indeed be yours.
Śibi said:
"I am Śibi, the son of Uśīnara; I ask you this:"
O father, if there are worlds for me here,
whether they be situated in the intermediate space or in heaven,
I consider you to be the knower of that dharma.
Yayāti said:
"O wise one, O lord of men, you have not disregarded those seeking your favor, neither in word nor even in thought."
"By that [merit], infinite worlds in heaven have been attained by you— worlds that are like lightning, resonant with sound,
and vast. Śibi said:
"O King, enter those worlds granted by me, if you do not desire to purchase them;
nor shall I enter them hereafter once they have been given."
"Having gone there, you indeed worship those worlds.
Yayāti said:
"Since you possess a power equal to that of Indra..."
And those worlds, O god among men, are likewise infinite;
yet today I find no delight in what is given by another.
Therefore, I do not rejoice in an inheritance from Śibi.
Aṣṭaka said:
"O King, if you do not welcome us individually to these worlds,
then we shall all go to hell after handing everything over to you."
Yayāti said:
"O virtuous ones, you have given this to one who is worthy, out of truthfulness and compassion;
however, I do not venture to accept it, as it was not performed by me in the past."
"O lion among kings, that which was said regarding me, who am free from desire— that this gift is as described— is not so in reality."
"That very act of giving shall bear fruit for him.
Aṣṭaka said:
"To whom do these five golden chariots belong that are visible here?"
Being exalted, they shine forth like blazing crests of fire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Vasumān—
Yayāti said: "O Vaiśampāyana,
in ancient times, during the great horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) ordained by the Self-born One,"
O Bhārata, having cut the limbs of the horse in their proper order, the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ, together with the Brahman priest—
all sixteen officiating priests— cast them into the fire according to the prescribed rite.

And those most sinful men on earth who smelled the fragrance of the smoke were instantly freed from their sins and became purified; and in that very interval, that Mādhavī, whose wealth was her asceticism—
With her limbs covered by a deer-skin and wearing the hide of a deer,
she moved about among the deer, subsisting on a diet of deer;
having entered the sacrificial enclosure with the herds of deer, she was filled with great wonder.

Sniffing the scent of the smoke, she wandered there with the deer; wandering through the sacrificial enclosure and beholding those unconquered sons as well as the majesty of the sacrifice, Mādhavī attained great joy.
Then, perceiving that Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, had reached heaven while remaining untouching the earth, he paid homage to his father. At that time, Vasumanas questioned his ascetic mother.
"Since you have performed this salutation at my feet here, tell me:
who is this king, resembling a god, whom you worship?
Listen together, my sons; this is my father, the son of Nahuṣa."

"Yayāti was known as the maternal grandfather of my sons; having installed my brother Pūru upon the throne, he departed for heaven. For what reason has that highly illustrious one come here in this manner?"
Having heard those words of his, she said, "She has fallen from heaven.
Hearing her son's speech, Mādhavī, her mind overcome with agitation, spoke to her father, who was surrounded by his grandsons.
"Accept these worlds won by my asceticism as my own,
like wealth acquired through righteousness that belongs to sons and grandsons.
Here, the seers who recite the Dharma speak only of their own self-interest."
"Therefore, through your gift and your austerity, ascend to heaven;
for if this is indeed the fruit of dharma, it shall be well for you. By your daughter and by your high-souled grandsons, I have been truly delivered."
Therefore, from this day forward, the daughter’s son is a purifier for the paternal ancestors.

At a *śrāddha*, three things are purifiers: the daughter’s son, the *kutapa* woolen blanket, and sesame seeds. Furthermore, three qualities are praised in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
Those who eat, those who serve, those who cause [the mantras] to be heard, and those who purify;
when the sun has grown dim during the eighth part of the day,
that time is called *kutapa*, and what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
Sesame seeds protect from the *piśāca* demons; *darbha* grass protects from the *rākṣasa* spirits;

those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) protect the assembly; and that which is eaten by ascetics (*yati*) is inexhaustible. Having found a worthy recipient who is wise, learned in the Vedas, firm in his vows, and pure—
"That time was granted by Time; Time is not subject to anything else.
Having spoken thus, the wise Yayāti spoke again:
"Since we have all performed the ritual ablutions at the conclusion of the sacrifice, hasten now out of respect for the gravity of our task."
Yayāti said:
"Indeed, these five golden chariots shall carry you;
standing high, they shine brightly like blazing crests of fire."
Aṣṭaka said:
"Ascend the chariot, O King, and traverse the sky with valor;
we too shall follow when the time comes."
Yayāti said:
"Now we must all go together, for we have conquered heaven.
This dustless path to the abode of the gods is visible before us."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having mounted their chariots, all those best of kings set forth,
traversing the heavens with their splendors and encompassing heaven and earth with their righteousness.
Aṣṭaka, Śibi, Pratardana the king of Kāśī,

and Vasumanas of the Ikṣvāku line— these four rulers of the earth were then all virtuous men who, having performed their ritual ablutions at the conclusion of the sacrifice, ascended together to heaven.
Aṣṭaka said:
"I thought that I alone was to go first;
Indra is my friend in every respect, for he is a great-souled one."
"Why did this Śibi Auśīnara alone overtake all the horses with such speed?
Yayāti said:
He gave away whatever wealth he possessed for the sake of the path to the gods;
this Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, is indeed the best among us,
for he is charity, austerity, truth, and also dharma.
O King, these qualities— modesty, prosperity, forgiveness, gentleness, and likewise endurance— resided in the intellect of the incomparable and compassionate King Śibi.
"Since one who behaves in such a manner is restrained by a sense of shame, Śibi therefore departed in his chariot.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Aṣṭaka, out of curiosity, questioned his maternal grandfather once more, who was like Indra himself:
"O King, I ask you; tell me the truth."
From where and whose son are you? And whose [son] are you?
For there is no doer of that which has been done by you;
in this world, there is no other kṣatriya or brāhmaṇa besides you.
Yayāti said:
"I am Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and the father of Pūru; I was once the sovereign lord of the whole earth."
"I declare this secret matter to my own kin:
I am your grandfather, manifest before you.
I have conquered this entire earth."
Having bound pure, one-hoofed, and well-formed horses to the sacrificial post, I gave them to the Brahmins;
at that time, the gods become partakers of merit.
I have indeed given this entire earth to the Brahmins— this whole land filled with vehicles,
cattle, gold, and the finest wealth.
There were a hundred arbudas of cows there;
by my truth, both heaven and earth,
as well as fire among men, blaze accordingly.
Not even a single word has been uttered by me in vain;
for the virtuous honor truth.
O Aṣṭaka, I speak this truth here: it is indeed so.
Pratardana, the son of Upadāśva,
as well as all the gods, sages, and worlds—
these are to be honored through truth; this is my firm conviction.
"Whoever, free from malice, shall report to the foremost of the twice-born all of us who have conquered heaven exactly as it occurred, shall attain the same world as ours.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus that great-souled king,
the subduer of enemies, having been rescued by his own grandsons,
abandoned the earth— he whose deeds were most noble.
Having ascended to heaven, he pervaded the earth with his deeds;
since your entire life story as the son of Nahuṣa has been related to you in detail and according to the facts.
O King, whose lineage is renowned as Kauraveya, and in whom you were born with the deeds of a lord of men— this great life-story of Yayāti is most meritorious.
"By hearing this and by causing others to hear it, a person here goes to heaven.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the kings who were the founders of Pūru’s lineage."

Tell me of the son of Yayāti, Pūru, the best among the upholders of dharma— what his vigor was, what he was like, how many there were [of his lineage], and what his prowess was; and tell me in due order of the others who increased the lineage of Pūru.
O best of the twice-born, tell me again in detail how King Bharata was born from Janamejaya, the son of Duḥṣanta;
for in his lineage there was no lord of men who was deficient in virtue or lacking in prowess.

O one rich in asceticism, I wish to hear in detail the life stories of those kings of celebrated conduct and profound wisdom, even though at some time in the past they may have been deprived of offspring.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Behold, I shall tell you that which you ask me concerning the heroic upholders of Pūru's lineage, whose splendor was equal to that of Śakra."
Pūru, that tiger among kings, remained established in his kingdom like his father the king, ever devoted to dharma and possessing the prowess and valor of Śakra;
he was endowed with abundant wealth and strength, and honored for all the auspicious marks of royalty.

Pravīra, Īśvara, and Raudrāśva—these three great chariot-warriors were born as the sons of Pūru by Pauṣṭī; among them, Pravīra was the founder of the lineage. From him was born Manasyu, the heroic and powerful son of Śyenī.
The lotus-eyed protector of the earth bounded by the four oceans was Subhrū,
the handsome and eloquent Saṃhanana; these three were the sons of Sauvīrī,
born of Manasyu— all of them heroes and great chariot-warriors.

The powerful King [Raudrāśva] begot upon Miśrakeśī the wise Anvagbhānu and others, as well as the illustrious Vasunābha and Garbhara, who were both beautiful, heroic, fearless, and givers of protection.
The youngest son of Sunvata was Rathantara; from him was born a hero, a firm-bowed man of beautiful form, that best of kings.
[He begat] Rudrāśva, Pṛṣadaśva, Rathāśva, Gaya, and Manu.
The younger brother begot upon a Gandharvī sons of terrible prowess.
To Raudrāśva were born ten sons, great archers, from an Apsaras; they were performers of sacrifices, heroes, possessed of offspring, and deeply learned in the scriptures.
All were experts in every weapon, and all were devoted to righteousness.
Then there were Ṛcepu, Kakṣepu, and the heroic Kṛkaṇepu, as well as Sthaṇḍilepu, Vanepu, and the great car-warrior Sthalepu.
Tejepu was powerful and wise; Satyepu possessed the prowess of Indra; Dharmepu was humble; and the tenth, Anādhṛṣṭi, possessed divine valor. Among them, the learned Arcepu became the sole sovereign.
Then Ṛcepu, valiant like Vāsava among the gods, was born;
O dear one, he was the son of Anādhṛṣṭi and a performer of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. From him, the learned King Matināra was born as the son of Ṛcepu.
O King, the four sons of Mātināra were of immeasurable prowess:
Taṃsu, Mahān, Atiratha, and Druhyu, who was of incomparable splendor.
That virtuous and illustrious Antinārā gave birth to these very men.
Tamsu, of great prowess, upholding the lineage of Puru,
acquired radiant glory and conquered the earth.
The heroic Tamsu begot a son named Ilina.
That best of victors also conquered this entire earth. Then, O King, Ilina begot five sons, beginning with Duḥṣanta, who were like the five elements, through Rathaṃtarī.
Duḥṣanta, Śūra, Bhīma, and Vasu preceded them;
of these, O Janamejaya, Duḥṣanta was the eldest and became king.
From Duḥṣanta was born the wise King Bharata, the son of Śakuntalā.
From Duḥṣanta and Lakṣmaṇā was born Janamejaya;
from Śakuntalā, Bharata was born as the son of Duḥṣanta. From him, the great glory of the Bharata lineage spread forth.

That son of Śakuntalā, King Bharata, the descendant of Duḥṣanta, performed sacrifices: a hundred horse-sacrifices along the banks of the Yamunā, thirty on the Sarasvatī, and four hundred along the Gaṅgā.
Bharata begot nine sons by his three wives;
however, the king did not welcome them, saying, "They are not worthy of me.
Thereupon, their mothers, filled with rage, sent those sons to the abode of Yama.
Then, having performed great sacrifices, Bharata at that time obtained from Bharadvāja a son named Bhumanyu, O Bhārata;
considering him to be a supreme person whose soul was dedicated to dharma.

Then, O best of the Bharatas, the delighter of the Pauravas, knowing himself to be a father of sons, consecrated Bhumanyu as the heir apparent. Thereafter, that lord of the earth had a son named Vitatha.
Then he who was named Vitatha became the son of Bhumanyu.
Suhotra, Suhotṛ, Suhavi,
and Suyaju were likewise the sons born to Bhumanyu by Puṣkariṇī, the daughter of Ṛcīka.
In the lineage of Bharata, there were four [sons], among whom Suhotra was the one who carried on the line.
Of them, Suhotra was the eldest, and he obtained the sovereignty over the kings;
he performed many sacrifices, such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha.
Suhotra enjoyed the entire earth, clothed by the oceans,
filled with elephants, cattle, and horses, and teeming with many jewels; the earth seemed to sink under him, oppressed by his immense weight.
01.089.024c–01.089.025ab At that time, while King Suhotra was ruling his subjects according to dharma, the earth was filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, and teeming with people;
it was marked by hundreds of thousands of sacrificial altars and stakes.
And Sahadevā, with its people and crops flourishing, shone brightly.
O Lord of the Earth, descendant of Bharata, the princess of Ikṣvāku bore to King Suhotra three sons: Ajamīḍha, Sumīḍha, and Purumīḍha.

O Indra among kings, Ajamīḍha was ever devoted to righteousness and renowned for his glory. Among them, Ajamīḍha was the preeminent one, and upon him this lineage was established. Ajamīḍha begot illustrious sons upon the princess of the Ikṣvāku line.
O Bhārata, he too begot six sons through three wives:
Dhūminī bore Ṛkṣa; Nīlī bore Duḥṣanta and Parameṣṭhin;
and Keśinī bore Jahnu and both Janarūpin.
The wise know Saṃvaraṇa to be a hero, the son of Rathaṃtara born from Ṛkṣa;
likewise, O King, all these Pāñcālas are descendants of Duḥṣanta and Parameṣṭhin, while the Kuśikas are of the lineage of Jahnu of immeasurable splendor.
They say that the eldest son of Janarūpin was the king named Ṛkṣa;
from Ṛkṣa, O King, was born Saṃvaraṇa, the perpetuator of your lineage. While Saṃvaraṇa, the son of Ṛkṣa, was ruling the earth, O King—
We have heard that there was a very great destruction of the people;
then the kingdom fell apart, struck by various kinds of calamities,
by famine and death, by drought, and by diseases.
The Bharatas were overwhelmed by their powerful enemies,
and they in turn struck down both the Bharatas and the forces of their adversaries,
shaking the very earth with their fourfold army.
The Pāñcālya king, having swiftly conquered the earth, marched against him;
with ten *akṣauhiṇī*s, he defeated him in battle.
Then [the opponent], together with his wives, ministers, sons, and friends, [fled].
King Saṃvaraṇa fled from that great terror; thus defeated, those Bhāratas took refuge in the western direction. Then they dwelt in the thicket of the great river Sindhu.
On the border of the river territory, near the mountain,
the Bhāratas dwelt for many years, taking refuge in that difficult terrain.
As they lived there, a thousand years passed.
Then the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha approached the Bharatas. Having gone out with great effort to meet him who had arrived and having saluted him,
all those Bharatas then presented him with the traditional water of honor (*arghya*).
Having reported everything with great honor to the illustrious seer, the king then personally chose him on the eighth day of the month, saying:
"May you be our domestic priest; let us strive for the sake of the kingdom."
Saying "Om," Vasiṣṭha likewise installed the Paurava among the Bhāratas;
we have heard that he then consecrated him in the sovereignty over all the Kṣatriyas, as a preeminent leader over the entire earth.

He occupied that preeminent city, which had formerly been inhabited by Bharata; furthermore, he made all the rulers of the earth pay him tribute. Then, having regained the earth, that mighty one performed sacrifices once again.
Ājamīḍha performed many great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
From him, Saurī Tapatī bore Kurus to Saṃvaraṇa;
all the subjects chose him for the kingship, saying, "He is a knower of dharma."
By his greatness, the Kurus gained profound confidence;
the region on earth known by his name as Kurujāṅgala,
that great ascetic made holy through his penance as Kurukṣetra.
We have heard that the wise Vāhinī gave birth to these five sons: Aśvavān, Abhiṣvān, the sage Citraratha, the renowned Janamejaya,
and his [other] sons.
Abhiṣvata, the powerful Parikṣit, and Śabalāśva; Abhirāja, Virāja, and the mighty Śalmala; Uccaiḥśravas, Bhadrakāra, and Jitāri is remembered as the eighth.
Śabalāśva and six others,
as well as other mighty ones; in their lineage were born Janamejaya and six others, likewise mighty, renowned for the virtues born of their deeds.
Parikṣit had sons who were all experts in dharma and artha:
Kakṣasena, Ugrasena, the heroic Citrasena,
Indrasena, Suṣeṇa, and Bhīmasena by name.
And Aśvasena the powerful— these seven are celebrated by name as the sons of Janamejaya, renowned on earth for their great strength;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the first-born, followed by Pāṇḍu and Bāhlīka.
Niṣadha of great splendor, the powerful Jāmbūnada,
Kuṇḍodara, Padāti, and Vasāti is remembered as the eighth;
all of them were skilled in dharma and artha, and all were devoted to the welfare of living beings.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra became king, and his son was Kuṇḍika; Hastī, Vitarka, Krātha, and Kuṇḍala as the fifth were also [his sons]. From Bhīmasena, the great archer Pratīpa was born.
Atirāja, Nahuṣa, and likewise Śakrapurañjaya;
after them, Paryaśravas is said to be the best among the upholders of dharma.
They know him alone to be the supreme sage, the foremost among those who have performed meritorious deeds.
O Bhārata, they say that Dhṛtarāṣṭra had three sons renowned on earth: Pratīpa, Dharmanetra, and Sunetra. Among them, Pratīpa became celebrated as peerless on the earth.
Haviḥśravas, Indrābha, Sumanyu, and Aparājita— O bull of the Bharatas, these three sons were born to Pratīpa:
Devāpi, Śaṃtanu, and the great chariot-warrior Bāhlīka.
Devāpi, however, went forth as a wandering ascetic out of a desire for dharma; Śantanu obtained the earth, as did the great chariot-warrior Bāhlīka.
Born in the lineage of Bharata were these powerful and great chariot-warriors.
O King, many excellent monarchs who were like celestial sages,
as well as other great car-warriors equal to gods,
have been born in the lineage of Manu, increasing the race of Aila.
The great deeds of Bharata are renowned among all kings; in ancient times, that son of Duḥṣanta, the great king Bharata, performed sacrifices with a thousand Aśvamedhas and a hundred Rājasūyas.
The noble-souled Cakravartin, unconquered by his enemies and victorious in battle,
approached the banks of the Gaṅgā, O Janamejaya,
and underwent initiation for a thousand horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
Furthermore, he performed great sacrifices with excellent gifts for the priests,
including Agniṣṭomas, Atirātras,
Ukthyas, and Soma rites, as well as thousands of well-prepared Vājapeya offerings and Satra sessions.
Having performed sacrifices and gratified the twice-born with wealth, King Bharata, the son of Śakuntalā,
the highly illustrious one, gave another thousand *padmas* of pure Jāmbūnada gold to Kaṇva.
His sacrificial posts were one hundred *vyāmas* in circumference and made of gold;
rising to a height of one thousand *vyāmas*, they were erected by the gods led by Indra—
well-adorned, radiant, and beautiful with every kind of jewel.
Gold, elephants, horses, buffaloes, camels, goats, and sheep;
female and male slaves, wealth, grain, and milch cows with their calves;
and land marked by thousands of sacrificial posts—[all this] as abundant sacrificial fees for Kaṇva.
Having given wealth for many Brahma-kalpas, having performed many sacrifices,
and having likewise given away villages, houses, and fields by the millions and tens of thousands,
that great chariot-warrior made his dwelling in the world of Pitāmaha.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, I have heard from you the great origin of my ancestors,
and I have also heard of the noble kings in this lineage."
However, this brief account of pleasant events does not satisfy me;
therefore, may you tell me more of it in detail—
this very divine narrative from Prajāpati down to Manu.
Whom would the meritorious birth of these [Buddhas] not bring joy? Their supreme fame, increased by the greatness of the qualities of the True Dharma, remains vast, pervading the three worlds.

"I am never satiated by listening to the stories of those endowed with virtue, power, heroism, vigor, courage, and energy— stories that are equal in taste to the nectar of immortality. Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen, O King, to what was heard by me in the past from Dvaipāyana;
I shall relate this entire auspicious account of the birth of my own lineage— the blessed dynasty of Pūru, consisting of kings of immeasurable splendor."
I shall proclaim to you the names of the ancestors; listen to them from me. Brahmā, whose origin is the Unmanifest, is eternal, constant, and imperishable.
From him Marīci was born, as well as Dakṣa, the lord of progeny.
Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci; Aditi was the daughter of Dakṣa; Dakṣa [beheld] Aditi;
from Aditi came Vivasvat.
From Vivasvat came Manu; from Manu came Ilā;
from Ilā came Purūravas.
From Purūravas came Āyu;
from Āyu came Nahuṣa;
from Nahuṣa came Yayāti.
From his thumb he created Dakṣa, and from his two eyes Marīci.
Yayāti had two wives:
Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
Regarding this, there is a genealogical verse:
"Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu, while Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru."
Among them, from Yadu came the Yādavas;
from Pūru came the Pauravas. Pūru’s wife was named Kausalyā.
From her was born to him a son named Janamejaya,
who performed three horse-sacrifices and,
having offered the Viśvajit sacrifice, entered the forest.
Janamejaya indeed married Mādhavī, named Anantā;
from her was born to him Prācinvān,
who conquered the eastern direction as far as the rising of the sun.
01.090.012D Thereupon, he [received] the name Prācinvat.
01.090.013A Prācinvat indeed married Aśmakī, and from her was born to him Saṃyāti.
Saṃyāti indeed married Varāṅgī, the daughter of Dṛṣadvat;
of her was born to him Ahaṃpāti. Ahaṃpāti, moreover, married Bhānumatī, the daughter of Kṛtavīrya.
From her was born to him Sārvabhauma.
Sārvabhauma, having conquered [the land], took as his wife the Kaikeyī named Sunandā.
From her was born to him Jayatsena.
Jayatsena indeed married the princess of Vidarbha named Suṣuvā;
from her was born to him Arācīna.
Arācīna also married another princess of Vidarbha named Maryādā.
From her was born to him Mahābhauma;
from her was born to him Ariha.
Ariha indeed married Aṅgī.
Mahābhauma married the daughter of Prasenajit, named Suyajñā. Of her was born to him Ayutanāyī,
who brought ten thousand human sacrifices (puruṣamedhas).
That was his leadership over ten thousand.
Ayutanāyin indeed married Bhāsā by name, the daughter of Pṛthuśravas;
from her, Akrodhana was born to him.
Akrodhana married a Kāliṅga princess named Karaṇḍu;
by her, Devātithi was born to him.
Devātithi married a Videha princess named Maryādā.
From her were born to him the *ṛc*s. He married Sudevā by name, the daughter of Aṅga;
from her he begot a son, Ṛkṣa.
Ṛkṣa indeed married Takṣaka’s daughter, named Jvālā;
through her, he begot a son named Matināra.
Matināra, for his part, performed a twelve-year sacrificial session on the Sarasvatī.
When the sacrificial session had concluded, Sarasvatī approached him and chose him as her husband;
she bore him a son named Taṃsu.
Regarding this, there is a genealogical verse:
Sarasvatī gave birth to Taṃsu as her son from Matināra.
Taṃsu begot his own son, Ilin, upon Kālindī.
Ilin, however, begot five sons, Duḥṣanta and the others, upon Rathantarī.
He begot Janamejaya. Janamejaya, for his part, married the daughter of Bhagīratha named Lakṣmaṇā; in her...
Duḥṣanta, however, married the daughter of Bhagīratha named Lakṣaṇā;
by her was born to him Janamejaya.
Duḥṣanta indeed married Śakuntalā, the daughter of Viśvāmitra.
From her was born to him Bharata.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father; he by whom one is begotten, he indeed is that [son]."
"Support your son, Duḥṣanta; do not despise Śakuntalā.
O god among men, the son who bears the seed rescues [his father] from the abode of Yama.
You are the progenitor of this child; Śakuntalā has spoken the truth."
01.090.033A From that came his name Bharata. 01.090.034A Bharata indeed married Sunandā, the daughter of Sarvasena, a princess of Kāśī.
01.090.034B Through her, Bhumanyu was born to him.
01.090.035 A Bhumanyu indeed married the daughter of the Daśārhas named Jayā;
from her was born to him Suhotra.
01.090.036 A Suhotra indeed married the daughter of Ikṣvāku named Suvarṇā.
From her was born to him Hastin,
who founded this city of Hāstinapura;
that is the reason for its name, Hāstinapura.
Hastin indeed married a princess of Trigarta named Yaśodharā;
by her was born to him Vikuṇṭhana.
Vikuṇṭhana indeed married Sudevā, a princess of the Daśārhas.
From her was born to him Ajamīḍha.
Ajamīḍha had one hundred and twenty-four sons by Kaikeyī, Nāgā, Gāndhārī, Vimalā, and Ṛkṣā;
they were all kings who each established their own separate lineages.
Among them, Saṃvaraṇa was the progenitor of the lineage.
Indeed, Saṃvaraṇa married Tapatī, the daughter of Vivasvat;
by her, Kuru was born to him.
Kuru indeed married the daughter of the Daśārhas named Śubhāṅgī;
by her was born to him Vidūratha.
Vidūratha, however, married the Māgadha princess named Saṃpriyā.
From her was born to him a son named Arugvān. Arugvān indeed married Amṛtā, the daughter of the Magadhas,
by whom he begot Parikṣit.
Parikṣit married Bāhudā, named Suyaśā;
by her, Bhīmasena was born to him. Bhīmasena married Kaikeyī, named Sukumārī.
From her was born to him Paryaśravas,
whom they call by the name Pratīpa.
Pratīpa indeed married Śaibya, named Sunandā.
Upon her he begot three sons: Devāpi, Śantanu, and Bāhlīka.
Now, Devāpi entered the forest while still a youth, whereas Śantanu became the protector of the earth.
Regarding this, there is a traditional verse:
"Whomever he touches with his two hands, even if aged, enjoys happiness;
he becomes young again, and for that reason they know him as Śantanu."
01,090.049A That was his Śantanu-hood. 01,090.050A Śantanu indeed married Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī. 01,090.050B By her, Devavrata was born to him.
Regarding him whom they call Bhīṣma:
Bhīṣma indeed married his mother Satyavatī out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his father—
her whom they call Gandhakālī.
From her, the maiden Parāśara begot the son Dvaipāyana;
from that same woman, Śantanu had two sons,
Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya.
01.090.053A While they were both yet to reach youth, Citrāṅgada was slain by a Gandharva;
01.090.053B Vicitravīrya, however, became king.
01.090.054A Vicitravīrya indeed married Ambikā and Ambālikā, the two daughters of the King of Kāśī, who were born of Kausalyā.
Vicitravīrya, however, passed away childless.
Thereupon Satyavatī reflected:
"The lineage of Dhṛtarāṣṭra is being cut off."
She thought of the seer Dvaipāyana;
he stood before her, asking, "What shall I do?
She said to him:
"Your brother Vicitravīrya has gone to heaven without issue; therefore, produce offspring for him. Having said "So be it," he begot three sons: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura.

In that regard, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra had one hundred sons by Gāndhārī, due to a boon granted by Dvaipāyana. Among those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, four were preeminent: Duryodhana, Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, and Citrasena.
Pāṇḍu, however, had two wives, Kuntī and Mādrī, both of whom were jewels among women.
Then Pāṇḍu, while out hunting, saw a ṛṣi engaged in sexual union with a doe;
though he had already entered upon it and had not yet attained the essence of desire, nor was he yet satiated, [Pāṇḍu] struck him with an arrow.
Pierced by the arrow, he said to Pāṇḍu:

"O you who practice this dharma, by means of which you, possessing supernatural knowledge (*abhijñā*), have struck me—who had not yet attained the essence of desire—with the flavor of sensual pleasure; therefore, you too, having reached this same state and not having attained the essence of desire, shall very quickly meet your end.
"O cruel one, he who struck me with an arrow while I was observing the vow of a deer and had not yet achieved my purpose—"
"Even for you, such a state will very soon arrive.
He, pale in appearance and wan, avoiding the curse, did not approach his wife,
and he spoke these words:
"Because of my own recklessness, I have come to this state,
and I hear that there are no worlds for one who is childless.
He said to Kuntī, "Therefore, you must bear sons for my sake."
There she gave birth to sons: Yudhiṣṭhira from Dharma, Bhīmasena from Māruta, and Arjuna from Śakra.
Seeing her joyful form, Pāṇḍu said to her, "This co-wife of yours is childless."
"Excellent! Let offspring be begotten upon her.
Having been told "So be it" by Kuntī, Nakula and Sahadeva were then begotten upon Mādrī by the two Aśvins.
Upon seeing Mādrī adorned with ornaments, Pāṇḍu was overcome by passion;
as soon as he touched her, he attained the state of being bodiless (died). Thereupon, Mādrī ascended the funeral pyre after him.
He said to Kuntī,
"The noble lady must remain vigilant regarding the twins.
Then those five Pāṇḍavas, together with Kuntī, were brought to Hastināpura and introduced to Bhīṣma and Vidura by the ascetics.

And as all the castes were looking on, those ascetics vanished from sight after their announcement. Upon hearing those words of the Blessed Ones, a rain of flowers fell from the sky and the celestial drums resounded.
Having been received, the Pāṇḍavas announced the death of their father; they performed his funeral rites according to the law, and while they were there...

From their childhood, Duryodhana could not tolerate the Pāṇḍavas as they lived [in exile]. Being of evil conduct and resorting to a demonic mindset, he endeavored to displace them by various means; yet, due to the inevitability of destiny, he was unable to displace them.
Thereupon, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, under a pretext, sent them toward Vāraṇāvata, and they consented to go.
Even there, they were prepared to burn them in a house of lac, but they were prevented from succeeding by the counsel of Vidura.
Then, having slain Hiḍimba along the way, they went to Ekacakrā;
there, too, having slain the Rākṣasa named Baka, they proceeded to the city of the Pañcālas. There they obtained Draupadī as their wife and returned safely to their own territory.
And they begot sons:
Yudhiṣṭhira begot Prativindhya,
and Vṛkodara begot Sutasoma.
Arjuna [gave] Śrutakīrti; Nakula, Śatānīka; and Sahadeva, Śrutakarman.
Yudhiṣṭhira, however, obtained at a svayaṃvara a maiden named Devikā from Govāsana of the Śibis;
he begot upon her a son named Yaudheya. Bhīmasena also married Baladhara, the daughter of the King of Kāśī, for whom valor was the bride-price.
In her, he begot a son named Sarvaga.
Arjuna, having gone to Dvāravatī, took as his wife Vāsudeva’s sister, named Subhadrā;
in her, he begot a son named Abhimanyu.
That Arjuna begot a son named Irāvān upon the Nāga maiden Ulūpī;
and upon Citrāṅgadā, the daughter of the lord of Maṇalūra, Arjuna begot a son.
He begot a son named Babhruvāhana.
Nakula, however, took as his wife Kareṇumatī, the daughter of the King of Cedi;
through her, he fathered a son named Niramitra.
Sahadeva also married a woman named Vijayā at her *svayaṃvara*,
and through her he begot a son named Suhotra.
Bhīmasena, however, had previously begotten a son named Ghaṭotkaca upon the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā.
These eleven sons of the Pāṇḍavas have been described by me to you, O lord of men.
Among them was born the high-souled progenitor of their lineage,
the heroic Abhimanyu, son of Subhadrā;
Abhimanyu married Virāṭa’s daughter, named Uttarā.
From her, his lifeless embryo was born. Pṛthā received him in her lap by the command of Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person,
who said, "I shall restore this six-month-old embryo to life."

He, whose strength, vigor, and prowess had not yet been produced, who was born out of season, and who had been consumed by the fire of the weapon, was restored to life by the splendor of the Blessed Vāsudeva himself.
Vāsudeva said:
"I shall restore the prince Anantavīrya to life;
as soon as he was born from Abhimanyu,
may this earth support him by means of truth!"
By the touch of Vāsudeva’s foot, he was restored to life. Having revived him, he said:
"Since he was born when his lineage had been nearly extinguished, let him be named Parikṣit."
When the lineage was nearly extinct, Parantapa was born of Uttara from the illustrious son of Subhadra; he was named Parikshit. Parikshit indeed married the woman named Madravati.
From him [Kuru] was born Janamejaya.
From Janamejaya, by Vapuṣṭamā, two sons were born: Śatānīka and Śaṅku.
Śatānīka, indeed, married a princess of Videha.
In her he begot a son named Aśvamedhadatta. Thus has this lineage of Puru, as well as that of the Pāṇḍavas, been proclaimed. By hearing this lineage of Puru, one is liberated from all sins.
Those Brahmins who shall cause this meritorious history to be heard in its entirety,
or those who, with self-restraint, free from envy, and friendly-minded, devoted to the gods, shall listen to it— they too,
being constant devotees of the gods, Brahmins, and men, become conquerors of heaven and possessors of the world of merit.

They are to be honored and worshipped. For this Bhārata, spoken by the Blessed Vyāsa, is supremely purifying for those castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas who are faithful, free from envy, friendly, and perfected in Vedic vows.
They too shall hear it; having conquered heaven, those virtuous ones become beyond grief regarding what has been done and what remains to be done. And on this point there is a verse:
"For this is equal to the Vedas, purifying, and supreme."
It is conducive to merit, fame, and long life; it should be heard by those of self-restraint.
Vaiśampāyana said:
There was once a lord of the earth, a king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
Known as Mahābhiṣa, truthful in speech and true in valor,
that lord gratified the Lord of the Gods with a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; thereafter, he attained heaven.
Remembering that youth had arrived for the prince, the best of speakers,
and recollecting the imperishable worlds known to him through his own deeds,
the gods once upon a time waited upon Brahmā.
There were royal sages there, and that king Mahābhiṣa was among them. Then Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, approached the Grandfather;
her garment, bright as the moon, was blown upward by the wind.
Then the hosts of gods suddenly cast their faces downward;
but the royal seer Mahābhiṣa looked upon the river without fear.
That Mahābhiṣa was then cursed by the blessed Brahmā.
And it was said: "Having been born among mortals, you shall again attain the worlds;
having stayed among men for a long time, you shall reach auspicious realms. O evil-minded one, you whose mind has been captivated by Gaṅgā."
"In the world of men, she will indeed act in ways that are disagreeable to you; when anger arises within you, then you shall be released from the curse.
Having reflected thus, the king [considered] all the kings and those whose wealth is asceticism.
She chose as her husband the father of great splendor, Pratīpa.
But seeing that King Mahābhiṣa had fallen from his steadfastness,
that best of rivers returned, meditating upon him alone in her mind.
Having fixed her mind upon that state, she went toward her husband, the king.
But as she was traveling along the path, she beheld the Vasus, the celestial dwellers of heaven, their bodies withered and their vital energy struck down by dejection.
Seeing them in such a state, the best of rivers asked:
"What is this? Why have you lost your natural luster? Is all well with the dwellers of heaven?
Why are your joys no longer bright, and why have you become so pale?"
"Why will men fall to the ground in suffering?
To them the Vasu gods replied: "O great river, we have been cursed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha out of anger for a minor offense."
Indeed, we were all utterly deluded; previously, we passed by the most excellent of sages, Vasiṣṭha, as he sat performing his twilight devotions, and we overstepped him in secret.
Because of that, we have been cursed by him in anger, saying, "Be born from a womb."
"What has been spoken by the teacher of Brahman cannot be made otherwise.
Therefore, having become a human woman, give birth to the Vasus as sons upon the earth;
we shall not enter the unpropitious womb of a mere mortal."
Having been addressed thus, Gaṅgā said "So be it" to those Vasus and spoke this:
"Among mortals, who will be the one to bring you forth, O best of men?
Thus addressed by Gaṅgā, the Vasus then spoke to her.
The Vasus said:
"In the world of mortals, there will be a righteous king named Śantanu, the son of Pratīpa; he shall be our progenitor."
Gangā said:
"O gods, my mind is also thus, exactly as you have spoken, O destroyers of pride. I shall do what is pleasing to him, and this is also your desire."
The Vasus said:
"O you who dwell in the three worlds, it is indeed fitting for you to cast your newborn sons into the waters, so that our atonement may be accomplished before long."
Gangā said:
"I shall do exactly this; let him be appointed as his son, so that his union with me for the sake of a son shall not be in vain."
The Vasus said:
"We shall each contribute a quarter of our own vigor;
by that vigor, a son shall be born to you who will fulfill his desires."
"His lineage shall not continue further among mortals;
therefore, that son of yours who is now childless shall become a powerful son.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus made this agreement with Gaṅgā, O King, the Vasus departed with delighted minds directly toward their intended destination; but she [Gaṅgā],
seeing him with his body shattered and overcome by dejection, [was filled with grief].
Vaiśampāyana said: Then King Pratīpa, who was devoted to the welfare of all beings,
sat for many years on the bank of the Gaṅgā, engaged in silent recitation.
To him, Gaṅgā— endowed with beauty and virtue, like the goddess Śrī incarnate,
possessing an exceedingly alluring form— emerged from those waters;
she was a high-minded woman of divine appearance as the royal seer was engaged in his studies.
The fair-faced woman took hold of his right thigh, which resembled a *śāla* tree.
But Pratīpa, the protector of the earth— the best among those skilled in speech and one who knew the true principles of the determination of dharma— spoke these words to that high-minded lady.
"O auspicious lady, what pleasing thing may I do for you that you desire?
The woman said:
"O King, best of the Kurus, I desire you; accept me."
"For the abandonment of women who are full of desire is censured by the virtuous.
Pratīpa said:
"O woman of excellent complexion, I would never approach another's wife out of lust."
"O auspicious lady, know from me that this is my righteous vow: never to take a woman of a different caste.
He who abandons his own wife and personally serves another's woman shall not be liberated from the cycle of existence until the dissolution of all beings."
The woman said:
"I am not one who brings misfortune, nor am I unapproachable, nor am I ever to be spoken against. O King, accept me, a maiden and an excellent woman, who am devoted to you."
Pratīpa said:
"This which you urge upon me as a pleasant thing has already been transcended by me;
otherwise, a violation of dharma would have destroyed me for having acted contrary to it."
“O beautiful woman, having reached my right thigh and embraced it,
O timid one, know this to be the seat for children and daughters-in-law. That portion on the left belongs to a lover, and that has been abandoned by you.”
"Therefore, O beautiful woman, I shall not act according to my desire toward you.
Become my daughter-in-law, O auspicious one; I choose you for the sake of my son.
For you have come and taken refuge in the side of the daughter-in-law, O lovely-thighed lady."
The woman said:
"O knower of dharma, let it be so; may I be united with your son.
Out of devotion to you alone, I shall honor the renowned Bhārata lineage."
On this earth, you are the ultimate refuge for all those who are kings among men.
Indeed, your virtues could not be fully described by me even in hundreds of years; such is the unsurpassed excellence of your lineage as it has been established.
"O Lord, he shall not question my lineage, nor shall your son ever scrutinize any of the actions I may perform.
Living in this manner with your son, I shall increase his prosperity."
"Through his meritorious and beloved sons, your son shall attain heaven.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having said, 'So be it,' O King, she vanished right there."
At that time, while the lion among kings was looking on, she became invisible;
yet the king, awaiting the birth of his son, continued to maintain his vigil. At this very moment, Pratīpa, the bull among Kṣatriyas—
O descendant of Kuru, he practiced austerities together with his wife for the sake of a son. Meanwhile, a glorious embryo grew within the womb of Pratīpa’s wife,
endowed with supreme splendor like the moon in the bright fortnight of autumn.

Then, in the tenth month, Queen Pratīpā gave birth to a prince who possessed the radiance of the sun and shone like the offspring of a god. Thus, that son Mahābhiṣa was born to those two who had grown old.

From Śānta was born a lineage; therefore, he was called Śaṃtanu. Once he was born, the powerful Pratīpa had the rites for him performed by a Brahmin according to the rituals prescribed in the Vedas, beginning with the *jātakarman*.

O protector of the earth, the Brahmins then performed the naming ceremony for Śantanu with the highest honors, according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas. Thereafter, King Śantanu, who was devoted to the dharma of the world, grew up.
Having attained the highest perfection, that best among the upholders of dharma reached the ultimate mastery in both the science of archery and the Vedas;
and the prince, the foremost of eloquent speakers, also entered his youth.

O best of the Bharatas, having seen him established in youth, that best of kings, Śaṃtanu, out of affection for him, consecrated him as the heir apparent (yauvarājya) and remained a king who performed his royal duties.
Remembering the imperishable worlds won by his own deeds,
that Mahābhiṣa was born in the lineage of that high-souled one;
Śaṃtanu, O best of the Kurus, was indeed a performer of meritorious acts.
Then Pratīpa instructed his son Śantanu, who was established in youth:
"O Śantanu, long ago a woman approached me for your welfare.
O son, if that fair-complexioned woman should come to you in secret..."

A celestial woman, beautiful and endowed with great form, desiring a son, must not be questioned by you as to who she is or whose she is, O lady. And whatever she may do, O sinless one, that should not be done; she is not to be questioned by you.
"You should accept her as she serves you at my command," he said to him.
Having thus instructed his son Śantanu,
King Pratīpa then consecrated him in his own kingdom and entered the forest.

That wise King Śantanu was renowned on earth as a great archer; he was esteemed by all the world as one whose word was truth. With broad shoulders and mighty arms, his prowess was like that of an elephant in rut.
Endowed with all the royal marks that fulfill every purpose,
possessed of the excellence of ministers, and a distinguished knower of the duties of the Kṣatriya,
he alone, having conquered the lords of the earth, brought the world under his control.
He caused the entire Vedas and all the duties of kings to be brought to him;
he performed many sacrificial sessions with rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
and he gratified the Brahmins who were experts in the study of the Vedas.
With various kinds of jewels, cattle, villages, horses, and even wealth;
endowed with youth and beauty, as well as manliness and strength;
and possessed of sovereignty, majesty, prowess, and riches.

And by means of truth, they made that lord of the earth— who was skilled in all dharmas— the king of kings; those protectors of the earth were free from sorrow, fear, and affliction, and they enjoyed sleep and awakening in happiness.
O tiger among the Bharatas, the lords of the earth were endowed with splendor;
the world was protected by sovereign rulers headed by Śantanu,
and it flourished with the Veda as supreme, according to the regulations for all social classes.
The Kṣatriyas attended upon the Brāhmaṇas, the Vaiśyas upon the Kṣatriyas,
and the Śūdras, following the natural order of the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, attended upon the Vaiśyas.
In this same manner, it was so for cattle, pigs, as well as deer and birds.
When Śantanu was established in the kingdom, the senseless slaughter of those who were miserable,
helpless, and dwelling in the wombs of animals ceased;
that very king became the father of all living beings.
Dwelling in Hastināpura, that righteous-souled joy of the Kurus was like the sun in splendor and equal to the wind in strength;
he was like the God of Death in anger and like the earth in forgiveness.
King Sumati, whose prowess was truth, was beloved by his subjects;
he was constantly devoted to hunting, dwelling perpetually in the forests among delightful woods, mountains, and waterfalls.
In forests, in wildernesses, and at mountain cascades,
that best of kings, Śantanu, slaying deer and buffaloes,
roamed along the river with supreme joy.
He wandered alone along the Gaṅgā, which is frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*. Once, O Great King, he beheld a most excellent woman;
she approached Śantanu, driving away his misfortune.
Blazing with her physical form like the goddess Śrī herself,
she was entirely faultless, possessed of beautiful teeth, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing fine garments, and alone, with a radiance equal to the interior of a lotus.
Having just bathed, wearing only her lower garment in a forest growing on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
with her hair disheveled, she was touching her locks with both hands—
she who was endowed with such beauty, youth, radiance, and the excellence of her bodily limbs.

With gestures (*hāva*), emotions (*bhāva*), and amorous playfulness (*vilāsa*), with the movements of the corners of her eyes, with the weight of her hips, her waist, her breasts, her chest, and her gaze; with the mass of her braided hair, her feet, her physical postures, and her smiles—
With her conversations as sweet as the warbling of the cuckoo, she eclipsed the speech of the three worlds,
as well as Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, and other celestial women;
that playful woman gazed longingly at the king with affection.
Seeing her, his hair stood on end and he was struck with wonder at the perfection of her form. O King, she surpassed all the women of the royal class in beauty;
by her beauty, she eclipsed all the women of the royal class.
Then the king spoke to that lovely woman, Manoramā;
drinking her in as it were with his two eyes, the lord of men could not be satiated.
And she, upon seeing the king of great splendor wandering there, [was filled with wonder].
Out of affection, her friendship having been aroused, the graceful woman was not satiated;
gazing at the king with longing,
that graceful woman moved before him like a *kiṃnarī*, resembling an *apsaras*.
Upon seeing her, Śantanu was filled with joy at the very sight; she stood surpassing all the women of the royal court in beauty. Then the king spoke to her, consoling her with gentle words.
Whether you are a goddess, a daughter of the Dānavas, a Gandharvī, or an Apsaras;
whether you are a Yakṣī, a Pannagī, or a human woman, O slender-waisted one— you who possess the luster of a celestial womb, become my wife, O beautiful one.
"For my life-breaths are centered in you, as is whatever wealth I possess.
Having heard these words of the king— gentle, charming, and spoken with a smile—
the illustrious lady then approached Śāntanu for his welfare.
And she, seeing that best of kings,
the lord of the earth Śantanu, the prince, walking along the shore, and remembering the words of Pratīpa, approached the king herself, desiring offspring.
Thinking, "This is the time," Gaṅgā, impelled by the curse of the Vasus, spoke to Śantanu: "O lord of men, accept me. Remembering the agreement with the Vasus, the blameless woman approached him.
And she spoke to the king, gladdening his heart with her voice:
"O protector of the earth, I shall become your queen, obedient to your will. You have been recognized by my father; O Lord, become my husband."
"Indeed, neither you nor anyone else should seek to know in any way whatsoever what I might do, O King, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
I am not to be restrained, nor should I be addressed with anything unpleasant."

"O King, as long as you conduct yourself in this manner, I shall dwell with you; but if I am obstructed or addressed with unpleasant words, I shall undoubtedly abandon you. This is my condition, O King: accept me as you desire."

"I have been entreated by your father; O Lord, become my husband. "So be it," the king replied to her then, O best of the Bharatas. Having obtained that foremost of monarchs, she experienced incomparable joy.
Having promised her "So be it," the lord of men placed the queen upon his chariot and departed with her;
she approached Śantanu like another personified Lakṣmī.
Having approached her, the self-controlled Śantanu enjoyed her according to his desire, having married her by the Gāndharva rite according to the prescribed rule. And she was wedded by the king...

Thinking that she was not to be questioned, he said nothing at all to her; yet the lord of the earth was secretly gratified by her character, conduct, beauty, nobility, virtues, and her service in private.
That king was supremely delighted, being cherished by that most excellent woman;
for that goddess Gaṅgā, the river that flows through the three paths, possessed a divine form,
yet that woman of beautiful complexion had assumed a glorious human body.
She appeared like a wife presented by destiny for Śantanu,
that lion among kings who possessed a splendor equal to the King of the Gods;
she captivated him with the intimacy of pleasure, her skillfulness, and her enchanting smiles and dances.
She delighted the king, and he likewise took his pleasure.
Because that king was so deeply attached to sensual enjoyment and captivated by the virtues of that supreme woman,
he did not perceive the many years, seasons, and months that had passed.
Taking delight with her as he desired, that lord of men,
the illustrious Śantanu, the scorcher of foes, enjoyed both celestial and human pleasures, O King, and rejoiced greatly.
In due season, that queen conceived a divine embryo;
she gave birth to eight sons who possessed the splendor of the immortals. O Bhārata, as each son was born, she cast him into the water.
Seizing them by the throat during their period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*), he led them to the abode of Yama.
Saying, "I gratify you," he submerged them in the current of the Gaṅgā.
That act was not pleasing to King Śantanu at that time.

And the lord of the earth said nothing at all to her, fearing abandonment; for Śantanu, remembering his father’s words, held that the source of action is beyond questioning and that scripture is authoritative, and thus he did not inquire about the sin regarding his son.
That woman indeed killed every son born to her, up to seven sons;
yet Śantanu, out of fear of violating dharma, did not question her in any way.
But when she sought to kill the eighth, Śantanu’s fortitude was shaken.
Then, when the eighth son was born, the king, afflicted with grief and desiring to save his own son, spoke to her as she seemed to be smiling;
seeing her then beginning [to act], that delighter of the Kauravas addressed her.
The best of the Bharatas, overcome with supreme grief, spoke these words:
"Do not kill! Who are you? Whose are you? Why do you harm your own sons?
O slayer of your children, do not incur this great sin; stop, you who are to be censured!"
The woman said:
"O you who desire a son, O best among those who possess sons, I shall not kill your son;
however, this garment of mine has grown old, according to the agreement that was made."

"I am Gaṅgā, the daughter of Jahnu, served by hosts of great seers; for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, I have dwelt together with you. These eight Vasus are gods of great fortune and great power."
Due to the fault of Vasiṣṭha’s curse, they have descended into human form;
there is no other progenitor for them on earth but you,
and there exists here no human nurse like me.

Therefore, for the sake of giving birth to him, you have attained human form; O King, those Vasus have been born as your sons for the glory of the world. Having fathered the eight Vasus, imperishable worlds have been won by you.
"This is the covenant of the gods, the Vasus, as it was heard by me:
'Whosoever is born, we shall release from birth after birth from the human state.
Thus you have been liberated from that curse of the high-souled Āpava."
"May it be well with you; I shall depart. Protect your son of great vows.
This son of yours, O delighter of your lineage, has been born through their power; he will surpass all other men, of this there is no doubt."
"This temporary residence of mine was made in the presence of the Vasus.
Know that this son, Gaṅgādatta, was begotten by me.
Therefore, he is both Devavrata and the heroic Gaṅgādatta."
The son of Śaṃtanu, who has two names and surpasses Śaṃtanu in virtues,
attains the worlds of those Vasus, O lord of the earth.
Śaṃtanu said:
"Who indeed was this one named Āpava among the Vasus, and what evil deed did he commit,
O auspicious lady of lovely appearance, because of which he cursed the Vasus,
so that through his curse they all came to assume human bodies?"
"And what has been done by this prince Gaṅgādatta,
on account of which he shall dwell among mortals?
And how is it that those Vasus, who are lords of all the worlds, [have come to this]?"
"Tell me that, O Jāhnavī, regarding how they were born among human beings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed, Gaṅgā then spoke this to the king.
The goddess Jāhnavī bore to her husband Śantanu, that bull among men,
the son whom Varuṇa had obtained in former times, O best of the Bharatas;
he was the sage known by the name Vasiṣṭha, and also as Āpava.
His holy hermitage, filled with flocks of birds and herds of deer and covered with flowers of every season, was situated on the side of Meru, the king of mountains. There,
O best of the Bharatas, that son of Varuṇa performed austerities.
In that forest, which abounded in sweet roots, fruits, and water, was the best of those who perform meritorious deeds.
O bull of the Bharatas, the goddess Surabhi, the daughter of Dakṣa who was exceedingly proud, gave birth to a cow through Kaśyapa.
For the sake of favoring the world, that righteous son of Varuṇa obtained that excellent cow, the fulfiller of all desires, as a sacrificial cow;
she dwelt in that forest of ascetics frequented by sages.
Then, free from fear, the cow roamed at will through that delightful and righteous forest. Now, O bull of the Bharatas,
once all the Vasus, headed by Pṛthu, came to that forest frequented by gods and celestial sages.
Accompanied by their wives, they roamed that forest in every direction;
they took delight upon the beautiful mountains and in the woods.
There, the wife of one Vasu, who possessed the prowess of Indra, indeed—
Wandering in that forest, the slender-waisted woman saw a cow— the supreme cow of plenty that granted all desires belonging to the sage Vasiṣṭha.
Overcome with wonder at her excellence of character and wealth, she stood there.
On the very next day, O bull-eyed one, he showed that cow to him— a cow with six elevated parts, beautiful flanks and thighs, broad and five-fold in her proportions,
and with a head and neck eight spans long; he beheld her as she stood there.
To Vasu, the daughter of Vasu gave a cow that was well-fleshed, an excellent milker, with a beautiful tail and face,
auspicious, endowed with every excellence and unsurpassed character—
thus possessed of all such qualities.
O Indra among kings, O delighter of the Pauravas, in ancient times Dyaus manifested himself; and upon seeing that cow, O king, you who possess the prowess of the lord of elephants and Indra,
spoke to that goddess of slender waist, O best of monarchs.
O King, speaking of her beauty and virtues, he said to that queen:
"O dark-eyed lady, O lady of excellent hips, this is the supreme cow belonging to that Rishi of Varuṇa’s lineage, whose forest is this most excellent one."
"O slender-waisted one, that mortal who drinks her sweet milk shall live for ten thousand years with eternal youth.
Having heard this, O best of kings, that goddess of slender waist—
She of faultless limbs spoke to her husband of radiant splendor:
"In the world of mortals, I have a friend who is the daughter of a king;
she is named Jinavatī, and she is endowed with beauty and youth."

The daughter of the royal sage Uśīnara— wise, true to his promise, and renowned in the world of men for her perfection of beauty— is my desired prize, O illustrious one, along with her calf. For her sake, [I have come].
"Bring her quickly, O best of immortals, O increaser of merit!
O giver of honor, let my friend drink her milk so that she alone among mortals may become free from old age and disease."
"O illustrious and blameless one, you ought to do this for me;
for there is nothing whatsoever that would be dearer to me than this.
Having heard these words of the queen, [he acted] out of a desire to do what was pleasing to her."
Then Dyaus, together with his brothers Pṛthu and the others, carried off that cow.
Directed by that lotus-eyed woman, O King,
Dyaus was unable even to look upon the intense ascetic power of that seer.
The cow was carried off by him at that time, yet the precipice was not perceived.
Then, having gathered fruits, the son of Varuṇa arrived at the hermitage grounds;
however, he did not see the cow there with her calf in that most excellent forest.
Then that ascetic, possessed of noble intellect, searched for the cow in that forest; yet, though he sought it, the sage of divine vision did not find it,
having realized that it had been carried away by the Vasus.
He immediately fell under the sway of anger and then cursed the Vasus:
"Since the Vasus have stolen from me my milch-cow with her beautiful tail, therefore they shall all be born among human beings; of this there is no doubt."

Thus did the illustrious Āpava, the best of sages, having fallen under the sway of anger, O bull of the Bharatas, curse those Vasus. Having cursed them, the highly blessed one set his mind once more upon ascetic penance.
O King, thus did that Brahmarṣi of great power and ascetic wealth, filled with wrath, curse the eight Vasus. Having been cursed in this manner by that sage of the Yamunā, they indeed departed.
O best of sages, all eight Vasus together, out of anger,
having reached the hermitage of that high-souled one and realizing they had been cursed, approached that ṛṣi.
O bull among kings, though the Vasus sought to propitiate that seer,
they did not obtain favor from that best of sages; indeed,
the blessed seer showed them no grace at all.
From Āpava, that tiger among men who was proficient in all dharmas,
that righteous-souled one said: "O you seven, Dharā and the others,
after one year you shall indeed obtain release from the curse."
But he on whose account you have been cursed by me shall dwell for a long time in the world of men as a mortal due to his own karma. I do not wish to make false that which I spoke to you in anger.
For by speaking a falsehood, he would likewise harm his own progeny;
moreover, this high-minded one shall not procreate among human beings. He will be a righteous soul, proficient in all the scriptures.
"Devoted to the dear welfare of his father, he will renounce the enjoyments of women.
Having spoken thus to all the Vasus, the blessed Rishi departed. Then all those Vasus approached me.
And they begged a boon of me, O King, and it was granted by me:
"O Gaṅgā, you yourself must cast us into the waters as soon as we are born.
Thus, O best of kings, were they cursed by me in accordance with their request.

"I have acted exactly as was necessary for the sake of liberation from the world of men. O best of kings, O Bhārata, by the curse of that ṛṣi, this Dyu alone shall dwell for a long time in the world of men."
"This prince, your son, shall return once he has grown up;
and I too, O King, shall come to you when summoned.
Having spoken thus, the goddess vanished on the spot.
Having taken that boy, he then departed as he desired.
Because of that, he became known as Devavrata and Gaṅgādatta; thus he was named Devavrata and also Gāṅgeya.
The son of Śaṃtanu, who bore two names and surpassed his father in virtues, [was born].
Then Śaṃtanu, afflicted by grief, departed for his own city,
[leaving behind] his fame, his conduct, and the great, noble qualities of that king.
I shall proclaim the immeasurable virtues of that Śantanu,
and the great fortune of the illustrious king of the Bharatas,
whose radiant history is called the Mahābhārata.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus was that wise Śantanu honored by the royal sages of the gods;
he was a righteous soul, renowned throughout all the worlds as one whose word is truth.
I shall proclaim all the virtues of Śantanu:
self-restraint, generosity, forgiveness, intelligence, modesty, fortitude, and supreme splendor—
these were ever present in that great-souled Śantanu, that bull among men.
Thus that king, endowed with virtues and skilled in both dharma and worldly affairs,
was the protector of the lineage of Bharata and of righteous people;
he possessed a neck like a conch shell, broad shoulders, and the prowess of an elephant in rut.
Endowed with all the marks of a king and possessed of every fulfilled purpose, men, constantly observing the conduct of that illustrious one,
became established in the conviction that virtue alone is superior to desire and wealth.
O bull of the Bharatas, these qualities resided in the Great Being Śantanu;
indeed, no kṣatriya was his equal in righteousness,
for he was the foremost among all knowers of dharma as he abided in his own duty.
The lords of the earth consecrated that protector of the earth in the sovereignty of kings;
free from sorrow, fear, and affliction, and awakening from sleep in happiness,
those rulers of the land attended upon the guardian of the Bharatas.
By that illustrious king, whose splendor was equal to Śakra’s,
other monarchs were likewise rendered disciplined and devoted to sacrifice, charity, austerity, and virtuous conduct;
for at that time, the world was protected by kings headed by Śantanu.
By virtue of the established order, the Brahmins stood supreme among all the social classes;
the Kṣatriyas attended upon the Brahmins, and the Vaiśyas were devoted to the Kṣatriyas. And the Śūdras, being attached to both the Brahmins and the Kṣatriyas, attended upon the Vaiśyas.
Dwelling in the delightful city of Hastināpura, the capital of the Kurus,
he indeed ruled the earth as far as the ocean's edge.
Resembling the king of the gods, he was a knower of dharma, truthful in speech, and upright.
Through his practice of the virtue of giving and austerity, he was endowed with supreme glory;
free from passion and hatred, he was as pleasing to behold as the moon;
in brilliance he resembled the sun, and in speed he was equal to the force of the wind.

In his anger he was like the God of Death, yet in forgiveness he was equal to the earth. O King, while Śantanu protected the world, the slaughter of cattle, boars, as well as deer and birds, did not occur in vain.
In that kingdom where Dharma was supreme, the self-controlled Śantanu,
free from desire and passion, ruled all beings with impartiality. He was a youth with eyes like those of the *cakora* bird, a copper-colored face, and the gait of a lion or a bull.
Endowed with all incomparable and desirable virtues,
profound and possessed of great strength, his face resembling the full moon—
at that time, rituals were undertaken for the sake of the gods, sages, ancestors, and sacrifices.
And there was no killing of any living beings through unrighteousness—
neither of those who were miserable, nor of the helpless, nor of those dwelling in the animal realm.
That very king became the father of all beings.
While that best of Kuru lords, the sovereign of kings, was reigning,
speech became rooted in truth and the mind took refuge in charity and righteousness.
Animals were created for the sake of sacrifice, and sexual union for the sake of progeny.
For sixteen years, eight years, four years, and another eight years,
he lived as a forest-dweller, finding no pleasure in women;
emaciated by fierce asceticism, he was constantly devoted to recitation and meditation.
Possessing such a form, such conduct, such behavior, and such learning,
he had a son by Gāṅgeyā named Devavrata, who was a Vasu.
He was thoroughly proficient in all weapons, both those of earthly kings and others.
Possessed of great strength, great being, great heroism, and a great chariot,
that King Śantanu once, having pierced a deer while pursuing it along the river Gaṅgā, beheld the Bhāgīrathī with its waters diminished.
Seeing her, Śantanu, that bull among men, reflected:
"Why does this best of rivers not flow today as she did before?
Then, seeking the cause, that high-minded one beheld it.
The prince was endowed with beauty, tall and lovely to behold;
manifesting divine weapons like the god Purandara,
he stood there having completely encompassed the entire Gaṅgā with his sharp arrows.
Seeing that river Gaṅgā covered with arrows near him,
King Śantanu was struck with wonder at witnessing such superhuman feat; he then beheld his son, whom he had not seen since the moment of his birth.

The wise one did not regain his memory to recognize that son; Śantanu likewise lacked the recollection to recognize his own offspring. But seeing his father, he bewildered him with his illusory power.
Having thus bewildered him, she quickly vanished right there.
Seeing that wonder at that time, King Śantanu,
suspecting [it was his son], said to Gaṅgā, "Show [him to me]."
Suspecting him to be her son, Gaṅgā approached and spoke these words;
then Gaṅgā, assuming a most excellent form, revealed herself to him,
taking that adorned boy by his right hand.
Although he had seen her before, Śantanu did not recognize her as she was adorned with ornaments and wearing stainless garments. Gaṅgā said:
"O King, that son whom you formerly begot upon me as the eighth—this is he, O tiger among men; take him to his home. He is unsurpassed in the knowledge of all weapons."
"O Great King, accept this son whom I have raised;
O tiger among men, having taken him,
the heroic youth studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches under Vasiṣṭha himself."
Having mastered the Vedas along with their secret Upaniṣads, their limbs and sub-limbs, according to the prescribed rules,
he became a supreme archer skilled in all weapons, equal to the King of the Gods in battle; O Bhārata, he was always esteemed by both the gods and the asuras.
Uśanas knows whatever scripture exists, and he knows it all completely; likewise, whatever scripture the son of Aṅgiras— who is honored by gods and asuras— knows,
that too is established entirely within him.
In your high-souled, mighty-armed son,
the powerful Rishi Jamadagnya— who is unassailable by others,
who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures, and who possesses perfect memory and eloquence— [the entire Veda with its limbs and sub-limbs has been established].

Whatever weapon Rāma knows, that too is established in him. O King, take this hero back to his home— this great archer, skilled in the duties and purposes of kingship, my own son, whom I have bestowed upon you.
01,094.037 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus permitted by her, Śantanu took his son,
who was radiant like the sun, and returned toward his own city.
Having spoken thus, that illustrious lady vanished right there.
Paurava, having returned to his own city, which was like the city of Purandara,
considered himself by himself to have all his desires fulfilled.
Then, among the Pauravas, he consecrated his son as the heir apparent (yauvarāja);
[he was] one who grants fearlessness for the sake of the kingdom,
virtuous, and high-souled.
O bull of the Bharata race, the highly illustrious son of Śaṃtanu delighted the Pauravas, his father, and the kingdom through his conduct;
for such was his behavior, such his practice, such his righteousness, and such his learning.
The son named Devavrata was superior to Śantanu in virtues;
he was authorized in all weapons among both kings and others,
and thus the son Devavrata became distinguished by many qualities.
Thus, that lord of the earth, possessed of immeasurable prowess, spent four years living happily with his son. Once, he went to the forest along the Yamunā river.
The lord of the earth smelled an unsurpassed fragrance that could not be identified;
seeking its source, he wandered about in every direction.
Then he beheld a maiden of the fishermen who possessed a celestial form.
Upon seeing that dark-eyed maiden, he asked her:
"To whom do you belong, who are you, and what do you intend to do, O timid one?
She replied: "I am the daughter of a fisherman; for the sake of dharma, I am rowing this boat."

By the command of his father, the high-souled king of the fishermen— blessings be upon you— he beheld that daughter of the fisherman, who possessed a divine form and was endowed with beauty, sweetness, and fragrance;
and having gazed upon her, King Śāntanu desired her.
Having gone there, he then requested her hand from her father;
subsequently, for his own sake, he questioned her father:
"I desire the blameless daughter of the fisherman as my wife."
And that king of fishermen replied thus to the lord of the earth:
"As soon as she was born, this woman of excellent complexion was to be given by me to a suitor;
however, O lord of men, there is a certain desire in my heart—heed it."

"O sinless one, if you seek this lawful wife from me, you are a speaker of truth; therefore, by your truthfulness, make a covenant with me. Then, O King, I shall give this maiden to you according to that agreement."
"For indeed, there shall never be any suitor for me equal to you. Śantanu said:
"O fisherman, having heard of your boon, I must decide whether I will accept it or not."
"If it is to be given, I shall give it; but that which ought not to be given, I will not give under any circumstances.
The fisherman said:
"Whatever son may be born of her, he shall be the king, the lord of the earth."
"O King, after you, no one else whatsoever shall be consecrated.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Śāntanu did not wish to grant that boon to the fisherman.
O Bhārata, although being consumed by that intense fever born of the body,
the lord of the earth, his mind stricken with grief, then returned to Hastināpura while still thinking only of the fisherman’s daughter.
Then, on one occasion, as Śantanu was grieving and absorbed in meditation, his son Devavrata approached and spoke these words to his father:
"In every respect, all is well with you; all the kings of the earth are subject to your will."
O tiger among kings, why do you grieve and burn with such distress? For what reason do you lament here so frequently, afflicted by sorrow?
And why, O King, do you remain as if lost in thought, saying nothing at all?
"You do not depart on horseback; you are pale, jaundiced, and emaciated.
I wish to know your ailment so that I may indeed provide a remedy for it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
His father was unable to explain to his son that unspeakable desire regarding the daughter of the fisherman, which had been so clearly revealed;
thus addressed by his son, Śantanu replied.
"Without doubt, I am exactly as you describe me—devoted to meditation.
O Bhārata, you alone are our offspring in this great lineage;
you are constantly devoted to weapons and ever established at the forefront of manly valor."
"The mortality of mortals is impermanent; therefore, my son, I grieve.
O Gāṅgeya, if you should meet with misfortune, our lineage would cease to exist in any way. Without a doubt, you alone are a son more excellent than even a hundred."
Nor do I venture here again to take a wife in vain;
I desire this for the sake of the non-extinction of our lineage—may prosperity be yours.
Those who speak of dharma say that having only one son is equivalent to being childless.
O Bhārata, between the eye and a son, both exist and do not exist;
for upon the loss of the eye comes the loss of the body, while upon the loss of a son comes the destruction of the lineage.
