The *agnihotra* sacrifice, the three Vedas, and the rituals accompanied by sacrificial fees—[all these are surpassed by a son].
All these [other merits] do not equal even a sixteenth part of the value of offspring.
This is exactly so among humans and indeed among all living beings;
regarding that which is offspring, O one of great wisdom, I have no doubt in this matter.
Through offspring, one is freed from debt to the ancestors in this world; of this there is no doubt.
This is the eternal tradition of the three Vedas and the supreme Purāṇas:
offspring, ritual action, and knowledge—these three are the lights, O Bhārata.
"O dear one, since this entire cause has been explained to you directly,
and since you, O Bhārata, are always brave, indignant, and constantly devoted to weapons—
therefore, O sinless one, your death shall not come by any means other than from a weapon."
"I have fallen into doubt as to how it will be when you have passed away;
thus, my dear, I have told you the cause of my suffering in its entirety. Having understood that cause in its fullness and without exception,"
The highly intelligent Devavrata proceeded, reflecting deeply;
[thus spoke] Sūta Vaiśampāyana.

Having heard these words of his father, which were connected with the fruit of obtaining offspring, he, being deeply distressed, summoned the charioteer once again. Then, by the command of the chief of the Kurus, the charioteer approached him.
The highly wise Bhīṣma spoke to his father’s charioteer:
"O charioteer, you are a friend of my father as he stands at the pole of the chariot;
do you know what the king's intention is?"
"Tell this to me when asked; I shall do it and not otherwise.
O best of men, the daughter of the fisherman has set her heart upon the king;
therefore, having been chosen by that lord of men, he then spoke these words."
"Whatever male child may be born from her shall be the king after you.
At that time, your father did not wish to grant him that boon;
yet his resolve was such that he would not give it otherwise.
"O hero, thus have I spoken to you; now do what must be done next.
Then, having received his father's command and having fully considered his intention, the son, perceiving that his father was despondent, set out toward the Yamunā.
At that very moment, he quickly approached his father’s well-wishing elder minister.
Having arrived, he then questioned him regarding the cause of his father’s grief.
To that leader of the Kurus, who was questioning him properly, [he spoke].
O bull of the Bharatas, he chose that maiden as his boon;
then Devavrata, accompanied by the elder Kṣatriyas,
approached the king of the fishermen and himself requested the maiden from her father.
The fisherman received him according to the prescribed rites and, having honored him,
spoke to him as he sat in the assembly of kings, O Bhārata:
"This is Uccaiḥśravas."
"O best of men, this maiden should be given as a bride-price for the kingdom to whoever asks for her;
whatever offspring she may bear shall be king after her father.
You alone, O bull among men, are a sufficient protector for Śāntanu."

O best among those who possess sons, what words indeed shall I say to you? O Bhārata, I shall say something regarding the bride-price for the maiden. For who would not desire such a praiseworthy and sought-after alliance through marriage?
Even Indra himself would not feel remorse for transgressing against this noble man,
who is equal to you all in virtues and from whose seed the illustrious Satyavatī was born.
"O dear one, for that reason my father has been praised by him many times,
O Bhārata, as the most worthy among all kings to wed Satyavatī. Indeed,
even the celestial sage Asita was previously rejected by me."
For that best of sages was intensely desirous of Satyavatī;
however, O bull of the Bharatas, because I am her father, I shall say something:
I see only the fault here of powerful rivalry.
O unconquered one, I perceive that very same fault in you in even greater measure.
For whoever— whether a Gandharva or an Asura— should have you as his rival,
he could never live in happiness while you are enraged, O scorcher of the foe.
"O King, this is the only fault here, and no other whatsoever;
know this, may you be blessed, O scorcher of foes, regarding both giving and taking.
Having been thus addressed, the son of Gaṅgā replied with what was appropriate.
"O Bhārata, best among those who speak the truth, accept this true resolve of mine while the kings are listening for the sake of my father:
neither one already born nor one yet unborn would venture to speak such a thing."
"I shall do exactly as you have said:
whatever son is born of her, he shall be our king.
Having been addressed thus, the fisherman then spoke to him once more.
O bull of the Bharatas, desiring to perform a difficult task for the sake of the kingdom,
you alone, O righteous-souled one, are the sufficient protector and the lord capable of bestowing the daughter of Śaṃtanu, whose splendor is immeasurable. You are the master and the authority.
"O gentle one, O subduer of enemies, listen now to these words of mine and understand my purpose. Regarding the character of young maidens, I shall speak to you,
O you who are devoted to truth and righteousness, concerning Satyavatī."
"That which was promised by you in the midst of the kings is indeed worthy of you alone;
it cannot be otherwise, O mighty-armed one, there is no doubt at all in this matter. There is no possibility of its being otherwise than through you, O destroyer of enemies."
"O tiger among men, O observer of great vows, truth indeed exists within you. However, regarding the offspring that might be born from you, we have a great doubt.
Having understood his intention, he who was devoted to truth and righteousness [replied].
O King, desiring to do what was pleasing to his father, he then made this promise.
Devavrata said:
"O King of the fishermen, O best of monarchs, listen to these words of mine."
Whether they be sages, gods, or hidden beings, let them all here hear this: there is no speaker equal to me;
take these words to heart as I speak them in truth.
"O lords of the earth, listen as I speak on behalf of my father:
O ruler of men, the kingdom was already renounced by me long ago;
nevertheless, for the sake of offspring, I now make this firm resolve."
"O fisherman, from this day forward, I shall observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Although I am childless, eternal worlds shall be mine in heaven;
for since my birth, not a single falsehood has ever been uttered by me here."
"As long as the vital breaths indeed remain supported within my body, I shall not procreate; give this maiden to my father. I renounce the kingdom and all sexual union whatsoever."
"I shall become one whose vital energy is drawn upward; O Daśārha, I tell you the truth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of his, his hair stood on end with joy.
"I shall give," the righteous Dāśa replied to him. Then, seeing that difficult feat, the Apsarases in the sky, the gods along with the hosts of ṛṣis, and the kings likewise, offered their praise.
They showered him with flowers and cried out, "This is Bhīṣma!
Then, for the sake of his father, he spoke to that illustrious lady:
"Mount the chariot, mother; let us go to our own home."
Having spoken thus, Bhīṣma placed that beautiful woman upon his chariot;
arriving at Hastināpura, he reported the matter to Śāntanu.
The lords of men praised that difficult feat of his.
Whether gathered together or separately, they all said, "This is Bhīṣma!
O Bhārata, seeing that difficult feat performed by Bhīṣma, King Śāntanu became sorrowful for many nights.
Pleased by that deed, the father himself, being satisfied, granted a boon to his son; he gave him the power to die at his own will:
"Death shall have no power over you as long as you wish to live."
"O sinless one, having obtained permission from you, Death shall prevail;
you shall act according to your own will, and never against your will.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having learned that the daughter of the Cedi king had been raised by the king of the fishermen,
he caused her marriage to be performed according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
Then, when the marriage was completed, King Śantanu, the ruler, [proceeded further].
He settled that maiden, endowed with great beauty, in his own home. Then, from Satyavatī, the wise son of Śāntanu begot a hero named Citrāṅgada, who surpassed men in prowess.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the powerful lord again begot upon Satyavatī another great archer, King Vicitravīrya;
yet he did not even reach youth before his death.

That wise King Śantanu eventually succumbed to the law of time. When Śantanu had ascended to heaven, Bhīṣma— abiding by the will of Satyavatī— installed Citrāṅgada, the subduer of enemies, upon the throne.
But Citrāṅgada, through his heroism, overthrew all those kings;
indeed, he did not consider any human to be his equal.
As he was thus casting down gods, humans, and likewise asuras, [the gods spoke].
Then the powerful king of the Gandharvas, bearing the same name, approached him and said:
"O son of a king, you indeed have a name identical to mine; give me battle!
Or else, take another name if you will not grant me combat."
"I desire battle with you; I have come before you for that very purpose. I shall not depart from here having spoken in vain.
Having said this, the two of them, roaring, took their stand on the bank of the Hiraṇyavatī.
Between him and that [Gandharva], a very great battle indeed took place on Kurukṣetra; between those two powerful ones, the Gandharva and the chief of the Kurus,
the combat lasted for three days on the bank of the river Hiraṇvatī.
In that tumultuous clash, crowded with a rain of weapons,
the Gandharva, superior in illusory power, slew the heroic Citrāṅgada, the best of the Kurus,
who possessed wonderful arrows and a bow.
Having brought about his end, the Gandharva then ascended to heaven.
When that tiger among kings, possessed of great splendor, had been slain,
O King, Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu performed the funeral rites.
Then, immediately thereafter, the mighty-armed one consecrated the youthful Vicitravīrya, who had not yet reached maturity, as the king of the Kurus. At that time,
Vicitravīrya remained steadfast in the word of Bhīṣma.
O Great King, they governed the ancestral domain inherited from their fathers and grandfathers.
That king, skilled in the treatises on dharma, honored Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu,
according to dharma, and he in turn protected him.
Vaiśampāyana said: O sinless one, when Citrāṅgada had been slain and his brother was still a child, Bhīṣma,
remaining steadfast in the opinion of Satyavatī, protected that kingdom.
Thus, seeing his brother Vicitravīrya— now in the prime of youth and enjoying incomparable happiness— Bhīṣma set his mind upon arranging a marriage for him, he who was the best among the wise.
Then, O King, Bhīṣma heard that the three daughters of the Lord of Kāśī, who were like apsarases, were together choosing a husband for themselves by *svayaṃvara*.
Thereupon, that best of chariot-warriors, clad in armor, set out on a single chariot.
With his mother’s permission, he went toward the city of Vārāṇasī. There, Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, beheld those maidens as well as the kings who had assembled there from all directions.
Intoxicated by desire for her, the people of Kāśī and Kosala, along with the Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras,
and Kaliṅgas, went together toward that city while the names of thousands of kings were being proclaimed by the king.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, seeing the aged Bhīṣma, the delighter of Śāṃtanu, all alone,
those most beautiful maidens appeared as if filled with agitation.
They all departed, thinking only, "He is old. That aged one, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma, bearing wrinkles and grey hair—
what is the reason that this shameless bull of the Bharatas has come here?
"O Bhārata, what will he say in the worlds, having made a false claim? For Bhīṣma is falsely renowned on earth as a *brahmacārī*. Speaking thus, those lowest of kings laughed."
O Bhārata, having heard the words of the Kṣatriyas, Bhīṣma became enraged;
O King, the powerful Bhīṣma then himself chose them as his wives.
And, O King, he spoke to the rulers of the earth with a voice like the roar of clouds.
Having placed those maidens upon the chariot, Bhīṣma, the best among strikers, summoned the wise and declared:
"The giving of daughters to virtuous men is prescribed by the learned;
having adorned them according to one's ability, one should also bestow wealth."

Some give away their daughters for a pair of cattle; others do so for wealth that has been specified, others by force, and others after obtaining her consent. Some approach a girl who is intoxicated with passion, while others obtain her of their own accord.
Others take wives by following the ancient (ārṣa) rite;
know that this is the eighth form of marriage remembered by the seers.
But the Kṣatriyas praise the self-choice (svayaṃvara) and enter into it.
"Those who speak of dharma say that a woman taken by force after her husband has been overcome is the superior [wife].
Therefore, O protectors of the earth, I desire to carry these women away from here by force. Strive with all your might for victory or its opposite."
"O protectors of the earth, I stand here having resolved upon battle.
Having spoken thus to the kings and the King of Kāśī,
that valiant descendant of Kuru caused all the maidens to ascend his own chariot.
Having addressed them and taken those maidens, he departed swiftly;
then all those kings, filled with indignation, sprang up,
wringing their own arms and biting their lips.
As they hurriedly cast off their ornaments and donned their armor,
a great commotion arose,
O Janamejaya, like the falling together of stars.
With their bright ornaments and armor on all sides,
they shone brilliantly here and there with their mail-clad decorations;
likewise, their brows were knit in anger and impatience, and their eyes were bloodshot.

Mounting chariots prepared by their charioteers— resplendent, with excellent horses harnessed to the poles— those heroes, equipped with all types of weapons and raising their arms, followed the lone Kuru prince as he proceeded.
Then, O Bhārata, there occurred between them and him— a battle between one and many— that tumultuous and hair-raising conflict. They simultaneously hurled ten thousand arrows at him.

Before those arrows could even reach him, Bhīṣma then cut them all down with a great shower of shafts that rose like a bristling coat of hair. Thereupon, all those kings surrounded him from every side.
They rained down a shower of arrows upon him, just as clouds rain upon a mountain.
Having warded off that rain of arrows on all sides with his own shafts,
he then pierced every one of those kings with three arrows each.
Then, O King, each one of them pierced Bhīṣma with five arrows;
and that valiant warrior pierced each of them in return with two.
That battle was tumultuous, terrible, and like the conflict between the gods and the asuras.
Filled with arrows and spears hurled by the heroes of the world,
Bhīṣma in that battle cut down bows, the tops of standards, armor, and heads by the hundreds and thousands.
Even his enemies praised his agility as he moved about in his chariot and his skill in protecting himself in battle, surpassing all other men;
having destroyed others without being wounded himself, his prowess was truly immeasurable.
That son of the daughter of the ocean, skilled in all weapons, having conquered those sons of Kāśya in battle,
set out toward the Bhāratas accompanied by the maidens.
Then, O King, the great car-warrior Śālvarāja,
of immeasurable soul, struck Bhīṣma, the son of Śaṃtanu, from behind in battle,
just as another elephant might strike an elephant in the hindquarters with its tusks.

Having encountered his mate, the leader of the herd, the best among the strong, that mighty-armed King Śālva, impelled by indignation, said to Bhīṣma, "Stop, stop! You lustful woman! (though addressed thus, he meant "Stop, you lustful man!").
Then that tiger among men, Bhīṣma, the scorcher of foes and crusher of enemy forces, turned back toward the King of Sālva,
highly incensed and blazing like a smokeless fire, agitated by his words and filled with wrath.
With bow in hand, his forehead furrowed with concentration,
like the Lord Agni fanned by the wind burning through dry grass,
he stood firm in the duty of a Kṣatriya, free from fear or agitation.
The great car-warrior turned his chariot back toward Śālva. Seeing him turning back, all those kings became mere spectators of the encounter between Bhīṣma and Śālva.
Like two powerful bulls bellowing toward one another in the presence of a cow in heat, those two,
endowed with strength and prowess, rushed at each other.
Then, seeing that king approaching, the son of Śantanu became enraged.
Enraged, he urged on the horses toward King Sālveśvara; and that bull among men, the invincible one, having touched his excellent bow and strung it,
stood ready with arrow and bow.
The bull among the Kurus, clad in armor, girt with a sword, and equipped with arm-guards, rushed toward the lord of the Sālvas for battle;
the son of Śaṃtanu addressed King Sālva, saying, "Stay! Stay!"
Then, for the sake of the maiden, the mighty Sālva set out; O King,
thereupon a battle took place at that *svayaṃvara* between the royal sage Bhīṣma and Sālva as well.
A most terrible battle, like that between Indralekhā and her enemy,
which produced fear in cowards and increased the joy of heroes;
it caused wonder among the gods and increased the delight of the wicked.
Unseen and unheard of by anyone, yet causing terror to all the worlds,
the king of Śālva, the best among men, then covered Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, with hundreds of thousands of swift-flying arrows.
Then, at that moment when speed was required, that best of the foremost Kṣatriyas swiftly pierced Bhīṣma between the breasts on his left side.
Having seen Bhīṣma previously afflicted by Śālva, those kings—
They were struck with amazement and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Having witnessed his agility in battle, all those kings and lords of men joyfully honored Śālva with their words.
Then, having heard the words of the kṣatriyas, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu and conqueror of enemy cities, became enraged and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
He then spoke to his charioteer in anger: "Go where that king is."
"Until today I slay him, like the king of birds slaying a serpent.
Having heard those words, the charioteer drove where Śālva was; [Kṛṣṇa said: "O charioteer, you must not fear that son of King Śālva."
"While you look on, I shall slay the lord of the Sālvas; behold my strength! Not even a single arrow shall fall upon you, for I am not Śantanu before the Sālva.
Then the Kaurava duly invoked the Vāruṇa weapon.

O lord of men, with those [arrows], that descendant of Kuru, Bhīṣma, having warded off the weapons of King Śālva with his own weapons, crushed the four horses of the King of Śālva and slew his charioteer, O tiger among kings.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, the son of Jahnu severed the bow;
then, with another single weapon, he struck down the excellent horses.
O King, Sālva was thus deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed.
Having cast down his bow upon the ground, the illustrious Bhīṣma, son of Śāntanu and best among men, then stood with his face turned downward for the sake of the maiden;
having conquered that most excellent of kings, he released him alive.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, Śālva departed for his own city;
and at that time, the king ruled his own kingdom with righteousness.
As for the kings who were there, desiring to witness the *svayaṃvara*, they [departed].
O conqueror of enemy cities, they too returned to their own kingdoms; having traversed delightful forests, mountains, and rivers,
those kings proceeded to their respective realms.

At the *svayaṃvara*, Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus, having conquered the maidens— Bhīṣma, the foremost of strikers, having thus won those maidens after slaying certain kings in battle and putting some of the soldiers to flight— [acted as follows].
Having stripped away the fame, renown, strength, and fortitude of the kings,
he proceeded to Hastinapura,
where that Kuru king Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, was then residing.
Having passed through their respective kingdoms, the kings proceeded to Kurukṣetra, the most meritorious land,
where the righteous-souled Vicitravīrya ruled this earth.
O best of kings, just as his father Śaṃtanu, the Kaurava, was a supreme ruler, he too, in a short time,
traversed forests, rivers, and mountains covered with various trees.
Having destroyed his enemies in battle without being wounded himself, he of immeasurable prowess—
the son of the River Ganges— brought back the daughters of the King of Kāśī;
that righteous-souled one treated them like daughters-in-law, and his younger brothers like sisters.
Having accepted them as his daughters-in-law, he departed for the Kuru land;
that mighty-armed one brought them back out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his brother.
All those women, endowed with every virtue, [were given] by the elder brother to his younger brother.

Having performed superhuman deeds in accordance with the dharma of the virtuous, Bhīṣma, the knower of dharma, bestowed upon Vicitravīrya those women won by his prowess and proceeded to arrange the marriage for his brother Vicitravīrya.
Having reached a private agreement with Satyavatī,
the self-possessed Bhīṣma was about to arrange the marriage;
then the eldest of those daughters, being virtuous, spoke these words to him at that time.

"Previously, the lord of Saubha was chosen by me in my mind as my husband; and I too was previously chosen by him. This was the desire of my father, that Śālva should be chosen by me at that *svayaṃvara*."
"O knower of dharma, having understood this, you must then practice righteousness.
Thus addressed by that maiden in the assembly of brahmins,
the heroic Bhīṣma fell into reflection regarding the appropriate course of action for that very matter.
"But this maiden, though won by me in the Kṣātra game, is attached to another;
she has been given in word, given in thought, and the auspicious benedictions have been recited for her.
Once designated as another's, she must be abandoned and considered as belonging to another."
Having spoken thus and having obtained the consent of his brother,
who was compliant with his will, that knower of dharma, having deliberated with brahmins who had mastered the Vedas,
then gave leave to his eldest mother, the daughter of the King of Kāśī.

Bhīṣma gave his two wives, Ambikā and Ambālikā, to his younger brother Vicitravīrya according to the rites prescribed by tradition. Having taken their hands in marriage, he, arrogant in his beauty and youth, [acted].
The righteous-souled Vicitravīrya became possessed by lust;
[then] Bhīṣma spoke to Vicitravīrya.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Ambā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
He did not desire her in any way at all.
When Ambā was being praised by another, he said to that beautiful woman:
"This desire, which yields its fruit only in direct perception, is wicked and useless."
"O Noble One, you ought not to speak to me as one who enjoys what belongs to another;
for, O dear one, you are established in the lineage of Śantanu. O righteous-souled one, since you act without selfish desire, I consider your opinion to be excellent."
Having spoken thus and looked upon his mother, he addressed her with words according to the prescribed rite:
"O blameless one, you have been dismissed; go now as you desire.
For I am not capable of commanding my beloved brother, who is beyond the need for such instruction."
"Furthermore, who would allow a woman who has gone to another man to dwell in his house? Therefore, I will not employ you; since your desire is for another, depart.
As for me, I am one whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), having desisted from the business of marriage."
"There will certainly be no union between us two by any means whatsoever.
Having spoken thus, she departed for that place, surrounded by her female companions;
and she was gradually directed toward the city of the King of Śālva, O King.
Then Ambā, having approached the king of the Śālvas, spoke with her mind set upon him: "O fair-faced one, having previously resolved my heart upon you, I have come to you,
leaving behind Devavrata, that bull among the Bharatas, along with his younger brothers."
"Accept me, may prosperity be yours, as I am offered according to the prescribed rite.
Thus addressed by her, Śālva laughed and said this:
"You have been conquered here by Bhīṣma after he had defeated me among kings."

"O blessed lady, I do not accept one who has been won by another and released from his house by him, O fair-hipped one; let us go back to that very place. Having been addressed thus, she approached Bhīṣma and spoke again.
Then Ambā said to Bhīṣma: "I was carried off by you by force;
observe the duty of a Kṣatriya! By law, you are my husband—whichever man wins a maiden at a *svayaṃvara* through the excellence of his heroism."
"Having conquered all the kings, he will certainly marry her. Therefore, you alone shall be my husband, since I have been won by you.
For that reason, O Bhīṣma, marry me, for I have been won by you in the assembly."
"I am indeed one whose vital energy is drawn upward," he replied again and again.
Then Ambā said to Bhīṣma, "Act in such a way that you have truly conquered me.
Thus did the lotus-eyed lady pursue Bhīṣma for six years.
"O blessed lady, I am one whose vital energy is drawn upward (an ūrdhvaretas), and thus I have been averse to marriage.
Go back to that very Śālva whom you previously chose in your mind. Why did you formerly describe yourself as being attached to another?"
"One should certainly not keep in one's own house a bride or a maiden who is attached to another. O auspicious lady, I will not marry you to my younger brother Vicitravīrya; go wherever you please."
Approaching Sālva once more, she said, "O King, take me!
But she was rejected by Sālva, who replied, "I do not take women won by another.
She was also rejected by Bhīṣma, who said, "I am one whose vital seed is drawn up."

O King, that high-minded woman, weeping and grieving, caused Bhīṣma to go to Sālva and Sālva to Bhīṣma again and again by means of this coming and going for six years, drenching the earth with her tears.
With a pair of full and elevated breasts, large hips and eyes,
her gait languid from the weight of her loins, and a face resembling the full moon,
she shone like a flickering lightning flash atop a rain-bearing cloud.
Then, for twelve years,

Seeing that ascetic power of hers, which caused agitation among the gods,

he indeed shall be the cause of Bhīṣma's death."
"The foolish Sālva does not welcome me because I have had another husband before; thus, deprived of both dharma and desire, bearing only grief,

"This is a garland for you, O Kṣatriyas, which shall slay Bhīṣma;
and I shall become the wife of him who causes Bhīṣma to be killed. Five years passed while she was wandering about.

"May neither righteousness nor defeat overcome those who are the elders of the Ikṣvākus and the best of the Pañcālas at this wedding through your grace.

"I know you; I am awakening you especially, O princess. To the best of my power and according to dharma, I maintain this strength for you, O daughter of a king, against whatever fear you might have from another monarch."
I am capable of providing the means for his removal;
however, I am not the master over Śāṃtanava, who wields great weapons,

Your brother Vicitravīrya has reached the end of his existence;

O knower of dharma, you know the laws both in brief and in detail;

"My son, your brother, was heroic and very dear to you; though he was but a youth and childless, O bull among men, he has gone to heaven. These two auspicious queens of your brother, the daughters of the King of Kāśī,"
O Bhārata, since she is endowed with beauty and youth and desires a son,

Take a wife according to the Dharma; do not let your ancestors sink into ruin. The *agnihotra* sacrifice, the three Vedas, and imperishable progeny—these three are declared to bestow the fruits of heaven and liberation.
Thus addressed by his mother and by his friends, that scorcher of foes,

"You know indeed my supreme vow concerning offspring:

"You know exactly what occurred regarding the matter of the bride-price between you [and me].
O Satyavatī, I swear to you again in truth:

Even if there were anything superior to these two, it could never be true;
for the earth might abandon its scent, the waters their own taste,

The sun might relinquish its radiance, and likewise the comet its heat; space might abandon sound, and the moon its cool-rayed nature.
The slayer of Vṛtra might forsake his prowess, and the King of Dharma might abandon righteousness.
But I shall never, under any circumstances, resolve to abandon the truth;
even at the destruction of the worlds,
or for the sake of immortality, or for the sake of the abode of the three realms, that [truth] must never be made otherwise.
Thus addressed by her son, who possessed great wealth and splendor,

If you so desired, you could create other three worlds by your own splendor;

Yet, consider the duty in times of distress and bear the burden of your grandfather’s lineage.
O scorcher of foes, act in such a way that your family lineage and your dharma do not perish, and that your friends may rejoice;
O dear one, O Bhārata, this will be for your own benefit and my pleasure as well.
To her, who was thus lamenting piteously, longing for her son, and speaking words contrary to dharma, Bhīṣma spoke this again:

"O Queen, deviation from the truth is not praised among the duties of a Kṣatriya,

"Having heard this, you should act upon it together with wise priests who are skilled in the dharma and purpose regarding times of distress, and having considered the governance of the world.

O highly fortunate lady, when Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, could not endure the slaughter of his father,

The thousand arms of the high-souled Hehaya Arjuna were indeed cut off;

The warrior class was repeatedly consumed by the chariot of him who conquered the earth;
thus, by means of various weapons, the high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu formerly cleared the earth of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times.
When the world had thus been rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas by that great ṛṣi,

"It is established in the Vedas that a son belongs to the one who took his hand;

Then, once again, the Kṣatriyas arose together at that time.
In this regard, I shall relate this ancient history:
long ago, there was a wise sage known as Utathya.
He had a wife named Mamatā, who was highly esteemed by him. Now, Utathya’s younger brother, Bṛhaspati of great splendor, was the priest of the gods; he pursued Mamatā.
Mamatā, however, spoke to her husband, the best of speakers:
"I am pregnant by my elder brother; let him desist. And this [child], O illustrious Bṛhaspati, is already within my womb."
At this very spot, Autathya studied the Veda along with its six auxiliary limbs;
you too, surely, ought to be one whose seed is never in vain. Therefore, since things have come to this, you ought to desist now.

Thus addressed by her, Bṛhaspati of great luster was unable to restrain himself, whose mind was possessed by desire. Then, filled with longing, he united with her, who was likewise filled with longing.
As he was about to emit his seed, the one staying within the womb addressed him:
"O father, younger brother, do not speak thus; there is no possibility for two [beings] to exist here.
Your semen is never in vain, and I have already arrived here first."
"You are one whose seed is never in vain; you ought not to cause her pain.
Yet, without even hearing those words of the one dwelling in the womb, Bṛhaspati proceeded to have sexual intercourse with the beautiful-eyed Mamatā.
Then, perceiving the emission of semen, the sage within her womb blocked the path with his feet; thus, that semen of Bṛhaspati was then repelled before it could reach its destination.

He suddenly fell to the ground; then Bṛhaspati became enraged. Thus addressed, the venerable sage Bṛhaspati, being filled with wrath, reviled the son of Utathya who was still within the womb and cursed him.
"Since you have spoken such words at a time when all beings desire it, therefore you shall enter into a long darkness.
By virtue of this curse, that seer was born by the name Dīrghatamas."
Like Bṛhaspati in splendor, the son of the far-famed Bṛhaspati—
who was born blind yet wise and learned in the Vedas— obtained through his own learning a young and beautiful Brāhmaṇa woman named Pradveṣī as his wife.

That man of great renown begot sons, Gautama and the others, for the sake of increasing the lineage and family of the seer Utathya; he was righteous-souled, high-minded, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Having studied the entire *godharma* from the bull Saurabheya, that sage,
full of faith, proceeded to practice it without hesitation. Then,

All those dwellers of the hermitage there, overcome by delusion and filled with anger, said:

"O best of Brahmins, do as you wish, so that I may not bear [another] as I did before.

O King, as he was then floating downstream on that raft,

Seeing him approaching through the current while he was submerged,

I might renounce the three worlds, or again, the sovereignty over the gods, or even something superior to these; but I shall never renounce the truth. The earth may lose its fragrance, and the waters their supreme flavor.
Light would abandon its supreme form, and wind would abandon the quality of touch; space would abandon its resonance, and the moon would relinquish its coldness;
the sun would cast off its radiance, and the comet its heat.
Vṛtra-slayer might abandon his valor, and the King of Dharma might abandon his righteousness;

"I know your truthfulness, O knower of dharma, best among those who possess truth.

Your friends would be greatly rejoiced; you ought to act accordingly.
You alone are the elder of the family, and you possess the highest respect;
therefore, you ought to tell us the supreme means for the continuation of our lineage.
For women indeed hold the supreme secret in every family; they also ensnare men with many illusions. Therefore, O Satyavatī, you who are devoted to truth, behold the dharma!
"So that I may not abandon the truth, and so that our lineage may not perish. "O mighty-armed Bhārata, what you say is indeed true.

"It is not possible for this calamity of such a kind to remain unspoken to you;

Listen to me regarding that which occurred in my youth when I was a maiden;

Once, when I had reached the prime of my youth, I went there and easily ferried people across to the other shore. Then,
O best among the upholders of dharma, the supreme seer Parāśara—

By which this sky was made to expand like a copper-colored garment; as soon as I had spoken there, the Lord Parāśara, whose resolve is truth, created a mist over the island in the waters of the Yamunā.

Overpowering me, a mere girl, with his splendor, he brought me under his control; having shrouded the world in darkness, O Bhārata, as if I were still upon a boat. Formerly, I had a great and loathsome odor of fish.

Then, O Bhārata, that high-souled Parāśara, being greatly delighted, begot a son upon me, his maiden daughter, right there on the island;
and the wise one produced both snow and the island in the waters of the Yamunā.
Then my father Vasu and the ancestors, whose wealth is asceticism, departed.
Thereupon, that sage, having cast off my embryo, said to me:

Having spoken thus, that seer, the knower of the supreme dharma, departed.
O Bhārata, at that very moment my own birth occurred;
he became the great yogin, the great seer Pārāśarya.
In former times, my daughter's son was known as Dvaipāyana,
that blessed ṛṣi who, through his ascetic power, divided the four Vedas; he attained the name Vyāsa in the world because of his "splitting" (vyāsa), and the name Kṛṣṇa because of his dark complexion.
A speaker of truth, devoted to tranquility, an ascetic whose sins were burnt away—
he was born instantly as a great being, and then departed with his father. O one of immeasurable luster, he has clearly been commissioned by me and by you.
"He will procreate auspicious offspring in the fields of his brother;
for he said to me there, 'Remember me in your duties.
O mighty-armed Bhīṣma, if you so desire, I shall remember him."
And with your permission, he may freely procreate offspring by these two;
for with your consent, O Bhīṣma,
that man of great asceticism will certainly beget sons in the wombs of Vicitravīrya’s wives.
As soon as this was said, Bhīṣma, with his hands joined in reverence over his head, was filled with joy;
and as the Great Seer praised him who is all-knowing and the creator of all, Bhīṣma spoke with palms pressed together.

"I know the place and the time; let it be done for the accomplishment of our purpose. He who perceives these three—dharma, artha, and kāma—as well as artha with its consequences and dharma with its consequences [should act accordingly]."

Having reflected with wisdom upon desire and its connection to further desires, as well as their various opposites, and likewise the auspicious and its connection to further auspiciousness— those threefold categories— he who correctly resolves them is wise.
He who, having reflected again and again with his intellect, correctly resolves upon action— he is the wise man among men, he is the man who performs all duties in their entirety.
This very matter is consistent with righteousness and is indeed for the welfare of our lineage.
"What you have said regarding that which is the highest good is pleasing to me. Then, O descendant of Kuru, when Bhīṣma had thus given his promise,
Kālī thought of the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.

Then, having offered worship to her son according to the prescribed rites,
and having embraced him with both arms and drenched him with the flow of her tears,
the daughter of the fisherman shed tears upon seeing her son after so long a time.
Having sprinkled her with water and saluted his afflicted mother, the great seer Vyāsa, her eldest son, spoke these words:

"Instruct me, O knower of the essence of dharma; I shall do what is pleasing to you. Then the domestic priest performed worship for that supreme seer, and he accepted it according to the rules, preceded by sacred mantras.
Honored according to the ritual preceded by mantras, he attained great joy. Once he was seated, his mother, having asked after his unchanging welfare,
explained in due order that which she had been contemplating for his sake.
Satyavatī, having gazed upon him, immediately said this:
"O sage, sons are born as common property to both mother and father;
of them, the mother is the owner just as the father is—of this there is no doubt."

O Brahmarṣi, just as Vicitravīrya was ordained by the Creator as my first son, so too is he my younger son; just as Bhīṣma is related to me through his father, so are you related to me through your mother.
"O son,
just as you consider him, this son of Śantanu, whose valor is truth, upholds the truth and does not set his mind upon offspring or the governance of the kingdom."
Therefore, O sinless one, out of regard for your brother, for the continuation of the lineage, at the word of Bhīṣma and by my command,
and out of compassion for all living beings, act for their protection.
"Having heard what I say out of compassion, you ought to do it:
according to dharma, the two wives of your younger brother are like the daughters of the gods, endowed with beauty and youth, and desirous of sons."
"O dear son, you are indeed capable of producing offspring for those two,
worthy of this lineage, both in terms of continuity and progeny.
Vyāsa said:
"O Satyavatī, you know the Dharma, both the higher and the lower;
and how your mind, O knower of Dharma, is fixed upon righteousness. Therefore, at your command, for the sake of Dharma as my motive,"
"I shall fulfill your desire, for this has been seen in ancient times.
I will grant you sons equal to Mitra and Varuṇa;
O two goddesses, you must observe the vow that has been prescribed here by me."
After a year, according to the prescribed rule, they shall both become pure; for no woman who has not observed her vows may approach me,
nor can the daughter of Kosala, while impure, attain me who am worthy.
"Since this is so, Satyavatī, you ought to know the supreme Dharma.
Satyavatī said:
"Act in such a way that the queen may conceive a child immediately."
In kingdoms without a king, there is no rain and no deities;
the protectors of the people perish,
and all ritual activities come to naught.
"O Lord, how can a kingdom without a king be maintained?
Therefore, conceive a child; Bhīṣma shall raise him.
Vyāsa said:
"If my son must be given away by me quickly and without delay, let him endure my deformity; this is her supreme vow:
if she can endure my odor, my appearance, my attire, and likewise my body."
"May Kausalyā conceive an excellent embryo this very day!
Of that [embryo], there shall undoubtedly be a hundred sons—
protectors of the Kuru lineage and destroyers of your grief."
01,099.044 Vaiśampāyana said:
01,099.044*1068_01 Having spoken thus to Satyavatī at that time, the highly resplendent Vyāsa [departed];
meanwhile, Kausalyā, dressed in pure garments and well-adorned, was upon her bed. 01,099.044*1069_01
"Desiring a reunion," said that sage as he vanished;
then the queen approached her daughter-in-law, who was gathered in private,
and spoke these beneficial words, consistent with dharma and endowed with purpose.
"O Kausalyā, listen to me as I speak of the course of dharma.
It is evident that the extinction of the Bharatas has occurred due to the exhaustion of my good fortune.
Having observed me thus distressed and my father’s lineage afflicted,"
Bhīṣma gave me this wisdom here for the increase of dharma;
O beautiful woman, having ascertained it with my own intellect, I shall speak to you today.
Having heard these words, O fair-browed one, you ought to act accordingly and not otherwise.
"And that wisdom is within your power, O daughter; I have understood this.
Restore the Bharata lineage which has been destroyed! Bear a child in your womb, O auspicious lady, for the sake of the high-souled god."
"O lady of beautiful hips, give birth to a son whose splendor is equal to that of the King of the Gods;
for he shall indeed bear the heavy burden of sovereignty for our lineage.
Having spoken thus to her daughter-in-law Satyavatī, the queen then—
Having somehow persuaded that practitioner of dharma with arguments based on righteousness,
she fed her, as well as the brahmins, the celestial rishis, and the guests.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at the proper time, Satyavatī, as her daughter-in-law had bathed after her menses, gently spoke these words as she laid her down upon the bed:
"Kausalyā, your brother-in-law exists; he shall enter you today."
"Wait for him vigilantly; he will arrive at midnight.
Having heard those words from her mother-in-law, she lay upon her beautiful bed and then thought of Bhīṣma and the other bulls among the Kurus.
Then, at midnight when most people were asleep, the venerable seer,
the truthful sage who had first been appointed to Ambikā,
entered her bedchamber while the lamps were burning bright.
Urged by Satyavatī, that best of sages, who was truthful in speech and established in vast asceticism, went to her bedchamber. That Kṛṣṇa had tawny matted hair and glowing eyes.
Seeing his tawny beard, the queen closed her eyes.
But Kausalyā, who was unaccustomed to such a sight, looked upon him and, terrified that he had become deformed,
sat there shrinking back with her eyes closed.
Indeed, he was ugly, with matted hair, ill-favored in complexion, and emaciated;
his scent was the opposite of fragrant, yet he was entirely invincible.
Out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his mother, he came into being with her during that night.
Out of fear, the daughter of Kāśi was unable even to look at him.
Then, having approached her son who had emerged [from the womb], his mother said to him:
"O son, will there be a virtuous prince born of this [womb]?"
Having been told this, he said, "O Mother, due to a fault of his mother,
the prince born from Ambikā’s womb will be blind and possess the strength of ten thousand elephants.
Upon hearing those words from his mother, Vyāsa, possessed of supreme intelligence, [reflected].

Impelled by the sacred injunctions, that wise and most excellent royal sage— possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, endowed with great fortune, great heroism, and great intelligence— spoke, having attained knowledge beyond the reach of the senses.
"He too shall have one hundred sons of great strength;
however, due to a defect in his mother, he himself will be blind.
Having heard those words of his, the mother then spoke to her son.
"If this son, obtained after such long effort, should indeed be blind,
then give birth to another son, a younger one, who shall be the protector of this lineage and the destroyer of the sorrow of the virtuous, a lord of men."

"O one rich in asceticism, this wife of my brother is endowed with beauty and youth; by my command, procreate upon her a son of superior qualities. The blind king of the Kurus is not a suitable match."

"You ought to grant a second king for the Kuru lineage— one who will be the protector of his kin and the increaser of the line of his ancestors. Having promised "So be it," that man of great asceticism departed.
In due time, Kausalyā gave birth to that blind son; then,
having established Ambālikā [in her place], Satyavatī again appointed her to ensure the continuation of the lineage.
The virtuous Ambālikā sat down upon an excellent couch, dejected;
meditating on who might come, she awaited him with self-restraint.
Because he was held (dhṛta) by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he became known as Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then that blameless goddess Satī, having again reproached her daughter-in-law, summoned the Ṛṣi just as before; thereupon,
by that very same rite, the great Ṛṣi approached her.
Then he approached Ambālikā; and upon seeing the ṛṣi, O Bhārata, she too became dejected and turned pale like a corpse.
Seeing her terrified, pale, and despondent, O King—
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, spoke these words:
"Since you have turned pale upon seeing even my deformed appearance,
therefore this son of yours shall indeed be named Pāṇḍu."
"And that very name shall be his here, O fair-faced one.
Having said this, the Blessed One, the best of sages, departed.
Then, seeing him gone, Satyavatī spoke to her son.
"O son, will this prince also be virtuous?
"The prince replied, 'Tell me, my son, will there be anything auspicious in this regard?
He then explained to his mother the paleness of that boy."
Then his mother said to him, "Will there also be an auspicious prince here? Tell me the truth. The seer replied to her:
"There will be a prince of great prowess, renowned in all directions."
"Due to a defect in his mother, his complexion will be pale.
Then the mother again requested another son from him,
and the great seer replied to that mother, "So be it."
Then that queen gave birth at the opportune time to a prince named Pāṇḍu, who was endowed with auspicious marks and radiant as if with splendor.
To him were born five sons, the Pāṇḍavas, who were great archers.
"Five sons indeed, all great archers, shall be born to him here.
Having spoken thus to his mother there and having paid his respects, he departed.
When the sage had gone, Ambikā gave birth to a highly fortunate son.
To the highly wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord who possessed the eye of wisdom,
Ambālikā gave birth at the proper time to a son named Pāṇḍu,
who was endowed with auspicious marks and radiant, enveloped in glory.
Bhīṣma had all the birth-rites for those two performed correctly and in due order by Brahmins who were masters of the Vedas,
after seeing that the son born to Ambikā, the offspring of Satyavatī, was blind.
Having summoned his son for the sake of Kausalyā, he requested another:
"I desire this blind man to have another auspicious son born of Kausalyā.
Thus addressed, the great seer replied to that mother.
"If Kausalyā shall again become auspicious and steadfast,
a prince shall be born to her who will know the true essence of the meaning of the treatises on Dharma.
Then Satyavatī, having once more consoled that daughter-in-law,"
Then, at the time of her season, she directed her eldest daughter-in-law to him.
But she, resembling a daughter of the gods, having reflected upon the appearance and the odor of the great seer, did not carry out the queen’s command out of fear.
Then, having adorned a maidservant with her own ornaments until she resembled an Apsaras,
the daughter of the King of Kāśī sent her to Kṛṣṇa. The maidservant went out to meet the sage who had arrived and saluted him.
Having been granted permission, she entered his bedchamber and attended upon him with great respect—
through her service, her character, and her perfection of beauty and youth; by means of her speech, her disposition, her gifts, and the touch of her limbs.
Through the enjoyment of desire, that great seer found satisfaction with her;
having spent the night with her as she was filled with joy, the rishi, rising, said to her: "You shall no longer be a slave."

"And this glorious embryo has entered your womb, O auspicious lady; he shall be righteous-souled in the world and the best among all the wise. He was born by the name Vidura, the son of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
And the brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu was the one of immeasurable intellect,
Dharma himself, who— due to the curse of that high-souled Māṇḍavya— appeared in the form of Vidura; he was a knower of the true essence of things and was entirely free from desire and anger.
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana also reported this to Satyavatī: his own deception and the birth of a son from a Śūdra woman. Having thus discharged his debt to Dharma, he returned once more to his mother.
Having informed her that she was pregnant, he vanished right there.
Thus, from Dvaipāyana, sons resembling the offspring of gods were born in the field of Vicitravīrya, increasing the Kuru lineage.
When those three princes were born, Kurujāṅgala,
the Kurus, and Kurukṣetra— all three— prospered.
Likewise, Gandhavatī spoke concerning her son who was of righteous form.
"O Mother, I am no longer able to be joined with my son.
Janamejaya said:
"What deed was committed by Dharmas, on account of which he incurred a curse?"
"And by whose curse, O Brahmarṣi, was he born from a Śūdra womb?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"There was a certain Brāhmaṇa renowned as Māṇḍavya."
Resolute, a knower of all dharmas, and established in truth and austerity,
he traveled on a pilgrimage as he pleased,
visiting whatever sacred fords were situated near the villages.
Having established a hermitage there, the great sage dwelt;
at the entrance of that hermitage, at the foot of a tree, that great ascetic,
a master of yoga, stood with his arms raised, observing a vow of silence.
After a long time, while he was remaining in that ascetic practice,
O bull of the Bharatas, some robbers carrying stolen goods arrived at that hermitage, being pursued by many guards.
Those plunderers went to that very dwelling from their village;
O best of the Kurus, they deposited the loot in that residence,
and having placed it there, they remained hidden out of fear when the army arrived.
When they had hidden there, O King, that force of guards quickly followed,
and even more swiftly than that, the great royal army arrived at the lodging where the sage of rigid vows was sleeping.
Then the pursuers of the thieves arrived and saw that seer; O King, they then questioned that ascetic, who was thus situated,
"O best of the twice-born, by which path have the bandits gone?"
"Therefore, O Brahmin, let us go by that path more quickly.
But even as those guards were speaking thus,
O King, that ascetic did not say a single word, whether good or bad.
Then those royal officers, searching that hermitage, saw the thieves hidden there along with the goods. Thereupon,
suspicion arose among the guards regarding that sage.
Having bound him, they then presented him and the bandits to the king.
The king ordered that he, along with those thieves, be put to death.
Unknown to the executioners, that man of great asceticism was impaled upon a stake.
Then, having impaled that sage upon a stake, the guards departed for the king, taking those riches with them. But that righteous soul, remaining on the stake, after a long period of time—
Though without food, the brahmin seer did not succumb to death;
he sustained his life-breaths and brought other seers to that place.
By that high-souled one, who was performing penance upon the tip of the stake, [they were likewise drawn].
Then, O scorcher of enemies, the sages fell into the utmost distress;
the ṛṣis dwelling there in the hermitage were then filled with grief. Having become birds, they gathered from all sides around him during the night.
Showing him as much respect as they were able, they questioned that best of the twice-born:
"O Blessed One, by what fault will you depart, O most excellent of the twice-born?
We wish to hear, O Brahmin, what sin have you committed?"
O best among the foremost of the twice-born, that great fear of suffering on the stake which has come upon you here is a source of immense doubt;
for such as you, O best of the twice-born, are engaged in fierce asceticism.
Then that tiger among sages spoke to those whose wealth is asceticism:
"In whom shall I find fault? For no one else has offended me.
Having seen him there on that many-thought day, the guards [reported it].
They reported to the king exactly what had occurred, O lord of men. Having heard their words regarding that best of sages impaled upon the stake,
the king, having heard of the seer, went out together with his ministers.
Then he sought to appease that best of sages who was fixed upon the stake:
"O best of sages, whatever wrong I have done out of delusion or ignorance, I seek your favor for that; you ought not to be angry with me."
Thus addressed by the king, the sage then showed favor;
once he had shown favor, the king then caused him to descend.
Having lowered him from the tip of the stake, he indeed pulled that stake out.
Unable to pull out the stake, he cut it at the base. Thus, with the stake remaining within him, the sage continued his journey;
the sage proceeded with the wooden pin situated between his throat and his side.
He became intent on the thought, "May I become one who carries a vessel of flowers.
By means of that asceticism, he conquered worlds difficult for others to attain;
therefore, he is called Aṇīmāṇḍavya among the people of the world.
Having gone to the abode of Dharma, that brahmin, a knower of the supreme truth,
saw Dharma seated upon his throne and then reproached the Lord:
"What evil deed have I committed, unknowingly?"
"Since such a fruition as this has been attained by me, tell me the truth of it quickly; behold the power of my asceticism! Dharma said:

"O one whose wealth is asceticism, you thrust a blade of grass into the tails of the insects; this is the fruit you have now obtained for that deed. Just as even a very small gift, when given, may become of great merit,"
"O Brahmin-sage, thus unrighteousness alone yields the fruit of manifold suffering.
Āṇimāṇḍavya said:
"Tell me truly, at what time was that committed by me?"
Then the King of Dharma was addressed by him: "In your childhood, you inflicted [this] upon me. Aṇīmāṇḍavya said: "For a minor offense, a massive punishment was inflicted upon me by you."
"Therefore, O Dharma, you shall be born as a human being from a *śūdra* womb.
For whatever you do before the age of twelve from birth,
there shall be no unrighteousness (*adharma*) therein, nor will you even perceive the directions."
Today I establish a boundary in the world that brings about the fruit of dharma:
until the fourteenth year, no sin shall exist;
for those who act beyond this limit, there will surely be fault.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"On account of this transgression, by the curse of that high-souled one,
Dharma was born from a Śūdra womb in the form of Vidura."
Skilled in both righteousness and worldly affairs, free from greed and anger,
far-sighted, devoted to tranquility, and intent on the welfare of the Kurus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Dharma is powerful in every respect; even greater than that is the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus did the blessed Bādarāyaṇa declare here.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and the high-souled Vidura—
these three princes—
were born, these three regions: Kurujāṅgala, the Kurus, and Kurukṣetra, flourished.
The earth was covered with standing crops, and the grains were laden with fruit;
Parjanya rained according to the seasons, and the trees bore many flowers and fruits.
The mounts were delighted, and the beasts and birds were joyful.
Fragrant garlands and succulent fruits were strewn about the cities by merchants and artisans;
and the brave, the learned, and the virtuous all became happy.
There were no robbers at all, nor were there people who took pleasure in unrighteousness;
even in the remote regions of the kingdoms, the Kṛta Yuga prevailed. People were devoted to the practice of giving and the performance of dharma, and were dedicated to sacrifices and vows.
At that time, the people grew up joined by mutual affection;
free from pride and anger, and devoid of greed,
they prospered one another, and righteousness prevailed supremely.
That city, filled like the great ocean, shone resplendently;
it was adorned with gates, archways, and turrets resembling masses of clouds,
crowded with hundreds of palaces, and comparable to the city of Mahendra.
In rivers, forest groves, ponds, pools, and mountain ridges,
as well as in delightful woodlands, the joyful people sported together with the Northern Kurus at that time, O Southern Kurus.
They moved about in competition with the perfected seers (*siddha-ṛṣi*) and celestial minstrels (*cāraṇa*).
In that delightful country, no one was miserable, nor were there any widowed women; many [amenities] were provided there by the Kurus.
In that kingdom, there were wells, groves, assembly halls, ponds, and dwellings for Brahmins; endowed with every prosperity, they were always filled with festivities.
That land was made fragrant by the constant sounds of *svāhā* and *svadhā*.
O King, while that region was protected on all sides by Bhīṣma according to the scriptures,
it became delightful, marked by hundreds of sacrificial altars and stakes;
having annexed the territories of other kingdoms, it flourished.
The wheel of dharma set in motion by Bhīṣma turned throughout the kingdom; while the duties of the high-souled princes were being performed,
all the people of the city and the countryside lived in constant celebration.
O lord of men, in the houses of the Kuru chiefs and the citizens, these words were heard everywhere: "Let it be given! Let it be eaten!
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and the high-minded Vidura—
Protected like sons by Bhīṣma from their very birth,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Kuru king, was consecrated by Bhīṣma; he was devoted to the study of the Vedas and had mastered the treatises on political ethics (*nītiśāstra*).
In the science of archery, in riding horses, in combat with the mace, and in the use of sword and shield;
likewise in the training of elephants, in various weapons,
and in the diverse branches of knowledge that prioritize wealth and virtue.
When Pāṇḍu had reached the further shore [of death], he was then made the commander-in-chief;
however, Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not assume the kingship because of his blindness, and Vidura did not because of his inferior status; thus, Pāṇḍu became the lord of the earth.
Even as a youth, Vidura was appointed by Bhīṣma as the minister of the illustrious lord of men; he was the guide to all dharmas,
a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures, and a young man sharp in intellect and wisdom.
Through his disposition joined with the sacred tradition, he caused the entire world to know [the truth]. The lineage of Śaṃtanu, which had perished, was raised up once more by Bhīṣma.
Therefore, this etymological explanation is recited among the virtuous.
Kausalyā is the foremost among women who give birth to heroes; Kurujāṅgala is the foremost among countries;
Bhīṣma is the best among upholders of dharma; and Gajasāhvaya is the foremost among ancient cities. O Janamejaya, those three became princes through the power of time.
Those great-souled ones grew up, bringing joy to their friends; having been refined by the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and devoted to vows and study,
they became skilled in physical exertion and exercise as they reached youth.

O Lord, they were masters of the science of archery, horsemanship, combat with the mace, and the use of sword and shield; likewise, they had reached the further shore of elephant training and the treatises on ethics,
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and various branches of learning.
Those who knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences were everywhere thoroughly proficient;
Pāṇḍu was preeminent among men for his prowess with the bow,
while King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was more powerful than all others.

In the three worlds, O King, there was no one equal to Vidura; he was eternally devoted to dharma and had attained the highest perfection in dharma. Then, from the Brahmins, he heard news concerning the Yādava king.
The son of the Ocean’s daughter [Bhīṣma] took as his wives the daughter of Subala, the king of Gāndhāra, who was endowed with beauty and youth,
and the daughter of the king of Madra, whose peerless form was unrivaled on earth.
Seeing that the lineage of Śantanu, which had been lost, was now restored, a saying then circulated throughout the world and all kingdoms:
"Among those who give birth to heroes, the daughter of the King of Kāśi is foremost; among countries, Kurujāṅgala is foremost."
Bhīṣma, the knower of all dharmas, [ruled] the ancient city called Gajasāhvaya;
however, Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not assume the kingship because of his blindness, and Vidura did not because of his status as a servant; therefore, Pāṇḍu became the lord of the earth.

Then, at one time, Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, who was skilled in all forms of policy, spoke these appropriate words to Vidura, who knew the true essence of dharma. Then, after a long period of time had passed, Bhīṣma addressed Vidura.
Bhīṣma said:
"This renowned lineage of ours is perfectly endowed with all virtues;
it surpasses other rulers of the earth and possesses sovereign dominion over the world."
Protected by former kings who were high-souled and knowers of dharma,
this lineage of ours has never at any time suffered decline;
it was protected by me, by Satyavatī, and by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
It has been firmly established once more within you, the continuers of the lineage. O son, so that this family may flourish like the ocean,
I must take such measures, and especially so must you.
It is heard that there is a Yādava maiden who is worthy of our lineage, as well as the daughters of Subala and the Lord of Madra;
they are all of noble birth, beautiful, and well-protected on every side.
"O best among the wise, O Vidura, those bulls among Kṣatriyas are indeed well-suited for an alliance with us; I believe they should be chosen as brides for the sake of this lineage,
or whatever else you may think."
Vidura said:
"You are our father, you are our mother, and you are our supreme preceptor.
Therefore, having reflected for yourself, do what is beneficial for this lineage."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then he heard from the brahmins about Gāndhārī, the daughter of Subala,
who had propitiated the boon-granting god Hara, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes.
"O Bhārata, having heard in truth that the auspicious Gāndhārī had indeed obtained a boon for a hundred sons, Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus,
then sent a messenger to the king of Gāndhāra."
"There he was [concerned] with the thought that [the king] was sightless;
yet, having carefully considered his lineage, reputation, and conduct with his intellect,
Subala gave that virtuous Gāndhārī to Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

Gāndhārī, however, O Bhārata, heard that Dhṛtarāṣṭra was sightless and that he had been offered himself by his father and mother. Then that auspicious woman, taking a cloth and folding it many times over, [bound her eyes].
O King, devoted to her vow of fidelity to her husband and having resolved, "I shall not eat more than my husband," she bound her own eyes. Then Śakuni, the son of the king of Gāndhāra, approached.
Taking his sister, who was endowed with supreme beauty, he then gave her to Dhṛtarāṣṭra among the Kauravas after honoring her most highly;
and with Bhīṣma’s consent, he performed the marriage ceremony.
Then, under a constellation approved by all, he performed her marriage ceremony.
The heroic Śakuni, the son of Subala, who was pleasing in appearance, O great king,
gave his sister along with suitable dowry and attendants.
He returned to his own city, honored by Bhīṣma;
and Gāndhārī too, O Bhārata, that woman of noble form, produced satisfaction among all the Kurus through her character, conduct, and deeds.
Seeing her husband, the lord who possessed the eye of wisdom, Gāndhārī was deeply terrified by her transgression and reflected upon her conduct toward her husband;
though she had withdrawn her gaze, she attained equanimity before her husband.
For even in the slightest transgression, she did not then turn away from her husband;
having gratified them all through her conduct, she who was devoted to her husband and firm in her vows did not even mention other men by name.
Subala, the King of Gāndhāra, who had been chosen as a suitor by Bhīṣma, then gave him ten more daughters who were his own uterine sisters:
Satyavratā, Satyasenā, Sudeṣṇā, and Susaṃhatā.
On a single day, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, accepted as his wives Tejaḥśravas, Suśravas, Nikṛti, Śubhā, Śambhavā, Daśārṇā, and the ten renowned Gāndhārīs.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, having purchased them from here and there with bows,
gave more than a hundred princesses to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
There was a best of the Yadus named Śūra, the father of Vasudeva.
He had a daughter named Pṛthā, whose beauty was peerless on earth.
That heroic man gave her to his paternal cousin, who was childless.
Having previously promised his foremost [daughter] to the first [suitor],
the heroic one gave that maiden, named Agrajā, to the high-souled Kuntibhoja, who desired the highest favor, as a friend to a friend.
Appointed in her father’s house to the worship of the deities and guests,
she attended upon a fierce and formidable brahmin of rigid vows,
who was known as Durvāsas and whose resolve in dharma was hidden.
With all her efforts, she gratified that fierce one of disciplined soul;
with curds, ghee, and other such items, as well as daily side-dishes, that auspicious and excellent woman constantly served the Lord of Yogins in thousands of varieties every day.
At the end of the year, Durvāsas gave her that unsurpassed mantra;
out of consideration for the duties required in times of distress, he bestowed that mantra upon her,
and the sage further spoke to her regarding its application in rites of sorcery.
The venerable sage explained to her ten thousand instances of the *abhicāra* rite:
"Whichever deity you shall summon with this mantra,
by that deity's grace a son will be born to you."
Thus addressed by that brahmin out of curiosity at that time,
Kuntī— the illustrious maiden, though still a girl— invoked the god Arka, the Sun, for the purpose of testing him.
Then, having created a dense cloud to obscure his path,
the Sun approached that maiden Pṛthā, whose eyes were wide;
descending from his own course, he himself assumed a divine form.
She beheld him approaching, the sun, the creator of the world;
and seeing that great marvel, Kuntī, whose limbs were faultless, was struck with wonder. Kuntī said:
Sūrya said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having approached her, the god Vivasvat spoke this.
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, here I am; tell me, what may I do for you?
O slayer of enemies, a certain knower of Brahman granted me a boon and sacred knowledge. It was out of a desire to test that knowledge, O Lord, that I have addressed you."
Therefore, for this offense, I seek to propitiate you by bowing my head;
for women must always be protected, even when they have committed a transgression.
I know all of this that Durvāsas gave to you.
Abandoning both pride and fear, let us be united;
my sight is never in vain, and I have been summoned by you, O auspicious one. For if you summon me in vain, O timid one, there will undoubtedly be fault for you.
Having been addressed thus with many kinds of both conciliatory and harsh words by Vivasvat,
that beautiful woman, O King, did not desire [him], thinking, "I am a maiden," for she was terrified by fear of her kinsmen and, being ascetic, was filled with shame.
O bull of the Bharata race, the Sun spoke to her once again:
"O Queen, by my grace, no fault shall befall you.
Having spoken thus to the daughter of Kuntibhoja at that time, the Blessed One—
Sūrya; Vaiśampāyana;
Sūrya.
Kuntī;
Sūrya; Vaiśampāyana.

She said, "O Blessed One, who are you that have appeared before me? He replied, "O auspicious lady, know me to be the god Arka, invoked by mantra and present here at your summons for the sake of obtaining a son, O lady of pure smiles."
"O fair-browed one, O lady of auspicious countenance, listen to what kind of son has been created for you:
he shall wear earrings from the Sun and my own armor, which,
O lady of pure smiles, will be impenetrable to all weapons and missiles."
There shall be nothing that he will not give to the brahmins;
even when urged by me, he will not hesitate to consider it appropriate,
for he will give to the learned priests and he will indeed remain honorable.
Thus addressed, Kuntī then replied to the Lord of Rays:
"I am a maiden under the authority of my father, and I have no power over men.
If you think this way, O timid one, why do you summon the Sun?"
If you despise me, he shall no longer be a seer,
for it was by the gift of a mantra from him that you have become arrogant with pride. Today, I shall consume your lineage with my eyes blazing with wrath.
Be gracious to me, O Blessed One; indeed, I have no arrogance.
It would be a disgrace to my maidenhood that must be avoided by me alone. Let your fear depart today, for you shall behold the prince.
"And by my permission, you shall become a maiden once again.
Having been addressed thus, Kuntī’s hair stood on end with joy;
then, O fair-browed one, she was united with the high-souled Āditya.
Then the Sun, whose function is illumination, deposited his seed in her;
from that he begot a hero, the best among all wielders of weapons,
glorious, born with divine luster, clad in natural armor, and enveloped in splendor.
Wearing his innate armor and with his face illuminated by earrings,
a son named Karṇa was born, renowned throughout all the worlds;
[he was placed] in a basket filled with jewels and designated by the name Karṇa.
And that one of supreme splendor restored her maidenhood to her;
having bestowed it, he, the best among givers, then ascended to heaven. Seeing the boy born, that Vārṣṇeyī became dejected in spirit.

With one-pointed mind, she reflected: "What must I do so that it may turn out well? Then, concealing her transgression out of fear of her kinsmen, Kuntī cast that boy, endowed with auspicious marks, into the water.
Then the highly illustrious husband of Rādhā, that delighter of the Sūtas, together with his wife, took that abandoned embryo and adopted it as their son;
and both of them gave a name to that child.
"Since he was born together with wealth (*vasu*), let him be named Vasuṣeṇa.
As he grew up, he became powerful and proficient in all weapons;
indeed, he became renowned in the world as the best among all wielders of arms.
That valiant hero, true to his promise, remained there performing his silent recitations (japa) until his back was scorched by the heat of the sun; at that time,
there was nothing that the high-souled one would not give to the brahmins.
Karṇa; Sūrya; Vaiśampāyana.
Then, at a certain time, while [Karṇa] was at the end of his sleep, the Sun, having become a Brāhmaṇa, spoke to Karṇa: "O hero, listen to my words;
when the night has turned to dawn, Vāsava will come to you."
Alms should not be given to him, for he will appear in the form of a Brahmin;
his intent is to steal from you your armor as well as your earrings. Therefore, I am warning you now, so that you may remember my words.
"O twice-born one, if Śakra indeed requests me in the form of a brahmin,
how could I not give it to him, as I have been instructed? For brahmins are always to be honored by the gods who desire what is pleasing."
Knowing him to be the God of gods, I am indeed unable to address him without formal invitation.
If it be so, listen to me, O hero; he will grant you a boon, and you too should ask for a spear that destroys all enemies.
Having spoken thus, the twice-born vanished right there in that dream.
Then Karṇa, having awakened, remained reflecting upon that dream.
Indra, the creator of beings, having become a Brāhmaṇa, [appeared] for the sake of alms.
The one of great splendor requested the earrings and the armor.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Brahmin,
Karṇa then cut off his earrings and, with palms joined in reverence, presented them to him.
Having cut the armor from his own body with a dejected mind, blood flowing from it,
Karna then cut off his earrings and presented them with palms joined in reverence.
Having accepted them, the Lord of the Gods was pleased by this deed of his.
"O, what audacity! said Vāsava, laughing within his mind, regarding Karṇa among the gods,
Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
"I do not see anyone who will indeed be the performer of this deed.
I am pleased with that action; choose whatever boon you desire.
"I desire, O Blessed One, a power granted by you that destroys enemies."
O Lord of the hosts of gods, Śakra, filled with wonder, gave him an infallible and irresistible spear from you, and spoke these words:
"Of gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas..."
"Whomever you cast your wrath upon, he shall cease to exist because of her;
having slain that one enemy in battle, he will then come to me. Having spoken thus and granted him this boon, Śakra indeed vanished.
Formerly, his name was heard to be Vasuṣeṇa;
thereafter, he became Karṇa Vaikartana because of that deed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Endowed with beauty, goodness, and virtue, delighting in the Dharma and observing great vows,
she was the daughter of Kuntibhoja, whom her father had intended for a *svayaṃvara*. That radiant maiden, possessed of beauty and youth—

No kings whatsoever could resist her who was endowed with such extraordinary feminine virtues; therefore, O best of kings, her father King Kuntibhoja summoned the lords of men and gave his daughter away in a *svayaṃvara*.
Then that high-minded woman beheld in the midst of the arena Pāṇḍu, the tiger among kings and best of the Bharatas—
mighty, with the fangs of a lion, the shoulders of an elephant, and the eyes of a bull.
The illustrious Kuntī chose as her husband the great archer Pāṇḍu,
who stood in the assembly of kings like a second Purandara, eclipsing indeed the splendor of all other monarchs like the sun.

Seeing that Pāṇḍu, the best of men, in the arena, the auspicious daughter of Kuntibhoja, whose limbs were faultless, became agitated in her heart. Then, her body overcome by desire, her mind trembled for a moment.

Feeling bashful, Kuntī placed the garland upon the king’s shoulder. Hearing that Pāṇḍu had been chosen by Kuntī, all those lords of men returned as they had come, by means of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Then, O King, her powerful father performed her wedding ceremony;
he chose Pāṇḍu from among thousands of lords of the earth.
That joy of the Kurus was united with that daughter of Kuntibhoja.
Possessing immeasurable good fortune, he was united with her as Maghavan was with Paulomī.
Having traveled to the capital of the Madras by means of Devavrata,
he found Mādrī, the daughter of the lord of the Madras, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Renowned among all kings and peerless in beauty on earth,
she was then purchased with great wealth for the sake of Pāṇḍu;
Bhīṣma then caused the marriage to be performed for the high-souled Pāṇḍu.

Seeing Pāṇḍu— that tiger among men, high-minded, with the chest of a lion, the shoulders of an elephant, and the eyes of a bull— the people on earth were filled with wonder. Then, having performed his marriage, Pāṇḍu was endowed with strength and energy.
The illustrious protector of the Bharata lineage, skilled in all weapons,
went forth desiring to conquer the earth and numerous enemies.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Indra among kings, after King Kuntibhoja had performed the marriage ceremony for Kuntī and Pāṇḍu, honoring them with various riches,
that monarch sent the best of the Kurus back to his own city.
Then, with a great army adorned with various banners and flags, being praised with benedictions by brahmins and great seers,
King Pāṇḍu, the delighter of the Kauravas, reached the city.
The lord established his wife Kuntī in his own palace. Then the wise Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, set his mind upon arranging another marriage for the illustrious King Pāṇḍu.
Accompanied by his ministers, elders, Brahmins, and great seers,
as well as his fourfold army, he went to the city of the Lord of Madra.
Hearing that Bhīṣma had arrived, the preeminent leader of the Bāhlīkas [prepared to meet him].

Having gone out to meet him and honored him, the king led him into the city; having offered him a bright seat, as well as water for his feet and the guest-offering (*arghya*), the Lord of Madra presented him with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and inquired about the purpose of his arrival.

Bhīṣma, the upholder of the Kuru lineage, replied thus to the King of Madra: "O subduer of enemies, know that I have come seeking a boon. It is heard that your virtuous sister, the illustrious Mādrī, is present."
"I shall choose that illustrious lady for the sake of Pāṇḍu;
for you, O King, are well-suited to this alliance—we are yours. Having reflected upon this, O Lord of Madra, accept us according to the prescribed rites."
To Bhīṣma, who was speaking thus, the King of Madra replied:
"Indeed, in my mind there is no other suitor better than you;
for something has been established in this lineage by the best of kings since the time of our ancestors."
Whether it be good or whether it be bad, I do not venture to transgress that;
this is clearly known to you as well, there is no doubt in this.
And it is not fitting for you, O most excellent one, to say "Give [me] this."
"O hero, that is our family custom, and it is our supreme authority.
For that reason, O slayer of enemies, I do not speak these words to you without hesitation.
To him, the high-minded Bhīṣma replied thus to the King of Madra:
O King, this is the supreme dharma spoken by the Self-Existent One himself;
there is no fault whatsoever in this, for this rule was established by the ancients.
O Śalya, you already know this boundary esteemed by the virtuous.
