Having spoken thus, that one of great splendor gave to Śalya thousands of articles of gold, both wrought and unwrought, as well as various jewels,
elephants, horses, chariots, garments, and ornaments.
The son of Gaṅgā bestowed beautiful jewels, pearls, and corals;
having accepted all that wealth with a joyful heart, Śalya adorned his sister and gave her to the bull among the Kurus.
Taking Mādrī with him, the wise Bhīṣma, son of the River Ganges, returned to the city and entered Hastināpura. Then,
when the auspicious day and the moment approved by the virtuous had arrived, he performed the ceremony.

King Pāṇḍu, the lord of men, took the hand of Mādrī according to the prescribed rites. Then, when the wedding was completed, that king, the joy of the Kurus, established his beautiful bride in a splendid residence.
That best of kings, the lord of monarchs, sported with those two wives, Kuntī and Mādrī, according to his desire and at his pleasure. Then that Kuru king, having passed thirty nights there...
O Lord, out of a desire to conquer the earth, Pāṇḍu departed from the city. Having saluted and bowed down before the elders headed by Bhīṣma,
as well as Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Kauravya and other best of the Kurus, he set forth.

Having taken his leave and being cheered by them, the king departed; he was greeted with blessings accompanied by auspicious rites and proceeded with a great army consisting of a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots.

That king Pāṇḍu, resembling the king of the gods and desirous of conquering the earth, set out with his army full of joy and vigor against numerous enemies. Having first gone against those who had committed offenses, he defeated the Daśārṇas in battle.
Then Pāṇḍu, that lion among men and upholder of the Kauravas' fame,
took up his army, which bore various kinds of banners and was teeming with numerous elephants, horses, chariots, and throngs of infantry.
An offender against all heroes, an enemy of all kings, the protector of the Magadha kingdom— Dārva has been slain at Rājagṛha.
Then, having seized his treasury, as well as his vehicles and forces, [the king departed].
Having gone to Mithilā, Pāṇḍu conquered the Videhas in battle;
likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, among the Kāśis, Suhmas,
and Puṇḍras, he established the glory of the Kurus through the strength and prowess of his own arms.

Having encountered that subduer of foes, who was like a fire of Pandu with a great blaze of arrow-showers and the radiance of weapons, the lords of men were consumed by fire. Those kings, together with their armies, had their forces utterly destroyed by him who possessed an army.
Having brought them under his control, Pāṇḍu employed them in the performance of taxes; by him all the kings on earth were utterly defeated,
and they regarded him alone as a hero, like Purandara among the gods.
With palms joined in reverence, all those lords of the earth bowed down and approached him, bringing wealth and various kinds of jewels— gems,
pearls, coral, as well as gold and silver.
The king, the lord of Nāgapura, accepted all of that: cattle-jewels, horse-jewels, chariot-jewels, and elephants; as well as donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and whatever goats and sheep there were.
Taking that [gift], Pāṇḍu departed once more with his joyful mounts,
intending to gladden his own kingdom and the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura),
as well as the lineage of Śaṃtanu, that lion among kings, and the wise Bharata.
The fame-born reputation that had perished was raised up once more by Pāṇḍu.
Those who formerly seized the Kuru kingdoms and the wealth of the Kurus were made to pay tribute by Pāṇḍu, the lion of Hastināpura.
Thus spoke the kings and the assembled royal ministers;
they indeed greeted Pāṇḍu with various kinds of blessings,
their minds confident and joyful along with the citizens and the people of the countryside.
All those inhabitants of Nāgapura, led by Bhīṣma, went out to meet him as he arrived. Having traveled but a short distance along the road,
they joyfully beheld the world crowded with many kinds of people.
Having received jewels of various kinds, both high and low, brought from diverse vehicles,
as well as elephants, horses, chariots, gems, cattle, camels, and sheep,
the Kauravas, together with Bhīṣma, could find no end to them.

Having saluted his father’s feet, he who increased the joy of Kausalyā honored the citizens and the people of the provinces as was their due. He had returned successful, having crushed the kingdoms of his enemies.
Upon reaching his son, Bhīṣma shed tears out of joy. Amidst the great sounds of hundreds of musical instruments and kettledrums,
he entered the city of Hastināpura, gladdening the citizens on all sides.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been authorized by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he offered the wealth won by his own arms to Bhīṣma, Satyavatī, and his mother.
And Pāṇḍu sent that wealth to Vidura; moreover, the righteous-souled one gratified his friends with that wealth. Then Bhīṣma [honored] Satyavatī and the illustrious Kausalyā.
O Bhārata, he gratified [his mother] with auspicious, white, and conquered jewels;
Kausalyā rejoiced, embracing that bull among men of incomparable splendor, as Paulomī embraced Jayanta.
By means of the heroic deeds of that hero, which were accompanied by hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees,
and by the countless riches won by the strength of Pāṇḍu’s arms, the king...

Dhṛtarāṣṭra performed hundreds of horse-sacrifices and other great rites; O bull of the Bharatas, he was accompanied by Kuntī and Mādrī. At that time, Pāṇḍu, having conquered all sloth, became a dweller of the forest.
Having abandoned his palace residence and beautiful couches,
he became constantly devoted to the forest and perpetually intent on hunting.
Wandering along the lovely southern slope of the Himavat mountain, he proceeded.

He dwelt upon the mountain ridges and in groves of great *śāla* trees. Living with Kuntī and Mādrī in the forest, Pāṇḍu shone like the glorious elephant of Indra standing between two female elephants.
The forest-dwellers beheld the Bharata prince, accompanied by his two wives, bearing arrows,
sword, and bow; clad in variegated armor, a hero, and a king skilled in supreme weapons,
they thought, "This is a god who wanders here."
And urged by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, men tirelessly brought him objects of desire and enjoyments from the forest regions. Then,
[he took] the daughter of King Devaka, who was born of a Pāraśava father.
The son of the River (Bhīṣma) heard that she was endowed with beauty and youth;
then, having chosen her and brought her back, that bull among men had the marriage performed for the high-minded Vidura.
And upon her, Vidura, the joy of the Kurus,
begot sons endowed with discipline and equal to himself in virtues.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Then, O Janamejaya, one hundred sons were born to Dhṛtarāṣṭra by Gāndhārī; furthermore, there was one more son by his Vaiśya wife beyond that hundred. And to Pāṇḍu, by Kuntī and Mādrī, five sons were born who were great chariot-warriors.
They were bestowed upon the gods for the sake of the lineage's continuity.
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, how was a hundred sons born to Gāndhārī?"
After how much time did their lifespan reach its maximum?
And how was it that he alone became the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through a Vaiśya woman?
And how did he obtain Gāndhārī as a wife, who was so well-suited to him and a practitioner of dharma?

While she was living in accordance with his wishes, Dhṛtarāṣṭra disregarded her. And how did the five sons, those great chariot-warriors, spring from the gods for Pāṇḍu, who had been cursed by that high-souled one?
"O knower of this, O one whose wealth is asceticism, tell me in detail exactly what occurred; I am not satiated as my kinsmen are being described.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Gāndhārī gratified Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, who had arrived exhausted by hunger and fatigue; Vyāsa granted her a boon,
and she chose for herself a hundred sons equal to her husband.
Then, in due time, she conceived a child from Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Once the embryo had been placed in Gāndhārī, Pāṇḍu, the son of Ambālikā,
experienced the greatest sorrow for the sake of offspring, O subduer of enemies.

Then, while Gāndhārī was pregnant, Pāṇḍu, being deeply afflicted by grief and lamenting for himself due to the curse of the deer, ceased all worldly activity. Having attained perfection through asceticism on earth, like Viśvāmitra, he—
With his mind set on casting off his body, he spoke these words:
"Gāndhārī bore that embryo for two years; though she remained childless, she carried it, and then grief took possession of her."
Having heard that the son of Kuntī had been born, possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun,
she regained her composure and reflected within herself:
"He must be kept secret from Dhṛtarāṣṭra through great effort."
Gāndhārī, fainting from grief, caused her uterine brother to fall.
Then there was born a mass of flesh, as hard as a lump of iron ore;
she proceeded to cast it out, though it had been nurtured in her womb for two years.
Then Dvaipāyana, having perceived this, arrived in haste;
that best of those who recite prayers beheld that mass of flesh.
Thereupon he said to the daughter of Subala: "What is this that you intend to do?"
And she declared her own thought to be the truth to the supreme seer:
"Having heard that the eldest son of Kuntī had been born, possessing a splendor equal to the sun,
my womb was brought down by this supreme grief."
"You previously granted me a hundred sons;
yet this mass of flesh has been born to me for a hundred sons.
Vyāsa said:
"It is so, O daughter of Subala; this shall never be otherwise.
Never before have I spoken a falsehood even in jest, so how could it be otherwise now?
Let a hundred jars filled with ghee be prepared immediately."
"Let protection be provided in well-guarded places,
and sprinkle this swelling with cold water.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As she was being sprinkled, that mass of flesh split into a hundred parts;
indeed, O lord of the people, there were exactly one hundred and one embryos, each the size of a thumb’s joint, according to their respective proportions.
Then, O King, having brought a hundred cauldrons there, that great ṛṣi, as time passed, gradually placed those pieces of flesh into them as embryos. Then he deposited them into those cauldrons.
Then, in well-guarded places, he established protection; Kṛṣṇa indeed commanded the guarding of the embryos at that time. And after such a period of time, the Blessed One commanded once again.
"These vessels are to be broken," said Vyāsa to the daughter of Subala;
"from these vessels the Kumāras shall arise.
Having spoken thus and having made such arrangements, the Blessed One Vyāsa departed.
The wise one went to the Himalayan mountain range for the sake of asceticism.
Having thus instructed him, O descendant of Kuru, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
firm in his vows, then departed for the mountain itself to practice austerity.
By this sequence, King Duryodhana was born among them;
however, by the measure of birth, King Yudhiṣṭhira was the eldest.
This was then reported to Bhīṣma and to the wise Vidura.
On the very day that the invincible Duryodhana was born, O King,
on that same day the mighty-armed and heroic Bhīma was also born;
and as soon as he was born, O monarch, he became the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
He brayed and roared with a sound like the braying of a donkey;
then the asses, vultures, jackals, and crows responded to him.
At that time, winds blew violently and a conflagration appeared in every direction.
As soon as that son was born, Dhṛtarāṣṭra said this:
"O Bhārata, as soon as Duryodhana was born, in all directions, O Bhārata,
terrible carnivorous beasts howled and jackals uttered inauspicious sounds."
The god sent down rain of blood, portending a great terror.
In the meantime, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
having summoned many brahmins as well as Bhīṣma and Vidura, [spoke].

"O King, [consider] our other friends and all the Kurus as well. Prince Yudhiṣṭhira, the eldest of us and the enhancer of our lineage, has obtained the kingdom by virtue of his own merits; there is nothing to be said against him by us."
"But this king here shall be the one immediately following him.
Tell me the truth of this: what will certainly come to pass?
For the omens portend great misfortune upon his birth."

Therefore, O Vidura, I say this to you: a great fear has entered me. At the conclusion of these words, O Bhārata, in all directions, terrible carnivorous beasts howled and jackals shrieked, foreboding evil.
Having observed those terrible omens on all sides,
O King, those brahmins and the high-minded Vidura said:
"O lord of men, since these omens are so terrible..."
O bull among men, these [omens] arose when your eldest son was born. This King Duryodhana, dark-complexioned with tawny eyes,
will bring about not only the end of his own lineage, but the end of the entire Kṣatriya order.
"It is evident that this son of yours will be the destroyer of your lineage.
Peace lies in abandoning him; otherwise, there will be great misfortune despite his prosperity.
O Lord of the Earth, let there be even ninety-nine other sons remaining for you."

"Abandon this one man, O Bhārata, if you desire peace for the family; by abandoning one, bring security to both the world and the family. One should abandon an individual for the sake of the family; one should abandon a family for the sake of the village."

"One should abandon a village for the sake of a district, and one should abandon the whole earth for the sake of the self. Though addressed in this manner by Vidura and all those best of the twice-born,
the king, overcome by affection for his son, did not act accordingly.
Then, O King, within a single month, all one hundred sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were born, along with one daughter in addition to the hundred,
while Gāndhārī was suffering from her expanding womb.
It is said, O King, that a Vaiśya woman attended upon the mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In that year, O monarch, the highly illustrious and wise Yuyutsu was born to Dhṛtarāṣṭra from her; he was a Karṇa (Kṣattṛ) by caste, O ruler of men.
In this manner, one hundred sons were born to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
heroes who were all great chariot-warriors— and also one daughter, Duḥśalā;
and furthermore, there was the highly energetic and powerful Yuyutsu, the son of a Vaiśya woman.
O King of kings, [this was told] to Dhṛtarāṣṭra by me just as it has been related to you.
Janamejaya said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
Vyāsa said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
You have related from the beginning the account of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons.
Through the grace of the seer, however, it was not proclaimed that there were one hundred daughters;
rather, Yuyutsu was the son of the Vaiśya woman, and there was one daughter in excess of the hundred—
the daughter of the King of Gāndhāra, O sinless one, who was known as Śataputrā.
It was spoken by that great seer Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor:
"But now, O Blessed One, why do you tell me that she was born as a girl?
If that great seer had divided the embryo into a hundred parts,"
"If the daughter of Subala were not to give birth again by any means,
O brahmin-sage, tell me how Duḥśalā came into being; it is fitting for you to do so here, for my curiosity in this matter is great."
"O son of Pāṇḍu, this question you have posed is excellent; I shall explain it to you.
The Blessed One himself, of great ascetic power, sprinkled that mass of flesh with cool water and divided it into portions."
O King, whatever portion was assigned to each person, the nurse then placed one by one into jars filled with clarified butter. In the meantime,
the virtuous Gāndhārī, firm in her vows, [remained there].

Reflecting upon her attachment and affection for her daughter, the noble lady, the queen, thought in her mind: "There is no doubt that I shall have these one hundred sons; the sage does not speak otherwise."
This would be my supreme satisfaction if I were to have a daughter;
she will be the youngest girl, one more than a hundred in number. Then that husband of mine shall not be excluded from the world of grandsons.
It is said that for women, affection for their son-in-law is indeed excessive;
if only I too had even one daughter in excess of a hundred,
I would truly have fulfilled my purpose, surrounded by sons and grandsons.
"If true austerity has been practiced, or if gifts have been given, or even oblations offered,
or if my gurus have been gratified, then let it be so for my daughter.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself appeared.
Then, having divided that embryo-mass and counted out a full hundred portions, the Blessed One, the best of sages, said to the daughter of Subala:
"This is a full hundred of sons; the word I have spoken is not false."
"By the turn of fate, this one portion remains out of the hundred;
O fortunate lady, this girl shall become yours according to your desire.
Then, having brought another jar of ghee, the great ascetic—
And the ascetic cast that portion of the maiden into it as well.
This, O King, descendant of Bharata, has been told to you regarding the birth of Duḥśalā.
Speak, O Indra among kings, sinless one; what more shall I relate to you?
Janamejaya said: O Lord,
proclaim in due order the names of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, as well as their seniority, one after another.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, Duryodhana, Yuyutsu, Duḥśāsana,
Duḥsaha, Duḥśala, Jalasaṃdha, Sama, and Saha—
Vinda and Anuvinda, Durdharṣa, Subāhu, Duṣpradharṣaṇa, Durmarṣaṇa, Durmukha, Duṣkarṇa, and Karṇa himself;
Vivimśati, Vikarṇa, Jalasaṃdha, and Sulocana.
Citra and Upacitra, Citrākṣa, Cārucitra, Śarāsana; Durmada, Duṣpragāha, Vivitsu, Vikaṭa, Sama;
Ūrṇanābha, Sunābha, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka.
The commander-in-chief Suṣeṇa, Kuṇḍodara, Mahodara,
Citradhvaja, Citraratha, Citrabāhu, Amitrajit,
Citrabāṇa, Citravarman, Suvarman, and Durvimocana.
Ayobāhu, Mahābāhu, Citrāṅga, Citrakuṇḍala, Bhīmavega, Bhīmabala, Balākī, Balavardhana,
Ugrāyudha, Bhīmakarman, Kanakāyu, and Dṛḍhāyudha.
Citrāyudha, Niṣaṅgin, Pāśin, and Vṛndāraka; likewise Dṛḍhavarman, Dṛḍhakṣatra, Somakīrti, and Anūdara;
Dṛḍhasandhi, Jarāsandhi, Satyasandhi, and Sadasuvāk.
Ugraśravas, Aśvasena, Senānī, Duṣparājaya, Aparājita, Paṇḍitaka, Viśālākṣa, Durāvara,
Ajita, Jayanta, Jayatsena, and Durjaya.
Dṛḍhahasta, Suhasta, Vātavega, Suvarcas,
Ādityaketu, Bahvāśin, Nāgadanta, Ugrayāyin, Kavacin, Niṣaṅgin, Pāśin, Daṇḍadhāra, and Dhanurgraha.
Ugra, Bhīmaratha, Vīra, Vīrabāhu, Alolupa, Bhīmakarman, Subāhu, Bhīmavikrānta,
Abhaya, Raudrakarman, and likewise Dṛḍharatha— these three.
Anādhṛṣya, Kuṇḍabhedin, Virāvin, Dīrghalocana, Pramatha, Pramāthin, the heroic Dīrghālāta,
Dīrghadhvaja, Dīrghabhuja, Adīrgha, and Dīrgha.
Dīrghabāhu, Mahābāhu, Vyūḍhoru, Kanakadhvaja,
Mahākuṇḍa, Kuṇḍa, Kuṇḍaja, Citraja,
Kuṇḍāśin, Virajas, and Duḥśalā, who was the hundredth and one.
O King, these one hundred and one sons and one daughter have been proclaimed;
know, O monarch, their order of birth according to the sequence of their names.
All of them were heroic Atirathas, all experts in warfare.
They were all knowers of the Vedas and experts in the treatises on statecraft; all were skilled in the sciences of social interaction and distinguished by their learning and noble birth.
O Lord of the Earth, wives were chosen for each of them according to their respective merits.
O Bhārata, having deliberated according to the rules at that time with Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the king then gave Duḥśalā in marriage to Jayadratha, the king of the Sindhus, with the approval of Saubala.
"Thus, O King, a hundred sons have been recounted by me, as well as Yuyutsu, who was one more than the hundred, and the daughter Duḥśalā. Janamejaya said:
O best of those who know the Veda, you have related the supreme, superhuman, and divine origin of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra among human beings;
and their names have also been recounted by you in their respective divisions.
"O Brahmin, I have heard [the accounts] from you; now please recount those of the Pāṇḍavas.
For they were all high-souled, possessing the prowess of the king of the gods, and by you alone were their divine portions proclaimed during their descent as partial incarnations."
"Therefore, I wish to hear all about the birth of those who performed superhuman deeds; O Vaiśampāyana, please narrate it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In the great forest frequented by deer and beasts of prey, King Pāṇḍu beheld a leader of a herd of deer engaged in the act of mating. Then,
with gold-feathered arrows equipped with excellent fletching, [he struck] both that doe and him.
Pāṇḍu pierced him with five sharp, swift arrows.
And he, O King, the son of a seer, possessed of great splendor and rich in asceticism, was united with his wife in the form of a deer. That radiant one was joined with her.

The sage was a deer and his wife was a doe; both were endowed with ascetic power. Having become unrestrained in their passion, they took delight in the forest. Yet, while he was joined with that doe, he spoke words in a human voice.
In an instant, he fell to the ground and lamented with his senses overwhelmed.
The deer said:
"Though overcome by desire and anger, and though deprived of the faculty of reason,"
Men who delight in evil deeds avoid cruel acts;
wisdom does not swallow up destiny, but destiny swallows up wisdom.
Wisdom does not attain those ends that have been brought about by destiny.
"O Bhārata, how has your mind, born in a preeminent family of those whose very nature is dharma, become so wavering, overcome as you are by desire and greed?
Pāṇḍu said:
"The conduct prescribed for the slaying of enemies is traditionally held to apply to the slaying of wild animals. O deer, you ought not to reproach me out of delusion;
the slaughter of animals is permitted through the use of nets, traps, and guile."
"That very same duty belongs to kings; knowing this, why do you reproach me?
The seer Agastya, while engaged in a sacrificial session, went out hunting in the great forest, having consecrated wild animals for all the deities."
"How can you reproach us, who act according to what is seen through valid means of knowledge?
Indeed, it was by the sorcery of Agastya that your sacrificial fat was offered as an oblation.
The deer said:
In former times, they did not discharge arrows specifically targeting enemies,
nor did those ancients seek to provoke a confrontation with their foes; rather,
it is especially at the moment of their vulnerability that the time for slaying them is praised.
Pāṇḍu said:
"Whether heedless or heedful, they strike with their might against those who are exposed, using means such as sharp arrows; why, O deer, do you reproach me?"
"O Great King, you have slain one who was engaged in sexual intercourse without cause.
The deer said:
"O King, I do not blame you for killing deer for your own sake."
"Out of compassion toward you, I must wait for my mating here;
for this is a time when all beings seek the welfare of all beings.
For what wise man would kill a deer wandering in the forest while engaged in mating?"
"O Indra among kings, out of passion I practiced sexual union with this doe;
that which you have rendered fruitless— the lovely fruit of human purpose—
belongs to the Pauravas and to those sages of unwearied deeds."
"O Kauravya, born as you are in this lineage, this is not worthy of you—
this most cruel deed, greatly despised by all the world,
which leads away from heaven, brings dishonor, and is utterly unrighteous, O Bhārata."

"O you who resemble a god, you who are a connoisseur of the pleasures of women and a knower of the true essence of the scriptures, dharma, and worldly purpose— you ought not to perform such an act that leads away from heaven.
By you, men who commit cruel deeds and follow sinful conduct [are to be judged]."

"O best of kings, those who are devoid of the three aims of life (trivarga) should be restrained. O best of men, O King, what wrong have I done to you that you would slay me— an innocent sage, subsisting on roots and fruits, wearing the guise of a deer?"
Since I have been harmed by you— who dwell constantly in the forests, ever devoted to tranquility— therefore, without doubt, I shall likewise [punish] you,
who are a perpetrator of cruelty toward both [father and mother], helpless and deluded by desire.
"The state that brings an end to life will surely come in this very way.
For I am a sage named Kiṃdama, peerless in asceticism;
yet, out of shame before men, I have engaged in sexual intercourse with a doe."
Having become a deer, I roam with other deer in the dense forest. Among quadrupeds such as elephants, horses, and buffaloes, there is no sense of shame;
devoid of modesty, apprehension, and fear, sexual union is their supreme pleasure.
That happiness does not exist for bipeds; it belongs to quadrupeds.
For kings, hunting is a lawful practice, and therein no killing is prescribed—even for a pair of deer whose minds are intent on mating, O Lord of the Earth.

"But this sin of killing a Brahmin shall not be yours, since you acted without knowing that it was I who had assumed the form of a deer and was thus deluded by desire. O fool, you shall indeed receive a fruit exactly like this."
Having obtained union with your beloved, you too, deluded by desire,
will go to the world of the departed in this very state; and at the time of death, you shall go to union with that same beloved.
"O best among the wise, she who has fallen under the power of the King of the Dead and is difficult for all beings to overcome will follow you out of devotion— she by whom I,
while dwelling in happiness, was reduced to such misery as I have now been brought to by you."
"So too, after you have attained such happiness, suffering shall come upon you.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, afflicted by intense grief, he was deprived of life.
And in an instant, the pale deer became afflicted with grief.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having passed beyond him, the king [beheld] as if his own kinsman.
Together with his wife, afflicted by grief and suffering, he lamented in distress.
Pāṇḍu said:
"Alas! Even those born in the families of the virtuous may fall into misfortune through their own actions."

Those of unrefined soul, deluded by the snare of desire, fall [into ruin]. We have heard that my father, though born with a soul ever devoted to dharma, reached the end of his life while still a child, because his soul was possessed by desire.
In the field of that king who was possessed by lust, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana— the Lord himself, whose speech is restrained— begot me. Today,
this base intellect of mine has become intent upon his misfortune.

"Abandoned by the gods due to this misconduct in hunting, I, being evil-minded, resolve only upon liberation; for bondage is a great calamity. I shall follow that eternal, virtuous conduct of my father."
"Without doubt, I shall yoke myself to extreme austerity.
Therefore, alone for one day at a time, wandering from tree to tree as a shaven-headed sage begging for alms, I shall traverse this earth."
Covered with dust, dwelling in empty huts or making his home at the foot of trees, having abandoned all that is pleasant and unpleasant,
neither grieving nor rejoicing, he regards blame and self-praise as equal.
Free from expectations, free from ritual salutations, free from the pairs of opposites, and free from possessiveness; never mocking anyone, nor ever knitting his brows;
always with a serene countenance, he is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Always practicing non-violence toward all four classes of beings, both moving and stationary, he remains impartial toward all living creatures as if they were his own offspring;
wandering for alms at a single time of day, he visits two or five households.
Or, in the event that alms-food is unavailable, even while practicing fasting,

he should eat only very little food as it is obtained, never by means of a previous acquisition; always remaining within the bounds of moderation when obtaining food, he should complete the seven [days] even when there is no gain.
Whether in loss or in gain, the one of great austerity views them with equanimity;
whether one person hacks at his one arm while another anoints the other with sandalwood paste,
he reflects upon neither as evil nor as good regarding both of them.
Acting neither like one wishing to live nor like one wishing to die, neither rejoicing in death nor hating life,
he performed whatever auspicious rites could be accomplished by a living being.
Having transcended all those states, he remains established even in moments such as the blink of an eye;
in all those conditions, he has abandoned the activities of all the senses,
completely relinquished the nature of dharma, and thoroughly cleansed the impurities of his own self.
Released from all evils and having passed beyond all snares,
he does not remain under the control of anyone, sharing the nature of the wind;
practicing constantly in this manner and of such a kind.
Established upon the fearless path, I shall sustain this body;
I would not take pleasure in the path frequented by dogs, which is suited for the weak and the wretched,
and from which one is eternally estranged from one's own duty, being devoid of vigor.
Whether honored or dishonored, he who, driven by lust, seeks another’s livelihood with a piteous eye, follows the path of dogs.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the king, afflicted by great sorrow and sighing deeply,
looked toward Kuntī and Mādrī and addressed them:
"Kausalyā, Vidura the steward, and the king along with his kinsmen— "
The noble Satyavatī, Bhīṣma, and those royal priests,
the high-souled Brāhmaṇas who drink the Soma and are firm in their vows, as well as the elders of the city who dwell there under our protection— [all these must be informed].

Having propitiated them all, he should say: "Pāṇḍu has departed for the forest. Hearing these words of their husband, who was resolved upon dwelling in the forest, Kuntī and Mādrī both spoke words to the same effect.

"O bull of the Bharatas, there are indeed other stages of life (*āśrama*) that we could consider, which would allow us to dwell together while adhering to dharma. Having performed great austerities together with me, your lawful wife, [we might find such a way]."
"Having attained the Dharma of great fruit for the liberation of the body,
you yourself will undoubtedly become a caravan leader even for heaven;
having restrained the collection of your senses, you are now intent upon the world of your husband."
"O one of great wisdom, O lord of the people, if you abandon us, we two shall indeed renounce the pleasures of desire and perform extensive austerities;
today itself we shall give up our lives— of this there is no doubt."
Pāṇḍu said:
"If this resolve of yours is indeed consistent with dharma,
then I shall follow that eternal way of life of my father."
Having abandoned the pursuit of vulgar pleasures, performing great austerities, clad in bark garments and subsisting on fruits and roots, I shall wander in the great forest,
offering oblations into the fire at both times and performing ritual ablutions at both times.
Emaciated, restricted in food, wearing rags, skins, and matted hair,
enduring cold, wind, and heat, and beset by hunger, thirst, and fatigue—
he was withering this body away through difficult ascetic penance.
Dwelling in solitude, reflecting deeply, and subsisting on both ripe and unripe forest produce, he gratified the ancestors and the gods with forest offerings, with prayers, and with water;
even the sight of forest-dwellers and those living in their ancestral homes was pleasing to him.
Never performing anything unpleasant, how much less so for those living in villages; thus,
desiring the fierce and even fiercer rule prescribed by the forest scriptures, I shall remain until the completion of this body.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to his two wives, the king born of the Kuru lineage then [gave] his crest-jewel, his golden neck-ornament, his armlets, and his earrings.
Diadems, pearl necklaces, waistbands,
as well as costly garments and the ornaments of women;
principal vehicles, weapons, and armor.
Divine golden vessels, couches, and coverlets;
jewels, pearls, corals, and various kinds of wealth;
and many excellent seats of diverse sorts.
Having given everything to the brahmins, Pāṇḍu spoke again:
"Go to Nāgapura and say: 'Pāṇḍu has gone forth into the forest;
[abandon] wealth, desire, pleasure, and even the highest sensual delight.'"
Leaving everything behind, that bull among the Kurus set out with his wife. Then his attendants and followers,
having heard those various piteous words of the lion of the Bharatas, [followed him].
Making a terrible sound of distress, they cried out "Alas! Alas!
Shedding hot tears as they left that lord of the earth, they departed quickly for Nāgapura, taking all those words with them.
Having gone to the city, they related everything that had occurred to the high-souled king, and they gave him various kinds of wealth.
And having heard from them all that had happened in the great forest, [the king was moved].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the best among men, grieved only for Pāṇḍu;
he found no pleasure whatsoever in beds, seats, or enjoyments,
being overwhelmed by grief for his brother and constantly reflecting upon that very matter.
But the Kuru prince Pāṇḍu, subsisting on roots and fruits,
went from there with his two wives to Mount Nāgasabha;
having reached Caitraratha and passed beyond Vāriṣeṇa.
Having crossed the Himavat, he proceeded toward Gandhamādana;
protected by great beings, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis,
the king then dwelt there upon both level and rugged terrain.
Having reached Lake Indradyumna and passed beyond Haṃsakūṭa,
O great king, the ascetic arrived at Śataśṛṅga.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Even while engaged in that most excellent asceticism,
that heroic one became a pleasing sight to the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
he was intent on service, free from egoistic speech, self-controlled, and a master of his senses.
O Bhārata, he strove with his own prowess to go to heaven;
for some he was a brother, for others he was a friend,
and other ṛṣis protected him as if he were their own son.
But after a long time, having attained stainless ascetic power,
O bull of the Bharatas, Pāṇḍu became like a Brahman-sage;
thus spoke Vaiśampāyana.
The sages;
Vaiśampāyana said:
On the new moon day, the sages, having undertaken their vows, gathered together.
Desirous of seeing Brahmā, those great seers set forth.
Seeing the seers departing, Pāṇḍu spoke these words:
"O best among speakers, tell me, where are you going?"
Today there is a great assembly of high-souled beings in the world of Brahmā—
of gods, sages, and ancestors. We shall go there, desiring to see the Self-Existent One.
Hearing those words of the great seers as Pāṇḍu suddenly rose up, desiring to depart, he spoke these words:
"I too shall come to where you will go."

Desiring to cross to the further shore of heaven, he set out from the Hundred-Peaked Mountain facing north with his two wives; there, as they were traveling higher and higher toward the north over the king of mountains, the ascetics spoke to them.
We have seen many inaccessible regions of this mountain,
crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots and resounding with the sound of singing; we have seen places guarded by yakṣas and rākṣasas, and frequented by gandharvas.
He saw the pleasure groves of the gods, as well as those of the gandharvas and apsarases;
the gardens of Kubera, both level and rugged;
the slopes of great rivers, and inaccessible mountain clefts.
There are regions of eternal snow, devoid of trees, deer, and birds; some are places of heavy rain, while others are difficult to traverse and hard to approach—
places that even a bird could not cross, let alone other animals.
"Only the wind can pass where the Siddhas and supreme ṛṣis go;
how then do these two princesses traverse this king of mountains?
O bull of the Bharatas, let them not perish, for they do not deserve such suffering; do not go [there]."
"O illustrious one, you who are childless, it does not behove you to go to heaven. O lord of men, O lotus-eyed one, do not [grieve] over this state of being childless.
Pāṇḍu said:
"O highly fortunate ones, they do not declare a door [to heaven] for one who is childless;
therefore, being tormented by that lack of offspring, I tell you this:
I, along with my wife, have abandoned all hope for life through fierce asceticism."
"Even though childless, may I attain heaven through fierce ascetic practice.
Men born upon this earth are burdened by four debts, to be paid in hundreds of thousands of ways: to the ancestors, the gods, the seers, and to men."
But that man who does not recognize these [periods] at their proper time—
those who know the Dharma have established that for him there are no worlds.
He pleases the gods with sacrifices, and the sages with Vedic study and austerity.
Through my sons, I have fulfilled my duties toward the ancestors through the *śrāddha* rites, and toward other men through compassion; thus,
in accordance with dharma, I am liberated from my obligations to the three classes of beings— sages, gods, and humans— while for the other three, their destruction occurs within myself as I perish.

"O ascetics, I am now unreleased from my debt to my ancestors; because I am unreleased from my debt to my ancestors, O you whose wealth is penance, I suffer. It is certain that with the destruction of the body, the destruction of the ancestors is inevitable—this is the settled conclusion."
For by the destruction of the debt to the ancestors, one does not suffer the destruction of progeny;
therefore, O best of men, offspring are produced here for the sake of progeny,
just as I was created in my father’s field by that great-souled one.
"In this very field of mine, how indeed might progeny come to be?
The ascetics said:
"O righteous-souled one, we know that you possess auspiciousness equal to that of a god."
"O King, O tiger among men, we see with divine vision that there shall be faultless offspring ordained by fate; accomplish this through action here,
for a wise man, remaining undistracted, obtains the fruit of his efforts without hardship."
"O dear one, since that fruit has been seen, you ought to exert yourself;
having obtained offspring endowed with virtues, you will attain joy.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of the ascetic, Pāṇḍu became lost in thought,
knowing that his own religious rites had been rendered futile by the curse of the deer.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O bull of the Bharatas, having summoned both Kuntī and Mādrī,
he announced to them the fulfillment of his acquisition of sons— a result surpassing all other rites—
for inferior men desire a son from a superior man in times of distress.
"Virtuous people desire offspring that yield the fruit of dharma from a superior man.
Having thus properly entreated him in the assembly of great brahmins,
the knower of dharma reflected upon a virtuous brahmin.
In a secluded place, he spoke to Kuntī, his illustrious lawful wife,
justifying the practice of procreating offspring as a means for times of distress:
"In this world, offspring are the foundation of one's standing, established in righteousness."
"O Kuntī, the wise have declared from the beginning that this is the eternal dharma:
sacrifice, charity, austerity, and well-performed self-restraint—
all these are said here not to purify one who is childless."
"O lady of pure smiles, having understood this,
I perceive that being childless, I shall not attain the auspicious worlds; thus I reflect,
for my procreative power has been destroyed by the curse of the deer, as I am one who has failed to master his self."
"O timid one, it is just as if something were defiled by a cruel deed.
According to the vision of Dharma, these six sons are indeed heirs to their kin;
hear from me, O Pṛthā, the six sons who are not heirs to their kin."

The son born of one’s own self, the excellent son, and the son purchased—these are equal to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*). The son born of one’s own self is a *kṣatriya*... [and so forth].
The son of a remarried woman, the son of an unmarried girl, and he who is born of an adulteress;

the given son, the bought son, the made son, and he who approaches [the father] of his own accord; the son received with a pregnant bride, the son of uncertain paternity, and he who is maintained by a woman of low birth.
If no son of each preceding type is available, one should indeed seek to obtain a son;
for in times of distress, those of lower status desire a son from a man of higher status.
The virtuous obtain an excellent offspring that yields the fruit of dharma.
"Manu, the son of Svayambhū, has declared that even one's own semen may be distinct [from the offspring].
Therefore, being myself deficient in procreative power, I shall send you forth today;
O illustrious lady, know that you shall obtain offspring from one who is either your equal or superior."
For that virtuous and illustrious sister of yours, Śrutasenā,
whom the great Kaikeya Śāradaṇḍāyani married—
listen, O Kuntī, to this story concerning Śāradaṇḍāyani.
O Kuntī, you who were the wife of a hero and were commissioned by your elders to procreate offspring,
having bathed with a flower while purified, you, devoted to auspicious vows, went at night to a crossroads for the sake of obtaining progeny.
Having chosen that perfected brahmin and performed the *puṃsavana* rite with fire,
she remained with him once that ritual was completed;
there she gave birth to three great chariot-warriors, Durjaya and the others.
"In the same way, O auspicious lady, at my command, you must strive with a Brahmin superior in asceticism to produce offspring quickly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, O Great King, Kuntī spoke to Pāṇḍu—
the hero, the bull among the Kurus, and her husband, the lord of the earth:
"O Knower of Dharma, you ought not to speak to me in such a manner under any circumstances."
"O lotus-eyed one, she is devoted to you as her lawful wife.
But you alone, O mighty-armed Bhārata, shall lawfully beget upon me sons endowed with heroic prowess."
"O tiger among men, may I go to heaven together with you. For the sake of offspring, do you yourself approach me, O joy of the Kurus;
for I would not go to any other man even in my thoughts, save for you."
And what other man on earth is superior to you? Now, O large-eyed one, listen to this ancient and righteous tale of mine, which has been heard by many and which I shall now proclaim.

Long ago, there was indeed a king renowned as Vyuṣitāśva, most virtuous and the enhancer of Puru’s lineage. While that high-souled and righteous-minded one was performing a sacrifice, [the following occurred].
Then the gods, together with Indra and the great seers, arrived there.
Indra was exhilarated by the Soma, and the twice-born were gratified by the sacrificial fees at the sacrifice of the high-souled royal sage Vyuṣitāśva.
Then the gods and the celestial sages themselves performed that rite.
Thereupon, O King, Vyushitashva shone forth, surpassing all mortals,
just as the sun outshines all beings at the end of the winter season.
Having conquered and captured those kings— the easterners, the northerners, the central ones, and those from the south— that most excellent of monarchs,
the powerful Vyushitashva, brought them together for the great horse sacrifice.
For that lord of kings was endowed with the strength of ten elephants.
Regarding this, O best of the Kurus, those people who are knowers of the Purāṇas sing this verse concerning Vyushitāśva, the increaser of glory and lord of men: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Vyushitashva gave away immeasurable and boundless wealth.
Having conquered this earth as far as the ocean's edge,
Vyushitashva protected all the social orders (varnas) like a father protects his own biological sons.
As a sacrificer, he bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins through great sacrifices; taking up infinite jewels,
he performed the great rites and pressed much soma, extending the soma-sacrifices.
And he had a wife, highly esteemed, named Bhadrā, the daughter of Kakṣīvat; O lord of men, she was peerless on earth in her beauty.
It is heard that the two of them were in love with one another.
Intoxicated by passion for her, he was seized by consumption;
in a short time, he set like the sun.
When that lord of men had passed away, his wife was deeply afflicted with grief.
"O tiger among men, we have heard that Bhadrā, afflicted by supreme sorrow because she was childless, lamented; understand that, O lord of men.
O knower of the highest dharma, every woman who is deprived of a son [is likewise afflicted]."
"She who lives without her husband does not truly live; she lives only in suffering.
O bull among Kṣatriyas, death is better for a woman than life without her husband.
I wish to follow your path; be gracious and take me with you."
"Deprived of you, I cannot bear to live for even a moment. O King, show me favor; take me away from here at once.
I shall follow behind you over both the level and the uneven ground."
"O tiger among men, O King, as you go forth never to return, I shall always remain by your side like a shadow that never departs,
ever obedient and constantly devoted to your pleasure and welfare, O tiger among men."
"O King, from this day forward, painful anxieties that wither the heart will overcome me, for I am deprived of you, O lotus-eyed one. Surely,
through my ill fortune, my companions have been separated from me."
O King, whether through union or separation in previous bodies,
this separation from you has now come upon me;
for she who lives even for a moment separated from her husband [is truly wretched].
O King, that wicked woman lives in misery like one dwelling in hell;
this suffering born of separation from you has now come upon me, O King, as the result of evil deeds accumulated in previous bodies.
"From this day forward, O King, I shall sleep upon a bed of kusha grass,
overcome by misery and intent only upon seeing you. Show yourself, O tiger among men, to me who am thus beset by sorrow."
O lord of men, while she was thus lamenting in many ways— miserable, helpless, pitiable, and wailing— while she was crying out again and again,
an invisible voice spoke from within that very corpse which she embraced.
"Arise, O blessed lady; go, for I shall grant you a boon here. O lady of lovely smiles, I shall procreate offspring through you.
And on the fourteenth day, O lady of excellent hips, [come] to my own bedchamber."
"Or, having bathed after your menses, you should lie with me on the eighth day.
Thus addressed, that goddess, devoted to her husband, did exactly as she was told; then Bhadrā, desiring a son, acted according to those words.
O lord of men, O best of the Bharatas, by means of that corpse, that goddess gave birth to three Śālvas and four Madras as her sons;
likewise, O bull among the Bharatas, you too [conceived] in me through my mind alone.
"By virtue of the power of his asceticism and yoga, he is capable of fathering sons.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by her, the king spoke again to that queen.
The knower of dharma spoke these supreme words, consistent with righteousness:
"O Kuntī, it was exactly as you have said; in former times, Vyushitashva did indeed act in this way, for he was like an immortal."
Now, however, I shall proclaim this dharma; listen to it from me. It is the ancient dharma perceived by the high-souled seers who were knowers of dharma.
O fair-faced one, in former times, women were indeed unconfined.

O lady of beautiful eyes, they lived according to their own will and were independent. O fortunate one, O woman of excellent hips, when they departed from their husbands after [their period of] maidenhood, no unrighteousness occurred; for that was the law in ancient times.
Even today, creatures born as animals continue to follow that very ancient dharma, free from desire and hatred;
this dharma, seen of old, is honored by the great seers.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, even today in the northern Kuru region,
that eternal dharma which bestows favor upon women still prevails.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean ever satiated with rivers.

Neither Death nor beautiful-eyed women are the end for all beings; likewise, O woman of pure smiles, there is no such thing as a woman who is forever inaccessible to every man, for craving is ever present toward each and every man.
Upon seeing a man here in secret— whether it be a son, a grandson, or even a brother— the womb becomes moistened; this,
O auspicious lady, is the natural state of women and is not caused by any external motive.
But in this world, O lady of pure smiles, listen to me in detail regarding how and by whom this boundary was established not long ago. We have heard that there was a great seer named Uddālaka.
He had a son known as Śvetaketu, who was a sage. O lotus-eyed one, we have heard that he established this law among human beings; learn from me the reason for which he did so out of anger.
Uddālaka,
the Brahmin Pāṇḍu.
O Goddess, Śvetaketu’s father undertook fierce asceticism;
in the summer he practiced the "five-fire" penance, in the rainy season he remained under the open sky,
and in the winter, that great ascetic stayed in the water together with his wife.
To Uddālaka, who was performing austerities, disciplined and composed in meditation,
his son Śvetaketu offered service. At that time, a certain twice-born man arrived, covered with wrinkles and grey hair.
Upon seeing him, the sage was delighted and honored him according to the scriptures,
O Bhārata, with a welcome, water for his feet, and gentle words;
he further honored him with vegetables, roots, fruits, and other forest products.
Afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, yet honored by the great seer, the twice-born man rested; having approached the sage, he then questioned him:
"O great seer Uddālaka, tell me the truth, not a falsehood."
"This prince, the son of a seer, is especially handsome;
I consider him to be your own son. Tell me, have you accomplished your purpose? O man of great wisdom, my wife is considered the daughter of Kuśika."
My wife, who has ever followed me and is constantly devoted to me, is like Arundhatī among wives, her breasts emaciated by asceticism. From her was born my son Śvetaketu, a man of great austerity.
O Brahmin, knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted to my command,
you are one who knows the world, renowned throughout all lands, truthful in speech, and compassionate.
I am old, my eyesight is failing, and I am without a wife and in need of wealth.
"Unreleased from my debt to my ancestors and having not yet fulfilled my duty toward women,
I have this wife, the source of progeny, who is endowed with noble lineage, character, and concentration; she is of a clan equal to mine, so I carry her— please forgive me."
Having spoken thus to the fawn-eyed woman, who was clad in bark and a black antelope skin, the twice-born man—
leaning on a staff, with failing limbs, dim sight, and lacking wisdom—
perceived that she was incapable of her own duties and indifferent toward him.
Long ago, it is said, while Śvetaketu was in the presence of his father, a certain Brahmin took his mother by the hand and said, "Let us go. Thereupon,
the son of the ṛṣi became indignant and gave way to anger.
Seeing his mother being led away as if by force,
Śvetaketu— whose prowess was kindled by asceticism— could not endure it.
Taking his mother by the hand, Śvetaketu spoke:
"O wicked Brahmin, release my mother, who is devoted to her husband!
This is my father, a brahmin-sage, patient and most eminent in Vedic knowledge;
he is capable of both cursing and blessing, yet remains silent, observing his great vow."
His wife, endowed with self-restraint, is especially my mother;
she is devoted to her husband, advanced in asceticism, and adorned by virtuous conduct.
O Brahmin, release her, who has been like a mother to me, by returning her to me.
Having spoken thus to him who was repeatedly entreating "Release me," O King, the twice-born man replied with these words, which were modest and lacking in arrogance:
"O Śvetaketu, I am old and my sight is failing; I am desirous of offspring."
"O Kāśyapa, through you as a son, your father has been released from his debt;
but I am not released from my debt. I am old and free from worldly desire;
who will give me his daughter, a maiden who has reached the prime of youth?"
"O you of great asceticism, release this wife, the source of progeny;
I shall give your mother to your parents with one offspring.
Thus addressed, Śvetaketu was overcome with anger out of shame.
Seeing him enraged, his father spoke to Śvetaketu, taking his mother by the hand:
"Do not be angry, my son; this is the eternal law."
For on this earth, women of all castes are indeed unrestrained;
just as cattle remain within their own respective pens, O dear one, so do people remain within their own castes. And likewise, within their households, they never become negligent.
When the time of their season arrived, they did not then forsake their husband. But Śvetaketu, the son of the ṛṣi, could not endure that practice;
he then established this boundary for men and women on earth.
"O highly fortunate lady, this applies among humans and not among other creatures;
we have heard that from that time forward this boundary has been established. From this day forth, it is a sin for a woman to transgress against her husband."

The sin committed by the destruction of an embryo will bring about unhappiness. Even today, O highly fortunate one, those in the northern Kuru region remain free from desire and hatred; thus it is, O illustrious lady.
Likewise, for one who commits adultery with a wife who was a virgin at marriage, who has observed lifelong celibacy,
and who is devoted to her husband— this shall be the sin on earth. And so too for a wife who, being commissioned by her husband, fails to bear offspring.
"She will not do it, and this very thing shall indeed come to pass"—
thus, O timid one, was that righteous boundary formerly established by force by Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka.
Listen now to that matter which was seen by him even more clearly than before:
if a wife, though appointed by her husband for the sake of offspring,
should not perform her duty, O timid one, she incurs very great sin.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, we have heard that Madayantī, commissioned by Saudāsa to produce offspring, approached the seer Vasiṣṭha; from him,
that beautiful woman obtained a son named Aśmaka.
The wife of Kalmāṣapāda, desiring to do what was pleasing to her husband, said:
"O lotus-eyed one, O timid lady, your birth from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana for the sake of increasing the lineage of the Kurus is also known to us."
Therefore, having duly considered all these reasons,
O blameless lady, you ought to carry out these words of mine which are in accordance with dharma. For, O princess of firm vows, it is the duty of a woman toward her husband in every season.
"Those who know the Dharma understand that this law must not be transgressed; however, at other times, a woman is said to deserve independence. Virtuous people declare this to be the ancient Dharma."
"O Princess, those who know the Dharma understand that whatever a husband may say to his wife— whether it be righteous or unrighteous— that must be done accordingly;
especially so when he is himself deficient in procreative power and longs for a son."
O lady of faultless limbs, just as I am longing for the sight of my son, so too, O auspicious one, do these hands— with their palms and fingers red like lotus petals—
raise this *añjali* to my head to seek your favor.

"O lady with beautiful hair, by my command, you ought to procreate sons endowed with excellent qualities through a brahmin of superior ascetic power. For your sake, O broad-hipped one, I shall attain the destination of those who possess sons."
"Therefore, O highly fortunate lady, do as you have said, for it is in accord with dharma.
Thus addressed, Kuntī, the woman of noble form who was devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, replied to Pāṇḍu, the conqueror of enemy cities.
O best of the Bharatas, this is a very great impropriety for women,
that a husband— who ought to be propitiated, O bull among Kṣatriyas— should instead have to be propitiated by them. Listen also, O mighty-armed one, to these words of mine which bring me joy.
While I was still a girl in my father’s house, appointed to the service of guests,
I attended upon a formidable brahmin of rigid vows there—
he whom they know as Durvāsas, whose resolve in dharma was hidden.
With all my efforts, I gratified him, whose soul was firmly disciplined. That blessed one granted me a boon involving the power of incantations;
he bestowed upon me a collection of mantras and spoke these words to me:
"Whichever deity you shall invoke with this mantra,
whether he be unwilling or willing, he will come under your control.
By his grace alone, O Queen, a son shall be born to you."
O Bhārata, having been addressed thus by that Brahmin in my father’s house, I said: "The time for his truthful words has now arrived;
permitted by you, O King, I shall summon the god."
"O royal seer, O Lord, by means of that mantra, may offspring be born to us both.
O Great King, that lore which the highly illustrious one gave to me—" Kuntī said:
[01,113.037d*1197=03] [01,113.037d*1197_01] "O Great King, that lore which the highly illustrious one gave to me..."
Summoned by her, the god will grant a son who is like unto a god;
O hero, he shall dispel the sorrow you feel on account of being childless. "May I have offspring"—such was the desire for progeny that arose within her.

Or [permit] a Brahmin endowed with virtues who delights in the welfare of all beings; may prosperity be yours, for the husband is indeed the deity of a woman. O knower of dharma, whatever god or Brahmin you shall name, [he it shall be].
"O hero, O mighty-armed one, I shall do exactly as you have instructed.
From a god, the fruit of a son is obtained immediately; from a brahmin, it occurs after some time.
Tell me, O best among those who know the truth, which god shall I invoke?"
"Know me to be standing ready for this task, awaiting your permission.
Pāṇḍu.
Vaiśampāyana.
I am blessed, I am favored; for you are indeed the sustainer of our lineage. Homage to that great seer by whom this boon was granted to you!
O knower of dharma, subjects cannot be protected through unrighteousness.
Therefore, O gentle lady, for the sake of obtaining a son and for my own lineage,
you must invoke Dharma, the most excellent of all the gods,
with the permission of the illustrious Pāṇḍu of the Bharata race.
At that time, O Great King, Pāṇḍu set his mind upon the invocation of Dharma.
Pāṇḍu said:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, strive this very day to perform the rites according to the prescribed rule."
"O auspicious lady, summon Dharma; for he is the one among the gods who possesses merit. Let us not be joined with unrighteousness by any means whatsoever.
Bhīṣma said:
Just as that punishment is constantly inflicted upon evildoers,
it is called *daṇḍanīti* (the science of government) here because of the administration of that punishment.
Then the Blessed Lord, the powerful wielder of the trident, meditated for a long time.
Mahādeva Maheśvara created all the scriptures,

as well as the means of valid knowledge in their entirety, for the purpose of applying the science of government (daṇḍanīti); these are the four foundational sciences, along with their various divisions and distinctions.
The auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya,
the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
It is certain that [the others] are Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda.
The science of polity (*arthaśāstra*) is the fourth; thus, there are indeed eighteen branches of knowledge. These eighteen are renowned as the compendia of Dharma.
Maheśvara has declared the detailed exposition (*vyāsa*) of these very sciences.
He stated that there are three hundred treatises (*śāstra*) and seventy tantras;
indeed, Vyāsa alone was proclaimed by Mahādeva as the knower of these sciences (*vidyā*).
Among them are the well-known *Pāśupata-tantra* and the *Pāñcarātra*.
The Yogaśāstra, Sāṃkhya, Tantra, and likewise Lokāyata;
the Tantra known as Brahmalulā, the science of logic for the denizens of heaven,
and that which is renowned as the cause for the inquiry into pleasure, pain, and objects.

Likewise, there are eight sciences of logic (*tarkavidyā*); the detailed [recension] consists of nine verses. It should be known that there are eighteen compendia of sacrifices belonging to the Purāṇas;
indeed, just as many compendia of the Purāṇa have been composed here.
The treatises on Dharma are his words; their purpose is one, and not otherwise.
The Purāṇas have a single purpose, and the Vedas are likewise compiled for a single purpose. Yet Śaṅkara [revealed] all those various scriptures with diverse purposes.
The Blessed Lord spoke those sciences of time,
the Ayurveda with its superior branches consisting of sixty-four measures, and the eternal science of government (Daṇḍanīti) with its eighteen divisions.

He has related the Gāndharva and the Itihāsa in their various extensive forms. Thus, these are the sciences proclaimed by Śaṅkara, consisting of words and meanings; furthermore, their expansion consists of thousands of divisions.

Together with the ṛṣis, gods, and gandharvas, it is constantly practiced in the world with its conceptual elaborations and in full detail; indeed, the Veda itself is practiced in every way. The four branches of knowledge are condensed therein, and they are remembered as the proclamations of the Veda.
He who has reached the further shore of these is said to have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Śakra, and Manu Svāyambhuva, the knower of the supreme dharma, are those who have reached the further shore of all that is to be known.
Brahmā is the supreme god, always honored by all the gods and asuras; Vyāsa, who has reached the further shore of the Vedas, is the bestower of grace upon all;
and I am Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, through the favor of Mādhava.
O best of the Kurus, by the grace of Śaṅkara and Brahmā,
Yājñavalkya was declared in every respect to have reached the further shore of the Vedas,
so he was called by the highly fortunate seers who perceive the truth in every aeon.
They are distinguished by the sons of the seers, by the hosts of seers, and even by those belonging to the hermitages;
they were fashioned by Śiva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu,
and in the first aeon, they were again divided by the virtuous ones.
Even now, this Sarasvatī is divided in many ways by learned men through their conceptual constructions, according to their previous births;
and this world, O lady of excellent hips, will consider it to be the Dharma.
He will undoubtedly be a righteous ruler of the Kurus;
even though he has been given [the kingdom] according to dharma, his mind shall not delight in unrighteousness.
For one who knows dharma, there is indeed dharma at the beginning, dharma at the end, and dharma in the middle.

Offspring is desired in the worlds, for it increases fame and renown. Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, placing dharma foremost and remaining self-controlled, you must indeed propitiate dharma through service and ritual practice.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed in this manner by her husband, that beautiful woman replied, "So be it," and having saluted him and received his permission, she circumambulated him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Janamejaya, when a year had passed since Gandhārī conceived,
Kuntī invoked the infallible Dharma for the sake of obtaining a child.
That goddess, acting with haste, offered the oblation to Dharma;
for she knew him to be the supreme Dharma and brought him under control through mantras. Summoned by Kuntī according to the ritual rules, he who is worshipped by all beings appeared.
The Blessed Lord Dharma appeared for the sake of procreation with the Pāṇḍava in that forest abounding in deer, on the supreme mountain Śataśṛṅga;
for the sake of Pāṇḍu, the highly fortunate Kuntī approached Dharma.
At the time of her season, having bathed pure, dressed in white garments, and being illustrious,
that woman of beautiful hips and firm vows took her place upon the bed with Dharma. She recited the prayers as prescribed, which had been given to her by Durvāsas in the past.

Then, by the power of the mantra, the god Dharma arrived from there in a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun, where Kuntī stood engaged in silent prayer. Smiling at her, he then said: "O Kuntī, what shall I give to you?"
Though she was smiling, she said this to him: "Give me a son.
Having united with him who had assumed a form through yoga by means of dharma, that woman of excellent hips obtained a son, the best among all living beings.
When the moon was in conjunction with the constellation Aindra, during the eighth *muhūrta* called Abhijit,
while the sun was at midday on an auspicious and honored lunar day,
Kuntī gave birth at the proper time to a son of abundant fame.
As soon as that son was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"He shall be the best among the upholders of dharma; of this there is no doubt. Valiant and truthful in speech, he shall become a king upon the earth."
The first-born son of Pāṇḍu shall be known as Yudhiṣṭhira;
he will become a celebrated king, renowned throughout the three worlds, endowed with fame, splendor, and virtuous conduct.
Having obtained that righteous son, Pāṇḍu spoke to her again:
"They say that the Kṣatriya is preeminent in strength; choose a son who is preeminent in strength.
Those learned in ritual action, O twice-born woman, have said that one should procreate many sons."
Then, O Bhārata, that exceedingly powerful god approached Kuntī and commanded her: "Invoke Vāyu!
The Aśvamedha is the best of sacrifices; the Sun is the best of luminaries."

"The Brāhmaṇa is the best among bipeds, and Māruta is the best among the gods. O woman of excellent complexion, by means of ritual observance, summon Māruta— the foremost of the Maruts, praised by all living beings— for the sake of a son."

"O lady of beautiful hips, whichever son he shall give us will be preeminent in strength among men, for rulers of the earth are foremost in power. Having been addressed thus by her husband, she then invoked Vāyu.
Then the mighty Wind-god, mounted upon a deer, arrived before her and said:
"O Kuntī, what shall I give you today? Tell me what dwells in your heart.
Smiling with bashfulness, she replied: "O best of gods, grant me a son."
Strong, with a massive body, and the shatterer of all pride—
he again recited the collection of mantras according to the previously stated procedure, while remaining established in those very same observances, accompanied by the second offering.
Then Vāyu arrived and said, "What shall I do?
Thereupon, Kuntī, filled with shame, desired a son of great strength;
saying "So be it," Vāyu touched her and departed for heaven.
From him was born the mighty-armed Bhīma, of terrible prowess. When that one of exceeding strength was born, an incorruptible voice spoke to him:
"O Bhārata, this one who has been born is the best among all the strong."
As soon as the prince was born, all the kings of the world discharged urine and fell into a state of distress;
their mounts collapsed, shedding drops of tears.
Just as a wind, when fully stirred up, is capable of shaking the earth,
so too Bhima, whose limbs were pervaded by wrath and who possessed fearsome prowess;
and this was a most wonderful thing that occurred the very moment Vṛkodara was born.
When he fell from his mother's lap, he crushed a stone with his limbs.
Janamejaya said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
How did that prince, whose body was as hard as a diamond, fall upon the mountain?
And how was the rock pulverized by his limbs as he fell? O Blessed One, best of the twice-born, I wish to hear this from you.
"O brahmin-sage, I have a great curiosity regarding this matter; it has been well-posed, O son of Pāṇḍu, and I shall tell you. Kuntī, having gone with her son to that most beautiful lake..."

O best of the Bharatas, on the tenth day, after bathing and taking her son with her, Pṛthā, the daughter of the Yadu clan, departed from the hermitage intending to worship the deities; as she was traveling along the side of the mountain, O best of the Bharatas.

A great tiger, desiring to kill, emerged from a mountain cave. As that leopard was rushing toward him, Pāṇḍu, whose prowess was equal to that of the gods, drew his excellent bow and pierced it with three arrows.
Seeing him filling the cave of the mountain with a great roar,
Kuntī then desired to climb the rock out of fear;
O bull of the Bharatas, out of that terror, her son fell from her lap.
Standing atop the mountain, the infant fell toward the ground below;
impelled by the wielder of the thunderbolt, he pulverized the rock like a thunderbolt itself.
Then, out of affection for his son, Pāṇḍu rushed to the slope of the mountain.
Agitated by the fear of tigers, Kuntī suddenly leapt up;
she did not realize that Vṛkodara was fast asleep in her own lap.
Then that prince, like a thunderbolt falling, crashed down upon the mountain.
As he fell, that rock was pulverized into a hundred pieces by his limbs;
seeing that rock crushed to dust, Pāṇḍu was filled with wonder.
He [had seen this] at the birth of Bhīma, when [the child] was crying out with a great roar.
Standing upon a mountain peak, he of tiger-like prowess beheld a tiger;
and for the sake of protecting his wife and protecting his son,
that joy of the Kurus always kept his bow and arrow in hand.
When the moon was in conjunction with the constellation Maghā, when Jupiter had risen in Leo,
when the sun was at midday during the day, on the auspicious thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī),
and during the Maitra muhūrta, Kuntī gave birth to the steadfast Bhīma.
O best of the Bharatas, on the very day that Bhīma was born,
Duryodhana also was born there, O lord of the earth. When Vṛkodara had been born, Pāṇḍu reflected further upon this.
"How might I have an excellent son, the best in the world?"—
for this world is established upon both destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*). Among these, destiny is obtained through the performance of rites at the proper time.
"For we have heard that Indra is indeed the king of the gods,
possessing immeasurable strength and energy, heroic, and of infinite splendor. By gratifying him through ascetic penance, I shall obtain a son of great power."
"He who gives me a son shall be most excellent;
he will slay both non-humans and humans in battle.
Therefore, through deed, mind, and speech, I shall perform great asceticism."
Then the immensely radiant Pāṇḍu, the descendant of Kuru, having consulted with the great seers,
prescribed an auspicious one-year vow for Kuntī;
and the mighty-armed king himself remained standing on one foot.
O Bhārata, that righteous-souled one undertook fierce asceticism with supreme concentration,
desiring to propitiate the Lord of the thirty gods;
he performed his circumambulations together with the sun.
After a long time, Vāsava replied to him:
"I shall grant you a son who will be renowned throughout the three worlds,
one who accomplishes the purposes of the gods, the brahmins, and his friends."
"I shall grant you an eldest son who will produce grief in the hearts of the wicked, bring joy to all his kinsmen, and destroy all enemies. Thus was the Kuru king addressed by the high-souled Vāsava.

O Bhārata, having determined that Dharma and Power were his strength, Pāṇḍu urged Kuntī, the princess, for the sake of offspring, saying, "So that it may come to pass. Then the righteous-souled one spoke to Kuntī, recollecting the words of the King of the Gods.
"O auspicious lady, the Lord of the hosts of gods is pleased with you;
he desires to grant you a son exactly as conceived in your heart— one of superhuman deeds, illustrious, and a subduer of enemies."

O lady of beautiful hips, give birth to a son who is possessed of statesmanship, high-souled, with splendor equal to the sun, invincible, devoted to action, and of most wonderful appearance— the very abode of the majesty of the kṣatriyas.
"Grace has been obtained from the Lord of the Gods; summon him, O lady of pure smiles.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"When the high-souled princes had been born to Dhṛtarāṣṭra..."
Having been addressed thus, the illustrious lady then summoned Śakra.
Thereupon, the Blessed One also served with that powerful one;
then the Lord of the Gods arrived and begot Arjuna.
Because he was born during the day under the two *pūrvaphalgunī* constellations, which precede the two *uttaraphalgunī* constellations,
he is therefore remembered as Phalguna, born in the month of Phālguna.
As soon as the prince was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
Causing all beings to rejoice,
she who was then in the state of childbirth made the sky resound with a great and profound roar.
While all beings and those dwelling in the hermitage were listening,
he addressed Kuntī of the radiant smile and spoke these words clearly:
"O Kuntī, [your son] shall be equal to Kārtavīrya and possess prowess like that of Śibi."
He shall be the foremost among the vigorous and remain unconquered;
likewise, he will acquire all the divine weapons in their entirety.
Invincible like Śakra, he will spread your fame far and wide.
Just as the affection between Aditi and Viṣṇu was increased and flourished,
so shall Arjuna, who is equal to Viṣṇu, increase your joy. Having brought the Madras under his control, along with the Kurus and the Kekayas, he will do so.
He will bestow the kingdoms of Cedi, Kāśi, Karūṣa, and Kuru upon him who bears the auspicious marks;
by the prowess of his arms, all enemies shall be terrified,
and all the Nivātakavacas shall lose their lives.
Having destroyed Hiraṇyapura in battle,
he will slay all the sons of Pulomā and the Kālakeyas;
and having gone to the northern quarter, the hero will conquer the kings in war.
The son of Pāṇḍu will bring back an immeasurable flood of wealth and jewels;
by the power of his arms, the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) shall indeed attain supreme satisfaction with the fat of all creatures at Khāṇḍava.
Having conquered the village chiefs and the protectors of the earth, this mighty hero,
together with his brothers, will perform three sacrifices,
O Kuntī; he is equal to Jamadagnya and possesses prowess like that of Viṣṇu.
He shall be the foremost among the heroic and remain unconquered.
In battle, he will propitiate Mahādeva Śaṅkara,
and from that gratified deity, he will obtain the weapon named Pāśupata.
There are Daityas named Nivātakavacas, enemies of the gods;
by the command of Śakra, your mighty-armed son shall slay them,
and he shall likewise acquire all the divine weapons in their entirety.
"This bull among men shall recover the lost royal fortune. Kuntī heard those most wonderful words spoken by Vāyu in the sky during the birth ceremony of her son.
Having heard that speech uttered so loudly by the ascetics,
there arose supreme joy among the inhabitants of Śataśṛṅga,
as well as among the celestial ṛṣis and the gods, including Indra.
In the sky, there arose a tumultuous sound of kettledrums;
a great roar rose up, enveloped by showers of flowers.
And the hosts of gods, having gathered together, paid homage to the son of Pṛthā.
The sons of Kadrū, the sons of Vinatā, the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), and the seven great Ṛṣis—
Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, and Gautama;
Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha,
as well as that venerable Atri who appeared when the sun had vanished—
he too arrived here.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Dakṣa Prajāpati, as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
wearing divine garlands and garments and adorned with every ornament.
And those luminous beings among mortals, provided with every necessity,
sang to Bībhatsu and danced before him;
likewise, the great ṛṣis also chanted there on all sides.
Then, while the musical instruments of the Gandharvas resounded in the sky,
the illustrious Tumburu, accompanied by the Gandharvas, began to sing;
as did Bhīmasena, Ugrasena, Ūrṇāyu, and Anagha.
Gopati, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Sūryavarcas as the seventh;
Yugapa, Tṛṇapa, Kārṣṇi, Nandi, and Citraratha; Śāliśiras as the thirteenth, and Parjanya as the fourteenth.
Kali was the fifteenth among them, and Nārada was the sixteenth;
then there were Sad, Bṛhad, Bṛhaka, and the highly illustrious Karāla;
and the one renowned as Brahmacārī, Bahuguṇa, and Suparṇa.
Viśvāvasu, Bhumanyu, and Sucandra as the tenth,
as well as the famous Hāhā and Hūhū, who were endowed with sweetness of song—
these divine gandharvas sang there for that bull among men.
In the same way, the highly fortunate apsarases, adorned with every ornament,
danced and sang, those large-eyed ones who were flawless,
irreproachable, beloved, foremost, and excellent in their qualities.
Adrikā, Sācī, Miśrakeśī, Alambuṣā,
Marīci, Śikhaṇḍinī, Vidyutparṇā, Tilottamā,
Agnikā, Lakṣaṇā, Kṣemā, and the goddess Rambhā, who is so enchanting.
And Urvaśī herself, O king of kings, danced to the sound of singing;
likewise Asitā, Subāhu, Supriyā, Suvapuḥ,
Puṇḍarīkā, Sugandhā, Surathā, and Pramāthinī.
Kāmyā and Śāradvatī danced there in groups; so too did Menakā, Sahajanyā, Parṇikā, Puñjikasthalā,
Kratusthalā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, and Pūrvacitti.
"Umloca is well-known, and Pramloca— these ten,
with Urvaśī as the eleventh," so sang those large-eyed women.
"Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga likewise..."
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ,
Parjanya, and Viṣṇu—
these are the twelve Ādityas, blazing with the splendor of the sun and possessing the radiance of fire.
Standing in the sky, they increased the glory of the Pāṇḍava: Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, the highly illustrious Nirṛti,
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Pinākin, the scorcher of foes.
O lord of the people, Dahana, Īśvara, Kapālī,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhava— the Rudras— stood there;
as did the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the mighty Maruts.
Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins; those two Aśvins, as well as the Sādhyas, were present at his birth,
along with Kratu, Dakṣa, Tapas, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, and Dhuri.
Kurumān, Madhumat, and Rocamāna by his splendor were there,
as were the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas, all stationed around him.
Then Karkoṭaka, Śeṣa, and the serpent Vāsuki were also present.
Kacchapa, Cāpakuṇḍa, Takṣaka, and the great serpent Mahoraga arrived, endowed with splendor, possessed of great wrath and great strength;
these and many other nāgas were stationed there.
Then the great grandfather, surrounded by royal sages such as Sagara, Ambarīṣa, Nahuṣa, and Yayāti, received his grandson with a stainless garment.
By the wise King Dhundhumāra Uparicara,
by Mucukunda, by Māndhātṛ, by Śibi, by Ariṣṭanemi, by Bharata, by Dilīpa, and by all others, O Janamejaya.
Pūru, together with the kings, received the bull among the Kurus;
and many other excellent monarchs were present there,
as well as these and many other lords of the world of men.
Having come here from the world of the gods, they gazed upon that bull among the Bharatas,
who was radiant with his physical form and illuminating the ten directions,
endowed with all the manifest marks indicative of his greatness.
