And those great seers perfected in asceticism beheld all those hosts of gods situated upon the mountain peaks and in their celestial chariots, but other people did not see them. Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, Garuḍa, and Asitadhvaja—
Aruṇa and Aruṇi, as well as the sons of Vinatā, took their positions there.
Seeing that great marvel, the best of sages were struck with wonder;
from then on, they maintained an even greater devotion toward the Pāṇḍavas.
With a joyful mind, Pāṇḍu worshipped the deities and others. The gods, honored by Pāṇḍu, replied to that best of kings:
"Indeed, this Dharma has appeared, born from the grace of the deities."
For this Mātariśvan is indeed formidable, powerful, and a crusher of enemies;
he was born directly as Indra himself through the grace of Śatakratu. Indeed, because of his status as the father of the gods, there is no one more meritorious than you.
"You are now freed from your debt to the ancestors; as a partaker of merit, you shall attain heaven.
Having spoken thus, all the deities departed as they had come.
But the highly illustrious Pāṇḍu, out of a longing for sons, once again [addressed her].
Then Kuntī, whose limbs were beautiful to behold, sent him forth and said to him:
"They say that even in times of distress, one should not have a fourth birth;
beyond this, a woman becomes unchaste, and in the fifth [birth], she becomes an adulteress."
O wise Pāṇḍu, how is it that you, understanding this dharma accessible to the intellect, speak to me as if out of negligence, transgressing it for the sake of offspring?
"01.114.066d *1232_01 It is exactly so; this treatise on dharma is just as you say.
01.115.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
"01.115.001a After the sons of Kuntī and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had been born,"
The daughter of the King of Madra spoke these words to Pāṇḍu in private:

"O scorcher of foes, I feel no resentment toward you, even though you are devoid of virtue. Nor do I feel any heat of anger toward one who has passed his youth; how then could there be defeat for us?"
O sinless one, although you have always remained unworthy of such honor while she deserved it,
O King, even upon hearing that a hundred sons had been born to Gāndhārī, my grief was not so great, O joy of the Kurus.
"But this is my great sorrow: that while we are equals, I am childless. By good fortune, however, my husband now has offspring through Kuntī.
If only the daughter of King Kunti would bestow the continuity of progeny upon me..."
"If you do this, it would be a favor to me and would also be for your own benefit.
For because I am her co-wife, I feel a sense of pride that prevents me from speaking to the daughter of Kunti;
therefore, if you are well-disposed toward me, please urge her yourself."
Pāṇḍu said:
"O Mādrī, this very same purpose has always revolved in my heart as well;
however, I did not venture to speak to you out of a desire to say what was pleasing or displeasing."
"But having understood this intention of yours, I shall strive from now on.
I believe that if she is addressed by me, she will certainly accept my words.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, in private, Pāṇḍu spoke again to Kuntī:
"O blessed lady, show favor also to the daughter of the King of Madra;
for the sake of my lineage and the world, do what is pleasing."
O auspicious lady, for the sake of the funeral offerings for myself, my ancestors, and yourself, and for the sake of my pleasure, perform this most excellent act of merit;
for it ensures the increase of the family's funeral offerings and the continuity of the lineage.
The attainment of my desired goal and your own supreme fame depend upon this;
for the sake of fame, you must perform this most difficult task,
just as Indra, desiring fame, performed sacrifices after attaining sovereignty.

Likewise, O beautiful lady, Brahmins learned in the mantras, having performed extremely difficult austerities, approach their gurus for the sake of glory; so too do all the royal sages and the Brahmins whose wealth is their asceticism.
For the sake of fame, they performed various difficult deeds;
likewise, O beautiful one, the wise royal sages such as Manu, Vainya, and others, individually performed deeds endowed with dharma for the sake of glory.
Therefore, O blameless one, ferry this Mādrī across as if by a boat;
by sharing the offspring with her, may you attain supreme fame.
Indeed, the dharma spoken of in the treatises on dharma is exactly as you say it is.
"Therefore, O lady of excellent complexion, show favor to Mādrī.
Thus addressed, she said to Mādrī: "Meditate upon a deity once;
from that, offspring worthy of you shall undoubtedly arise."
When that mantra had been uttered by Kuntī according to the ritual prescribed by rule,
the princess, having bathed, then lay down upon her bed.
Thereupon Mādrī, after reflecting, went mentally to the Aśvins.
Having arrived, those two begot twin sons upon her:
Nakula and Sahadeva, who were peerless on earth in beauty. And likewise, an incorporeal voice spoke to those twins as well.
In terms of their actions, their devotion, their strength, and likewise their conduct,
these two— endowed with beauty, noble character, and virtue— outshine all other people, shining exceedingly with splendor through the perfection of their form and wealth.
O lord of the people, the inhabitants of Śataśṛṅga bestowed names upon them through devotion, ritual action, and benedictions:
they called the eldest Yudhiṣṭhira and the middle one Bhīmasena.
And with "Arjuna," they designated the third son of Kuntī; then, with "Nakula" for the eldest and "Sahadeva" for the other, those brāhmaṇas, their minds filled with joy, named the two sons of Mādrī.
Although they were born year after year, those best of the Kurus,
the sons of Pāṇḍu, shone like the five years [of the cycle];
and the sons of Pṛthā, as well as the two sons of Mādrī, followed along with them.
Seeing those sons of his— great beings of great heroism, possessing great strength and prowess, white-complexioned, godlike in form, and endowed with great majesty—
the lord of men attained supreme joy and rejoiced.
They became dear to all the sages dwelling on Mount Śataśṛṅga, and likewise to the wives of those munis. Then Pāṇḍu urged Kuntī once again for the sake of Mādrī.
O King, Pṛthā, who had always been addressed in secret, said to him:
"She was told only once that she would obtain a pair [of children], and by that I was deceived.
I fear her contempt; such is the nature of women."
"O fool, I did not realize that there were two fruits at the invocation of the *dvandva* [sacrifice];
therefore, I should not be commanded by you—let this be my boon.
Thus were the five sons of Pāṇḍu born, granted by the gods and possessed of great strength.
They were born illustrious, increasing the Kuru lineage;
endowed with divine vigor and great strength, they were experts in all the scriptures.
All possessed celestial frames, and all were of radiant form.
Endowed with auspicious marks, as pleasing to behold as the moon,
possessing the pride of lions, they were great archers who moved with the stride of lions;
they had lion-like chests, the courage of lions, the eyes of lions, and the prowess of lions.
Those lords of men, with necks like lions and godlike prowess, grew up there on the holy Himalayan mountain; as they increased in stature,
they inspired wonder in the great seers who had assembled there.
Those five hundred and one [sons], who increased the Kuru lineage,
all grew up in a short time like lotuses in the water.
Vaiśampāyana said:
From the moment they were born, the ascetics dwelling on Mount Śataśṛṅga regarded the sons of Pāṇḍu as their own children.
Then all the Vṛṣṇis, led by Vasudeva, [acted likewise].
Fearing the dread of a curse, Pāṇḍu went to Mount Śataśṛṅga;
there, together with the sages, he became an ascetic practicing austerities,
subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, a practitioner of penance with his senses restrained.
"Many bards, emaciated by grief upon hearing that the king had become devoted to yoga and meditation,
spoke with hearts filled with affection for Pāṇḍu: 'When shall we hear his excellent stories?'"
Speaking thus with their kinsmen, all those Vṛṣṇis,
having heard of the arrival of Pāṇḍu’s sons, were filled with joy;
honoring one another, they spoke these words to Vasudeva.
"The sons of Pāṇḍu, possessed of great strength, would not remain devoid of ritual action;
therefore, seeking what is dear and beneficial to Pāṇḍu, do you dispatch the family priest. Having said, "So be it," Vasudeva dismissed the priest.
O Bhārata, he sent numerous gifts suitable for the princes, and having instructed Kuntī and Mādrī, he dispatched male and female servants, as well as household goods, cattle, gold, and silver.
Having gathered all those items, the family priest set forth.
Upon the arrival of that best of the twice-born, Kāśyapa, the family priest,
Pāṇḍu, the conqueror of enemy cities, honored him according to the prescribed rites.
Pṛthā and Mādrī, filled with joy, praised Vasudeva;
thereafter, Pāṇḍu caused all the rites for the Pāṇḍavas to be performed—
the ceremonies beginning with the impregnation, as well as the tonsure and the initiation.
O Bhārata, Kāśyapa performed all the preparatory rites (*upākarma*); thereafter, those illustrious ones with bull-like eyes became masters of the study of the Vedas.
The son of Śaryāti and Pṛṣata was Śuka by name, a scorcher of his enemies,
by whom the earth as far as the ocean was conquered with his bow;
that great-souled one performed hundreds of horse sacrifices and other grand rituals.
Having propitiated all the deities and the ancestors as well, the high-minded one performed austerities on Mount Śataśṛṅga, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits. By him,
[the disciples] were strengthened through excellent implements and instruction.
Through his grace, they attained mastery in the science of archery; Bhīma became a master of the mace, Yudhiṣṭhira of the javelin,
and the twins, the best among the courageous, were proficient in sword and shield.

Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, has reached the further shore of the science of archery (Dhanurveda). O Lord, having been authorized by Śuka with the words, "This one is equal to me," the king then gave his permission for [the receipt of] the spear, the sword, and likewise the arrows.

And the best of givers, being greatly delighted, gave to Pārtha a bow of great luster measuring a palm-tree in length, along with decorated arrows— Vipāṭhas, Kṣurans, and Nārācas— with feathers like vultures' wings, possessing the splendor of great serpents.
Having obtained all the weapons, the son of Vāsava was delighted;
he considered all the rulers of the earth to be insufficient in their own splendor.
Yet those subduers of enemies were separated from one another by only a single year’s interval.
The sons of Pṛthā and the two sons of Mādrī likewise grew up.
O joy of the Kurus, hear now the lifespan of the Pāṇḍavas:
Yudhiṣṭhira went to Hastināpura at the age of sixteen.
Bhīmasena [lived there] for fifteen years, Bībhatsu for fourteen,
and the twins for thirteen;
during those thirteen years, they dwelt together with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
For six months he was freed from the house of lac, and Ghaṭotkaca was born;
for six months he stayed at Ekacakrā, and for one year in the house of the Pāñcāla king;
and, O Bhārata, he lived with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for five years.
They dwelt there in Indraprastha for twenty-three years;
then, having been defeated at the deceptive game of dice, they lived for another twelve years and one year [in exile].
Having enjoyed sovereignty over the earth bounded by the oceans for thirty-six years, they [departed].
After six months, all those great-souled ones, devoted to Kṛṣṇa,
having installed Parīkṣit upon the throne, attained their desired goal.
Thus, the lifespan of Yudhiṣṭhira was also one hundred and eight years.
The mighty-armed Keśava was three months older than Arjuna;
the exceedingly powerful Saṃkarṣaṇa was three months older than Kṛṣṇa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, in that great forest, Pāṇḍu beheld his five handsome sons;
seeing them protected by the strength of his own arms, he took delight upon the mountain.
Once, during the time of the months of Madhu and Mādhava, when the forests were in full bloom, he rejoiced there.
When the fourteenth year had been completed, during the month of Phalguna,
under the asterism of Uttaraphalguni, while the recitation of auspicious benedictions was underway,
Kunti, preoccupied with feeding the Brahmins, forgot about the protection [of the child].
Together with the family priest, she served the brahmins. At that time, having summoned Mādrī, the king, deluded by passion,
wandered through the forest with his wife in order to bewilder all living beings.
With *palāśa*, *tilaka*, mango, *campaka*, and *pāribhadraka* trees,
and with many other trees abounding in fruits and flowers—
*karṇikāra*, *aśoka*, *kesara*, and *atimuktaka*.

Then, with *kurabaka* trees resounding with the humming of intoxicated bees, with mango trees in full bloom, and even with groves of *pārijāta* trees, there was the music of the *parapuṣṭa* birds and the humming of six-legged bees.
With *jambu*, *udumbara*, *saihuṇḍa*, *vaṭa*, *āmrātaka*, and *dhava* trees;
with *nīpa*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *badara*, and *nāgakesara*; and with *tamāla*, *bilvaka*, *tāla*, *panasa*, and wild *kiṃśuka* trees.
It was blended with the songs of intoxicated bees and the warbling of cuckoos; it was filled with *hintāla*, *kadalī*, and *śāla* trees, with *panasa*, wild *kiṃśuka*,
*bakula*, *tilaka*, *tāla*, and forest *kiṃśuka* trees.
Adorned with various water-bodies and lotus ponds,
resounding with the cries of diverse flocks of birds and the songs of cuckoos,
he then beheld there the delightful, blossoming trees.
Beholding the forest of Pāṇḍu, love was born in his heart— a place filled with the songs of intoxicated bees mingled with the warbling of cuckoos,
just as it had been in the city of the Nāgas when Gandharvas were singing in former times.
While he was dwelling there with a joyful mind like an immortal,
Mādrī alone followed him, wearing a beautiful garment. But he, gazing at her— young in years and clad in thin clothing— [was filled with desire].
His desire flared up like a fire rising in a thicket;
seeing that lotus-eyed woman, who was his own equal, in private, the king,
overcome by the power of passion, was unable to restrain that desire.

Then, in the eighteenth year, during her season, Pāṇḍu, his mind overcome by passion, summoned the illustrious Mādrī who was adorned with ornaments. Thereupon, the king forcibly seized her as she stood alone in private.
Though he was being restrained by the queen as she struggled with all her might,
his soul was so overwhelmed by passion that he did not perceive that curse as he approached Mādrī for sexual union as if by force.

Falling under the sway of the god of love, the Kaurava, casting aside the fear born of the curse, went by force toward his beloved even at the cost of his life. The intellect of that lustful man was directly deluded by Time itself.
Having utterly overwhelmed the collection of his senses, Pāṇḍu— whose mind was utterly lost—
united with that wife of his, O joy of the Kurus,
and that most righteous-souled man was joined with the law of time (death).
In an instant, the king indeed reached the capital city of Yama.
Then Mādrī, embracing the lifeless king,
let out a cry born of grief again and again, most excessively.
Hearing that piteous sound which had suddenly arisen,
Kuntī, along with her sons, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
then went together to the place where the king was situated in such a state.
Then, O King, the distressed Mādrī spoke these words to Kuntī:
"Come here alone; let the children remain right here.
Having heard her words, she kept the children there.
Crying out, "I am slain!", she suddenly approached.
Seeing both Pāṇḍu and Mādrī lying upon the surface of the earth,
Kuntī, her limbs overwhelmed by grief, lamented in great distress.
"Though this hero, ever self-possessed, was constantly protected by me,
how is it that you have transgressed the curse, knowing well the power of the forest-dwellers?
O Mādrī, surely this lord of men ought to have been protected by you!"
O Mādrī, how did you entice the lord of men in that desolate place,
having seen him in the lonely forest when he was impelled by destiny?
Without considering that curse, great joy arose within him.
How is it that, though constantly distressed, he experienced such joy upon finding you in solitude and reflecting upon that very curse?
"O Bāhlīkī, you are blessed; indeed, you are more fortunate than I, since you have beheld the face of the king when he was filled with joy. Mādrī said:
Though I repeatedly tried to dissuade him while he was being enticed,
my own self was not restrained by him as he sought to fulfill his destiny—
so Vaiśampāyana said.
01,116.022d Vaiśampāyana;
01,116.022d Vaiśampāyana.
Having heard those words of hers, Kuntī, inflamed by the fire of grief,
suddenly fell to the ground like a tree whose roots have been severed;
though she lay fallen on the earth motionless, she did not stir from her state of unconsciousness.
At that moment,
having raised up Kuntī— who was dressed in spotless garments, adorned with ornaments, and lying upon a beautiful bed— Mādrī’s consciousness was overcome by delusion.
Saying "Come, come," he revealed the Kuru prince to Kuntī.
Kuntī fell at his feet, and rising again, she beheld the lord of the earth,
whose limbs were smeared with red sandalwood paste and who was clad in garments of great silver.
Embracing him as he seemed to speak words with his smiling face,
she then lamented, her senses overwhelmed by delusion;
and Mādrī also, having embraced the king, lamented.
Approaching the pale king as he lay there in that manner, all the ṛṣis together with the cāraṇas gathered and, out of grief, shed tears for him—
as if for the sun that has set, or for the ocean that has run dry.
Seeing Pāṇḍu, that tiger among men, the great seers grieved;
the seers and the Pāṇḍavas became equal in their sorrow.
Consoled by the brahmins, those two blameless women lamented.

"Alas, O King! Abandoning us both, where are you going to the abode of the thirty gods? Alas, O King! How is it that you have met with death after uniting with Mādrī, O King, due to the total exhaustion of my own ill fortune?"
"O Lord of the People, why have you departed, leaving behind Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and both the twins— your beloved sons?
Surely the thirty gods, the Tridaśas, rejoice at you, O Bhārata!"
"O King, since you have performed such fierce asceticism in the assembly of Brahmins,
you shall go together with us two to the auspicious heaven—
the destination attained through the deeds of the Ajamīḍhas and the descendants of Ajamīḍha."
"O best of the Kurus, when you arrived at the forest, did you not indeed promise us, 'I shall go together with both of you'?
O lord of the people, you shall go only in the company of us two."
"O King, please forgive us for a moment; we shall ascend your funeral pyre.
Having lamented thus most bitterly, they both fell senseless upon the ground, like two female deer in the forest pierced and slain by hunters.
All the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira and masters of the Vedas,
also arrived at their father’s side; losing consciousness, they fell to the ground,
and embracing the feet of Pāṇḍu, the Pāṇḍavas began to lament.
"Alas, we are ruined, O father! Alas, we have become protectorless!
Deprived of you, O one of great wisdom, how shall we children survive? We are the sons of the Lord of the World, yet we have no protector."
In an instant, O Great King— oh, how wondrous is the variety of the world!
There are no princes more unfortunate than we, O Bhārata,
due to your destruction and likewise the collapse of the kingdom, O Indra among kings.
"O King, it is through our ignorance regarding our kinsmen that we have fallen into this calamity.
What shall we do? Be gracious to us; tell us what must be done. Having abandoned both kingdom and enjoyments, [we have come] to the dweller on Śataśṛṅga."
"O Indra among kings, through your great asceticism we have been rescued by you;
having abandoned pride and gone to the forest,
you yourself have provided for our sustenance by gathering wild vegetables, roots, and fruits for our food."

O King, descendant of Bharata, that time has now arrived for which fathers desire sons of great soul— those who seek the fruit of the three aims of life. You ought not to depart, O Bhārata, without having first enjoyed that fruit.
Having spoken thus to his father, Bhīma also lamented:
"The Bhārata lineage, which had perished, was raised up once more by Pāṇḍu;
yet now that he has gone to the forest of asceticism, the kingdom along with the entire realm has been lost."
"The Kṣatriya order has been rescued once again by the high-souled sons of Pāṇḍu.
Having heard this, O Kaurava, you ought to depart with joy. Having spoken thus to his father, Dhanañjaya lamented.
O bull of the Bharatas, having performed austerities difficult to accumulate and having obtained this boat,
you have not attained even a fraction of the great fruit of obtaining a son through service and other virtues, such as the sovereignty that your father enjoyed in former times.
Having spoken thus, the twins also lamented, being deeply distressed.
Kuntī said:
"I am the eldest lawful wife; the foremost fruit of dharma belongs to me."
"O Mādrī, do not turn me back from these events that must inevitably come to pass.
I shall seek out my husband here, who has fallen under the power of death. Rise up, leave him, and protect these children."

Having obtained sons and attained her true self, she requested the status of being the wife of a hero; then the daughter of the King of Madra spoke these words to Kuntī: Vaiśampāyana said: "Having obtained sons and attained her true self, she requested the status of being the wife of a hero; then the daughter of the King of Madra spoke these words to Kuntī."
Mādrī said:
"I myself shall follow my husband, who did not flee;
for I am not yet satiated with desires, so let my elder sister grant me permission."
"Having approached me, this best of the Bharatas has been exhausted by his desire.
How might I cut away that desire of his so that he may go to the abode of Yama? For my sake, that king, the most excellent of royal seers, has departed to heaven."
Such wisdom as that is no longer mine, nor are my kinsmen such as they once were;
deprived of my husband, I have no desire to sustain my life.
Therefore, I shall follow him as he departs for the abode of Vaivasvata.

Nor shall I, O noble lady, conduct myself toward your sons without distinction; for were I to do so, sin would touch me. You, however, must always be equal toward my two sons and your own sons at all times.
Therefore, O Kuntī, you must treat my two sons as you would your own children;
for this king, desiring me, has fallen under the power of death,
and I shall follow my husband as he departs for the abode of Yama.

"This body of mine must be burned along with the king's body, well-concealed; O noble lady, do this which is pleasing to me. And you must be vigilant regarding the children and remain devoted to my welfare."
"I see nothing else that remains to be instructed.
Having heard these words of hers, Kuntī, inflamed by the fire of grief,
suddenly fell to the ground like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Motionless, she fell upon the ground and did not stir from her fainting;
at that moment, he lay upon a beautiful bed, having performed his ablutions, clothed in fine garments, adorned with ornaments, and pale.
Having raised Kuntī up, Mādrī, whose consciousness was overcome by delusion, said: "Come, come, Kuntī! Do not weep; I shall show you my own marvel.
Then Kuntī, having fallen at his feet, rose again toward the lord of the earth.
His limbs were smeared with red sandalwood paste and he was clothed in garments of great gold;
Vaiśampāyana said:
Kuntī—
Mādrī;
Vaiśampāyana said:
The sages, having consoled those Pāṇḍavas of true prowess, [spoke].
Having comforted Kuntī and Mādrī, the ascetics said:
"O fortunate ladies, you must not die under any circumstances while your sons are still children.
We shall also lead the Pāṇḍavas, those scorchers of foes, to the kingdom of the Kurus."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is full of greed for wealth that is contrary to dharma;
he might at some time fail to behave toward the Pāṇḍavas according to what is right.
Moreover, the Vṛṣṇis are the protectors of Kuntī, as is Kuntibhoja.
And for Mādrī, O best of the strong, her brother Śalya—a great chariot-warrior—will surely die together with his wife; there is no doubt that this will bear fruit.
Furthermore, the foremost of the twice-born say that this is a difficult task for the two of you.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman, established in celibacy and exhausted by restraints and observances— pure deeds of mind, speech, and body—
while constantly thinking of her husband, that auspicious woman shall cross over [the world] together with her husband.
The husband shall be delivered, as shall the self and the sons; therefore,
we know that this life of yours is indeed auspicious,
in accordance with the command of Pāṇḍu and likewise that of the assembly of Brahmins.
The command has been placed upon my head, and I shall carry it out exactly as such;
for whatever the Blessed Ones have said, I consider that to be most excellent—
for my husband, for my sons, and for myself, without a doubt.

Kuntī is capable of providing for the welfare and security of her sons; indeed, even Arundhatī would not be her equal in intelligence. Furthermore, the Vṛṣṇis and Kuntibhoja are the protectors of Kuntī.
"I am not as capable as you are in supporting sons. Therefore, I shall follow my husband; may the eldest queen, who is satisfied with that world of her husband, grant me her permission."

"I shall serve the feet of that wise one who knows the Dharma, who is grateful, and who is true to his promise; may the noble lady grant her permission. Having spoken thus, O Great King, the beautiful daughter of the King of Madra—
Mādrī, having bowed her head in salutation, gave the twins to Kuntī;
she then paid homage to the great seers, embraced the Pāṇḍavas,
and repeatedly smelled the heads of the sons of Pṛthā as well as her own two sons.
Taking Yudhiṣṭhira by the hand, Mādrī spoke these words:
"I am Kuntī, your nurse; your father is dead.
Yudhiṣṭhira is always the eldest of the four according to dharma."
Those who are devoted to serving elders and others, and who are dedicated to truth and righteousness—
such as these do not perish, nor do they suffer defeat.
Therefore, all of you should indeed practice the conduct toward gurus without laziness.
Having bowed down again and again to the sages and to Pṛthā, Mādrī, distressed by exhaustion, then replied to Pṛthā:
"O Vārṣṇeyī, you are blessed; there is no woman equal to you."
O Kuntī, you shall behold the vigor, splendor, discipline, and majesty of these five illustrious sons of yours, possessed of immeasurable power,
in the presence of the sages, for which reason these words were uttered by me.

"Since I desire to see heaven, this [journey] of mine shall not be in vain. Noble lady, you are to be saluted and honored by me in every way; O Goddess, you are the eldest and most excellent, adorned with your own auspicious virtues."
O delight of the Yādavas, I wish to be permitted by you so that,
for your sake, I may attain dharma, heaven, and fame; therefore,
ordain this for me here and do not hesitate.
With a voice choked with tears, the illustrious Kuntī said:
"O auspicious one, you have been granted permission; may you be reunited with your husband in the third heaven, O large-eyed and radiant lady, this very day."
"Reunited in the heavenly world, may you rejoice for eternal years.
Then the family priest, having bathed and being an expert in the rites for the deceased,
[prepared] fragments of gold, clarified butter, sesame seeds, curds, and rice.
Having brought water-jars and axes together with ascetics,
and having fetched the fire for the horse-sacrifice from all sides according to the prescribed rule,
Kāśyapa performed the funeral rites for the deceased Pāṇḍu.
Following the ritual prescribed by the family priest, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu,
cremated Pāṇḍu with that fire after having performed the funeral rites. Then, weeping and tormented by grief, the Pāṇḍava fell to the ground.
Having bid farewell to the sages, his sons, Pṛthā, and the princes,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having spoken thus to that bull among men who stood upon the funeral pyre, the lawful wife [addressed him]."
The illustrious daughter of the King of Madra quickly ascended after him;
and the sinless one, clothed in new garments and accompanied by his brothers, offered water libations there, abiding by the counsel of his family priest.
The ascetics dwelling on Mount Śataśṛṅga,

together with the *cāraṇa* seers, performed the funeral rites for that Arhat according to the prescribed rules; the ascetics likewise caused their own sons to perform the ritual acts according to the ordinance.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having performed the final purificatory bath for Pāṇḍu, those great seers, who were like gods,
then gathered together and, being ascetics, held a consultation.
Having abandoned both his kingdom and his realm, that great-souled one of mighty asceticism went to this place to perform penance, seeking refuge among the ascetics;
and he [left behind] his wives and sons here with you as soon as they were born.

"Having entrusted the deposit to the king, Pāṇḍu has departed from here to heaven. Taking these sons, the body, and the wife of that great-souled one, let us go to our own kingdom; for this is the duty remembered by us."
"Therefore, examine what ought to be done," said Śuka, the knower of dharma, the supremely auspicious one, as he addressed them with his voice. Then,
having consulted one another, those who delight in the welfare of all beings—
Placing righteousness foremost, they formed this excellent resolution:
"Let us take Kuntī along with her sons from here to Kurukṣetra, and then, honoring the sons of Pāṇḍu, let us lead them to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura)."
Those of noble mind set their hearts on going,
indeed to give the Pāṇḍavas to Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
at that very moment, they all departed, taking them with them.
Taking Pāṇḍu’s wives, his sons, and even his body, all those ascetics set out from Śataśṛṅga, the best of mountains. She,
who had previously been happy and was ever devoted to her sons, [was now led away].
Having set out upon that long journey, she perceived it as short;
in no long time, she reached Kurujāṅgala,
and the illustrious lady arrived at the gate of the city of Vardhamāna.
The ascetics said to the gatekeeper, "Announce us to the king. Having gone there, they were announced in the assembly hall in a mere moment;
at that time, the arrival of thousands of *cāraṇas* and sages was reported.

Upon hearing this in Nāgapura, amazement arose among the people. When the sun had risen for a mere moment, all the city-dwellers, placing dharma foremost, went out with their wives to see the ascetics.
Multitudes of women and multitudes of kṣatriyas, mounted upon various vehicles,
went forth together with the brahmins and the wives of the brahmins; likewise,
there was a great thronging of the multitudes of vaiśyas and śūdras.
No one harbored envy; they were all possessed of a mind devoted to righteousness.
Thus it was with Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, as well as Somadatta and Bāhlika, and the royal sage whose wisdom was his eye, and Vidura himself, the Kṣattṛ.
The queen Satyavatī, the illustrious Kausalyā,
and Gāndhārī, surrounded by the king’s wives, went forth;
as did the heirs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, led by Duryodhana.
Adorned with various ornaments, those women numbered in the hundreds went forth.
Having saluted all those hosts of great seers with their heads bowed and having uttered words of welcome, they entered the palace of Pāṇḍu.
All the Kauravas, together with their family priests, sat down nearby;
likewise, all the citizens and countryfolk, having saluted and bowed down with their heads to the ground, also sat down nearby.
Perceiving that the entire multitude of people was then as if silent,
O Lord, Bhīṣma honored them according to custom with water for the feet and the arghya offering, and he offered the kingdom and the realm to the great seers.
Then the eldest among them, wearing matted hair and deerskin, rose up;
and having ascertained the opinion of the great seers, that great seer spoke these words:
"That heir of the Kauravas, the lord of men named Pāṇḍu—"
Having renounced the enjoyments of desire, he went from here to Śataśṛṅga;
having renounced the enjoyments of desire, he indeed became an ascetic. There, subsisting on roots and fruits, he practiced the austerities as prescribed.
For some time, that righteous-souled one, unwearied, remained with his two wives;
by his conduct and ascetic practices,
he gratified the ascetics dwelling on Mount Śataśṛṅga.
The ascetics, having restrained him as he was desirous of going to the heavenly world,
addressed these words to that Brahmin who was setting out with his two wives:
"O Indra among kings, for one who is childless, there are no worlds of merit."

Therefore, O Indra among kings, together with your two wives, propitiate the deities Dharma, Vāyu, Mahendra, and likewise the Aśvins. When they are satisfied, they will grant you sons, and you shall be released from your debt.
"Through our ascetic power and divine vision, we see your sons in that manner. Having heard our words, Kuntī then propitiated the gods according to the law of the practice of the celestial women."
By means of certain meritorious narratives, O noble lady,
and through the power of the sage’s mantras— [the sage] who was devoted to Śiva as his portion—
he summoned Dharma, Vāyu, Mahendra, and likewise the two Aśvins.
Kuntī gave birth to sons, and Mādrī also gave birth to two sons;
for him who was established in the vow of celibacy, this son Yudhiṣṭhira was born from Dharma himself through a divine cause.
Likewise, Mātariśvan gave to that high-souled king this son, the best among the strong, named Bhīma, who possessed great might;
born of Kuntī from Puruhūta, he was one whose valor was truth.
His fame shall surpass all those who wield great bows.
When this great archer was born, the gods, including Indra, spoke thus:
"By my grace, he has been born of Kuntī, possessing true prowess."

Invincible in battle, he is the conqueror of enemies, including the gods; of this there is no doubt. Having relieved the earth of its burdens, that Nara was directed by Hari to enter me, O Kuntī; for they know Nara to be half of Viṣṇu.
"O blessed lady, I have entered you; I am born with the name Phalguna.
Therefore, he shall be invincible even by the fourteen worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira shall obtain the Rājasūya sacrifice through the prowess of his brothers."
Having heard Indra’s words, Pāṇḍu attained great joy:
"He shall conquer all men, as well as all the Gandharvas and Rākṣasas;
he shall surpass Duryodhana and the Bhāratas in fame."
Through the heroic exploits of that one hero, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
will always perform sacrifices such as the Rājasūya; he is indeed another Dharma personified,
for having conquered all kings and made them tributary, he is their lord.

That righteous-souled one shall himself enjoy the earth girt by the oceans; as a peerless warrior on a single chariot, he shall conquer by his prowess even the gods, asuras, and serpents. Ajātaśatru, the righteous-souled one, will be honored for his sovereignty over the earth.
Moreover, those two great archers whom Mādrī bore, the best of the Kurus—
these two tigers among men,
Nakula and Sahadeva, who possess immeasurable splendor— they too remain here.
These two Pāṇḍavas, tigers among men, are likewise unconquered. While leading a life in the forest, ever devoted to dharma and illustrious,
this ancestral lineage was raised up once again by Pāṇḍu.
As Pāṇḍu constantly beheld the birth and growth of his sons and their Vedic studies, his joy increased perpetually; for,
conducting himself according to the way of the virtuous, he had attained the gain of sons.
On the seventeenth day from now, Pāṇḍu has gone to the world of the ancestors;
learning that he had entered the funeral pyre and was offered as an oblation into the mouth of Vaiśvānara,
Mādrī abandoned her own life and entered the fire.
Devoted to her husband, she has gone with him to the world of husbands.
Let that which must be done for her and for him be performed immediately thereafter;
[and likewise for] Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the high-minded Vidura.
Grant refuge to Pṛthā who has sought it, and show favor to the illustrious Pāṇḍavas as is fitting, for this is the eternal dharma. O Bhīṣma, their maintenance is likewise a great dharma.
You ought to show special honor to the body of the steward Dhṛtarāṣṭra and especially to Gāndhārī, as well as to the bodies of those two, to Pṛthā who has come to you for refuge,
and to all their sons who are knowers of dharma.
"These two bodies of theirs, and these excellent sons of theirs— let these subduers of enemies, together with their mother, be assisted by the performance of the funeral rites.
And when the rites for the deceased have been completed, let the highly illustrious one perform the *pitṛmedha* sacrifice."
"May Pāṇḍu, the knower of all dharmas and the upholder of the Kuru lineage, obtain [this].
Having spoken thus, while all the Kurus were looking on,
all the Cāraṇas together with the Guhyakas vanished in an instant.

Seeing that host of ṛṣis and siddhas, which had appeared like a city of the Gandharvas and then vanished right there, the Kauravas were filled with supreme wonder; springing up suddenly, they cried out in amazement, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all the Kurus, headed by Bhīṣma, having heard of that arrangement regarding Pāṇḍu, accepted those sons along with their mother.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O Vidura, perform all the funeral rites for Pāṇḍu like those for a king— for that lion among kings— and especially for Mādrī."
Bestow cattle, garments, jewels, and various kinds of wealth upon Pāṇḍu and Mādrī, as much as each desires and to whomever it is due. Act in such a way that Kuntī may show honor to Mādrī.
Just as neither the wind nor the sun can see her when she is so well-concealed,
so too the sinless Pāṇḍu is not to be pitied; that lord of men is to be praised,
for he has five heroic sons born who are like the sons of the gods.
"And that Pāṇḍu, the most eminent among those of meritorious deeds, would not be one to be grieved for.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Bhārata, Vidura, having said 'So be it' to him, [departed] together with Bhīṣma."
He had Pāṇḍu cremated in a most secluded place. Then, from the city, the royal priests quickly brought forth blazing fires, preceded by oblations of clarified butter.
With wood from the stalks of *palāśa*, and with *kuśa*, *muñja*, and *kabalvaja* grasses,
they quickly fashioned the two bodies according to the procedure prescribed in the ritual manuals.
Then, O King, having made effigies of the two upon *darbha* grass, they proceeded.
Then, having placed him upon a decorated palanquin adorned with ornaments,
they further embellished the palanquin with seasonal perfumes and various excellent garlands, covering it entirely with cloth.
Adorned with garlands of pearls, coral, rubies, and gold,
and likewise beautified with flower wreaths and costly garments,
it was further graced with mirrors and [images of] the Aśoka, Punnāga, Mallikā, Jāti, and Campaka flowers.
With coconut fruits, flowers, and betel nuts well-offered,
the ministers, kinsmen, and friends attended upon him,
that lion among men, who was mounted on a highly adorned chariot drawn by men.
He was carried away in a preeminent vehicle, well-attended by Mādrī,
with a white parasol and yak-tail fans;
then they adorned him with the sounds of all musical instruments.
And taking up many hundreds of jewels, men there gave them to those who desired them for the funeral rites of Pāṇḍu. Then [they brought] white, bright, and large umbrellas.
For the sake of the Kaurava, they brought forth beautiful garments;
while the sacrificial fires were being offered by the priests clad in white robes, those well-adorned flames went before him, blazing brightly.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras by the thousands,
weeping and tormented by grief, followed after the lord of men;
and likewise, the women followed, weeping.
With their hair disheveled and their hands placed upon their heads,
all the devoted women wept while beating their breasts;
they were all clad in single garments and devoid of any ornaments.
"O Great King, all the men and women, their heads uncovered, joyless and deeply distressed, [cried out]:
'He has abandoned us and cast us into eternal suffering.'"
Having made us protectorless, where will that supreme protector, the lord of men, go? O King,
having failed to establish in the kingdom your illustrious sons born for the forest, where will you go, leaving behind this abundance of offspring?
All the Pāṇḍavas, Bhīṣma, Vidura,
Bāhlīka, Somadatta, and King Bhūriśravas,
crying out and embracing one another, followed by the thousands.
Then, in a delightful, level, and auspicious forest region on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
they set down the palanquin of that truthful lion among men,
Pāṇḍu, whose deeds were untiring, together with his wife.
Having removed [the garments] and wrapped it in clean cloth, they performed the purification of the site.
Then that body of his was treated with all kinds of perfumes,
anointed with pure kālīyaka and other substances, and scented with the finest bathing powders.
He quickly sprinkled [the body] with water from jars made of gold,
and anointed it with the finest white sandalwood paste,
as well as with black aloe-wood and the resin of *tuṅga*.
Then they dressed him in white garments produced in that region;
covered by those clothes, that bull among men, a tiger among men accustomed to a costly couch, shone as if he were still alive.

By means of the sacrificial fire of the horse sacrifice (*hayamedha*), all the officiating priests together with the family chaplains performed the rites according to the injunctions declared in the Vedas, accompanied by the sacred mantras.
When the officiating priests had completed the funeral rites, they gave their formal permission.
The king, together with Mādrī, was well-adorned and sprinkled with clarified butter;
he was anointed with fragrant sandalwood mixed with tall *padmaka*,
as well as *sarala*, *devadāru*, *guggulu*, and lac.
They cremated him with red sandalwood logs, with *haribera* and *uśīra*,
and with various other abundant perfumes; likewise, they burned garments soaked in ghee and costly outer robes.
Then they cremated the king with jars filled with ghee. Having seen their two bodies, Kausalyā fell suddenly to the ground, overcome by delusion, crying out, "Alas, alas! My son!"

Seeing her fallen and afflicted, all the people of the city and the countryside wept aloud, filled with compassion and devotion to the king; and as if exhausted by that sound of wailing, all creatures cried out together.
Together with the humans, all beings— even those born of animal wombs— wailed along with those people, sharing in their common sorrow.
Likewise did Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, and the high-minded Vidura.
In every way, the Kauravas, deeply afflicted by grief, wailed aloud;
all the Pāṇḍavas and Dhṛtarāṣṭra also cried out, O Bhārata.
Then Bhīṣma, Vidura, and the king, together with their kinsmen, [fell silent].
All the Kuru women offered water for him;
likewise, all the Pāṇḍavas, Bhīṣma the son of Śāntanu,
Vidura, and his kinsmen wailed and performed the water-rites.
In a single vessel, they offered the funeral cakes separately and the water for the rites separately;
all of them, including all the Kuru women, offered the water of dharma. Taking those Pāṇḍavas, who were emaciated by grief after having performed the water-libations, [the people departed].
O King, all the subjects, filled with grief, gathered around; just as the Pāṇḍavas had slept upon the ground together with their kinsmen, O King,
so too did the citizens, including the Brāhmaṇas and others, lie down.
For twelve nights, that city, together with the Pāṇḍavas, remained joyless, uneasy, and devoid of cheer from its children onward. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the Steward (Vidura), the King, and Bhīṣma, together with their kinsmen and assisted by the family priest,
performed the śrāddha for Pāṇḍu, offering that nectar-like svadhā according to the prescribed rites.
Having fed the Kurus and the foremost of Brahmins by the thousands, both together in a single cooking and separately according to the prescriptions stated in their own Vedic branches,
he gave heaps of jewels and even excellent villages to the best of the twice-born.
Then, having taken those Pāṇḍavas, the bulls of the Bharatas, who had performed their purificatory rites,
the citizens entered the city named after the elephant.
They constantly grieved for that very bull of the Bharatas.

At the conclusion of the *śrāddha*, Vyāsa spoke to his mother, who was bewildered and afflicted by grief and sorrow, seeing all the people of the city and the countryside as distressed as if they were mourning their own deceased kinsman.
Times of great happiness have passed away, and dreadful times have arrived;
day after day, the days become more evil, for the earth has lost its youth. It is now filled with many deceptions and agitated by various faults.

A terrible time will come when the performance of righteous deeds has ceased; moreover, due to the misconduct of the Kurus, the earth shall no longer exist. Then, indeed, all the kings—sons and grandsons alike—[shall perish].
The Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty over the kingdom,
will mercilessly slaughter one another for the sake of the earth;
the interests of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas shall become the cause of the destruction of the world.
Having encountered one another in a terrible conflict, they will leave this earth submerged in a flood of blood, with only children and the elderly remaining—
this horrific time that brings about the destruction of all, which they have not yet perceived.
"O Mother, having seen this joy and happiness with affectionate eyes, listen to me:
go now, adopting renunciation, and dwell disciplined in the forest of asceticism;
do not witness the terrible destruction of this lineage and yourself."
Saying "So be it," she gave her consent; then, having entered, she said to her daughter-in-law:
"O Ambikā, we have heard that due to the misconduct of your son, the Bharatas, along with their followers and even your grandsons, will surely perish."
"Therefore, if you agree, may you be blessed; let us take this Kausalyā, who is distressed and oppressed by grief for her son, and go to the forest.
When Ambikā had said "So be it," she took leave of Bhīṣma, she of virtuous vows.
O descendant of Bharata, Satyavatī went to the forest together with her two daughters-in-law.
O best of the Bharatas, having performed most severe austerities, those goddesses,
O great king, cast off their bodies and then attained their desired goal.
Then the Pāṇḍavas received the sacraments prescribed in the Vedas,
and they grew up enjoying pleasures in their father’s house,
playing together with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In all childhood games, the Pāṇḍavas were preeminent:
in speed, in hitting targets, in eating, and in wrestling in the dust;
Bhīmasena overwhelmed all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Out of joy, seizing those boys as they were playing at hide-and-seek,
the Pāṇḍava grabbed them by their heads and made them fight.
There were one hundred and one of those princes of great prowess.
Vṛkodara alone, without great effort,
crushed them; seizing them by their feet, the powerful one struck them down with force and dragged them across the ground as they cried out, their knees, heads, and eyes being bruised.
While playing in the water, he would seize ten children with his two arms and remain submerged in the water, releasing them only when they were nearly dead;
and whenever they climbed a tree to gather fruit, he would do the same.
Then Bhīma made the tree tremble with a kick at its foot;
seizing the base of the tree with both hands and shaking it,
he felled to the ground those creatures clinging to the tips of the highest branches.
With their feet, thighs, and backs broken, and their heads and sides shattered,
the young princes— struck by the force of the impact— then tumbled rapidly from the tree, whirling about like fruit loosened from its stalk.
Some with shattered heads and chests, others with broken waists—
all those brothers fell, oppressed by the strength of Bhīmasena’s arms; for they were never his equal in wrestling, in speed, or in any martial exercises.
The princes, competing with Vṛkodara, performed the *uttara* [exercises].
Thus, though competing with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vṛkodara remained extremely indifferent toward what was unpleasant to them; it was out of childishness, not from a mind intent on malice.

Then the powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having recognized that extraordinary strength of Bhīmasena, displayed his wicked intent. As he had strayed from righteousness and was looking toward sinful deeds, [Bhīma acted].
Out of delusion and greed for power, an evil thought arose:
"This Vṛkodara, son of Kuntī, is the foremost among the strong;
let this middle son of Pāṇḍu be slain by means of treachery."
Endowed with vital strength and prowess, and possessed of great heroism,
Vṛkodara alone challenges all of us together;
yet we shall cast him, while he sleeps, into the Ganges in the city garden.
"Then, having forcibly bound both his younger brother and the eldest, Yudhiṣṭhira, in captivity, I shall rule the earth. Having thus made this resolve, the wicked Duryodhana then—

He was constantly watching for an opportunity against the high-souled Bhīma. Then, O descendant of Bharata, he had large and wonderful pavilions constructed of cloth and wool for the purpose of sporting in the water.
Filled with all desirable things and adorned with raised banners,
he had many various houses constructed there;
O descendant of Bharata, he caused them to be called "Water-Sports."
Having approached a certain spot on the shore of the ocean,
there were presented to him foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk, sucked, and licked,
all brought by men skilled in the art of cooking.
Then those men reported that matter to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Thereupon the evil-minded Duryodhana said to the Pāṇḍavas:
"Let us go along the Gaṅgā, which is adorned with gardens and groves."
"All of us brothers together shall enjoy water-sports.
Yudhiṣṭhira replied to him, "So be it.
Then, with chariots as large as cities and the finest elephants bred in that region, they set out.
The heroic Kauravas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, departed from the city;
having reached the pleasure grove and dismissed the great multitude,
those heroes then entered it like lions entering a mountain cave.
Beholding the garden, all those brothers saw it adorned with bright audience halls and gabled roofs,
as well as with windows, lattices, and water-channels.
It was swept clean by masons and adorned with paintings by artists; and indeed,
that water, covered by full oblong ponds as well as lotus-pools,
shone brightly with blossoming water-lilies.
The earth was covered with seasonal flowers as if concealed by them;
there all those Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas sat down,
and they enjoyed many pleasures that were likewise concealed here and there.
Then, in that excellent garden, while they were thus engaged in play,
they gave edible foods from their mouths to one another here and there.
Then the wicked Duryodhana placed *kālakūṭa* poison in that food.
Desiring to kill Bhīmasena,
he himself rose up with a heart like a razor, and cast poison [into the food],
though his speech was like nectar and he acted toward him like a brother and a friend.
The evildoer himself threw food into the mouth of Bhīma; and it was accepted by Bhīma, who was unaware of that offense. Then Duryodhana, as if laughing in his heart, [departed].
The lowest of men considers himself as one who has accomplished his purpose. Then all of them together— the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— engaged in water-sports with joyful minds.
At the conclusion of their play, all of them, dressed in clean garments and well-adorned,
slowly partook of that food which was abundant in every desired enjoyment. At the end of the day, those scions of the Kuru lineage, having enjoyed themselves, became weary.
In the very dwellings of the monastery, the heroes chose to take up residence.
Then the powerful Bhīma, exhausted by his excessive exertion, the lordly one,
having made those princes engage in water-sports, [rested].
Seeking a place to stay at Pramāṇakoṭi, he climbed up that spot and slept there;
having found a cool dwelling, the Pāṇḍava, exhausted and stupefied by intoxication,
O King, lay motionless as if dead.
Then Duryodhana, having slowly bound Bhīma— the best among the strong— who was fast asleep at Prabhāsa-koṭi on the Gaṅgā with nooses of creepers,
cast him from the dry land into the deep water of terrible current.
Then, unconscious, that son of Pāṇḍu entered the depths of the water; advancing into the abode of the Nāgas,
he then encountered many highly venomous Nāgas.
He appeared utterly terrifying with his great fangs, which were overflowing with poison.
As he was being bitten by them, that Kālakūṭa poison of his was neutralized by the snake's poison,
just as a stationary poison is overcome by a mobile one.

Then, having awakened, the son of Kuntī, Bhīma— the best among strikers— cut all his bonds and rose once more from the water. Released, that one of great splendor did not realize what had been done by him.
Once again, the powerful one fell under the sway of sleep and slept right there. Then, when the night had passed, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas rose;
but Duryodhana, seeing the son of Kuntī, was overcome with despondency.
Then, having encountered some [opponents], he crushed their heads;
with head against head, the hero waged a wondrous battle.
Likewise, on another day, he again [slew] those who were asleep with serpents of terrible countenance.
And he was bitten again by angry,
massive-bodied snakes with sharp fangs and potent venom; while he slept, they bit him once more on all his limbs and vital points.
The fangs of those fanged creatures, though struck even in his vital spots,
did not pierce the skin of that broad-chested one because of its toughness;
but Bhīma, having awakened, crushed all those serpents.
Vaiśampāyana said;
Vidura said;
Vaiśampāyana said.
The serpents who had survived the slaughter by Bhīma approached Vāsuki;
and they spoke to Vāsuki, the king of snakes, who was like Indra himself:
"O lord of the Nāgas, this man was indeed bound and cast into the waters."
O Hero, it was our thought that he would have died from the poison;
yet, having reached us motionless after being bitten, he regained consciousness and,
once restored to his senses, quickly severed our bonds.
"You ought indeed to recognize that mighty-armed one who is striking [the earth].
Then Vāsuki, followed by the *nāgas*,
approached and beheld that mighty-armed one, terrible and of fearsome prowess.
He was seen by his maternal grandfather, Pṛthā’s grandfather; then that grandson of a daughter’s son was embraced very tightly by him,
and the highly illustrious Vāsuki became exceedingly pleased with him.
And the lord of the *nāgas* said to him, "What pleasing service may be done for him?
Let a flood of wealth, a heap of jewels, and riches be given to him.
Being thus addressed, the *nāga* then replied to Vāsuki.
"O Lord of Nagas, if you are pleased, what need is there for him to have stores of wealth?
Since you are gratified, this mighty prince shall drink the nectar;
the strength of a thousand nagas is established within that vessel."
"Let as much as this fool drinks be given to him.
Vāsuki replied to that Nāga, "So be it.
Then Bhīma, having been purified by the Nāgas who performed rites for his well-being, became clean.
Sitting facing the east, the Pāṇḍava drank the liquid;
then, with a single breath, the one of great strength drank the entire vat.
In this manner, the son of Pāṇḍu drank eight vats.
Then the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, the subduer of enemies, lay down at his ease upon that divine bed given by the Nāgas. Then all those Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas remained there, except for Bhīma.
Having finished their sports and pastimes, they set out for Hastināpura by means of chariots, elephants, horses, and various other vehicles in great numbers;
meanwhile, Bhīmasena spoke, saying, "He has indeed gone ahead of us."
Then the wicked Duryodhana, not seeing Vṛkodara there,
entered the city joyfully together with his brothers;
but the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira found no fault within himself.
By his own inference, he perceived that another virtuous man was there. Then Pārtha, who is devoted to his brothers, approached his mother;
having saluted Kuntī, he said, "Mother, Bhīma has arrived here."
"Where could he have gone, O mother? I do not see him here, O auspicious one.
Gardens and the forest have been searched thoroughly on all sides, yet we have not seen that hero Vṛkodara."
Thinking thus, they all said: "O illustrious lady, he has already departed before us; we have arrived with our inner selves agitated.
Having come here, where indeed has he gone, or where has he been sent by you?"
"O illustrious lady, tell me of the mighty-armed Bhīmasena; for my mind finds no peace regarding that hero, O beautiful one. Since I think Bhīma is still asleep, I believe he has not been slain."
Having been addressed thus by the wise Dharmarāja, Kuntī, crying out "Alas! Alas! in her agitation, replied to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O son, I do not see Bhīma; he does not come to me, O Lord."
"Make haste and exert effort in searching for him together with his younger brothers. Having spoken thus to her eldest son with a grieving heart,
Kuntī then summoned the Steward (Kṣattṛ) and addressed these words to him.
"O Kṣattṛ, where has the Blessed One Bhīmasena gone? He is not to be seen.
All the brothers have departed from the garden together with their siblings;
yet that one mighty-armed Bhīma does not come here to me."
He never pleases the eyes of Duryodhana;
for that Suyodhana is cruel, evil-minded, base, greedy for the kingdom, and shameless— he would even slay that hero were he provoked to anger.
"Because of that, my mind is agitated and my heart seems to burn.
Do not speak thus, O auspicious lady; preserve what remains of us. For if that evil-souled one is rejected, he might strike even at what is left of you."
"O long-lived one, your son shall be as the great sage foretold; your son will come and bring you joy. Having spoken thus, the wise Vidura departed for his own abode.
Kuntī, remaining in the house with her sons, became lost in thought. Then, on the eighth day, when that elixir had been digested, the mighty Pāṇḍava of immeasurable strength awoke.
Seeing that the Pāṇḍava had awakened, those serpents calmly comforted him and spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed one, this essence, gathered from your own prowess, which you have drunk— "
Therefore, you shall possess the strength of ten thousand elephants and be invincible in battle.
Go now to your own home, having bathed in these divine waters;
for your brothers, O bull among the Kurus, are grieving because of your absence.
Then the mighty-armed one, having bathed, being pure and wearing white garments and garlands,
performed the auspicious marriage rites in the abode of the Naga with fragrant herbs that especially counteract poison.
The mighty hero, having eaten the supreme food offered by the Nāgas,
was honored by the serpents and greeted with blessings;
adorned with divine ornaments, the Pāṇḍava took his leave of the Nāgas.
With a joyful heart, the subduer of enemies rose up from the world of the Nāgas;
lifted by the Nāga from the water, that lotus-eyed joy of the Kurus was set down in that very forest region.
Those nāgas vanished even as the Pāṇḍava was looking on. Then the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, arose and went straight to his mother’s side.
Then, having saluted his mother and his eldest brother,
and having smelled the heads of his younger brothers— that crusher of enemies—
was himself embraced by them and by his mother, those bulls among men.
Out of mutual affection, they exclaimed, "By good fortune! By good fortune!
Then Bhīmasena, endowed with great strength and prowess, related all those deeds of Duryodhana to his brothers.
And the Pāṇḍava related in its entirety everything that had occurred in the world of the Nāgas, including all its virtues and faults. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these meaningful words to Bhīma.
"Be silent; you must not speak at all regarding this matter. Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, remained vigilant along with all his brothers.
And with a slap of his hand, he struck his beloved charioteer;
the righteous Vidura then gave counsel to those sons of Pṛthā.
Struck by him, that charioteer likewise went to the abode of Yama.
Then on another day, O King, that man of extreme intolerance, desiring to kill him and abiding by the counsel of Saubala,
consulted with Valala and again had poison mixed into Bhīmasena’s food.

The son of the Vaiśya woman then announced that fresh, sharp *kālakūṭa* poison had been prepared, which causes the hair to stand on end; yet Vṛkodara consumed it and digested it without any change in his condition.
For that poison, though extremely sharp, produced no transformation in him;
Bhīma, possessed of formidable strength, then digested it as well.
Then, O King, on the following day, he desired to kill Vṛkodara.

With Saubala as his companion, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra reflected; reflecting thus, he found no sleep, remaining vigilant day and night. In this manner, Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni the son of Subala [remained].
By means of many stratagems, they sought to slay the Pāṇḍavas;
yet the dull-witted Pāṇḍavas did not perceive those occurrences.
And the Pāṇḍavas, the subduers of their enemies, recognized all of that.
Remaining steadfast in the opinion of Vidura and refraining from making any public display [of their power],
the king, seeing those princes playing about with extreme arrogance and seeking someone for the purpose of their formal instruction, presented them to Gautama.
Born from a clump of reeds and having mastered the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras,
all those whom the king had presented to him were indeed appointed [as teachers];
and from Kripa, those Kurus learned the science of archery (Dhanurveda).
Vaiśampāyana;
Vidura;
Vaiśampāyana.
Then those men, led by Duryodhana, took counsel together:
"Vṛkodara alone is a destroyer of lives, full of prowess, established in great heroism, and he constantly vies with us."

"But while he is asleep in the city garden, we shall cast him into the water-pit. Then, O Bhārata, for the purpose of sporting in the water, he had various beautiful and auspicious pavilions made of cloth and wool constructed.
There, O Bhārata, they constructed many various dwellings; he had them built for the purpose of sporting in the water, having prepared the equipment on the site at the edge of the shore.
There, men presented to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra various kinds of food— solid, soft, drinkable, suckable, and likewise lickable— which had been acquired by men and prepared there by cooks.
Then the evil-minded Duryodhana said to the Pāṇḍavas:
"Let us all, together with our brothers, pay our respects today to the Gaṅgā, adorned with its gardens and groves, and enjoy sporting in the water."

"So be it," Yudhiṣṭhira replied to him as well. Then those heroes, the Kurus together with the Pāṇḍavas, set out from the city on chariots resembling fortified towns and drawn by the finest horses bred in their own lands.
Having reached the garden grove and unyoked their mounts,
those of great heroism entered like lions into a mountain cave;
then all those brothers beheld the garden.
It was adorned with pure pavilions for attendance and with balconies, as well as with windows, lattices, and water-circulating devices; it was well-serviced by plasterers,
painters, and artisans.
The water shone, covered with sacred long ponds as well as *kāraṇḍaka* pools and blossoming lotuses; likewise,
the earth was strewn with flowers according to the seasons.
Then all the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus sat down;
having enjoyed many excellent pleasures here and there,
they then proceeded to that garden grove for their diversion.
Then they gave food from here and there into one another’s mouths. Then the wicked Duryodhana,
desiring to kill Bhīmasena, caused the Kālakūṭa poison to be mixed into that food.
Then, rising up himself with a heart like a razor,
that evildoer treated him with the respect due to a brother and, with words like nectar,
personally placed the food into Bhīma’s mouth.
And Bhīma had indeed devoured it, unaware of its defect;
then Duryodhana, that lowest of men, as if laughing in his heart, considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Then they all, united together, engaged in water-sports; at the end of the day, having sported until they were exhausted, those heroes, the joy of the Kurus,
chose to take up residence in the pleasure-pavilions.
But the mighty Bhīma, having eaten and exerted himself excessively in the water,
and having caused those princes to perform their aquatic sports, the one of great strength climbed up to that dry land at Pramāṇakoṭi and slept there, seeking a place to rest.
Having reached that spot, he was indeed exhausted, especially from his exertions in the water;
with his limbs overcome by fatigue, he fell asleep as if he were dead.
Then Duryodhana himself bound Bhīma with nooses of creepers.
Having quickly driven spikes into the water, he caused the water to fall from the dry land;
yet because there was still a remnant [of his merit], the Pāṇḍava did not reach the water where the spikes were.
Wherever he fell, by chance, no spike was found there for him.
Deprived of consciousness, that Pāṇḍava indeed entered the depths of the water;
having stepped into the abode of the Nāgas, he likewise encountered the young Nāga-kumāras. Then, many highly venomous Nāgas gathered together.

There the Pāṇḍava was bitten by great serpents smeared with poison; as he was being bitten, that *kālakūṭa* poison was quickly neutralized by the venom of the snakes, the mobile [poison] overcoming the stationary.
Then the son of Kuntī, having awakened, tore that bond asunder;
he struck them all down and deprived some of their lives.
As they were being slaughtered by Pārtha, those serpents fled toward Vāsuki.
And they spoke to Vāsuki, the king of serpents, who was like Vāsava:
"O lord of the *nāgas*, this man has indeed been bound and cast into the waters; O hero, it is our conviction that he will drink the poison."
Having entered and reached the interior, he was indeed bitten many times; yet,
having regained consciousness and quickly severed our bonds,
that mighty-armed one began to crush us— you ought truly to know him.
Then Vāsuki, followed by the *nāgas*, approached;
that great *nāga* beheld Bhīma of terrible prowess.
And having been seen by his grandfather, he was likewise seen by Pṛthā’s grandfather.
Then the Pāṇḍava was seen by him and embraced; Vāsuki, the highly illustrious lord of the Nāgas, became very pleased with him and said to him, "What may be done for him?"
"Let a dear mass of wealth and jewels be given to him as much as he desires.
Thus addressed, the Naga then replied to Vāsuki:
"O Lord of Nagas, if you are pleased with him, what need has he for hoards of wealth?"
"Since you are pleased, let this boy drink the *rasa*; he shall become possessed of great strength.
A thousand elephants' worth of power is contained within this vessel;
let it be given to him while this boy drinks it."
"So be it," Vāsuki replied to that Nāga. Then the Pāṇḍava Bhīma, having had the rites for success performed by the Nāgas, being pure and seated facing the east, began to drink the fluid.
Then, with a single breath, that one of great strength drank from the vessel;
in this manner, the son of Pāṇḍu drank from eight such vessels.
Thereafter, the mighty-armed one lay upon a celestial bed provided by the Nāgas.
And at that time, Bhīma lay there for eight days; meanwhile,
the evil-minded Duryodhana, having cast Bhīma into the pool of venomous serpents,
then considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
When the night had turned to dawn, they entered the city from the forest.
Bhīmasena, however, was speaking as he went at the very front,
while the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira reflected upon the sin within himself.
Then, by his own inference, he perceived him from afar.
Thereupon, the sons of Pṛthā, who were devoted to their mother, approached her; having offered their salutations, they said, "O Mother, Bhīma has arrived here."
"‘No,’ Kuntī said then; thereupon they became distressed. Going quickly to the city garden, the Pāṇḍavas searched for him, constantly crying out the words ‘Bhīma! Bhīma! in a loud voice."
Then, searching everywhere, they all could not see their brother;
having returned once more to their own home, they then said this to Pṛthā:
"O Mother, the mighty-armed Bhīma is not seen in the forest."
All the pleasure gardens as well as the rivers were searched.
Then Kuntī, having summoned Vidura to her own residence, said:
"O Kṣattṛ, the powerful Bhīmasena is not to be seen."
All the brothers have gone out from the garden together with their brothers;
for there, the one mighty-armed Bhīma does not come here to me,
and he never pleases the eye of Duryodhana.
"Therefore, I think my son was killed by a wicked person while he was fast asleep.
"Do not speak thus, O blessed lady; protect those who remain.
"For once the evil-souled one has been repulsed, he might strike at those who are left behind."
"Your sons shall be long-lived, for so the seer has declared;
your son will come and increase your joy.
Having been addressed thus, Kuntī then sighed again and again.
Then that illustrious woman, surrounded by her sons, remained devoted to her bed.
On the eighth day thereafter, the son of Pāṇḍu,
the mighty one of immeasurable strength, awoke once that elixir had been digested.
Adorned with fragrant, poison-destroying herbs, the mighty-armed one, whose eyes were like lotuses, ate the exquisite food offered by the nāgas; and then,
the nāgas lifted him up from the water.
In that very forest region, the son of Pāṇḍu was stationed;
and those Nāgas vanished even as the Pāṇḍava watched.
Then Bhīma, having risen, went to his own home.
Having been saluted, embraced, and smelled upon the head,
he then bowed to the Son of Dharma and embraced Phalguna;
and having been saluted by those heroes, he also embraced the twins.
Vṛkodara related all of that exactly as it had happened;
but when the Pāṇḍavas understood that deed of his,
they did not at all exert themselves extensively in guarding their secret counsel.
The righteous and wise Vidura gave them his counsel;
but Duryodhana, seeing that Pāṇḍava had returned once more,
sighed and brooded, burning with grief day after day.
Thus the wicked Duryodhana and Śakuni, the son of Subala,
sought to slay those Pāṇḍavas by means of many stratagems;
and the Pāṇḍavas, the subduers of their enemies, recognized all of that.
Without making any display of their prowess, they remained under the guidance of Vidura;
and from Kṛpa, those Kurus learned the science of archery.
Janamejaya said:
"O Great Brahmin, you ought also to tell me the origin of Kṛpa:
how was he born from a clump of reeds, and how did he obtain his weapons?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O great king, the great seer Gautama had a son known by the name Śaradvat; O lord, he was indeed born with arrows. Yet, his intellect was not so inclined toward the study of the Vedas.
Just as his intellect had become perfected in the science of archery, O scorcher of foes,
and just as those who discourse on Brahman acquire the Vedas through austerity,
so too did he, endowed with austerity, obtain all the divine weapons.
Because of his devotion to the science of archery and his immense asceticism,
that Gautama caused the king of the gods to suffer greatly.
Thereupon, the lord of the gods [sent] a celestial maiden named Jālapadī.
"O Kaurava, she was sent with the command: 'Create an obstacle to his asceticism.
Having approached the delightful hermitage of Śaradvat, that young woman tempted Gautama, who was carrying his bow and arrows."
Seeing that Apsaras in the forest, clad in but a single garment and possessing a form unparalleled in the world, Gautama’s eyes widened with wonder; indeed,
both his bow and his arrows fell from his hands to the ground.
Upon seeing her, a trembling arose throughout his body; yet,
because of the greatness of his knowledge and the power of his asceticism,
that man of great wisdom remained firm through supreme fortitude.
But because a transformation came upon him suddenly, O King, his semen was discharged; and he did not perceive it. Leaving that hermitage and that very apsaras, the sage—
That seed of his went forth and fell indeed upon a clump of reeds;
and having fallen upon the clump of reeds, O King, it split into two parts.
Thereupon, a pair was born from that seed of Gautama Śaradvat.
Near the hermitage of this great seer Gautama, a certain soldier of King Śantanu, while wandering at will on a hunt in the forest, beheld that couple.
Seeing the bow with its arrow as well as the black antelope skins,
and having determined that this was the offspring of a Brahmin who had reached the furthest limits of the science of archery,
he then presented that pair along with the arrow to the king.
Then the king, filled with compassion, took that pair and returned home, saying, "These are my sons. Thereupon,
he raised them and endowed them with the sacred rites of initiation.
The son of Pratīpa, the best among men, gave that pair to Gautama;
and Gautama, having received them, became devoted to the science of archery,
thinking, "Out of compassion, these two children were raised by me."
Therefore, that lord of the earth gave them those very names;
thus he became known as Kṛpa, and she became the maiden Kṛpī.
Gautama discovered the two of them there by means of his ascetic power.
Having approached him, he then declared everything to him, beginning with his lineage;
he then explained to him in its entirety all four branches of the science of archery (dhanurveda) and various weapons, including every secret.
And within seven nights, Kṛpa became devoted to the science of archery;
in a very short time, he attained the status of a supreme teacher.
Then the son of Gaṅgā, summoning Kṛpa, said, "These are your pupils."
Then, having gathered his grandsons together, he propitiated them out of compassion;
thereupon, all those great chariot-warriors—
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the mighty Pāṇḍavas— mastered the science of archery.
The Vṛṣṇis, other kings, and various others gathered from many lands,
having approached the teacher Kṛpa, attained supreme mastery in the knowledge of weapons.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Bhīṣma, seeking excellence for his grandsons and desiring their disciplined training,

inquired after teachers renowned for their prowess and skilled in the science of archery; for one who is not of small intellect, nor of great fortune, nor proficient in various weapons, [could not have done so].
"Only one who is not a god among beings can subdue the Kurus, who are possessed of great strength in weaponry.
Having reflected thus, O best of the Bharatas, the son of Gaṅgā then [approached] the wise Droṇa, the son of Bharadvāja, who was a knower of the Vedas.

O bull among men, that illustrious one, the best among those skilled in weapons, was honored according to the scriptures by that high-souled Bhīṣma and, being well-pleased, gave the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas as his disciples.
The highly illustrious Droṇa accepted them all as his disciples and instructed them in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) in its entirety. In a very short time, they became experts in all weapons.
The Kauravas and the Pandavas, O King, were possessed of immeasurable prowess.
Janamejaya said:
Vaishampayana said:
How was Droṇa born, and how did he acquire his weapons? O Brahmin, how did he come to the Kurus, whose son was that heroic man,
and how was his son Aśvatthāman born, who was the most skilled in weapons?
"I wish to hear this; please proclaim it in detail. At Gaṅgādvāra there lived a great and venerable ṛṣi known as Bharadvāja, who was always firm in his vows."
Then, he went first to the river Gaṅgā in order to perform the consecration. Long ago, while the great seer Bharadvāja was performing a sacrifice,
the seer beheld the Apsaras Ghṛtācī herself as she was bathing.
She was endowed with beauty and youth, intoxicated with pride and languid with passion; as the wind blew her garment away,
passion arose in his mind from the sight of her private parts.
Then his semen was discharged, and the seer placed it in a wooden vessel (*droṇa*).
Having seen her with her garments cast aside, the seer then desired her;
thus the mind of the wise Bharadvāja became fixed upon her.
O King, having seen her with her beautiful secret parts and full, elevated breasts,
Droṇa was born from the water-jar of that wise man.
He mastered the Vedas and all the Vedāṅgas in their entirety. Having received from the sage Kāśyapa the weapon of Agni,
Bharadvāja acquired that divinely wrought weapon.
The powerful Bharadvāja, the best among the upholders of dharma, imparted the Āgneya weapon to the highly fortunate Agniveśya. O best of the Bharatas, that sage was born from Agniṣṭu.
Then Agniveśya, like a brother to his brother,
imparted that great fiery weapon, the Āgneya, belonging to Bhāradvāja, to Droṇa.
"If a teacher here desires happiness, he should indeed be disciplined," Bhīṣma spoke thus out of a desire to win over Bhāradvāja. Furthermore,
there was a king named Pṛṣata who was a friend of Bharadvāja.
To him, too, was born at that time a son named Drupada. That son of Pṛṣata, a bull among Kṣatriyas, would constantly go to the hermitage with Droṇa, where he played and pursued his studies.
Then, after Pṛṣata had passed away, that mighty-armed king Drupada became the lord of men among the Northern Pañcālas. At that time, the blessed Bharadvāja also ascended to heaven.
Dwelling in that very place, Droṇa, a man of great asceticism, performed penance;

he was a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, his sins consumed by his austerity. Then, with his mind directed by his father and out of a longing for a son, the highly illustrious one [continued his practice].
Then Droṇa took Kṛpī, the daughter of Śaradvat, as his wife; she was constantly devoted to the sacred fire, dharma, and self-restraint. Gautamī bore him a son named Aśvatthāman.
As soon as he was born, he neighed just like the horse Ucchaiḥśravas.
Hearing that, an invisible being situated in the intermediate space said:
"The power of this [child], as he neighs, has reached the quarters of the sky like that of a horse."
