"This child shall be known by the name Aśvatthāman (Horse-tusk) himself. Because of that son, the son of Bharadvāja became exceedingly pleased;
and dwelling right there, the wise one became devoted to the science of archery.
O King, he heard that the high-souled son of Jamadagni, the scorcher of foes,
a Brahmin who possessed all knowledge and was the foremost among all wielders of weapons,
was then desiring to bestow all manner of wealth upon the Brahmins.
Having heard of Rāma’s science of archery and his divine weapons, he set his mind upon them, as well as upon the treatises on political ethics (*nītiśāstra*). Then,
that one of great ascetic power was attended by disciples who were observant of vows and devoted to austerity.
Surrounded [by his followers], the mighty-armed one set out for Mahendra, the best of mountains. Then, having reached Mahendra, the son of Bharadvāja, a man of great asceticism,
beheld the descendant of Bhṛgu, who was patient, self-controlled, and the slayer of his enemies.
Then Droṇa, surrounded by his disciples, approached the descendant of Bhṛgu;
he announced his own name and his birth in the lineage of Aṅgiras,
and having prostrated himself with his head upon the ground, he saluted his feet.
Then, hearing that he— who was skilled in all weapons and missiles— had arrived there desiring to depart for the forest and renounce everything,
that high-souled crusher of all kṣatriyas spoke to him.
"Welcome to you, O best of the twice-born; tell me what you desire.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Bhāradvāja spoke these words:
"Bhāradvāja then spoke to Rāma as he was setting out for the forest."
"Born from Bharadvāja, know me to be Droṇa, a bull among the twice-born, who has come to you— though not born of a womb— and who desires wealth;
I am Rāma, the best of strikers, wishing to bestow various riches."
"O you of extensive vows, I indeed seek infinite wealth.
Rāma said:
"Whatever gold and whatever other riches I possess exist [only for you]."
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, everything has been given by me to the Brahmins;
likewise, this goddess Earth, bounded by the oceans and adorned with cities, has been given by me in its entirety to Kaśyapa."
Today, only this body and these highly precious missiles and various weapons have been left by me.
Choose either the weapons or the body; choose whichever is offered by me.
"Choose, O Droṇa! Tell me quickly what I shall give to you.
Droṇa said:
"O Bhārgava, [grant me] all my weapons, together with the methods for their withdrawal."
O best of Brahmins, you ought to grant [these teachings], together with their practical applications and secret mysteries, in their entirety;
for this is indeed the wealth of all the Vasus.
Rāma said:

"O Blessed One, grant this boon to me, which I have chosen. Having obtained the boon, O best of the twice-born, I shall have my purpose fulfilled. Accept it from me, O chief of Brahmins, O Droṇa, if you so desire."
"O best of the twice-born, I grant you today the boon that you have requested.
Accept these divine weapons and my own science of archery. O Droṇa, I grant this great boon to you along with your son."
"O best of Brahmins, go now with your purpose accomplished; go back just as you came.
Having mastered the weapons, being heroic, and being learned in all the scriptures, he shall become a renowned great chariot-warrior (mahāratha) known as Aśvatthāman."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having said "So be it," Bhārgava then bestowed upon him the weapons,
along with their secret mantras and the required observances, as well as the entire science of archery (Dhanurveda) in its completeness.
Having accepted all of that, the best of the twice-born, now proficient in weapons,
departed with great joy toward his dear friend Drupada.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having approached Drupada, the powerful son of Bharadvāja said to the son of Pṛṣata, "O King, know me as your friend.
Thus addressed by his friend with affection, that lord of men [replied].
Bhāradvāja could not endure those words of the Pāñcālya king.
With his eyebrows knitted in anger and indignation, and his eyes reddened,
the king— filled with the intoxication of power— spoke this to Droṇa.
Drupada said:
"O Brahmin, this wisdom of yours is unrefined and not very appropriate,
since you speak to me so imperiously, saying, 'I am your friend,' O twice-born one."

For kings who have risen to power never form friendships with men such as these— O dull-witted one— with those devoid of prosperity and fallen from wealth. Even friendships decay as time itself decays.
For previously there was friendship between us, bound by our mutual capability;
yet in this world, an undecaying friendship is never seen at any time,
for desire distracts it and anger cuts it down.

"It dwells for a time and perishes in that very time; do not attend upon such a decayed friendship, but cultivate a new one. O best of the twice-born, my friendship with you was based on a specific purpose."
A poor man is not the friend of the wealthy, nor is the ignorant man the friend of the learned;
a eunuch is not the friend of a hero. Why is friendship sought with one who was previously a friend?
Only between those whose wealth is equal and whose lineage is equal [can true friendship exist].
Friendship and marriage can exist between two who are equal, but not between the prosperous and the destitute.
One who is not a Vedic scholar cannot be the friend of a scholar, nor can one without a chariot be the friend of a charioteer;
there is no alliance for a king with one who is not a king—why then is such a friendship sought?

"O dull-witted one, friendship can never exist between those like you and those like me who are destitute of wealth; why do you desire such a former friendship? O wise Brahmin, it is exactly so; you shall never be a king anywhere."
"Do not stand near one who has not yet crossed over; establish a new friendship.
O sage, how can one such as you become the friend of a king?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Drupada, the powerful Bhāradvāja reflected for a moment, overwhelmed with indignation. Having resolved within his mind regarding the Pāñcāla king, the wise one—
Having made that vow which he was soon to fulfill,
the illustrious one, surrounded by his disciples and followed by his son,
then went to the city named after the elephant, the capital of the Kuru chiefs.
Seeing the Kurus assembled together, the highly energetic Brahmin Droṇa, desiring to obtain a livelihood, came toward Nāgapura;
having been thus addressed by him, he then departed for the Kurus along with his wife.
Droṇa, together with his wife and his son Aśvatthāman, who was possessed of great strength, arrived at the house of his brother-in-law;
having reached Nāgapura, he went to the residence of Gautama.

There, the best of the twice-born, Bhāradvāja, lived in disguise. Then his son, the lord Kṛpa, taught the sons of Pṛthā their weapons immediately after [the instruction of] Kṛpa; and the people did not recognize him.
Thus, with his identity concealed, he dwelt there for some time.
Then those heroic princes, having departed from Hastināpura,
roamed about there in joy, playing with a ball.
While they were playing there,
a ring fell into a well from their ball as they were sporting at that time. Then,
with great care, they made an effort to retrieve the ball.
But that [ball] was hidden by water like a star-form in the sky;
seeing it, the princes indeed surrounded it with effort,
yet they were unable to perform the action required to recover the ball.
Then, with their faces bowed down in shame, they looked at one another;
finding no way to approach her, they became deeply distressed.
They saw a dark-complexioned brahmin who was grey-haired and emaciated.
Seeing that high-souled one, who was occupied with his duties, nearby, and preceded by the sacred fire-offering, those young boys approached him and,
their own efforts and enthusiasm shattered, surrounded the brahmin.
Then the heroic Droṇa, seeing those princes intent on their task, smiled gently out of affection and addressed them. Having observed those princes who were so intent yet bewildered, he spoke.
The Brahmin, smiling gently, addressed them with skill:
"Alas! Shame on the power of the Kshatriyas, and shame on this mastery of weapons of yours—you who, born in the lineage of Bharata, do not even find a small ball!"
"Indeed, I could pull out even these two—a ball and a ring—with blades of grass;
let food be given to me.
Having spoken thus to those princes, Droṇa [took] the bandage from his own finger.
Into that waterless well, the tamer of foes threw him.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, spoke to Droṇa:
"O Brahmin, with Kṛpa’s consent, receive from us eternal alms."
Thus addressed, he laughed and replied this to the Bharatas:
"This is a handful of reeds consecrated by me with a mantra;
behold its power, which is not found in any other."
I shall pierce that ball with a blade of grass, and that blade of grass with another;
and that [second blade] with yet another blade,
and that [third] with yet another— such is the conjunction for me in seizing the ball.
Then, everything was performed exactly as Droṇa had instructed, swiftly and without error.
Seeing that, the princes, their eyes wide with wonder,
retrieved the ball that had been thrown and spoke to the one who had shot it.
"O brahmin-sage, quickly extract this seal-ring as well!
Then the highly illustrious Drona, taking up his bow and arrow,
pierced that seal-ring with the shaft and, being a master, drew it upward.
Taking up an arrow, he then gave a finger-ring from the well to the astonished princes; seeing the ring drawn out, those young princes said to him:
"We pay homage to you, O Brahmin; this [power] is not found among others. Who are you? Whom do we recognize you to be? What shall we do?
Thus addressed, Droṇa then replied to the youths.
Droṇa said:
"Describe me to Bhīṣma according to my appearance and my qualities;
he alone, possessed of great intelligence, will understand me at once."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having said, "So be it," they all spoke to their grandfather Bhīṣma:
"The word of the Brāhmaṇa is true, and his deed was indeed extraordinary."
Having heard this from the princes, Bhīṣma recognized Droṇa as such;
reflecting that he was indeed a most worthy preceptor,
he then personally brought him there and honored him with great respect.
He honored him with due rites and offerings according to custom;
then Bhīṣma, the best among wielders of weapons, questioned him skillfully. Droṇa then explained the entire reason for his arrival.
O Acyuta, in former times I went into the presence of the great seer Agniveśya for the sake of weapons, desiring to master the science of archery;
there I lived as a humble-minded celibate student with matted hair for many years.

I dwelt there for a very long time with the desire to master the science of archery. The mighty Yajñasena, the son of the King of Pañcāla, practiced this science together with me under our preceptor, exerting himself with focused concentration.
He was my friend there, helpful and dear to me; having come together with him, I indeed took delight for a very long time,
O Kauravya, from childhood onwards, even sharing our studies.
Having approached me there, O Bhīṣma, that dear-doer who speaks kindly addressed me with these words that increased my joy:
"O Droṇa, I am the most beloved son of my high-souled father."
"When that Pāñcālya consecrates me in the kingdom, then,
O friend, the wealth of your friend shall become your own enjoyment,
just as my kingdom shall be your enjoyment; I swear this to you by the truth."
"My enjoyments, my wealth, and my pleasures are all dependent on you;
O illustrious one, my kingdom should be enjoyed by you, if you so desire.
Thus addressed, I, having mastered the use of weapons, went forth into the forest out of a desire for wealth.
At that time, I constantly held those words in my mind. By the command of my father and out of a desire for a son,
I married the illustrious Nādikēśī, who was possessed of great wisdom and observed great vows.
Gautamī, who was constantly devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, truthfulness, and self-restraint,
obtained as her own biological son Aśvatthāman,
whose deeds and prowess were formidable and whose splendor was equal to that of the sun.
I was as delighted by that son as Bharadvāja was by me;
yet, seeing the wealthy sons there drinking cow’s milk,
the young Aśvatthāman wept, and that made the very quarters of the sky seem uncertain to me.

"A Snātaka should not fall into distress while remaining steadfast in his own duties"— reflecting thus in his mind, O son of Gaṅgā, he wandered many times through that region, seeking a pure place for receiving gifts that was endowed with righteousness.
Having wandered from end to end, I did not find a milch cow;
then children tempted me with flour-water. Having drunk that flour-liquid, the child thought, "Milk has been drunk by me as well."

O descendant of Kuru, rising up, he danced, delighted and deluded by his own childishness. Seeing my son dancing, surrounded by children, and having become an object of ridicule, a dejection came over me there.
"Fie on Drona, the penniless man who does not obtain wealth!
Having drunk water mixed with flour as if it were milk out of a thirst for milk,
he danced, overcome with joy, thinking, 'Milk has been drunk by me as well.'"
Having heard these words spoken by them, my intellect failed me;
reproaching myself by myself, I reflected thus in my mind:
"Indeed, in the past, I was avoided and severely censured by the brahmins."

Thinking, "I shall not engage in the most wicked service of others out of a desire for wealth," I then took my beloved son Bhīṣma and, out of affection born of former love, went with my wife to the Saumaka king.
Hearing that he had been consecrated, and thinking "I have achieved my purpose," I returned with great joy to my dear friend now established in his kingdom,
recollecting both our meeting and those words of his.
Then, O Lord, having approached Drupada— who was formerly my friend— I said, "O tiger among men, know me as your friend.
But Drupada, upon seeing me approach and greeting him as a friend, [did not acknowledge it].
Laughing at me as if I were formless, he said this to me:
"O Brahmin, this wisdom of yours is unrefined and not very consistent,
since you have so forcefully told me, 'I am your friend,' O twice-born one."
In this world, associations decay as time wears them away;
for previously, my friendship with you was bound by mutual capability.
One who is not learned in the Vedas cannot be a friend to one who is learned, nor can one who is not a charioteer be a friend to a charioteer.
For friendship arises from equality; it does not occur through inequality.
In this world, no one's friendship is ever found to be ageless;
either time wears it away, or anger carries it off.
"Do not treat this worn-out friendship with such indifference; let it be restored.

O best of the twice-born, there was once a friendship between you and me based on a mutual purpose. For one who is not wealthy is not the friend of the wealthy, nor is one who is unlearned the friend of the learned."
A eunuch cannot be the friend of a hero; why seek a former friendship with him? A non-king cannot be the friend of an earthly monarch either; why seek a former friendship with him?
For it never happens that kings who have risen to power [form such ties] with men of this sort.
O dull-witted one, friendship exists with those devoid of fortune and fallen from wealth. I do not recognize any agreement made by you for the sake of the kingdom;
however, O Brahmin, I shall gladly give you food for a single night.
Having been addressed thus by him, I then set out with my wife,
having made that vow which I shall fulfill before long.
"Accept this, O best of the twice-born, for friendship is indeed bound by purpose."

"One who is not a Vedic scholar cannot be a friend to a scholar; one without a chariot cannot be a friend to a charioteer; nor can one who is not a king be a friend to a monarch. Why, then, do you desire such a former friendship? Addressed thus by Drupada, I was overwhelmed with indignation.
"I came to the Kurus, O Bhīṣma, seeking disciples endowed with virtuous qualities.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Bhīṣma said:
"Then I have come to fulfill your desire;
this is the delightful city of the Nāgas—tell me, what shall I do for you?
Thus addressed, Bhīṣma then spoke to the son of Bharadvāja.
"Let the bow be strung; properly take up your weapon.
Enjoy pleasures with great delight, being honored in the abode of the Kurus. Whatever wealth the Kurus possess, as well as this kingdom together with its territories, is yours."
"You alone are the supreme king, and all the Kurus are yours.
O Brahmin, let it be considered that whatever you have requested has already been accomplished.
By good fortune you have arrived, O brahmin-sage; a great favor has been bestowed upon me."

Droṇa, having been addressed thus by Bhīṣma, was honored as he was being led to his residence; at that moment, the endeavor of the Kurus became fruitful with the arrival of Droṇa. He imparted the entirety of the fourfold weapons to the princes.
In that world of the Kṣatriyas, there were princes of great strength.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Droṇa, the best among men, was honored by Bhīṣma.

Honored in the house of the Kurus, the one of great splendor took his rest. Then, once that preceptor had rested, Bhīṣma took the Kauravas, his grandsons, and gave them over as disciples along with various riches.
And the lord, being well-pleased, bestowed upon Bhāradvāja a house that was well-sheltered and filled with wealth and grain;
Bhīṣma, together with the sons of Pāṇḍu, accepted him as their preceptor.
Taking all those grandsons and various kinds of wealth,
O King, he gave them to Droṇa according to the prescribed rites as his pupils;
and that great archer accepted the Kauravas as his pupils.
With a joyful heart, Droṇa received both the Pāṇḍavas and the Dhārtarāṣṭras;
having welcomed them all, Droṇa, being confident in himself, then spoke these words in private to those who had approached him for instruction.
"O sinless ones, there is a certain task desired by me that revolves within my heart; you who have mastered all weapons must grant it to me—speak the truth.
Having heard this, O lord of the people, those descendants of Kuru remained silent.
Then Arjuna, the scorcher of enemies, promised to do all of it. Thereupon, having smelled Arjuna’s head again and again and having embraced him with affection, he wept with joy.
Having summoned Aśvatthāman, Droṇa spoke these words:
"Know Pārtha to be your friend; accept him as given by me.
Saying "Excellent! Excellent! Pārtha embraced him and spoke thus.
"From this day forward, O best of Brahmins, I am yours in accordance with dharma;
by your grace, O most excellent of the twice-born, I live as your disciple.
Having spoken thus, the son of Pṛthā, the Pāṇḍava, then grasped his feet.
Then the valiant Droṇa caused the sons of Pāṇḍu, as well as other princes who had assembled there, O bull of the Bharatas, to master various divine and human weapons.
Then the Vṛṣṇis, the Andhakas, and kings from various lands approached Droṇa, the best of the twice-born, for the sake of weapons;
and the Sūta’s son, Rādheya, also went then to his teacher Droṇa.
But the son of the Sūta, being highly intolerant and vying with Pārtha,
relied upon Duryodhana and held the Pāṇḍavas in contempt;
he then approached Droṇa with the desire to master the science of archery.

Among all of them, Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, became preeminent through his training, physical strength, and exertion, as well as his passion for the science of weapons; for even when their application of weapons was equal, he excelled in swiftness and elegance.
Among all his disciples, Arjuna became preeminent;
Droṇa regarded him as the peerless son of Indra in the matter of instruction. In this manner, he imparted the science of archery to all the princes.
He gave a water-pot to all of them for the sake of delay,
but he gave a jar to his son so that there would be no delay; meanwhile, while they had not yet returned, he performed for him the supreme rite.
Droṇa related that deed to his son, and how Jiṣṇu had countered it;
then, having filled his water-pot with the Vāruṇa weapon,
Phālguna approached his preceptor together with the preceptor’s son.
But from that son of the preceptor,
the wise Pārtha, the best among those skilled in weapons, did not fall behind in the accumulation of special excellence.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Arjuna, however, exerted the greatest effort in honoring his teacher and applied himself with supreme diligence to the science of weapons; thus he became dear to Droṇa. Seeing Phālguna constantly devoted to the practice of archery and weaponry, [Droṇa was pleased].
Then Droṇa spoke to him in the king’s very residence;
having summoned the food-preparer in secret, Droṇa said:
"In the darkness, you must not give food to Arjuna under any circumstances."
"And furthermore, this speech of mine must not be told by you to Vijaya.
Then, while Arjuna was eating, a wind blew forth;
by that wind, the lamp that was burning there was extinguished.

Arjuna indeed ate his food, yet his mouth did not become bewildered; for the hand of that radiant one was always occupied with the act of taking up the food. Considering this to be the result of practice, the Pāṇḍava practiced it during the night.
The mighty-armed son of Pāṇḍu made himself proficient with the bow.
O Bhārata, Droṇa heard the sound of his bowstring and palm-strike;
approaching him, rising up, and embracing him, he spoke these words.
I shall strive to act in such a way that no other archer today possesses weapons like yours,
nor seeks after weapons as you do;
even in the mastery of the bow, you shall become my distinguished disciple.
Then this instruction of Droṇa took root in the heart of Jiṣṇu;
and Arjuna, that tiger among men and the best of all wielders of weapons, the scorcher of foes, exerted supreme effort in the science of archery.
Having authorized all activities, he thus brought his disciples together:
Duryodhana, Citrasena, Duḥśāsana, Vivimśati,
Arjuna, and Aśvatthāman.
Then the mighty-armed Droṇa, having fashioned a clay doll of a child, threw it into the waters of the Gaṅgā while his disciples looked on;
and having bound their eyes with a cloth, he gave them a bow.

"Shoot this young boy while he stands in the water with his eyes bound! At that very moment, the self-controlled Bībhatsu pierced the boy submerged in the water with ten arrows from his quiver, striking him with five on each side.
Having observed all his actions, Droṇa considered the Pāṇḍava to be superior to all his disciples, and he was filled with joy at that time. Then Bhāradvāja spoke to the high-souled great car-warrior:
O Pāṇḍava, learn this weapon which is superior to all others and does not exist among them, together with its method of withdrawal and application; observe the vow,
for this weapon named Brahmashiras could consume even the entire earth.

Even as far as the application of mantras is concerned, it shall occur during the ritual deployment; however, at the very least, that same [application] must be performed during the withdrawal. Furthermore, the Brahmā-weapon must never, under any circumstances, be employed against a human being.
"When a non-human enemy anywhere oppresses human foes,
then this eternal Brahma-weapon must be employed. And Bībhatsu, with palms joined in reverence, replied, "So be it."
And the bull among men performed everything exactly as he had been told. Then,
having instructed Bībhatsu— who had now acquired the weapons— the high-minded one,
exceedingly pleased, said to the Pāṇḍava, "You are equal to me."
"I tell you this as the truth: there shall be no one equal to you in the world.
Then Droṇa further instructed Arjuna in the art of combat on chariots, elephants, horses, and even on the ground.
In the proper movements of weapons, Droṇa’s pupil practiced;
in mace-fighting, sword-play, and with the tomara, prāsa, and śakti missiles,
as well as in combined combats, Droṇa instructed the Pāṇḍava.
Seeing that skill of his, thousands of kings and princes, desiring to master the science of archery, gathered together;
Drona, the best among the wielders of weapons, instructed them all.
Then, O great king, Ekalavya, the son of Hiraṇyadhanus, the king of the Niṣādas, approached Droṇa; however,
Droṇa did not accept him as a pupil, reflecting that he was a Niṣāda.

The knower of dharma, out of consideration for them alone, made his disciple practice on the bow. "O Niṣāda, you are my disciple; your application [of force] is too great. Return to your home; you are forever granted permission."
But that scorcher of enemies, having fashioned an image of Droṇa out of earth, approached the forest while grasping Droṇa’s feet with his head;
at that time, he maintained the highest conduct toward him as toward a teacher.
Adhering to the highest discipline, he applied himself to the yoga of archery;
endowed with supreme faith and the highest mastery of yoga,
he attained the utmost lightness in the release, the drawing, and the aiming of his arrows.
In no long time, he attained both agility and mastery in the use of weapons.
Then, once permitted by Droṇa, all the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas—
those crushers of enemies— went out on horseback for a hunt.
There, O King, a certain man, taking up some provisions and carrying a dog, followed the Pāṇḍavas alone by chance as they were wandering about,
desiring to perform various tasks for them.
Wandering lost in the forest, that dog went toward the Niṣāda. O noble one, as it was crying out, lost in the lonely forest, the Niṣāda heard the sound of that dog.
Seeing the son of Niṣadha in the forest— dark-skinned, his limbs smeared with dirt, and wearing a black antelope skin—
a dog stood near him and began to bark.
Then, as that dog was barking, [the prince] discharged seven arrows into its mouth.
Displaying his lightness of hand with the weapon, he released [the arrows] simultaneously;
like a whirlpool in a forest,
they appeared beautiful in their length and curvature as those sprout-like arrows.
With straight, swift, and whistling arrows of equal length, those subduers of enemies covered him,
just as a mountain is struck by stone-tipped flames.
Then that dog, its mouth filled with arrows, rushed toward the Pāṇḍavas.
Seeing him, the heroic Pāṇḍavas were filled with the utmost wonder;
beholding that supreme lightness of hand and skill in hitting targets by sound alone,
they were both abashed and praised him from all sides.
But seeing the dog, O King, the Pāṇḍavas’ eyes widened with wonder;
searching for that forest-dweller throughout the woods,
the Pāṇḍavas then beheld him incessantly discharging arrows.
And they did not recognize him at that time because of his deformed appearance;
then they questioned him, "Who are you, and to whom do you belong?
Having heard those words of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, he...
Ekalavya said:
"Know me to be the heroic son of Hiraṇyadhanus, the lord of the Niṣādas,
a pupil of Droṇa who has exerted himself in the science of archery."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having learned that [news] in its true essence, the Pāṇḍavas returned and related everything exactly as it had happened, including that marvel, to Droṇa.
O King, Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, remembering Ekalavya,
approached Droṇa in private and spoke these words out of affection:
"Surely, having embraced me alone with love, you once spoke these words..."

"You have said that no disciple of mine shall be superior to you; yet why is there another disciple of yours, more distinguished than I and even more heroic than anyone in the world— the son of the lord of the Niṣādas?"
Having reflected for a mere moment and reached his decision, Droṇa took Savyasācin and proceeded toward the son of the Niṣāda;
there he beheld him with limbs smeared with dirt, wearing matted hair and garments of bark.
Seeing Ekalavya with bow in hand, incessantly discharging arrows,
Ekalavya, upon seeing Droṇa approaching from nearby,
went up to him, touched his feet, and prostrated his head upon the ground.
Then, having duly honored Droṇa, that son of a Niṣāda presented himself as a pupil and stood before him with palms joined in reverence. Then,
O King, Droṇa spoke these words to Ekalavya:
"If you are my pupil, let the fee be paid quickly.
But Ekalavya, hearing this, spoke these words with joy:
"What shall I give, O Blessed One? Let the Guru command me."
"O best of those who know the Veda, there is indeed nothing that I cannot give to my teacher.
He said to him: "O Ekalavya, let your right thumb be given to me;
if it must certainly be given by you, then give it to me."
"It is my opinion that [the fee] shall be one thumb from the right hand," he said. "Very well," replied the Niṣāda; and having cut off both thumbs, he then gave them.
But Ekalavya, having heard those harsh words of Droṇa, [was overcome with grief].
Protecting his own vow and always devoted to truth, with a joyful countenance and an undepressed mind,
he cut off his own thumb and gave it to Droṇa without hesitation.
Undaunted, he cut through Droṇa’s fee and gave it to them;
seeing the Niṣāda prince true to his promise, he was pleased and said this:
"O hero, by your power you have fulfilled the desire of my preceptor."
"Thus it must be done," he said to Ekalavya.
Thereafter, however, the Niṣāda prince drew [the bow] with his fingers;
yet, O lord of men, he was not as swift as he had been before.
Then Arjuna became joyful in mind and free from distress;
Droṇa’s word had proven true, for no one else could surpass Arjuna.
Having witnessed this deed performed by us, he then [spoke].
The sky-dwellers spoke thus: "Prajñā,
Droṇa, and Pārtha—
let these wise ones go now to their own abode."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Droṇa, receiving the highest honor from the Kurus and wealth,
imparted the entire science of weapons, consisting of four divisions, to the princes.
Then the mighty princes of the Pārthiva Kṣatriya clan followed Droṇa among the Kurus, desiring to learn the science of weapons. Among them,
Yudhiṣṭhira became the best of charioteers and superior in the use of javelins.
At that time, Duryodhana and Bhīma, the two disciples of Droṇa, excelled especially in the practice of the mace among the Kurus;
however, Aśvatthāman became superior in all secret techniques.
Likewise, those two twin brothers, both armed with spears, surpassed all other men; that son of Rādhā, possessed of great strength, excelled them all in the use of *tomara* javelins.
Arjuna is the best among victors;
Yudhiṣṭhira is the best of chariot-warriors; but Dhananjaya is renowned everywhere throughout the earth bounded by the oceans as the leader of the leaders of chariot-divisions.

Through the power of his intellect, yoga, and energy, and in all weapons, Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, became distinguished by his devotion to his teacher; and though the instructions on the weapons were equal for all, the heroic one excelled through his skill.
Among all the princes, Arjuna alone was an *atiratha*;
O lord of men, the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra could not tolerate Bhīmasena, who surpassed them in strength, nor Dhanañjaya, who was accomplished in learning.
Having assembled all of them, who were proficient in every branch of knowledge, Drona— desiring to test their skill in the use of weapons, O bull among men—
had craftsmen place a lifelike decoy bird upon the top of a tree.
He taught it to the princes as something to be observed, though it was not yet understood by them.
Droṇa said:
"All of you, indeed, quickly take up your bows with haste."
"Aiming at this Bhāsa, stand ready with your arrows fixed.
At the very moment my words are spoken, let his head be struck down.
I shall assign you each one by one; act accordingly, my sons."
01.123.049 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the best of the Aṅgirases first spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O invincible one, fix your arrow and release it at the conclusion of my speech."
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, first taking up his great-sounding bow,
stood facing the bird, impelled by the words of his preceptor.
Then Droṇa [beheld] that joy of the Kurus with his bow drawn.
After a moment, O bull of the Bharata race, he spoke these words:
"O son of the best of men, do you see this bird perched on the top of the tree?
Yudhiṣṭhira replied to the teacher, "I see it."
After a mere moment, Droṇa addressed him again:
"Do you see this tree, or me, or even your brothers?
To him, that son of Kuntī replied: "I see this lord of the forest."
To him— addressing you, his brothers, and Bhāsa again and again—
Droṇa, as if displeased in mind, said,
"Withdraw! You are not capable of hitting this mark," thus reproaching him.
Then the highly illustrious one, desiring to test them, questioned Duryodhana and the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in that same sequence;
he also questioned his other disciples, Bhīma and the rest, as well as kings from other lands.
"And thus we all see everything," they said contemptuously.
Then Drona, smiling, addressed Dhanañjaya:
"Now you must strike; behold this target."
"Simultaneously with my word, an arrow must be released by you here;
O son, draw your bow and wait for a moment.
Thus addressed, Savyasācin drew his bow into a circle.
Urged by the words of his preceptor, he stood aiming at the target.
After what seemed like a mere moment, Droṇa addressed him in the same manner:
"Do you see this bird perched there, the tree, and me as well?"
"I see this bird, Bhāsa," Pārtha said to Droṇa;
"but I do not see you, sir, nor the tree," he added, O Bhārata.
Then, with a pleased mind, Droṇa [spoke] to him again after a moment.
The invincible one replied to that bull among the charioteers of the Pāṇḍavas:
"If you see this bird, then speak these words again:
'I see the head of the bird, but not its body. He said this.
Thus addressed by Arjuna, Droṇa, his hair standing on end with joy, said to Pārtha, "Release it! He released it without hesitation;
then, with that sharp razor-headed arrow, [he struck] him as he stood upon the tree.
Having swiftly severed the head, the Pāṇḍava caused it to fall. When that deed was accomplished, he embraced Phalguna; and he considered Drupada, along with his followers, defeated in battle.

Then, after some time had passed, O bull of the Bharatas, that best of the Aṅgirases, accompanied by his disciples, went to the Gaṅgā to bathe. Having plunged into the water, Droṇa was [seized] by a creature dwelling in the water.
Driven by Time, a powerful crocodile seized him by the calf of his leg.
Although he was capable of liberating himself, he urged all his disciples on, as if in haste, saying: "Kill the crocodile and set me free!"
Simultaneously with those words, Bībhatsu struck the crocodile submerged in the water with five sharp arrows from his quiver;
the others, however, were utterly bewildered and fled here and there.

And seeing him endowed with such skill, Droṇa considered the Pāṇḍava to be superior to all his disciples and was filled with joy at that time. Yet he [the Pāṇḍava] was reduced to many fragments by the arrows of Pārtha.
The crocodile met its death, having released the thigh of the high-souled one.
Then Bhāradvāja spoke to that great car-warrior, the high-souled one:
"O mighty-armed one, take this preeminent [bow] which is exceedingly difficult to withstand."
This weapon named Brahmāśiras, along with its method of employment and withdrawal,
must never be used by you against human beings under any circumstances;
for if it were discharged against one of little power, it would utterly consume the world.
"O dear one, this weapon is said to be without equal in the worlds;
you should wield it with self-restraint. Listen now to these words of mine:
O hero, whenever any non-human enemy should oppress you,"
"You should employ this weapon in battle for his destruction.
Having promised "So be it," Bībhatsu, with palms joined in reverence, took up that supreme weapon; and the Teacher spoke to him again:
"There shall be no other man in the world equal to you as an archer.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Bhārata, [having seen] the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the sons of Pāṇḍu accomplished in weapons..."
Having seen this, O King, Droṇa spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
in the presence of Kṛpa, Somadatta, the wise Bāhlīka, Gāṅgeya, Vyāsa, and Vidura.
O King, O best of the Kurus, those princes have acquired all branches of knowledge; like the Lord of Creatures presiding over the three worlds,
they should now display their training with your permission, O King.
Then the great king, with a joyful heart, said:
"O Bhāradvāja, best of the twice-born, a great deed has been performed by you!
Whenever you deem it the right time, in whatever place, and in whatever manner—"
"In whatever way you deem necessary, command me yourself. Out of despair, I long today to see my sons, who possess keen eyesight, exerting their prowess for the sake of the weapons."
"O Kṣattṛ, do exactly as the venerable teacher says;
for I do not think, O lover of dharma, that anything dearer than this will ever happen.
Then, having taken leave of the king, he went outside followed by Vidura.
The highly wise Bhāradvāja measured out the ground for the sacrificial hall according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures; he selected a site that was level,
free of trees and shrubs, and situated with a gentle slope toward the north.
On that day, under an auspicious lunar mansion and on a sacred date, he offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) upon that ground,
O best of speakers; and in the city as well, a great proclamation was made for that purpose regarding the vast arena prepared according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures.
O bull among men, there the artisans constructed a well-arranged viewing hall for the king, equipped with all kinds of weapons, as well as for the women; and,
desiring to see them, he erected spacious platforms for the spectators.
On that day, when it had arrived, the king together with his ministers then had the local people construct platforms there— extensive and provided with high elevations— as well as costly palanquins.
Then, with the approval of Vyāsa, he [Yudhiṣṭhira], together with his inner apartments and his ministers,
placed Bhīṣma at the head, along with Kṛpa, the best of teachers,
as well as Bāhlīka, Somadatta, and Bhūriśravas.
Taking the Kurus and his other ministers outside the city,
the king, accompanied by the brahmins, reached the arena,
which was draped with nets of pearls and adorned with lapis lazuli gems.
He arrived at a divine assembly hall made of gold.
O best among victors, the highly fortunate Gāndhārī and Kuntī,
along with all the women of the king, including their attendants and retinues, were there as well.
In their joy, they ascended the platforms like the celestial women ascending Mount Meru;
and the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, quickly came from the city,
desiring to behold the mastery of weapons by the princes.
In an instant, desiring to see him, he went to that place where they were gathered;
with musical instruments being played and because of the people's curiosity,
that assembly then became as turbulent as a great ocean.
Then the preceptor, wearing white garments, with a white sacred thread,
white hair, and a white beard, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
entered the center of the arena together with his son.
Like the moon accompanied by Mars when the sky is devoid of clouds,
that best among the powerful performed his sacrificial offering according to the prescribed time;
and there, he had the Brahmins, who were masters of the mantras, recite auspicious blessings.
The king bestowed as sacrificial fees gold, gems, jewels, and various kinds of garments upon Droṇa and Kṛpa;
and immediately after that auspicious proclamation of the merit of the day, there followed the sound of the sacred recitation.

Taking up various weapons and implements, the men entered; then those mighty bulls of the Bharata race, having donned their armor, fastened their waist-bands, and equipped themselves with quivers and bows, entered.
Then those bulls among men, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, having saluted Droṇa as he stood in the midst of the arena according to their seniority,
paid him due honor, as well as Kṛpa, in accordance with the prescribed rules.
With blessings uttered, all were delighted in their minds;
having again saluted the weapons, which had been worshipped with offerings and flowers,
the Kauravas themselves honored them with red sandalwood paste mixed [with other perfumes].
Anointed with red sandalwood and wearing red garlands,
all of them bearing red banners and having eyes reddened at the corners,
those subduers of enemies took up their weapons, permitted by Droṇa.
First taking up their bows adorned with refined gold,
the Kauravas readied their weapons of various forms and, fixing them with arrows,
honored all beings by making the sound of their bowstrings and the slapping of their palms.
All those bulls among men moved along the paths of their weapons as they were discharged;
the princes of great prowess performed most wonderful feats with their missiles.
O King, in some places, arrows fell at the roots of trees.
In some cases, arrows fell upon flower crowns;
others struck their targets with various shafts marked by the signs of impact, piercing both heavy and light objects with ease through their swift release.
Some men lowered their heads out of fear of being struck by arrows;
others, filled with wonder, looked on boldly.
They pierced the targets with arrows adorned with their own names.
Carried swiftly by horses released with various displays of agility,
that army of youths, grasping their bows and arrows,
appeared like a city of the Gandharvas; seeing this, they were filled with wonder.

O Bhārata, hundreds of thousands of men there suddenly cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! their eyes wide with wonder, after he had repeatedly displayed his skill upon the bow and in the maneuvers of the chariot.
Possessing great strength on the backs of elephants and horses, and in hand-to-hand combat,
they took up swords and shields and, thereafter, struck out again;
they moved across all terrains according to the prescribed methods of drawing the sword from its scabbard.
They all beheld therein the agility, grace, splendor, steadiness, and firmness of grip displayed by everyone in the practice with sword and shield.
Then those two, Suyodhana and Vṛkodara, who were ever joyful, [prepared for battle].
Having descended, mace in hand, they were like two single-peaked mountains;
with their girdles fastened and their mighty arms bared, they stood firm in their manly prowess, trumpeting like two rutting elephants for the sake of a female.
Those two of great strength, wielding spotless maces, moved in circles to the right and to the left like two rutting bull elephants.
Vidura [reported this] to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the son of Pāṇḍu to Gāndhārī.
They reported all those actions of the princes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While the Kuru king was present in the arena, as was Bhīma, the foremost among the strong...
The people there were divided into two groups by their affection born of partiality;
from those crying out, "Alas, O hero, O King of the Kurus! and "Alas, O Bhīma!", a massive clamor suddenly arose among the men.
Then, beholding the arena resembling an agitated ocean,
the wise son of Bharadvāja spoke to his beloved son Aśvatthāman:
"Restrain both of these men of great prowess, who are equally well-trained."
"Let there not be this provocation on the stage arising from Bhīma and Duryodhana.
Then Aśvatthāman rose up with speed and restrained him, saying, "O Gāndhārī's son, it is the command of the preceptor; it is the preceptor’s instruction that Bhīma [be spared]."
"Enough with this forceful display of skill! Enough with such rashness!"—
thus spoke the son of the preceptor as he restrained those two,
who were like two oceans of great velocity agitated by the winds at the end of an eon, with their maces raised high.
Then, having entered the arena, Droṇa spoke these words,
silencing the ensemble of musical instruments whose sound was like the roar of a great cloud:
"He who is dearer to me than my own son, the best among all those skilled in weapons— "
"Let that son of Pṛthā, who is equal to Indra’s younger brother [Arjuna], be seen!"— at these words of the teacher, the youth then had the rites for success performed;
he donned his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, and equipped with a full quiver and his bow, he set forth.
Wearing golden armor, Phalguna appeared like a cloud at twilight, accompanied by the sun, Indra’s bow, and lightning. Then,
a great tumult arose from the entire assembly.
And musical instruments, along with conchs, were sounded on all sides:
"This is the illustrious son of Kuntī; this is the middle Pandava;
this is the son of Mahendra; this is the protector of the Kurus."
He is the foremost among those skilled in weapons; he is the best among the upholders of dharma. He is also the supreme treasury of virtue and knowledge among the virtuous;
he is the very life of Kaṃsa’s slayer, his friend as dear to him as his own soul.
"He shall reach the further shore of whatever he promises"—
as Kuntī heard these incomparable words uttered by the spectators, her chest became drenched with tears mingled with the flow of her milk.
Then, his ears filled with that great sound,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the best of men, spoke with a joyful heart to Vidura:
"O Kṣattṛ, what is this immense noise, resembling the agitated ocean?"
Suddenly rising up on the stage as if splitting the very vault of heaven,
Vidura said:
"O great king, this is Pārtha Phalguna, the son of Pāṇḍu."
Having descended there clad in armor, he let out a very great roar.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O high-minded one, I am blessed, I am favored, and I am protected."
By the three Pāṇḍava fires produced from the friction-stick of Pṛthā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When that assembly had somehow been gathered together and settled, it was as follows.
Bībhatsu displayed his dexterity with weapons before the teacher:
with the Āgneya weapon he created fire, with the Vāruṇa weapon he created water,
with the Vāyavya weapon he created wind, and with the Pārjanya weapon he created clouds.
With the *bhauma* weapon he entered the earth; with the *pārvaṇa* weapon he created mountains;
and by means of the *antardhāna* weapon, he became invisible once more.
In one moment he was tall, in another short, and in another moment he stood upon the pole of his chariot.

In one moment standing upon his chariot, in the next he descended to the earth; and he, who was dear to his preceptor, being endowed with great skill, pierced various targets— whether delicate, subtle, or heavy—
with diverse arrows.
And as the boar was running,
he released five arrows in quick succession from his bow, which were unattached to one another yet appeared like a single shaft,
at the head of the iron [target] suspended by a rope and moving within the hollow of a cow-horn.
The one of great prowess buried twenty-one arrows; such were the many great feats he performed with his sword and bow, while,
skilled in weapons, he displayed various maneuvers with his mace.
He displayed his dexterity in the use of the discus, the *tomara* spear, and the noose, as well as the *bhiṇḍipāla* javelin and the battle-axe,
and in the training of other weapons too.
Then, O Bhārata, when that performance was almost completed—
When the assembly had grown quiet and the sound of musical instruments had subsided,
there was heard from the gateway a sound of arms like the crash of a thunderbolt, signaling his greatness and power.
That sound was exceedingly great, as if filling the two worlds;
"Are the mountains splitting? Is the earth being torn asunder?
Or is the sky being filled with clouds dense with the weight of water?"
O lord of the earth, in an instant such was the thought that arose among the spectators;
then all the onlookers turned toward the gate.
Surrounded by the five Pārtha brothers, Droṇa shone resplendent.
Joined with Pañcatāra, like the moon with the constellation Sāvitra,
he surrounded the hundred powerful brothers led by Duryodhana— the slayer of enemies— who had risen up together with Aśvatthāman.
Surrounded by those brothers who stood with their weapons raised, he remained with mace in hand;
he shone like [Viṣṇu] in ancient times at the destruction of the Dānavas.
Puraṃdara, surrounded by the hosts of gods—
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time, in that gathering of people...
When space had been granted by the men whose eyes were wide with wonder,
Karṇa, the conqueror of enemy cities, entered the vast arena,
wearing his natural armor and his face illuminated by his earrings.
With bow in hand and sword girded, he was like a mountain walking on foot;
born from the womb of a maiden, the son of Pṛthā, of wide fame and large eyes,
Karṇa— the slayer of enemy hosts— is a portion of the sun, the sharp-rayed Bhāskara.
Equal in vigor and prowess to lions, bulls, and lordly elephants, he was like the sun, the moon, and fire in his qualities of brilliance, beauty,
and luster; tall as a golden palm tree, the youth possessed the powerful build of a lion.
The illustrious son of the Sun-god, possessed of countless virtues,
being mighty-armed, surveyed the entire arena from all sides and offered salutations to Droṇa and Kṛpa that appeared somewhat lacking in formal respect.
That entire assembly became motionless, their eyes fixed;
overcome with agitation, they were filled with curiosity, wondering, "Who is this?
Then that best of speakers addressed them in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
"O Pārtha, son of Sāvitrī, you who are like Indra, brother to your unknown brother—
whatever extraordinary deed you have performed, I shall do even more than that before the eyes of men; do not be filled with pride within yourself."
Then, O best of speakers, before his speech was finished,
the entire assembly rose up quickly as if propelled by a machine;
and, O tiger among men, joy then took hold of Duryodhana.
Shame and anger entered Bibhatsu in an instant.
Then, permitted by Droṇa, Karṇa, who always delights in battle,
performed there whatever was done by Pārtha, for he was possessed of great strength.
Then, O Bhārata, Duryodhana, together with his brothers, embraced Karṇa with joy and spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one! By good fortune have you arrived, O giver of honor."
"Both I and the Kuru kingdom shall be enjoyed as you desire.
Karṇa said:
"I have had enough of everything else; I choose only friendship with you."
"O Bhārata, I wish to engage in a duel with Pārtha.
When Karna had spoken thus, King Duryodhana then embraced Karna,
whose long arms were well-rounded, and said this to him:
Duryodhana said:
"Enjoy pleasures together with me; be a bringer of joy to your kinsmen.
O subduer of enemies, place your foot upon the heads of all those who bear you ill will."
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
regarding himself as if insulted, Pārtha addressed Karṇa,
who stood like a mountain in the midst of his assembly of brothers.
"O Karṇa, you shall go to those worlds that belong to those who approach uninvited and those who converse uninvited; slain by me, you shall attain them. Karṇa said:
"This arena is common to all; what is there for you here, O Phalguna?
Among the Kṣatriyas, valor is supreme, and righteousness follows strength. Brāhmaṇas are said to possess the power of speech, and Vaiśyas possess the power of wealth."
The Śūdras were ordained by the supreme Brahmā to be those whose strength lies in labor. O Bhārata, what is the use of these feeble, breathless reproaches with your arrows?
Tell me, for today I shall take away your head with my shafts right before your preceptor.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, permitted by Droṇa, Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities,
was embraced with haste by his brothers and advanced toward him for battle.
Then Karna, standing ready for battle with his bow grasped and arrows fixed, was embraced by Duryodhana along with his brothers. Thereupon,
[the sky was filled] with lightning and thunder, accompanied by Indra’s bow and swift portents.
The sky was covered with clouds that seemed to laugh with rows of white cranes;
then, out of affection upon seeing the sun-horsed god (Agni) watching the arena,
the Sun-god (Bhāskara) caused the clouds nearby to vanish.
Then the Pāṇḍava was seen shrouded by the shadow of clouds,
while Karṇa was also clearly visible, surrounded by the sun’s rays;
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remained stationed in that region where Karṇa stood.
Bhāradvāja, Kṛpa, and Bhīṣma turned wherever Pārtha went;
the assembly was split in two, and a division arose among the women.
The daughter of Kuntibhoja, having understood the situation, fell into a swoon.
Vidura, the knower of all dharma, comforted Kuntī, who was thus overwhelmed by delusion, by sprinkling her with water scented with sandalwood. Thereupon,
having regained her senses, she saw that both of them were clad in armor.
Seeing her two sons, she was deeply distressed and did not know what to do.
Then Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat— who was skilled in the conduct of duels and knew all the laws of righteousness— spoke to those two who stood with their great bows raised.
"This youngest son of Pṛthā, the joy of Pāṇḍu and a Kaurava, shall engage in a duel with you. You too, O mighty-armed one, [consider] your mother, your father, and your lineage."
"Tell [us] of those kings, O enhancer of their lineages, for whom you are the progenitor;
then, having learned this, the son of Pṛthā will decide whether or not he shall fight against you.
Sons of kings do not fight with those whose family traditions are in vain."
When Karna had been addressed in this way, his face, bowed down with shame,
shone like a fallen lotus wet with rainwater.
Duryodhana said:
O Teacher, according to the determination of the treatises, there are three sources for kings:
one born of that same lineage, a hero, and one who leads the army.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone.

"Their all-pervading energy is extinguished within their own wombs if this Phalguna does not wish to fight against one who is not a king. Therefore, he shall be consecrated by me to the kingdom in the territory of Aṅga."
Then, having taken leave of the king and his grandfather, the son of Gaṅgā,
he had the twice-born gather the requisites for the consecration and gave ten million cows to those of meritorious deeds who were so engaged.
"He is worthy of the kingdom of Aṅga"—thus it was to be declared by the twice-born.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, at that moment, Karṇa [was honored] with jars containing parched grain and flowers.
On a golden throne made of gold, the great chariot-warrior, possessed of great strength and endowed with splendor, was consecrated in the kingdom of Aṅga by those learned in the mantras;
he was adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and hand-ornaments.
Adorned with the insignia of royalty and other auspicious ornaments, and accompanied by the royal umbrella and yak-tail fan amidst shouts of "Victory!",
King Vṛṣa then spoke to that Kaurava king.
Being honored by the brahmins and having bestowed immeasurable wealth, [the king said]:
"O tiger among kings, tell me what I may give you that is equal to this gift of sovereignty; for I shall do so, O monarch."
"I desire eternal friendship," Suyodhana said to him;
thus addressed, Karṇa then replied, "So be it," O Vaiśampāyana.
Having given the King of Aṅga the appropriate royal regalia,
they both embraced him with joy and attained supreme delight.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Adhiratha entered the arena, his upper garment slipping, perspiring and trembling, his life-breath sustained only by a staff, as if calling out [to his son].
Seeing him, [Arjuna], constrained by respect for his father, cast aside his bow.
With his head still wet from the consecration, Karṇa bowed his head in salutation.
Then, hurriedly covering [Karṇa’s] feet with the hem of his garment,
the charioteer addressed him, fulfilling his desire, saying, "O son!"
Then, overcome with affection, he embraced his head and again drenched it with tears,
which were moist from the consecration for the kingdom of Aṅga.
Seeing him, the Pāṇḍava concluded, "This is the son of a charioteer."
Then Bhīmasena spoke these words as if laughing:
"O son of a Sūta, you do not deserve death at the hands of Pārtha in battle;
you are worthy of your own lineage. Take up the whip immediately!"
"O lowest of men, you do not deserve to enjoy the kingdom of Aṅga,
just as a dog does not deserve the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) placed near the fire at a sacrifice.
When he was addressed thus, Karṇa’s lower lip quivered slightly.
Sighing, he gazed up at the sun situated in the sky;
then the mighty Duryodhana sprang up in anger from that lotus-forest of his brothers, like an elephant intoxicated with rut.
He spoke to Bhīmasena, who stood there performing terrible deeds:
"O Vṛkodara, it is not fitting for you to speak such words.
For Kṣatriyas, strength is paramount; one must fight with a fellow of the warrior class."
The origins of heroes and of rivers are indeed difficult to discern.
From the waters arose fire, by which the world of moving and unmoving beings is pervaded;
and from the bones of Dadhīca was fashioned the thunderbolt that destroys the Dānavas.

The Lord Guha is heard of as being born of Agni, the son of Kṛttikā, and as the son of Rudra and Gaṅgā; he is the divine one who embodies all secrets. And those who were born from Kṣatriya women but became Brāhmaṇas are likewise renowned.
Viśvāmitra and others attained the imperishable state of Brahmanhood;
they say these were born of Kṣatriya women by Brāhmaṇas during the decline of the Kṣatriyas. The Teacher (Vasiṣṭha) was born from a water-jar, and the preceptor Kṛpa from a clump of reeds.
Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons,
was born in the lineage of Gautama; and how you yourselves were born has also been learned by the kings.
"How can a doe give birth to a tiger, resplendent like the sun, adorned with earrings and armor, and marked with divine characteristics?
The charioteer shall beget him."

Thus, this lord of men, endowed with the qualities of a kṣatriya and appearing resplendent in assembly, is worthy of the sovereignty of the entire earth, not merely the kingdom of Aṅga; for he possesses such strength of arm, and I am ever obedient to his command.
"Or if there is any man who does not tolerate this deed of mine, let him mount a chariot or, on foot, bend the bow! At that, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the entire assembly.
Accompanied by shouts of "Well done!", the sun went down.
Then, O King, Duryodhana, taking Karna by the hand,
departed from that arena, illuminated by the light of the lamps' fires.
O lord of the people, the Pāṇḍavas, together with Droṇa and Kṛpa,
all accompanied by Bhīṣma, went each to his own quarters. O Bhārata, some among the people cried out, "Arjuna!", while others cried, "Karṇa!"
Then, calling out "O Duryodhana!",
they set forth; and Kuntī, recognizing her son— the lord of Aṅga— by his divine marks, felt her love for him increase, though she remained concealed by affection.
O King, when Duryodhana had obtained Karna at that time,
the fear born of Arjuna quickly vanished from him.
And that hero was one who had completed his training in the use of weapons.
He addressed Suyodhana with great conciliation;
at that time, Yudhiṣṭhira also thought:
"There is no archer on earth equal to Karṇa."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Droṇa, having summoned all his disciples without exception,
and having observed that both the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were proficient in the use of weapons, [spoke].
When the time for the teacher’s fee had arrived, the preceptor reflected upon it;
then the preceptor urged his disciples, who were now masters of weapons, saying,
"Having gathered the disciples together, urge them toward the purpose of the teacher."
When they had completed their training in weaponry and arrived at Gaṅgādvāra,
Bhāradvāja then addressed them all:
"I desire that you grant me, acting together, a most excellent sacrificial fee."

Thus addressed, those disciples then approached Droṇa and said, "O Blessed One, what shall we give? Let our preceptor command us. O lord of the earth, Droṇa [spoke] to them all without exception regarding the matter of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

"Having captured Drupada, the king of the Pañcālas, at the head of the battle, bring him back—may prosperity be yours; that shall be your supreme sacrificial fee. Having said, "So be it," all those strikers quickly departed on their chariots.
They went together with Droṇa for the purpose of giving the preceptor’s fee;
then those bulls among men proceeded toward the Pañcālas, slaughtering [the enemy].
Arjuna—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Duryodhana, Karṇa, the mighty Yuyutsu,
Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, Jalasaṃdha, and Sulocana.
These and many other youths of great prowess, those bulls among the Kṣatriyas, cried out, "I first! I first! Then there were multitudes of chariots, infantry, elephants, and horsemen.
Having entered the city, they all proceeded along the royal highway.
At that time, the King of Pañcāla, having heard of and seen the great force,
went out from his palace in haste accompanied by his brothers.
Then, having donned their armor, the brothers of Yajñasena,
discharging showers of arrows, roared in every direction;
thereafter, they encountered the Kauravas in a brilliant chariot.
The invincible Yajñasena rained down terrible arrows in battle.
But Pārtha, having already deliberated with Droṇa, then said to him:
"O best of the twice-born, the pride and arrogance of these princes is irresistible."
"At the end of their prowess, we shall perform our own bold deed;
the Pāñcāla prince cannot be captured at the head of the battle by these youths.
Having spoken thus, the sinless son of Kuntī, together with his brothers, [prepared for action].
At a distance of half a *krośa* from the city, Drupada remained stationed outside;
seeing the Kauravas, he rushed forward from all sides,
bewildering the Kaurava army with a great net of arrows.
As he advanced alone in his chariot, acting with such swiftness in battle,
all the Kauravas, out of sheer terror, perceived him as if he were many.
Drupada’s terrible arrows coursed in every direction.
Then, O Great King, thousands of conchs, kettledrums, and clay drums were sounded in the camp of the Pāñcālas,
and a lion’s roar arose from those high-souled Pāñcālas.
The sound of bowstrings slapping against palms reached the vast sky;
then Duḥśāsana, Vikarṇa, Subāhu, Dīrghalocana,
and the enraged Duryodhana covered him with showers of arrows.
O Bhārata, that great archer, the son of Pṛṣata, who was difficult to defeat in battle, having been deeply pierced, instantly scattered those armies—
Duryodhana, Vikarṇa, and the mighty Karṇa as well.
Moving like a whirling circle of fire, he gratified the various heroic sons of kings and the diverse armies with his arrows. Then all the citizens, clubs and staffs in hand, [advanced].
They rained [arrows] upon the Kauravas like clouds pouring rain;
then the people of Kāmpilya, including both children and the elderly, marched against the Kauravas.
And having heard of that tumultuous battle, O Bhārata, the citizens [also gathered].
They rushed forward, crying out and shouting toward the Pāṇḍavas.
But the Pāṇḍavas, hearing that hair-raising clamor of the distressed,
then saluted Droṇa and mounted their chariots.
Having quickly restrained Yudhiṣṭhira, saying "Do not fight," O Pāṇḍava,
Phalguna then made the two sons of Mādrī the protectors of his wheels;
Bhīmasena, with mace in hand, stood roaring at the head of the army.
Then, having sounded his conch, the sinless son of Kuntī, accompanied by his brothers,
advanced with speed, making the earth resound with the roar of his chariot;
he then approached the army of the Pāñcālas, which possessed the sound of a surging ocean.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena, like Death himself with staff in hand,
entered the great army as a makara enters the ocean;
wielding his mace, Bhīma personally rushed against the elephant division.
Skilled in combat and peerless in the strength of his arms, Pārtha,
assuming the form of Death himself, struck down the elephant division with his mace.
Those elephants, resembling mountains, vomited forth copious amounts of blood.
With their frontal globes split by Bhīmasena’s mace,
elephants fell to the earth like mountains struck by a thunderbolt;
the Pāṇḍava brought down elephants, horses, and chariots alike.
The elder brother of Arjuna did not slay the foot soldiers or the citizens,
just as a cowherd with his staff drives herds of cattle in the forest; Vṛkodara moved about, driving away the chariots, elephants, and horses.
Then Phalguna, the son of Pandu, intent on doing what was pleasing to Bharadvāja’s son,
quickly covered the son of Pṛṣata with a net of arrows,
as well as the multitudes of horses, elephants, and chariots on all sides.
O King, felling [his foes] in battle like the blazing fire at the end of an eon,
the Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas, being thus slaughtered,
quickly covered Pārtha from all sides with various kinds of arrows.
Uttering lion-like roars, they fought against the son of Pāṇḍu;
that battle was terrible and most wonderful to behold.
Hearing the sound of those lion-roars, Dhanañjaya could not endure it.
Then Kirīṭin suddenly rushed toward the Pāñcāla prince,
covering him with a great net of arrows as if to bewilder him,
while he was swiftly discharging and incessantly fixing his shafts.
Not the slightest interval could be seen around the illustrious son of Kuntī;
neither the cardinal directions, nor the intermediate space, nor the earth itself—
nothing at all could be discerned there in that battle, O great king.

When the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow created a darkness with his arrows, a great roar of "Excellent! Excellent! arose from both the Pāñcālas and the Kurus, followed by the sound of trumpets and the loud blast of conch shells.
And a lion’s roar arose, mingled with shouts of "Excellent!
Then the King of Pañcāla, together with Satyajit,
rushed forward in haste like Śambara against Mahendra.
With a great shower of arrows, the son of Pṛthā overwhelmed the prince of the Pañcālas. Then a tumultuous roar arose among the Pañcāla forces,
like that of a great lion seeking to seize the leader of a herd of elephants.
Seeing Pārtha approaching, Satyajit, whose prowess is truth,
desiring to protect the Pañcāla prince, rushed toward Dhanañjaya;
then Arjuna and the Pañcāla prince came together for battle.
Those two agitated the armies like Indra and Virocana.
Then, O King, Pārtha powerfully pierced Satyajit with ten arrows that pierce the vital organs; it was like a marvel.
Then the Pāñcāla swiftly afflicted the son of Pṛthā with hundreds of arrows;
but the great car-warrior Pārtha, being covered by that shower of shafts,
wiped his bowstring and, possessing great speed himself, exerted his own momentum.
Then, having severed Satyajit’s bow, he rushed toward the king.
Thereupon, taking up another more powerful bow,
Satyajit swiftly pierced Pārtha along with his horses, charioteer, and chariot.
Pārtha could not endure that he had been struck by the Pāñcāla in battle;
thereupon, for the sake of his destruction, he swiftly discharged arrows at his horses,
his standard, his bow-grip, and both his outrider-charioteers.
As his bows were thus broken again and again and his horses were cut down, he turned away from the battle.
Beholding Satyajit thus turning his back on the field of combat, [he pursued him].
With great speed, O King, he rushed toward the son of Pṛṣata;
then Arjuna, the best among victors, engaged in a great battle with him. Pārtha brought down his banner, his umbrella, and his bow to the earth.
With five arrows he pierced his horses and his charioteer;
then, casting aside that bow and taking up a quiver,
the son of Kuntī drew his sword and let out a lion’s roar.
Leaping onto the shaft of the Pāñcāla’s chariot, Dhananjaya suddenly roared; then, remaining undaunted,
he seized that chariot just as Tārkṣya seizes a serpent after agitating the ocean.
Then all the Pāñcālas fled in the ten directions; meanwhile,
Dhananjaya, displaying the strength of his own arms to all the troops,
let out a lion’s roar and emerged.
Seeing Arjuna approaching, the princes then united and laid siege to the city of the high-souled Drupada;
for Drupada, the best of kings, was a kinsman of the Kuru heroes.
"Do not slay that force, O Bhīma; let a heavy gift be bestowed. Then, O King, the great car-warrior Bhīmasena, though unsated in the duties of battle, was restrained by Arjuna and turned back.
They crushed the city of that Drupada of great prowess.
Having captured Yajñasena Drupada at the head of the battle along with his ministers, those bulls of the Bharata race brought him before Droṇa.
His pride shattered, his wealth taken, and thus brought under his control,
Droṇa, brooding over their enmity in his mind, said to Drupada:
"Having crushed your kingdom by force, your city has been laid waste by me."
"Having fallen alive into the power of the enemy, what is desired from one who was formerly a friend?
Having spoken thus, he laughed at him and, having made his resolve, spoke again:
"Do not fear for your life, O King; we brahmins are forgiving."
O bull among kṣatriyas, because of that play which we engaged in together during our childhood in the hermitage, my affection for you has grown;
O bull among men, I seek friendship with you once again.
"I grant you a boon, O King; receive half of the kingdom.
Indeed, one who is not a king does not deserve to be a friend of kings.
Therefore, O Yajñasena, I have striven for this kingdom of yours."
"You are the king on the southern bank of the Bhāgīrathī, and I am on the northern. Know me as your friend, O Pāñcāla, if you so deem it fit.
Drupada said:
"O Brahmin, this is no wonder among those high-souled ones who possess such prowess;
I am pleased with you, and I desire from you a friendship that is eternal.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, O Bhārata, Droṇa released him;
and having honored him with a joyful heart, he bestowed upon him half of the kingdom,
namely Mākandī, which lay on the bank of the Gaṅgā and was filled with many districts.
With a dejected mind, he dwelt in Kāmpilya, the best of cities,
as well as in the southern Pañcāla country as far as the river Carmaṇvatī;
for Drupada, remembering his enmity with Droṇa, could find no peace.
And by means of his kṣatriya power, he saw no possibility of defeat; yet,
perceiving himself to be inferior in brahminical power,
that king, desiring the birth of a son, maintained his resolve.
And Droṇa took possession of the district of Ahicchatra.
Thus, O King, the city of Ahicchatrā, together with its surrounding countryside,
having been conquered in battle by Pārtha, was handed over to Droṇa.
Vaiśampāyana; Pṛṣatī;
Yāja.
Vaiśampāyana;
Janamejaya;
Vaiśampāyana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Remembering his enmity with Droṇa, Drupada could not sleep;
and by means of his Kṣatriya strength, he hoped for Droṇa’s defeat and destruction.
Having realized himself to be inferior in both spiritual power and physical strength to the Brahmin,
King Drupada, out of indignation and seeking the success of his undertaking, wandered through many dwellings of the twice-born in search of that best of brahmins.
"There is no offspring superior to me; fie upon my kinsmen! he said.
Indeed, he was consumed by sighs, desiring to do what was unpleasant for Droṇa:
"I have no friends in this world, nor is there anyone as valiant."
Desiring indeed the birth of a son, he searched this entire earth;
yet, despite striving to achieve it through Droṇa’s power, training, discipline, and the strength of his weapons, he was unable to bring about his defeat.
Then, wandering about on the bank of the Gaṅgā near the dappled cow,
that lord of the earth reached a holy dwelling of brahmins.
There, there was no twice-born man who had not completed his student vows, nor any who was without religious observances.
In that very same way, the son of Pṛṣata beheld those two illustrious Brahman-sages, Yāja and Upayāja,
who were firm in their vows, exerting themselves in the study of the Saṃhitās, and who by lineage were also both Kāśyapas.
In the forest, those two brahmins, the best of sages, were appropriately engaged; he,
unwearied, invited them with all objects of desire,
having perceived their strength and intelligence near the younger one.
Desiring to win him over with all manner of pleasures, he sought refuge with Upayāja, who was firm in his vows;
for he was devoted to serving his guru, acting for his pleasure, and granting every wish,
honoring him with water for the feet, a seat, the respectful offering (arghya), and fruits.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rule, Upayāja then said:
"For what specific purpose do you desire us?
From where does this mobilization come? May your lordship tell us."
Having understood that supreme sage’s words filled with joy,
Drupada then spoke to the ascetic, seeking to entice him with objects of desire:
"O Brahmin, by what ritual may I have a son who will be the death of Droṇa?"
"Whichever woman of excellent complexion shall become the wife of Arjuna— O Upayāja, perform this service for me, and I shall give you a hundred million cows.
Thus addressed by him, the ṛṣi replied to him once again.
"O Drupada, I do not seek any reward; he who would seek one should go there. Thus rejected by him in the presence of virtuous men, Drupada then began to attend upon him, desiring to win his favor."
Then, at the end of a year, Upayāja, the best of the twice-born, addressed these words to Drupada at the proper time in a sweet voice:
"While wandering by a forest waterfall, my eldest brother seized [a deer]."
Following after my brother, I saw that fruit fallen upon ground where purity was not maintained; yet he would never,
under any circumstances, have entertained any hesitation regarding the taking of that fruit.
He who, having seen the fruit [of ritual action], did not perceive its subsequent defects,
how could he ever distinguish [the true] purpose of purity even in other matters?
Having explained the five sacrifices at the conclusion of the study of the *Saṃhitā*, [he proceeds].
Eating from time to time that alms-food gathered by gleaning,
O royal sage, he would repeatedly speak of the flavor of the meal,
even while dwelling in the forest hermitage and engaged in the study of the *Saṃhitā*.
At that time, he would constantly eat the alms-food left over by others,
repeatedly praising the qualities of the food with great joy. Therefore,
by the eye of my reasoning, I consider him to have been one who sought only the fruits [of his actions].
"O King, you should indeed go to him; he will perform the sacrifice for you.
Hearing Upayāja’s words, King Drupada, who was conversant with all duties, felt loathing for the impure destiny resulting from such fruits [of the sacrifice].

Having honored the sage Yāja, who was worthy of worship, he spoke to him: "O Lord, I give you eight thousand cows; O Yāja, perform a sacrifice for me, for I am distressed, having come to you for refuge after being tormented by the enmity with Droṇa."

A Kshatriya cannot conquer a Kshatriya who has been incited by a mere Brahmin; therefore, you ought to protect me here, for I am afflicted by the fear of Drona. You should gladden me, who have been scorched by the fire of Bharadvaja’s son.
For he is the best among the knowers of Brahman and unsurpassed even in the weapons of the Kṣatriyas; therefore,
let Droṇa not defeat me for the sake of a dispute with a friend,
for there is no leading Kṣatriya on earth who is his equal.

The net of arrows belonging to the wise Droṇa, the preeminent teacher of the Bhāratas and son of Bharadvāja— arrows that snatch away the bodies of enemies— and his six-cubit bow and his great, incomparable sword.
For that high-minded son of Bharadvāja moves about having undoubtedly struck down the Kṣatriya force with the power of a Brāhmaṇa; indeed,
he is equal to Kārtavīrya or even comparable to Khaṭvāṅga.
Indeed, the power of the Brahman has now been joined with the force of the Kṣatriya;
for I consider the illustrious son of Bharadvāja to have become like the son of Jamadagni, raised up and intent upon the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.

Neither missiles, nor spears, nor swords could prevail against him; for his Brahman-splendor would consume them, just as oblations poured with mantras consume [the fire]. Indeed, the terrible power of his weapons was irresistible by others on earth.
Having encountered his enemies, he conquers them by placing the duty of the Kṣatriya at the forefront;
yet when Brahmanical power and Kṣatriya power are united, the splendor of Brahman prevails.
Thus, being deficient in the strength of the Kṣatriya, I have sought refuge in the splendor of Brahman.
Having approached you, who are superior to Droṇa and the most eminent among those who know the Veda,
may I obtain a son who is invincible in battle and who shall be the death of Droṇa;
may a heroic son be born to me today as the very death of Droṇa.
"O Yāja, perform that rite for me; I shall offer up Arbuda as a sacrifice of cattle.
Having said "So be it," Yāja spoke these words regarding the purpose of the sacrifice:
"Do not fear; I shall provide a son for you through this ritual."
"Arise quickly and without distraction, and prepare the necessary materials.
Having spoken thus and made his promise, the sage undertook the ritual;
Yāja officiated for that king in order to destroy Droṇa.
While performing the ritual for his preceptor’s sake, Upayāja,
a man of great asceticism, approached Yāja and then explained the Vaitāna sacrifice to that lord of men for the purpose of obtaining a son.

And that son, O King, shall be of great heroism, great splendor, and great strength; he will be exactly as you desire him to be. Having resolved upon the slayer of Bhāradvāja, that lord of the earth [spoke thus].
Drupada prepared that sacrifice for the successful accomplishment of his task;
and a Brahmin, the best among bipeds, offered the oblations according to the prescribed rites.
For him, who was longing for a son, they performed that rite known as the Kaukilī.
Then, at that time, during the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the officiating priest approached his wife;
at the conclusion of the oblation, he then called out to the queen:
"Come, O Queen Pṛṣatī! A pair has presented itself before you."
The prince and the princess were born for the increase of their father’s lineage.
My mouth is indeed not smeared with [worldly] things; I bear only meritorious fragrances. I am not your wife for the sake of procreation; stay, O Yaja, for my sake, my dear one.
The oblation cooked by the *yāja* and consecrated by the *upayāja*—how could it not fulfill one's desire? Whether you go forth or stay, O spotted cow!
When this had been said, the sacrificial offering was offered and consecrated by the *yāja*.
From that fire arose a youth equal to a god,
having the form of a flame and a terrible complexion, wearing a diadem and armor;
a hero equipped with sword, arrows, and bow, he roared repeatedly.
He ascended that excellent chariot and set forth with it at that time.
And as soon as the prince was born, an invisible voice spoke:
"This one shall become both the disciple and the death of Bhāradvāja."
