Then the Pāñcālas, filled with joy, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
For this prince, the dispeller of fear and the bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas, has been born as the remover of the king's grief for the sake of slaying Droṇa.
Thus spoke that great being, invisible and moving through the sky, at that time.
And when the oblation had been offered and consecrated with mantras during the second *hotrā*,
the princess of Pañcāla arose from the center of the sacrificial altar.
O bull of the Bharatas, when the Pṛṣatī had rejected the officiating priest,
that most fortunate maiden, the daughter of the Pañcāla king, who was born from the middle of the sacrificial altar,
emerged as a most enchanting girl within the Vedic enclosure.
Dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals and dark, curly hair,
she was a woman of celestial beauty who had assumed a human form;
her fragrance, equal to that of the blue lotus, wafted for a full *krośa*.

She who bears a supreme form, for whom there is no comparison on earth, desired by gods, dānavas, and yakṣas— she, the goddess-like woman with beautiful hips, was born, and an incorporeal voice spoke to her.
Kṛṣṇā, the most excellent of all women, desires to bring about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas. At the proper time, this woman of slender waist will accomplish the work of the gods;
for her sake, a great fear shall arise among the Kṣatriyas.
Hearing this, all the Pāñcālas roared like a pride of lions;
the earth could not bear them as they were so filled with joy.
Thus was a pair born to the high-souled Drupada.
O bull of the Bharatas, at that time there was a prince and a princess, both charming and endowed with supreme splendor and the physical form of a Kṣatriya. O King,
seeing them, Pṛṣatī, desiring sons, approached them.
"Let these two not know of any mother other than me," she said;
Yāja replied "So be it" to her, desiring to do what was pleasing to the king.
Then the twice-born ones, their hearts fulfilled, bestowed names upon the two of them.

"Because of his boldness (*dhṛṣṭatva*), because he is invincible (*apradhṛṣyatva*), and because of his splendor (*dyumna*) arising from *dharma*, let this boy be Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Drupada. Thus they spoke; and as for Kṛṣṇā, she indeed became "Kṛṣṇā" by virtue of her complexion.
Thus that pair was born at the great sacrifice of Drupada.
At that time, Dhṛṣṭadyumna had reached the furthest limit in the study of the Vedas;
and having brought Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Drupada and prince of the Pañcālas, [to the assembly].
The powerful Bhāradvāja, the high-minded Droṇa, initiated [the weapon] for the sake of the missile; yet, because destiny is inescapable due to past deeds,
he acted in such a way for the sake of protecting his own fame.
He acquired all weapons instantly upon merely seeing them.
O Brahman-sage, I wish to hear the origin of Drupada as well:
how was he born, and how did he obtain those weapons?

"O Blessed One, O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear this from you; for my curiosity is indeed great as my past births are being recounted. There was once a king of Pañcāla who, desiring a son, sought the means to obtain one."
Having gone to the forest, the great king performed most severe asceticism,
striving with great effort for the sake of obtaining offspring. While he was thus performing penance in the forest filled with herds of deer,
But a very long time passed, O King, due to the delay caused by the birth of his son.
That king of great prowess then undertook intense asceticism;
for some time he subsisted on air alone, and likewise remained without food.
While he was thus engaged, O mighty-armed Bhārata,
a great deal of time passed there, O King, best of monarchs;
then, O great king, when spring had arrived, which kindles all desires.

O best of the Bharatas, at that time, when the forest of *aśoka* trees was in full bloom— a season most enchanting to living beings— the lotus-eyed king went to the bank of the river Gaṅgā and remained there established in his vows.
Then, not long thereafter, O lord of men,
a woman renowned as Menakā suddenly arrived at that forest, O King;
she was wandering and sporting repeatedly on the bank of the river.
Tearing down flowering trees, she came into the king’s sight;
yet, O King, she did not see the monarch standing in his place.
But upon seeing that apsarā, the king’s semen fell to the ground.

But that king, O Indra among kings, being himself overcome with shame, O long-lived one, stepped upon it with his own feet; thus Drupada came to be. Then, through the ascetic power of that royal sage of purified soul, [he became a daughter].
A son was born from Ārdra, between the feet;
O protector of the earth, all those sages rich in asceticism, having assembled together,
gave him the name Drupada, for they were wise.
O King, descendant of Bharata, he grew up happily there in the hermitage of that very Bharadvāja, O best of monarchs, provided with all his desires;
for the powerful Pāñcāla king, O lord of kings, had also returned to his own kingdom.
Having given his son to the high-souled Bharadvāja for the purpose of instruction, O King,
that prince, accompanied by Droṇa,
then studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) in the forest, O Bhārata.
Filled with supreme joy, he roamed happily through the forest. While he was thus living in the forest with the forest-dwellers, O King, before long his father passed away to heaven.

Having joined with the Pāñcālas, he was consecrated among the Pāñcālas; and having obtained the kingdom, O Indra of kings, he increased the joy of his friends and protected the realm righteously, just as Indra does in Triviṣṭapa.

O Indra among kings, I have thus related to you exactly as it happened the birth of Drupada and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O royal sage; and as for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Indra among kings, he was the delighter of the Pauravas.
Knowing Yudhiṣṭhira to be indeed capable of sustaining the kingdom,
he consulted with his ministers regarding his consecration as the heir apparent.
But when the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra learned of this, they were then filled with remorse.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, then at the end of a year, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, was installed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra as the heir apparent.
Due to his fortitude, steadfastness, endurance, benevolence, and likewise his straightforwardness,
as well as his compassion for his dependents and his constant friendship,
Kuntī’s son Yudhiṣṭhira [attained sovereignty] in no long time.
Through his character, conduct, and meditative composure, he eclipsed the fame of his father;
and in sword-fighting, mace-fighting, and chariot-fighting, Vṛkodara, the son of Pāṇḍu,
indeed received constant instruction from Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Bhīma, having completed his training, was equal to Dyumatsena in strength;
endowed with great prowess, he remained under the command of his brothers. He was likewise preeminent in the firmness of his tight grip, in agility, and in the precision of his aim.

Phalguna became a knower of the true nature of razors, iron arrows, crescent-headed shafts, and *vipāṭha* bolts; he was the one who could employ them straight, curved, or broad. In both dexterity and elegance, there was no one else like him.
"Droṇa was of the firm conviction that there is no one in the world equal to Bībhatsu.
Then, in the assembly of the Kauravas, Droṇa said to Guḍākeśa:
'In the science of archery, my preceptor in former times was the disciple of Agastya.'"
O Bhārata, I am known as Agniveśya, and I am his disciple. I am now intent upon leading you from one sacred ford to another,
for that which has been attained by me through austerity is unfailing and possesses eternal radiance.
"The weapon named Brahmashira, which could burn even the earth,
was given to you by your preceptor with these words: 'O Bhāradvāja, O Lord, this must not be released by you against human beings, even those of little prowess.'"
"O hero, this divine [weapon] which has been obtained by you, no one else deserves it but you.
Yet, O lord of people, the agreement established by the sage must be observed by you. Give the teacher’s fee while the assembly of kinsmen looks on."
When Phālguna had promised, "I shall give it," the Preceptor said:
"O sinless one, I must be fought by you in battle while we are both fighting. And having promised "So be it" to Droṇa, that bull among the Kurus [departed].
Having clasped his feet, he departed toward the northern direction. By its very nature, his fame spread across the earth girdled by the ocean;
there was no archer in the world equal to Arjuna.

In combat with maces, in combat with swords, and in chariot warfare, the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya then became a master; he was proficient in archery and possessed the entire science of policy from the Lord of the Gods.
Sahadeva, too, having obtained [this knowledge], remained under the control of his brothers;
and Nakula, beloved of his brothers, was likewise trained by Droṇa himself. Renowned as a versatile warrior, he became celebrated as an Atiratha.

The Sauvīra king, who had performed sacrifices for three years during the invasion of the Gandharvas, was slain in battle by the Pārthas led by Arjuna— he whom even the heroic Pāṇḍu had been unable to bring under his control.
That king, the lord of the Yavanas, who was exceedingly endowed with strength and always proud toward the Kurus, was brought under the control of Arjuna; he,
the Sauvīra named Vittalas, was slain by the wise Pārtha.

Arjuna, with Bhīmasena as his companion, subdued with his arrows the Sauvīra king named Sumitra, who was renowned as Dattamitra and was determined for battle, along with other chariot-warriors in the desert regions.
Arjuna, on a single chariot, conquered all the easterners in battle;
likewise, traveling on a single chariot, he conquered the southern quarter. Dhanañjaya brought back a flood of wealth to the Kuru kingdom.
Thus, in former times, all those great-souled Pāṇḍavas, the best of men, having conquered the kingdoms of others, expanded their own realm; then,
they recognized the renowned power of those firm bowmen.
The disposition of Dhṛtarāṣṭra toward the Pāṇḍus was suddenly corrupted;
that king, consumed by anxiety, found no sleep at night.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said;
Vaiśampāyana said;
Kaṇika said.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Kaṇika said:
The jackal said:
Kaṇika said;
the tiger said;
the jackal said.
The tiger said;
the jackal said;
the mongoose said.
Kaṇika said;
Vaiśampāyana said;
Vaiśampāyana said.
Janamejaya said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu were heroes, overflowing with strength and possessed of great majesty...
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the protector of the earth, fell into anxious thought;
then, having summoned Kaṇika— the foremost of ministers, an expert in counsel and most proficient in the meaning of the treatises on statecraft— Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words.
"O best of the twice-born, the Pāṇḍavas are ever arrogant, and I feel envy toward them. In this matter, my mind is firmly resolved regarding the cause for peace or war;
tell me your opinion, Kaṇika, and I shall act according to your word."
With a serene mind, that best of the twice-born, being thus questioned by him,
spoke these sharp words illustrating the science of kingship:
"Listen, O sinless King, to this which is being declared by me in this regard."
O best of the Kurus, having heard this, you should not harbor ill-will toward me.
You should always have the rod of punishment raised, always manifest your prowess,
remain without flaws yourself while observing the flaws of others, and pursue their vulnerabilities.
For people tremble greatly before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should carry out all affairs by means of the rod alone.
Let another not perceive his own vulnerability, and let him pursue the enemy through the latter's vulnerability.
One should hide one's limbs like a tortoise and guard one's own vulnerabilities;
having undertaken an action, one should never perform it imperfectly,
for even a thorn, if poorly extracted, may cause a chronic discharge.
They praise indeed the slaughter of enemies who have done harm:
a well-executed breach, a well-displayed valor, a well-fought battle, and a well-timed retreat;
one should act thus in calamity and at the proper time without hesitation.
My son, an enemy must never be disregarded, however weak he may be;
even a tiny fire burns down an entire forest by relying upon its fuel.
One should be blind at the time for blindness, and one should likewise resort to deafness when appropriate.
One may even make a bow out of grass and sleep the sleep of a deer;
yet, by means of conciliation and other such methods, one should strike down an enemy who has been brought under control. One should not show mercy toward him simply because he has come for refuge.
For one who is undisturbed, fear does not arise from being struck;
thus, one should strike back at an enemy with a gift, even one who has previously done harm. One should strike the entire opposing faction—three, five, or seven members in every way.
One should constantly cut off the very root of the enemy's faction from the beginning; thereafter, one should destroy their allies and all those belonging to that side.
For when the foundation has been severed at its root, all who depend upon it are destroyed.

How indeed could the branches remain upon a tree whose root has been severed? One should be single-minded, unyielding, and ever-watchful for vulnerabilities; O King, one should conduct oneself in the kingdom amidst rivals with constant vigilance.

Having gained the world’s trust through the establishment of the sacred fires, through sacrifice, by wearing saffron robes, and by carrying matted hair and skins, one may then plunder [them] like a wolf.
They say that purity is a hook for the seizing of wealth.
Bending down a branch laden with fruit, one should pluck it ripe by ripe;
for this is the endeavor of wise men in this world who seek fruit.
One may carry an enemy upon one's shoulder as long as the turn of time has not yet arrived.
Then, when the right time has come, one should shatter him like a jar against a stone;
an enemy must not be released, even if he speaks piteously at great length. One should show no mercy toward him, but must surely slay the wrongdoer.
One should destroy an enemy by means of conciliation, or again by means of gifts; likewise, one should pacify him through all possible means, such as sowing dissension and the use of force.
How, then, [should one act] by means of conciliation, gifts, dissensions, or force?
"An enemy can be slain; tell me that according to the truth.
"Listen, O King, to what happened long ago while [I] was dwelling in the forest, concerning a jackal, O Great King, who perceived the meaning of the treatises on statecraft (nītiśāstra)."

Now there was a certain jackal, wise and skilled in his own interests, who lived together with his friends— a tiger, a mouse, a wolf, and a baboon. They saw in that forest a powerful leader of a herd of deer.
Unable to seize him, they then consulted with one another regarding the mantra:
"O tiger, though he has been repeatedly attempted to be killed by you in the forest,
this youth— endowed with speed and possessed of intelligence— is not to be overcome."
"Let this mouse devour his feet while he lies there;
then let a tiger seize him once his feet have been eaten;
thereafter, we shall all eat him with joyful hearts."
The jackal’s words were carried out by them with focused attention.
Then, with legs gnawed by mice, the tiger killed the deer.
But seeing the body of the deer writhing upon the ground, he [the jackal]—
"Go after bathing; may it be well with you; I shall guard [the meat]," said the jackal. At the word of the jackal, they all then went to the river.
The jackal remained right there, absorbed in thought.
Then, having first bathed, the mighty tiger arrived;
he saw the jackal, whose mind was agitated by anxiety.
"Why do you grieve, O highly wise one? You are the best among us who possess intelligence."
"Having eaten the flesh today, we shall enjoy ourselves.
Listen to me, O mighty-armed one, as to what the mouse said:
'Fie on the strength of the king of beasts! This deer has been slain by me today.'"
"Relying on the strength of my arms, he will today attain satisfaction.
Since he is roaring in this manner, I do not find his being food agreeable,
even though he has been awakened at this very time and speaks thus."
"Relying on the strength of my own arms, I shall slay the forest-dwellers;
I shall eat their flesh there," he said, and set out for the forest.
At that very moment, however, a mouse also arrived.
Seeing that he had arrived, the jackal also spoke these words:
"Listen, O mouse—may prosperity be yours—to what the mongoose said here: 'I shall not eat the deer-meat; this is poison, it does not please me.'"
"I shall eat the mouse; may you grant me your permission.
Having heard those words, the mouse, terrified, fled in fear.
Then, O King, having bathed there, the wolf returned.
When he had arrived, the jackal then spoke these words to him:
"The king of beasts is indeed enraged; it will not be well for you.
He approaches here with his family; do what must be done next."
Thus urged by that jackal, the wolf,
the eater of flesh, made a springing leap toward the jackal and set out;
at that very moment, however, a mongoose also arrived.
O great king, the jackal said to Nakula in the forest:
"Relying on the strength of your own arms, you have conquered them; they have fled elsewhere.
Having given me a wrestling match, eat as much meat as you desire."
"The king of beasts, the wolf, and even the wise mouse—
since these heroes were conquered by you, you are therefore more heroic than they.
Having said, "I do not venture to fight with you," he also approached.
When they had thus departed, the jackal, his heart filled with joy,
then ate the meat alone by virtue of his secret plan.
Acting in this manner constantly, the king prospers in happiness.
One should divide a coward by means of fear, a hero by joining one’s palms in salutation, a greedy man by the gift of wealth, and an equal or inferior by means of prowess.
Thus has this been told to you, O King; now hear another matter as well.
Whether it be a son, a friend, a brother, a father, or even a teacher,
if they occupy the positions of enemies, they should be treated in a way that increases one's prosperity.
One may strike down an enemy even by means of an oath, or again, by the giving of wealth.
One should never overlook [an offense], even by means of poison or illusion;
for if both parties are equally beset by doubt, it is the one possessed of faith who prospers therein—
even toward a teacher who is arrogant and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done.
For one who has set out upon a wrong path, instruction that is consistent with reason is appropriate. Even when angry, he should appear as if not angry, speaking with a smile;
and even when possessed by anger, he should never disparage another.
O Bhārata, one who is about to strike should speak kindly; even while striking, he should speak kindly;
and having struck, he should show compassion, grieve, and weep.
He should also console the other person with soothing words, through the practice of dharma, and for the sake of worldly benefit.
Then, at the proper time, one should strike him when he has strayed from the path—
even if he has committed a terrible offense— provided he remains steadfast by taking refuge in dharma;
for that fault is concealed, just as a mountain is covered by dark clouds.
One should set fire to the house of anyone who has committed murder. One should not allow those who are penniless, hypocrites, or thieves to dwell within one's own domain.
Nor should one provide them with any form of hospitality, such as rising to greet them, offering a seat, or any other kind of gift.
One who strikes down those who have placed their trust is like a sharp-toothed crocodile that has submerged itself;
one should fear those who inspire no suspicion, and one should be wary of all those who do inspire suspicion. For danger arising even from one who is not suspected cuts away the very root.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place excessive trust even in the trustworthy. Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts down even the very roots.
One should employ well-organized spies both for oneself and for others.
He should employ heretics, ascetics, and others in foreign kingdoms; likewise,
he should station them in gardens, monasteries,
temples, taverns, on the highways, and at all sacred fords.

One should investigate [the king's conduct] at the four gambling houses, on mountains, in forests, in all public assemblies, and by the rivers. He should be exceedingly humble in speech, yet like a razor in his heart.
One should speak with gentleness first, even if one has been provoked by fierce deeds.

One who desires prosperity must perform these single acts: joining the palms in salutation, taking an oath, speaking soothingly, bowing the head at the feet [of others], and fulfilling their expectations.
A tree may be in full bloom yet bear no fruit; it may bear fruit yet be difficult to climb;
it may be unripe yet appear as if ripe, and never decay at any time.
In the three aims of life (trivarga), there are likewise three kinds of affliction and their corresponding consequences.

The consequences should be known as auspicious, but one should avoid afflictions; for even the affliction that befalls one practicing Dharma is restrained by two [means]. Wealth belongs to one greedy for wealth, and sensual pleasure to one who indulges excessively in desire.
Free from pride, disciplined, gentle in speech, and devoid of malice,
he should deliberate with the twice-born, having examined the matter and being pure in soul;
by whatever means possible here, whether mild or harsh, [he should act].
One should rescue oneself from distress; once capable, one should practice righteousness. A man who has not entered into uncertainty does not behold auspicious things;
but having entered into uncertainty, if he survives, he beholds them.

One whose intellect is superior should be conciliated by referring to the past; one of dull intellect by referring to the future; and a wise man by referring to the present. He who, having made peace with an enemy, lies down as if his task were accomplished, [is a fool].
Like one who has fallen asleep at the top of a tree and awakens upon falling,
one should always exert effort in concealing one's counsel without malice;
one’s own outward expression must be guarded and maintained even by means of a spy.
Without piercing the vital organs of others, without performing cruel deeds,
and without killing like a fisherman, one does not attain great prosperity.
[One should avoid] those who are emaciated, diseased, or soaked with water, those who have no water, and those who have no food.

One should strike the enemy's force when it is completely trusting and sluggish; for one who has no need does not approach one who has a need, and there is no association once the purpose has been achieved.
Therefore, one should cause all undertakings to be carried out with something remaining unfinished.
One who is free from envy should exert effort in both conciliation and conflict;
and one who desires prosperity should also apply diligent energy. His undertakings should remain unknown to his friends as well as his enemies.
One should see that undertakings have indeed been begun and brought to a successful conclusion.
One should prepare like one who is afraid as long as danger has not yet arrived;
but having seen that danger has arrived, one should strike fearlessly.
The man who favors an enemy subdued by force embraces his own death, just as a she-mule conceives a fetus.
For he should perceive what is yet to come and that which is the task standing before him.
One should not let any purpose pass by due to a deficiency of intellect;
rather, one who desires prosperity must exert effort with enthusiasm,
having carefully distinguished between place and time, as well as the three factors of destiny, dharma, and so forth.
It is an established principle that those two—place and time—are to be known as conducive to the highest good.
A foolish enemy who is neglected establishes his roots like a palm tree;
like a fire let loose in a thicket, he quickly grows great.
The man who kindles himself like a small spark of fire,
as he grows, consumes even a vast accumulation.
He should make his hope timely and join the time with obstacles.
One should declare that an obstacle arises from a sign, and that a sign arises from a cause.
Having become a razor, sharpened as the instrument of Time, it shall take away their lives—
hidden, hair-bearing, and the cutter of enemies.

O bull of the Kurus, by conducting yourself toward the Pāṇḍavas and others according to what is right, you shall not sink; act accordingly. It is certain that you are endowed with every excellence and are preeminent.
Therefore, O lord of men, protect yourself from the sons of Pāṇḍu;
for the sons of Pāṇḍu are powerful, O lord of men. Therefore, O subduer of enemies, I speak clearly as to what must be done.
O King, listen to this along with your sons, and having heard it, be diligent; O lord of men, act in such a way that there is no fear from the Pāṇḍavas,
and let policy be established so that there shall be no regret later.
Having spoken thus, Kaṇika then departed for his own home;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the descendant of Kuru, was likewise overcome with grief.
Then the son of Subala and King Duryodhana—
Duḥśāsana and Karṇa deliberated upon a wicked plot;
having obtained the permission of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Kaurava lord of men,
they set their minds upon the burning of Kuntī along with her sons.
Vidura, who understood gestures and dispositions and perceived the truth, recognized that secret counsel of those evil-minded men by their very facial expressions alone.
Then, he whose soul had known all that is to be known, remained devoted to the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas.

The sinless one set his mind on flight together with the sons of Kuntī. Then, having prepared a sturdy boat capable of enduring the waves, equipped with oars, fitted with a rudder, and adorned with a banner, he spoke thus to Kuntī:
This Dhṛtarāṣṭra, born into this lineage with a corrupted soul, destroys the family’s tradition of fame and abandons eternal dharma. This [ship],
however, is fitted for the waterway and is capable of enduring waves and wind.

"O auspicious lady, by this boat you shall be released from the noose of death along with your sons. Having heard this, the illustrious Kuntī, distressed, boarded a boat on the Gaṅgā together with her sons, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then, following the words of Vidura, the Pāṇḍavas set out a boat,
took the wealth given by them, and entered the forest safely; meanwhile,
the Niṣāda woman with her five sons remained there in that house made of lac.
Having arrived there for a specific purpose, we were burned along with our innocent sons;
and that lowest of Mlecchas, the wicked Purocana, was also burned there.
Thus have the evil-minded sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with their followers, been deceived.

The high-souled sons of Kuntī, unknown to the people and thus unhurt, were released along with their mother from the plot devised by Vidura. Then, in that city, in the capital of Vāraṇāvata, the people—
Seeing the house of lac consumed by fire, they grieved in their suffering;
they dispatched messengers to inform the king of exactly what had occurred:
"Your great desire has been fulfilled; you have burnt the Pāṇḍavas."

"O descendant of Kuru, let your desires be fulfilled; enjoy the kingdom together with your sons. Having heard this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, grieving along with his son, performed the funeral rites for the deceased together with his kinsmen.
O best of the twice-born, I wish to hear again in detail, as well as from Kṣattṛ and Bhīṣma, the best of the Kurus,
about the burning of the house of lac and the escape of the Pāṇḍavas.
"This deed of theirs was cruel and accompanied by violence.
Relate it to me exactly as it happened, for my curiosity is great.
Listen in detail, O King, subduer of enemies, as I speak."
"This was the burning of the house of lac and the liberation of the Pāṇḍavas.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Bhīmasena, who is dearer to him than life, and Dhanañjaya, who is accomplished in learning—"
Having observed this, the evil-minded Duryodhana was consumed by grief.
Then Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, and Śakuni, the son of Subala,
sought to slay those Pāṇḍavas through numerous stratagems.
The Pāṇḍavas, those subduers of enemies, acknowledged all of that,
remaining steadfast in the counsel of Vidura and refraining from any self-display.
Then, seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu endowed with every virtue, the citizens [were filled with joy].
O Bhārata, they recounted their virtues in assemblies,
and having gathered together in courtyards and halls, they spoke of how the eldest son of Pāṇḍu had then attained the kingdom.

Because he lacked the eye of wisdom, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, did not obtain the kingdom previously; how then could he become king? Likewise was Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, true to his word and observer of great vows.

Having previously renounced the kingdom, he will certainly never accept it now. Furthermore, because Vidura is his instrument, let the Pāṇḍava be consecrated. Thus, we [shall install] the eldest Pāṇḍava, who is young yet possesses the character of the aged.
"Let us now duly consecrate him who is truthful and compassionate.
For that highly illustrious son of Pāṇḍu will always honor and worship the elders, the ministers, and his kinsmen, all of whom are worthy of reverence."
For he, the knower of dharma, honoring Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu and Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his sons, will provide them with various enjoyments. Having heard those words spoken by them, Duryodhana—
The evil-minded one was consumed with grief by those who were devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Tormented and unable to endure their words, that wicked-souled man,
burning with envy, approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, seeing his father departed and having paid him due honor, he,
tormented by the affection of the citizens, spoke these words afterwards:
"O Father, I have heard the inauspicious words of the citizens as they were speaking."
O Bhārata, having heard the words of those citizens who are devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira and their ill-omened cries, I shall suffer greatly. O one of great wisdom, I have come to your feet; hear my words.
Disregarding you and Bhīṣma, they desire the Pāṇḍava as their husband. This is the opinion of Bhīṣma as well; he does not wish to rule the kingdom.
Furthermore, the people in the city intend to cause us supreme suffering.
In former times, Pāṇḍu obtained the kingdom from his father through his own virtues;
you, however, did not obtain the kingdom you had acquired because of your lack of virtue. If this son of Pāṇḍu now receives the inheritance of Pāṇḍu, [it is only right].

"His son will surely obtain it, and his son after him, and so on for others. Thus, O Lord of the World, we shall be deprived of our royal lineage along with our sons, and we shall be held in contempt by the world."
"O King, act quickly so that we, who constantly subsist on the alms of others, do not fall into hell.
O Indra among kings, may you likewise continue the royal lineage."
"O King, had you remained steadfast in the kingdom in the past,
we certainly would have obtained the sovereignty even while the people were under your control; provided, O Great King, that you yourself do not depart from the royal lineage."
"We ourselves shall indeed strive [to save you] from that impure, bottomless hell;
therefore, O Kauravya, act accordingly so that we, your kinsmen, may be protected while you yourself obtain the kingdom— deliberate on this with your followers."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Duryodhana:
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard such words from his son,
[considered] Bhīmasena, who is dearer to him than life, and Dhananjaya, who is accomplished in learning.
Having reflected for a moment, he then spoke to Duryodhana.
Observing this, the evil-minded Duryodhana was consumed by grief,
as were Vaikartana Karṇa and Śakuni Saubala.
Pāṇḍu was always devoted to righteousness and well-behaved toward me out of respect,
as well as toward all my kinsmen, especially so. Yet,
by many means, they sought to slay the Pāṇḍavas.

He did not know anything of this at all, yet he desired to prepare meals; and the Pāṇḍavas, abiding by the counsel of Vidura, carried out all of that according to their strength, without making it known.
The steward of dharma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
informed me that when he saw the sons of Pāṇḍu endowed with such virtues,
he then regarded them as his own sons; for Pāṇḍu was always devoted to righteousness.
O Bhārata, they would recount his virtues in assemblies, saying:
"He is virtuous, world-renowned, and firmly established in the city;
how can he be removed by us, O bull among men?"
Then, having gathered together in the courtyards and in the assembly halls, they spoke of the eldest son of Pāṇḍu who had attained the sovereignty:
"For he has obtained the kingdom for us, especially since he is accompanied by allies."
Since his blind brother Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, whose eye is wisdom, has always been supported by his brothers, the Pāṇḍavas, and by the army and the ministers,
how could that king have previously obtained the kingdom?
Their sons and grandsons were also especially cherished;
O dear one, those men in the kingdom were thus honored by Pāṇḍu,
as was Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, who was true to his promise and had conquered his senses.

"How might they not slay us along with our kinsmen for the sake of Yudhiṣṭhira? Having once renounced the kingdom, he will never accept it today. Therefore, we [should approach] that best of the Pāṇḍavas, who is young yet possesses the character of the aged."
They would not desire these objects of sense, especially the abandonment of dharma;
let us therefore duly consecrate here one who is truthful and compassionate—
both we ourselves and these high-souled Kauravas.

For he, the wise one, will honor Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu and Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his sons by providing them with various enjoyments; O dear one, how then shall we not incur the censure of the world?
"Bhīṣma remains perpetually neutral, while Droṇa’s son is stationed with me;
where the son is, there will Droṇa be—of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words of theirs, O Bhārata, Duryodhana...
The evil-minded one burned with grief for those who were devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira;
both Kṛpa and Śāradvata [were likewise affected], for wherever we were,
that wicked-souled man, being tormented, could not endure their words.
Therefore, he will not abandon his nephew, the son of Droṇa, under any circumstances.
Bound by his purpose toward us, Vidura remained hidden from the enemies;
yet, tormented by envy, he approached Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But he alone is not capable of harming us for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore, seeing our father deprived [of his power] and having paid him due honor,
exile the sons of Pāṇḍu along with their mother, while they are completely unsuspecting.
Having seen what had occurred previously regarding Pāṇḍu, he then spoke these words:
"I have heard the inauspicious words of the citizens as they were speaking;
today itself we shall go to Vāraṇāvata, and no harm shall come to us here."
"O one of great wisdom, I have come to your feet; hear my words. A terrible sleeplessness, like a dart fixed in the heart, has arisen; extinguish that fire of grief born from that deed."
Disregarding you and Bhīṣma, they desire the Pāṇḍava as their husband;
and Bhīṣma’s mind is set on Saumya, and he does not wish for the kingdom.
His son has certainly obtained it, and another says, "It belongs to him and him."
O Lord of the World, deprived of our royal lineage along with our sons, we shall remain unrecognized by the world,
constantly fallen into misery and subsisting on the alms of others.
"O King, act quickly so that we may not come to such a state;
for you too, O Indra among kings, shall continue the royal lineage,
provided that you, O monarch, are established in the kingdom as before."
"Surely we too shall obtain the kingdom by your power alone;
therefore, O Kauravya, act in such a way that we, your kinsmen, may be protected so that we ourselves may attain the kingdom. Deliberate on this together with your followers."
Duryodhana;
Vaiśampāyana:
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard those most grievous and unpleasant words...
The wise [Vidura] spoke these words to Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies:
"O dear one, although I am born blind, I have been greatly honored by Pāṇḍu;
for even kings, though they be most excellent, act out of regard for righteousness."

One who lacks the eye of wisdom is incapable of protecting a kingdom due to his blindness; yet one who is merely blind does not repel enemy forces in battle. My son, I have studied the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*) as well as the Vedas with all their auxiliary branches.
O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, a king who desires righteousness must fight in person;
for a kṣatriya, death in battle is ordained as the path to heaven. Alternatively, having transferred his royal fortune to his son, he may retire to the forest to dwell there.
Although he was physically impaired, Pāṇḍu was established in the kingdom as the eldest;
having conquered the kingdoms of others, he presented them to me. For the sake of upholding the family dharma, I am the eldest, yet I do not receive the portion of the eldest.
Among many brothers, the eldest is indeed the best by virtue of his seniority;
even if he is younger, he is the eldest, the most excellent, and truly the one who brings prosperity to the family.
Therefore, Pāṇḍu was the eldest and the most excellent, the best among those who uphold dharma. His sons are renowned for their virtues and are resolute in matters of purpose;
skilled in weapons and having attained their mark, the sons of Pāṇḍu are great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
They are always devoted to both the Dharma and the treatises on ethics;
moreover, the citizens and the people of the countryside hold them in especially high regard.
My child, how could I bear to exile them from the city?
The Brahmins, together with the citizens and the people of the countryside, constantly say:

"Because he lacks eyes, the one whose eye is wisdom is incapable of protecting the kingdom. Therefore, let us [install] the best of the Pāṇḍavas, who is young yet possesses the character of the aged."
"Let us consecrate as king one who is truthful and compassionate;
for that highly illustrious Pāṇḍava will always honor and worship the elders, ministers, and kinsmen who are worthy of reverence."
"Respected and honored, he will cause the grandfather Śāntanava and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with his sons, to dwell in comfort with various enjoyments according to dharma"—
thus did people lament and speak repeatedly.

"O King, hundreds of thousands of citizens are overwhelmed by hundreds of sorrows. Having heard those inauspicious words of the citizens who are devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall suffer greatly, O Bhārata."
But Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard the words of his son, said: "O son, act in such a way that we do not fall into reproach. Having heard these words of his, he entered his great palace.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus heard the words of his son, and having heard those words of Kaṇika in their entirety, the lord of men, whose eye was wisdom, [acted accordingly].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra became divided in mind and overcome with grief;
then Duryodhana, Karṇa, Śakuni the son of Subala,
and Duḥśāsana as the fourth, deliberated together in private.
Then King Duryodhana spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"We have cause for fear of the Pāṇḍavas; may your majesty exile them by some clever stratagem to the city of Vāraṇāvata."
Having heard such words from his son, Dhṛtarāṣṭra reflected for a moment and then spoke to Duryodhana:
"Pāṇḍu was always constant in righteousness; he was my benefactor and well-wisher."
He was thus toward all his kinsmen, but he was especially so toward me.
I knew nothing that he did not know, whether it concerned food or whatever else he desired to do;
for he, firm in his vows, constantly reported everything regarding the kingdom to me.
His son was devoted to righteousness just like Pāṇḍu;
he was virtuous, world-renowned, and highly esteemed by the citizens. Conducting himself in that manner, he was like a younger brother to Dharmaputra.
How can he be forcibly removed from here by us,
especially since he has allies?
For the ministers of Pāṇḍu have been maintained [by us], and the army has been constantly supported.
Their sons and grandsons have been supported by you, especially so.
O dear one, those Paurava people were formerly honored by Pāṇḍu;
why would they not slay us along with our kinsmen for the sake of Yudhiṣṭhira?
Duryodhana said:
"O father, it was indeed with this very thought that I perceived the fault within myself;
having seen it, I have gratified all the subjects with wealth and honors."

"O Lord of the Earth, it is certain that they will become our principal allies; for today the entire body of wealth, along with the ministers, is under my control. Therefore, you ought to quickly exile the Pāṇḍavas."
O King, when the kingdom has been firmly established in me at Vāraṇāvata by means of gentle stratagems,
then, O Bhārata, Kuntī shall return with her children.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Duryodhana, this very thought also revolves in my heart;
however, because the intention is sinful, I do not reveal it."
Neither Bhīṣma, nor Droṇa, nor the Steward (Vidura), nor Gautama (Kṛpa) will ever approve of the sons of Kuntī being sent into exile;
for these men and we are equal toward the Kauravas, O dear son.

"These wise men, devoted to righteousness, would never desire anything unjust. Therefore, O dear one, how might we, as well as these high-souled Kauravas and the world at large, avoid being put to death?"
Duryodhana said:
"Bhīṣma is always impartial, while the son of Droṇa stands with me;
where my son is, there will Droṇa also be—of this there is no doubt."
"Since Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, and these other three [Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, and Kṛtavarman] are present,
he will never abandon Droṇa or his sister's son. However, Vidura, though bound to our cause by his purpose, is secretly aligned with the enemy."
He alone is not capable of harming us for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas;
therefore, with confidence, exile the sons of Pāṇḍu along with their mother this very day to Vāraṇāvata— there shall be no fault in this.
"This terrible thing, which causes sleeplessness and is like a dart fixed in my heart—
extinguish this kindled fire of grief by means of this deed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Duryodhana, together with his younger brothers, gradually won over all those subjects by means of wealth and honors,
with the single exception of Yuyutsu, who remained loyal to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But certain skillful ministers employed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke of the delightful city of Vāraṇāvata:
"This great assembly is the most beautiful on earth."
"Present in the city of Vāraṇāvata,
which is filled with all kinds of jewels and is a delightful place for men—
thus, at the word of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they held this conversation."
While that delightful city of Vāraṇāvata was being described in this manner,
O King, the sons of Pāṇḍu set their minds on going there;
for the king perceived that they were filled with curiosity.
Then the son of Ambikā spoke to those Pāṇḍavas:
"The scriptures have been studied by you here in their entirety,
as well as the weapons from Droṇa and from Gautama, the son of Śaradvat."
"O father, this being the case, I reflect on all sides:
these men who are constantly devoted to the protection and administration of the kingdom always speak thus to me again and again."
"Vārāṇavata is the most delightful city in the world. Therefore, dear ones, if you so desire, celebrate a festival in Vārāṇavata;
go there with your retinues and attendants, and enjoy yourselves like the immortals."
"Give jewels to the Brahmins and to the singers in every way, according to their desire, like gods of great splendor. Having thus enjoyed yourselves for some time and experienced supreme delight,"

"O subduers of enemies, you shall indeed return again to this city of Hastināpura when you are happy; dwell right there, devoted to its protection, for a great transformation will surely take place there."
"You shall indeed return to this city, O Pāṇḍavas.
Having understood Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s wish and his own lack of assistance, Yudhiṣṭhira replied to him, "So be it."
Then [he addressed] the highly wise Bhīṣma and the great-minded Vidura,
as well as Droṇa, Bāhlika, and Somadatta the Kaurava,
Kṛpa the son of the preceptor, and the illustrious Gāndhārī.
...and Bhūriśravas himself,
as well as other venerable ministers, Brahmins rich in asceticism,
domestic priests, and the citizens.
Having touched all his mothers and the wife of Vidura,
Yudhiṣṭhira then spoke these words slowly and dejectedly.
"O dear ones, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, we shall dwell with our followers in the delightful city of Vāraṇāvata, which is crowded with people; all of you,
with cheerful minds, utter auspicious words."
"Evil shall not overcome us, who have been strengthened by these blessings.
Having been addressed thus by the son of Pāṇḍu, all those Kauravas,
with serene countenances, turned back toward the Pāṇḍavas.
"May there be well-being for you always on the road, and from all beings in every way; and may no inauspicious thing befall you from any quarter, O sons of Pāṇḍu!
Then, having performed the rites for auspiciousness for the sake of regaining their kingdom, the Pāṇḍavas—
Having completed all their duties, they set out for Vāraṇāvata.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had been thus addressed by the king...
The evil-minded Duryodhana attained the highest joy.
Then the son of Subala, Karṇa, and likewise Duryodhana,
resolved upon the burning of Kuntī along with her sons.
Having consulted with them, that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
O bull of the Bharatas, brought Purocana aside in private;
taking his minister by the right hand, he spoke these words.
"O Purocana, this earth, filled with wealth, belongs to me; as it is mine, so is it yours, and you ought to protect it. For indeed, there is no one else who is more trustworthy to me than you."
"O father, protect this counsel with which I may deliberate as an ally with you; uproot my rivals by means of a skillful stratagem,
and do exactly as I say."

"The Pāṇḍavas have been sent by Dhṛtarāṣṭra to Vāraṇāvata; by Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s command, they will enjoy themselves at the festival. Therefore, you [should go] on a swift-moving chariot yoked with donkeys."
"Act in such a way that you may depart for Vāraṇāvata this very day.
Having gone there, take refuge in the armory and have a magnificent, well-concealed four-winged mansion built at great expense."
"Whatever substances there may be here, such as hemp, resin, and so forth,
which are fiery in nature— have all of them brought forth,
mixed with *balvaja* grass and beeswax."
Mixing clay with clarified butter, oil, and a generous amount of lac,
you should apply it as a plaster upon the walls,
exactly as commanded by the illustrious Kuru king.
For these sons of Pāṇḍu, he had a terrible house constructed;
you should place hemp, bamboo, ghee, wood, and various mechanical devices throughout that entire dwelling.
"And so that the Pāṇḍavas, as well as other men, might not suspect you even upon examination, saying,
'This is the fire-weapon (āgneya),' you must act accordingly.
Having thus prepared that house, treat them with the highest honor."
You should provide lodging for the sons of Pāṇḍu, Kuntī, and their circle of friends;
there, excellent seats, vehicles,
and beds must be prepared for the Pāṇḍavas so that my father may be satisfied.
"Everything must be arranged so that they may enjoy themselves with confidence in the city of Vāraṇāvata, until the turning of time [death] arrives.
But once you know them to be fully trusting, sleeping, and free from fear from any quarter,"
Then you must set fire to that house from its doorway.
In this way, when people see their own home burnt down, they will say, "The kinsmen have burned it," perhaps even for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having promised "So be it" to the Kaurava,
Purocana set out for the city of Vāraṇāvata in a donkey-drawn carriage.
O King, having arrived there in haste, he remained intent on the will of Duryodhana.
Purocana carried out everything exactly as the prince had instructed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But the Pāṇḍavas, having yoked their chariots with excellent horses that were like the wind, [set forth].
As they were ascending, they seized the feet of Bhīṣma like those in distress, and likewise the feet of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the high-souled Droṇa,
and other elders, as well as Vidura and Kṛpa.
Having thus saluted all the elderly Kurus, those of firm vows embraced their equals and were in turn greeted by the children; likewise,
having questioned all their mothers and circumambulated them, they departed.
All the Pāṇḍavas, grieving for the one of immeasurable prowess as was fitting,
along with all the subjects, set out for Vāraṇāvata.
The highly wise Vidura and other bulls among the Kurus,
as well as the citizens, followed those tigers among men, emaciated by grief.
There, some fearless brahmins then spoke as follows:
O bull of the Bharatas, grieving excessively for the sons of Pāṇḍu,
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra— shrouded in total darkness and possessed of a very wicked intellect— views things with partiality and does not perceive what is righteous.
For neither the sinless-souled Pāṇḍava Bhīma— the best among the strong— nor Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, will take pleasure in evil;
how much less, then, could the two sons of Mādrī, who are possessed of great wisdom, ever do so?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot endure that this kingdom, obtained from his father,
has been seized; why indeed does Bhīṣma acquiesce in this entire unrighteousness,
as the sons of Kuntī, those bulls among the Bharatas, are being exiled to an improper place?
"For in the past, the son of Śantanu was like a father to us—
the royal sage Vicitravīrya and Pāṇḍu, the joy of the Kurus.
Now that that tiger among men has passed away through the power of fate,"
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot endure these young princes;
unable to bear this, we shall all depart from this best of cities,
leaving our homes behind, and go wherever Yudhiṣṭhira goes."

To those citizens who were speaking thus, distressed and emaciated by grief, the King of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira— himself wasted by sorrow yet supremely pleased— spoke: "Whatever the lord of the earth, our father, our venerable and most excellent elder, has said,"
"That task must be performed by us without hesitation; this is our vow.
You are our friends; having circumambulated us from left to right and honored us with blessings, please return to your respective homes."
"But when our business shall arise,
you must then perform what is pleasing and beneficial for me.
Having promised "So be it," they circumambulated him.
Having greeted them with blessings, they indeed departed for the city.
But when the citizens had returned, Vidura, who knew all the laws of righteousness,
spoke these words to the best of the Pāṇḍavas to awaken his understanding:
The wise man, knowing how to speak wisely and seeing correctly the meaning of the Dharma,
spoke these words to the wise man who knew how to speak wisely and understood correctly the true nature of the Dharma and its purpose.
He who understands the wisdom of others according to the treatises on policy (*nītiśāstra*),
having understood this, should act accordingly so that he may overcome calamity— just as one uses a sharp, non-metallic weapon to cut through the body.

The enemies do not strike down him who knows how to repel their blows; he who protects himself with the thought, "Let not the fire that consumes dry grass and destroys the cold burn me," survives even in a great forest where creatures dwell in holes.
One without eyes does not know the path; one without eyes does not find the directions.
One who lacks fortitude does not attain prosperity—be awakened by this awakening. A man accepts a weapon that is not made of iron when it is given by those who have not attained [their goal].
A porcupine, having found a refuge, may escape from the fire;
one who knows the paths as he travels finds his directions by means of the stars.
By himself, and not by another, he afflicts the five [senses] and is not himself afflicted.
Thus addressed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and son of Pāṇḍu, replied to Vidura, the best among the wise, saying, "It is understood.
Having instructed them, followed them, and circumambulated them, he departed.
Then, having saluted Kuntī, Vidura wept as he thought of Pāṇḍu;
having taken leave of the Pāṇḍavas, Vidura departed for his home. When Vidura had returned, as well as Bhīṣma and the citizens, [the king remained there].
Addressing Ajātaśatru, Kuntī spoke these words:
"The message that the Steward (Kṣattṛ) spoke in the midst of the people, as if not speaking at all,
and which you confirmed by saying 'So be it'— we do not understand its meaning."
"If that can be heard by us and is not fraught with fault,
I wish to hear that entire conversation between you and him.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Vidura told me that one must be wary of poison and fire;
he said that no path should remain unknown to you,
and he told me that you would obtain the earth once you had conquered your senses."
"I have understood all of that," Vidura said to me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
On the eighth day, under the asterism Rohiṇī, those sons of Phalguna set out.
Having reached Vāraṇāvata, they saw the citizens.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then all the subjects from the city of Vāraṇāvata...
Accompanied by every auspicious rite and acting according to the scriptures without weariness,
they heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu had arrived in thousands of various vehicles;
and upon hearing this, they went forth to meet those best of men with supreme joy.

Having approached the sons of Kuntī, those people from Vāraṇāvata all offered blessings for their victory and stood surrounding them. Surrounded by them, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and tiger among men, [proceeded].
Resplendent like a god, he shone like the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi) among the immortals.
Honored by the citizens and having honored the citizens in turn, those sinless ones entered Vāraṇāvata, which was adorned and crowded with people.
Having entered the city, those heroes then quickly went to the houses of the brahmins devoted to their own duties, O protector of the earth,
as well as to the homes of the city officials and the chariot-warriors.
Those best of men went even to the houses of the Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
honored by the citizens, the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls of the Bharatas,
then proceeded to their dwelling with Purocana leading the way.
To them, that Purocana gave food, drink, and various kinds of edibles, as well as beautiful beds and excellent seats. There, they were honored by him with very costly furnishings.
Being attended by the men residing in the city,
they dwelt there; and when they had stayed for ten nights, Purocana then presented to them a house called Śiva, which was in fact inauspicious.
There those tigers among men, together with their attendants, entered at the word of Purocana, like Guhyakas entering Kailāsa. But having gazed upon that house, he who was expert in all dharmas—
Smelling the odor of fat mixed with clarified butter and lac, O gentle one, Yudhiṣṭhira said to Bhīmasena:
"O scorcher of foes, this house is clearly prepared by means of fire."
This clay clearly belongs to a house mixed with fiery substances; hemp and resin were evidently brought for the construction of the dwelling.
All materials such as muñja grass, balvaja grass, bamboo, and the like have been sprinkled with clarified butter.
Hemp, balvaja grass, cotton, bamboo, wood,
and mats were likewise placed around the house as incendiary materials;
for the construction of the dwelling had been well-executed by trustworthy artisans skilled in their craft.
"This wicked Purocana desires to burn me while I am trusting him;
for that fool acts in such a manner, remaining under the control of Suyodhana. But at that time, the highly intelligent Vidura perceived this very danger."
O Pārtha, it was he who previously alerted me to the impending calamity;
by the good fortune of our high-souled Vidura, that beautiful and auspicious house made of fire has now been seen.
Awakened by him, we have realized that the home is not auspicious;
[we were thus enlightened] by our father, who ever desires our welfare, out of affection for his younger son.
"This was well-contrived by the teachers who remained hidden, acting under the influence of Duryodhana.
Bhīma said:
"As for this house which you consider to have been prepared with fire—"
"Having burned this Purocana, we shall go to Vāraṇāvata. Let us go directly there, to where we previously dwelt.
It does not seem right to me that we should depart separately after having shown ourselves [to him]."

Whether it be inauspicious or auspicious, we shall dwell together with them. From this day forward, once we have departed, that lord of men, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, will become firmly established in his kingdom, overwhelmed by fear.
That kingdom shall be his, and these subjects shall be his;
therefore, we shall dwell together with him, placing our feet upon his neck,
once we have reached our time and seized the kingdom from the enemy.
"We shall enjoy half of our paternal inheritance as eternal happiness;
why then do we acquiesce to the words of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? O King, from where does this weakness come to you, such that you would go otherwise out of fear of them?"
In times of calamity, we have the high-minded Vidura as our protector; the son of Gaṅgā remains neutral, being averse to the enjoyment of the kingdom;
and the elders, headed by Bāhlīka, are always impartial.
Droṇa would become ours, for he is filled with affection for Phalguna;
therefore, O King, you must dwell together and not go apart.
Or else, what could they do against us, being powerless in their prowess?

O Lord of Men, what would these petty, deceitful, and rogue creatures not do while I am awake? What poison was not previously given to me? And by those most terrible serpents, the venomous snakes, was I not bitten?

O King, when I was bound at the edge of the measuring-line and overcome by sleep, why did those fierce, venomous serpents not strike me with their gaze upon the bed of spikes in the Ganges? Why did my vehicle not perish then?

O best of kings, where indeed has that God gone today— he who protected us from most terrible calamities brought about by the wicked, and under whose control stands this entire world consisting of the moving and the unmoving?
"As long as we must endure [this], I shall endure it with effort;
but when we are no longer protected by them, then we shall see what is for our own benefit.
What should we see then? We should seize [the opportunity] with speed and force."

We shall strive through conciliatory speech, by gifts, and even by sowing dissension to obtain half of the kingdom; thereafter, the use of force is recommended. Therefore, one must dwell together with him as if he were a thorn implanted in one's mind.
"Having shown [the way], one should not depart as if in great fear.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I prefer that we dwell here, remaining vigilant and free from outward signs."
"Is this all there is, or will something more come after this?
Reflecting thus while awake, those beings who desire their own welfare should remain right here; this is what pleases my mind, O younger brother."
Like those searching for a lost and certain destination from here, what more could they do, seeking fearlessly? For if Purocana were to discover our whereabouts...
Becoming swift in action, he might even forcibly burn us down.
This Purocana fears neither reproach nor unrighteousness;
for thus does that fool behave, remaining steadfast in the opinion of Suyodhana.

Moreover, if we were to be burned here, our grandfather Bhīṣma would surely become enraged; for what purpose would he provoke the Kauravas? Or rather, even if we were burned here, Bhīṣma, our grandfather—
Dharma alone would be provoked to anger, as would the other bulls among the Kurus;

for when the lineage has been consumed by fire, even those who know the Dharma and the other preeminent Kurus would be justified in their wrath if they were to proclaim the names of their family lineages.
If we were to flee out of fear of being burned, Suyodhana, greedy for the kingdom, would surely have us all killed by his spies—
he who stands on firm ground while we are without a foothold, and who possesses wings while we are wingless.
One with a great treasury can certainly destroy those with depleted treasuries through strategic means.
Therefore, we must dwell here deceiving this wicked man and that wicked Suyodhana, living in disguise in various places.
"Being habituated to hunting, we shall roam this earth;
thus the paths will be known to us should we need to flee.
Moreover, let us construct a well-concealed subterranean cave this very day."
"Ensuring our breathing remains hidden there, the fire shall not consume us;
and while we dwell here, we must act with vigilance so that neither Purocana nor any of the townspeople discover us."
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, a certain friend of Vidura, a skilled digger,
spoke these words to the Pāṇḍavas in private.
"I have been sent by Vidura as a highly skilled miner;
since the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas must be accomplished, what may I do for you?
Vidura has secretly told me that you are the best course of action here for the Pāṇḍavas."
"Entrust it to us out of trust; what may we do for you?
On the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight, Purocana shall set fire to this house of yours at its entrance."
"The Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men, must be burned to death along with their mother"—
this was the resolution of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son that I heard, O Pārtha. Furthermore, O Pāṇḍava, you were addressed by Vidura in the Mleccha language.
"And you replied, 'So be it'—this is the reason for my trust.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, firm in truth, said to him:
"O gentle one, I truly recognize you as a friend of Vidura."
He is pure, trustworthy, dear, and always firm in his devotion;
for Kavi, there is no need for any token of recognition.
As he is to us, so are you to us; we are no different toward you.

"O you two, protect us as he [the sage] protected us; act as a wise man would. It is my conviction that this Agni-shelter was constructed by Purocana for my sake, under the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son."
That wicked and evil-minded man, possessing both wealth and allies,
constantly oppresses us as well.
May your lordship exert effort to deliver us from this fire.

"If we are indeed consumed here, Suyodhana will have his desire fulfilled. This great armory of that evil-minded one, situated at the edge of the rampart, has been rendered defenseless; let him seize it."
"This must surely be that inauspicious deed he intended to perform;
Vidura knew of it beforehand and therefore warned us.
That very calamity has now arrived, which the Kṣattṛ foresaw long ago."
"Deliver us from Purocana while we remain unknown to him.
Having promised "So be it," the digger applied himself with effort and,
while ostensibly digging a moat, constructed a very large subterranean cavern.
And in the middle of that house, O Bhārata, he constructed a door that was not too large, fitted with panels and made level with the floor;
out of fear of Purocana, he kept the entrance concealed.
Having indeed returned here from heaven, he was a great favorite of Indra;
then, sent by Indra to act for the benefit of the Pāṇḍavas,
he remained constantly devoted to eating clay for ten days.
Having made a very large hole, he departed from here to heaven once more;
then, having reported everything to Indra, he returned again from heaven. That one of evil intent dwells there constantly at the door of the house.
There, O King, they all dwelt through the nights with their weapons ready;
by day, the sons of Pāṇḍu roamed from forest to forest on hunts,
appearing as if trustful while remaining distrustful, thus deceiving Purocana.
O King, though they were extremely distressed, they lived there as if content, appearing satisfied;
and the people dwelling in the city did not perceive their condition,
except for the minister Vidura, that best of diggers.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having seen them with cheerful minds after they had lived there for a full year,
and perceiving that they were as if completely trusting, Purocana was filled with joy.
With a joyful inner soul, he reflected:
"I believe this is the opportune moment for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas. Then, having discerned that internal disposition of his, the bull among the Kurus—
The wise Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, reflected upon this;
and when Purocana was thus delighted, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
who knows the dharma, spoke to Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the twins.

"This wicked Purocana knows us to be completely trusting; this cruel-souled man has been deceived. I believe the time has come for our escape. Having set fire to the armory and burned Purocana to death,"
"Having placed six living beings here, let us depart unobserved. Then, O King, under the pretext of giving alms, Kuntī prepared a great feast for Brahmins at night; many women arrived there.
O Bhārata, having sported as they pleased and having eaten and drunk,
they departed for their homes at night after taking leave of Mādhavī; she, it is said,
was serving Pṛthā, who had been placed there by Purocana.
The Niṣādī woman, wicked-hearted and always moving about within [the palace],
had five sons; through her former habit, she felt affection for that food by chance, and she became a friend to Kuntī, equal to her own sons.
Having brought honey, roots, and various kinds of fruits, she,
driven by fate, came seeking food together with her sons.
That wicked woman, who had five sons, considered herself a friend of Pṛthā.
Having drunk the wine, O King, she became intoxicated; overwhelmed by intoxication along with all her sons, she slept in that very dwelling,
deprived of consciousness and resembling one who is dead, O lord of men.
Then, O Lord, when a tumultuous wind was blowing and the people were asleep at night,
Bhīma set fire to that place where Purocana lay;
thereafter, the Pāṇḍava ignited the door of the house of lac.
Then, he set fire to that dwelling on all sides. When the sons of Pāṇḍu realized that the entire house was ablaze,
those subduers of enemies quickly entered the tunnel together with their mother.
Having first cleared the cave, the high-minded Bhīmasena led Kuntī, together with the Pāṇḍavas, into that cave; then,
having quickly provided fire, Bhīma himself emerged through the opening.
Then, around that house, the wise one [beheld] the household's accumulated wealth;
thereafter, there was a very great heat and a sound like that of fire.
Then that mass of people was awakened by it as it appeared;
seeing their house ablaze, the citizens, with distressed faces, said: The citizens said:

"Alas, what a tragedy! All the Pāṇḍavas are being consumed by fire! they cried out, as the house—which had been built for his own destruction and set ablaze by the wicked and evil-minded Duryodhana—was burning.
And those men made the utmost effort for their deliverance;
then they beheld that hair-raising house of lac,
constructed by one of cruel deeds for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas.
"Alas, fie upon the intellect of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which is not at all sound, since he had the pure and young Pāṇḍavas burned by the wicked Purocana out of a desire for Duryodhana's welfare!"
"By good fortune, this evil-souled and most wicked-minded man has now been consumed—
he who burnt those best of men, who were innocent and full of trust.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus did the people of Vāraṇāvata lament;
surrounding that house, they remained there on all sides throughout the night.
And the Pāṇḍavas also, O King, together with their mother, were deeply distressed.
Having emerged through that opening, they went away secretly and unobserved;
yet, due to that deprivation of sleep and their agitation, those Pāṇḍavas,
the subduers of foes, were unable to proceed quickly with their mother.
But Bhīmasena, O king of kings, possessing terrible speed and prowess,
departed taking all his brothers and his mother; the heroic one placed his mother upon his shoulder and the twins in his arms.
Taking hold of the two Pārtha brothers with their hands, those two brothers of great strength went through a tunnel for a distance of one *yojana* to the auspicious Siddhapada;
there, at the foot of a banyan tree, they lay down with their eyes sealed in sleep.
Emerging suddenly from the cave, the son of the Wind-god reached his brothers and mother,
and having arrived at the forest on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he proceeded onward,
swiftly breaking down trees and tearing up the earth with his feet.
The radiant Vṛkodara, possessing the speed of the wind, proceeded swiftly,
breaking through thickets of shrubs and creepers along the indistinct forest paths.
Vaiśampāyana said:
At that very time,
however, the wise Vidura, according to his understanding, dispatched a pure man to that forest.
Having gone to the designated place, he beheld the Pāṇḍavas in the woods.
O descendant of Kuru, as they were measuring out the river water together with their mother,
that was known to the high-minded and wise Vidura; and thus, through his own spies, he learned of the conduct of that evil-minded man.

Then, dispatched by Vidura, that wise man showed the sons of Pṛthā a boat that moved with the speed of mind and wind, equipped with machinery, adorned with banners, and capable of withstanding all winds.
On the auspicious bank of the Bhāgīrathī, built by men who felt secure,
he then spoke again that which was previously enjoined as an indicator:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O sage, understand this speech for the sake of recognition."
The fire that destroys the thicket and the cold season does not kill those dwelling in a cave within a great forest; he who protects himself in this way survives.
Know that I have been sent by him, having placed my trust in this sign.
Furthermore, Vidura, the steward who knows all matters, said to me:
"O son of Kuntī, you will undoubtedly defeat Karṇa, Duryodhana along with his brothers, and Śakuni in battle."
"This boat, properly equipped for the water-path, will glide easily upon the waters;
it will deliver you all from this place, of this there is no doubt.
Then, seeing those best of men distressed along with their mother—
Having helped them board the boat on the Gaṅgā, Vidura spoke again to those who had set forth:
"Having smelled your heads and embraced you repeatedly, he said,
'Go safely and with undistracted minds upon the path.'"
Having spoken thus to those heroes, O king of kings, that man, urged by Vidura, ferried those bulls among men across the Gaṅgā by boat. Then,
having ferried them across the Gaṅgā, he brought them all safely to the further shore.
Having offered blessings of victory, he then departed by the way he had come.
And the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, having taken leave of the sage,
crossed the Gaṅgā with speed and proceeded on their way, hidden and unobserved.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
when the night had passed,
all the people of the city arrived there in haste, desiring to see the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Then those people, while extinguishing the fire, saw that house made of lac consumed by flames, along with the minister Purocana. "Surely this evil deed was orchestrated by Duryodhana."

"The sons of Pāṇḍu shall be destroyed"—thus did the people cry out. Once this was known by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra undoubtedly caused the heirs of Pāṇḍu to be burned; for he did not restrain him.
Surely Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, does not follow righteousness;
nor do Droṇa, Vidura, Kṛpa, and the other Kauravas—
though they know what is right, alas, O Fate, they disregard righteousness as if it were slain!
Alas! Even those who are learned and wise, like wealthy men, have fallen under the power [of fate];
even great men do not look after the virtuous, the helpless, the righteous, and those devoted to the vow of truth—for them, destiny is their ultimate refuge.
"We shall now send word to that evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
'Your supreme desire has been fulfilled; you have burned the Pāṇḍavas to ashes. Then, for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, they shall drive away that fire."
They beheld Niṣādī, innocent and with her five sons, consumed by fire.
"Look here! This illustrious Kuntī lies burnt;
look, O citizens, at this daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, who perished together with her sons!"
While that very excavator was clearing the house,
the opening was covered over with dust by those men so that it remained unnoticed;
thus they all grieved and spoke in this manner, each separately.
Then those citizens sent word to Dhṛtarāṣṭra that the Pāṇḍavas and the minister Purocana had been consumed by fire.
Upon hearing that most grievous news, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was deeply distressed.
Deeply distressed, he lamented the destruction of the sons of Pāṇḍu;
with joy within his heart yet overwhelmed by outward sorrow,
he was like a bottomless lake that is cool within but hot without in the summer heat.
"Today King Pāṇḍu has died, my brother so difficult to find,
now that those heroes— especially his mother— have been burned.
Let men go quickly to the city of Vāraṇāvata."
Let them honor those heroes and that daughter of Kuntirāja;
let them construct large and bright funeral mounds for them,
and let their friends also pay homage to those who have died there.
"My high-souled kinsmen, who increased the lineage of our family, have been consumed by fire.
This being the case, whatever beneficial acts can be performed by me—
whatever is for the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī— all that should be done with wealth."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all the Kauravas together with Bhīṣma,
as well as Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his sons, set out toward the Gaṅgā.
Clad in single garments, joyless, and devoid of ornaments and head-dresses, they—
along with their sons, kinsmen, and ministers, having abandoned their auspicious vehicles— were indeed desirous of offering water to the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.

O King, without umbrellas, they proceeded toward the Ganges along the way. Having spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, surrounded by his kinsmen, then offered the water libations for the sons of Pāṇḍu.
All the Kauravas, overcome by intense grief, cried out:
"Alas, Yudhiṣṭhira, O Kauravya! Alas, Bhīma! others cried;
"Alas, Phālguna! said some, and "Alas, the twins! said others.
The people, distressed and grieving for Kuntī, offered water libations;
other citizens likewise lamented for the Pāṇḍavas,
repeatedly exclaiming, "Oh, what beauty, grace, learning, and strength!"
"Was it propriety or was it love? Why do we grieve so?"—speaking thus at great length, the citizens wept bitterly;
but Vidura grieved only slightly, for he knew the supreme truth.
01,137.016 Vaiśampāyana;
01,137.016 Vaiśampāyana.
Then Bhīṣma, deeply distressed upon hearing that the sons of King Pāṇḍu had died along with their mother,
lamented and wept.
"Alas Yudhiṣṭhira! Alas Bhīma! Alas Dhanañjaya! Alas the twins!
Alas Pṛthā, you have gone to heaven in a single night along with your sons! Your young children, together with their mother, all remain right there."
For indeed, Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya,
with their selves impelled by speed, would not fail to shatter even this palace by their force;
nor do I see how Pṛthā could meet her end along with the Pāṇḍavas.
In every way, that [destruction] would have been a calamity if they had met their end;
for Yudhiṣṭhira has indeed been designated by the Brahmins as Dharmarāja,
and he, Dhananjaya, will become the foremost among those who move upon the earth.

How did Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu— firm in his vows, devoted to dharma, truthful in speech, and endowed with auspicious marks— come under the power of Time? He who conducts himself toward others by taking himself as the standard of comparison.
How did that descendant of Kuru, along with his mother, fall under the power of Time—
he who had been protected for a long time, yet like a tree at the time of its fruition,
was broken by the force of the wind, even so was King Yudhiṣṭhira?
He who, having been consecrated as crown prince, acquired glory for his father— and likewise for himself— through truth, righteousness, and noble conduct; he,
devoted to the Brahmins and observant of others, has placed my grief within his heart.

For he was destroyed by Time; fie upon Fate, which bestows misfortune! And because she was so devoted to her son, Kuntī—though she suffered through dwelling in the forest and shared in its hardships—did not die after her husband.

"She who, having been born into this family for but a short time, had attained the affection of her husband— she has today been consumed along with her sons, her desires yet unfulfilled. As he reflected upon this, his mind was deeply distressed in many ways.
And though my body has been cast aside, the fire does not burst forth within my heart;
hearing that the youth, with his thick shoulders and beautiful arms, resembling a peak of Mount Meru,
is dead— though his name was Bhīma— my mind cannot believe it.
He is one who excels in relinquishment, a yogi, swift-handed, and firm with his weapons; he is active, has hit his mark, and is an expert in chariot warfare;
he is a long-distance shooter, undaunted, of great heroism, and a knower of mighty missiles.
That tiger among men, whose soul was never dejected, was the foremost of all archers;
by him the easterners, the Sauviras, and those of the south were utterly defeated,
and by that hero his manliness was proclaimed throughout the three worlds.
How did Jishnu— who, upon his birth, brought an end to the sorrow of Kuntī and the heroic Pāṇḍu,
and who was equal to Purandara— come under the power of Time?
How did those two, with shoulders like bulls and a gait as powerful as lions’, [fall]?
The twins, the destroyers of their enemies, having succumbed to the condition of mortals,
heard his lamentation and poured out water for him;
then Vidura, discerning the proper place and time, replied:
"Do not grieve, O tiger among men; cast off your sorrow, O you of great vows. No sin exists for them, as that which was done has reached its appointed time by me.
And let him, O Bhārata, sprinkle water over them from those [vessels]."
Having uttered something while the Kauravas did not hear him, he addressed the Steward (Vidura),
his voice choked with a flood of tears:
"How, dear father, do those great chariot-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu, survive?"
How was it that the side of Pāṇḍu was not struck down for our sake? How were we all, led by me, released from such great danger? Those princes were rescued, like a mother [rescued] by Garuḍa.
Thus addressed, while the Kauravas were listening,
that righteous-souled one related [the matter] to Bhīṣma of wondrous deeds,
concerning Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śakuni, and King Duryodhana.
