Having resolved my mind upon the destruction of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
and having likewise ascertained that wicked resolve,
I too, desiring to slay him, remained intent upon their approval.
Then, having gone to the house of lac, when this fire was set by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra against Pṛthā and her sons,
he then summoned a digger and [constructed] a tunnel in that hollow.

"Having had a house with a secret passage constructed for them, those sons of Pāṇḍu were previously led out by me along with Kuntī; do not set your mind on grief. Then, having placed Pṛthā together with her sons upon a boat,"
Having granted safety to Kuntī and her sons, I set fire to the house.
Therefore, let there be no grief for you; the Pāṇḍavas have been released from that sin.
O King, the Pāṇḍavas, those subduers of enemies, have emerged together with their mother.
Therefore, do not grieve over those most terrible fires caused by me through that stratagem; for the Pāṇḍavas are indeed alive and will wander in disguise until the turn of time.
At that time, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
men on earth shall behold him as pure as the risen moon at the end of the dark fortnight;
I see no destruction for him whose brother is Dhanañjaya.
O Bhārata, the invincible Bhīmasena and the two sons of Mādrī,
as well as the other Pāṇḍavas, having departed from the city of Vāraṇāvata,
reached the river Gaṅgā accompanied by their mother, all possessing great strength.
By the strength of the arms of the fishermen, by the swift current of the river,
and by a favorable wind, they quickly reached the opposite shore; with great speed, O King, they proceeded, taking their course toward the southern direction.

Having discerned their path by the stars at night, O King, they headed southward and, exerting themselves, entered the dense forest. Then the sons of Pāṇḍu became exhausted, afflicted by thirst, and blinded by sleep.
Once again, they spoke these words to the immensely powerful Bhīmasena:
"What indeed could be more miserable than this, that we are in a dense forest,
do not know the directions, and are unable even to move forward?"
"And we do not know whether that wicked Purocana has been burnt;
how indeed may we escape from this danger unobserved?
O Bhārata, take us once again and proceed just as before."
"For you alone among us are powerful, just as Satatakami was.
Thus addressed by the King of Dharma, the mighty Bhimasena,
endowed with great strength, took Kuntī and his brothers and departed swiftly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As he strode swiftly, the forest, shaken by the force of his thighs,
seemed as if it were being whirled around along with its trees and branches.
O King, the wind blew as it does at the onset of the bright summer months;
the one of great strength cleared a path by bending over the creepers and trees. He crushed both the flowering and the fruit-bearing lords of the forest.
Tearing up the thickets of wood growing near that path,
like one enraged and furious as he breaks down great trees in the forest,
the majestic sixty-year-old king of elephants, his ichor flowing in three streams, advanced.
Thus, breaking down the trees, he of immeasurable prowess proceeded;
the exceedingly terrifying sound of the wind arising from his two armpits was heard, pervading every quarter of the horizon.
By its force, a kind of swoon seemed to come over the Pāṇḍavas.
Having repeatedly crossed the river Ganges— which has a far shore and whose waters are filled with the cries of birds— by means of their arms as rafts, they emerged from it.
Carrying their mother and their brothers without fatigue, the sons of the Wind then proceeded along the road, concealed out of fear of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for it was with great difficulty that they carried their single mother, who was delicate and illustrious.
There, on the ridges and uneven ground, they carried him on their backs;
at evening, those bulls of the Bharata race arrived at a forest region that was terrible, filled with fierce birds and beasts, and where roots, fruits, and water were scarce.
A terrible and dreadful twilight set in, and the beasts and birds became fierce; all the directions were shrouded in darkness by unseasonable winds,
O King, and the trees were filled with many shrubs and bushes whose leaves and fruits had withered away.
Filled with many trees that were mostly broken and bent,
the Kauravas— afflicted by exhaustion and thirst,
and overcome by increasing sleep— were unable to proceed at that time.
They all entered that exceedingly dense, terrible, and in some places a path difficult to discern great forest, which was devoid of any pleasant taste;
then Kuntī, emaciated by thirst, spoke to her sons.

Standing in the midst of the five Pāṇḍavas, she who was their mother, being overcome by thirst, spoke urgently to her sons. Hearing those words spoken by Bhīmasena out of maternal affection, [he replied].
With a mind burning with compassion, he set out to depart.
During the night itself, they traveled swiftly twenty-four yojanas;
beyond this point, I am no longer able to go even a single step on foot.
"I shall lie here at the foot of this tree; let the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra carry me away!
Listen to my words, Bhīma: in the presence of the strength of your arms, the Kauravas are not able to stand. Why do you fear in vain, O son?"
"I have no other enemies on earth except Bhīmasena and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you coward; you desire me to sleep here in vain. Thus, seated upon Bhīma’s back with a grieving heart," [she spoke].
Weeping with a sound of tears, she fell under the power of sleep.
Then Bhīma, having entered the vast and formidable forest devoid of people,
approached a beautiful banyan tree of wide-spreading shade.
Having set them all down there, O bull of the Bharatas, that lord said:
"I am searching for water here; you must rest.
For these water-faring cranes are crying out sweetly.
"It is my conviction that there is surely a great body of water here. O descendant of Bharata, having been permitted by his eldest brother to depart,
he went to the place where the aquatic creatures were crying out.
Having drunk water there and bathed, O bull of the Bharatas,
he who was devoted to his brothers took up lotus leaves for the sake of his brothers and bound them together to form reservoirs of water.
Then, O King, having returned from a distance of one *gavyūti*, he hurried toward his mother, bringing water in his upper garment;
his soul overwhelmed by grief and sorrow, he sighed like a serpent.
He gave water to his brothers and his mother to drink;
once they had drunk the water, they all, overcome by exhaustion and their fortitude stolen by sleep, fell into a deep slumber, utterly overwhelmed.
Seeing his mother and his brothers asleep on the ground in that most terrible and fearsome forest, at the cool foot of a tree,
with their hands and feet sprawled out and their heavy breathing loud and long, he [remained there].
With his face turned upward and his body trembling, Vṛkodara— like five Indras upon the earth,
yet terrified by the unknown tree-dwelling spirits, ghosts, and Rākṣasas—
lamented with a soul overwhelmed by intense sorrow.
What indeed could be more painful than this that I must now behold? For I, unfortunate as I am, see my brothers today sleeping upon the earth,
whereas formerly at Vāraṇāvata they lay upon most excellent beds.

At that time, they found no sleep; yet today they lie asleep upon the ground— Kuntī, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, endowed with every auspicious mark, the sister of Vasudeva, the crusher of hosts of enemies.
The daughter-in-law of Vicitravīrya and wife of the high-souled Pāṇḍu— she who always slept upon palatial couches, possessed the radiance of the interior of a white lotus,
was more delicate than the most delicate of women, and was accustomed to costly beds.
Behold her here today lying upon the earth, though she is unaccustomed to such a state—
she who gave birth to these sons from Dharma, Indra, and Vāyu;
yet now she lies exhausted upon the ground, though she is so ill-suited for it.
"What indeed could be more painful for me to behold than this—
that I today see these tigers among men lying asleep upon the ground?
For a king who knows the dharma deserves the sovereignty over the three worlds."
How is it that he,
who is dark as a blue cloud and peerless among men on earth, now lies upon the ground like an ordinary man, exhausted? What indeed could be more painful than this?
These two, dark as blue lotuses, peerless among men on earth,
who by their perfection of form are like the Aśvins among the gods—
these two now lie fast asleep upon the surface of the ground like common folk.

He who has no kinsmen who are discordant or who bring disgrace to the family shall live in great happiness in this world, like a solitary tree in a village. For indeed, that single tree which stands in a village and is endowed with leaves and fruit [is cherished].
He becomes a shrine for his kin, worthy of worship and well-honored;
those whose many kinsmen are brave and devoted to the Dharma live happily in this world and remain free from affliction.
"Powerful, their purposes fulfilled, and bringing joy to their friends and kinsmen,
they live by relying on one another, like trees born in a forest. But we have been treated thus by the evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons."
Greedy for the kingdom, foolish, accompanied by evil counselors, wicked, unrighteous in character, and with a mind focused solely on his own self-interest—
by the command of such a man, they were exiled and somehow not burned.
"Therefore, having escaped from that burning heat, we have taken refuge under this tree.
To what direction shall we turn now, having encountered such unsurpassed suffering?
O evil-minded one of little vision, son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, let your desires be fulfilled!"

Surely the gods are pleased with you, O evil-minded one, for Yudhiṣṭhira does not grant you permission to slay me; that is why you still live. Indeed, today [I shall destroy] you along with your sons, ministers, Karṇa, his younger brothers, and Saubala.
"Filled with rage, having gone there, I shall send him to the abode of Yama.
O you of sinful conduct, what indeed can I do so that Yudhiṣṭhira— the righteous-souled best of the Pāṇḍavas— does not become angry with you, O King?"
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one, his mind inflamed with anger, crushed hand against hand and sighed with a dejected heart; then,
becoming once more dejected in spirit, he was like a fire whose flames have been extinguished.
Vṛkodara beheld his brothers sleeping on the surface of the earth,
lying there as if full of trust and appearing like common folk;
and he perceived that the city was not far from this forest.
"While they sleep when they ought to be awake, alas, I myself shall remain awake. "Having awakened and overcome their fatigue, they will drink water later.
Having thus resolved, Bhīma then kept watch himself.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While they were sleeping there, a Rākṣasa named Hiḍimba was perched upon a śāla tree not far from that forest.
Cruel, a devourer of human flesh, possessed of great heroism and great strength; dark as a rain-cloud, with tawny eyes and a formidable appearance;
his face terrifying with fangs, he was tormented by hunger and longing for flesh.
With pendulous buttocks and a protruding belly, with red beard and hair,
with the shoulders of a great tree and spike-like ears, he was terrifying;
by chance, he beheld those sons of Pāṇḍu, the great chariot-warriors.

Deformed in appearance, tawny-eyed, terrifying, and fierce to behold, he was hungry and longing for flesh; by chance, he saw them. Scratching himself with his fingers pointed upward, he shook his coarse hair.
Yawning with his great mouth and looking again and again,
that wicked eater of human flesh, possessing a massive body and great strength,
sniffed the scent of humans and spoke thus to his sister:
"After a long time, today my prey, so dear to my heart, has appeared. My tongue, dripping with saliva, flows forth and moves around my mouth.
My eight fangs, with their exceedingly sharp tips, have not been able to strike for so long."
I shall plunge into bodies and into moist flesh;
having attacked the human throat and even severed the artery,
I shall drink copious amounts of warm, fresh, and frothy blood.
"Go and find out who these are lying here, having taken refuge in the forest. A strong human scent satisfies my nostrils as it were.
Having slain all these men, bring them into my presence."
"You have no fear from these who sleep within our domain;
having prepared the flesh of these humans, let us both eat it together as we please. Quickly do as I say."
"And having eaten human flesh to our heart's content,
we two shall dance together many times, keeping time. Thus was Hiḍimbā addressed by Hiḍimba then in the forest.
Leaping from tree to tree, she went toward the Pāṇḍavas;
having received her brother’s command, the Rākṣasī proceeded with great haste,
O bull of the Bharatas, to where the Pāṇḍavas were.
Having gone there, she saw the Pāṇḍavas together with Pṛthā lying down, and the unconquered Bhīmasena, who remained awake,
being attended by Bhīma, who was endowed with beauty and youth.
To those delicate sons of Pṛthā, who were emaciated by physical exertion, joined with suffering, and overcome by their elder brother, she—
being fierce yet beautiful— showed herself to the princes.
Upon seeing Bhīmasena, who rose up like the trunk of a *śāla* tree and was peerless on earth in beauty, that rākṣasī felt desire for him;
with her mind inwardly turned, the rākṣasī reflected:
"This dark-complexioned one, mighty-armed, with shoulders like a lion's and great splendor,
with a neck like a conch shell and eyes like lotuses— he would be a fitting husband for me. I would never carry out the cruel words of my brother."
Affection for a husband is exceedingly powerful, yet brotherly love is not so;
satisfaction would last but a moment for both my brother and myself. But by slaying these [enemies], I shall rejoice for eternal years rather than by leaving them unslain.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the exceedingly fierce Hiḍimbī cast off her Rākṣasa form and assumed a human shape;
being able to take any form at will, she fashioned for herself an excellent human appearance.
Skilled in interpreting gestures and facial expressions, she approached the mighty-armed Bhīmasena very slowly; adorned with all her ornaments, she drew near like a bending creeper.
Then Bhīma, watching her as she drew near very slowly,
beheld that slender woman with full breasts,
a moon-like face, lotus eyes, and dark, curly hair.
Seeing her, endowed with such beauty— dark-skinned with very white teeth, having lips like the *bimba* fruit, and lovely to behold— Bhīma was struck with wonder;
she was possessed of the qualities of refined conduct, graced by playful and charming smiles.
Then, having approached Bhīma, that fair-faced woman spoke these words to the Pāṇḍava at the proper time for speech,
appearing as if bashful, adorned with divine ornaments like a flowering creeper.
Then, with a smile, he spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"From where have you come, and who are you, O bull among men?
And who are these men of godlike form lying here?"

"O sinless one, who is this large, dark-complexioned, and delicate woman lying here in this forest as if she were in her own home, so full of confidence? She does not realize that this is a dense forest inhabited by *rākṣasas*."
"For here dwells a wicked-souled Rākṣasa named Hiḍimba.
I have been sent here by that evil-minded brother, the Rākṣasa,
who desires to devour your flesh, O you who are like unto the immortals."

Having beheld you, who possess a radiance equal to that of a divine child, I desire no other husband; I tell you this truth. Knowing this, O knower of dharma, act toward me in a manner that is fitting.
"Accept me, whose body and mind are overcome by desire as I serve you. O mighty-armed one, I shall protect you from the man-eating Rākṣasa;
let us dwell in the mountain fastnesses. O sinless one, be my husband."
"I desire this, O hero—may it be well with you—do not let me lose my life.
For if I am abandoned by you, O subduer of enemies, I shall not live. Indeed, I am one who travels through the air and wanders at will."
"May you attain incomparable joy with me in various places;
this is my eldest brother, none other than my supreme teacher. As long as he remains unmarried, I shall by no means marry."
Bhīma said:
"O Rākṣasī, who indeed would abandon his mother, his eldest brother, and these other younger brothers today, while still possessing the power to do so?"
For what man like me, afflicted by passion, would go away after offering these sleeping brothers as food for the Rākṣasa, and likewise his mother?— O Rākṣasī!
"O scorcher of the enemy, I shall liberate you alone along with your mother;
leave these brothers behind and mount upon my hip."
"O Rākṣasī, I have no hope of living if I must abandon my brothers;
go back the way you came alone, for you speak what is disagreeable to me.
The Rākṣasī said:
"I shall do what is pleasing to you; awaken all of these. I will surely liberate you from the man-eating Rākṣasa.
Bhīma said:
O Rākṣasī, out of fear for your evil-minded brother, I shall not wake my brothers and mother as they sleep peacefully in the forest; for,
O timid one, the Rākṣasas are not capable of withstanding my prowess.
"Neither humans, nor Gandharvas, nor Yakṣas [can harm you], O lovely-eyed one.
Go or stay, O blessed lady, or do whatever you desire;
or else, O slender-limbed one, send that man-eating brother of yours away."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having learned that she had been gone for a long time, Hiḍimba, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
descended from that tree and then approached the Pāṇḍavas.
Red-eyed, long-armed, with hair standing erect, possessed of great strength,
with a body like a mass of clouds, and a face radiant with sharp fangs—
he struck palm against palm and repeatedly brandished his arms.
With eyes rolling and enraged, grinding his teeth against his teeth, he thought:
"Does Hiḍimbī not fear me? Why has she been sent and does she not yet arrive?
Seeing him approaching with such a hideous appearance, [he spoke].
Terrified, Hiḍimbā spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"This evil-minded man-eater is rushing toward us in a rage;
do exactly as I tell you, along with your brothers."
"O hero, I am capable of going wherever I desire and am endowed with the strength of a rākṣasa.
Mount upon my hips; I shall carry you through the air.
O scorcher of foes, awaken these who are fast asleep, as well as their mother."
"I shall take you all and travel through the sky.
Bhīma said:
"Do not fear, O lady of broad hips; as long as I am standing here, no one can harm you."
"It is my firm conviction that no *rakṣasa* could possibly harm him;
whether it be a god or even a *dānava*, none is capable of oppressing these [sages].
O slender-waisted one, I shall slay him while you look on."
"O timid one, this lowest of Rākṣasas is not capable of enduring my prowess in battle, nor indeed can all the Rākṣasas together.
Behold these two well-rounded arms of mine, resembling the trunks of elephants."
"My thighs are like iron clubs and my chest is broad;
today, O beautiful one, you shall behold my prowess equal to that of Indra.
Do not despise me, O lady of broad hips, by thinking that I am merely a human here."
Hiḍimbā said:
"O tiger among men, I do not disregard you who possess the form of a god;
however, I have seen a rākṣasa among humans who has performed great deeds."
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, while Bhīmasena was thus conversing,
the enraged man-eating Rākṣasa heard those words.
And Hiḍimba beheld her human form,
with hair adorned by garlands of flowers, a face resembling the full moon, with beautiful eyebrows,
nose, eyes, and hair-ends, and with delicate nails and skin.
Adorned with every ornament and clothed in very fine garments,
she bore a most enchanting human form;
the man-eater beheld her thus before Bhīma.
Suspecting that she desired a man, the man-eater grew enraged.
O best of the Kurus, the Rākṣasa, filled with rage toward his sister,
then widened his large eyes and spoke this to her.
"Who is this evil-minded one who creates an obstacle for me when I desire to eat?
Are you not afraid, Hiḍimbā? Have you been utterly deluded by my wrath?
Shame on you, you unchaste woman, who lusts after men and acts against my will!"
This act, which brings dishonor to all the former lords of the Rākṣasas,
you have committed by relying on these [monkeys] and doing me such great harm;
today I shall surely slay them all along with you.
Having spoken thus to Hiḍimbā, the red-eyed Hiḍimba rushed toward her for the sake of killing her, gnashing his teeth against teeth;
Bhīmasena beheld him roaring in that desolate place.
Protecting the vigilance of his brothers and his mother, that slayer of enemy heroes,
the radiant Bhīma— the best among strikers— beholding him rushing toward him, rebuked him and said, "Stay! Stay!"
Vaiśampāyana said:
But Bhīmasena, seeing that Rākṣasa enraged at his sister, spoke these words as if laughing:
"O Hiḍimba, what is the use of waking these people who are sleeping so peacefully? Approach me, O evil-minded eater of men, and confront me with force!
Strike at me alone; you ought not to kill a woman."
Especially since no harm was done by me and harm has been done by another,
this young woman, who is not her own mistress, does not desire me here today;
for she has been impelled by the bodiless god who wanders within the body.
"O evil-minded one, she is your sister, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas' fame. At your command, and having beheld my form, this timid woman now desires me; she does not defile her family."

"O evil-minded Rākṣasa, you ought not to kill her here for an offense committed by the bodiless god of love; if you are a hero, then destroy Smara himself! O wicked-souled one, while I am standing here, you ought not to kill a woman."
"O Rākṣasa, I shall kill you, who are afflicted by the arrows of desire for my sake. Come together with me, one-on-one, O devourer of men;
I alone shall lead you today to the abode of Yama."
"O Rākṣasa, today let your head, crushed by my palm,
shatter into a hundred pieces like a full water-jar struck against a stone,
as if trampled by the foot of a powerful elephant."
"Today, let the flesh-eaters— hawks and jackals—
joyfully drag your limbs upon the earth once you have been slain by me in battle.
In an instant today, I shall rid this forest of its thorn."
"O wicked one, you who have constantly defiled [the world] by devouring men from the very beginning—
today, O sinner, your sister shall see you being dragged upon the ground by me,
looking like a mountain, like a great elephant being dragged by a lion."
"O vile Rākṣasa, when you have been slain by me, these forest-dwelling men shall roam this forest free from all affliction. Hiḍimba said:
O man, what is the use of your roaring and your boasting?
For your roar is as fruitless as that of an autumnal cloud. Having accomplished all this through action, you should boast; do not delay.

Since you consider yourself strong and devoid of prowess, today, upon encountering me, you shall know yourself to be surpassed in strength. For now, I will not harm these; let them sleep as they please.
"O evil-minded one, I shall slay you first, you who speak so unpleasantly;
having drunk the blood from your limbs,
I will afterwards kill these others, and after that, this woman who has done me harm."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the man-eater then seized Bhīmasena, the tamer of foes, by the arm and rushed at him in a great rage.
As he was rushing forward swiftly, Bhīma of terrible prowess,
as if laughing, seized his outstretched arm with force.
Having restrained him by strength, Bhīma dragged him about as he struggled.
Eight bow-lengths from that spot, like a lion toward a small animal,
the enraged Rākṣasa, forcibly seized by the Pāṇḍava,
embraced Bhīmasena and let out a terrifying roar.
Then the mighty Bhīma, possessing great strength, forcibly dragged him away,
thinking, "Let there be no noise that might wake my brothers who are sleeping peacefully.
Seizing the *rākṣasa* by the hand, he carried him far away to another place.
Having seized him by the tail with his beak like a *garuḍa* seizing a serpent,
the two of them, having encountered one another, dragged each other with great force;
the *rākṣasa* and Bhīmasena both displayed supreme prowess.
Having broken down trees with massive branches, they struck them out in their fury:
*sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, mango, *vaṭa*, and *arjuna* trees; *vibhītaka*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, date palms, breadfruit trees, and *aśmakaṇṭaka* trees.
Having uprooted all these and other great trees with force,
they tossed them about and struck one another in their mutual rage during the battle,
until the entire forest, once thick with trees, became treeless.
Then those two enemies, having uprooted and taken stones, thickets, and thorny trees, as well as mountain peaks, cloud-licking mountains, and boulders from the slopes, [advanced].
Desiring victory over one another in that battle, the two hurled [their weapons] at each other from above;
they utterly cleared the forest for five *yojanas* around it, making it devoid of trees, creepers, shrubs, stones, and wild animals.

O Indra among kings, through the battle of those two Bhīma and Rākṣasa, that forest in a mere moment became smooth and level like the back of a tortoise. Then they both broke down the great trees and dragged away the creepers.
Like two sixty-year-old elephants in rut, highly agitated,
they rushed forward with the speed of their thighs, uprooting trees and tearing apart masses of creepers by grasping them all around with their legs.
Terrifying all the beasts and birds on every side with their roars, those two powerful and intoxicated warriors, each desiring to slay the other,
engaged in a fierce battle between the two terrible rākṣasas.
Exerting themselves against one another with their thighs and arms,
pulling, dragging, and hauling each other to and fro,
they then roared at one another with a great sound.
They struck each other with blows resembling the clashing of stones; embracing one another and dragging each other back and forth,
a terrible hand-to-hand combat ensued, like that between Bali and Vāsava.
The sound of their hissing, issuing forth from the fury of battle,
was like that of Vṛtra and Vāsava in the ancient war between the gods and the asuras; by that great noise, those bulls among men were awakened.
Together with their mother, they saw Hiḍimbā standing before them.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having awakened, they beheld the superhuman form of Hiḍimbā.
Those tigers among men, together with Pṛthā, were filled with wonder.
Then Kuntī, beholding her and being herself amazed by the perfection of her beauty,
spoke these sweet words slowly and with conciliation:
"To whom do you belong, O you who shine like the offspring of a god? And who are you, O woman of excellent complexion?
For what purpose have you come, O lady of beautiful hips, and from where have you arrived? Are you perhaps the deity of this forest, or are you an *apsaras*?"
"Tell me all of that; for what purpose do you stand here?
Hiḍimbā said:
"This great forest which you see, resembling a dark cloud—"
"This is the dwelling of the Rākṣasa Hiḍimba and of myself as well.
Know me, O beautiful lady, to be the sister of that lord of Rākṣasas,
sent here by my brother who desires to kill you and your son, O noble lady."
"O auspicious one, at the command of that man of cruel intellect, I have come here;
I beheld your son of great majesty, radiant with the luster of gold.
Then, O beautiful one, I moved among the hearts of all living beings."
Urged by your son’s god of love, she became subject to his will;
therefore, your mighty son was chosen by me as my husband,
and though I strove to dissuade him, I was simply unable to do so.
Knowing that I was delaying, that man-eater then came himself to kill all these sons of yours.
He was encountered by my beloved, your wise son.
Having violently crushed him here, he was dragged away by that high-souled one;
behold those two, the man and the rākṣasa, both valiant in battle, dragging each other with great speed and roaring at one another.
Fighting with the desire for victory, the dull-witted Rākṣasa said:
"I do not wish for the life of my brother, that man of evil deeds, at any time."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Upon hearing her words, Yudhiṣṭhira,
Arjuna, Nakula, and the heroic Sahadeva sprang up at once.
They saw those two locked together, dragging each other about,
both desiring victory like two lions fierce in battle;
they clung to one another, pulling each other to and fro.
They raised a cloud of earthly dust resembling the smoke of a forest fire; enveloped by the dust of the earth, those two who resembled mountains shone like two peaks shrouded in mist.
Beholding that great battle, they were all distressed in heart;
yet, seeing Bhīma thus being tormented by the Rākṣasa,
and observing those two who had been fighting for a long time with a mutual desire for each other's destruction, [they watched].

Pārtha spoke these words, laughing softly as it were: "O Bhīma, do not fear, O mighty-armed one! Exhausted by fatigue, we were fast asleep and did not perceive you when you arrived in this terrifying form."
"O Pārtha, I stand here to assist you; I shall fight the Rākṣasa.
Nakula and Sahadeva will protect our mother.
Bhīma said:
"Look on with indifference; you must not be agitated.
Having come between my arms, this Rākṣasa shall never live again once he has reached the space between Bhīmasena’s arms."

"O Pārtha, by my prowess I shall not release him, lest he die; let there be this sound [of my resolve]. O Pārtha, this Rākṣasa shall never slay us. I will not let him go alive; do not fear, O bull of the Bharatas."
Arjuna said:
O Bhīma, you were awakened in the early part of the night by a cruel rākṣasa;
the night has now dawned, yet you have not finished the great battle.
"O Bhīma, what is the use of this wicked Rākṣasa living any longer?
O subduer of enemies, he cannot remain here for much more time. Before the eastern quarter grows red, before the dawn twilight sets in,"
"In this *raudra* moment, the *rākṣasas* become powerful.
Hasten, Bhīma! Do not play; slay the terrifying *rākṣasa* before he manifests his magic. Apply the full strength of your arms!"
"You know your own greatness out of a desire for the welfare of men;
slay this Rakshasa as Shakra slew Vritra of old in the great forest.
Vaishampayana said:
Thus addressed by Arjuna, Bhīma,
blazing as if with rage at the terrifying Rākṣasa,
summoned that strength which [he had displayed] when the world was destroyed by Vāyu.
Then,
having lifted up the body of that one who resembled a cloud— [a body] exceeding a hundred qualities— he whirled it rapidly;
and as he whirled the Rākṣasa, he spoke thus in a state of great anger.
The mighty-armed Bhīmasena, roaring again and again, said:
Bhīma said:
"Rearing on meat obtained in vain, nourished in vain, grown old in vain, and possessing a mind devoted to what is vain—"
"You deserve a useless death; today you shall no longer exist in vain. Today I shall make the forest secure, free from thorns, so that you, O Rākṣasa, shall never again kill and devour human beings."
Arjuna said:
"Or, if you consider this Rākṣasa a burden in battle, I shall provide you assistance; let him be slain immediately."
"Or rather, Vṛkodara, I myself shall slay him;
you have performed your task and are exhausted, so rest well for now.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Hearing those words of his, the highly intolerant Bhīmasena violently threw him down upon the ground and killed him like an animal; then,
having seized him by force, he likewise slew him as one slaughters livestock.
Being struck by Bhīma, he let out a tremendous roar,
filling the entire forest like a drum dampened with water;
then the powerful son of Pāṇḍu bound him with his two arms.
Having whirled his head along with his neck, he carried it upward;
having split his head in the middle, he cast Sugrīva’s [head] aside.
It was devoid of ears and eyes, tongueless, and drenched in blood.
Cast aside by Bhīmasena, that head, gnashing its teeth, shone forth;
with its arms outstretched and its flesh and skin torn open,
it became a headless trunk (*kabandha*) there, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Having broken him in the middle, that powerful one gladdened the Pāṇḍavas.
Seeing Hiḍimba slain, those energetic warriors were filled with joy; and Hiḍimbā too, beholding the Rākṣasa killed in battle, was likewise delighted.
And those invisible beings who dwell in their own realms, the speakers of truth, gathered together and, being greatly delighted, honored the son of Pāṇḍu, crying out, "Excellent!
Excellent! And his brothers as well, led by Yudhiṣṭhira, were filled with joy.
They honored Bhīmasena, that tiger among men and subduer of foes. Having paid homage to the high-souled Bhīma of terrible prowess,
Arjuna spoke these words once more to Vṛkodara.
"O Lord, I think the city is not far from this forest;
let us go quickly—may you be blessed—so that Suyodhana may not discover us.
Then all those subduers of enemies, having said "So be it," departed together with their mother.
Those tigers among men departed, as did the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the sister of that Rākṣasa quickly descended from there.
The Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, however, without speaking to the Pāṇḍavas,
then saluted Kuntī and the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja;
having honored them all, she addressed Bhīmasena.
From the mere sight of you, I fell under the power of the god of love;
disregarding the cruel words of my brother and devoted solely to you,
I witnessed your conduct toward that Rakshasa of fierce appearance.
"I desire to serve you and attend to your person.
Bhīma said:
"Rākṣasas remember their enmity by resorting to delusive magic."
"O Hiḍimbā, go along the path frequented by your brother.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhīma, tiger among men, even though you are enraged, do not slay a woman."
O Pāṇḍava, protect the dharma that is superior even to the protection of the body;
O Pāṇḍava, protect the dharma by concealing one who has come for refuge. You have slain a man of great strength who came with the intent to kill you.
"What can the sister of that *rākṣasa*, even if she is angry, do to us?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Hiḍimbā, having saluted Kuntī with joined palms, spoke.
And he spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī:
"O noble lady, you know the suffering born of love that women endure here;
that very suffering has now come upon me, O auspicious one, caused by Bhīmasena."

I have endured that supreme suffering while awaiting my time; now that very time has arrived, and it shall surely bring me happiness. For I have renounced my friends, my own duty, and likewise my kinsmen.
"O auspicious one, this tiger among men, your son, has been chosen as your husband by this boon and by you as well, O illustrious lady. Therefore,
O woman of excellent complexion, you ought to show me compassion."
For having spoken thus at that time, being rejected regarding the ritual action,
I shall undoubtedly go to the worlds of evildoers on earth—
whether you consider me a fool, or think I am devoted, or think I am merely following you.
"O highly fortunate one, unite him with this husband, your son;
taking him, who possesses the form of a god, I shall go wherever I desire. And I shall surely return again—place your trust in me, O auspicious lady."
Indeed, I intended to seize him at the proper time before my elder brother could deliver him;
then, during the night, he rushed forward with the desire to kill Bhīmasena—
just as he strides, just as he sports, and just as he stands.
In whatever way she tried to entice the Pāṇḍava, being deluded by passion, that Yātudhānī said:
"Noble lady, I am not a Yātudhānī, nor am I a night-stalker (Rākṣasī).
I am Īśā among the Rākṣasas, a virtuous queen named Sālakaṭaṅkaṭī."
Accompanied by your son, O lady of celestial complexion,
I shall attend upon all of you, placing Vṛkodara at my head—
vigilant among the heedless, devoted to service, and free from pride.
"For I, meditated upon by you in your minds, shall always lead you all;
I shall carry across those bulls among men through calamity and over difficult terrains. I shall bear you on my back as you desire a swift course."
"Show me favor; let Bhīmasena accept me.
Then Kuntī spoke to the Rākṣasī named Hiḍimbā:
"By whatever means necessary, one should preserve one's life in order to cross over calamity."
Everything must be performed with due regard by one who follows the dharma;
he who maintains the dharma even in times of distress is the highest among those who know the dharma, for it is said that for those devoted to dharma, adversity itself is their trial.
Merit sustains the vital breaths; merit is said to be the giver of life.
Whatever righteous path one may follow, there is no censure found therein.
— Vaiśampāyana.
"Save me as well, for I am oppressed here by a woman out of lust.
The virtuous show compassion toward those seeking dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
and the sages who cherish dharma call that very quality ‘dharma’."

With divine knowledge, I behold the past and the future; therefore, I shall tell you of the supreme lake that brings about the highest good. Having reached the lake today, bathed, and rested beneath a tree—
Tomorrow at dawn, having seen the great being, the Lord of the World,
Vyāsa with eyes like lotus petals, you shall cast off your grief;
as well as [the sorrow over] Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s exile and the burning at Vāraṇāvata.
They know you to be their protector; this is known by me through the eye of wisdom. In the dwelling of Śālihotra, he shall provide you with shelter;
this sacred tree is capable of enduring rain, wind, and heat.
As soon as the water is drunk, hunger and thirst perish. By Śālihotra, through his ascetic power, a lake and a tree were created,
where kādamba ducks, cranes, swans, and kurarī birds dwell together with kurara falcons.
They sing sweetly, their songs mingled with the sounds of celestial music.
Having heard those words of hers, Kuntī spoke these words to the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, who was proficient in all the scriptures.

"For you are the best among the upholders of dharma; listen, O Bhārata, to what I have said. This Rākṣasī indeed speaks of dharma with her words, yet she is evil in her true nature; what will that Rākṣasī do to Bhīma?"
"If you desire offspring, worship the heroic Pāṇḍava.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Hiḍimbā, it is exactly as you say; there is no doubt in this matter."
"But you must abide by the dharma as I shall instruct you, O slender-waisted one. Having always performed your daily rites, bathed, and purified yourself, you should remain beautiful in form.
[Likewise,] O blessed lady, [attend to him] who has bathed, performed his daily duties, and completed the auspicious rites of consecration."
"You should attend upon Bhīmasena before the sun has set;
during the days, you may sport with him as you desire, moving with the speed of thought.
But this Bhīmasena must always be brought back to you at night."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Before the morning twilight, [the child] must be released and constantly protected. Thus, enjoy yourself with Bhīma until the time of the fetus's birth.
"O blessed lady, this is your duty; you must serve with vigilance, always being well-disposed, and you must act beautifully.
Having been addressed thus by Yudhiṣṭhira, she was taken onto Kuntī’s lap.
Positioned between Bhīma and Arjuna and preceded by the two twins,
Hiḍimbā, who moved with the gait of a lioness, walked sideways toward Yudhiṣṭhira;
then, seeking water, they reached the delightful Śālihotra lake.
Having promised "So be it," the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā then went to the foot of a great tree and, having swept it like a house,
constructed a leaf-hut for the residence of the Pāṇḍavas.
And she prepared a separate place for herself and Kuntī.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, having bathed and become pure, performed their twilight devotions;
though afflicted by hunger and thirst, they subsisted on water alone.
Then Śālihotra, perceiving that the Pāṇḍavas were afflicted by hunger,
thought in his mind of providing them with water and a great feast.
Thereupon, all those Pāṇḍavas, together with Pṛthā, became rested.

Having recounted various stories concerning what occurred in the house of lac and what was done by the Rākṣasa, Kuntī, the daughter of a king, then addressed these words to Bhīmasena, the joy of the Pāṇḍus, at the conclusion of their talk.

Just as Pāṇḍu was, so too is your elder brother Yudhiṣṭhira to be honored by you. According to the ordinances of dharma, I am even more worthy of your honor. Therefore, for the sake of Pāṇḍu’s welfare and for my own, act for the benefit of the crown prince.
O Vṛkodara, I see no means of retaliation for the wrongs committed by the evil and undisciplined son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
therefore, within a few days, our security and well-being will be restored.
"We shall dwell in this secure and inaccessible abode at our ease. Today, O Vṛkodara, there is great sorrow and a hardship regarding the Dharma;
for as soon as I saw you, O highly wise one, I was impelled by the bodiless god [Kāma]."
"He has chosen both Yudhiṣṭhira and me according to dharma.
For the sake of dharma, give us your son; he will bring about our welfare. I do not desire a reply; simply grant our request."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus promised "So be it," the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā then [departed];
and Bhīmasena spoke this.
"I shall carry out your command, even as the command of a god," Bhīmasena said this in the presence of his brothers.
"Listen, O Rākṣasī; by truth I declare this covenant to you."
"O fair-waisted one, for as long as it takes to produce a son,
for that long I shall go with you. In particular, do not reveal my low status in my presence."
"Endowed with the highest qualities of a woman, O lady of excellent complexion, you should serve me.
When the day has passed, bring food fit for a king to the dwellings. Once, Hiḍimbā, who could move at will, went out for the sake of recreation.
Taking Bhīmasena with him, he then ascended upward toward delightful mountain peaks and divine sanctuaries,
which were always resonant with the cries of beasts and birds and ever enchanting.
Having assumed a supreme form and adorned with all ornaments,
she delighted the Pāṇḍava with her exceedingly sweet conversation.
Likewise, in the forest fastnesses where the mountain peaks were covered with flowering trees, she continued to please him.
In delightful lakes filled with lotuses and water-lilies,
in regions of river islands with sands of beryl,
and likewise in mountain rivers possessing excellent bathing-places, forests, and waters;
In various wonderful forests with flowering trees and creepers,
in the groves of the Himalaya mountains and in diverse caves,
and by lakes of pure water filled with blossoming lotuses.
In the regions of the ocean studded with jewels and gold,
in delightful cities, in great groves of *śāla* trees,
in sacred divine forests, and likewise upon mountain peaks.
Bearing her supreme beauty, she delighted the son of Pāṇḍu in the abodes of the Guhyakas, in the hermitages of ascetics, and by the Mānasa lakes which possess fruits and flowers of every season.
Vaiśampāyana said:
After the venerable Vyāsa had departed, the Pāṇḍavas, their fever of anxiety gone,
dwelt there for six months at the banyan tree as they pleased.
O Great King, having been permitted, Kamalapālikā then [departed], while the Pāṇḍavas performed austerities, subsisting on vegetables, roots,
and fruits; and just as a man of meritorious deeds rejoices in heaven together with an apsaras.
Thus, filled with supreme delight, that one of great splendor took his pleasure with her.
For his joy, Bhīmasena could not be satiated as he repeatedly caressed her auspicious hips, which were adorned with a girdle of gold and jewels.
Then, gladdening Bhīma here and there with her mind-swift movements,
she took delight with him out of great joy, never satiated again and again;
she wandered with the Pāṇḍava during the days and returned at the times of night.
Having brought her to his own home, he showed her to his mother;
then the Pāṇḍava, together with his brothers, would always sleep there. She, serving Kuntī, dwelt by her side throughout the night.
He will bring mouth-perfumes and other such things, as well as food. When that night had passed, Mahāvratapārāśarya arrived— he who is possessed of great wisdom, divine vision, and great austerity.
Having then saluted the high-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, they all stood with palms joined in reverence, along with Mādhavī and her daughters-in-law; and there,
the swift-moving Ramayantī likewise attended to Bhīma in various places.
With her limbs adorned with divine ornaments and garments, and anointed with divine garlands and unguents,
the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā, who could assume any form at will, thus caused the seven Pāṇḍavas to dwell in the forest for seven months for the sake of Bhīmasena.
While dwelling in happiness, Bhīma enjoyed her company for that period of time; then that Rākṣasī, who could assume any form at will, conceived a child,
having been united with Bhīmasena for seven months without being satiated.
The Rākṣasī gave birth to a son of great strength from Bhīmasena—
one with deformed eyes, a massive mouth, and spike-like ears, who was terrifying,
of fearsome form, with copper-red lips, sharp fangs, and immense power.

The great archer of great heroism, the great being with mighty arms, possessing great speed and a massive body, the subduer of enemies who employs great illusion— long-nosed, broad-chested, and with formidable, well-developed calves.
O lord of the people, though he was born among humans, he possessed superhuman power, terrible speed, and great strength;
he surpassed all other piśācas and even all human beings.
Although he was but a child, O ruler of men, he attained the vigor of youth.
The powerful hero attained supreme excellence in all weapons. For Rākṣasīs conceive and give birth instantly; they can assume any form at will and possess many shapes.
Having prostrated, the supreme archer Vikaca then grasped the feet of his father and his mother; they both gave him a name,
and he addressed his mother as Ghaṭabhāsotkaca.
Because of that, his name became Ghaṭotkaca.
And that Ghaṭotkaca was devoted to those Pāṇḍavas;
for with disheveled hair, he would dance here and there before his parents.
In the presence of the Pāṇḍavas,
Ghaṭotkaca was always beloved by them and became like their very own self.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The massive-bodied Ghaṭotkaca, having saluted the Pāṇḍavas along with Pṛthā according to custom and addressed them, said:
"O sinless ones, tell me without hesitation what I may do for you, my noble lords."
To the son of Bhīmasena as he was speaking thus, Kuntī addressed these words:
"You were born in the lineage of the Kurus; indeed, you are equal to Bhīma himself.
You are the eldest son of the five; therefore, O dear son, provide them with assistance."
Thus addressed by Pṛthā, he bowed and spoke these words:
"Just as Rāvaṇa or the mighty Indrajit were in the world,
so have I become distinguished among men, equal to them in stature and prowess."
Then Hiḍimbā said to him, "The time for our living together has passed," and she replied to her,
"You shall see those established in their kingdom again."
"O beloved lord, whenever you remember me while desiring pleasure in secret,
O Bhārata, I shall quickly come back under your power.
Having spoken thus, she departed swiftly, fixing her heart upon the Pāṇḍava.
Having made this agreement, Hiḍimbā returned to her own abode.
Then all the Pāṇḍavas, having been honored by him with forest produce at the hermitage of Śālihotra, took leave of that great sage.
"I shall attend upon the ancestors at the time of the funeral rites," said Ghaṭotkaca;
"by the mere remembrance of you,
[I shall be saved] from great hardship in this difficult forest."
Having taken leave [of them], the best of Rākṣasas set out toward the northern direction;
for he had been created by the high-souled Maghavan for the sake of the spear,
in order to bring about the destruction of the great-souled Karṇa of matchless heroism.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, those heroic great chariot-warriors, slaying many herds of deer, departed from that forest for another forest, proceeding with haste.
Passing through the Matsyas, Trigartas, Pañcālas, and the Kīcakas,
they beheld delightful forest regions and lakes; then,
all of them fashioned matted locks for themselves and donned garments of bark and deerskin.
Together with Kuntī, those great-souled ones, assuming the form of ascetics,
carried their mother at times with haste; those great chariot-warriors performed their daily rites, subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
Sometimes traveling according to their own will, they proceeded with force;
on the way, they all beheld Dvaipāyana, their own grandfather,
studying the Veda of Brahman and all the Vedāṅgas in their entirety.
Those knowers of dharma beheld the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the treatises on statecraft;
having obtained [the teachings] through the grace of Śālihotra and having attained joy,
they then paid their respects to the high-souled Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
All those subduers of enemies stood with their hands joined in reverence along with their mother.
O Vyāsa,
O bulls among men, I have learned of their departure from that hermitage.
Having learned of the birth of Ghaṭotkaca, his joy increased.
Vyāsa said:
"O bulls among the Bharatas, this was previously known to me by my mind."
Since we were exiled by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra through unrighteousness while they remained [in their own lands],
and since we have always been driven away by our mother due to the evil counsel of the wicked,
I have come here having learned of this, desiring to accomplish what is supremely beneficial.
"You should not despair in this matter; all of this is for your own happiness.
O subduers of enemies, this is the ripening of an action born from separation from friends that was performed in the past.
This result has now been attained; do not grieve, O harassers of foes."
When your evil deed has been completed, you and your kinsmen will undoubtedly roam about in your own kingdom;
all of them and you are indeed equal to me, there is no doubt.
Relatives show affection out of pity and childishness;
therefore, my affection for you now is even greater.
Out of this love, I wish to do what is beneficial for you; listen to that.
This city nearby is delightful and free from harm;
dwell here in concealment, longing for my return.
This lake was indeed created by the ascetic power of Śālihotra.
"This water is delightful, removing hunger, thirst, and fatigue;
therefore, you who have business to attend to, may you dwell here at your pleasure for six months.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having thus comforted those sons of Pṛthā, the subduers of enemies, the lord Vyāsa went to Ekacakrā and consoled Kuntī, speaking these words: "Daughter-in-law, do not weep; do not weep. Thus spoke Vyāsa.
And once again, the righteous-souled Vyāsa spoke these words:
"A man should not perform only virtuous deeds; likewise, he may also commit evil."
"O beautiful one, there is no doer of good or evil deeds in this world;
the doer inevitably receives the fruit of both merit and sin.
It is by the very fruit of his evil deed that he has encountered this supreme calamity."
Therefore, O Mādhavī, who are worthy of honor, do not set your mind on grief. O mother of living sons, this son of yours, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and king of righteousness,
shall rule over all the kings upon the earth.
Having conquered the entire earth through righteousness, the self-controlled knower of dharma—
having subdued the whole earth girt by the oceans,
including its mountains and forests, and having brought it all under his auspicious sway.
"By the strength of Bhīmasena and Arjuna, he will undoubtedly enjoy [the kingdom];
and all your sons and the sons of Mādrī, being great chariot-warriors,
shall then dwell happily and with cheerful minds in their own kingdom."
Having conquered this earth, those tigers among men will perform sacrifices such as the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha with abundant sacrificial fees,
bestowing wealth and happiness upon their circle of friends.
"Your sons shall enjoy here the kingdom inherited from their fathers and grandfathers;
this lotus-petal-eyed daughter-in-law, Kamalapālikā by name, being under Bhīma’s control, shall give birth to a son."
"By that son, you shall be delivered from your hardships. Having spoken thus and having settled them in the house of the Brahmin,
the seer Dvaipāyana then addressed the best of kings.
"Wait for me here; I shall return again. Having understood the proper place and time, you will experience supreme joy.
O lord of men, he was addressed with "So be it" by all of them with palms joined in reverence.
The venerable seer Vyāsa, the lord, departed as he desired.
Janamejaya said:
"Those great chariot-warriors, the sons of Kuntī, having gone to Ekacakrā..."
01.145.001 After this, O best of the twice-born, what did the Pāṇḍavas do?
01.145.002 Vaiśampāyana said:
01.145.002a Having gone to Ekacakrā, those great chariot-warriors, the sons of Kuntī, [remained there].
They dwelt for no very long time in the house of the brahmin,
beholding various delightful forests,
as well as royal regions, rivers, and lakes.
O lord of the people, they all then wandered for alms,
constantly attending upon Yudhiṣṭhira and Kuntī while reflecting on them;
wearing matted hair and living as celibates, they always subsisted by begging.
And by their own virtues, they were pleasing to behold for the citizens;
those twice-born ones were handsome, pure, auspicious, and like the offspring of gods.
"Delicate ascetics are worthy of alms, not worthy of kingship;
though endowed with all auspicious marks, they do not deserve to beg for alms constantly. Speaking thus, he reasoned that they were wandering about for the sake of some purpose.
Constantly reflecting upon the arrival of their kinsmen,
the citizens prepared full meals consisting of various kinds of food and edibles; meanwhile, the Pāṇḍavas, observing a vow of silence, accepted alms.
Seeing that their mother has been gone for a long time, the Pāṇḍavas grieve; constrained by reverence for their mother, they return in haste. These Brahmins are not truly delicate ascetics.
They wander here upon the earth in disguise for some particular reason;
with eyes filled with tears of sorrow,
they scratch the surface of the ground while begging at the houses of the twice-born and thinking of their mother.
And every night they would present their alms to Kuntī;
all the food obtained from begging was given by their mother separately to each of them,
and they ate those allotted portions individually.
Half of it those heroes, the subduers of their foes, eat together with their mother;
the other half of all that alms-food, the mighty Bhīma eats. Yet he was never satiated in the past, even when nourished with excellent food.
He underwent a change of complexion and became emaciated from lack of satiety,
just as a drop of clarified butter [disappears] in a great blazing fire;
so it was with that half-portion of Bhīma’s alms-food, O best of kings.

While those high-souled ones were thus dwelling there, O King, a very long time passed by, O bull of the Bharata race. Bhīma, too, having sported among those who were like kinsmen of Brahmins, engaged in mutual play.
Then that large vessel obtained a connection with the potter;
he gave that great vessel to Bhīma as if laughing,
and having performed that wonderful feat, he took up a heavy load of clay.

His burden was a hundredfold greater than that of others; he pleased the potter by constantly bringing alms and fashioning earthen vessels wheel after wheel. Seeing him go away with those [alms], people laughed and mocked him.
Taking various kinds of food and eatables, they cast them [into the fire].
Having thus always eaten, he would speak to his mother in private:
"The potter gave me a large vessel, having fashioned it as a bowl."
Laughing at Bhīmasena, amazed by his deed, [he spoke].
Thus was the Pāṇḍava always questioned by the citizens when he appeared hungry.
Then, on one occasion, those bulls of the Bharata race went out for alms.
Bhīmasena remained there together with Pṛthā. Then, O Bhārata, Kuntī heard a loud, terrible, and intense cry of distress arising from the brahmin’s dwelling.
O King, as they all wailed and lamented,
the queen, out of compassion and her virtuous nature, could not bear it;
then Pṛthā’s heart was churned by grief as if by a fire.
The auspicious lady spoke these words, full of compassion, to Bhīma:
"O son, we have lived very happily in the house of this Brāhmaṇa,
unknown to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, well-honored and free from anxiety."

"O son, she would constantly think: 'What indeed can I do that is pleasing to this brahmin?'—thinking of what those who dwell happily in one's house might do for him. For a man is truly great, my dear, in whom a service rendered is never lost."
Whatever another might do for him, he would surely repay it with even more;
yet this suffering has certainly befallen this Brāhmaṇa. If we were to provide him assistance in this matter, it would be a virtuous deed.
Bhīma said:
"Let it be known what his sorrow is and from where it has arisen;
once it is understood, I shall determine the course of action, even if it should be very difficult to accomplish."
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lord of the people, as they were thus conversing, they again heard the sound of that distressed Brahmin and his wife.
Then Kuntī quickly entered the inner apartments of that high-souled Brāhmaṇa, like a cow with her calf tied up.
Then she [found] that Brāhmaṇa there, together with his wife and son.
And he saw him with a deformed face, accompanied by his daughter.
The Brahmin said:
"Fie upon this life in the world, which is useless and lacks the essence of effort!"
The root of suffering is dependence on others, and one experiences intense unpleasantness.
In life there is supreme suffering; in life there is supreme fever.
For one existing in life, the arrival of dualities is certain.
For even a single individual cannot pursue dharma, artha, and kāma simultaneously;
moreover, separation from these is considered the supreme suffering. Some say that liberation (mokṣa) is the highest [goal], but that does not exist in any way whatsoever.

Upon the acquisition of wealth, one falls entirely into hell; the desire for wealth is supreme suffering, and the acquisition of wealth is even greater than that. For one who has developed attachment to objects, the suffering upon their loss is even more intense.
However many desirable things one has conjoined with,
so many spikes of sorrow are driven into one's heart;
having obtained this life, which is of such short duration and great peril, [one must not be heedless].
This great sacrifice has been undertaken even by me together with my wife;
indeed, I see no means by which I might be liberated from this calamity,
nor any way to flee to safety along with my sons and wife.
"O Brahmin lady, I have indeed previously endeavored as you know;
yet you did not listen to me when I said, 'Go from here to where there is safety.
For I was born here, I grew up here, and my father is here."
O dull-witted woman, you spoke thus even though you were entreated by me repeatedly:
"My aged father has gone to heaven, as have your mother and your former kinsmen for a long time; what pleasure, then, can there be in dwelling there?"
Food shall not be an obstacle, nor shall women or the place of residence be a hindrance.
For the sake of one's duty, one should travel even to the farthest distance, like Garuḍa or a swan.
This very person [is here] for you, who desire your kinsman, while you have not heard my words.
"The loss of my kinsmen has occurred, causing me intense suffering.
But since it has come to pass, O auspicious lady, enjoy it as you wish. [The Brahmin’s wife:
"O Brahmin!"
"Send me indeed today as tribute to Baka;
O twice-born one,
this sacrifice has now come upon either me or my son."
Whether it be yours or that of your daughter, this is the fruit of dwelling here.
O beautiful lady, you do not heed my words; therefore, you must now experience the consequence.
Or else, I shall not be able to die myself while my son remains.
Thus, I am unable to abandon you, nor even my own daughter;
or rather, this shall be my own destruction, for as long as I live, I cannot bear to abandon any kinsman like a cruel man.
She is my companion in dharma, self-controlled, and always like a mother to me;
she was ordained by the gods as my friend and my supreme refuge,
and she has been destined by her mother and father to share forever in the life of a householder.

Having chosen you according to the prescribed rule and having wedded you with the sacred mantras— you who are of noble birth, endowed with virtuous character, the mother of my offspring, and a faithful wife who has done me no wrong— I have done so for the sake of my very life.
I cannot bring myself to abandon my wife, who is ever devoted to me;
how much less could I possibly abandon my own daughter herself—
so young, not yet reached by puberty, and whose physical characteristics have not yet emerged?
Nor shall I be able to abandon this daughter of mine under any circumstances. I seek supreme joy, as well as the fruits of heaven, in him;
how then could I bring myself to abandon my beloved child here?
He, upon whose birth his ancestors ascended to heaven upon seeing his face;
he, by whose splendor upon birth his parents were liberated from their debt to the ancestors—
him, my eldest son, the savior of my lineage on earth, [I shall install].
"How shall I abandon my little son, who is a treasure of food and water for me? How indeed could I myself ever forsake my daughter,
who was entrusted as a deposit by the Great-Souled Creator for the sake of her husband?"
"How can I bear to abandon this young girl, upon whom I hope for worlds to be won through her daughters' sons, together with my ancestors, after having fathered her myself?
Some men consider a father's affection for a son to be greater."
"However, I do not consider either of them to be my equal regarding a daughter.
In whom the worlds, progeny, and constant happiness are established—
how could I bear to abandon that innocent girl?"
How can I bear to abandon this young daughter of mine— intelligent, faultless, obedient, and free from pride—
who yearns for love and many pleasures?
They produce offspring for the sake of dharma, pleasure, and wealth; yet,
having fallen under the power of the hungry ghosts, I shall suffer even at the cost of sacrificing myself—
just as I am unable to abandon them myself.
It is evident that these have been abandoned by me; they will certainly not be able to live here.
Furthermore, the abandonment of any one of these is cruel and condemned by the wise;
yet, if I were to abandon myself, they too would perish without me.
"Having fallen into this hardship, I am unable to cross over this calamity.
Alas, what a pity! To what fate shall I go today along with my kinsmen?
Death together with all of them is better; life is no longer fit for me."
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"You should never feel distress as an ordinary person might;
for this is no time for you, a learned man, to grieve."
All human beings in this world must inevitably go to their death;
indeed, when a matter is inevitable, no grief should be felt here. A wife, a son, and a daughter—all are desired for one's own sake.
"Cast off your distress through your own wisdom; I myself shall indeed go there. For this is the supreme, eternal duty of a woman in this world:
that she should act for the welfare of her husband, even at the cost of her own life."
And that action performed there brings you happiness here as well;
it is inexhaustible in the hereafter and brings glory in this world.
This indeed is the weighty dharma which I shall proclaim to you.
In this matter, both your worldly purpose and your merit are seen to be greatly served;
for that purpose for which a wife is desired has been attained by you through me. Both a daughter and a son have been secured, and I have been made free from my debt to you.
"You are capable of nourishing and likewise protecting my two sons;
I, however, am not so able to protect and nourish them.
For me, deprived of you, all desires become calamities."
"How might the two young children survive, and how might I myself endure? For how shall I, widowed, protectorless, and with infant sons, live without you,
remaining on the path trodden by the righteous?"
"How shall I be able to protect this daughter of yours when she is sought after by those who are arrogant with egoism and unsuitable for alliance with you—
just as birds flock to meat cast upon the ground?"
"All people desire a woman who is bereft of her hero; thus, being pursued and shaken by those evil-minded men,
O best of the twice-born, I shall not be able to remain on the path cherished by the virtuous."
"O Lord, birth as a woman is despised in this world filled with wicked people.
A maiden is under the control of her mother and father; likewise, once married, she is under the control of her husband.
And in the absence of these two, a woman who is independent among her sons is censured."

Women are a state of helplessness; indeed, that door to the wicked is wide open. Just as a piece of cloth smeared with ghee is dragged along by dogs, so too, O Lord, are women seen [and seized] by those arrogant with the power they have sought.
"How can I venture to establish this one young girl of your family, who has not yet been consecrated,
upon the ancestral path of her fathers and grandfathers? How shall I be able to instill the desired virtues in this child?"
"O you who perceive the Dharma, just as this boy has acted wickedly for twelve years while being orphaned and destitute on all sides,
those who speak of the Dharma say that such evil belongs to his parents."
"Father and mother teach this through their conduct, as does the son;
yet these unworthy men, having disregarded me and this helpless girl of yours, will seek her just as Śūdras seek the hearing of the Vedas."
If I were not willing to give her away, who has been so highly exalted by your virtues,
they would carry her off by force, like crows stealing the sacrificial oblation from a ritual.
Who indeed could stand against her?
"O learned one, while I look on and cry out, these shameless men continue to carry her away;
for I am helpless, O wise one, as I behold your daughter who does not seem at all like your son."
"O Brahmin, having fallen under the power of one unworthy, and likewise despised by the world, this daughter of yours— being ignorant of her own self— I shall die, there is no doubt."
Though we are innocent and feel ashamed,
because of our powerlessness and lack of a protector,
it is certain that we must go with you once you have died.
When their husband has died, women find not even a trace of happiness. These two young sons of mine, deprived of both me and you,
will perish without a doubt, like two fish when the water dries up.
"Even in every way, this triad will undoubtedly perish;
therefore, since it is deprived of you, you ought not to abandon me.
For this is the supreme prosperity for women, and the husband is their ultimate refuge."
But for the sons of Brahmins, it is not permitted to move within the kingdom;
even though she is virtuous and endowed with auspicious items such as turmeric, collyrium, and flowers,
she who drinks the water offered by her husband goes to death.
With her mind offered at the feet of her husband, she goes to the abode of Girijā;
having become a friend of Girijā, she rejoices with the daughter of the mountain.
For a father gives but little, a brother gives but little, and a son gives but little.
Who would not rejoice in a husband who is the giver of the immeasurable?
This son has been abandoned by me, as has this daughter;
for your sake, my kinsmen have been forsaken, and even my own life.
Through sacrifices, austerities, observances, and various kinds of gifts,

a woman’s constant abiding in what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband is distinguished above all; even more so than the stages of life, the consecration of the sacred fires, recitations, oblations, and vows.
These [vows] should not be undertaken by women without a blameless husband;
for a woman, it is known that her duty consists only of forbearance, purity, and fasting. Therefore, this which I desire to do is righteous and highly esteemed.
It is both desirable and beneficial for you and for your family;
likewise, children, wealth, dear friends,
and even a wife are considered by the virtuous to be for the sake of liberation from calamity.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
For it is for the sake of results both seen and unseen that one possesses a wife, a son, wealth, and a home.
"All this must be ordained; this is the certainty of the wise.
O increaser of the lineage, either the entire family or the self alone [should be protected], for not everything is equal—this is the certainty of the wise."
Of these two, which is superior, O wise one? The self is indeed superior to one's lineage.
Because the self exists, O tiger among the twice-born, the fourteen worlds exist; therefore, the self must always be protected by you.
If the self does not exist, then nothing here belongs to it;
indeed, this entire world is not equal to the self. Therefore, perform for me what must be done, and deliver yourself by means of your own self.
"Grant me leave, Noble One, and protect my two sons.
Furthermore, O Lord, hear from me what else I shall say for your benefit;
having heard it, let it be taken to heart by you, and then act accordingly for your own welfare."

"Women are not to be slain," say those who know the Dharma when determining the law; they say that Rākṣasas are knowers of the Dharma, and thus he would not kill me either. For the killing of men is certain, while the killing of women is uncertain.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, you ought to send me away.
I have enjoyed pleasures, attained what is dear to me, and practiced dharma;
furthermore, my fame has become incomparable, born from my service to you.
Your beloved daughter has been found; she will not cause me grief by being dead. Having given birth to a son, she is now aged and always desirous of your welfare.
Considering all this, I have therefore made this resolution.
"O Noble One, even after abandoning me, you shall find another woman;
take a maiden of noble birth, and your dharma will be restored once more.
A twice-born man should not remain without an āśrama for even a single moment."
"Then, O auspicious one, dharma will be established once more for you; indeed,
it is not unrighteous for men to have many wives,
but it is a very great unrighteousness for women to transgress against their first husband."

"Having considered all this, O Lord, and the fact that the abandonment of one's own life is censurable, follow my word; do not let your mind be otherwise. Save yourself by means of me, as well as this lineage and these two children."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by her, O Bhārata, her husband embraced her and,
deeply distressed along with his wife, slowly shed tears.
Immediately after that, his daughter prepared to speak:
"Do not say such a thing, O auspicious one; stay at home, O slender-waisted lady. A wise man should never abandon his own wife or even his sons."
In this world, a wise man should especially protect his wife;
yet, even if he must abandon her, he should live on, for these [other things] should never be forsaken. He does not truly understand dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa in their true essence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those exceedingly piteous words of the two of them,
the maiden, her limbs overwhelmed by intense grief, addressed them both.
"Why do you two cry out so piteously like those who are helpless?
Listen to something from me as well; having heard it, do what is appropriate. According to dharma, I am to be abandoned by you both; there is no doubt in this."
"Having abandoned me, who am destined to be forsaken, everything has been saved by me alone"—
it is for this purpose that offspring is desired, thinking, "He will deliver me.
Now that the time has arrived, cross over [the flood] with me as your raft.
Whether he delivers him from misfortune in this world or delivers him after death, in every way a son delivers; therefore he is called "putra" by the wise.
Because he protects [his father] from the hell named Put, he is called a son (*tanaya*).
"Grandfathers always desire even grandsons;
I myself shall surely protect them, guarding my father's life.
And this brother of mine is but a child, now that you have departed for the other world."

In a very short time, he would undoubtedly perish. For when my father has gone to heaven and my younger brother is destroyed, the ancestral offering (*piṇḍa*) for the ancestors would be cut off; that would be displeasing to them.
"Abandoned by my father, as well as by my mother and brother, I shall undoubtedly fall from sorrow to even greater sorrow and perish, though I am undeserving of such a fate.
But when you are free from illness and released [from this place], my mother and my infant brother— "
The lineage and the family estate will undoubtedly be established.
It is said that one's self, son, friend, and wife are easy to maintain, but a daughter is indeed a hardship;
therefore, deliver yourself from this hardship and unite me with righteousness.
"O father, deprived of you, I shall become helpless, miserable, and childlike, wandering aimlessly; alas, I shall indeed be wretched!
Or rather, I shall effect the liberation of this lineage."
"Having performed this most difficult task, I shall attain the fruit [of my labor].
Or else, O best of the twice-born, you will go there leaving me behind;
I shall be afflicted, so please look after me as well."
"Therefore, O best of beings, for our sake, for the sake of dharma, and for the sake of progeny,
protect yourself and abandon me, who must be abandoned. Let not this time pass you by regarding a matter that must necessarily be done."
"By the water given by you, there will be welfare for me.
What indeed could be a greater misery than this: that while you have gone to heaven, we, begging for food from others, must run about like dogs?"
"But when you are free from disease and liberated from this affliction along with your kinsmen,
and are dwelling in the world of the immortals, I shall be endowed with happiness.
We have heard that by giving from here, both the gods and the ancestors [are satisfied]."

"O dear one, having considered both of these points— what is beneficial for you, as well as what is beneficial for your mother and for your own son— you must resolve accordingly. For sons endowed with virtues shall once again come to be for their parents."
"But the parents shall never again become the parents of a son.
Having heard her lamentation of many such kinds,
the father, the mother, and the maiden— these three— all wept aloud.
Then, hearing them all weeping, their young son, with eyes wide open, spoke in sweet and indistinct tones:
"Do not weep, father; do not weep, mother; do not weep, sister."
As if laughing, he approached each of them one by one;
then, taking up a blade of grass, he spoke again with great joy:
"With this, I shall slay that man-eating Rākṣasa."
Nevertheless, hearing those indistinct words of the child, great joy arose within them who were overwhelmed by sorrow. Knowing that this was the right moment, Kuntī approached them.
Reviving them as if with nectar, she spoke this;
Kuntī said:
"I wish to know the truth of what the root of this suffering is."
"Having understood this, I shall remove it, if it is possible to remove.
The brahmin said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, what you say is appropriate for the virtuous."
"But this suffering cannot be dispelled by a mere human being;
nevertheless, I shall explain the true origin of this suffering. Whether it can be remedied or not, listen, O blessed lady, to the truth as it is."
Near this city dwells a rākṣasa named Baka. At a distance of only one *gavyūti* from here, there is a cave in a thicket on the Yamunā;
in that cave dwells that terrible man-eater, seeking to kill.
He was indeed named Baka by name, a wicked-souled and lowest of Rākṣasas;
he was the lord of this country and city, possessed of great strength.
That very powerful Rākṣasa was Pralambaka, capable of assuming any form at will.
Afflicted by him today for the thirteenth year, this city has been overrun.
That evil-minded man-eater, nourished on human flesh,
the powerful king of the *asuras*, constantly protects this district.
Endowed with the power of the *rakṣas*, he shall protect both the city and the country;
because of that, we shall have no fear from foreign armies or from malevolent spirits.
[Yet] we are being devoured by a fierce and evil-minded man-eater.
The city, being without a protector, finds no lord or savior;
while he dwells there in his cave, that evil-minded one constantly oppresses the people— women, children, the elderly, and the young alike.
There, that evil-minded Rākṣasa was praised with mantras, oblations, and feasts by the foremost of the twice-born, and thus honored;
and so he continued to slaughter everyone in this manner.
Then all the brahmins bound him by an agreement:
"O Rākṣasa, do not slay us out of desire; we shall always provide you with meat and rice here at your pleasure in turn, O Lord."
Food combined with meat and mixed with sesame powder,
prepared with clarified butter and adorned with various side dishes; colorful garlands, sesame seeds, funeral cakes, parched grain, cakes, wine, and spirituous liquors.
Jars of boiled and unboiled drinks, large pieces of meat— both boiled and unboiled—
various jars of clarified butter, and many other diverse kinds,
all filled today with prepared sesame flour.
"From family after family, you shall obtain a man and two black oxen;
without anger, you shall receive the portion assigned to the Rākṣasa.
Thus did those twice-born ones entreat him, saying, "Stay here according to our agreement."
"So be it," the Rākṣasa replied, accepting those words. Fearing no enemy armies, he undertook the protection [of that region] and,
remaining steadfast in the portion assigned to him, the powerful one observed his agreement.
The wage prescribed for that rice-transporter was food,
along with two buffaloes and one man who would go taking it;
and each man provided that food individually.
That ford remains difficult for men to cross even after many years;
moreover, that *rakṣas* kills and devours those men who anywhere strive for liberation from it, along with their sons and wives.
In the house at Vetrakīya, this king does not abide by right policy;
that dull-witted man does not employ the means by which there might be eternal well-being for these people today, even though he exerts effort toward it.
"Truly, we deserve this: that we dwell here in the territory of a weakling, perpetually anxious, having taken refuge under a bad king;
