and [we have lost] our former dwelling, house, field, and so forth."
Not wishing to abandon [our word], we therefore dwell in the city;
even in Ekacakrā, we remain because our own word is so difficult to relinquish,
while the Bakas and Rākṣasas constantly offer us hell as their fee.
To whom should Brahmins be said to belong, or whose followers are they?
For by their own virtues they are attracted [to others], like birds that fly according to their desire. One should first obtain a king, then a wife, and then wealth.
"O King, if this world did not exist, where would there be a wife, and where would there be wealth? Through the accumulation of these three, one supports one's kinsmen and sons;
yet all these three have been acquired by me in a contrary manner."
Having encountered this calamity, we shall suffer greatly. This very turn has now come upon us, which brings about the destruction of the family;
a meal and one man must be provided by me as the wage.
I possess no wealth anywhere with which to ransom a man,
nor am I able in any way to provide for my friends; furthermore,
I see no means for my liberation from this Rākṣasa.
"I am deeply submerged in this great ocean of suffering that is impossible to cross;
today I shall go to the Rākṣasa along with these very kinsmen of mine.
Then that base creature will devour us all together."
"O blessed and sinless lady, I have explained this root of suffering to you in response to your question. Kuntī said:
"You should not feel any despondency whatsoever out of fear of this."
A means has been perceived here for the liberation of the Rākṣasa;
therefore, I do not at all approve of your going there yourself with your son.
You have but one young son and one daughter who is a mere child.
"I do not approve of your going there with those two or with your wife. O Brahmin, I have five sons; one of them shall go for your sake, taking an offering for that wicked Rākṣasa."
The brahmin said:
"Desiring life, I will never under any circumstances perform the depriving of life for my own sake, nor for the sake of a brahmin guest."
But this [disposition] is not found among women of low birth nor among those who are unrighteous—
that they would sacrifice even themselves or their own children for the sake of a Brahmin. Rather, I prefer that I should understand what is truly for my own highest good.
Whether it be the killing of a Brahmin or the killing of myself, the killing of myself is better for me;
the killing of a Brahmin is the supreme sin, and for me, the killing of myself is better. The killing of a Brahmin is the supreme sin; there is no atonement found for it.
"The instigator, the consenter, and the slayer—these three are equal.
Even by committing it unintentionally, my own death would be better for me, O auspicious lady;
yet I do not desire to bring about my own destruction myself."
"If the killing were committed by others, no sin whatsoever would exist in me;
but since that killing of a Brahmin was committed by me intentionally,
I see no atonement for such a cruel and base act."

The abandonment of one who has come to one's house, as well as the killing of one who seeks refuge or begs for help, is considered the height of cruelty. One should never perform a censurable act, nor ever an act of cruelty.
"Thus did the great-souled ones of old understand the duties in times of distress. Yet,
for me today, it would be better to perish along with my wife than that I should ever,
under any circumstances, consent to the killing of a Brahmin."
Kuntī said:
"O Brahmin, this resolve of mine is firm: that Brāhmaṇas must be protected.
Even if I were to have a hundred sons, not one would be more dear to me than a son who is undeserving."
"And that Rākṣasa is not capable of destroying my son;
for my son is heroic, perfected in mantras, and full of splendor.
He will deliver all that food to the Rākṣasa."
"It is my firm conviction that he will liberate himself;
for those powerful and massive-bodied Rākṣasas whom we have encountered before have been slain by this hero on numerous occasions."
"But, O Brahmin, this must not be disclosed to anyone under any circumstances;
for those seeking knowledge might, out of curiosity, cause my sons to quarrel. Moreover, one who has not been authorized by his preceptor should not be made to learn it."
"One should not employ that knowledge for such a purpose; this is the opinion of the virtuous.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus by his wife Pṛthā, that brahmin, together with her...
Delighted, he honored those words which were like nectar.
Then Kuntī and the brahmin, together, said to the son of the Wind-god,
"Do this," and he replied to them, "So be it."
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Bhārata, when Bhīma had pledged, "I shall do it," all those Pāṇḍavas then returned, bringing alms-food with them.
Then, seeing Bhīmasena with his face beaming,
Dharmarāja understood that the steadfast Bhīma was delighted;
the elder brother pondered in his mind the cause for which he was so joyful.
O King, having observed him at that time, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu and lord of warriors, desiring to hear [his words], recognized his intention by his very appearance; then,
sitting alone in private, he questioned his mother.
"What deed does this Bhīma of terrible prowess intend to perform?
Does he wish to do this here with your permission? Kuntī said:
"At my very word, this scorcher of foes will perform a great task for the sake of the brahmins and for the protection of the city;
O son, he has prepared a vast and excellent offering intended for Baka."
"O son of austerity, Bhīma eats sumptuously even for a single day.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is this rash and cruel misdeed that you have committed?"
"Indeed, the virtuous do not praise the abandonment of one's own son.
Why do you wish to abandon your own son for the sake of another's? By abandoning your son, you have indeed acted in a manner contrary to the ways of the world."
Relying upon whose arms we all sleep in comfort,
we now desire to reclaim the kingdom that has been seized by the base;
for Duryodhana, contemplating the prowess of him who possesses immeasurable energy, [is filled with fear].
He does not sleep through all his nights, for he suffers alongside the bird;
by the prowess of that hero we were released from the house of lac and from other evils, and Purocana was slain.
"O Mother, relying upon whose prowess we desire to enjoy the earth filled with wealth without rivals, O high-minded one— we consider this earth already won, having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."

Having resolved upon the abandonment of Karṇa, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni the son of Subala, what kind of reasoning have you adopted? Is it not possible that your intellect has been clouded by sorrows, and your mind has lost its composure?
Kuntī said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should not feel any grief regarding Vṛkodara;
nor was this resolve made by me out of any weakness of intellect."
My intellect has not been clouded by grief, nor has my consciousness departed;
O son, we have lived happily here in this brahmin’s house,
unknown to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, well-honored and free from anxiety.
"O dear one, this remedy for that has been considered by me:
a man is truly great only so long as what he has done does not perish.
A great merit lies in the cause of a Brahmin; Vṛkodara, you who know this, act accordingly."
"Whatever another might do for him, he would repay many times over;
having witnessed Bhīṣma’s great prowess at the house of lac and from the slaying of Hiḍimba, I have full confidence in Vṛkodara."
For the great strength of Bhīma’s arms is equal to ten thousand elephants,
by which you all— resembling elephants yourselves— were carried out from Vāraṇāvata.
There has never been another, nor will there ever be, whose strength equals that of Vṛkodara.
He who could have risen up in battle even against the wielder of the thunderbolt himself;
yet, as soon as he was born, he fell from my lap onto a mountain,
and by the weight of his body, the rock was crushed to pieces by his limbs.
For indeed, after the night had passed, I saw in a great dream that Bhīma,
having eaten and slain the crane, surrounded by the citizens,
returned joyfully to this dwelling, adorned with auspicious things.
O Pāṇḍava, having recalled that through my wisdom and considering the power of Bhīma as well as the need for recompense toward the brahmin, I then made this resolve;
it was not determined out of greed, nor out of ignorance, nor out of delusion.
But this determination regarding dharma was made by me with prior reflection;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, both objectives will be accomplished:
the repayment for our dwelling and the practice of great dharma.
"I have heard that a Kṣatriya who should ever provide assistance to a Brāhmaṇa in his affairs would attain auspicious worlds.
A Kṣatriya likewise [attains them] by effecting the release from execution of another Kṣatriya."
He attains vast fame both in this world and in the next. Furthermore, a Kṣatriya who provides assistance to a Vaiśya in battle certainly delights all subjects in every world.
But by releasing a Śūdra who has come to him seeking refuge,
a king obtains birth here in a family that possesses wealth and is honored by kings.
Thus did the venerable Vyāsa speak of old, O delighter of the Kauravas.
The exceedingly wise one spoke further regarding this which he desired to do.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Mother, this which you have done with deliberate intent is entirely appropriate."
Out of compassion for this distressed Brāhmaṇa, you have done this;
surely this Bhīma will come, having slain the man-eater,
since you are so full of pity for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa in every way.
This was proclaimed by Manu and other great-souled sages who were knowers of the Vedas:
for the sake of a cow or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, one should immediately sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a Brāhmaṇa is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
He shall come to the city and thereby be liberated from that sin;
however, so that the men living in the city do not discover this,
this brahmin must be spoken to and carefully concealed.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O subduer of enemies, having consulted with Yudhiṣṭhira for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas,
Kuntī entered and comforted them all, O Bhārata.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
when the night had passed, the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena took food and went to where that man-eater was.
Vaiśampāyana;
Bhīmasena;
Vaiśampāyana.
Then, when the night had passed, the mighty Bhīmasena approached the brahmin and spoke these words:
"O lover of brahmins, I shall deliver you from this calamity along with your sons."
"Do not fear that *rākṣasa*; you should offer me as a sacrificial gift (*bali*).
O best of the twice-born, strive to feed me here;
then I shall surrender myself to that terrible *rākṣasa*."
"Hasten! Why do you delay? Do not tarry long, O sinless ones!
Today, indeed, I shall resolve to protect you even at the cost of my own life.
Thus addressed by Bhīma, O bull of the Bharatas, the Brāhmaṇa—
Having related that to his friends, he served them well-prepared food;
then the city-dwellers brought him rice mixed with meat,
along with ghee, various side dishes, and diverse soups.
Having eaten that, as well as various kinds of meat, excellent sweetmeats, and many heaps of variegated rice, Bhīmasena then drank very many jars of curds,
measured by droṇas.
When he had finished eating, the citizens, their minds full of joy, then presented him with the portion of the sacrificial offering that they had duly prepared. Then,
when the night had passed, [he partook of] that which was soaked in curds and various condiments.
Having mounted a cart filled with food, Vṛkodara departed,
surrounded by the citizens and accompanied by the blaring of trumpets;
he intended to offer himself as food to the Rākṣasa.
Young, handsome, sturdy, robust, and youthful,
Vṛkodara, being praised with such words as these,
urged on the two yoked oxen that were dark in all their limbs.
Amidst the resounding noise of musical instruments, he, surrounded by men, approached that man-eater with great joy; and having reached that place,
he drew near alone.
Terrified by the fear of the man-eater, the multitude of people remained right there.
Having traveled a long distance toward the southern direction,
he saw a tree with spreading branches at the spot as it had been described.
Then, all around that lord of the forest, the ground was strewn with hair, marrow, bones, fat, and even arms, thighs, and feet— both moist and dry—
covered with the carcasses of vultures and herons, and teeming with packs of jackals.
Having entered that dreadful place, which possessed a foul stench, was unpleasant to the sight, and resembled a cremation ground,
the valiant one reflected upon that great tree as long as the demon Baka, arrogant in his strength, was not in view.
As long as the Rākṣasa beholds this cart, piled high with various kinds of food and rice resembling mountains and filled with soups,
so long indeed shall I eat; for it will surely be difficult to obtain again.
For if I were to fight with the Rākṣasa in battle, everything would be scattered;
and once Baka was seized, it would become unfit for consumption due to contact with a corpse.
But Bhīmasena, having observed that he was indeed one of such terrible deeds, [acted accordingly].
Seated there, he slowly partook of the most excellent food.
Then the citizens, having climbed trees on all sides, watched him;
for men should not eat an offering that lacks a protector, even if it be so abundant.
"He eats in the form of a Brāhmaṇa; he is a crane," they said. That radiant one laughed after consuming that food.
Then the powerful Pāṇḍava reached the forest of that Rākṣasa.
Then, while consuming that food, he called out to it by name.
Hearing those words of Bhīmasena, the Rākṣasa arrived,
highly incensed, at the place where Bhīma was stationed.
Of massive body and great speed, as if tearing asunder the earth,
with blood-red eyes, formidable, and with red beard and hair;
with a mouth split open to his ears, spike-eared, and terrifying.
Knitting his brows into three furrows and biting his lip,
that Rākṣasa, seeing Bhīmasena eating the food,
rolled his eyes in anger and spoke these words.
"Who is this evil-minded person who eats this food prepared for my sake, while I am looking on and about to depart for the abode of Yama?
Bhīmasena, however, O Bhārata, hearing this, spoke as if laughing.
Disregarding that rākṣasa, he continued to eat with his face turned away.
Then, letting out a terrible roar and raising both his arms,
that man-eater rushed at Bhīmasena, desiring to kill him.
Nevertheless, Vṛkodara, the Pāṇḍava and slayer of enemy heroes, disregarded him and did not even look at the Rākṣasa as he continued to eat the food;
yet the Rākṣasa was filled with indignation toward the son of Kuntī.
Standing behind him, he struck Bhīma on the back with both his hands.
Though thus violently struck by the powerful one with his two palms, Bhīma did not even look at the Rākṣasa; he simply continued to eat.
The balls that had entered Bhīma’s belly, numbering more than a hundred with the spaces between them,
became fused together like a single mass by the blow of the Rākṣasa’s hand.
Then, becoming even more enraged, that Rākṣasa seized a tree.
Intending to strike Bhīma, the powerful one then rushed at him again.
Then Bhīma, that bull among men and possessor of great strength, having slowly eaten that food and sipped water, stood in the battle rejoiced.
Having stood for a moment and rested while maintaining the heroic posture (*vīrāsana*),
the hero saw the one of terrifying appearance approaching, brandishing a great tree;
seeing him, he rose up in battle and let out a lion’s roar.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
having displayed the force of his arms, a crackling sound, and a loud roar,
the enraged Bhīmasena challenged the Rākṣasa.
O lowest of Rākṣasas, your body has been well-nourished for a long time;
relying on the strength of my arms, you shall no longer exist. Crushed by my arms today, you will go to the abode of Yama.
From this day forward, the inhabitants shall sleep without anxiety, scattered about as this city’s thorn has been uprooted by me;
today in battle, your body will be [devoured] by herons, jackals, and crows.
"Let them eat and tear apart on the ground that which has been slain by me!
Having spoken thus, Pārtha, filled with great rage and desiring to slay Baka, rushed toward him;
and Baka likewise rushed toward Pārtha, O best of kings.
Possessing a massive body and great speed, as if tearing the earth asunder,
he of hideous form and tawny eyes rushed toward Bhīmasena,
knitting his brows into three furrows and biting his lip.
He spoke with a voice like the sound of a thunderbolt, as if terrifying them;
then, having eaten the cart-load of food along with the Rākṣasa’s hand, [he consumed] many meats of bipeds and quadrupeds and mountains of boiled rice.
Seizing the great tree, which was as massive as a mountain, Bhīmasena laughed; having eaten the rākṣasa until nothing remained,
and having drunk from hundreds upon hundreds of jars full of curds and pots of clarified butter, he cast him aside.
Seizing with his left hand that tree, a lord of the forest with massive branches sent forth by the rākṣasa, and raising it up with his other hand,
he glared at the rākṣasa’s face, which was made hideous by a frown.
Displaying his teeth to the Rakshasa, he laughed with a sound like a thunderclap. O Bharata, the heroic Bhima, as if laughing, caught that tree hurled by the enraged one with his left hand.
Then that powerful one again raised up various kinds of trees and hurled them at Bhīmasena; but Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu,
warded off all those trees with a tree held in his own hand.

O great king, that great battle between Baka and the Pāṇḍava, involving a struggle with trees that caused the destruction of many trees, was terrible in form. Then Baka, having proclaimed his name, rushed toward the Pāṇḍava.
With both arms, he seized the mighty Bhīmasena;
and the powerful Bhīmasena, too, having embraced that Rakṣasa with his great arms,
forcibly dragged it as it struggled with great speed.
By means of whirling, throwing, embracing, and hurling down; by rising up and falling back, those two obstructed one another,
as well as by lifting up, raising, moving, and setting down.
Bhīma seized him with both hands, and having grasped him, he threw him down.
Though thrown down by Bhīmasena, he rose up again laughing;
then, having embraced and squeezed him, he struck him down upon the surface of the earth.
Bhīma dismissed him, saying, "Take heart," and that powerful one slapped his arms and said, "Rise! Then,
rising up in anger, he assumed a much larger form.
Virūpa suddenly stood there, threatening Vṛkodara;
then Bhīmasena laughed at the Rākṣasa of fearsome appearance.
Bhīmasena then seized the fearsome-looking creature by the neck.
With both arms and one knee, he pressed down upon the demon's back. Then, enraged, Bhīma released him and,
slightly lifting his own hips, seized the demon's two arms.
Seizing his two arms, Vṛkodara, acting with haste,
lifted him up and shook him; the powerful one,
filled with rage and possessing terrible prowess, threw him down upon the ground, striking him with his left foot.
Bhīma struck him on the chest as he lay fallen upon the ground;
then, rising up in a rage, he violently struck Bhīma,
opening his mouth wide with his flaming tongue and raising his right arm.
Rushing forward in a rage, he struck Bhīma on the head with his fist and hit him on the left side with his knee;
thus was he being beaten by the more powerful Rākṣasa.
Overcome by great rage, Bhīma of terrible prowess then rose up in fury and seized the Rākṣasa;
thus Vṛkodara and the man-eater tormented one another.
Like two great elephants in rut, they dragged each other about;
and by the sounds of the two terrifying rākṣasas’ flailing arms,
the entire city of Vetrakīya was thrown into a state of panic.
By the great force of those two, the earth there trembled;
they both pulverized the trees and the creepers as well.
And those two heroes, having encountered one another, were each desirous of slaying the other.
Then, with stones and the force of their feet, the two of them crushed him.
Then, having whirled him around, the mighty Bhīmasena seized him,
embracing him with both arms, O bull of the Bharatas.
With his two knees, Bhīmasena forcibly seized Baka;
the mighty one dragged the large-bodied demon as he writhed.
Being dragged by Bhīma while simultaneously dragging the Pāṇḍava in the combat, [he struggled].
The man-eater was overcome by intense exhaustion as he was dragged by Bhīma and, in turn, dragged the Pāṇḍava. The man-eater was overcome by intense exhaustion.
By the great force of those two, the earth trembled,
and they then pulverized the massive trees.
But beholding that *rakṣasa* being diminished, O bull of the Bharatas, [he grew in size].
Having crushed him against the ground with his two hands, Vṛkodara struck him repeatedly; then, pressing down upon his back with his knee as if with great force,
he seized his neck with his right arm.
Placing his back upon [Bhīma’s] knee, he broke it with a great roar;
having thrown him to the ground, he crushed him against the earth with both hands.
Then the Pāṇḍava seized him by the waist-cloth on his left side.
That *rākṣasa* redoubled its efforts, emitting terrifying roars;
then, O lord of the people, blood issued from the mouth of that fierce *rākṣasa* as he was being broken by Bhīma.
The Brahmin said:
Jñānasāgara said:
"O best of the twice-born, thereupon that young Yājñasenī grew up."
In due course, she attained youth, becoming a lamp for the fire of the god of love.
Seeing her of faultless limbs wandering at will in the assembly hall, Drupada, with a joyful heart, addressed her.
"I give [him] to Arjuna"— he then revealed his heart thus.
Having heard these words of King Drupada, the minister named Vasuprada was then distressed and spoke this slowly:

O best of kings, how could you give Pāñcālī, the daughter of Pṛṣata, to Arjuna— those great archers, the Pāṇḍavas, who were sleeping together with Kuntī in the house of lac, having been burned there in secret by the design of Duryodhana?
Having heard those words of his, the king became deeply distressed.
Seeing Drupada thus afflicted, the family priest, an ocean of knowledge, said:
"O King, I know from the omen that you have not been consumed by fire."
Then the king, delighted, said: "O twice-born one, how are you to see them?
"O lord of men, you shall see them through a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage); therefore, perform that.
Having heard this, all the Pāñcālas cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Then he caused a proclamation to be made regarding the *svayaṃvara* of his daughter:
"On the seventh day from now, in the month of Phālguna on the seventh lunar day.
The king also had many platforms constructed, suitable for royalty.
Resembling Mount Meru and Mount Mandara and adorned with gold and jewels,
Drupada had a wonderful bow made, difficult for kings to bend,
as a prize for the sake of Arjuna’s exhibition of skill.
And he set up a fish-mechanism at a distance, adorned with various colors;
"Whoever indeed shall strike down this aquatic creature with an arrow from this bow,
he shall make the princess of Pañcāla his own wife."
"O twice-born ones, that day of festival is now near.
Kings, princes, and all those who are elegant on this earth, as well as brahmins, bards, panegyrists, and heralds, are setting forth."
"I shall go to see that festival and to acquire wealth;
as for your departure, O best of the twice-born, you must make an effort.
Thus has everything been told to you, exactly as it was seen and heard."
Having heard what had occurred in the house of lac, the Brahmins, together with the family priest, [approached] Vaiśampāyana, the Brahmin.
Having consulted with one another, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with their ministers, spoke these words to Drupada, the king of Pañcāla:
"They have formed a most difficult resolve for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas."
It is heard that one sent by Duryodhana, known as Purocana,
having reached Vāraṇāvata and constructed a great house of lac,
[placed] the Pāṇḍavas along with Pṛthā in that house, full of confidence.
"O Great King, at midnight that Purocana set the house on fire;
he himself was consumed by the flames like a base and cruel man.
Upon hearing this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his kinsmen, was filled with joy.
But having heard that the Pāṇḍavas had been burned, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
with his grief diminished and his soul rejoicing, then commanded Vidura:
"O highly wise one, perform the rites of funeral cakes and water for the Pāṇḍavas."
Having spoken thus, O noble one, the compassionate Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Kṣattṛ, today Pāṇḍu has died at the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas;
alas, by the power of fate alone, they have gone to the abode of Yama."
Having spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with the son of Subala, wept there.
Having heard that Bhīṣma had performed the funeral rites according to the rules,
[the king reflected on] the deed committed by that evil-minded one for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas.
"Thus, an agent of this deed has neither been seen nor heard of before.
O Great King, we have heard this account concerning the Pāṇḍavas.
Having heard their words, the high-minded Yajñasena—
Just as a father would grieve at the loss of his own biological son,
so did the King of Pañcāla suffer at the prospect of the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas;
having summoned the subjects together with all their kinsmen.
Out of compassion alone, the King of Pañcāla then spoke these words:
"Oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what valor and training!
O kinsmen, day and night I think only of Arjuna."
Together with his brothers and his mother, he was consumed by fire.
What wonder is there in this world? For time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having failed in my promise, what shall I say now to the people of the world?
Burning day and night with inward grief,
O sinless ones, I have honored Yāja and Upayāja and made this request of you:
[to provide] a slayer of Bhāradvāja and likewise a divine weapon for Arjuna.
The world knows that, and so too have we heard from Yāja;
having offered the Putrakāmīya sacrifice, both were produced—
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Kṛṣṇā— who are both the source of my joy.
"What shall I do for you? The Pāṇḍavas, along with Pṛthā, are lost.
Having spoken thus, the Pāñcāla king, overcome with extreme distress, lamented.
Seeing the Pāñcāla king grieving so intensely, he (Bhīṣma) spoke this to him.
The family priest is endowed with goodness and possesses distinguished knowledge;
the Pāṇḍavas are practitioners of dharma who are devoted to the instructions of their elders.
Such as they are, they do not perish, nor do they suffer defeat.
O lord of men, hear this truth as it was seen by me:
it was spoken truly by the Brahmins and heard by me in the Vedas;
furthermore, in former times, it was heard even by Paulomī according to the opinion of Bṛhaspati.
Indra was lost within the knot of a lotus stalk when he was released by Upaśruti;
O Great King, I have heard that Upaśruti exists for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Wherever those Pāṇḍavas live, there is no doubt.

I have seen the omens that the Pāṇḍavas will arrive right here. O lord of men, hear the reason why they are coming: the *svayaṃvara* has been shown as the method for giving a daughter in marriage among the Kṣatriyas.
"O best of kings, let the *svayaṃvara* be proclaimed throughout the city;
whether the Pāṇḍavas are living there together with Pṛthā,
or whether they are far away, nearby, or even in heaven— let the Pāṇḍavas be summoned."
"O King, having heard of the *svayaṃvara*, they will surely assemble; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, O King, let the *svayaṃvara* be proclaimed; do not delay.
Having heard what was spoken by the family priest, the King of Pañcāla was then filled with joy.
He caused a proclamation to be made throughout the city regarding the *svayaṃvara* of Draupadī:
"In the month of Puṣya, under the asterism Rohiṇī, on an auspicious lunar day in the bright fortnight,
the *svayaṃvara* shall take place in seventy-five days."

Gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism are surely going, desirous of beholding the svayaṃvara; of this there is no doubt. Your sons are high-souled and especially handsome to behold.
"Or perhaps the princess of Pañcāla might go to the middle husband by chance;
for who among men knows the auspicious decree of Prajāpati?
Therefore, O Brāhmaṇī, you should go with your sons, if it pleases you."
O lady rich in asceticism, those Pāñcālas are always well-supplied with food;
that King Yajñasena is devoted to the Brahmins and true to his word,
all the citizens are devoted to the Brahmins, and the Brāhmaṇas are fond of guests.
They will constantly provide for those who arrive without being asked;
I too shall go there along with these disciples of mine. We shall travel as one caravan, if it pleases you, O Brāhmaṇī.
Having spoken these words, the brahmin fell silent.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, with his ribs and limbs broken, he let out a terrible roar.
Resembling the king of mountains, Baka became lifeless. At that sound, O King, the people of that Rākṣasa’s dwelling were terrified and rushed out of the house along with their attendants.
Then, seeing that the mighty lord of the rākṣasas had been slain,
the followers of Baka, overcome with supreme terror, sought refuge with Bhīma.
They were the attendants of Baka.
Stationed in groves, gardens, and sacred shrines, and taking refuge in minor temples,
they were struck with fear upon seeing Bhīma, that mass of valor; then Bhīma, the best among strikers, assailed those who had lost their presence of mind.
The powerful one consoled them and established them in an agreement:
"Human beings must never again be harmed by you here at any time;
for those who do harm them, their own destruction shall swiftly come to pass in this very same way."
Having heard those words of his, O Bhārata, those Rākṣasas said to him,
"So be it," and they accepted that agreement.
Then Baka’s brother, together with his followers, bowed down to the Pāṇḍava.

Leaving behind the city’s groves, gardens, shrines, and parks, they fled in terror, trembling with fear and overwhelmed by dread, taking refuge in a forest of *bhibītaka*, *kapittha*, *arka*, *plakṣa*, and *śālmali* trees.
Leaving the banks of the Yamunā, he entered the cemetery of his ancestors.
From that time forward, O Bhārata, gentle-looking *rākṣasas* were seen there in the city by the people dwelling in the city.
Then Bhīma, taking up that lifeless man-eater—
whose ears and eyes were gone, whose tongue was protruding, who was unconscious due to the pressure on his throat, and who was struggling with many convulsions— dragged that cannibal away.
"Surely that very Rākṣasa is coming again toward our city," they cried;
terrified, the men, including children and the elderly, fled in all directions.
Then Vṛkodara, having severed their arms, feet, and heads, [departed].
Having thrown [the corpse] at the four gates, that son of the Wind-god returned;
having cast it down at the gateway, he departed unobserved.
Then, seeing Baka, who had been shaken by Bhīma’s strength, slain.
His kinsmen, agitated by fear, fled here and there. Then Bhīma, having slain him, went to that brahmin’s house and offered the two oxen and the cart to the brahmin.
Having told the best of the twice-born, "Go silently into the inner apartments," she went before her mother and brother, and having approached the bed,
she related everything that had occurred concerning the king in its entirety.
"O Mother, I have eaten today; my satisfaction shall last for ten years.
Then, at the very break of dawn, men emerged from the city and beheld the Rākṣasa slain upon the ground, drenched in blood.
Seeing him, who resembled a mountain peak, scattered about and terrifying,
the citizens there stood with their hair bristling in awe;
then others went to Ekacakrā and spread the news.
Then, O King, thousands of city-dwellers—
accompanied by women, the elderly, and children— came there to see Baka.
They all beheld Baka, who was without head, hands, or feet.
Like a mountain stripped of its peaks, devoid of trees, and shorn of its shrubs, so it appeared;
then they were all struck with wonder upon seeing that superhuman feat,
their eyes wide with amazement and their fingers pressed against their noses.
O lord of the people, they all worshipped the deities;
then they began to calculate whose turn it was for the meal that day.
Having learned [the answer], they approached that brahmin and all of them questioned him about it.
Thus questioned repeatedly, while protecting the Pāṇḍavas,
that bull among brahmins then said this to all the citizens:
"I was commanded by Aśani while I was weeping along with my kinsmen."
A certain Brāhmaṇa, accomplished in mantras and possessed of great power, saw [them] and said:
"Today is your turn as a Rākṣasa; it was informed to me yesterday by a village spy who is common to all the inhabitants of the city."
Having first questioned me regarding the suffering of the city,
that best of brahmins spoke, consoling me as if with a smile:
"I shall deliver this food to that evil-minded one."
"Furthermore, one who possesses vigor should not feel fear on account of me. Taking that food, he departed toward the forest of Baka;
surely it was for this purpose that he performed this deed for the benefit of the world.

Then all those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were greatly amazed and, being delighted, performed a great sacrifice to Brahman. Thereafter, all the people from the countryside arrived at the city.

The Pārthas remained right there to witness that most wonderful sight. O Indra among kings, if a man hears of the slaying of Baka and honors the reciter, there shall be no fear of Rākṣasas even within his lineage.
His enemies perish, and likewise his calamities;
he attains great merit by hearing [the account] of Bhīma’s prowess.
In the house of Vetrakīya, they all surrounded Vṛkodara.
Filled with wonder, they approached Bhīma of terrible prowess;
"Nothing indeed is impossible for high-souled Brāhmaṇas"—
thinking thus, the citizens honored him and surrounded him on all sides.
For he is indeed our protector of all, like a father in the ultimate sense;
desiring to serve him, we attend upon his feet,
offering food consisting of meat and curds, along with the finest rice.
When he was slain, those men, terrified and seeking to understand what had happened, fled; then the sons of Pṛthā, the subduers of enemies, together with their mother,
departed for Ekacakrā, those Pāṇḍavas of firm vows.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas, with matted hair and observing the vow of celibacy,
they lived there for a long time in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, dwelling together with Mātṛ in Ekacakrā.
Janamejaya said:
O Brahmin, after those tigers among men had thus slain the Baka Rākṣasa, what did the Pāṇḍavas do next?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having slain the Rākṣasa Baka, they continued to dwell right there in the residence of the Brāhmaṇa, studying the supreme Brahman.
Then, after a few days had passed, a brahmin of rigid vows came to that house of the [other] brahmin seeking lodging.
Having honored him properly, that wise bull among brahmins then—
He, who was ever devoted to the vow of hospitality toward all guests, granted him shelter.
Then all those Pāṇḍavas, bulls among men, together with Kuntī,
sat around that brahmin as he related various stories.
He spoke of various countries and diverse sacred fords,
as well as the various exploits of kings and many different cities;
there, O Janamejaya, that Brahmin recounted these matters at the conclusion of his discourse.
The wonderful self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of Yājñasenī among the Pāñcālas,
the birth of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and the birth of Śikhaṇḍin,
as well as the fact that Kṛṣṇā was not born from a womb at Drupada’s great sacrifice.
Having heard that most wonderful account concerning that great-souled one in the world,
those bulls among men questioned him further in detail regarding that story:
how it was that Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Drupada, [was born] from the fire.
How did the wondrous birth from the center of the black sacrificial altar occur?
How did the great archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna learn all the weapons from Droṇa,
the great bowman, and how was he the one who brought death to Droṇa?
"How were those two dear friends separated, and by whose doing?
Thus urged by those bulls among men, O King,
that brahmin then related everything concerning the birth of Draupadī.
The Brahmin said:
At Gaṅgādvāra there lived a great ṛṣi of mighty asceticism,
the highly wise Bharadvāja, who was ever firm in his vows.
Having gone to the Gaṅgā to perform his ablutions,
the seer beheld there the Apsaras Ghṛtācī, who had already arrived and was bathing.
Then, on the riverbank, the wind blew away her garment.
Seeing her with her garments disarrayed, the seer then desired her; his mind was fixed upon her, even though he had been a celibate since childhood,
as he gazed at the arrangement of her private parts and the beauty of her other limbs.
The seed of the delighted sage spilled forth, and he deposited it in a wooden vessel (*droṇa*).
From that, the son Droṇa was born to that wise man.
He mastered the Vedas and all the Vedāṅgas in their entirety.
Now, Bharadvāja had a friend, a king named Pṛṣata;
he too then had a son named Drupada. That son of Pṛṣata used to go constantly to the hermitage together with Droṇa.
That bull among Kṣatriyas engaged in play and indeed pursued his studies.
Then, after Pṛṣata had passed away, Drupada became king;
meanwhile, Droṇa heard that Rāma was desirous of giving away all his wealth.
To Rāma, who was setting out for the forest, the son of Bharadvāja said:
"O bull among the twice-born, know me to be Droṇa, who has come desiring wealth.
Rāma replied:
"O Brahmin, today only this body of mine remains. Choose either the weapons or the body—whichever you prefer.
Drona said:
"You ought to grant me all the weapons, as well as their withdrawal and the method for employing them all. The Brahmin said:
Saying "So be it," the descendant of Bhrigu then gave it to him.
Having accepted it, Droṇa then felt his purpose was fulfilled;
with a joyful heart, he received from Rāma that which is highly esteemed.
Having mastered the Brahmāstra, he became superior among men. Then, having approached Drupada, the powerful son of Bharadvāja, that tiger among men, said: "Know me as your friend."
Drupada said:
"One who is not a Vedic scholar cannot be a friend to a scholar; one who is not a charioteer cannot be a friend to a charioteer;
nor can one who is not a king be a friend to a monarch. Why, then, do you desire a former friendship?"
"Between two whose wealth is equal and whose learning is equal,
there may be marriage and friendship, but not between one who is prosperous and one who is destitute.
The Brahmin said:

Having resolved in his mind regarding the prince of Pañcāla, that wise man went to the city of the Kuru leaders, named after the elephant (Hastināpura). Taking his grandsons and various riches with him, he departed for that city.

When he had arrived, Bhīṣma gave his disciples to the wise Droṇa. Then the learned Droṇa, having gathered all his disciples together, spoke these words for the purpose of bringing unhappiness upon Drupada.
Service to the preceptor and likewise the preceptor’s fee—
some such remuneration for the teacher revolves within his heart.
"O sinless ones, that [weapon] should be given to those who have mastered the arts of weaponry; this is the truth spoken by me.
Then the preceptor said "So be it" to those led by Arjuna, and having said "So be it," the wise son of Pṛthā grasped his feet.
"O Guru, tell me what wealth should be given as the fee for the knowledge [of weapons] that has been acquired?
And when all the Pāṇḍavas had mastered their weapons and completed their training,
Droṇa then spoke these words again regarding the payment."
"The son of Pṛṣata, named Drupada, is the lord of men in Chatravatī.
Having seized his kingdom, it must be returned to me immediately.
Then the Pāṇḍavas, together with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, went toward the Pañcālas.

Having encountered Yajñasena, Karṇa, Duryodhana, and others were defeated, as were other bulls among the Kṣatriyas; they then retreated. Thereafter, the five sons of Pāṇḍu, having conquered Drupada in battle, [proceeded].
Then, having bound him along with his ministers, they presented him to Droṇa;
just as the invincible Mahendra [once] confronted the Dānava,
so did Arjuna, the son of Mahendra, then conquer the Pāñcāla king.
Seeing that great hero of Phalguna, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
all the kinsmen of Yajñasena were filled with wonder,
saying, "There is no prince equal to Arjuna in prowess."
Droṇa said:
"O lord of men, I seek friendship with you once again;
for indeed, one who is not a king cannot be the friend of a king."
"Therefore, O Yajñasena, I have striven for your kingdom.
You shall be king on the southern bank of the Bhāgīrathī, and I on the northern.
When these words had been spoken by Drupada, O best of the twice-born, [he replied], "So be it."
Having honored Drupada, Droṇa, the knower of reality, sent him away, saying:
"O best of men, you should dwell in Kanyakubja or Kāmpilya;
O King, I myself dwell in Ahicchatra together with the Brahmins."
The Brahmin said:
"That great lack of hospitality does not depart from the king's heart even for a moment; dejected in mind, he has become emaciated."
Thus addressed by the wise Bhāradvāja, the Pāñcālya, the best among those skilled in weapons, spoke to Droṇa, the most excellent of Brahmins:
"So be it; may prosperity be yours, O high-minded Bhāradvāja."
"Let that very friendship be eternal which you desire.
Having spoken thus to one another and having established an unsurpassed bond of friendship, Drona and the Panchala prince, both subduers of enemies, departed as they had come.
Having heard his words and taken them to heart, the Brahmin became dejected in mind and said:
"King Drupada is impatient with those foremost of the twice-born who have accomplished their task."
Remembering his enmity with Droṇa, Drupada could not sleep;
seeking him out, he wandered through many dwellings of Brahmins,
his mind stricken with grief as he longed for the birth of a son.

He constantly thought, "I have no superior offspring," and out of despondency he said of his born sons, "Fie upon my kinsmen! He was consumed by sighs, driven by the desire to take revenge upon Droṇa.

O Bhārata, although that best of kings exerted himself, he could not find a way to counteract Droṇa’s power, discipline, training, and deeds, nor his strength born of the kṣatriya code, even as he reflected upon them.
Then, wandering about on the bank of the Gaṅgā near the dappled cow,
that lord of the earth reached a holy hermitage of Brahmins.
There, there was no twice-born man who had not returned from his studentship, nor any who lacked the observance of vows.
In that very same way, the son of Pṛṣata beheld those two Brahman-sages, Yāja and Upayāja, who were of noble lineage, firm in their vows, tranquil,
and devoted to the study of the Saṃhitās; they were both descendants of Kaśyapa.
Those two brahmins, the best of sages, were most appropriately suited for the rescue;
he, unwearied, addressed them with all desirable things,
having perceived their strength and intelligence near his younger brother.
Seeking to win over Upayāja, who was firm in his vows, he approached him while gratifying him with all his desires.
Devoted to serving at his feet, speaking kindly, and granting every wish,
he honored Upayāja according to custom and spoke to him.
"O Brahmin, by what rite may I have a son for the death of Droṇa,
and likewise a wife of excellent complexion for Arjuna? O Upayāja, if that is accomplished, I shall give you ten billion cows."

"Or whatever else, O best of the twice-born, may be very dear to your mind, all that I shall grant to you; indeed, I have no doubt in this matter. Thus addressed, the ṛṣi replied to him, "I am not [interested]."
Desiring to please him, Drupada attended upon him once more.
Then, at the end of a year, O King, that best of the twice-born, Upayāja,
spoke to Drupada at the proper time in a sweet voice:
"My eldest brother, while wandering by a forest waterfall,
picked up a fruit that had fallen upon ground whose purity was unknown. Following after my brother, I saw that he had acted improperly."
One should never, under any circumstances, engage in critical deliberation regarding the acceptance of mixed [impure] things;
for having seen the fruit, one does not perceive the defects that follow from it. How could he who does not distinguish purity in this matter be capable of doing so in any other?

"With the eye of reasoning, I consider that brother of mine to be one who desires the fruit [of the sacrifice]. Go to him, O King; he will perform the sacrifice for you. Thinking this, the king was filled with loathing in his mind.
Having heard the words of Upayāja, the king, who was conversant with all duties, honored the ṛṣi Yāja—who was worthy of honor—and said to him:
"O Lord, I shall give you eighty thousand cows; please perform the sacrifice for me."
"You ought to gladden him who is tormented by his enmity toward Droṇa;
for he is the best among those who know the Veda and is unsurpassed even in the Brahmāstra. It was because of that [enmity] that Droṇa defeated me in our conflict as friends."
There is no Kṣatriya on this earth who is his equal, for he is the foremost leader among the wise Bhāradvāja, the preeminent teacher of the Kauravas,
Droṇa, whose nets of arrows snatch away the bodies of living beings.
A great and peerless bow of six *aratnis* is seen in his hand;
for that high-minded Bhāradvāja, a mighty archer, undoubtedly strikes down the power of the Kṣatriyas with the power of a Brāhmaṇa.
He stood there like the son of Jamadagni, ordained for the extermination of the Kṣatriyas;
for his terrible power of weapons was irresistible by men on earth,
as he discharged the Brāhma energy like a fire fed with oblations.
Having come together, he, preceded by the Brahmin, consumes the warrior class in battle;
and when both the Brahmin and the warrior are established, the spiritual power of the Brahmin excels.
Thus, being deficient in the strength of the warrior, I have resorted to the spiritual power of the Brahmin.

Having approached you, the most eminent knower of Brahman and superior even to Droṇa, may I obtain a son invincible in battle who shall be the destroyer of Droṇa. O Yājña, perform that rite for me; I offer ten million cows as the sacrificial fee.
Having said "So be it" to him, Yāja prepared everything for the sake of the sacrifice;
and he urged Upayāja, though he was unwilling, saying, "This is for the sake of our preceptor.
Then Yāja, the best among those who perform sacrifices, gratified the carrier of oblations (Agni).
Yāja promised to bring about the destruction of Droṇa, and he did accordingly. It was my intention that there should be a daughter for the sake of Pāṇḍu’s daughter-in-law;
having said "So be it," he undertook the rite intended for the king's desire for a son.
Then, for that lord of men, the great ascetic Upayāja explained the sacrificial ritual (*vaitāna-karman*) intended to yield the fruit of a son;
and the king, as instructed, had that sacrifice prepared by the Brahmin.
"And that son shall be of great heroism, great splendor, and great strength;
O King, he whom you desire will be exactly such as that. Having resolved upon the slayer of Bhāradvāja, that lord of the earth—"

Drupada provided all of that accordingly for the successful completion of the ritual. Then, at the conclusion of the oblation, Yāja summoned the queen, saying: "Come to me, O Queen Pṛṣatī; a pair has presented itself before you."
The prince and the princess were for the sake of increasing the lineage of their husband.
The queen said:
"O Brahmin, my face is anointed, and I wear holy fragrances."
"I am detained for the sake of my daughter; stay, O Yāja, for my sake.
Thus addressed by the king, Yāja, who was himself a treasury of Brahmanic luster, endured it all and spoke to the queen.
Yāja said:
"The oblation cooked by Yāja and consecrated with mantras by Upayāja—how could it not fulfill one's desire? Therefore, you may either depart or stay."
The Brahmin said:
When Yāja had spoken thus, and the consecrated oblation had been offered into the fire,
a boy resembling a god rose up from that flame.
Flame-colored, of terrible form, wearing a diadem and excellent armor,
bearing a sword, arrows, and a bow, and roaring repeatedly,
he ascended that best of chariots and then set forth with it.
Then the Pāñcālas, filled with joy, shouted, "Excellent! Excellent!
But the earth could not bear them as they were thus overcome by exultation;
for that prince was the dispeller of their fear and the bringer of glory to the Pāñcālas.
"He has been born indeed to remove the king's grief and for the sake of slaying Droṇa"—
thus spoke a great, invisible being moving through the sky at that time;
and the princess of Pañcāla also rose up from the middle of the altar.
Fortunate, with limbs beautiful to behold, with a waist like the middle of an altar, and enchanting; youthful, with eyes like lotus petals and dark, curly hair;
with copper-colored high nails, beautiful brows, and lovely, full breasts.
Having assumed a human form, she was visibly like a celestial maiden;
from her, a fragrance like that of a blue lotus wafted for a *krośa*,
and she possessed a supreme beauty for which there is no equal on earth.

"O Bhārata, with hearts full of joy and motivated by devotion to the king, they said: 'She is desired by the gods, Dānavas, and Yakṣas; she possesses a divine form and is a fitting match for Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu.'"
And when that woman of beautiful hips was born, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"Kṛṣṇā, the best among all women, intends to bring about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas; this woman of slender waist will, in due time, accomplish the work of the gods."
"Because of her, a great fear will arise among the Kṣatriyas.
Upon hearing this, all the Pāñcālas roared like a pride of lions;
and the King of the Pāñcālas, seeing her, shed tears out of joy.
Embracing his daughter Kṛṣṇā and saying, "She is the daughter-in-law of Pāṇḍu," the king took the princess of Pañcāla onto his lap and attained great joy; indeed,
even this earth could not contain them as they were so full of delight.
Seeing them, Pṛṣatī, desiring a son, approached Yāja,
saying, "May these two not recognize anyone other than me as their mother.
Yāja said to her, "So be it," out of a desire to do what was pleasing to the king.
And the twice-born, their hearts fulfilled, bestowed names upon the two:
"Because of his boldness, his extreme audacity, his righteousness, and his birth from fire (dyut),
let this youth be Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Drupada."

They called her Kṛṣṇā because she was indeed black by complexion; she arose from the essence of the earth when it was ploughed and from the sacrificial oblation. Thus that pair was born at the great sacrifice of Drupada.
Indeed, Drupada performed all the necessary rites for him; Dhṛṣṭadyumna reached the furthest limit in the study of the Vedas. Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, making the Pāñcālas resound with his lion-like roar—
He mounted that excellent chariot and proceeded with him to his home;
and Kṛṣṇā, having reached a palanquin, entered her residence.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the prince of the Pañcālas, having brought [them] to his own residence, entered it.
The noble-minded Droṇa honored the son of his friend;
having honored Droṇa according to the prescribed rites as his preceptor in accordance with dharma,
Somaka then entrusted that disciple, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, to him.
"O King, may you be gracious! so spoke those who were pleasant of speech.
Then the powerful Brahman-sage Bhāradvāja, having understood his origin and possessing great majesty, initiated him for the sake of the weapons.
Considering that destiny is indeed inescapable and bound to happen, the high-minded Droṇa acted accordingly to preserve his own reputation;
for he had acquired all weapons instantly upon merely seeing them.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard this, the sons of Kuntī became like men pierced by arrows; the Pāṇḍavas were struck with grief.
Afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, they went mentally to Draupadī.
Then, O King, during that night...
all those great car-warriors became uneasy in mind.
Then, seeing her sons bewildered and deprived of their senses, Kuntī,
who always speaks the truth, addressed Yudhiṣṭhira with these words:
"We have stayed for many nights here in this brahmin’s dwelling."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O subduer of enemies, having obtained alms, we have been enjoying ourselves in that delightful city;
all those forests and groves here that are beautiful have been seen by us again and again.
"O hero, those very same sights no longer please us as they did before; nor, O joy of the Kurus, is alms-food obtained in such abundance. Therefore, if you agree, let us go properly to the Pañcālas."
"O dear one, it will be a delightful sight for us to see what we have never seen before.
O crusher of enemies, it is heard that the Pāñcālas are well-supplied with food,
and we have heard that this King Yajñasena is devoted to the Brahmins."
"Indeed, dwelling in one place for a long time is not appropriate, nor is it my view;
therefore, let us go there, my son, if you agree.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Whatever you deem to be the proper course of action is for our supreme benefit;
however, I do not know whether my younger brothers will go or not.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Kuntī spoke to Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the twins regarding their departure; they then replied, "So be it.
Thereupon, O King, Kuntī took leave of that brahmin together with her sons.
He set out for the beautiful city of the high-souled Drupada.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While those high-souled Pāṇḍavas were living there in disguise...
Then Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, arrived to see them.
Upon seeing that he had come, those subduers of enemies rose to meet him,
and having prostrated and saluted him, they then stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having taken leave of all those who were seated, the sage,
being gratified and honored by the sons of Pṛthā, spoke these words with affection:
"O harassers of the foe, do you conduct yourselves in accordance with dharma and the sacred scriptures?"
"Does your worship of the Brahmins, who are worthy of honor, not diminish?
Then, having spoken words consistent with dharma and artha, that blessed Ṛṣi,
after various and diverse discourses, spoke this once again.
In a penance grove, there was a certain daughter of a high-souled rishi;
she had a slender waist, beautiful hips, lovely eyebrows, and was endowed with every virtue.
Yet, due to her own past actions, she became unfortunate.
But that beautiful maiden, though virtuous, did not find a husband;
thereupon, being unhappy, she began to perform austerities for the sake of a husband. She indeed gratified Śaṅkara with her fierce asceticism.
The Blessed One, pleased with her, said to that ascetic woman:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I am a granter of boons, O beautiful lady. Then she spoke these beneficial words to the Lord concerning herself:
"I desire a husband endowed with all virtues," she said again and again. Then Īśāna, the best of speakers, Śaṅkara, replied to her: "O blessed lady, you shall have five husbands."
Thus addressed, the maiden then spoke to the boon-granting god Śaṅkara: "Grant me a single husband. To her, as she was thus responding, the god again spoke these excellent words.
"I have been told by you five times, 'Give me a husband. When you have gone to another body, that which was spoken shall come to pass:
she shall be born as a daughter of Drupada’s lineage, possessing the form of a god."
"Your blameless wife Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Pṛṣata, has been pointed out to you. Therefore, O mighty ones, enter the city of the Pañcālas;
having reached her, you will undoubtedly be happy."

"O Pārthas, the kingdom has indeed come to you. Having spoken thus to the Pāṇḍavas after entering Indraprastha, the highly fortunate grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas, a man of great asceticism, took leave of the sons of Pṛthā and Kuntī and departed.
01,157.016 Vaiśampāyana said:
01,157.016 Yudhiṣṭhira said: 01,157.016 The Brahmins said:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Those tigers among men, the scorchers of their foes, set out together with their mother and saw many Pāñcālas traveling with their retinues along with Brāhmaṇas.
Then those brahmins spoke to the dharma-practicing Pāṇḍavas:
"Where will you go, and from where have you come?"— thus they addressed the brothers, who were departing from Ekacakrā and seeking a vision of the gods.
"O sirs, may you recognize us as those who have traveled together following our mother;
we are going toward the Pāñcālas, to the city of Drupada. We wish for you to know us, for our curiosity is great."
"We too are traveling along this same caravan, bound for that very place;
there, moreover, a great festival of wondrous appearance will take place. Then, [we shall go] to the high-souled Yajñasena Drupada."
That maiden who is not born from a womb shall stand at her own choice of husband (svayaṃvara);
she is beautiful, with faultless limbs, delicate, and illustrious—
the sister of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the powerful enemy of Droṇa.

Born from the fire as a hero, equipped with arrows and a bow, that highly fortunate great car-warrior of the Somakas emerged from the well-kindled flames; and as he was being born, an incorporeal voice spoke.
At that great sacrifice, this Mṛtyu was born as the disciple of Bhāradvāja; moreover,
his sister Vedyā was also born there,
a jewel among women with dark-cornered eyes, as youthful and dark as a blue lotus.
"Let us go there indeed to see that daughter of Yajñasena, Draupadī, the most excellent of women, and also her svayaṃvara;
[there] kings and princes who have performed sacrifices and given profuse sacrificial fees [will be gathered]."

Devoted to sacred study, pure, high-souled, and firm in their vows; youthful, handsome, powerful, and difficult to overcome— these great chariot-warriors, skilled in weapons, shall assemble here as lords of the earth.
There, for the sake of victory, those lords of men will bestow various gifts— wealth, cows, and all kinds of food and drink— in their entirety;
and having obtained all that and seen Kṛṣṇā at her svayaṃvara.
And whichever Kṣatriya that maiden shall choose in the arena—
actors, bards, dancers, Sūtas, and Māgadhas,
as well as mighty wrestlers from various lands, will all assemble there.
Having seen this curiosity there and having accepted it,
you high-souled ones shall return together with us and your mother;
for all of you will appear beautiful, standing there with one and the same form.
Having observed them, Kṛṣṇā may choose one of you as her husband by lot. This one brother of yours is handsome and mighty-armed;
if he fights, he will win great wealth by lot.
"O sirs, we shall go to see the supreme self-choice ceremony (*svayaṃvara*) there—
the daughter of Yajñasena, Draupadī, and likewise her festival.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the Blessed Vyāsa had departed, those bulls among men, the Pāṇḍavas, with joyful hearts, set out placing their mother at their head;
they first took leave of the Brahmin, saluted him, and paid him due honor.
Traveling by level paths toward the north as directed, those subduers of enemies proceeded day and night toward the holy ford of Somaśravāyaṇa and toward the city of the Pañcālas.
They approached the world-river Gaṅgā, the daughter of Bhagiratha,
at the hour of moonset, at midnight, during their gathering,
while immersing themselves in the water.

Those tigers among men, the sons of Pāṇḍu, sat down upon the Gaṅgā. Then the highly illustrious Dhanañjaya, raising a torch, went before them there for the sake of illumination and for their protection.
There, in the delightful and secluded waters of the Gaṅgā, while sporting with his women,
the jealous king of the Gandharvas arrived for a water-sport. He heard the sound of them approaching the river.
Pervaded by that sound, the powerful one became violently enraged.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas, those subduers of foes, there together with their mother,
he stretched his terrible bow and spoke these words.
The twilight that becomes terrible at the onset of the early night is said to be a *muhūrta* lacking eighty *truṭis*;
it is ordained for the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas who move according to their own will.
The rest of human conduct here is recorded as being according to their own will.
When men wander about during those specific times out of greed, we, along with the *rākṣasas*, seize those foolish ones once they have been attacked.
Then, as they were reaching the water at night, those people who knew the Veda censured all men, even kings established in power, saying:
"Stand far off! Do not approach me!"
"Why do you not recognize me who has come to the waters of the Bhāgīrathī?
Know me to be the Gandharva Aṅgāraparṇa, relying upon my own strength. For I am proud, envious, and the dear friend of Kubera."
This forest of mine, situated along the Gaṅgā and the Vākā, is known as Aṅgāraparṇa; it is wondrous, and there I dwell.
Neither corpses nor horned beasts, neither gods nor humans may enter here.
"They are approaching this; why then do you approach it?
Arjuna said:
"O evil-minded one, [this is] at the ocean, on the side of the Himavat, and at this river."
By whom has possession been ordained for the night, the day, or the twilight?
O sky-ranger, whether one has eaten or not eaten,
there is no restriction of time once one has reached the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers.
"Though we are endowed with power, we did not dare to challenge you at an improper time;
for men worship you during this cruel hour when they are powerless.
Long ago, she emerged from the golden peak of the Himalayas."
Having reached the waters of the ocean, the Gaṅgā divides into seven streams:
the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī born from the Plakṣa tree,
the Rathasthā, the Sarayū, the Gomatī, and likewise the Gaṇḍakī.
Those who drink from the seven rivers have their sins not lingering; having become this single-banked river, pure and moving through the sky,
O Gandharva, Gaṅgā attains the state of being the Alakanandā among the gods.
O Gandharva, as Dvaipāyana has declared, the Vaṅkṣu and the Bhadrā flow northward from the foot of the Himavat;
likewise, the Vaitaraṇī is difficult for those of evil deeds to cross,
yet it becomes the Gaṅgā.
The auspicious celestial river is unobstructed and brings about the attainment of heaven;
how can you wish to block it? This is not the eternal Dharma. How could we, by your word alone, obstruct that which is irresistible and unimpeded?
"May we not touch the holy waters of the Bhāgīrathī as we please.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that, Aṅgāraparṇa became enraged and bent his bow.
He released blazing arrows like venomous serpents; meanwhile,
the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya, swiftly brandishing a torch and his excellent shield,
warded off all of those arrows.
Arjuna said:
"O Gandharva, this intimidation is not employed against those who know weapons;
when used against those skilled in weapons, it dissolves like foam."
"O Gandharva, I perceive that all the Gandharvas surpass humans;
therefore, I shall fight with a divine weapon and not with illusion. Long ago, it is said, Bṛhaspati bestowed this Āgneya weapon upon me."
Bharadvāja was the preceptor of the Gandharvas and the son of Śatakratu;
from Bharadvāja came Agniveśya, and from Agniveśya my preceptor. That Droṇa, the best of Brahmins, bestowed this [knowledge] upon me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the enraged Pāṇḍava released the blazing Āgneya weapon at the Gandharva; it then consumed his chariot.
Dhanañjaya seized by the hair that mighty Gandharva, who was deprived of his chariot, overwhelmed, bewildered by the energy of the weapon, and falling headlong.
Then he dragged Yudhiṣṭhira toward his brothers, who had lost consciousness from the discharge of the weapon; his wife, named Kumbhīnasī, approached him seeking refuge,
desiring protection for her husband.
The Gandharvī said:
"Save me, O Great King, and release this husband of mine;
I am a Gandharvī named Kumbhīnasī who has come to you for refuge, O Lord."
Having heard those piteous words, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke;
indeed, having looked at Phālguna, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira spoke;
and out of a disposition toward showing favor, Pārtha spoke to Pārtha.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O slayer of foes, who indeed would kill an enemy such as you—one defeated in battle, stripped of glory, a protectorless woman, and devoid of prowess? Release him!"
Arjuna said:
"O Gandharva, receive this body and go; do not grieve.
Today King Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of the Kurus, grants you freedom from fear."
The Gandharva said:
"I am conquered; I relinquish my former name, Aṅgāraparṇa. I do not boast today of my strength, nor of my name, in this assembly of people."
"Excellent is this gain I have obtained, that I, though superior in age, desire to fight with one who wields divine weapons by means of Gandharva illusion!
This wonderful and supreme chariot of mine has been consumed by the fire of his weapons."
Having been Citraratha, I became known by the name Dagdharatha.
This science was previously acquired by me here through ascetic penance;
today I shall impart it to that high-souled giver of my life.
For what blessing does he not deserve, who restores to life an enemy who has been paralyzed by force, conquered, and come for refuge?
This is the science called Cakṣuṣī, which Manu gave to Soma.
He gave her to Viśvāvasu, and Viśvāvasu gave her to me.
Thus, having been bestowed by her preceptor, she has fallen into the hands of a coward and is being lost.
I have declared her lineage; now learn of my prowess.
Whatever one might wish to see with the eye anywhere in the three worlds, that one shall see; and in whatever manner one wishes to see it, one is capable of seeing it in that very manner.
By remaining for six months on a single mat, one may obtain this knowledge.
"I myself shall impart this knowledge to you once the vow has been performed.
For by means of this knowledge, O King, we are distinguished from other men and,
empowered by its majesty, are not inferior even to the gods."
O best of men, I shall give to each of your five brothers a hundred horses born of the Gandharvas—
steeds that carry the celestial Gandharvas, possessing divine fragrance and traveling at the speed of thought.
Though they are worn away again and again, these do not lose their momentum.
Long ago, when Mahendra hurled his thunderbolt for the destruction of Vṛtra,
it shattered into ten and even a hundred pieces upon Vṛtra’s head.
Then, having been divided by the gods, the portion of the thunderbolt (*vajra*) was worshipped;
whatever means of accomplishment exists in the world, that indeed is remembered as the body of the thunderbolt.
A Brahmin may have the thunderbolt in his hand, and the Kṣatriya is remembered as having the thunderbolt in his chariot.
The Vaiśyas are indeed the thunderbolts of the Dānavas, while the Karmavajras are the youngest;
the Vajras are known as the swift ones of the Kṣatriya, and the swift ones are considered invincible.
The mare gives birth to the chariot-wheel, and those who are considered Sūtas are among the horses.
"These horses, born of the Gandharvas, possess the colors of desire, the speed of desire, and appear at will; they shall fulfill your every wish. Arjuna said:
"O Gandharva, whether it be given by one who is pleased, or at the risk of my very life, I do not desire that knowledge, wealth, or even sacred learning. The Gandharva said:
"Indeed, union is seen to bring joy in assemblies.
I am pleased by your gift of life and shall grant you knowledge;
for from you, I shall receive the supreme *āgneya* weapon."
"Even so, O Bībhatsu, O bull of the Bharatas, let our friendship endure for a long time.
Arjuna said:
"I choose horses from you in exchange for my weapons; let our union be eternal."
"O friend, O Gandharva, tell us that by which we may cast off our fear.
Arjuna said:
"O Gandharva, tell us the reason; what is it by which we have been thus overcome?"
"O subduer of enemies, while all those who were knowers of Brahman were departing during the night,
the Gandharva said: 'They have no sacred fires, they offer no oblations, and they are not preceded by Brahmins.'"
Therefore, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas, you have been overcome by me;
for neither Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas,
nor humans can overcome those who are preceded by Brāhmaṇas, O tiger among men.

O best among those who possess the sacred fire, knowing both your splendor and your noble lineage, I have indeed made up my mind to challenge you. For who in the three worlds does not know you, O bull of the Bharatas?
They proclaim the extensive and glorious, preeminent fame of those of great splendor through their own virtues; they recount the expansion of the illustrious Kuru lineage,
which I have heard from Nārada and the other celestial rishis.
O hero, while those wise ancestors of yours were recounting your virtues,
I too, as I wandered across this entire earth girt by the ocean, personally witnessed the majesty of your lineage.
"O Arjuna, I recognize your teacher in both the Veda and the bow—
the illustrious Bhāradvāja, renowned throughout the three worlds,
the best among all knowers of the Vedas, and the foremost of all wielders of weapons."
I know Droṇa, who is skilled in the science of archery and the best among the descendants of Aṅgiras;
likewise, I know Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and the two Aśvins,
as well as Pāṇḍu— these six, O tiger among the Kurus, who increase their lineage.
"O Pārtha, these ancestors of yours are the best among gods and men;
they are divine-souled, high-minded, the foremost among all wielders of weapons—
your heroic brothers, all of whom have been steadfast in their vows."
O Pārtha, although I was aware of the supreme mental resolve of you whose souls are purified, I nevertheless committed this act of provocation here against you. Furthermore,
O Kauravya, no man ought to forgive such an offense in the presence of a woman.
Seeing my own humiliation and relying on the strength of my arms,
and because our power increases even further at night,
O Kaunteya, wrath entered me as I thought of myself along with my wife.

"O enhancer of the Tāpatyas, I have been defeated by you here in battle according to that very rule; listen now as I describe it to you. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the supreme duty, and that too is firmly established in you."

Therefore, O Pārtha, I have been conquered by you in this battle. But any Kṣatriya whatsoever who, O scorcher of foes, acts according to his own will and fights in battle at night, could not possibly survive in any way.
But a king of the Tāpatyas, even if he acts according to his own desires,
shall conquer all night-stalkers in battle by relying upon his domestic priest.
Therefore, O Tāpatya, whatever welfare is desired by men in this world—
In that undertaking, the domestic priests should be appointed— those who have subdued their selves,
who are devoted to the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs, pure, truthful, righteous in nature, and self-disciplined; such should be the domestic priests of kings.
Victory is certain for the king, and heaven shall follow immediately thereafter,
provided he has as his domestic priest a man who knows the dharma, is eloquent, virtuous, and pure—
one capable of gaining what has not been gained and preserving what has already been gained.

A king should appoint as his domestic priest one endowed with all virtuous qualities; for a monarch who desires to obtain the entire earth, bounded by the oceans and crowned by Mount Meru as its preeminent ornament, should abide by the counsel of his domestic priest.
For no lord of the earth who is not a Brahmin can ever conquer the land by mere valor alone, nor even by his descent from the Tāpatya lineage. Therefore,
O enhancer of the Kuru race, understand this to be so.
"A kingdom with the Brahmins at its head can be protected for a long time.
Arjuna said:
"As for those words you have spoken here to me, calling me 'Tāpatya'—"
Therefore, I wish to know the definitive meaning of the term *Tāpatya*.
Who is this woman named Tapatī, on account of whom we are called *Kaunteyas*, O virtuous one? I desire to know the truth of this.
"O Aṅgāraparṇa, tell all that to me in its entirety.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, that Gandharva [spoke] to Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī.
He caused this story, renowned throughout the three worlds, to be heard.
The Gandharva said:
"Behold, I shall relate to you this delightful tale."

O Pārtha, best among the upholders of dharma, I have already spoken to you in full regarding that righteous speech by which I addressed you as "Tāpatya. I shall now relate that to you; listen to me with an attentive mind.
He who pervades the celestial vault with his splendor by means of his radiant power— O son of Kuntī, O lord, that Vivasvat had an incomparable daughter named Tapatī, who was younger than Sāvitrī.
Renowned throughout the three worlds and endowed with ascetic power, Tapati was such that no goddess, nor asura, nor yakṣī, nor rākṣasī,
nor apsaras, nor gandharvī possessed a form like hers.
With well-proportioned and faultless limbs, dark and long eyes,
virtuous conduct, and being a faithful wife of beautiful appearance—
O Bhārata, there was no one equal to her in the three worlds.
Seeing that his daughter had reached her youth, Savitṛ considered a husband for her who was distinguished by beauty, character, lineage, and learning;
and beholding her, endowed with such beauty, at the age of sixteen, he [reflected].
Reflecting upon that gift, he found no peace; then,
O son of Kuntī, the powerful Saṃvaraṇa, the son of Artharṣi and bull among the Kurus, constantly propitiated the Sun.
The king, the delighter of the Pauravas, was constantly intent upon offering respectful salutations, garlands, and gifts; he was devoted to observances, fasts, and various forms of austerity,
being pure, free from egoism, and desirous of serving [the sages].
The devoted man worshipped the rising sun, Aṃśumat. Then the Sun, considering Saṃvaraṇa— who was grateful, knew the dharma, and was peerless in beauty on earth— to be a worthy husband for Tapatī.
Then, O Kauravya, he desired to give that maiden to Saṃvaraṇa,
that best of kings of renowned lineage;
for just as the sun of blazing rays illuminates the heavens with its splendor, so did he shine.
Likewise, Saṃvaraṇa became a protector of the earth on this world through his splendor;
O Pārtha, just as those who discourse on Brahman worship the rising sun, so did the subjects, including the lower castes, revere Saṃvaraṇa.
That illustrious king surpassed the moon in loveliness and the sun in splendor, both toward his friends and even toward his enemies.
O Kaurava, such was the king, possessed of such virtues and such conduct.
The Sun himself set his mind upon giving Tapatī to him. Then once, O Pārtha, that illustrious king of vast fame wandered for the hunt in a forest at the foot of a mountain on this earth.

O son of Kuntī, while he was hunting, the king’s peerless horse died on the mountain, overcome by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. With his horse dead, O Pārtha, the king continued his journey on foot across the mountain.
He beheld a long-eyed maiden, peerless in the world. Having approached that solitary maiden, that tiger among kings, the crusher of enemies, stood gazing at her with an unblinking gaze.
For the king conjectured her to be the goddess Śrī herself;
he further reflected that she was like the radiance fallen from the sun,
or like the crest of fire by virtue of her form and splendor.
With her serene countenance and radiant beauty, she was as stainless as the crescent moon. Standing upon that mountain plateau, the fair-eyed lady shone brilliantly, like a golden image.
By her form and especially by her attire, that mountain,
along with its trees, shrubs, and creepers, appeared as if it were made of gold.
And having seen that woman of beautiful limbs and lotus-like eyes, the king—
Seeing her, who embodied the form of all living beings, the king felt she was beyond contempt; he considered that he had finally attained the true fruit of his eyesight—
whatever he had seen since the time of his birth.
He could not conceive of anything that her form was like;
with his mind and eyes bound by her with snares made of the qualities (*guṇas*),
he did not move from that spot nor was he aware of anything at all.

"Surely, having churned the entire world— including its gods, asuras, and humans— the Creator has manifested and fashioned this form for this large-eyed woman. Thus he reflected upon her perfection of beauty and wealth of form.
At that time, King Saṃvaraṇa saw a maiden who was peerless in the world;
and upon seeing that auspicious girl, the king of noble lineage was afflicted by the arrows of love and his mind was filled with anxious thought.

Burning with the intense fire of love, that bold king spoke to that modest and illustrious woman: "Who are you? To whom do you belong, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks? And for what purpose do you stand here?"
And how is it that you wander alone in the desolate forest, O lady of pure smiles? For you, with your entirely faultless limbs, adorned with every ornament,
are like the desired object of these very ornaments themselves.
I do not consider her to be a goddess, nor an asura, nor a yakṣī, nor a rākṣasī; I do not think her to be a bhogavatī, nor a gandharvī, nor a human woman—
whatever excellent women have been seen or even heard of by me.

O intoxicated one, I do not consider you to be their equal; O fair-faced one, upon seeing your face— which is more lovely than the moon and has eyes like lotus petals— the god of love truly churns me.

Thus that protector of the earth spoke to her, but she did not say anything in reply at that time to him who was afflicted by desire in the lonely forest. Then, as the king continued to lament, the large-eyed woman—
Like a flash of lightning among the clouds, she vanished right there;
searching for her, the king then wandered through that forest like one driven mad, seeking the lotus-eyed woman.
Not seeing her, that best of the Kauravas lamented there at length and remained motionless for a moment. The Gandharva said:
Then, while she remained invisible, the king, deluded by passion—
that slayer of hosts of enemies— fell upon the surface of the earth.
When he had fallen to the ground, that woman of lovely smiles [vanished].
Once again, she of the full and broad hips revealed herself to the king;
then that auspicious woman addressed the king, the sustainer of the Kuru lineage whose mind was overcome by desire, with sweet words.
Tapatī spoke these sweet words, as if smiling:
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you. O subduer of enemies, O tiger among kings, you who have appeared upon this earth do not deserve to fall into delusion."
Thus addressed with sweet words,
the king then beheld her of broad hips standing directly before him;
