then the lord of men spoke to that woman with dark-cornered eyes.
"My soul overwhelmed by the fire of love, with words of faltering syllables:
'O dark-eyed one, O beautiful woman, favor me, who am afflicted by desire and devoted to you;
for my very life-breaths are deserting me.'"
"O large-eyed one, for your sake this Kāma, piercing me with sharp arrows, finds no rest, O lady with the luster of the lotus's interior. Thus,
O blessed one, I am seized by the great serpent of desire in a place where there is no refuge."
O you with full and broad hips, O lady of beautiful countenance, encompass me!
For my life-breaths depend upon you, O singer of kinnara songs,
you whose every limb is lovely and faultless, and whose face resembles both the lotus and the moon.
"O timid one, indeed I shall not be able to live by myself without you;
O lotus-petal-eyed one, this desire pierces me.
Therefore, O large-eyed lady, O beautiful woman, show compassion toward me."
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, you ought not to abandon me, who am devoted to you;
for you, O beautiful woman, ought to protect me through the bond of affection.
My mind, its love aroused by the sight of you, trembles violently."
"O auspicious lady, having seen you, I have no desire to see any other woman again.
Be gracious; I am under your power. O beautiful one, accept me, your devotee.
O lady of lovely limbs, the moment I saw you, O fair one, the god of love has taken firm hold of my body."
O large-eyed one, O lotus-eyed one, he pierced the burning heat arising from the fire of love within me with his feathered arrows;
refresh me with these waters joined with the union of affection.

O auspicious lady, O noble one, pacify with the gift of yourself that invincible god whose weapon is the flower, who wields a fierce bow and arrows, and who pierces you with unbearable shafts born from the sight of you.
"O timid one, O beautiful lady, come to me through the Gāndharva form of marriage;
for among all forms of marriage, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, the Gāndharva is said to be the best.
Tapatī replied:
"O King, I am not the mistress of myself, for I am under the protection of my father. If you have affection for me, ask my father for my hand;
for just as my life has been taken by you, O lord of men, so too must he grant his consent."
"O best of kings, it was by your mere sight that you took away my life-force so completely; yet I am not the mistress of my own body,
and therefore I do not approach you, for women are never independent."

For what maiden in all the worlds would not desire as her lord and husband a king of renowned lineage who is affectionate toward his devotees? Therefore, since time is thus passing, ask my father [for my hand].
"O crusher of enemies, if the Sun, through my prostrations, ascetic penance, and self-restraint, should desire to give me to you,
then, O King, I shall forever remain under your control."
"O bull among Kṣatriyas, I am indeed his daughter, named Tapati, born of Savitṛ, the lamp of this world; I am the younger sister of Sāvitrī. The Gandharva said:
Having spoken thus, the blameless woman then quickly ascended upwards;
the king, distressed, cried out "Tapati! Tapati!
and the monarch repeatedly stumbled, yet rising again, he ran after her.
But the lord of the earth, running along and not seeing the Tapatī at all,
that king fell down again upon the ground right there. Searching for that best of kings, he went with his army.

The minister, accompanied by his retinue, beheld him in the great forest fallen upon the ground like the lofty banner of Śakra brought down at the appointed time. Indeed, having seen that great archer fallen on the earth, deprived of his horses—
He became his minister, as if set ablaze by fire;
and approaching with haste, overcome with affectionate agitation,
he raised up that king who was deluded by desire.
Like a father seeing his son fallen upon the ground, the king of the earth—
advanced in wisdom and age, and distinguished by fame and self-restraint— had him raised up from the ground; and having done so, the minister was freed from his distress.
And she spoke to him with sweet and auspicious words as he stood there:
"Do not fear, O tiger among men; may it be well with you, O sinless one.
She then perceived that the king was exhausted by hunger and thirst.
Having felled him— the one who caused his enemies to fall— upon the surface of the earth in battle,
he then consecrated the king’s head with very cool water,
which was as fragrant as a lotus, without touching the crown.
Then, having regained his breath, the powerful king dismissed that entire army, with the exception of that one minister alone. Thereupon,
by the command of the king, the great host departed.
But that king sat down once more on that mountain plateau,
O bull of the Bharatas; reflecting upon Tapati, his mind captivated by her form, he remained there like one who has lost his senses, devoid of awareness.
Then, having purified himself on that excellent mountain and joining his palms in reverence,
the lord of the earth, filled with devotion, stood upon the ground with upraised arms, desiring to propitiate the Sun and worshipping the Maker of Day.

Then King Saṃvaraṇa, the slayer of enemies, went in his mind to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and his domestic priest. At that time, while that lord of men remained in one place day and night, [the sage was present].
Then, on the twelfth day, the brahmin-sage arrived;
having understood through divine means that the king’s mind had been captivated by Tapatī, that great rishi, whose soul was purified, knew this.
Then that righteous-souled one, desiring to accomplish his purpose, addressed that best of kings who was thus self-restrained:
"May it be well with you, O tiger among kings; for I am entreating Tapati."
Having said, "And for that purpose, [I shall go] to Vivasvat," the best of sages departed.
While that lord of men looked on, the blessed seer,
possessing the radiance of the sun, ascended upward to behold the Sun-god.
Having traveled a million *yojanas* in an instant, the ascetic,
that brahmin, approached the thousand-rayed sun with palms joined in reverence;
out of affection, he announced himself, saying, "I am Vasiṣṭha."
The immensely radiant Vivasvat spoke to that best of sages:
"O great seer, welcome to you; tell me whatever you desire.
[Gandharva]
Vasiṣṭha is 64 yojanas [in diameter], and Sūrya is likewise 30 yojanas in a nimeṣa.
He who always travels by means of horses, standing at his side, spoke this:
"To Aja, the creator of the three worlds; to the Self of all beings, the Lord of Cows, the Bull."
Homage to Sūrya, the abode of creation and dissolution;
homage to the supreme among the greatly compassionate; homage to Vivasvat, the bearer of knowledge, the inner self.
Homage to the lamp of the world, who desires the welfare of the world;
homage to the Self-Existent One, who possesses a thousand radiant eyes, the supreme among gods, of immeasurable splendor.
"I have been praised by you, O Giver of Boons; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. This hymn spoken by you for the sake of devotees shall be recited as a prayer; I am the Giver of Boons.
Homage to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world!"
To the cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the world;
to the one consisting of the three Vedas, who assumes the nature of the three *guṇas*; to the one whose essence is Viriñci, Nārāyaṇa, and Śaṅkara.
"O illustrious one, best among speakers, whatever you desire from me,
I shall grant that which you intend, even if it be very difficult to obtain.
Thus addressed by him, the seer Vasiṣṭha replied.
Having prostrated before Vivasvat, the radiant one,
the great ascetic Vasiṣṭha said:
"This daughter of yours named Tapati, who is younger than Sāvitrī— "
"O Vibhāvasu, I choose you for the sake of Saṃvaraṇa.
For that king is of great fame, a knower of dharma and worldly purpose, and possessed of noble intellect;
O bird, Saṃvaraṇa is a fit husband for your daughter."
The Gandharva said:
Thus addressed by him,
the Sun, having resolved "I shall give," replied to that brahmin, greeting him with joy.
"Saṃvaraṇa is the best among kings, and you, O Sage, are the best among seers;
Tapatī is the most excellent among women—what else remains but her being bestowed [upon you]?
Thereupon, the Sun himself [bestowed] Tapatī, who was entirely faultless, upon Agni.
He gave her for the sake of Saṃvaraṇa to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha; then the great seer Vasiṣṭha accepted that maiden Tapatī. Having been dismissed, Vasiṣṭha then returned once more.
Where that bull among the Kurus, whose fame was renowned, had come to be;
there the king, possessed by the god of love and with his inner self entirely captivated,
beheld that celestial maiden Tapati of the lovely smile.
Accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, she shone with exceeding joy;
that fair-browed woman, descending from the sky,
gleamed all the more like a flash of lightning fallen from the heavens, illuminating everything with her own splendor.
When that king’s twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance had been completed,
the blessed seer Vasiṣṭha, his soul purified,
arrived there after propitiating through austerity the boon-granting Lord, the divine Master of Rays (the Sun).
By the very power of Vasiṣṭha, Saṃvaraṇa obtained a wife;
then, on that best of mountains frequented by gods and Gandharvas,
that bull among men took the hand of Tapatī according to the prescribed rites.
Permitted by Vasiṣṭha, that royal seer desired to sport with his wife on that very mountain. Then,
[he took leave] of the city, the kingdom, the mounts, and the armies.
Then the protector of the earth commanded that very minister.
Having given that beautiful Tapatī to the protector of the earth, he said:
"Stay here, O lady of fair hips; I shall depart. O auspicious one, you must take refuge with your husband."
Having taken leave of the king, Vasiṣṭha then departed;
the king, too, like an immortal, sported upon that mountain.
Thereafter, for twelve years, he dwelt in the forests and by the waters.
The king sported on that mountain together with that very wife of his.
In that city of the king, for twelve years in every respect,
the thousand-eyed Indra did not send rain anywhere throughout his kingdom.
Then, O subduer of enemies, when that drought had set in,
all creatures— both stationary and moving— came to ruin.
While that most terrible time was thus prevailing, [the people perished].
No dew fell upon the earth, and consequently the crops did not grow. Thereupon, with bewildered minds and tormented by the fear of hunger,
the people abandoned their homes and wandered aimlessly in every direction.
Then, in that city and kingdom, people who had abandoned their wives and possessions,
lacking restraint toward one another and tormented by hunger, began to slaughter each other.
At that time, those men were like corpses— joyless and afflicted by hunger.
The city of the King of the Dead became as if filled with ghosts—
devoid of flesh, consisting only of sinews and bones, and intensely covered with a network of veins.
Then, having seen it in such a state, that very same venerable seer [spoke].
The righteous-souled Vasiṣṭha approached that best of kings and brought that tiger among monarchs back to his city,
O King, together with Tapatī, after he had dwelt there for twelve years.
Then,
once that tiger among kings had re-entered the city, the slayer of the enemies of the gods,
the thousand-eyed Lord Indra, began to rain down as he had done before, bringing forth crops for the people.
Then that city, along with its kingdom, rejoiced with supreme joy, being graced by that foremost of kings, whose soul was purified. Thereafter,
the lord of men performed sacrifices again for twelve years.
Just as Śakra, the lord of the Maruts, is accompanied by his wife Tapatī,
so too was there in former times that highly fortunate woman named Tapatī,
O Pārtha; she was the daughter of Vaivasvata, by whom you are considered a Tāpatya.
Upon her, Tapatī, King Saṃvaraṇa begot Kuru, O best of those who heat; therefore, O Arjuna, you are a Tāpatya. Having sported with her for ten thousand years, he—
Having consecrated Kuru in the kingdom and performed austerities, that one whose wealth is penance then went to the world of the Ādityas, O bull of the Bharatas;
from him you were born as Kurus, and thus you are known as the Kauravas.
O bull among the Bharatas, the Pauravas, Ājamīḍhas, and Bhāratas—
this entire account of your ancestors, known as the Tāpatya, has been told to you. With me as your priest at the head, may you enjoy this earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O bull of the Bharata race, having heard those words of the Gandharva at that time,
Arjuna shone with supreme joy like the full moon.
And that great archer, the best of the Kurus, spoke to the Gandharva,
his curiosity greatly aroused by the power of Vasiṣṭha’s asceticism:
"Regarding this name of the seer which you have mentioned— 'Vasiṣṭha'— "
"I wish to hear this; tell it to me exactly as it is.
O Lord of the Gandharvas, who was this venerable ṛṣi who served as the domestic priest for our ancestors? Tell me this."
"Indeed, through the power of Vasiṣṭha’s asceticism, a kingdom with abundant food was obtained.
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā born of his mind, is the husband of Arundhatī.
The Gandharva said:
He whose two feet— desire and anger, which are eternally unconquerable even by the immortals— have been trampled down through asceticism;
he who has brought the senses under his control is called Vasiṣṭha.
Just as desire and anger were conquered— though unconquered by other men— by him,
his enemies were defeated, the worlds were won, and the paths to heaven were secured;
for that noble-minded one did not bring about the extermination of the Kuśikas.
On account of Viśvāmitra’s transgression, he maintained the utmost indignation;
though he was a powerful lord tormented by the calamity of his son's death,
he did not conceive of any cruel deed for the destruction of Viśvāmitra.

He who sought to bring back even the dead sons from the abode of Yama did not overstep the End-maker (Kṛtānta), just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore. Having obtained him, the self-conquered and high-souled one, the lords of men [attained their goals].
The Ikṣvākus, those protectors of the earth,
obtained this world after securing Vasiṣṭha, the best of priests and the foremost of sages; and those kings, O descendant of Kuru, performed sacrifices with various rites.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, that Brahmarṣi officiated at the sacrifices for all those most excellent kings, just as Bṛhaspati does for the immortals;
likewise, Saudāsa was then joined together with Vasiṣṭha.
But once separated from the Rākṣasas and joined by Viśvāmitra,
O hero, neither Gandharvas nor Rākṣasas, however mighty they may be, are able to even mentally covet him who has a Brahmin as his companion.
Therefore, let some virtuous Brahmin, whose soul is preeminent in dharma and who is learned in the Vedic law, be sought out as a desired domestic priest;
for by one born a Kṣatriya who desires to conquer the earth, [such a priest is required].
"O Pārtha, a domestic priest (purohita) must first be appointed for the prosperity of the kingdom;
by a king desiring to conquer the earth, the power of the Brahman (brahma) must be placed at the forefront. Therefore, let there be some virtuous twice-born man as your domestic priest."
"May the learned Brahmin, who knows the true nature of dharma, desire, and purpose, be your guide.
Arjuna said:
"What was the cause of the enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha?"
"Relate all of that to us concerning those two while they dwelt in their holy hermitage.
The Gandharva said:
"This ancient narrative concerning Vasiṣṭha is what they proclaim."
O Pārtha, learn from me exactly how it was in all the worlds.
O bull of the Bharatas, there was once a great king in Kanyakubja,
renowned in the world as Gādhi, who was devoted to truth and righteousness.
The son of that righteous-souled king, known as Viśvāmitra, who possessed abundant forces and vehicles and was a crusher of his enemies,
went out to hunt in the dense forest together with his ministers.
Piercing deer and wild boars in the delightful desert wastes,
that best of men, exhausted by exertion, seeking game, and parched with thirst,
then arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Seeing that he had arrived, the preeminent seer Vasiṣṭha received Viśvāmitra, the best of men, with honor,
O Bhārata, offering water for his feet, the guest-offering, water for sipping, and words of welcome.

In that same manner, he accepted it as an offering of forest produce. Then, for that high-souled Vasiṣṭha, there was a wish-fulfilling cow; when told, "Grant my desires," she then milked out all his wishes.
There were mounds of steaming rice resembling mountains, along with finished dishes, soups, and streams of curd; likewise,
there were wells filled with ghee and heaps of various foods.
In various places there were thousands of costly foods:
sugarcane, honey, parched grain, maireya wine, and excellent liquors;
as well as precious garments and thousands of woolen blankets.
She milked out both cultivated and wild herbs, as well as milk itself—
the six-flavored nectar, the unsurpassed elixir of immortality— and various kinds of foods to be eaten, drunk, and chewed.
O Arjuna, there were foods to be licked and likewise foods to be sucked that were like nectar;
there were also highly precious jewels and various kinds of garments.
Honored with all these objects of desire provided in full, that lord of the earth was gratified.
Together with his ministers and his army, that king was exceedingly gratified.
It is said that these are the auspicious, elongated features of cows: the head, the neck, the two thighs, the dewlap, the tail, and the udders.
Adorned with five broad colors and possessing six proportions—
the forehead, the two ears, and likewise the pair of eyes—
these five broad features of cows are praised by the wise.
Thus, like a frog that has swollen,

she whose six parts were expanded— she who had broad sides and thighs, the three-fold width, and the five-fold contraction; she with frog-like eyes, of beautiful form, with full udders, and beyond reproach.

Beholding her—possessing a beautiful tail, spike-like ears, lovely horns, and a charming form; with a well-nourished and long head and neck; well-fleshed in her limbs and of noble birth—he was filled with wonder.
Seeing that cow of Vasiṣṭha— her flanks and udders well-filled, her tail long, her belly broad, a first-calf mother, and full of milk— the king rejoiced in that source of joy for the sage.
And then Viśvāmitra, being greatly pleased, said to the sage:
"O Brahmin, give me Nandinī in exchange for a hundred million cows or even my kingdom; enjoy the kingdom, O great sage."
Vasiṣṭha said:

"O sinless one, this milch-cow Nandinī, who provides milk for the sake of the gods, guests, and ancestors, and for the purpose of sacrificial ghee, must not be given away by me even for your kingdom."
Viśvāmitra said:
"I am a kṣatriya, while you are a brahmin whose means are austerity and Vedic study. How can there be such prowess in brahmins who are peaceful and self-controlled?"

"O Blessed One, this is indeed a jewel, and the king is a thief of jewels, since you do not give me my desired cow for ten million cows. I shall not abandon my own duty; I will take the cow from you by force."
"I am a Kṣatriya, not a Brahmin; by my very nature, I possess the prowess of arms.
Therefore, while you look on, I shall take this [Sītā] here by the strength of my own arms.
Herein lie the offerings for the gods and ancestors, as well as the means for sustaining life."
"The Agnihotra sacrifice and the hospitality due to guests depend upon her, there is no doubt.
What is the use of much talk? I will not give away this cow that milks all desires.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"You are powerful, you are a king, and you are a Kṣatriya of great physical prowess;
therefore, act quickly as you wish, without hesitation.
On this earth, there are two treasures belonging to a Brāhmaṇa that must not be seized by kings."
"The Agnihotra cow and the wife, who is the unsurpassed source of progeny.
The Gandharva said:
"O Pārtha, having been addressed thus, Viśvāmitra then [acted] as if by force."
He carried off that cow Nandinī, who resembled a swan or the moon.
As she was being forcibly carried away by Viśvāmitra’s troops,
she was struck with whips and sticks and driven here and there.
Then the auspicious Nandini of Vasiṣṭha,
lowing softly, O Pārtha, came forward facing him and stood with her face turned toward the Blessed One;
even though she was being struck severely, she did not depart from the hermitage.
Having shaken off their powers and severed the bonds of their fetters,
they did not go toward the hermitages at all, but bellowed with loud "hum" sounds.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I hear your cry, O blessed one, as you lament again and again. You are being carried off by force, Nandini; for I am a patient Brahmin, O Nandini, by Viśvāmitra."
"What should I do there? [he wondered].
Then the soldiers of Viśvāmitra, with whips and stones in their hands, began to strike Nandinī from all sides once again.
The Gandharva said:
O bull of the Bharatas, Nandini, agitated by fear of Viśvāmitra, approached Vasiṣṭha out of the strength of those other bulls.
The cow said:
"O Brahmin, why do you neglect me, who am being struck by stones and sticks, crying out like one who is helpless, and who is devoted to serving your lotus feet?"
"O Blessed One, why do you look on with indifference while Viśvāmitra’s terrible forces [attack]?
The Gandharva said:
"O Pārtha, when she had thus been assaulted at that time, the great sage..."
He did not waver, nor did he deviate from his fortitude, for he was firm in his vows.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The strength of Kṣatriyas is their splendor; the strength of Brāhmaṇas is forbearance."
"Forgiveness attends me; therefore, let it be done if it pleases you. The cow said:
"O Blessed One, why do you speak thus to me as if I were one to be abandoned?"
"O Brahmin, since I have not been abandoned by you, I cannot be taken away by force.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I do not abandon you, O blessed lady; stay, if it is possible for you to do so."
"Bound with a firm rope, this calf of yours is being carried off by force;
by whatever means possible, you must prevent the calf from being taken.
The Gandharva said:
Hearing those words of Vasiṣṭha, "Stay!", that milch-cow,
with her head and neck raised high, appeared terrible to behold;
her eyes were bloodshot with rage, and she bellowed with a deep, thundering sound.
Viśvāmitra’s entire army was put to flight in every direction. Struck by the tips of whips and rods, and driven hither and thither, she,
her eyes blazing with rage, summoned even greater fury.
With his body blazing with anger like the sun at midday, he shone;
repeatedly emitting a great shower of glowing coals from his tail,
he produced the Pahlavas from his tail, the Śabaras from his dung, and the Śakas from his urine.
From the region of her womb she created the Yavanas, and likewise from the region of her dung the Śakas;
and from her urine, overcome with rage, she also produced the Yavanas,
and from her side the Barbaras.
From his nostrils he emitted these:
the Puṇḍras, Kirātas, Dramiḍas, Siṃhalas, and Barbaras;
as well as the Cibukas, Pulindas, Cīnas, Hūṇas, and Keralas.
In that very same way, she produced the Darada barbarians from her froth.
With those various hosts of Mlecchas who were thus released— covered in diverse armor and bearing various weapons— a great army was then formed.
While Viśvāmitra looked on, the army was overwhelmed by the enraged [Gandharvas];
then each individual warrior was surrounded by five or seven [of them],
and the host was driven back by that great rain of missiles.

While Viśvāmitra looked on, that fourfold army of his— formidable, exceedingly difficult to withstand, and once full of vigor— was utterly broken and fled in all directions. Deprived of its strength, it was struck with terror on every side.
Yet none of those soldiers were deprived of their lives by the enraged Vasiṣṭhas, O bull of the Bharatas;
that cow merely drove the entire army far away from Viśvāmitra.
Viśvāmitra’s army, being driven for three yojanas,
crying out and agitated by fear, found no protector.
Then Viśvāmitra, seeing this, was overcome with anger toward both heaven and earth.
He rained down showers of arrows upon Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages—
terrible-looking iron shafts, razor-edged arrows, and broad-headed missiles; yet the great sage neutralized those weapons discharged by Viśvāmitra with his bamboo staff.
Then, having witnessed Vasiṣṭha’s skill in action during the combat,
Viśvāmitra— the slayer of enemies— once again, out of wrath,
furiously unleashed a rain of divine weapons upon that sage.
O highly fortunate lady, when Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, [was struck], the weapons belonging to Agni, Varuṇa, Indra, Yama, and Vāyu were released;
emitting flames from all sides, they fell upon him.
At the time of the end of the eon, like the terrible rays of the sun,
even Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great splendor, smilingly warded off all those weapons with a staff empowered by the power of Brahman.
Then, reduced to ashes, they fell upon the surface of the earth.
Having warded off those divine weapons, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words:
"O great king, you are defeated, O evil-minded son of Gādhi!"

"If you possess supreme valor, then display it while I stand here. Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, O lord of men, King Viśvāmitra, his great strength having been humiliated and filled with shame, said nothing at all.

Having witnessed that great marvel born of Brahmanic splendor, Viśvāmitra, despondent with his status as a Kṣatriya, spoke these words: "Fie on the strength of a Kṣatriya! The strength of Brahmanic splendor is true strength!"
Having determined the relative strength of all things, he concluded that asceticism alone is the supreme power.
Abandoning his prosperous kingdom and that radiant royal splendor,
and casting all enjoyments behind him, he set his mind solely upon asceticism.
Having attained perfection through asceticism and pervaded the worlds with his splendor, he of blazing power scorched all beings and attained the status of a Brahmin;
and the descendant of Kuśika drank the pressed Soma together with Indra.
Thus did that royal seer, Arjuna, become a brahmin seer of such valor;
it was for his sake that enmity arose between the two seers Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha.
O Lord of the Gandharvas, tell me all of that:
the greatness of Vasiṣṭha, who possesses Brahmanic power,
as well as that of the high-souled Kṣatriya Viśvāmitra.
"O sky-walker, even though I am listening, I do not reach satiety.
O Lord of the Gandharvas, tell me more; you speak of wondrous things here, and you recount the greatness of Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra."
The Gandharva said:
"O Pārtha, there was once a king in this world named Kalmāṣapāda, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, who was peerless on earth in his splendor."
O Great King, there was no [fear] there for him who possessed a splendor equal to Vaiśvānara.
Once, that king, the crusher of enemies, went out from the city into the forest for the hunt; piercing deer and boars, he roamed about.
In that most terrible forest, he slew many rhinoceroses;
having hunted for a very long time and becoming exhausted, the king then turned back from there.
The powerful Viśvāmitra desired him as his patron for a sacrifice.

But that king, unconquered in battle, afflicted by thirst and hunger while traveling along a narrow path, beheld the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, approaching him from the opposite direction.
"O illustrious one, [the king spoke thus] to Śakti by name, the delighter of Vasiṣṭha’s lineage,
the eldest son among the hundred sons of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha:
'Depart from our path.'"
Then the seer spoke to him, consoling him with gentle words:
"O Great King, this is my path; it is the eternal dharma.
According to all codes of righteousness, the king must grant way for the twice-born."
In this way, the two spoke words to one another regarding the matter of the path; they offered the verbal retort, "Move aside! Move aside!
But the seer, remaining firm on that path of dharma, did not step back.
Neither out of pride nor out of anger did the king yield to the sage. But as that seer would not give way, the best of kings,
out of delusion, then struck the sage with a whip like a rākṣasa.
Then, struck by the lash, that best of sages,
the son of Vasiṣṭha, overcome with rage, cursed that foremost of kings:
"Since you strike an ascetic like a Rākṣasa, O lowest of kings!"
"Therefore, from this day forward, you shall become a man-eater;
addicted to human flesh, you shall roam this earth. Thus was he addressed by Śakti, the possessor of heroic power: "Go, O lowest of kings!"
Then, on account of their respective patrons, a feud arose between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha; at that time, Viśvāmitra pursued him,
and as the two were thus disputing, he approached them.
O Pārtha, the powerful sage Viśvāmitra was one of fierce asceticism;
then that best of kings later recognized him as the son of the sage Vasiṣṭha, equal to Vasiṣṭha himself in splendor.
Then, O Bhārata, Viśvāmitra, having concealed himself,
approached those two, desiring to accomplish his own purpose. But that best of kings was then cursed by Śakti.
And the king remained there, filled with despondency.
"O King, the end of your curse shall come in the twelfth year," Śakti said; and having been thus addressed by Śakti, the king stayed right there.
He went for refuge to Śakti, seeking to propitiate him with honor. O descendant of Kuru, having understood the king's disposition, Viśvāmitra then dispatched a Rakṣasa toward the monarch.
Due to the curse of that brahmin-sage and by the command of Viśvāmitra,
the rākṣasa named Kiṃkara then entered the king. Having realized that he was possessed by the rākṣasa, the sage then [acted].
Viśvāmitra also departed from that place, O subduer of enemies;
then that wise king, protecting himself by his own effort,
remained there even though he was being powerfully tormented by the Rākṣasa within him.
A certain twice-born man saw that king as he was setting out once more;
hungry, he then begged him for a meal consisting of meat.
Then the royal sage Mitrasaha spoke to that twice-born man:
"Stay right here for a moment, O Brahmin," he said, consoling him;
"I shall return and give you food as you desire.
Having spoken thus, the king departed, while that best of the twice-born remained there.

Then that speech uttered by the brahmin was taken to heart by the king; having entered the inner apartments, the lord of men retired to rest. Thereafter, the king, having wandered about as he pleased and as he desired, [fell asleep].
Having turned back, O Pārtha, the high-minded king entered the inner apartments.
Then, rising at midnight and summoning the cook with haste,
the king spoke, remembering his promise to the brahmin.
"Go! In that place, a brahmin is waiting for me;
he is seeking food, so provide him with meat and rice.
Thus addressed, the cook then searched everywhere but could find no meat anywhere.
Then, overcome with distress, he reported this to the king.
But the king, possessed by the Rākṣasa, became free from his own pain and said to the cook again and again,
"Feed him even with human flesh."
Saying "So be it," the cook then went to the execution grounds and,
free from fear, quickly brought back human flesh. Having prepared it according to the rules and mixed it with the food, he served it immediately.
He gave it to that hungry, ascetic Brahmin.
Having seen that food with his perfected vision, that best of the twice-born,
his eyes clouded with anger, said, "This is unfit to be eaten."
"Because that lord of men gives me food that is unfit to be eaten, therefore he himself,
that fool, shall become greedy for it here,
as was previously declared by Śakti when he was addicted to human flesh."
Terrifying to all living beings, he shall wander this earth.
When the king’s curse was uttered twice, it became powerful;
then, possessed by the strength of a *rākṣasa*, he lost his senses.
Then, O Bhārata, that best of kings, his senses impaired by the Rākṣasa, spoke to Śakti upon seeing him, as if after no long time:
"Since this improper curse has been cast upon me by you..."
"Therefore, from you I shall proceed to devour human beings. Having spoken thus, he immediately deprived him of life and devoured Śaktin, just as a tiger devours its desired prey.
Seeing Śakti slain, Viśvāmitra then once again directed that Rākṣasa against the sons of Vasiṣṭha. He [attacked] those hundred sons of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha who were younger than him.
Enraged, he devoured them like a lion devouring small deer. Having heard that those sons had been slain by Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha bore that grief as a great mountain bears the earth.
That best of sages formed the intention to bring about his own destruction;
however, that foremost of the wise did not at all consider the extermination of the Kuśikas.
Then the venerable ṛṣi threw himself down from the peak of Mount Meru.
His head fell upon the rock as if onto a heap of cotton; and when he did not die from that fall, O Pāṇḍava,
the Blessed One then kindled a fire and entered it in the great forest.

Then, although it was well-kindled, the consumer of oblations did not burn him; though blazing, O slayer of enemies, the fire became cold. Then that great sage, overcome with grief, set out toward the ocean.
Having tied a heavy stone around his neck, he threw himself into that water.
By the force of the ocean waves, that great sage was cast onto dry land;
yet even then, the Brahmin of firm vows did not die by any means.
Dejected, he then returned once more toward the hermitage.
The Gandharva said:
"Then, seeing the site of the hermitage devoid of those sons, the sage—"

Afflicted by extreme sorrow, he departed once again from that hermitage. O Pārtha, he saw a river filled with fresh rainwater during the monsoon season, carrying away many various kinds of trees growing along its banks.
Then, O descendant of Puru, overcome with grief, he fell into deep thought once more: "I shall drown myself in these waters. Thereupon, the great sage firmly bound himself with ropes.

Deeply distressed, he sank into the waters of that great river. Then, having severed the snares of the river, O crusher of enemy forces, she set that ṛṣi free, making him Vipāśa (the "snareless") as he stood upon the bank.
Then that great ṛṣi crossed over, freed from his bonds;
and the great ṛṣi gave that river the name Vipāśā. O Bhārata, she became renowned in the worlds as the river Vipāśā.
O tiger among men, at the words of that wise seer,
the venerable sage, O King, having emerged from there, was filled with sorrow;
he then set his mind upon grief and could not remain in one place.
He traveled across mountains, rivers,
and lakes; then that seer, seeing once again the river Haimavatī with its fierce crocodiles, leaped into its current.

Afflicted by grief and having resolved upon death, he immersed himself [in the waters]. Having reflected upon that Brahmin who was like fire, that best of rivers fled in a hundred directions; therefore, she is renowned as the Śatadru.

Then, seeing himself once again on dry land there, he said to himself, "It is not possible to die," and returned once more to the hermitage. Having traveled across various mountains and many different regions, he [arrived].
Followed by his wife Ādṛśyantī, as he was walking toward the hermitage,
he then heard from behind him the sound of Vedic recitation,
adorned with the six ancillary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) whose meanings were complete.
"Who is this that follows me? he asked. His daughter-in-law replied to him, "I am Adṛśyatī by name, O illustrious one; I am the wife of Śakti, an ascetic devoted to penance."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O daughter, whose is this sound of Vedic study, including the auxiliary sciences?
Previously, I heard such a recitation of the Vedas with their limbs from Śakti."
Adṛśyantī said:
"O Sage, this embryo of your son, born from Śakti, has been in my womb for twelve years while he was studying the Vedas here."
The Gandharva said:
Thus addressed, O Pārtha, the preeminent rishi Vasiṣṭha was delighted;
saying, "There shall be progeny," he turned back from Mṛtyu.
Then, having returned with his bride, that sinless man saw Kalmāṣapāda seated in the lonely forest.
O Bhārata, as soon as the king saw him, he rose up in a rage.
Possessed by a fierce *rākṣasa*, he then desired to devour him.
But Adṛśyantī, seeing that man of cruel deeds before her,
spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha with a voice trembling with fear:
"O Blessed One, that terrifying Rākṣasa approaches from here like Death itself with a fierce staff; he comes brandishing a wooden club.
There is no one else on earth capable of warding him off."
"O highly fortunate one, best among those who know all the Vedas, except for you,
O Blessed One, save me today from this evil of dreadful appearance;
for this rākṣasa surely intends to devour us both here."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Do not fear, daughter; you must not be afraid of the rākṣasa in any way. This is no rākṣasa from whom you perceive this danger approaching."
"This is King Kalmāṣapāda, renowned on earth for his prowess;
he dwells in this forest region, most terrifying.
The Gandharva said:
Beholding him as he was rushing forward, the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha,
O Bhārata, being full of splendor, warded him off with a mere "huṃ" sound;
and then, having sprinkled him again with water purified by mantras, he restrained him.
He indeed liberated that best of kings from the terrible Rākṣasa;
for he had been seized by the very splendor of Vasiṣṭha for twelve years, like the sun eclipsed by Rāhu during the time of a lunar node.

Then, released from the rākṣasa, that king illuminated that great forest with his splendor, like the sun illuminating the clouds at twilight. Having regained consciousness, he then saluted him with palms joined in reverence.
At that time, the king spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages:
"O highly fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, I am Saudāsa, your patron for sacrifices.
Tell me what you desire at this time; what may I do for you?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
"This has transpired according to the proper time; go and rule that kingdom.
And as for the Brahmins, O lord of men, never hold them in contempt."
The king said:
"O Brahmin, I shall never disregard the bulls among Brahmins;
remaining ever under your instruction, I shall honor the twice-born."

"O best of the twice-born, O foremost among those who know the Vedas, I wish to obtain from you a boon by which I may become free of my debt to the Ikṣvākus. You ought to go to my queen for the sake of obtaining the desired offspring."
[Endowed] with virtue, beauty, and good qualities, for the prosperity of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
The Gandharva replied to the king there, saying, "I give her."
Then, O sinless lord of men, that best of the twice-born, Vasiṣṭha— true to his promise and possessed of a supreme bow—
set out at the proper time accompanied by Vasiṣṭha toward Ayodhyā,
the most famous of cities in all the worlds.
Then all the subjects, rejoicing, went out to meet him—
that sinless and high-souled one— just as the inhabitants of heaven go to meet their Lord.
Before long, that lord of men reached the city of those who perform meritorious deeds.
Accompanied by that high-souled Vasiṣṭha, he entered;
then, O King, the people dwelling in Ayodhyā beheld him like the sun risen at the proper time in conjunction with the Puṣya constellation.
For he, the best among the fortunate, filled that city with his splendor,
just as the cool-rayed moon risen in the autumn season fills the sky;
its streets were sprinkled and swept, and it was adorned with hoisted banners.
That supreme city gladdened his heart;
O descendant of Kuru, that city, crowded with contented and well-nourished people,
then shone like Amarāvatī with Śakra.
Then, when that king, the lord of kings, had entered the city, the queen approached Vasiṣṭha by the command of the monarch. Then,
during her season, that great seer united with her.
The preeminent sage Vasiṣṭha, according to the divine ritual of the goddess, [conceived a son]. Then, once the embryo had been produced in her, that best of sages,
having been saluted by the king, returned again to his hermitage.
When she did not give birth to the fetus that had been carried for a long time, the queen then pierced her own belly with a stone. Then,
in the twelfth year from that, O bull among men, he was born.
The royal seer named Aśmaka, who founded the city of Potana—
Gandharva said:
"Then Adṛśyantī, while staying in her hermitage, gave birth to a son."

O King, that bull among sages, the blessed one himself, performed the birth rites and other ceremonies for his grandson Śakti— the founder of a lineage who was like a second Śakti— O best of the Bharatas.

Because Vasiṣṭha was then established by him while he was still in the womb, he is therefore remembered in the world as Parāśara. At that time, that righteous-souled one considered Vasiṣṭha to be his father.
From his very birth, he behaved toward him as if toward a father;
O Kaunteya, O scorcher of foes, he addressed the brahmin-seer Vasiṣṭha as "Father" in the presence of his mother Adṛśyantī.
Hearing those sweet words of his, "Father," which were full of meaning, Adṛśyantī, her eyes filled with tears, said to him:
"Do not say 'Father, Father, Father,' for that great sage is not your father."
"O dear one, your father has been devoured by a *rākṣasa* in the depths of the forest.
O sinless one, he whom you consider to be your father is not your father;
rather, this noble man is the father of that high-souled father of yours."
Thus addressed, that best of sages, truthful in speech and great-minded, being afflicted by grief,
set his mind upon the destruction of all the worlds. To that high-souled one who was thus resolved, the ascetic of great penance—
The seer Vasiṣṭha, the best among the knowers of Brahman, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, whose intellect was directed toward the ultimate, restrained him for a specific reason; hear that reason.
Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a king on earth renowned as Kṛtavīrya,
a bull among monarchs who was the patron of the Bhṛgus, the knowers of the Vedas in this world. O dear one, he [provided] those who eat first with grain and with wealth.
At the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice, the lord of the people gratified [the gods] with abundant offerings.
Then, on a certain occasion, after that tiger among kings had ascended to heaven,
a need for wealth arose among his kinsmen.
O dear one, having learned that the Bhṛgus possessed wealth, all those kings indeed went to those best of the Bhṛgus as supplicants.
Some of the Bhṛgus, however, buried their inexhaustible wealth in the earth.
Some gave to the twice-born out of fear of the Kṣatriyas;
others, however, the Bhṛgus, gave them wealth as they desired,
O dear one, at that time because they perceived a different underlying motive among the Kṣatriyas.

Then, O dear one, while a certain Kṣatriya was digging at random on the surface of the earth, he discovered wealth in the dwelling of a Bhṛgu. All those bulls among Kṣatriyas, having gathered together, beheld that treasure.
Then, out of anger, they held those Bhrigus who had sought refuge in contempt; those great archers slaughtered them all with sharpened arrows,
wandering across the earth cutting them down even from the womb.
Then, while the Bhrigus were thus being exterminated out of fear,
O dear one, the wives of the Bhrigus fled to the Himavat mountain.
Among them, one woman, out of fear, carried a fetus of fiery splendor within her womb.
With one thigh, that woman of beautiful thighs, for the sake of increasing her husband’s lineage, quickly conceived a child in her womb; then, a certain Brahmin woman, afflicted by fear,
went and spoke of it in secret to the Kṣatriya women.
Then those kṣatriyas, intent on destroying that embryo, went there;
they beheld that brahmin woman blazing with her own splendor.
Thereupon, that embryo emerged, having burst through the thigh of the brahmin woman.
Stealing away the sight of the kṣatriyas like the sun at midday,
they were then deprived of their vision and wandered through mountain fastnesses.
Thereupon, those bulls among kṣatriyas, their resolve frustrated and afflicted by fear, [fell into despair].
They sought refuge with that blameless woman of the Brahmin caste for the sake of sight;
those Kṣatriyas, deprived of their vision and afflicted by grief like fires whose flames have been extinguished, spoke to that illustrious lady.
"By the grace of the Blessed One, may the Kṣatriyas regain their sight;
and having desisted from evil deeds, may we all go together. You, along with your sons, ought to show us favor."
"Furthermore, you ought to save the king by restoring his sight.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"O dear one, I do not take back your sight; I am not possessed by anger."
"But this descendant of Bhṛgu, born from the thigh, is surely angry with you today.
O dear ones, it is certain that by that great-souled one, remembering his slain kinsmen, your eyes have been taken out in his wrath; of this there is no doubt."

"O sons, when you were even destroying the embryos of the Bhṛgus, this embryo was held by me within my thigh for a hundred years. Indeed, while still remaining in the womb, he mastered the entire Veda along with its six auxiliary limbs."
Desiring to do what was pleasing to the lineage of Bhṛgu, he entered once more.
"Surely, because of the slaughter of his father, he wishes to slay you out of anger—
he by whose divine splendor your eyes have been robbed of their sight."
"O dear ones, beg this Aurva, my most excellent son;
being satisfied by your prostration, he will restore your sight.
The Gandharva said:
When they had spoken thus, all those kings then said to that son of the thigh, "Be gracious! And he granted them his favor;
by this very name, that best of beings became renowned throughout the worlds.
That brahmin-seer Aurva was born after splitting open the thigh;
then, having regained their sight, the kings departed from there.
But the sage Bhārgava resolved upon the destruction of all the worlds.
O dear one, that high-minded one, the best of the Bhṛgus, desiring to avenge the Bhṛgus, directed his entire mind toward the total destruction of all the worlds.
Nourished by great ascetic power for the sake of destroying the entire world,
he scorched the worlds— including the gods, asuras, and humans—
desiring to delight the Grandfathers (Pitāmahas) with his fierce and mighty penance.
Then, O dear one, having recognized him as the best of the Bhrigus,
all the ancestors came from the world of the Pitris and spoke these words:
"O Aurva, O son, the power of your fierce asceticism has been witnessed."

"Show favor to the worlds and restrain your own anger. For at that time, O dear one, all those Bhṛgus of purified souls, though they were not powerless, overlooked the slaughter of the Kṣatriyas who were inflicting harm."

"O dear one, when exhaustion overcame us despite our great longevity, we ourselves then desired death at the hands of the Kṣatriyas. For that wealth was indeed buried by someone in the dwelling of the Bhṛgus."
That [wealth] was deposited at that time solely for the sake of enmity by those wishing to incite anger among the Kṣatriyas.
For what use have we for wealth, O bull among the twice-born, when we desire heaven?
Since the Lord of Wealth has brought us abundant riches.
But when death is unable to seize us in every way, then,
dear son, this method approved by us has been seen;
for a man who takes his own life, dear son, does not attain the auspicious worlds.
Therefore, having reflected thus, we have not destroyed ourselves by our own hands.
To avoid this [consequence], you must practice righteousness (*dharma*). And this which you wish to do, dear son, is not pleasing to us.

"Restrain this mind from evil, which brings about the downfall of all the worlds. For there are no Kṣatriyas for us, nor are there the seven worlds, O son; do not let them corrupt the power of our asceticism—abandon this arisen anger."
Aurva said:
"O ancestors, that vow which I uttered then out of anger for the destruction of all the worlds— let it not be in vain."
For I cannot bear to live with a vow of anger made in vain;
indeed, such unfulfilled wrath would consume me like fire consumes the friction-stick.
For he who is able to forgive anger that has arisen from a specific cause [is truly wise].
That man is not capable of properly protecting the three aims of life (trivarga),
for it is the restrainer of the undisciplined and the protector of the disciplined; anger employed in the proper place by kings desiring to conquer heaven is indeed appropriate.

At that time, while still situated in my mother’s womb upon the bed of the womb, I heard the wailing of the group of mothers as the Bhṛgus were being slaughtered by the Kṣatriyas together with the gods—
those lowest of Kṣatriyas who, along with the worlds, joined in the destruction of the Bhṛgus.
When the extraction of the embryo was permitted, then anger took possession of me.
Indeed, my mothers and fathers, their treasuries filled,
found no refuge in all the worlds out of fear.
At that time, no one would approach those wives of the Bhṛgus. Then this auspicious lady bore me on her single thigh;
for when there is someone in the worlds who restrains evil, [it does not take root].
At that time, no evildoer is reborn in any of the worlds.
But when a sinner finds no one anywhere to restrain him,
then many people in the world persist in sinful deeds.
Even he who, though knowing a sin to be evil, does not restrain it despite having the power to do so—
even being a lord— he too is joined with the fruit of that very action.
This is true even if my ancestors were kings and lords.
Though capable, they were unable to save him, considering life here to be dear;
therefore, although I am now the lord of these worlds, I am enraged and am not able to disregard your words.
Even for me, though I am the Lord, it would be a great fear that the worlds might suffer from sin while I remained indifferent;
and this fire born of my wrath desires to consume the worlds.
If he were restrained, he would consume me with his own splendor;
yet I recognize that you all desire the welfare of the entire world.
Therefore, O lords, ordain whatever is for the benefit of the worlds and for me.
The Pitṛs said:
"This fire born of your wrath which desires to consume the worlds—release it into the waters; may prosperity be yours, for the worlds are established upon the waters."
"O dear one, follow our words; do not destroy the worlds now.
All juices consist of water, and the entire world consists of water.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, release this fire of your wrath into the waters."
"O Brahmin, let this fire of your wrath remain here in the great ocean if you so desire; for it is known that the waters consume water, and all the worlds are composed of water.
In this way, O sinless one, this vow of yours shall become true."
"And the worlds, together with the gods, shall not suffer defeat.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Then, O dear one, Aurva cast that fire born of his wrath into the abode of Varuṇa."
He discharged those waters and drank them back in the great ocean;
having become the great horse-headed one (Hayagrīva), as those who know the Vedas understand him,
he drinks the waters in the great ocean while vomiting that fire from his mouth.
"Therefore, may you be blessed; you ought not to destroy the worlds, O Parāśara, best among the wise, knowing the supreme duties.
The Gandharva said:

Thus addressed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, that brahmin-seer restrained his anger, which had been directed toward the destruction of all the worlds. And he, possessed of great splendor and the best among those who know all the Vedas, performed sacrifices.
Then the great sage Parāśara, the descendant of Śakti, performed a Rākṣasa-sacrifice; remembering the slaughter of Śakti, he consumed the Rākṣasas— both old and young— in that extended sacrifice.
Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him from the slaughter of the Rākṣasas, out of the firm resolve: "Let me not break his second vow.
At that sacrificial session, the great sage [performed] three fires.
He stood before the blazing [fires] like a fourth fire itself;
by that pure sacrifice being offered with proper ritual application,
the sky was illuminated as if by the sun at the end of the rainy season.
All the sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, perceived him there as a second sun blazing in the sky with his splendor. Then,
that sage of noble intellect [beheld] that which is otherwise extremely difficult for others to attain.
Desiring to complete the sacrificial session (*satra*), Atri approached him;
likewise, O slayer of enemies, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu also came to that great sacrifice out of a desire for the lives of the *rākṣasas*.
O bull of the Bharatas, O Pārtha, upon the slaughter of those Rākṣasas, Pulastya spoke these words to Parāśara, the subduer of enemies:
"My son, I hope there are no obstacles to your ascetic practice; I hope you are joyful, my child?"
"O best of Soma-drinkers, because of the slaughter of all these Rākṣasas who were ignorant and innocent, this total destruction of my progeny has occurred.
My dear son, this is not the dharma seen for ascetic twice-born men."
"Peace alone is the supreme dharma; practice that, O Parāśara. Being the most excellent of men, you act most unrighteously, O Parāśara.
Furthermore, O knower of dharma, it does not behove you to transgress your own power here."
And you ought not to bring about the destruction of my progeny in this way;
for by a curse or by Śakti, O son of Vasiṣṭha, that has already been brought to pass, since Śakti has been sent from here to heaven by his own wrathful son.
"O Sage, no *rākṣasa* whatsoever was able to devour him;
for he had himself become his own death, created by himself. Viśvāmitra and Parāśara were merely the instrumental causes in that matter."
The Vasiṣ�ṭhas were devoured by the Rākṣasa unleashed by Kauśika;
yet they did not utter a curse, for that which is their ultimate refuge is the weapon of speech. Being full of forbearance, they did not burn his body, as they indeed pass on to another body.
And King Kalmāṣapāda desires to ascend to heaven;
and those sons of the great sage Vasiṣṭha who were inferior in power—
they all, filled with joy, rejoice together with the gods.
"O great sage, all this was indeed known to Vasiṣṭha; O dear one, this destruction of the ascetic Rākṣasas has you as its instrumental cause here at this sacrifice, O joy of the Vasiṣṭhas."

"Relinquish the sacrificial session; may it be well with you; let this be completed for you. Thus addressed by Pulastya and the wise Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, the son of Śakti, then brought the sacrificial session to its conclusion.
The sage cast that fire— which had been gathered for a sacrifice against all *rākṣasas*—
into the great forest on the northern slope of the Himalayas. Even today,
it consumes there the *rākṣasas*, as well as trees and stones.
The fire-god was seen constantly devouring [the offerings] at every change of the moon; furthermore, that one of great splendor, desiring to slay Viśvāmitra, became a Gandharva.
The son of Śakti, a man of great asceticism, had kindled a terrible fire;
and that fire, kindled by the descendant of Vasiṣṭha, was swallowed up by the wise Skanda, who desired the welfare of Viśvāmitra, with his own splendor equal to that of fire.
Arjuna said:
For what reason did King Kalmāṣapāda employ his wife toward his preceptor, the best among those who know Brahman?

"O friend, knowing the supreme dharma that pertains to the world, why did that great-souled Vasiṣṭha engage in approaching one who should not be approached? Furthermore, O friend, what most unrighteous act was previously committed by Vasiṣṭha?"
"In this regard, a doubt has arisen in me concerning the determination of what ought and ought not to be done.
You should explain everything that was performed by him in the past, as I am asking you.
The Gandharva said:
"O Dhanañjaya, learn this which you ask me concerning Vasiṣṭha, that invincible king who endures his enemies. I have previously told you how that monarch was cursed."
O best of the Bharatas, by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha’s son Śakti,
that king, the scorcher of foes, fell under the power of a curse; with eyes clouded by anger, he departed from the city together with his wife.
Having gone to the deserted forest, he wandered about together with his wife;
it was filled with various herds of deer and teeming with diverse creatures,
covered with various shrubs and creepers, and surrounded by various trees.
Wandering through the forest of terrifying sounds, seized by a curse,
he once, overcome by hunger and searching for food for himself,
saw [it] at a certain forest waterfall while greatly distressed.

Seeing a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Brāhmaṇa man who had come together for sexual union, they both fled in terror, their purpose unfulfilled; and as they were running away, the king seized the Brāhmaṇa by force.
Seeing her husband captured, the Brahmin woman then spoke:
"Listen, O King, to my words which I shall say to you, O observer of noble vows;
for you are renowned throughout the world as one born of the Solar dynasty."
Vigilant, established in the Dharma, and devoted to serving his guru—
O protector of the earth, you are a Vaiṣṇava who increases the solar dynasty,
for by you, through auspicious deeds, Viṣṇu was formerly propitiated.

Having regarded yourself as a blade of grass and having offered your life to Hari, you were indeed protected at that time by the powerful Viṣṇu. O invincible one, you have received this curse; you ought not to commit further sin.
"Now that my season has arrived, I have come together with my husband today. For I have not yet fulfilled my purpose with my husband, and my need for offspring is great.
Be gracious, O best of kings; let this husband of mine be released."

While she was thus crying out, that perpetrator of a most cruel deed devoured her husband, as a tiger devours its desired prey. As she was overcome with rage, the tears that fell from her onto the ground—
That fire blazed up and illuminated that entire region. Then,
tormented by grief and distressed by the calamity that had befallen her husband,
the Brahmin woman cursed the royal seer Kalmāṣapāda in her rage.
"O base one,
because my illustrious husband, my lord, has been devoured by you today while I was looking on and my purpose remained unfulfilled, you too, O evil-minded one, shall be mangled by my curse."
"Having approached your wife during her season, you shall immediately lose your life. Being thus entreated by him, she then granted her favor;
for it was the wife of that seer Vasiṣṭha whose sons had been destroyed by you.

"Having united with him, your wife shall give birth to a son; that son, O lowest of kings, shall be the perpetuator of your lineage. Having thus cursed the king, that auspicious lady of the Aṅgiras clan departed.
In his very presence, [the sage] entered the blazing fire;
and the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha beheld all of this through his great yoga of knowledge and his ascetic power, O scorcher of foes.
Moreover, O mighty-armed one, no unrighteousness is incurred here when a Brāhmaṇa bestows his offspring upon one who has requested it. But when a man,
O King, approaches another's wife out of lust, [then he incurs sin].
Then, O King of kings, the fruit of unrighteousness spoken of regarding another's wife shall accrue to him; yet, O best of the twice-born, being free from deceit, he shall emerge from this,
for he is the teacher of the world, O best of the Bharatas.
Then, after a long time, the royal seer was released from the curse;
yet when he approached Madayantī during her fertile season, he was turned away by her,
for the king, deluded by the curse, did not remember it.
Then, having heard the words of the goddess and recollecting that curse, that best of kings was deeply distressed. For this reason, the king appointed Vasiṣṭha [to perform the sacrifice].
O best of the Bharatas, when Kalmāṣapāda, afflicted by the fault of a curse, attained the state of a Rākṣasa while with his own wife,
Vasiṣṭha was then invited by Kuru for the sake of a sacrifice.
When Kalmāṣapāda had cast off his state as a Rākṣasa,
he was then reconciled with King Vasiṣṭha;
thus, Vasiṣṭha became your domestic priest.
Arjuna said:
"O Gandharva, tell us of one who is worthy of us and learned in the Vedas as our domestic priest (purohita); for everything is known to you."
The Gandharva said:
"This is the younger brother of Devala; he is performing austerities in the forest at the sacred ford of Utkocaka. If you so desire, choose him as your priest."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Arjuna, being pleased, duly bestowed that Āgneya weapon upon the Gandharva and spoke these words.
"O best of Gandharvas, let the horses remain with you for now;
I shall take them at the time of action. May it be well with you," he said.
Then the Gandharva and the Pāṇḍavas, having honored one another, departed.
From the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī, they set out according to their desire.
Then, having gone to the holy ford of Utkocaka and to the hermitage of Dhaumya,
those Pāṇḍavas, O Bhārata, chose Dhaumya for the office of family priest.
Dhaumya, the best among those who know all the Vedas,
received them with water for their feet, fruits and roots, and by accepting the office of domestic priest.
Then the Pāṇḍavas hoped to regain their prosperity and their kingdom.

Placing that Brahmin at their head, those bulls of the Bharata race, accompanied by their mother as the sixth, then joined with that preceptor for the svayaṃvara of the princess of Pañcāla; they considered themselves as having found a protector.
For he, noble-minded and knowing the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas, was their preceptor;

by him, the knower of dharma and all things, the sons of Pṛthā were made his sacrificial patrons (yājya). Indeed, he considered those heroes to have already attained their kingdom through their own duty.
Endowed with intelligence, heroism, strength, and energy like other gods,
those lords of men, having had the rites for success performed by him,
then resolved together to go to that svayaṃvara of the princess of Pañcāla.
The illustrious Dhaumya, the best of the twice-born, was a knower of the Vedas and an eloquent speaker; in brilliance, intellect, beauty, fame, and splendor,
as well as in various sacred mantras, Dhaumya was equal to Bṛhaspati.
And that brahmin also considered them to be superior by nature on this earth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then those five Pāṇḍava brothers, tigers among men—
Assuming the forms of Brahmins, with matted hair and observing the vows of celibacy,
the sons of Pṛthā set out to see Draupadī and that great divine festival. Those tigers among men, the subduers of enemies, departed together with their mother.
On the road, they saw many Brahmins traveling in groups.
O King, those Brahmins said to the Pāṇḍavas, who were living as celibate students:
"Where are you going, and from where have you come?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"May you recognize these brothers who have come from Ekacakrā, who have beheld the gods, and who are traveling together with their mother."
The Brahmins said:
"Go this very day to the residence of Drupada in the land of the Pañcālas;
a great svayaṃvara, attended by many wealthy suitors, will take place there."
"We too are traveling along this same caravan, bound for that very place;
for there a truly magnificent festival will take place, resembling something miraculous.
It concerns the daughter of the high-souled Drupada, Yajñasena."
Born from the center of the sacrificial altar, with eyes like lotus petals,
beautiful, with faultless limbs, delicate and high-minded—
she was the sister of the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the enemy of Droṇa.
He who was born already clad in armor, bearing a sword, arrows, and a bow—
the mighty-armed one, radiant as fire— appeared in the well-kindled sacrificial fire;
and at the moment of his birth, an incorporeal voice spoke:
This disciple and this Death are born of Bharadvāja;
his sister is the faultless-limbed Draupadī of slender waist,
whose fragrance, like that of a blue lotus, wafts for a *krośa*.
"Let us go to see that daughter of Yajñasena, who has set the time for her *svayaṃvara*, and to behold that great divine festival;
[there will be] kings and princes who have performed sacrifices and given abundant sacrificial fees."

Devoted to sacred study, pure, high-souled, and firm in their vows; young, handsome, and hailing from various lands— great chariot-warriors skilled in weapons, these rulers of the earth shall assemble there.
There, those lords of men will bestow various gifts for the sake of victory— wealth, cattle, and all kinds of food and drink.
Having accepted all that and having witnessed the svayaṃvara itself, [he shall depart].
Having enjoyed the festival, we shall depart as we desire. Actors, bards, dancers, sūtas, māgadhas,
and mighty wrestlers from various lands will also assemble there.
Having thus satisfied your curiosity, having seen [us], and having received [our hospitality],
you high-souled ones shall return again with us,
seeing all of you standing there, beautiful to behold and possessing the forms of gods.
"Having observed [the suitors], Kṛṣṇā shall choose one of the suitors as her husband. This brother of yours is illustrious, handsome, and mighty-armed;
by engaging in combat, he may win great wealth."
"Surely, by bringing this [news], he will increase your joy.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O venerable one, we shall go to see that great festival of the gods."
"All of you together with me shall attend that svayaṃvara of the maiden.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Janamejaya, having been thus addressed, those Pāṇḍavas set out."
Then, O King, those Pāṇḍavas beheld on the road that high-souled, pure-minded, and sinless Dvaipāyana, who was being escorted by King Drupada from the southern Pañcāla country.
Having offered him due hospitality and being comforted by him,
they were granted leave at the conclusion of their conversation and set out for Drupada’s abode,
beholding delightful forests and lakes along the way.
Dwelling here and there, those great chariot-warriors proceeded slowly;
devoted to sacred study, pure, sweet-natured, and pleasant of speech,
the descendants of Kuru reached the Pañcāla country in due course.
Having seen that city and the military encampment, the Pāṇḍavas then took up residence in the workshop of a potter; there,
adhering to the Brahmanical way of life, they collected alms.
And when those heroes had arrived, no men anywhere recognized them.
But Yajñasena of the Pañcālas, realizing that he himself was guilty toward Bhīṣma and Droṇa, then began the appropriate rites for his own protection.

Having obtained Dhṛṣṭadyumna, he no longer thought of Droṇa; and because of his involvement in the enmity with his son, he did not fear Bhīṣma. However, that lord of the earth considered the giving away of his daughter to be his refuge.

Because of his alliance with the strength of his son-in-law, he considered himself even more powerful. Yet, although Yajñasena always desired to give Kṛṣṇā to the diadem-wearing Pāṇḍava, he did not reveal this intention.
O Janamejaya, while that Pāñcālya was searching for the sons of Kuntī,
he recalled that a boon had been granted to him by the high-souled Śaṅkara when he was pleased;
having reached the conclusion that "it shall not be fruitless for me," he took it as authoritative.

"Now I must perform this difficult feat of piercing the target," he resolved in his mind; having so decided, O Bhārata, he caused an excellent target to be prepared and had a firm bow made that could not be drawn.
Vaiyāghrapadya brought forth that formidable bow named Kiṃdhura, which had been given by the gods, belonging to Sṛñjaya, the lord of the earth;
its string was made of iron and was exceedingly powerful.
But no other bow could withstand that great and excellent bow;
moreover, he had a mechanical device fashioned in the air,
and with that machine, the king [set up] a golden target.
Drupada said:
"Having strung this bow and, with these arrows,
having pierced the target beyond it— he who does so shall win my daughter."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus King Drupada caused a proclamation to be made everywhere. Having heard that, O Bhārata, all the kings assembled there.
And the high-souled sages came out of a desire to witness the *svayaṃvara*,
as did the Yādavas— the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis— along with Vāsudeva;
and kings and princes, young men wearing polished earrings.
The lords of various kingdoms were performers of sacrifices who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees;
they possessed charming forms and beauty, and their prowess was equal to that of Mahendra. In anger they were like fire, yet in forbearance they were equal to the earth.
Steadfast as Mount Meru, wise, and comparable to the sun and fire— those kings upon the earth and the sages whose wealth is asceticism—
all have assembled here, with the exception of children and the elderly.
O King, all the gods of the Thirty-three, stationed in their celestial chariots in the sky,
as well as the Kurus led by Duryodhana and including Karṇa,
and highly fortunate Brāhmaṇas arrived from various lands.
Those hosts of kings, having been honored by the high-souled Drupada,
sat down together with the Brahmins; and so did the Pāṇḍavas, along with the bards, dancers, heralds, chroniclers, and panegyrists.
Seated upon thrones, they were eager to witness the *svayaṃvara*.
Then all the citizens, their voices raised like the roar of the ocean,
reached Śiśumārapura, and those kings took their seats.
To the northeast of the city, on a level and auspicious plot of ground,
the assembly grove shone, surrounded on all sides by dwellings;
it was provided with walls and moats, and adorned with gates and archways.
It was covered everywhere with a variegated canopy,
filled with the sounds of hundreds of musical instruments, perfumed with the finest aloe-wood incense,
sprinkled with sandalwood water, and adorned with garlands of flowers.
It was enclosed on all sides by well-constructed, lofty palaces that resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, scraping the surface of the sky;
they were draped with golden lattices and adorned with floors of inlaid jewels.
With stairways easy to ascend, furnished with great seats and coverings, draped with exquisite fabrics, perfumed with the finest aloe-wood,
white as the color of swans, and fragrant for many yojanas;
Adorned with couches and seats, featuring hundreds of unobstructed doors,
and with their parts inlaid with many minerals like the peaks of the Himalayas—
there, in those various kinds of celestial palaces, they were beautifully adorned.
Then all the kings, vying with one another, took their seats. There they saw those lions among kings, highly fortunate and possessed of great courage and prowess, adorned with black aloe-wood paste.

The people of the city and the countryside sat upon most excellent platforms— men of great devotion, devoted to Brahmins, protectors of their own kingdom, dear to all the world because of their auspicious and well-performed deeds.
For the sake of finding Draupadī and out of joy at her discovery, they sat down together on all sides; those Pāṇḍavas sat down accompanied by the Brāhmaṇas,
beholding that unsurpassed prosperity of the King of Pañcāla.
Then, O King, that assembly continued for many days,
abounding in the distribution of jewels and graced by actors and dancers. While this delightful assembly was proceeding on the sixteenth day—

In the auspicious hour of Maitra, the royal wives, who were conversant with ancient lore and possessed sons, dressed in fine garments and adorned themselves with ornaments; they prepared a golden vessel, silk cloth, and *dūrvā* grass together with the ingredients for the ritual success.

Having set aside the oil for the purpose of bathing, the young women, beloved of Hari, took the oil for anointing prepared with a paste of *lodhra*, as well as *kāleyaka* and sandalwood; then the women led her, facing the four-cornered bath-platform, toward the ritual ablution.

Then they bathed Draupadī, who was seated upon a pedestal of lapis lazuli, with water contained in golden jars accompanied by the sound of musical instruments; and once her ablutions were completed, she was dressed in two silken garments.
The delighted female adorners, their eyes wide with wonder, led her to a well-prepared altar supported by jeweled pillars; having seated her facing the east,
they looked at one another, wondering, "By what cause has she come to this?"
Dispelling the moisture from her hair with the heat of incense smoke, they bound her braided hair (dhammilla) with fragrant garlands;
they placed in her hand a wreath fashioned of *dūrvā* grass and madhūka flowers.
And they fashioned leaf-designs with black aloe-wood upon her two breasts;
she shone like the excellent, long river of gold (the Gaṅgā) marked by the *cakravāka* birds.
With her curling locks of hair, her blossoming face gleamed.
That flower, with a bee clinging to it, surpassed the orb of the moon;
they applied black collyrium to their eyes for the sake of propriety,
and adorned themselves as was fitting with ornaments inlaid with gems.
And her mother, taking yellow orpiment and red arsenic with her two fingers, applied a tilaka mark upon her face. Seeing the bride thus adorned, the women were filled with joy.
Her mother did not rejoice, wondering, "What will her husband be like? Then,
at the command of Drupada, the chamberlains approached and caused her to mount a female elephant adorned with a rich housings.
Then auspicious musical instruments were sounded, reaching toward the heavens;
and a group of graceful women, singing auspicious songs, proceeded on both sides with a preeminent hundred female elephants.
Attentive attendants went before him to clear the way of people;
at that time, a great clamor arose in that excellent city.
O Bhārata, Dhṛṣṭadyumna went at the head, having mounted his horse.
Drupada, joined by a great force,
stood upon the arena ground after having arrayed his vast army, which was protected by firm bowmen. As that lady of beautiful limbs approached, the best of kings sat upon their thrones.
Upon seeing her, they were indeed possessed by the god of love and displayed various amorous gestures.
One of them repeatedly twirled a most enchanting lotus,
its petals fluttering, its bees moving, and its filaments curled around.

A certain playful man, turning his lotus-face sideways, took a necklace that had slipped off and caught on the tips of his armlets and placed it upon his shoulder; he then scratched the golden footstool with his toe, which was illuminated by the oblique radiance of his face.
Another man, though he was skilled in drawing auspicious lines with the tips of his nails, tore the *ketakī* petal— a beloved ornament for the ear— with those very nails.
Another, with a hand marked by the *svastika*, used a nail as red as a lotus to do the same.
The wise man cast down the dice with the radiance of his jewel-ring;
just as his stainless light moved from its place,
so did someone manipulate the jewel-ring upon his hand.
There, the lotus-eyed Draupadī gazed upon such sights in great abundance, as if she were creating a region composed entirely of blue lotuses;
her limbs bathed, dressed in fine garments, and adorned with every ornament.
Taking up a hero’s brass vessel adorned with gold,
Draupadī then descended onto the arena, O bull of the Bharatas; meanwhile,
the pure Brahmin priest of the Somakas, learned in the sacred mantras, [stood ready].
Having strewn the sacrificial ground, he then offered oblations of clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rite.
Having satisfied the blazing fire and caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings,
he caused all musical instruments to cease on every side.
O lord of the people, when that silence had been established, Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
whose voice resounded like a cloud or a drum, took Kṛṣṇā according to the prescribed rites and,
standing in the midst of the arena, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
He spoke these words aloud—smooth, meaningful, and excellent:
"Here is the bow, here is the target, and here are the arrows;
let all the kings hear me!"
"Passing through the aperture of the machine,
you must strike the target with five arrows.
He who accomplishes this most difficult task— "
Endowed with noble lineage, beauty, and strength— his wife today shall be this sister of mine,
Kṛṣṇā; I speak not falsely.
Having spoken thus to them, the son of Drupada then addressed Draupadī by name, by lineage, and by her deeds:
Proclaiming the names of those assembled kings,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna said:
"Duryodhana, Durviṣaha, Durmukha, and Duṣpradharṣaṇa."
Viviṃśati, Vikarṇa, Sahadeva, Duḥśāsana, Sama, Yuyutsu, Vātavega, Bhīmavegadhara,
Ugrāyudha, Balākī, Kanakāyu, and Virocana.
Sukuṇḍala, Citrasena, Suvarcā, Kanakadhvaja,
Nandaka, Bāhuśālī, Kuṇḍaja, Vikaṭa, as well as Vinda, Anuvinda, Sajīvī, Vikala, and Karī.
These and many other mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
heroic warriors accompanied by Karṇa, have assembled for your sake;
they are high-souled, numbering in the hundreds, and renowned as the bulls among the Kṣatriyas.
Śakuni, Bala, Vṛṣaka, and Bṛhadbala—
all these sons of the king of Gāndhāra have assembled here;
as well as Aśvatthāman and the Bhoja, both of whom are the foremost among all wielders of weapons.
These two high-souled ones have assembled for your sake, fully adorned:
Bṛhanta and Maṇimān, the heroic Daṇḍadhāra,
Sahadeva, Jayatsena, and Meghasaṃdhi the Māgadha.
Virāṭa, together with his two sons Śaṅkha and Uttara;
Vārdhakṣemi, Suvarcā, and King Senābindu; Abhibhū with his son Sudāmā and Suvarcas.
Sumitra, Sukumāra, Vṛka, and likewise Satyadhṛti; Sūryadhvaja, Rocamāna, Nīla, and Citrāyudha;
Aṃśumat, Cekitāna, and the mighty Śreṇimān.
And the powerful Candrasena, son of Samudrasena; Jalasandha and his son; Sudaṇḍa and Daṇḍa;
Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva; and the heroic Bhagadatta.
Kaliṅga and Tāmralipta, the lord of Pattana;
likewise Śalya, the king of Madra and a great car-warrior, together with his son,
along with the hero Rukmāṅgada and Rukmaratha.
Kauravya Somadatta and his sons, those great car-warriors— the three heroes Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala—
as well as Sudakṣiṇa the Kamboja and Dṛḍhadhanvan the Kaurava, have all assembled together.
Bṛhadbala, Suṣeṇa, Śibi the son of Uśīnara,
the slayer of the Paṭaccaras, and likewise the lord of the Kārūṣas— the three lords of the Pāṇḍyas, Keralas, and Colas, like the three sacrificial fires.
Seated upon their thrones, they shine resplendent, having taken refuge in the lineage of Agastya:
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, and the heroic son of Rukmiṇī;
as well as Sāmba, Cārudeṣṇa, Sāraṇa, and Gada.
Akrūra, Sātyaki, and the mighty Uddhava; Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika, Pṛthu, and Vipṛthu;
Viḍūratha, Kaṅka, Samīka, and Sāramejaya.
O Kṛṣṇa, know quickly that those others who are Yādavas have likewise arrived for your sake,
as well as Kṛtavarman, the son of Hṛdika.
Śaṅku, Sagaveṣaṇa, Āśāvaha, Aniruddha,
Vīra, Vātapati, Jhillī, and Piṇḍāraka as well.
The valiant Uśīnara and the Vṛṣṇis are thus celebrated;
