as well as Bhagīratha, Bṛhatkṣatra, Jayadratha the king of the Sindhus,
Bṛhadratha, Bāhlika, and the great car-warrior Śrutāyus.
King Ulūka Kaitava, Citrāṅgada and Śubhāṅgada, the resolute Vatsarāja, the lord of Kosala,
and the heroic Karṇa together with his son Vṛṣasena.
And the powerful Bṛhadbala, and King Durjaya,
and the mighty Śiśupāla, the son of Damaghoṣa—
the heroic and powerful lord of the Cedis, who is like Death itself.
The lords of the earth from the east, the north, the west, and the south— Śiśupāla, the valiant, and likewise Jarāsaṃdha;
these and many other rulers of various realms.
"O blessed lady, these kṣatriyas renowned throughout the earth have come for your sake. These valiant men shall seek the supreme target on your behalf;
O auspicious one, choose today him who pierces this mark."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Adorned with earrings, those youths gathered together, vying with one another.
Considering themselves to possess both weapons and strength,
they all rose up out of egoism,
[priding themselves] on their appearance, heroism, and lineage.
By virtue of their wealth and their youth,
they were puffed up with pride and shattered by the force of intoxication,
like the rutting lordly elephants of the Himalayas.
Gazing at one another with rivalry,
their limbs overwhelmed even by the power of thought,
they cried out, "Kṛṣṇā is mine!"
From their royal thrones,
those assembled Kṣatriyas suddenly rose up, having entered the arena and desiring to win that daughter of Drupada.
They shone like the assembled hosts of gods gazing upon Umā, the daughter of the King of Mountains,
their limbs tormented by the arrows of Kandarpa.
With their hearts fixed on Kṛṣṇā, those lords of men entered the arena for the sake of Drupada’s daughter;
there, they treated even their friends as enemies.
Then the hosts of gods arrived in their celestial chariots—
the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and the two Aśvins—
as well as all the Sādhyas and the Maruts.
Placing Yama and Dhaneśvara at their head,
the Daityas, Suparṇas, and Mahoragas,
as well as the celestial sages, Guhyakas, and Cāraṇas [followed].
Viśvāvasu, Nārada, and Parvata, as well as the chief Gandharvas together with the Apsarases, were there,
along with Halāyudha and Keśava.
The Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas,
those preeminent bulls among the Yadus, looked on and remained steadfast in the counsel of Kṛṣṇa.
For he saw them, possessing the forms of great rutting elephant-kings like five lordly tuskers with their trunks upraised,
resembling sacrificial fires whose bodies were covered in ashes.
That hero of the Yadus turned his thoughts toward the sons of Pṛthā and spoke of Yudhiṣṭhira,
Bhīma, Jiṣṇu, and the two heroic twins to Rāma.
Gazing at them very slowly, Rāma,
with a joyful heart, beheld Janārdana;
others, however, were the sons and grandsons of various kings.
With their eyes and minds drawn toward Kṛṣṇa,
they watched her as she whirled about, striving with effort,
her copper-colored face baring her teeth.
In the same way, all those sons of Pṛthā with their broad arms,
and the two heroic twins of great majesty,
having then beheld that Draupadī—
All the gods, together with their hosts, having assembled, were struck by the arrows of Kandarpa;
even the Vasus and the Aśvins were desirous of beholding her.
The Rudras, Soma, Varuṇa, and Yama,
placing Śakra at their head, as well as Dhaneśvara,
Viśvāvasu, Nārada, and Parvata.
The celestial sages and hosts of apsarases were there;
it was crowded with divine sages and gandharvas,
and frequented by suparṇas, nāgas, asuras, and siddhas.
It was filled with divine fragrance and strewn with celestial garlands,
while the great sounds of drums resounded.
The sky became crowded with that [host],
filled on all sides with a throng of celestial chariots,
and resounded with the music of flutes, lutes, and drums.
Then those hosts of kings, standing upon the assembly grounds like clouds thundering on all sides, proceeded in due order.
O King, for the sake of Kṛṣṇā,
Karṇa, Duryodhana, Śālva, Śalya, the son of Droṇa, Krātha, Sunītha, and Vakra exerted their prowess.
The lords of Kaliṅga, Vaṅga, Pāṇḍya, and Pauṇḍra; the king of Videha and the sovereign of the Yavanas;
and various other sons and grandsons of kings.
The lords of the realm, with eyes like lotus petals,
their broad arms adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, and bracelets;
Endowed with successive valor and courage, roaring with strength and vigor,
they [approached] that bow which was possessed of firm construction.
Though they exerted themselves with great force, those lords of men were unable to string the bow, as it was being pulled by its firm, throbbing power.
Lying upon the surface of the earth, writhing about,
they appeared wretched and broken in spirit;
their vigor gone, their crowns and necklaces had fallen away.
Sighing deeply, they became composed;
the daughter of the Pāñcāla king, of noble form, having witnessed the agitation caused by the bow along with her companions.
With the corners of her eyes dancing with playful grace, she laughed at those kings of great prowess;
then, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose because of that firm bow.
With their armlets and earrings crushed and broken,
and their resolve turned back for the sake of Kṛṣṇā,
that circle of kings was then in a state of distress.
Having surveyed all those kings, Karṇa,
the foremost of archers,
quickly raised his uplifted bow and advanced.
He quickly strung it and fixed the arrows; seeing the charioteer, the sons of Pāṇḍu thought that the excellent target had been pierced and brought down to the earth.
Seeing that archer, who had made a vow out of passion,
who surpassed Agni, Soma, and Arka, and was moreover the son of the Sun,
Draupadī spoke these words aloud:
"I do not choose the charioteer," he said,
looking at the Sun with a scornful laugh; then Karṇa cast aside that quivering bow.
When those Kṣatriyas had thus retreated from all sides,
the heroic and powerful lord of the Cedis,
the son of Damaghoṣa, the wise and great-minded Śiśupāla— resembling Death himself— [advanced].
Taking up the bow, he fell to the ground upon his knees;
then King Jarāsaṃdha, of great heroism and immense strength,
approached the vicinity of the bow and stood firm like an immovable mountain.
But being struck by the bow, he fell to the earth upon his knees;
then, rising up, that king returned to his own kingdom.
Then Śalya, the king of Madra, possessed of great heroism and immense strength—
Even as he was being lifted up, he fell to the earth on his knees;
struck by the tip of the bow, he fell face-down upon the ground.
Due to his fury, the other kings, overcome with fear, retreated to a distance of one *krośa*.
Then Karna Vaikartana, the son of a Suta and a true bull among men,
struck the bowstring at the very tip of a single hair as it was being drawn. He,
with his conch-like neck and broad shoulders, possessed the prowess of an elephant in rut.
With eyes as copper-red as an elephant in rut and possessing the speed of an elephant in rut,
Karṇa— the conqueror of the three worlds and renowned throughout the three worlds for his courage— struck the bow being strung at a distance of only a mustard seed.
"He too was shaken off by the bow"— thus all were overwhelmed with fear.
When Karṇa had been thus shaken off by the bow,
the other excellent kings could not even look with their eyes, their lotus-like faces cast down.
Seeing Karṇa cast down, those world-heroes, the best of kings,
became hopeless both regarding the lifting of the bow and the winning of Draupadī.
Then King Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and scorcher of his foes—
Proud, possessed of firm weapons, and endowed with all the marks of royalty,
that mighty one suddenly rose up there in the midst of his brothers;
beholding Draupadī, he approached the vicinity of the bow with joy.
Taking up the bow, he shone like Śakra bearing his own bow;
he then strung it and struck it with a mere sesame seed.
As that bow was being strung by the powerful king, it then [broke].
He did not fall from his standing position; though struck on the tip of his finger, he departed like a king feeling ashamed, having been struck by him.
Then, as he was being lifted up, [the other] struck him when he was only the size of a mung bean.
He fell from the arena to the earth at a distance of half a yojana;
in that same manner, he returned to his own kingdom, never looking back.
Then Karna, the son of Vaikartana, the bull-like delight of the Sūtas—
Having approached the vicinity of the bow, he took up that bow;
and as it was being strung, he struck it at the very tip of a single hair.
Then [he stood] as the most excellent among the gods and the Dānavas.
The noble-minded hero of the Vṛṣṇi clan rejoiced, as he grasped the hand of Rāma,
perceiving that he had come into the hand of the son of Pāṇḍu.
The other leading heroes among kings did not recognize the sons of Pāṇḍu, who were disguised in their forms,
except for Bhīṣma and the two foremost heroes of the Yadus.
And Dhaumya, Dharma,
and his brothers, while that assembly was in a state of agitation and the lords of men had ceased their debate.
Kuntī’s son Jiṣṇu, that hero, desired to string that bow and fix an arrow upon it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the kings had desisted from the act of stringing the bow,
King Yudhiṣṭhira then gave an order to Arjuna by means of a sign; and the wise Dharmarāja’s intention having been understood, [Arjuna acted].
Then Jiṣṇu, of noble intellect, rose up from the midst of the Brahmins. As that foremost of the Pāṇḍavas descended into the center of the arena, the chief Brahmins cried out, shaking their deerskins.
Seeing Pārtha set forth, radiant like the banner of Indra,
some were despondent while others were filled with joy; and some among them, who were skillful and lived by their intellect, spoke to one another.

"How could that [bow], which was not bent even by world-renowned kings led by Karṇa and Śalya— men who were powerful and devoted to the science of archery— be bent by you, who are unskilled in weapons and weaker than them in strength?"
"O twice-born ones, it is indeed possible for a mere boy to string this bow;
but if he has strung it, how could he possibly hit the target? The Brahmins will become objects of ridicule among all the kings."
If this task remains unaccomplished due to his fickleness and lack of deliberation—
whether he has set out to draw his bow out of pride, rashness, or the mere restlessness of a youth— he should be properly restrained; let him not go.
"We shall not become objects of ridicule, nor shall we fall into contempt; nor shall we incur the enmity of the rulers of the earth. Some said, "Victory is ours; there is victory, no defeat."
"Whether there be defeat or victory, O twice-born ones, he would string his bow.
Some say he is a youth of glorious splendor, with arms like the trunk of a Naga king; with broad shoulders, thighs, and arms, he is like the Himalayas in steadfastness."

With the playful gait of a lion, glorious, and possessing the prowess of an elephant in rut, this deed is worthy of him; it is inferred from his enthusiasm. His power is great and full of energy, for one who is powerless would not go forth of his own accord.
There is no action whatsoever in the worlds that cannot be accomplished by Brāhmaṇas who move within the three orders of life;
they subsist on water, subsist on air, or feed on fruits, remaining firm in their vows.
For the weak are indeed stronger than the strong, for the Brahmins possess the splendor of Brahman.
A Brahmin must not be treated with contempt, whether he behaves rightly or wrongly; whatever karma has come upon him, whether it be great or small, it brings both happiness and suffering.
The Kṣatriyas on earth were conquered by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni;
the unfathomable ocean was drunk up by Agastya through the power of his Brahmanic luster.
Therefore, let everyone here say: "This boy possesses a great bow."
"Let him be placed [upon the funeral pyre] quickly! "So be it," said the bulls among the twice-born.
Formerly, Vātāpi, who caused the increase and depletion of barren women, was devoured by the high-souled Bhṛgu, who turned the fire into a consumer of all things.
In the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), in the Vedas, and in various forms of yoga,
I do not see anyone on this earth who would be superior to a Brāhmaṇa,
whether by the power of mantras and yoga or by great personal strength.
"O best of the twice-born, they might even cause this world or that one to tremble.
While those brahmins were thus uttering various lamentations,
Arjuna stood near his bow, as immovable as a mountain.
While the son of Indra, Arjuna— the best of the Pāṇḍavas— was listening to all of them, he then spoke to Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"Is this bow of the Brahmins capable of being strung?"
Having heard those words of his, Dhṛṣṭadyumna spoke these words:
"Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra—
whosoever among these, O best of the twice-born, can string this most excellent bow."
"To him my sister shall be given; truly have I spoken these words.
Having heard those words of his, he set out, surrounded by brahmins;
following behind him was the son of Pāṇḍu, possessed of great splendor and invincible in battle.
Having circumambulated that bow clockwise, the scorcher of enemies, filled with joy, bowed his head in reverence and took up the bow of the Lord Īśāna,
the giver of boons.
And having fixed his mind upon Kṛṣṇa, [he beheld] that which was done by the kings Rukma, Sunītha, Vakra,
the son of Rādhā (Karṇa), Duryodhana, Śalya, and Śālva.
Then, although it was attempted with great effort by those lions among men who were experts in the science of archery, they could not string it;
yet Arjuna, full of pride, [strung it]— he of all the heroic ones.
Then Aindra, possessing the power of Indra’s younger brother,
strung his bow within the blink of an eye and took up five arrows.
He pierced the target, and it fell,
suddenly shot through with a hole into the earth;
then a roar arose in the sky.
And a great roar arose in the midst of the assembly;
the god rained down divine flowers upon the head of Pārtha, the slayer of his enemies.
Then the disciples raised their garments on all sides and let out cries of "Alas!
Alas! They rejoiced and danced there, waving fans, dancing before the kings and displaying the row of brahmins.
Roaring and laughing, with matted hair as yellow as lightning, they descended from the sky on all sides; and showers of flowers fell there,
while musicians played upon hundreds of lutes and instruments.
And there, throngs of bards and panegyrists with melodious voices offered praise.
Seeing him, Drupada, the slayer of enemies, became filled with joy;
together with his army, he desired to provide assistance to the son of Pṛthā.
When that great noise had arisen,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the best among the upholders of dharma,
quickly went to his dwelling.
Having observed the target pierced by the two Yamas, those best of men, and having beheld Pārtha who resembled Śakra, Kṛṣṇā [was filled with wonder].
While Arjuna looked on with joy and as many people watched, the Goddess threw it around his neck;
though her form was ever perfectly familiar to him, she appeared to him as if newly manifest.
Though without laughter, she seems to laugh through her radiance; though without intoxication, she seems to stumble through her gestures;
and though without speech, she seems to speak through her gaze.
Taking up a beautiful white garland of flowers,
she went toward the son of Kuntī with a smile;
that floral wreath [she placed] in the midst of the lords of the earth.
At that moment, she placed it around his neck;
afterwards, having gone and observed it, Kṛṣṇā fearlessly fastened it upon Pārtha’s chest.
Having cast it into the midst of that assembly of kings,
she chose Agni as her husband from among the heroes of the twice-born, just as Śacī chose the Lord of the Gods.
Like Svāhā to Lakṣmī, as immeasurable as the dawn to the sun, like Rati to Madana,
and like the daughter of the mountain king to Maheśvara.
Just as the princess of Mithilā [Sītā] toward Rāma,
and just as Damayantī toward Nala, the best of kings,
she approached him and cast her gaze upon him with affection.
Having placed the garland before the assembled kings with humility,
the king’s daughter suddenly withdrew from the monarch and stood there.
Having taken her and having triumphed in the arena,
he of inconceivable deeds emerged from the arena while being honored by those twice-born men.
Followed by his wife,
Vaiśampāyana said:
"As he was about to give his daughter to that high-souled Brāhmaṇa..."
Anger arose among the kings as they looked at one another from close by:
"Passing us by and treating our assembled company as mere straw,
this man wishes to give Draupadī, the best of women, to a brahmin!"
180.002d*1855_01 Disregarding his old age here, Kālikā is cast down.
180.002d*1856_01 But having planted a tree here, it is felled at the time of its fruiting.
180.002d*1857_01 The spotted deer should be disregarded; by that high-souled one, his task shall be accomplished.
"Let us slay this evil-souled one who does not respect us;
for he does not deserve honor, nor does he merit precedence among the elders by virtue of his qualities. Let us kill this man of wicked conduct along with his son, for he is a hater of kings."
For he, having summoned all these lords of men and honored them, and having fed them with excellent food, subsequently reviles them in this assembly of kings,
which is like a gathering of the gods.
"Has he not seen any king at all who is his equal? Furthermore, Brahmins have no authority regarding the act of choosing a bride;
it is a well-known tradition that the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice) belongs to Kṣatriyas."
"Or rather, if this maiden does not desire anyone here,
let us cast her into the fire and depart for our kingdoms, O lords of the earth.
Or perhaps a Brahmin has done this out of childishness or greed."
"He must not be killed under any circumstances, for he has displeased the lords of the earth; indeed,
our kingdom, our lives, our wealth, our sons, our grandsons, and whatever other riches we possess exist solely for the sake of the Brahmins."
"Out of fear of dishonor, for the sake of protecting our own dharma,
and so that other self-choice marriages (*svayaṃvara*) may not meet with such a fate," having said this, those tigers among kings, whose arms were like iron maces, were filled with joy.

Desiring to seize Drupada, they rushed forward armed with weapons. Seeing those kings approaching in a rage, carrying their quivers and bows, Drupada, out of sheer terror, sought refuge with the Brahmins.

Neither out of fear, nor out of meanness, nor for the sake of protecting his own life did Drupada flee from the brahmins; seeking peace, he submitted to them. But as they rushed forward with speed like elephants in rut with temples bursting, [he stood his ground].

The two sons of Pāṇḍu, of great heroism and subduers of their enemies, advanced against them. Then those kings, with weapons raised and their hands encased in leather guards and finger-protectors, sprang up.
Desiring to slay the two sons of the Kuru king and unable to endure Arjuna and Bhīmasena,
Bhīma— whose deeds and prowess were marvelous— then [acted].
Possessing great strength and valor equal to a thunderbolt,
that solitary hero uprooted the tree with his two arms and stripped it of its leaves,
just as a lordly elephant does.
Taking up that tree like the King of the Ancestors (Yama) wielding his fierce staff, the crusher of enemies stood near that bull among men.
The son of Pṛthā, whose arms were broad and long, spoke to Pārtha;
Bhīma said:
"O kings, if there is nothing at all that brings glory to the earth..."

Why did that desire arise in the son of Pṛṣata toward the daughter? And how did that desire come to be produced, or how did it arrive? And why was there such a persistent attachment to the bow, which is dearer to him than life itself?
Whose preceptor was not Droṇa in archery? May it be well with Devavrata!
This Lord of the Kurus has grown lax in his practice due to the distractions arising from prosperity.
O Karṇa and the others, listen quickly to the sweet words of this Brāhmaṇa!

Let Rādhā set up the mechanical device again; though it has been pierced, let it be as if unpierced. In the meantime, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) also went there and, in an instant, learned that Kuntī was well.
Having arrived, that foremost of heroes stood together with his two brothers, those bulls among men;
then Jishnu, of noble deeds, spoke.
Do not let out lion-roars here before your ancestors;
do not display ferocity in the midst of the enemy. First, fight as a common soldier, O noble one.
Beholding that deed, Jiṣṇu, possessed of superhuman intellect and of inconceivable actions,
was struck with wonder and cast off all fear.
He stood holding his bow, performing deeds like those of Mahendra.
Beholding that feat of Jiṣṇu, whose intellect is superhuman and whose actions are inconceivable, [Arjuna] stood with his brother.
Dāmodara spoke these words to his brother Halāyudha of fierce valor:
"This one who moves with the gait of a rutting bull— "
He draws a great bow as long as a palm tree;
this is Arjuna, there is no doubt about it—
if I am indeed Vāsudeva, O Saṃkarṣaṇa.
He who, having swiftly uprooted this tree,
has suddenly returned from the royal palace— Vṛkodara, no one else here could have done this today.
He who was formerly on earth a mortal subject to human laws— lotus-eyed, slender, with the gait of a great lion, and humble— is now capable of acting [thus].
O Acyuta, that fair-complexioned Dharmarāja, with his long, radiant, and beautiful nose, has emerged;
he who is like two Kumāras, the two Kārttikeyas.
"It is my conviction that the two sons of Aśvinī have escaped from that fire in the house of lac; for I heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu and Pṛthā were saved."
To him, who resembled a cloud free from impurity, Halāyudha, being pleased, spoke to his younger brother:
"I am delighted; by good fortune, our paternal aunt is here."
Why do you sit here, O Puruṣottama, together with the foremost of the Kauravas, even though Pṛthā has been liberated?
Come and fight so that they may not overbear us.
Just as kings [surrounded] the Pāṇḍava in the midst of battle,
then the wielder of the discus, Halāyudha, the Supreme Person, knowing his strength, spoke to him.
O noble one, you need not be anxious;
Bhīma’s younger brother is capable of fighting alone against many gods and asuras, O Pārtha.
Enough with conquering mere human kings!
O hero, if Savyasācin desires our assistance, let us exert ourselves.
"The sons of Pāṇḍu do not suffer defeat.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Shaking off their deerskins and water-pots, those bulls among the twice-born..."
They said to him, "Fear not; we shall fight the enemies.
To those Brahmins speaking thus, Arjuna, as if laughing, replied, "Stand aside as spectators."

"I shall ward off these enraged men with hundreds of straight-pointed arrows, just as one restrains venomous serpents with mantras. Having said this, the great chariot-warrior took up that bow which he had obtained as his bride-price.
Accompanied by his brother Bhīma, he stood firm like an immovable mountain. There,
a battle took place between those two and the valiant bulls among Kṣatriyas,
as well as the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, like the conflict between Viṣṇu and Vāsava.
With falling trees Bhīmasena and with nets of arrows Dhanañjaya struck down those foremost of men who stood there in front;
then Vṛkodara, with his right hand grasped, [felled them as well].
Performing a marvel, he struck down heroes with a tree using his left hand;
he slew elephant with elephant, supreme chariot with chariot,
horse with horse, and likewise man with man.
Having seen that most wonderful sight, they all stood at a distance;
then Śalya, seeing that the mace was not like a tree,
engaged in hand-to-hand combat with that mighty one.
Then those two, fearless as elephants encountering rival elephants, rushed toward those enraged Kṣatriyas led by Karṇa who had risen up in fury.
And those kings, desiring to slay him, spoke harsh words.
"For even the killing of a twice-born man is seen [permissible] in battle when he desires to fight.
Having spoken thus, the kings suddenly rushed toward the twice-born.
Then Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, advanced against Arjuna with vigor.
Like an elephant seeking battle for the sake of a female,
the powerful Śalya, lord of the Madras, advanced against Bhīmasena;
Duryodhana went against Dharmarāja, and Nakula went against Śakuni.
Duḥśāsana advanced against Sahadeva, that best among victors who strikes with the form of a god, like fire covered by ashes;
indeed, no one mounted a horse, an elephant, or even a chariot.
All the foot soldiers fought back against their enemies;
there, Karṇa encountered Arjuna, the son of Pṛthā, who was moving in disguise,
while Duryodhana and the others were joined together with the Brahmins.

Then, in that battle, they fought back with ease and without effort, beginning gently. Thereupon, the wise Arjuna, having drawn his bow with great force, pierced the attacking Karṇa Vaikartana with three arrows.
With great force and well-aimed shafts, he warded off that which was otherwise irresistible; bewildered by the impact of those sharp and fiercely blazing arrows,
the son of Rādhā pursued him with great effort.
Both of them, the best among victors, were indescribable in their swiftness;
they fought with great fury, each desiring victory over the other.
"Behold my retaliation for what was done! Behold the strength of my arms! he cried.

Thus they addressed one another with words meaningful to heroes. Then, having recognized the peerless strength of Arjuna’s arms on this earth, Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, fought him with great fury.
Having warded off those swift arrows discharged by Arjuna,
he roared loudly, and the troops honored him.
Karna said:
I am pleased with you, O foremost of brahmins, at your prowess of arm in battle,
at your lack of despondency, and at your mastery of weapons and missiles.
Are you the Dhanurveda itself in person, or are you Rāma, O best of brahmins?
Now, whether you are Hariya himself or Viṣṇu Acyuta in person, relying on the strength of your arms for the sake of concealing your true nature,
you have assumed this form of a brahmin and are therefore fighting against me.

Indeed, no other man besides the Lord of Śacī himself or the diadem-wearing Pāṇḍava is capable of fighting me when I am enraged in battle. At that time, all the Pāṇḍavas, including Arjuna, were burnt in the house of lac.
"O Brahmin, tell me, who are you? Are you Arjuna, or perhaps Pinākin himself?
"I am Karṇa, O best of the twice-born, the foremost among all wielders of weapons; I am firmly established in the Brahma-weapon and in the Vedas through the instruction of my preceptor."
"O mighty-armed one, having encountered you, my strength is being thwarted.
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, and being unable to strike him back,
Vaiśampāyana said:
To him who was speaking thus, Phalguna replied there, his hand resting on the tip of his bow, his lotus-like face wearing a gentle smile:
"I am not the science of archery, O Karṇa; nor am I the powerful Rāma."
"I am not Viṣṇu, nor am I Śakra; I am someone else endowed with strength.
I am a Brāhmaṇa, the best among warriors and the foremost of all weapon-bearers.
O hero, fight if you wish to fight, or else withdraw."

"Trained in the Brahma and Paurandara weapons through the instruction of my preceptor, I stand today in battle to conquer you; O hero, remain unshakable! A Brahmin shall not fight with you, yet you shall not depart from me alive."
"Or say, 'I am defeated,' and then depart as you please.
Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava severed Karṇa’s bow;
then, taking up another bow, he fixed an arrow to fight.
Seeing that too, the son of Kuntī cut down his bow along with the arrow;
yet again and again, the mighty son of Rādhā,
his bows shattered and his limbs deeply pierced by arrows, then took to flight.
Returning in a mere moment and taking up his bow with an arrow fixed,
the son of Vaikartana then rained a shower of arrows upon Pārtha;
but the son of Kuntī, having cut through those nets of arrows, struck him back with his own shafts.
Having recognized all those terrible arrows, Karṇa then quickly went outside. Then Arjuna fixed an arrow for the destruction of Karṇa;
Karṇa said, "I am conquered," and thereupon Arjuna withdrew it.
In that battle, Pārtha severed a hundred bows of Karṇa with his own bow;
having cut down Karṇa’s bows, he struck him in his vital organs. With his bows repeatedly severed, his quivers and sword-sheaths likewise destroyed, [Karṇa remained there].
He struck Phalguna’s entire body with a net of arrows,
and having severed his hand-guard, he let out a great roar.
The son of Kunti, also violently enraged, drew his bow fiercely in the battle.
Having tormented him severely with arrows, the Pāṇḍava put him to flight;
for he considered the strikes of those arrows to be as unbearable as those of the twice-born Śacīpati (Indra), thinking,
"This is Indra in the form of a brahmin, or Viṣṇu, or even Śaṅkara."
"Whether it be Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, or Rāma, the son of Jamadagni"—
having been addressed thus, Karṇa, the great car-warrior, withdrew from the battle,
considering that Brahmanic splendor to be invincible.
"A Kṣatriya born of noble lineage should not defeat a Brāhmaṇa in battle"—
thinking thus, Karṇa departed quickly for his camp.
But there, O King, Śalya and Vṛkodara engaged in combat.
Strong, intoxicated at once by both rivalry and physical power,
those two challenged one another like two great elephants in rut,
striking each other with fists and knees.
By pulling forward and drawing back, by dragging and dragging away, they dragged each other about and struck one another with their fists;
then a most terrible *caṭacaṭā* sound arose from them.
They struck each other with blows resembling falling rocks;
for a moment, the two of them dragged one another about in that battle.
Then Bhīma, lifting Śalya up with his two arms in the fray, [threw him down].
The best among the strong struck him down, and then the Brahmins laughed;
having embraced him and lifted him up with his two arms in the midst [of the assembly], O best of the Bharatas,
Bhīmasena, that bull among men, performed a marvel there.
That shaft which, having fallen upon the ground, the powerful one had not struck down against his stronger foe— then,
while the assembly of kings looked on, he shattered that tree.
Thereupon, the King of Dharma restrained Bhīma with words of command.
Then the Pāṇḍava, who knew the forms [of his enemies], turned back from his brother;
and Dharmarāja pierced the intolerant Kauravya Duryodhana with a straight-jointed arrow in that interval.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, addressed Duryodhana, the slayer of enemies.
Thereupon Duryodhana, enraged like a serpent struck by a staff,
exerted the utmost effort and fought back against the king.

Having cut the strung bow of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in battle, the king showered him with volleys of arrows; leaving that [battle] behind, he fled from the fray. But Duḥśāsana, O King, was enraged by Sahadeva.
Having fought for a very long time with his bow, that great car-warrior cast aside his bow in the battle, took up a radiant armor,
and rushed toward the Pāṇḍava with a sword as bright as the sky.
The Kaurava was seized by Vikarṇa and Citrasena,
and Duḥsaha was also dragged away from Nakula by the Kauravas; therefore, let your honors turn back— for whence can there be conflict with Brahmins?
These are not merely Brahmins, nor do they possess only human strength;
among them are two cruel Brahmins, both equal to Indra in power. Whether they be who they may be, let us pay them homage and return to our own city.
Having spoken thus, those Kuru heroes turned back;
the Brahmins there took their leave of that assembled circle of kings,
and those Kṣatriyas then departed from that front of battle.
And the Brahmins, having achieved victory, departed taking the maiden with them;
for Śalya had been struck down by Bhīmasena, Karṇa was filled with apprehension,
Duryodhana had fled, and Duḥśāsana likewise withdrew from the battle.
All the kings, filled with apprehension, surrounded Vṛkodara;
and gathered there, they said, "Let it be well ascertained where these bulls among brahmins were born and where they dwell."
For who indeed is capable of fighting the son of Rādha in battle,
other than Rāma, or Droṇa, or Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat,
or Kṛṣṇa the son of Devakī, or Phalguna the scorcher of foes?
Who indeed is capable of fighting Duryodhana in battle,
or likewise Śalya, the King of Madra and the foremost among the powerful—
save for the heroic Baladeva or Vṛkodara, the son of Pāṇḍu?
"Other than the heroic Duryodhana, no one is capable of striking him down in battle.
Let a withdrawal be made from this war involving the Brahmins;
for Brahmins must always be protected, even when they have committed an offense."
"Having encountered them here, we shall fight them again.
Having observed all those lords of the earth speaking thus,
and having surpassed even other men in that deed in battle, [he spoke].
Having observed that deed of Bhīma, Kṛṣṇa,
apprehensive regarding those two sons of Kuntī,
restrained those lords of the earth.

Having conciliated them all by saying, "It was obtained through righteousness," those very kings, experts in war, desisted from battle and all returned to their respective dwellings in great astonishment.
"The assembly has been presided over by a Brāhmaṇa; the Pāñcālī bride has been chosen by the Brāhmaṇas"—saying this, those who had gathered there departed.
Meanwhile, the two [Nala and Damayantī] were concealed by the Brāhmaṇas, who were dressed in the skins of the ruru deer.
Having escaped from the throng of people and being wounded by their enemies, Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya proceeded there with difficulty;
followed by Kṛṣṇā, those two heroes among men shone resplendent.
Like the moon and sun risen on the full-moon day, freed from the clouds,
their mother contemplated their various kinds of destruction as her sons failed to return while the time for alms-gathering was passing away.
If the bulls among the Kurus had known [the truth], they would not have been slain by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
whether by those possessed of illusion or by most terrible Rākṣasas who were their firm enemies—
even the high-souled Vyāsa’s mind became perverted.
Thus did Pṛthā reflect, filled with affection for her son.
Then, during a great afternoon when the people were mostly asleep, on a foul day overspread with clouds,
she was like the sun enveloped by thick mists.
Accompanied by those Brahmins who were learned in the study of the Vedas, Jishnu entered there, preceded by the Brahmins;
having arrived at the door of the house where Pritha was staying, he stood there.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gone to that workshop of Bhārgava and reached Pṛthā, the two sons of Pṛthā, who were of great majesty, [approached her].
When the three brothers had already entered the palace, those two foremost of men, filled with supreme joy, announced Yājñasenī to them, saying, "Alms! (bhikṣā).
"O Mother, we have brought alms," said Bhīma and Phalguna.
But she, remaining in her hut and not looking at her sons,
said, "All of you, come together and eat."
But later, having observed the girl, Kuntī said,
"Alas, I have spoken wrongly," for she was both afraid of the consequences and filled with shame.
Taking the hand of that highly delighted Yājñasenī,
Kuntī approached Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke these words.
"For this maiden, the daughter of King Drupada,
has been entrusted to me by your two younger brothers;
O son, I have also spoken as was appropriate."
"O King, bull among the Kurus, tell me how it could be that I have not spoken a falsehood today by saying, 'Having come together, eat,' out of negligence."
"Unrighteousness, such as never before existed, would not have occurred had the king reflected for even a moment regarding the daughter of the Pāñcāla king."
Having comforted his mother Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, the hero of the Kurus and possessor of supreme energy,
addressed these words to Dhanañjaya.
"O Pāṇḍava, Yājñasenī has been won by you;
the princess will find satisfaction in you. Let the fire be kindled and let the oblations be offered."
"Take her hand according to the prescribed rite.
Arjuna said:
"O lord of men, do not make me a partaker of unrighteousness!"
For this dharma is indeed desired by others; first you must be established [in it],
and then this Bhīma of mighty arms and inconceivable deeds.
After me comes Nakula,
and after him Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, who is the youngest.
Then come Vṛkodara, myself, and the twins, O King.
And this maiden belongs to you all;
since things have come to this pass, reflect upon what must be done here that is both righteous and conducive to fame.
"Tell us what would be pleasing to the King of Pañcāla; we shall all remain under your command.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having understood the words of Jiṣṇu, which were filled with devotion and affection,
the sons of Pāṇḍu cast their gaze upon the princess of Pañcāla.
Seeing the illustrious Kṛṣṇā standing there, they all looked at her.
Gazing at one another as they sat, they held her within their hearts.
For upon seeing Draupadī, the god of love appeared, utterly churning the collection of senses of all those men of immeasurable splendor.

For the desirable form of the princess of Pañcāla was fashioned by the Creator himself; perceiving her to be enchanting to all beings, the sons of Kuntī— endowed with goodness and impelled by the Creator— were filled with desire for her.
It was superior to all others and enchanting to the hearts of all beings.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, who understood their gestures and inner dispositions,
O bull among men, recollected the entire speech of Dvaipāyana.
Out of fear that they might become divided among one another, the king said to those brothers:
"The auspicious Draupadī shall indeed be the wife of us all.
Thereupon, the Pāṇḍavas accepted the word of their eldest brother.
Not harming one another, they attained their desired objects of dharma and pleasure.
Janamejaya said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
Why was that ready bow not strung by Keśava, though he is both virtuous and powerful? And for what reason was the target not pierced?
"Tell me that, O best of bipeds;
for though Kṛṣṇa was capable, he did not string that bow, desiring to know [the prowess] of the sons of Pṛthā."
It was precisely from his own exertion that he gained the certainty in the world that the sons of Pṛthā were still alive,
having observed other kings who were powerless.
At the svayaṃvara, having observed that the peerless hero Dhanañjaya was stringing that supreme bow,
Kṛṣṇa [acted].
Thus Vāsudeva himself, having reflected and desiring to test the sons of Pṛthā by various means,
did not wish to string that bow.
For the sons of Pṛthā were indeed most dear to him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having all considered those words of their brother...
Then the sons of Pāṇḍu, the eldest,
possessed of immeasurable splendor, remained there with their minds meditating upon that very matter.
But the hero of the Vṛṣṇis, apprehensive of the heroes of the Kurus,
went together with the son of Rohiṇī to that workshop of Bhārgava.
There, where those heroes among men were seated,
Kṛṣṇa, together with the son of Rohiṇī, beheld him sitting— broad-chested and long-armed.
Having approached Ajātaśatru and those who were seated around him, radiant as blazing fires,
Vāsudeva then spoke.
Kṛṣṇa, pressing his feet to those of King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and the best among the upholders of dharma, said, "I am Kṛṣṇa."
In the same way, the son of Rohiṇī greeted him;
and both the Yadu heroes were joyfully welcomed by the Kurus and their paternal aunt.
O chief of the Bharatas,
Ajātaśatru, that hero of the Kurus, having offered his greetings, asked Kṛṣṇa about his welfare as they did not grasp his feet.
"O Vāsudeva, how were we all discovered by you while living here in concealment? To him,
Vāsudeva replied with a smile:
O King, even a hidden fire is indeed known;
who else among men could have performed such valor, surpassing even the sons of Pāṇḍu?
"By good fortune, you have all been released from that fire, O Pāṇḍavas, subduers of enemies!
By good fortune, the wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— "
The minister would not have been successful;
by good fortune, Kṛṣṇā has been won by relying on his prowess;
by good fortune, we have once again and forever thus accomplished our purpose.
May it be well with you; may that which is hidden in the cave increase like a fire being kindled. Let no kings here recognize you.
"Let us go back to the camp for now. Having been thus permitted by the Pāṇḍava, he of undecaying glory departed quickly together with Baladeva.
Right there sat the heroic Pāṇḍavas, none of whom were inferior, together with their mother and Kṛṣṇā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the prince of the Pañcālas, followed behind the two descendants of Kuru as they proceeded toward the dwelling of Bhārgava;
remaining unobserved, he stationed men all around them.

He himself stayed at a distance, having settled in the residence of the descendant of Bhṛgu; desiring to test them, that prince dispatched men for the sake of Draupadī, saying, "Find out who these brahmins are."
Then at evening, Bhīma, the crusher of enemies,
as well as Jiṣṇu and the two high-souled twins,
having gone out for alms, returned to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Those of undaunted spirit made their report.
Then Kuntī, the eloquent one, spoke these words at the proper time to the daughter of Drupada:
Therefore, O blessed lady, take the best portion and prepare the sacrificial offering;
give alms to the brahmin and to those who desire food, give it to them.
And those men who were gathered all around,
having quickly divided the remainder—
half for the four [others] and half for myself.
"And give half to Bhīma, O blessed lady—
this youth who is dark-complexioned, endowed with a firm physique, and whose form is like that of a rutting bull."
"For this hero is always a great eater," yet the princess remained cheerful in appearance,
placing no doubt in his words as she considered them virtuous.
The virtuous woman performed everything exactly as she had been instructed;
they all likewise partook of the food,
while she prepared her bed upon the ground with *kuśa* grass.
The impetuous Sahadeva, son of Mādrī,
and all the other heroes, having spread out their own deerskins, slept upon the ground.
To the direction presided over by Agastya were the heads of those best of the Kurus;
Kuntī, however, was at their front.
Kṛṣṇā lay her head upon the feet of the sons of Pāṇḍu as they slept on the ground,
like a pillow made of kuśa grass.
There was no sorrow for her there,
nor did she hold those bulls among the Kurus in contempt;
there, those heroes engaged in conversation.
Various discourses concerning the leadership of armies,
divine weapons, chariots, and elephants;
as well as swords, maces, and battle-axes.
As those stories were being recounted,
the son of the Pāñcāla king then heard of Kṛṣṇā as she sat there.
And all those men saw it as well;
however, Prince Dhṛṣṭadyumna heard everything that had occurred and was told to them during the night.
Intending to report everything in its entirety to King Drupada, he departed in haste; meanwhile,
the King of Pañcāla appeared dejected in form.
Not finding those Pāṇḍavas, the high-souled one questioned Dhṛṣṭadyumna:
"Where has Kṛṣṇā gone, and by whom has she been led away?"
I hope that [this city] has not been overrun by a Śūdra of low birth,
or by a Vaiśya who pays taxes;
I hope that no foot has been placed upon my head.
I hope no garland has fallen into a cemetery;
I hope there is no man here who is superior in caste,
or even one of exalted caste.
"O son, I hope my foot has not been placed on my head by Kṛṣṇa’s touch today;
and I hope I shall perform the sacrifice with supreme joy."
Having united with Pārtha, that bull among men,
tell me truly, O high-souled one:
who is this victor of my daughter today?
Do the sons of Vicitravīrya, that hero of the Kurus, still survive today?
And by the fruit of my sacrifice, O son, do you live?
By my good fortune, or perhaps by the merit of my lineage,
has the younger brother of Pārtha today taken up the bow and struck the target?
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having been addressed in this manner, that prince, appearing exceedingly delighted, reported it to his father.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the foremost of the Somakas, [spoke] of how the event occurred and by whom Kṛṣṇā was carried off—
that youth with long, red eyes.
Clad in a black antelope skin and possessing a form equal to that of a god,
he who strung his preeminent bow and struck down that target upon the earth.
Moving without attachment, the energetic one proceeded,
surrounded by the foremost of the twice-born who honored him,
like the wielder of the thunderbolt among the sons of Diti.
Honored by all the gods and sages,
dark-complexioned and youthful, with the gait of an elephant in rut,
he had performed that great and most difficult deed.
Having agitated and put those kings to flight,
Kṛṣṇā, her form difficult to behold due to her own splendor, followed him, taking hold of his deerskin.
Just as a female elephant is delighted by a male elephant, I suspect that Arjuna— whose prowess is equal to the Lord of the Thirty-three— took up arms against the son of the Sūta.
While those lords of men were unable to endure it and were rushing toward him there in their anger,
another [hero] then appeared in the midst of the kings.
Having uprooted that flourishing tree growing from the earth,
he drove away the multitudes of kings,
just as the enraged God of Death drives away living beings.
O lord of men, I consider that Bhīmasena to be [the one] who,
while the kings looked on, struck down Śalya in battle.
Taking Kṛṣṇā with them, those two foremost of men went forth, shining like the sun and the moon,
to the workshop of Bhārgava outside the city.
Seated there like a flame of fire, she is,
in my estimation, the mother of those very heroes among men.
Then those two, having saluted her feet while she sat with the three [sages] who were like fires,
said to her, "Salute Kṛṣṇā."
Having informed Kṛṣṇā that they were staying right there,
those foremost of men went out to wander for alms;
and Kṛṣṇā, having received their alms—
Having made an offering to the Brahmins and having served that aged woman as well as those heroic men, he himself also ate.
But they all, O King, fell fast asleep;
Kṛṣṇā, however, became their pillow for their feet,
and the earth was their bed.
Provided with a supreme covering of darbha grass and deerskin,
they, like roaring clouds at the end of time,
engaged in various wonderful conversations.
Those heroes do not tell stories suited for Vaiśyas or Śūdras,
nor do they speak of them to the twice-born; undoubtedly, they are bulls among Kṣatriyas.
For just as they speak of the battle, O King,
our hope has clearly been fulfilled;
for we hear that the sons of Pṛthā have escaped from the fire.
For just as the target was struck down and the bow was strung by him with force,
so too do they speak to one another.
"The sons of Pṛthā are surely moving about in disguise.
Then King Drupada, filled with joy,
dispatched his family priest there.
"May we know you," he said, speaking thus;
"Are you perhaps the sons of the high-souled Pāṇḍu?"—
the royal priest, having grasped the king's words, [spoke].
Having approached them and offered his praise, he,
who was skilled in proper sequence, spoke their entire message to the king exactly as it was, in due order.
O you who are worthy of the best, Drupada, the king of the Pañcālas and lord of the earth, desires to know you;
for having seen this man who has pierced the mark, he seeks to identify you.
He sees no end to his joy;
therefore, declare the lineage of your kinsmen in succession,
and place your feet upon the heads of your enemies!
"Gladden this heart of mine,
along with that of the King of Pañcāla and his followers;
for King Pāṇḍu was the father of King Drupada."
"He was his dear friend and like his own self;
this daughter of mine is the object of that Kuru's desire, so that she might become his daughter-in-law."
And this desire, O lady of faultless limbs, has always remained in the heart of King Drupada:
that Arjuna, indeed, should have broad and long arms.
"Let him obtain my daughter according to dharma"—
having heard those words spoken by King Drupada, all the Pāṇḍavas indeed [acted accordingly].
Those heroes among men honored Kuntī as well as Mālinī, and they likewise honored their family priest; for they thought,
"This shall be a good deed done for me."
"This shall bring him fame, merit, and welfare.
Having spoken these words, the king gazed upon his domestic priest, who stood before him with humility.
He commanded Bhīma, who was standing nearby:
"Let water for the feet and the guest-offering be given to him;
he is the venerable priest of King Drupada."
To him, Bhīma, the lord of men, offered worship that was indeed exceeding;
and having accepted that very worship, [the guest departed].
When the domestic priest was seated comfortably,
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke thus to that Brāhmaṇa:
"The daughter has been bestowed by the King of Pañcāla."
Having been offered as a bride-price by King Drupada according to his own dharma and as he desired,
she was treated accordingly by this hero.
In that matter, no distinction was made based on caste; neither on livelihood, nor on family, nor on lineage.
For it was by means of a strung bow that [distinction was made].
Just as this [target] was released by him when the mark was pierced, so too has this Kṛṣṇā been won here by this great-souled one in the midst of the assembly of kings.
Since things have come to this, the king of the Somakas does not deserve to give way to grief that would lead to unhappiness;
nor indeed is this the desire of King Drupada.
And he too shall obtain that princess of unattainable beauty belonging to the king;
O Brahmin, I consider this to be excellent.
That bow cannot be strung with a bowstring by one of feeble strength; for likewise,
it cannot be done by one untrained in weapons or one of low birth.
For it is indeed possible to strike the target in that manner;
therefore, the King of Pañcāla ought not to feel distress on account of his daughter today.
"Nor can that downfall be otherwise brought about here on earth by any man.
While Yudhiṣṭhira was speaking thus, [the messenger]—
From the presence of the Pāñcāla king,
another man arrived there quickly as a second messenger, intending to announce that the food was ready.
The messenger said:
"King Drupada has prepared food for the sake of his kinsmen, and it has been specially prepared for the purpose of the wedding."
Therefore, accomplish all that needs to be done and reach that place;
do not delay Kṛṣṇā there for long. Here are these chariots, adorned with golden lotuses.
Mounting these chariots, yoked with excellent horses and worthy of lords of the earth, all of you proceed to that residence of the Pāñcāla king.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then those bulls among the Kurus set forth,
having first dispatched that family priest ahead of them.
Having mounted those great vehicles,
Kuntī and Kṛṣṇā departed together;
they were well-bathed with parched grain and fried rice.
With excellent jars filled with sandalwood water,
and with women adorned with fragrant garments, garlands,
and various ornaments.
Accompanied by the enchanting sounds of auspicious songs and the resonance of musical instruments, which had increased for the meritorious,
they proceeded joyfully while being celebrated in song.
Accompanied by Brahmins holding blazing lamps,
that foremost priest of the King of Pañcāla was thus addressed by Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having gone, he reported everything exactly as spoken by the joy of the Kurus to the king; and having heard the words of the domestic priest, [the king...]
O Bhārata, whatever the Dharmarāja had spoken out of a desire to know, he then gathered many kinds of articles for the sake of the best of the Kurus.
Fruits, well-prepared garlands,
skins, armor, as well as seats, O King, and likewise cattle and ropes;
And whatever other materials there may be for the purpose of agriculture,
as well as those required for other crafts—
all these were prepared there in their entirety.
And whatever objects were for the purpose of play,
the king brought them all there,
as well as radiant chariots, horses, and armor.
There were great swords and variegated horse-chariots,
as well as excellent bows and preeminent arrows;
there were also spears and double-edged swords adorned with gold.
Spears, *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, and battle-axes,
as well as everything pertaining to warfare,
and beds and seats of the finest craftsmanship;
And likewise, various seats were there;
then Kuntī, taking hold of the virtuous Kṛṣṇā,
entered the inner apartments of Drupada.
And those women of undaunted spirit paid their respects to that wife of the Kuru king,
as they gazed upon her who moved with the majestic stride of a lion.
Those heroic men had eyes like great bulls, wore deerskins as upper garments, possessed broad shoulders hidden by their robes, and had arms hanging down like the coils of the lords of serpents.
O King, all the kings and their ministers,
as well as the king’s sons, his friends,
and all his servants in their entirety;
There, those heroes, free from hesitation, experienced extreme joy as they sat upon the excellent seats provided with footstools.
Then those foremost of men entered in due order into the costly [seats], not feeling any astonishment at the various royal foods provided.
In vessels made of Jāmbūnada gold and silver,
male and female servants of well-groomed appearance,
as well as food servers, brought forth the food.
Having eaten there, those heroes among men,
being exceedingly well-satisfied according to their desire,
departed from all those riches there.
The heroic men entered the battle arrays;
having observed that, the son of Drupada and the king, together with all his chief ministers, [prepared for action].
Approaching with joy, they paid their respects to the sons of Kuntī, those princes and grandsons of kings.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the King of Pañcāla,
of great splendor and undepressed soul, having summoned Prince Yudhiṣṭhira and embraced him with a Brahmanical embrace, questioned the son of Kuntī, who was possessed of radiant luster.
"How shall we know whether you are Kṣatriyas or Brāhmaṇas,
Vaiśyas endowed with virtues, or those born of Śūdra wombs;
or perhaps you are Siddhas wandering in all directions, having resorted to illusion?"
"Please tell us the truth regarding those who have arrived from heaven for the sake of Kṛṣṇā and seek an audience with her; for our doubt here is great.
Only at the end of this uncertainty may satisfaction enter our minds."
"O scorcher of foes, may our fortunes be auspicious.
Speak the truth as you desire; truth is the ornament of kings. One should speak in accordance with one's sacrifices and meritorious works, but never speak untruth."
"O subduer of enemies, O one who resembles an immortal, having heard your words,
I shall certainly proceed with the performance of the marriage according to the prescribed rites.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, do not be dejected; O Pāñcālya, may you have joy. That desire which you wished for has surely been fulfilled, without a doubt.
For we, O King, are the Kṣatriyas who are the sons of the high-souled Pāṇḍu."

"Know me to be Kaunteya, the eldest; these two are Bhīmasena and Arjuna, by whom your sons were defeated in the assembly of kings, O King. And the twins are there, O Indra among kings, where Kṛṣṇā is stationed."
"Let the sorrow of your mind depart; we are kṣatriyas, O bull among men.
Like a lotus plant, this daughter of yours has merely gone from one lake to another.
Thus, O great king, I tell you all this as the truth.
"For you are our preceptor and our supreme refuge.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Drupada, his eyes overflowing with joy, spoke.
At that time, he was unable to offer a reply to Yudhiṣṭhira;
however, having restrained that great joy with effort, that scorcher of foes,
the king, then replied to Yudhiṣṭhira in a fitting manner.
The righteous-souled king asked him how they had previously fled;
that son of Pāṇḍu related everything to him in due order.
Having heard those words spoken by the son of Kuntī, King Drupada [was moved].
Then he censured Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
and comforted Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī;
and Drupada, the best among speakers, pledged to restore the kingdom.
Then Kuntī, Kṛṣṇā, Bhīmasena, Arjuna,
and the twins, having been commanded by the king, entered the great palace. There, O King, they dwelt, honored by Yajñasena.
Then the king, together with his sons, spoke to them once they had recovered their breath:
"O descendant of Kuru, let the mighty-armed Arjuna take her hand this very day according to the prescribed rites; on this auspicious day, let him perform the ceremony."
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, said to him:
"O lord of the people, I too must first form a marriage alliance;
therefore, I shall first perform that which you approve."
Drupada said:
"Either you yourself may take the hand of my daughter according to the prescribed rites,
or, O hero, bestow Kṛṣṇā upon whomever you deem fit."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, O Lord of the People, Draupadī shall be the queen of us all;
for this was previously declared by my mother."
I am indeed unmarried, as is Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava;
and this daughter of yours, who is like a jewel, has been won by the son of Pṛthā.
O King, this is our agreement: that the jewel shall be enjoyed in common.

O best of kings, we do not wish to abandon that agreement; for if you enter [the city] by an improper means, there would be a great loss of dharma. Furthermore, your daughter has been won by Pārtha and is like a precious jewel to you.
"According to dharma, Kṛṣṇā shall become the queen of us all;
let her take the hand of each one of us in turn before the blazing fire.
Drupada said:
O descendant of Kuru, many queens are ordained for a single man,
but never are many men ordained for a single woman;
this practice is never praised as dharma, either in the world or in the Veda.
"O son of Kuntī, you who are righteous and pure ought not to commit an unrighteous act that contradicts both the world and the Vedas; why has your mind become such as this?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Great King, the Dharma is subtle; we do not know its course.
We follow the path traversed by our predecessors in due succession.
O best among the upholders of Dharma, this Dharma is contrary to the ways of the world."
"My speech has never uttered an untruth, nor is my mind ever fixed upon unrighteousness. My mother speaks exactly as it is in my heart;
I heard this from Vyāsa, who was directed by Rudra while we were in the hermitage."
"O King, this is the eternal dharma; practice it without hesitation. O Ruler of the Earth, let there be no doubt in you regarding this in any way whatsoever.
Drupada said:
"You, Kuntī, O son of Kuntī, and my son Dhṛṣṭadyumna—
let us discuss what must be done so that we may perform it at the time of tomorrow.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having gathered together, O Bhārata, they all began to converse.
Then, O King, Dvaipāyana arrived there by chance.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all those Pāṇḍavas and the highly illustrious Pāñcālya,
seeing the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, rose up and honored him. Having greeted them all and inquired after their welfare in detail, he [spoke].
The high-minded one sat down upon a bright golden seat; then, permitted by Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor,
all those best of men sat upon costly thrones.
Then, after a moment, having uttered sweet words, the son of Pṛṣata,
the lord of the people, questioned that high-souled one regarding Draupadī:
"How may one woman belong to many without there being a confusion of dharma?"
"May the Blessed One explain all this to us exactly as it is.
Vyāsa said:
"Regarding this dharma which is deceptive and contrary to both worldly custom and the Vedas..."
"Whatever opinion each of you holds, that very thing I wish to hear.
Drupada said:
"In my view, this is unrighteousness, contrary to both worldly custom and the Vedas."
For there is no single wife found for many men, O best of the twice-born;
nor has this practice been followed by the high-souled ones of old,
nor should the eternal dharma be practiced when it resides in many.
"Therefore, I do not make such a resolution regarding this action;
for this matter appears to me as being clouded by doubt concerning dharma.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna said:

"O bull among the twice-born, O Brahmin rich in asceticism, how may an elder brother of virtuous conduct approach the wife of his younger brother? Because of the subtlety of dharma, we do not understand its course in any way whatsoever."

"O Brahmin, it is impossible for those such as us to determine whether this is unrighteousness or righteousness; therefore, I cannot resolve that Kṛṣṇā should become the queen of the five by any means whatsoever."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"My speech has never uttered untruth, nor is my mind set upon unrighteousness;
for my heart inclines toward this, and it is by no means unrighteous."
For it is heard even in the Purāṇa that there was a daughter of Gautama named Jaṭilā,
the highly wise and illustrious daughter of Gautama,
who, O best among the upholders of dharma, attended upon seven sages.
In the same way, Vārkṣī, born of a sage, whose self was purified by ascetic penances,
became united with the ten brothers named Pracetas;
and those best among the knowers of dharma declared that the word of the preceptor is dharma.
Of all gurus, the mother is the supreme guru.
She too spoke these words: "Let it be eaten like alms.
Therefore, O best of the foremost of the twice-born, I consider this to be dharma.
Kuntī said:
"I urged Arjuna, saying, 'Eat together with your brothers';
this is exactly as this righteous Yudhiṣṭhira has said."
"I have a sharp fear of falsehood; how may I be released from falsehood?
Vyāsa said:
"O blessed lady, you shall be released from falsehood, for this is the eternal dharma."
But I shall not speak for all; O Pāñcāla, listen to me yourself regarding how this dharma was ordained, from whence it is eternal,
and how the son of Kuntī has declared it— this is indeed the dharma, without a doubt.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the venerable lord Vyāsa Dvaipāyana, having risen,
took the king by the hand and entered the royal palace.
The Pāṇḍavas, Kuntī, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
being distraught, waited right there for those two.
Then Dvaipāyana spoke to that high-souled lord of men.
He related how it is the dharma for many men to have a single wife,
and how in former times the gods granted this boon to the princess; how Dharma and the other lords, gratified by her asceticism, [granted] that she should have five husbands.
Vyāsa;
the seer Vyāsa; Vyāsa.
Nāḷāyanī,
Vyāsa,
Drupada.
Vyāsa,
Nāḷāyanī,
and Maheśvara.
Nāḷāyanī;
Maheśvara;
Nāḷāyanī.
Maheśvara,
Vyāsa,
and others said: "O King, let there be no mental anguish within you."
"She is the wife of five [men], my daughter"— O King, she might have been sought by her mother,
thinking, "She is the wife of five, my daughter."
Yāja and Upayāja, devoted to dharma, through their ascetic penances brought about her state of having five husbands;
she was thus obtained by the sons of Pāṇḍu in accordance with dharma.
Your wife Kṛṣṇā shall indeed rejoice, and your lineage shall prosper. O King, there is no one else in this world more fortunate than you; you are invincible to all your enemies.
Furthermore, listen to this from me, O Viśoka;
according to tradition, she has had five husbands. Formerly, this Nāḷāyanī had the Elder Maudgalya as her husband.
Then that blameless woman attended upon that leper,
who was reduced to skin and bone, bitter, fickle, envious, and prone to anger; he was filled with a foul odor, and bore wrinkles and grey hair.
She, observing a great vow, attended upon the elder who was of deformed appearance, with decaying nails and skin, while she herself ate his leftovers.
Then, on one occasion, as he was eating, his thumb fell off.
Having extracted that food from the [remaining] food, she consumed it without hesitation. Then,
by him who was pleased and who spoke of her desires, she was told repeatedly, "Choose a boon," and she then chose a boon.
I am neither old, nor harsh, nor envious, nor excessively wrathful; I have no foul-smelling mouth, I am not emaciated, nor am I greedy.
How shall I delight you here? How shall I cause you to dwell with me?
"Speak, O auspicious lady, may it be well with you, according to whatever you desire in your heart.
To him— the performer of effortless deeds, the giver of boons, the granter of all desires— she,
whose limbs were faultless, replied with a serene countenance.
O high-minded one, I have been pierced by the five arrows of Manmatha; therefore, may you,
the illustrious and world-renowned Lord who has divided yourself fivefold, delight me once again after assuming oneness, O you of inconceivable soul.
The wise Brahmarṣi of great asceticism replied to her, "So be it.
Having assumed five forms, he delighted Nāḷāyanī, who possessed beautiful hair-ends and a lovely smile, in every way.
Furthermore, being honored even more highly by the great seers in the hermitages,
he wandered at will once again, assuming a body according to his desire;
and when he went to heaven, he was there together with the celestial seers.
Subsisting on the essence of nectar and ambrosia, he wandered through the world of the gods;
likewise, being honored by Śacī even in the palaces of Śakra,
he ran about with Mahendra’s army out of a desire for pleasure.
Having ascended the divine chariot of the Sun,
the venerable Lord returned once more to Meru and took up residence on Meru; having bathed in the celestial Gaṅgā, that treasury of austerity dwelt there together with her.
And as the wind dwells within the networks of rays of the moon, so did he dwell there;
when that great seer assumed the form of a mountain,
by his power a great river was born from its midst.
When the Lord Sage became a *sāla* tree covered in blossoms,
she then turned into a creeper and entwined herself around him; and she further nourished his body, following after him once more.
She nurtured him, and she even walked with her husband upon her own shoulders;
thus, the equal affection between him and her increased,
for the Blessed One, the best of sages, was pleased with her.
And there, by the turn of fate, that beautiful woman became aware [of his presence];
and he, through the power of yoga, delighted that goddess with his ascetic fervor.
Having formerly been a devoted wife, the illustrious lady remained ever steadfast at his side.
Like Arundhatī and like Sītā, she became exceedingly devoted to her husband;
she surpassed even Damayantī’s mother in this regard.
This is the truth, O Great King; let not your mind think otherwise.
O King, by some divine conjunction, this Nāḷāyanī gave birth to your daughter Kṛṣṇā, who was radiant and auspicious upon the sacrificial altar;
her mind remained attached to him and could never turn away from him.
"For her soul was thus fixed upon that best of the twice-born.
O Brahmin, best among those who know all the Vedas, tell me the reason why my daughter Kṛṣṇā was born at my sacrifice as an ascetic woman."
Listen, O King, to how this boon was indeed granted to her by Rudra,
and for what purpose this illustrious lady was born at your sacrifice;
I shall tell you of Kṛṣṇā’s former life.
Formerly known as Indrasenā, the auspicious daughter of Nala,
she became the wife of Maudgalya and lived there free from all distress. Indeed, she took delight with the great ṛṣi Maudgalya.
O King, then many series of years passed by as if they were a mere moment.
Then, at one time, that righteous-souled one, having become satiated with desire, grew dispassionate;
seeking the supreme Brahman, he became devoted to the dharma of renunciation.
That brahmin released her, and she then fell to the earth.
O tiger among kings, Maudgalya, who was always purified by his ascetic penances,
approached her as she was afflicted by lust and enjoyment, and spoke these words.
"Be gracious to me, O Blessed One; you ought not to abandon me.
O Brahman-sage, I am not yet satiated by the indulgence of sensual desires. Māra oppresses me excessively; may your lordship show me favor."
Satisfy my senses; a secret distresses me incessantly. Since you speak what should not be spoken to me without hesitation, while causing an obstacle to my ascetic practice, therefore hear my words.
In the world of men, you shall become a renowned princess,
the daughter of the high-souled Drupada, the king of Pañcāla;
there, five illustrious husbands shall be yours.
"You shall enjoy pleasure for a long time together with those of sweet appearance.

Having been cursed in this manner, the illustrious lady became despondent; though she had reached the forest, unsatiated by worldly enjoyments, she then propitiated the Lord of Gods through ascetic penance.
Free from desire, subsisting on air, and likewise without food, she followed the sun and practiced the penance of the five fires. Paśupati himself was pleased by her intense austerity.
Then Rudra, the Lord and Master of all the worlds, granted a boon:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, you shall have a supreme rebirth among human beings;
and, O blessed one, you shall have five husbands who are observers of excellent vows."
All of you possess bodies like that of Mahendra and have prowess equal to Mahendra.
While staying there, you shall perform great deeds for the sake of the gods.
"I have chosen only one husband; how then can it be five? [she asked].
"Tell me, how many husbands will there be for me alone?
For you have said to me five times, 'I shall give you a husband. Therefore, O blessed lady, you shall have five husbands who will bring you happiness."
Dharma alone was ordained of old as the husband of women; polygamy was established by the ancestors as the duty of men. This law for women was fashioned long ago by the sages.

It is said that for one man there is only one wife who shares his religious duties, and for a woman there is only one husband from her youth; this is the worldly rule. However, in times of distress or for the sake of progeny, another husband is prescribed by tradition.
If she should go to a third [man], her expiation is prescribed;
at the fourth [man], she falls from dharma; at the fifth, she becomes a *vardhakī*.
Since this is the path of dharma, I do not choose to have many husbands.
"How may I be released from that confusion of conduct practiced by the world?
For in former times, women were uncovered and were purified by their menses;
you have said once before that there would be no unrighteousness for you in this."
"If I have five husbands, I desire this boon from them:
that I remain a virgin in every union with each of them,
and that through service to my husbands, I may attain perfection as I did in the past."
I have experienced the desire for enjoyments, yet those enjoyments have not come to me; O auspicious one, pleasure and spiritual success do not coexist with one another.
You shall attain success through non-enjoyment, and even through yoga, you shall reach greatness.

And in another body, endowed with beauty, fortune, and virtues, you, O highly blessed one, shall attain youth through five [husbands] and become great. Go now, O auspicious lady, and stand in the waters of the Gaṅgā; whatever man you see there, [he shall be yours].
"O lady of pure smiles, bring that king of the gods into my presence.
Having been thus addressed by Viśvarūpa, she circumambulated Rudra and went toward the holy Gaṅgā, the river that flows through the three paths.
Vyāsa said:
Long ago, O King, the gods were performing a sacrificial session (sattra) in the Naimiṣa forest;
there, at that time, Vaivasvata performed the duties of the *śamitr*.
Then, O King, while Yama was consecrated there,
he did not cause even the slightest harm to his subjects;
consequently, those subjects became numerous.
Through the passing of time and death, they were abandoned;
O dear one, having been initiated there, he named Yama began to strike down living beings,
yet the creatures did not die.
Then Śakra, Varuṇa, Kubera,
the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins [honored] Prajāpati, the leader of the world.
Then the gods and others gathered there,
and having assembled, they said to the Teacher of the World:
"We have a great fear due to the increase of human beings."
"Therefore, trembling with fear and desiring happiness,
let us all go to you for refuge.
Brahmā said:
"What fear do you have of humans, since you are all immortal? Let there never be any fear for you from the presence of mortals.
The gods said:
"For mortals have indeed become immortal; there is no distinction whatsoever. Trembling at this lack of distinction, they have come here for the sake of distinction.
Brahmā said:
Vaivasvata is occupied for the sake of the sacrificial session;
therefore, these men do not die while he is thus single-mindedly engaged in all his duties.
Therefore, their time of destruction shall surely come;
even the body of Vaivasvata has been multiplied, being impelled by your own prowess.
"For this shall be their end at the time of destruction,
for the physical strength of men will indeed diminish.
Vyāsa said:
Then, having heard the words of their elder brother, those mighty gods assembled together and sat down at the place where the gods perform sacrifice.
On the Bhāgīrathī they saw a lotus;
having seen it, they were struck with wonder,
and Śūra, the Indra among them, went there.
Then he saw a woman with the brilliance of fire at the place where the Gaṅgā flows forth constantly;
there that woman was weeping, seeking water.
Having plunged into the goddess Gaṅgā, he stood there;
a single tear-drop of his fell into the water,
and it then became a golden lotus.
Beholding that marvel at that time, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin) questioned that woman from close by:
"Who are you? Why do you weep? For what reason?"
"Speak here a truthful word that you desire.
The woman said:
"O Śakra, you shall know who I am here."
"O King, come before me; I, unfortunate as I am, shall go on ahead. You shall see that for which I weep."
Vyāsa said:
As she was going away, he followed after her and then saw nearby a youth who was handsome to behold.
Seeing him seated upon a lion-throne, accompanied by young women,
playing with dice on the summit of the king of mountains,
the King of the Gods said to him: "This [kingdom] is mine."
"Know that the entire universe stands under my control," he said with great indignation, seeing him utterly intoxicated by the dice: "I am the Lord."
But seeing Śakra enraged, the god laughed and looked slowly at Śakra;
then the king of the gods became paralyzed.
Gazed upon by him, he stood still like a pillar.
But when his play here had reached its full measure,
he then spoke to that weeping goddess.
"Let him be brought here from afar,
lest pride should enter him once again.
Then Śakra, as soon as he was touched by her—
With his limbs collapsing, he fell to the earth.
The Blessed One of fierce splendor said to him:
"O Śakra, never act in this manner again under any circumstances."
Turn back this great king of mountains; your strength and heroism are immeasurable. Having turned it back, enter into its center.
There, where those like you, radiant as the sun,
were seated, he opened that peak of the great mountain and beheld four others of equal splendor.
Beholding them, he became sorrowful, thinking,
"Shall I not indeed become like these?
Then the god Giriśa [spoke] to the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Opening his eyes in anger, he said:
"O Śatakratu, enter this cave,
since you formerly treated me with contempt out of childishness."
Thus addressed by the Lord, the king of the gods,
trembling violently from his affliction,
with his limbs drooping as if blown by the wind, [spoke].
On the summit of the king of mountains, like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree,
he stood with palms joined and face bowed down,
trembling as he was suddenly addressed in this way.
And he said this to the many-formed and fierce one:
"O Blessed One, may you today be the beholder of Śeṣa.
To him, Ugradhanvan replied with a laugh:
Those who do not possess such virtue do not attain the remainder here;
these too shall become so in the future.
Therefore, having entered this cave, you should rest.
"Śeṣa shall also become thus for you, there is no doubt;
all of you enter human wombs. There, having performed unbearable deeds,"
Having brought many others to their end,
having caused men to fight with divine weapons,
and having conquered all those heroes in battle;
They shall return once more to the world of Indra,
that highly precious realm previously won by their own deeds.
All this has been spoken by me exactly so.
"Other various matters must also be attended to," [they said].
Then the former Indras said: "We shall go from the world of the gods to the world of men."
Where liberation is ordained as difficult to attain,
may the gods— Dharma, Vāyu, Maghavan, and the two Aśvins— place us within our mother.
"Having fought with humans using divine weapons,
they shall return once again to the world of Indra.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, Vajrapāṇi spoke again to the best of gods:
"For the sake of my task, I shall [summon] that man by means of my prowess."
I shall give them my own fifth son: Viśvabhuj, Ṛtadhāman, Śibi, the powerful Indra,
Śānti as the fourth among them, and the one known as Tejasvin as the fifth.
To them, the Blessed One Ugradhanvan granted their desired wish exactly as requested by his own inclination; and he also gave them that woman, beloved of the world.
Having established Śrī as the wife among human beings,
that god then departed together with them toward the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa.
Infinite, unmanifest, unborn, ancient,
eternal, the universe itself, and of infinite forms—
he indeed ordained all that.
Then they all came into being upon the earth;
having fashioned the fifth as Indra, the victorious Jishnu, the god among men and the foremost of the wise.
And Hari also plucked out two hairs—
one white and the other black—
and those two hairs entered the Yadus.
In the family, there were two women, Rohiṇī and Devakī.
That hair of the white god became one of those two, namely Baladeva.
Keśava became the second [incarnation], Kṛṣṇa;
he whose hair (keśa) was described as black (kṛṣṇa) by color— those who were previously restrained in the form of Śakra;
In that very cave on the northern side of the mountain are those heroic Pāṇḍavas;
the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin is a portion of Śakra.
Thus, O King, these Pāṇḍavas were born, who had previously been Indras;
and this prosperity of theirs was ordained from the very beginning.
How indeed could this wife of theirs, Draupadī of divine form,
rise from the surface of the earth at the end of her karma, unless it were by the power of destiny?
"O Lord of Men, her form possesses the brilliance of the moon and the sun,
and her supreme fragrance wafts for the distance of a *krośa*; furthermore,
this other thing [is given] out of affection."
"I grant you a most wonderful boon:
