behold with divine vision the sons of Kuntī, endowed with their former bodies through their merits."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Vyāsa, whose deeds were most noble,
being pure through the ascetic power of that king, [spoke] to the Brahmin.
He bestowed divine vision upon them all;
the king saw them exactly as they were in their former bodies. Then he beheld those celestial beings, adorned with golden crowns and garlands.
He saw youths who resembled Śakra, possessing the luster of fire and the sun, wearing beautiful turbans, handsome in form,
broad-chested, and as tall as palm trees.
Shining exceedingly with divine, dustless garments, golden ornaments, and the finest garlands—
like the three-eyed gods themselves, or the celestial Vasus;
Seeing those former Indras, endowed with all virtues and so handsome,
King Drupada was both pleased and amazed.
Having beheld the son of Śakra in the form of Indra,
having attained that immeasurable divine illusion,
and seeing her who was like the foremost Goddess Śrī incarnate in bodily form;
The lord of kings beheld a divine, prosperous wife, who was visibly radiant like the moon and fire, and worthy of them in her beauty, splendor, and fame.
Seeing that great and wondrous form,
he grasped the feet of the son of Satyavatī,
saying, "O supreme ṛṣi, this is not surprising in you."
With a serene mind, he spoke to him.
Vyāsa said:
"In a forest of asceticism, there was a certain daughter of a high-souled seer."
But that beautiful maiden, though she was virtuous, did not find a husband;
she propitiated Śaṅkara with fierce ascetic penance. The Lord himself, being pleased, said to her, "Choose a boon."
Thus addressed, the maiden spoke again and again to the boon-granting Lord, the God: "I desire a husband endowed with every excellence. Then the Lord of Gods, being pleased, granted her that boon.
"Śaṅkara said, 'You shall have five excellent husbands.
Then, seeking to propitiate the god, she spoke this further:
'I deserve only one husband endowed with all virtues from you.'"
The God of gods, his soul delighted, spoke these auspicious words to her again:
"Five times you have said to me, 'Give me a husband.
It shall be so, O blessed lady; may prosperity be yours."
When you have gone to another body, that which was spoken shall come to pass:
she herself, having become Nālāyanī, peerless in beauty upon the earth,
and having obtained her husband Maudgalya and received an auspicious boon, [shall attain her goal].
"Listen attentively, O protector of the earth, as I speak this secret;
have faith in my words, and then you shall see the Pāṇḍavas.
Having slain Vṛtra, the lord of the gods fell from heaven after killing the son of Tvaṣṭṛ."
Then, having incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin and being deprived of his righteousness and other virtues, the power of Indra went to Yama; his strength entered Vāyu;
and his excellent vigor and wisdom went to the two Aśvins.
Modesty, Fortune, Fame, Humility, and Intelligence—
these emerged from Indra and took refuge in the Goddess of Speech (Sarasvatī),
O King, due to a previous boon granted by Indra and by the command of Maheśvara.
Know that the Pāṇḍavas are Dharmarāja and the others, and Draupadī is likewise Hrī;
therefore, O King, these Pāṇḍavas are Indra alone, there is no doubt.
And Draupadī alone, O King, is Paulomī, there is no doubt.
Listen to another most secret mystery fashioned by the gods,
hearing which your doubt today shall shatter into a hundred pieces.
[These are] the faces of Maheśvara, beginning with the Sadyojāta face.
The five Pāṇḍavas are those who were, and this Draupadī is Pārvatī;
this is another secret of yours, an eternal mystery of the gods,
which is a great means for your conviction and for removing all doubt.
And the four arms of Viṣṇu were marked with the conch, the discus, and other signs;
Dharmarāja, Bhīma, and the two Yamas were there, O best of kings,
while Arjuna was Viṣṇu himself and Pāñcālī was Kamalāvatī.
O Lord of the Earth, know that Viṣṇu himself, the four forms of Viṣṇu, and the daughter of the ocean are the four Pāṇḍavas— Jiṣṇu and Kṛṣṇā;
he who possesses these four forms is the Caturvyūha together with Vāsudeva and the others.
Viṣṇu has descended to the earth, and Pāñcālī is Kamalā herself;
and Sadāśiva, who possesses five forms, is known as the Pañcāyatana.
O King, know that Pāñcālī consists of the five [tattvas] beginning with Nivṛtti.

Therefore, let there be no doubt in you; let Kṛṣṇā be given to the Pāṇḍavas, O King, for she was born before them as their sister. The Pāṇḍavas shall be like five fires, and Kṛṣṇā is proclaimed to be their Svāhā.
For this daughter of Drupada, Kṛṣṇā, the faultless Pārṣatī of divine form, was born for you as the destined wife of the five; she is the very goddess Śrī of heaven,
arisen from the great sacrifice for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having performed severe austerities here, she has become your daughter.
This very goddess Rucirā, beloved by the gods,
is one of five [sisters] due to her own past actions.
"O King, having heard what Drupada desires, do it; for she was created by the Self-born One himself as the wife of a god."—
Vyāsa.
O protector of the earth, listen also to this ancient account concerning the marriage of former royal sages as it is being told:
there was a royal sage named Nitantu, renowned throughout the world.
He had five sons who were great archers and rulers of the earth:
Sālveya, Śūrasena, the heroic Śrutasena,
Tindusāra, and Atisāra— all of whom were Kṣatriyas who performed Vedic sacrifices.
Speaking kindly to one another, they did not transgress each other’s bounds.
At that *svayaṃvara*, Naitantavā Pañca and Śaibyā obtained these five heroic lords of men as husbands, along with Bhaumāśvī.
Then Bhaumāśvī became the most excellent among all women, her voice as sweet as a lute resonating with the *gāndhāra* note;
she who had five husbands, bulls among Kṣatriyas, for whom no other [wives] were woven upon the loom.
There were protectors of the earth endowed with all virtues;
O King, they had one wife in common, the daughter of Uśīnara named Bhaumāśvī, who was then possessed of beauty and excellence— may prosperity be yours.
From the five [husbands], she gave birth to five heirs in five ways;
from those Naitaṇṭavas, O tiger among kings,
there then arose a separate designation for those Matsyas on earth in five divisions.
Listen to me, O best of kings, as I describe them to you exactly as they are:
the Sālveyas, the Śūrasenas, the kings of the Śrutasenas, the Tiṇḍusās, and the Atisārās; these are their lineages, O foremost of monarchs.
Thus, Bhaumāśvī became one wife, renowned throughout the earth.
Drupada said:
"O Great Seer, it was only after hearing these words of yours that [I acted];"
Having previously striven for this task,
and having heard these true words of great significance,
O Greatly Powerful One, my delusion has vanished.
Indeed, it is not possible to escape what has been ordained;
this very ordinance has now come to pass.
The knot of destiny is irreversible.
Nothing here is ordained by anything other than one's own karma; for a deed performed is indeed the sole cause for obtaining a boon,
and thus this has come to pass for many.
"Just as Kṛṣṇā had previously said,
'May the Blessed One grant me not one husband,' he likewise replied to her, 'So be it, a boon.'"
For the god knows what is supreme here,
or if this has been ordained by Śaṅkara;
whether it be dharma or adharma, there is no fault of mine in this matter.
"Let these take her hand according to the prescribed rite;
for Kṛṣṇā has been assigned to them according to their pleasure.
This is not the rule for the marriage of mortals."
For these gods and Draupadī herself are Lakṣmī;
by her own past deeds and through the grace of the God of Gods, she obtained five husbands.
This righteous marriage was ordained for them alone—
that Draupadī became the wife of the Pāṇḍavas;
other men and women would not have been so.
"O lord of men, the Dharma spoken by Manu would not exist [otherwise].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the Blessed One spoke to the King of Dharma.
Today is indeed an auspicious day, O son of Pāṇḍu;
today the moon enters the conjunction with the asterism Puṣya;
therefore, you should take Kṛṣṇā’s hand first today.
"O lord of men, first take the hand of this daughter of the Pāñcāla king.
Then both Kṛṣṇa and Drupada arrived there.
Where Kuntī remains with her sons, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, thereupon Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Today is an auspicious day; the moon will be in conjunction with Rohiṇī."

"In due order, let all these tigers among men, the Pāṇḍavas, take Draupadī’s hand according to dharma; this has been foreseen of old, O sinless one. Then King Yajñasena, together with his son, [spoke].
Having brought together many excellent gifts suitable for a bridegroom, he bathed his daughter Kṛṣṇā and adorned her with numerous jewels.
Then all his friends,
counselors, and ministers gathered there,
filled with supreme joy, to witness the wedding.
The twice-born and the citizens, according to their rank, [gathered there];
his palace was graced by those seeking wealth,
and its courtyard was adorned with scattered lotuses and water-lilies.
Variegated with a multitude of highly precious gems, it shone like the sky filled with spotless stars;
then those sons of the Kuru king—
Adorned with earrings, young men—
clad in costly garments, anointed with excellent sandalwood paste, having performed their ritual ablutions and completed the auspicious ceremonies— [approached].
O Lord, together with the family priest Dhaumya, who possessed a splendor equal to fire,
they all entered that assembly hall in due order according to the prescribed rite.
Like great bulls rejoicing in the cow-pen,
he then, having composed himself, that master of the Vedas,
offered oblations with mantras into the blazing fire.
The knower of mantras, having led Yudhiṣṭhira together with Kṛṣṇā,
caused them both to perform a circumambulation while holding hands.
That master of the Vedas caused the brahmins to be summoned; Yudhiṣṭhira, having gratified them with food,
cows, and various unprecedented jewels.
He took the hand of the daughter of the king of men when the fire had been duly kindled by Dhaumya with sacred mantras;
then flowers fell from the sky.
A wind blew with most delightful fragrance;
then, having given leave to him who graced the arena,
the domestic priest departed from Rājagṛha.
And in this order, O lord of men, those sons of kings then took the hand of that excellent woman day after day,
they who possessed the most sublime forms.
These great chariot-warriors, who increase the Kaurava lineage,
were there; and then the brahmin-sage spoke this supreme, wondrous account that transcends the human realm.
That woman of great majesty and slender waist remained indeed a maiden day after day;

for with respect to her elder brother, she was devoted to the status of a wife to a father-in-law, and with respect to her younger brother, she was devoted to the status of a wife to a husband’s younger brother.

And among the Pāñcālas of middle rank, three each were given for the three [classes]. When the marriage was performed, Drupada gave wealth of many forms and of the highest quality to those great chariot-warriors.
A hundred chariots adorned with excellent gold,
each yoked to four horses and featuring golden bridles and garlands; likewise, a hundred elephants accompanied by female elephants.
A hundred mountains as if made of golden peaks;
a hundred horses adorned with jewels and gold,
swift as thought, each twelve years of age.
Likewise, there were a hundred female slaves in the prime of their youth, adorned with costly garments, ornaments, raiment, and garlands;
and there were couches, seats, and vessels made of gold.
And Saumaki gave other great treasures and various riches, numbering ten times ten thousand each, with fire as witness.
In the same way, garments and ornaments, endowed with splendor and of great value, [were given].
And when the wedding was completed, the Pāṇḍavas then...
Having obtained that splendor abounding in jewels,
those mighty ones, who were like Indra himself,
lived there in the city of that Pāñcāla king.
O King, all the sons of Pāṇḍu were likewise gratified by her auspicious conduct, character, and composure;
and at that time, Yājñasenī was likewise [gratified] by them.
He increased his joy by his own virtuous deeds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But for Drupada, who had entered into an alliance with the Pāṇḍavas...

There was no fear whatsoever, even from the gods, in any way. Having thus performed the marriage in the palace of Drupada, all those heroes dwelt there, just as merit-bestowing beings who travel through the atmosphere.

Having approached Kuntī, those women of the high-souled Drupada announced their names and touched her feet with their heads. And Kṛṣṇā, clothed in silk and having performed the auspicious marriage rites, [stood there].
Having offered her salutations to her mother-in-law, she stood bowed with palms joined in reverence.
Then Prithā, out of affection, spoke words of blessing to her daughter-in-law Draupadī, who was endowed with beauty and auspicious marks and possessed of virtuous conduct and refined manners.
Just as Indrāṇī is to Indra, Svāhā to Agni,
Rohiṇī to Soma, and Damayantī to Nala;
just as Bhadrā is to Vaiśravaṇa and Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha.
As Sītā was to the son of Daśaratha, as the daughter of the mountain was to Rudra, as Lopāmudrā was to Agastya, as Jānakī was to Rāma,
and as Lakṣmī is to Nārāyaṇa— so may you be toward your husbands.
Just as Vāgdevī is to Caturānana, Girijā to Giriśa, and Uṣā is firmly established in Bhānu,
so too are you firm and beloved.
O blessed lady, you shall be a mother of living sons and a mother of heroes, endowed with great happiness;
you shall be fortunate, possessed of enjoyments, the wife of a sacrificer, and devoted to your husband.
You shall likewise [honour] guests who have arrived, the virtuous, children, the elderly, and teachers.
While you honor them according to the law, may your years pass by constantly;
may you follow the king who is devoted to dharma as he is consecrated over the principal kingdoms and cities of Kurujāṅgala.
"O you who are endowed with virtues, make the entire earth— which was conquered by your husbands of great strength through their prowess—
belong to the Brahmins at the great Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha). O virtuous one, whatever jewels exist upon the earth, let them all be yours."
"Attain those [happinesses], O auspicious lady, and may you be happy for a hundred autumns. And just as I rejoice today, O daughter-in-law, seeing you clothed in silk,
so shall I rejoice even more when your sons are endowed with virtues."
Then Hari, Mādhava, sent to the Pāṇḍavas, who had taken wives,
golden ornaments variegated with pearls and lapis lazuli,
as well as costly garments from various regions.
There were woolen blankets, skins, and precious gems, all soft to the touch and auspicious;
various large beds, seats, and vehicles;
and hundreds of vessels variegated with lapis lazuli and diamonds.
Endowed with beauty, youth, and grace, and well-adorned,
they had faces like the full moon; born of the lotus lineage,
they possessed the fragrance of lotuses, faces like lotuses, and eyes resembling lotus petals.
With ears beautifully adorned with pearls and strings of gems, and foreheads marked with seven dots;
burdened by the weight of their full breasts, with necks like conch shells and shapely noses;
possessing long, black, beautiful hair and slender waists that could be grasped in a single fist.

Kṛṣṇa bestowed upon him thousands of female attendants from various lands— women whose hair was like a row of bees, whose navels resembled whirlpools, whose broad hips were like planks, and whose pairs of thighs were like the trunks of plantain trees.
He gave them well-trained elephants of the *bhadra* breed and excellent horses beautifully adorned;
he also gave chariots yoked to docile steeds and decorated with auspicious golden bands,
as well as crores of unrefined gold.
The immeasurable-souled Madhusūdana sent that which had been prepared for the feast;
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira accepted it all,
filled with supreme joy and desiring to please Govinda.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, through the trustworthy spies of the kings, this report was brought forward:
that the auspicious Draupadī had been united with the Pāṇḍavas as her husbands.
He by whom that bow was drawn and the target pierced by that great-souled one—
he is Arjuna, the best among victors, the wielder of mighty arrows and the bow.
He who, being powerful, lifted up Śalya, the king of Madra, and whirled him around.
Enraged, he even terrified men in battle with his tree,
yet there was no agitation whatsoever in that high-souled one;
for Bhīma was of terrible touch, the one who struck down the limbs of the enemy host.
He who then, fighting in battle, overcame Duryodhana—
he is that king, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, the recipient of the highest fortune, the enhancer of wisdom;
he who fought with the younger brothers of Duryodhana as if they were his equals.
Those two twins, endowed with virtuous conduct and possessed of perfected strength and prowess,
were like kings who have dispelled their feverish anxiety once they have dispatched their spies;
so it was when the kings heard that the sons of King Pāṇḍu had assumed the forms of Brahmins.
A great wonder arose among the sons of Kuntī and the lords of men,
for it had been heard previously that Kuntī, along with her sons, had been burnt in the house of lac;
so too was it known by all the kings and the illustrious rulers of the realms.
"All the kings then considered them as if born again,
censuring Bhīṣma and Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Kaurava for that most cruel deed committed by Purocana."
Vaiśampāyana; Śakuni;
Vaiśampāyana.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When he ought to destroy those sons of Pṛthā, who are righteous, endowed with good conduct, and devoted to their mother’s pleasure and welfare— such as they are.
Then, O Bhārata, when the *svayaṃvara* had taken place, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, corrupted by Karṇa and Saubala, deliberated together:
"Some enemy must be weakened, and likewise another must be oppressed."
"O son of Kuntī, all the Kṣatriyas are, in my view, to be exterminated. If you all depart after being thus defeated,
without having made some agreement, it will undoubtedly cause you grief."
"This place and this time are for our rescue of the Pāṇḍavas;
if you do not act thus, you will become objects of ridicule in the world, [especially] since these people have taken refuge with you and desire a ruler of the earth."
In my view, King Drupada possesses little vigor or strength,
as long as these bulls among the Vṛṣṇis do not know that they are alive;
and so too does the powerful Śiśupāla, the tiger among men, the king of Cedi.
Having attained union with the high-souled King Drupada,
O King, they will become most difficult to overcome; of this there is no doubt,
until all the lords of men attain immovability.
We shall resolve upon the slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas at that very moment,
lest they escape again from this place— having been freed from Bhīma, who was like the mouth of a venomous serpent— and a great fear should enter us.
For those who have arrived here and for these city-dwellers,
it is as difficult for me to stand between them as it would be between two great rams; the armies of the mighty, led by the wielder of the plow himself, are already drawn up.
"O bulls among men, before the birds [of war] descend upon the army of the Kurus,
let this city be destroyed by a total assault;
I consider this to be the supreme course of action for the present time."
Having heard the words of the evil-minded Śakuni as he spoke,
the son of Somadatta then uttered these supreme words,
having understood the seven constituent elements of both himself and his opponent.
Likewise, one should take into account the place and the time, as well as the sixfold elements:
stability, growth, decline, the territory, allies, and prowess;
having thus scrutinized these, one should then attack an enemy who is afflicted by calamity.
Therefore, I consider the Pāṇḍavas to be endowed with friends and a treasury;

established in strength and established in valor, they are beloved by their subjects because of their own deeds. By their very form, they captivate the eyes and the minds of all beings upon this earth.
Arjuna delighted the ears of men with his sweet speech; indeed,
the subjects did not serve him out of mere divine right alone,
but performed whatever action was pleasing to his mind.
For the speech of Pārtha, who speaks so beautifully, was never found to be improper, nor unattached, nor untrue, nor unpleasant; indeed,
those sons were thus endowed with virtues and possessed the marks of royalty.
I do not see those who are capable of uprooting them by force;
for the power of majesty is vast, the power of counsel is abundant,
and likewise the power of energy is always superior among the sons of Pṛthā.
Yudhiṣṭhira, truly knowing the proper time for his hereditary allies and friends,
strives to conquer the enemy through conciliation, gifts, sowing dissension, and force, and not through anger; such is my opinion.
Having purchased his enemies with wealth and having secured both allies and riches,
and having made his own foundation very firm, the son of Pāṇḍu then slays his foes;
I consider the Pāṇḍavas to be invincible even by the gods led by Vāsava.
Both Kṛṣṇa and Saṃkarṣaṇa are always intent upon their welfare; if you consider this to be for your own benefit, and if my opinion is approved by you,
let us make peace with the Pāṇḍavas and return whence we came.
This most excellent of cities is protected by high gate-towers and hundreds of upper chambers, and it is surrounded by water;
it is likewise stocked with grass, grain, fuel, liquids, as well as machines, weapons, and medicines.

For it was properly equipped with wide gate-panels, storehouses for goods, and granaries; it possessed formidable, lofty great wheels and was enclosed by massive watchtowers; it had strong ramparts and turrets, and was covered with a network of *śataghnī* weapons.
Among the ramparts known to be made of brick, wood, or earth by human builders, O hero, that which contains a human embryo is honored by those who construct walls; therefore,
this city shines brilliantly with its pale white inner core of human origin.
The city was surrounded on all sides by many *sāla* trees;
the subjects of the high-souled Drupada were devoted to him—
both those from within and those from without— all of whom were honored with gifts and respect.
Knowing that these [Pandavas] have been obstructed by kings of terrible prowess,
the Dasharhas will arrive with their weapons raised high.
Therefore, let us make peace between the son of Dhritarashtra and the Pandavas.
"If my word is to be trusted, let us go to our own kingdom;
if it pleases you all, let this be my will. I consider this to be well-done and a source of security for the rulers of the earth."
Having heard the words of the son of Somadatta, Karṇa Vaikartana,
the bull among men and knower of the proper time for all actions, spoke these meaningful words at the right moment, preceded by sound policy.
I do not find fault with these words; let my established position be heard:
men should not resort to duplicity in any undertaking, for when the mind is divided, no action is successfully accomplished.
But by means of marching, sitting in wait, and likewise by causing exhaustion—this city cannot be destroyed by those means; moreover, its siege is inauspicious.
As I reflect upon it, I consider this to be the time for a direct assault.
As long as the Vṛṣṇis— those who delight in battle, powerful, joyful, contented, and endowed with the strength of their own arms— do not seize our rear,
let them crush the rampart and let the iron bars fill [the gates].
"Let them release water; let the uneven ground be made level. Let the ditch be filled with a great quantity of grass and wood.
Let it be proclaimed among the enemy kings' armies: 'Whoever shall slay [him]..."
He shall receive elephants, horses, or foot soldiers, along with gifts and honors:
ten thousand for an elephant, and five thousand each for horses and foot soldiers;
for a chariot, the kings will give twice as much wealth as for an elephant.
Whether it be a fool or an elder who is attached to the pleasures of desire, or those whose minds are not set on battle— let such cowards remain where they are;
no breach should be made, nor should one go unless commanded.
"Protect your glory—blessings be upon you! We shall surely conquer the city. The winds blow favorable to us from all sides, as do the beasts and birds;
the fires blaze forth, and so too do our weapons and armor."
Then, having heard Karna’s words, those rulers of the earth, desiring the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, marched forth, shaking their enemies in battle;
for their minds were entirely unattached to the objects of the senses.
Furthermore, for those who slay their enemies, the very birth and the battle itself are like this:
with the son of Vikartana as the preceding wind, the roar of the Sindhu waves,
Duḥśāsana as the great fish, and Duryodhana as the mighty crocodile.
That terrifying ocean of kings, formidable in appearance and with a fearsome roar,
rushed with speed toward that city, keeping it to its right;
that invincible host was ablaze with the fire of weapons and like venomous serpents.
Perceiving that [the enemy] had been driven out, the sons of Drupada cried out;
those mighty warriors, on excellent chariots with a roar like the clouds,
emerged from the city gate, terrifying their enemies in battle.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, Sumitra, Priyadarśana,
Citraketu, Suketu, and the heroic Dhvajāsena—
these powerful sons of King Drupada are seekers of victory.
And Drupada, of great heroism, with his white turban as his banner,
possessing a white fan and a white umbrella, and with a white standard and vehicle, shone resplendent in the midst of his circle of sons, O best of kings.
Like the moon risen on the full-moon night in the midst of the luminaries,
the Kuru army then rushed toward the approaching host of Drupada, which possessed straight-flying arrows and was as imperishable as a banner-top raised aloft.
From both of them there arose a terrible and tumultuous sound,
like that of two colliding rivers as the two armies struck one another;
and in every direction, those divisions were scattered with chariots, elephants, and horses.
The scattered celestial lights shone forth on all sides as the great, tumultuous sound of beaten kettledrums arose;
then the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, filled with indignation, marched out from there.
Then, having mounted resplendent chariots that rumbled like clouds and were yoked with excellent horses—

chariots equipped with bows and banners— the bulls of the Bharata race, the sons of Pāṇḍu, stood there with their bows raised. Having seen those sons of Pāṇḍu stationed upon their chariots with bows in hand, [the enemy forces prepared for battle].
A trembling and a quivering arose in the hearts of the kings.
Then, as the sons of Pṛthā set forth in battle, that army of Drupada was filled with supreme joy and exultation regarding their victory.
For a moment, there was a great confusion among the troops;
then they fought in single combat, making death their only point of retreat.
In that battle, Sumitra and Priyadarśana struck one another.
While Jayadratha and Karṇa looked on,
Arjuna, seeing that those two who were dear to their friends had been slain,
killed the son of Jayadratha there in the presence of his father.

Dhanañjaya struck down Subāhu, the younger brother of Vṛṣasena and the highly heroic son of Karṇa, from the seat of his chariot. Seeing those two sons slain, the two powerful lions among kings [fainted].
Those two mighty-armed ones did not flinch, like two noble elephants at a blow;
undaunted, they both advanced toward Phalguna’s chariot,
their hand-guards fastened and protecting one another.
A clash occurred between those two in that great battle,
like that of Vṛtra and Śambara with the wielder of the thunderbolt in a great conflict;
there, those two bulls among men slew Phalguna’s three horses.
Then a tumultuous roar of "kili-kili" arose among the Kurus.
Seeing those horses slain, the powerful Bhīmasena yoked his chariot with new horses in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Seeing the chariot approaching, the two subduers of foes— the son of Subala and the son of Somadatta— advanced with Duryodhana at their head.
Then the mighty Bhimasena, undaunted in spirit, [encountered] those five.
He fought with those powerful heroes as a lord fights against the objects of the senses; though hemmed in by them, that victor in assembly did not succumb to fear,
like a lion hemmed in by five rutting elephants.
With five sharp arrows each, those five simultaneously sent his charioteer and horses to the abode of Vaivasvata;
then, descending from that excellent chariot whose horses had been slain, the great car-warrior—
Raising his sword, the Pāṇḍava traversed various paths;
he moved about, striking down his enemies upon the necks of horses, upon wheels, upon yokes, and even upon shafts, just as Suparṇa strikes down serpents.
Seeing him without bow, without armor, and without a chariot,
the car-warriors led by Arjuna— Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandin, and the two invincible twins in battle— rushed toward that tiger among men.
When that battle involving the son of Daśaratha had commenced with showers of arrows,
chariots, banners, and flags— all was obscured.
That battle, having continued for a long time, seemed to be equal on both sides.
Then the mighty-armed Arjuna rushed forward again on his chariot. Seeing him approaching, the mighty-armed bowman Karṇa, the best among those skilled in weapons, checked him with his arrows.
Struck by him, the son of Pṛthā, the descendant of Vāsava, the Pāṇḍava, filled with rage, fixed three arrows resembling thunderbolts for the purpose of slaying Karṇa.
Struck by those arrows, Karṇa leaned against his flagpole.

The charioteer quickly bore away that conqueror of enemy cities in his chariot. Then, once Karṇa had been defeated, a great fear entered the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra upon seeing the highly exultant Pāñcālas.
Seeing that army of Saubala trembling excessively,
the hero repeatedly comforted them with deep-toned words,
along with all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra led by Duryodhana.
That army, though shaken by the son of Pṛthā, rallied once again.
Then, seeing Duryodhana, Bhīma of terrible prowess,
that mighty-armed one, became enraged as he recalled the house of lac.
Then, at the head of the battlefield, he beheld a vast tree standing like a long-stretched line, fifty fathoms high,
with a massive trunk and great height, rising up like the banner of Śakra.
Wearing variegated garlands and garments, and adorned with hundreds of banners,
the powerful one raised a *sāla* tree with his two hands and, lifting it up in battle,
charged at his enemies in the fray like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the asuras.
Afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena and struck down by Phalguna,
those armies protected by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were unable to hold their ground;
their warriors were bewildered, and their horses and elephants were exhausted.
Bhīma drove them in all directions, like the wind scattering clouds in the sky.
As they retreated, joyless and deprived of their elephants and horses,
[the Pandavas] did not pursue them, nor did they strike them, nor did they say anything harsh.
The Kṣatriyas, wounded by arrows, returned to their own camps;
the others also, joyful and bringing happiness to the citizens, marched toward the city. For but a moment did enmity exist between them and the Pāṇḍavas.
As long as that great battle continued, resembling the conflict between the gods and the asuras,
they all conducted themselves with perfect propriety and spoke of the bride as one truly obtained.
They declared Drupada to have achieved his purpose, as did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
Śakuni, the King of Sindhu, Karṇa, and Duryodhana—
these too felt that grief in their hearts, though they did not speak it with their voices.
Then all the kings departed, each returning by the way he had come.
For all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had already departed for Hastināpura even before the siege of the city by the Pāṇḍavas; therefore, O horsemen,
go and report that we are safe to Śauri.
Having reached the city of Dvāravatī in a short time,
Saṃkarṣaṇa and Upendra, who were skilled in speech, spoke these words:
"The Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis ask after the welfare of all the Pāṇḍavas."
They said that they themselves were unhurt and liberated from the house of lac;
they spoke of the lotus-eyed Draupadī as won at the assembly,
saying she was equal to themselves in character, conduct, and composure.
Having heard those words, Kṛṣṇa spoke these further words to them:
"I know all this; however, regarding the slaying of that Rākṣasa, Keśava then mobilized the fourfold army."
He quickly set out toward the city of Pañcāla to offer his service;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa and the mighty Keśava,
together with all the Yādavas, went to the Pāṇḍavas.
Having honored his father’s sister and Drupada according to the prescribed rites,
and having adorned Draupadī with brilliant and costly ornaments,
she was duly honored by the high-souled King Drupada.
Then, in the city of the Pañcālas, they beheld [the king] together with the Pāṇḍavas;
and when the *svayaṃvara* had concluded, all those kings departed as they had come, having learned that the Pāṇḍavas had been chosen.
Then King Duryodhana, dejected along with his brothers,
Aśvatthāman, his maternal uncle, Karṇa, and Kṛpa,
turned back upon seeing that Śvetavāhana (Arjuna) had been chosen by Draupadī.
But Duḥśāsana, feeling ashamed, spoke very softly;
the king, his face parched with distress and his heart burning with grief, said:
"If that man were not a Brāhmaṇa, he would never have won Draupadī."
"O King, no one truly knows that Dhanañjaya [in his true nature];
I consider destiny supreme, while human effort is useless. Fie on our human effort, my dear, since the Pāṇḍavas are carrying away [the wealth] here!"

Having bound our eyes, the sons of Pṛthā married the daughter of Drupada before the kings; having caused those kings to place their left feet [upon the scale], they were released by the sons of Pṛthā. How have they been liberated from this consumer of the sacrificial offering—the house of lac?
"Where has our manliness, our courage, and even our intelligence gone?
Today we have been slain by our maternal uncle, who trusted Purocana;
having failed to burn the Pāṇḍavas, he himself has been consumed by fire."
"O uncle, I consider the Pāṇḍavas to be even wiser than I;
they have no fear of death, having been delivered from the house of lac. Thus they conversed, while censuring Purocana.
The five sons of the Kirātī, and the highly intelligent Vidura,
entered Hastināpura dejected and dispirited;
terrified and devoid of resolve upon seeing the Pārthas of great prowess.
Having considered them as liberated from the consumer of oblations (Agni) and joined with Drupada,
and likewise reflecting upon Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin,
as well as the other sons of Drupada who are all experts in every form of warfare.
Seeing the faces of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vidura was filled with joy;
his lotus-like heart and face blossomed like a lotus flower beholding the sun.
Then Vidura, having heard that the Pāṇḍavas had been chosen by Draupadī...
Seeing all those powerful heroes joined with Drupada,
and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra arriving ashamed and with their pride shattered,
the steward Kṣattṛ, O lord of people, then became joyful in mind toward Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Filled with wonder, Vaiśampāyana said: "By good fortune the Kurus are prospering;
they have been liberated from all calamities and released from the conflict of kings."
Enveloped by the splendor of Kṛṣṇā as well as by the glory of heroes,
and having heard Vidura’s words— referring to the Kauravas in general—
that king, filled with contentment, leaped up with joy.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, green with joy, stood as if paralyzed for a moment.
But King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Vicitravīrya, having heard those words of Vidura, spoke, being exceedingly pleased: "By good fortune! By good fortune! O Bhārata.
For the lord of men, whose wisdom was his sight, through lack of discernment thought that Duryodhana had been chosen by Drupada’s daughter as his eldest son;
yet he then ordered many ornaments for Draupadī.
"O Kṛṣṇa, let all manner of excellent and variegated ornaments be brought for my sons," he then said to his son Duryodhana. Thereafter, Vidura informed him that the Pāṇḍavas had been chosen.
Do not think of your sons merely as "the Kauravas" out of common usage; they are filled with the joy and satisfaction of seeing their sons grow,
for by my word, these sons of Pāṇḍu have been raised.
The sons of Pṛthā, protected by Kṛṣṇā, were liberated from that royal conflict; all those heroes were safe and sound, honored by Drupada,
and received with great respect by Saṃkarṣaṇa and Kṛṣṇa— the joy of the Pāṇḍus.
Having heard these words of Vidura, the lord of men, in order to conceal his true feelings, said, "By good fortune! By good fortune! "It is so, Vidura; may you be blessed, if the Pāṇḍavas are alive."

Kuntī was likewise of virtuous conduct, and there was a kinship with Drupada. Born in the lineage of Vasu within the preeminent Matsya clan, he was advanced in conduct, learning, and austerity, and was a leader among kings.
His sons and likewise his grandsons were all firm in their virtuous vows. O Kṣattṛ, the joy born from the nectar of your words did not fit within my body; "Embrace me! you said to me again and again.

Extending his arms far out to conceal his wicked intent, he said: "Come, come, wise Vidura! You ought to embrace me. Having spoken thus, he drew Vidura toward him, knowing the state of his own inner mind.
The evil-minded one firmly embraced them with his arms until they were breathless;
and he likewise seized many other kinsmen of theirs who were endowed with strength and had assembled at that very *svayaṃvara* along with the Pāṇḍavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Just as those sons of Pāṇḍu are mine, so too are they even more so for me.
O Vidura, I consider this increased affection of mine to be a source of growth."
"O Lord, that affection which I have for the sons of Pāṇḍu does not exist elsewhere;
this is my constant and firm conviction, O Kṣattṛ, and I swear it to you in truth by truth.
Furthermore, they have many other kinsmen who are exceedingly powerful."
"It is my conviction that my sons have perished because they were wicked-souled,
whereas those heroic Pāṇḍavas are well and possessed of allies; meanwhile,
my sons, headed by Duryodhana, were always devoid of friends."
When I heard that the sons of Pāṇḍu had been consumed by fire, from that moment on I have burned with grief day and night; I neither eat nor sleep.
My sons were without allies, like birds whose wings have been clipped.

"Listen to me in truth, O Kṣattṛ: with my sons as my good allies, my empire has today become stable for as long as the moon and sun endure. For who, O Kṣattṛ, having encountered Drupada along with his kinsmen as an ally..."
"A king, even if he has lost his fortune, should not desire to exist merely for the sake of wealth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To him who was speaking thus, Vidura replied.
O Great King, this understanding has taken root in your heart; O Lord of Men, if it remains steadfast through deed, mind, and speech,
may this understanding of yours endure forever, O King, for a hundred years.

Having spoken thus, O King, Vidura departed for his own residence. Having spoken thus, O high-minded one, the Kṣattṛ went forth to his own home. Then, O lord of the people, both Duryodhana and the son of Rādhā [proceeded].
Then, approaching Dhṛtarāṣṭra, they spoke these words:
"O King, we were unable to speak to you in the presence of Vidura; therefore, we shall speak when you are alone. What is it that you intend to do?"
"O dear one, O best of men, that you consider the prosperity of your rival to be your own prosperity,
and that you offer praise in the presence of the Steward (Kṣattṛ),
while there is another duty to be performed, O sinless king, you are doing something else."

"O dear one, we must constantly strive to strike at their strength. Therefore, let us deliberate on what we should do now that the time has come, so that they— with their sons, armies, and kinsmen— may not devour us."
01,193.000*1959 = 00 Vaiśampāyana said:
01,193.000*1959_01 O lord of the people, having been addressed thus by Duryodhana and by Karṇa,
01,193.000*1959_02 Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to his son and to the Sūta’s son.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I too think this very same thing as you two;
however, I do not wish to reveal my true disposition toward Vidura."
Therefore, I shall specifically proclaim their virtues alone,
lest Vidura perceive my intention through my gestures.
And as for what you consider appropriate, O Suyodhana, speak that.
"O son of Rādhā, you too must say what you consider to have been achieved.
Duryodhana said:
"Today, by means of skilled brahmins who are well-trained and effective in their tasks..."
"Let us create a division among the sons of Kuntī and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī;
or else, let King Drupada and all his sons and ministers be enticed away by means of vast accumulations of wealth."
"Abandon King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī;
or else, let them choose to dwell right there with him. Alternatively, let them describe his residence here as being full of faults, one by one."
Let those Pāṇḍavas, being divided, set their minds upon that very place;
or else, let certain men who are skillful and expert in stratagems cause the sons of Pṛthā to be alienated from one another through the manipulation of their affections.
Or let them alienate Kṛṣṇā from him, for that would be easy to accomplish due to their numbers;
or else, O King, let men skilled in stratagems cause a rift between her and the Pāṇḍavas, or specifically with Bhīmasena.
"Let his death be carried out by those in disguise, for he is superior in strength to them.
Relying upon him, the son of Kuntī has long held us in contempt;
for he is both fierce and heroic, and indeed their ultimate refuge."
But when he has been slain, O King, they will strive no longer for the kingdom, their enthusiasm destroyed and their vigor lost, for he was their refuge. Indeed,
Arjuna is invincible in battle when Vṛkodara protects his rear.
Without him, Phalguna is not even a quarter-match for the son of Rādhā in battle.
Knowing their own great weakness and excluding Bhīmasena,
they will perish as weaklings once they realize we are strong.
O King, when the sons of Pṛthā have arrived here, acting under the power of our command,
we shall proceed with their destruction according to our resolve;
yet among them, some wise men will display their pride.
"O King, let the sons of Drupada be divided from their enemies;
or else, let them be enticed by beautiful women so that each son of Kuntī may become detached from Kṛṣṇā."
"Or let the son of Rādhā be dispatched to bring them here;
having formed an alliance with these thieves, let them be slain by trusted agents.
Of these proposed methods, whichever you consider to be faultless,"

"Adopt a plan against him before time passes us by. As long as trust has not yet been established in Drupada, that bull among kings, you will be able to act today; but after that, you will no longer be able to do so."
"O father, this resolve of mine proceeds for the sake of subduing him—whether it be right or wrong; what do you think of it, O son of Rādhā?
Karṇa said:
"O Duryodhana, it is my opinion that your wisdom is not sound. For the Pāṇḍavas cannot be overcome by you through stratagem, O joy of the Kurus;
indeed, they were already sought out by you with subtle means in the past."
O hero,
O king, when they were still staying right here in your presence like infants whose wings had not yet grown, you were not able to subdue them, nor were you able to cause them harm.
"O Acyuta, my mind is this: today those sons of Kuntī have grown their wings, are established in a foreign land, and have prospered in every way; they cannot be overcome by any stratagem.
Nor can they be brought to calamity, for they are protected by destiny."
Apprehensive yet desirous of their ancestral station,
it is impossible to sow dissension among them;
for those who are devoted to a single wife do not divide against one another.

Nor could Kṛṣṇā have been alienated from them by others, for she chose those who were emaciated; how much less so today, when they are radiant? Moreover, having many husbands is a quality desired by women.
And Kṛṣṇā has obtained him; she cannot easily be alienated from him.
Furthermore, the King of Pañcāla is of noble conduct and that monarch is not fond of wealth;
he will certainly not abandon the sons of Kuntī even for the gift of his kingdom.
Likewise, his son is virtuous and devoted to the Pāṇḍavas;
therefore, I do not think they can be overcome by any means whatsoever. O best of the Bharatas, let prowess alone be your recourse against the Pāṇḍavas.
But this, O bull among men, is what we ought to do now:
O lord of the people, as long as those sons of Pāṇḍu have not yet established their roots, they must be struck down; let your prowess be approved by you.
"As long as our side is great and the Pāñcāla king is weak, so long must you strike at them; do not hesitate. Our mounts are numerous and our allies are many."
O Gāndhārī, exert your prowess quickly while they have not yet reached you;
and as long as the Pāñcālya king does not set his mind upon an effort together with his sons of great heroism, exert your prowess quickly even now.

Drupada has always been an enemy who was constantly humiliated by you; while he has not yet grown strong through his allies, let your prowess be directed toward him. Before the descendant of Vṛṣṇi arrives, leading the Yādava host, [act now].
O lord of the earth, for the sake of the kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas, display your prowess immediately;
there is nothing— be it wealth, various enjoyments, or even the entire kingdom—
that Kṛṣṇa would not sacrifice for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
The great-souled Bharata obtained the earth through prowess;
and Indra, the subduer of Pāka, conquered the three worlds through prowess. O lord of the people, they praise the prowess of a Kṣatriya.
"For valor, O bull among kings, is indeed the innate duty of heroes. Therefore,
O King, having quickly crushed Drupada with our great fourfold army, let us bring the Pāṇḍavas here."
For the Pāṇḍavas cannot be overcome by conciliation, nor by bribery, nor by sowing dissension; therefore, destroy them by valor alone. Having conquered them through valor, enjoy this entire earth.
"O lord of men, I see no other means for accomplishing this task here.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard the words of the son of Rādhā, the powerful Dhṛtarāṣṭra—"
Having honored him, he then spoke these words:
"O woman of great wisdom, this speech, endowed with such prowess, is fitting for you, the son of a Sūta who has mastered the use of weapons."
"Furthermore, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Vidura,
as well as you two, should deliberate upon that plan which will result in our happiness.
Then, the highly illustrious king summoned all those ministers.
Then, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra held a consultation.
Bhīṣma said:
"A conflict with the sons of Pāṇḍu does not appeal to me in any way whatsoever."
Without a doubt, Pāṇḍu was to me exactly as Dhṛtarāṣṭra is;
and just as the sons of Gāndhārī are regarded by me, so too are the sons of Kuntī. Just as they are to be protected by me, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, so are they to be protected by you.
"O Bhārata, just as it is for me and for the king, so it is for Duryodhana, for all the Kurus, and for others as well. Since things have come to this, I do not approve of war with them."
"O heroes, let the earth be given today in accordance with the agreement;
for this kingdom belongs to their great-grandfathers, as well as to the father of those best of the Kurus."
"O Duryodhana, my dear son, just as you regard this kingdom as yours, so too do the Pāṇḍavas regard it as their paternal inheritance. Had those ascetic sons of Pāṇḍu not obtained the kingdom..."
How much less could this have happened to you or to any other descendant of Bharata?
O bull of the Bharatas, if you obtained the kingdom through righteousness,
it is my opinion that they too had already obtained the kingdom long ago.
"Let half of the kingdom be given to them with sweetness alone;
for this, O tiger among men, is for the welfare of all people.
If it is done otherwise than this, it will not be for our benefit."
"Your infamy as well will be complete, there is no doubt.
Devote yourself to the preservation of your reputation, for reputation is the supreme strength. Perform the duty that is appropriate for your lineage."
Fame, however, is the supreme splendor; for it is said that the life of a man whose fame has perished is indeed fruitless. O Kaurava, as long as a man's fame does not perish, [his life endures].

O son of Gāndhārī, he lives only so long as his fame remains; once his reputation is lost, he perishes. Therefore, O mighty-armed one, attend to this duty befitting the Kuru lineage; perform that which is worthy of yourself and your ancestors.

"By good fortune those heroes survive; by good fortune that Pṛthā lives; by good fortune the wicked Purocana, who desired our ruin, has met his end. From the moment those sons of Kuntibhoja’s daughter were thought to have been burnt..."

From that time forth, O Gāndhārī, I have not been able to look upon anyone among the living beings in this world when I hear that Kuntī has met with such a fate, even though you, O son of Pṛthā, had previously attempted to burn them in the house of lac.

"O King, suffering does not arise [from me], for you are the cause of everything. Furthermore, the world does not perceive Purocana as guilty in the same way that it attributes guilt to you, O tiger among men."

Therefore, O Great King, this life of theirs— which destroys your own defilement— and the sight of the Pāṇḍavas must be welcomed; for as long as those heroes live, O joy of the Kurus, [your purpose will not be fulfilled].
Even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself could not have taken their paternal share by force;
for they all stood firm in dharma, all being of one mind,
and were especially excluded from the kingdom through unrighteousness despite its being common to all.
"If dharma must be practiced by you, if my dear wish is to be fulfilled,
and if their welfare is to be secured, then let half [of the kingdom] be given to them.
Droṇa said:
"O King, we have heard that when brought together for counsel, those who act for the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra must speak what is righteous, beneficial, and conducive to fame.
O dear one, this is my own opinion as well, which is the same as that of the high-souled Bhīṣma."
The sons of Kuntī must share [the wealth]; this is the eternal dharma. O Bhārata, let some pleasant-spoken man be sent quickly to Drupada, taking with him abundant jewels for their sake.
Let him take many mutual gifts for him and depart;
likewise, let him speak of the highest prosperity arising from that alliance. And let him say to you, O King, as well as to Duryodhana, that they are being well-pleased.
O Bhārata, he should repeatedly describe Drupada and Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s long-standing intimacy, their affection, and their fitness for the alliance;
and he should repeatedly offer words of consolation to the sons of Kuntī and the two sons of Mādrī.
O Indra among kings, at Draupadī’s request, let him bestow many bright, golden ornaments;
likewise, O bull of the Bharatas, for all the sons of Drupada.
"Having given those highly precious items belonging to all the Pāṇḍavas and to Kuntī, gladden the Pāṇḍavas. Thus,
[speak] words joined with conciliation to Drupada together with the Pāṇḍavas."
Having spoken thus, he should immediately thereafter say regarding their arrival:
"O best among those who know the truth and possess discernment, let peace be established according to your wisdom.
Once the heroes have given their consent, let the auspicious army advance.
"Let Duḥśāsana and Vikarṇa bring the Pāṇḍavas here;
then, O best of kings, being constantly honored by you and with the approval of the subjects, they shall be established in their paternal station."
"O Great King, O Bhārata, I consider such conduct toward those sons of yours to have been entirely appropriate, along with Bhīṣma. Karṇa said:
Bound by wealth and honor, acting as intermediaries in all affairs,
they do not consult for your welfare— what could be more extraordinary than that?
Indeed, he who possesses a wicked mind and a concealed inner self...
One might ask: how can one bring about that which is called the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), as intended by the wise?
Friends do not act for the sake of one's welfare or otherwise during times of financial distress;
for everything—whether it be suffering or happiness—is preceded by destiny.
Whether one's wisdom is cultivated or uncultivated, whether a person is a child or an elder,
whether they have companions or are alone— they find everything everywhere.
Indeed, it is heard that in ancient times there was a certain man known as Ambuvīci.
In Rājagṛha, there was a king of the Magadhas among the rulers of the earth.
That monarch, deprived of all his faculties and reduced to mere breathing,
remained at that time entirely dependent upon his ministers for all affairs of state.
At that time, his ministers were united with one another.
Formerly, there was a minister of his named Mahākarṇi who was the sole ruler;
considering himself to have acquired power, he treated others with contempt.

That fool then seized everything— the king’s women, his jewels, and his wealth— as well as the sovereignty itself. Having taken all that, the greed of that covetous man increased even further through his gain.

For it has been heard by us that, although he strove to seize it, he was unable to take that kingdom from him who had been deprived of all his faculties and whose sole remaining function was breathing. Having taken everything else, he desired to seize even this [kingdom].
Surely that sovereignty of his was ordained by no other [cause] than destiny,
since even he, together with his ministers, is unable to increase his kingdom— provided,
O lord of the people, that his kingdom was indeed ordained for him.
"While all the world looks on, that [result] will certainly remain with you;
if it were ordained otherwise, you would not obtain it despite your efforts.
Knowing this, O wise one, properly discern the competence and incompetence of your ministers."
One must understand the speech of both the wicked and the virtuous.
Droṇa said:
We know that this which is being said is due to a defect in your disposition.
"O wicked one, for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, you proclaim our faults.
But, Karṇa, I speak what is supremely beneficial for the prosperity of the Kurus;
yet if you consider that to be evil, then tell me what is truly supreme benefit."
"If what I say for your supreme benefit is done otherwise,
it is my conviction that the Kurus will perish before long.
Vidura said:
"O King, there is no doubt that you ought to be told what is for your welfare by your kinsmen;
yet words do not find a firm footing in those who are unwilling to listen.
For the best of the Kurus has spoken those words which are indeed for your benefit."
O King, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, did not accept those words;
nor did Karṇa, the son of Rādhā, consider as beneficial for you that excellent and most salutary advice spoken in many ways by Droṇa.
O King, though I reflect upon it, I do not see anyone who is your dearest friend,
nor anyone who might surpass these two lions among men in wisdom or in sacred learning;
for they are both advanced in years, in wisdom, and in Vedic knowledge.

O Indra among kings, you are equal toward them and toward those sons of Pāṇḍu; O King, O Bhārata, you are not inferior to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, nor to Gaya in virtue and truthfulness— of this there is no doubt.
Neither of them has ever spoken anything that was not for your welfare, nor is any harm whatsoever seen to have been done by them toward you;
yet these two tigers among men [behave thus] toward you, O King, though you are innocent.

"O lord of men, how could these two, who possess truth as their prowess and are wise, not advise you for your own welfare? These two best of men in this world will not say anything crooked on your account."
"For this purpose, O King, these two high-souled and immensely radiant ones [have come];
such is my firm conviction, O joy of the Kurus. And out of a desire for wealth, these two knowers of dharma will not speak out of partiality."
O Bhārata, Duryodhana and your other sons considered this indeed to be the highest good; O King, the sons of Pāṇḍu are just as much your sons as these others, O King— of this there is no doubt.
If those ministers should, out of ignorance, deliberate upon anything harmful toward them, they do not perceive what is truly for their own welfare, especially so. Yet,
O King, if there exists a particular distinction in your heart toward them...

"Those who reveal what lies within [the heart] will certainly not bring about your welfare. For this reason, O King, these two great-souled and highly effulgent ones did not say anything openly; for this was not your firm resolve."
And as for what those two bulls among men declared regarding their invincibility—that was indeed so, O tiger among men; may prosperity be yours!
For how could the illustrious Pāṇḍava Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, [be otherwise]?
O King, even Maghavan himself might be able to conquer in battle that great Bhīmasena of mighty arms, who possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants;
for how indeed could he be defeated in combat even by the immortals?
O Bhārata, he by whom Hiḍimba— the destroyer of Rākṣasas, possessed of mighty arms and great strength— was slain in a hand-to-hand struggle;
he who was equal to Rāvaṇa in battle, as well as the Rākṣasa Baka.
O Indra among kings, while Bhīma of terrible prowess was thus fighting,
he heard of the preparations you had made for war with the Pāṇḍavas;
then all the Yādavas will surely come like a swarm of locusts.
Likewise, how can those two skilled warriors in battle— who are like the twin sons of Yama—
be endured in combat by one who desires to live?
In whom reside fortitude, compassion, forgiveness, truthfulness, and prowess.
How could he be defeated in battle, O best of the Pāṇḍavas,
when he has Rāma as his partisan and Janārdana as his counselor? What indeed remains unconquered in combat for those who have Sātyaki on their side?
Those whose father-in-law is Drupada, whose brothers-in-law are the sons of Pṛṣata,
those heroic brothers— the sons of Drupada— headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
and for whom Śiśupāla, the great chariot-warrior of Cedi, is a brother.
O Bhārata, having recognized their incapacity and their right to the inheritance according to dharma, conduct yourself properly toward them.
This great infamy, brought about by Purocana, has been smeared upon us.
O King, by favoring them today, wash away your own [sins];
for this favor toward them is a favor to all of us in our lineage,
as well as the supreme good and the prosperity of the kṣatriya order.
"King Drupada is also a great monarch who has long held enmity toward us;
O King, winning him over would increase our own faction.
Furthermore, O Lord of Men, the Daśārhas are numerous and powerful."
Where Kṛṣṇa is, there they shall be; where Kṛṣṇa is, there is victory.
O King, what man cursed by fate would seek to accomplish through conflict that which can be achieved by conciliation alone?
And having heard that the sons of Pṛthā were alive, O King, the people of the city and the countryside,
intensely longing to see them, desired what was pleasing to them.
So too did Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
"Unrighteous, lacking wisdom, and childish—do not heed their words.
O King, I told you this long ago when you were possessed of virtue:
'This people shall perish through the transgression of Duryodhana.'"
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The Pāṇḍavas are invincible in battle even by Hara or Hari, or even by the three worlds, O protector of the earth; how much less so by those mere mortals?"

The sons of Kuntī are favored by fate; fate is their ultimate refuge. This is evident to everyone, for they were released from the fire of the lacquer house, and having conquered the king of the Gandharvas, they obtained Dhaumya as their priest.

Having reached the city of Pañcāla and slain a hundred thousand non-human beings, and having bent the unbendable bow along with the heads of the kings— what was achieved there by the rulers such as the King of Cedi, the King of Magadha, Karṇa, and the rest?
Do not think that the sons of Pṛthā, though their roots are firmly established, can be conquered simply because they are poor and destitute; the Pāṇḍavas cannot be defeated even by the gods,
as long as Kṛṣṇa, born of the Yādava lineage, remains in this world.
Murāri, the slayer of Keśin, who assumes a human form through his divine play;
the Yogi who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions;
he who is affectionate toward his devotees and likewise dwells within the house of the hearts of his devotees.

The son of Dharma, O great king, does not deserve even this entire earth bounded by the four oceans, let alone the three worlds. Enough of this mindset, O Karṇa; do not incite Suyodhana to further exertion.
"O Śakuni, go; do not sink into the bottomless hell along with the Kauravas!
For we are all the Pāṇḍavas, the lords of the earth together with our kinsmen, as well as the Yādavas led by the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, together with Keśava."

"May we all live together, along with our sons, cattle, and kinsmen; may you likewise awaken us in this manner for a hundred autumns. O King, let not your son, who is so evil-minded, fall under the sway of his own passions."

Having brought together the virtuous Pāṇḍavas and your sons in their entirety, regard them without distinction; do not allow a rift between your eyes. With a heart full of affection, remain inseparable, like the nail from its flesh.
"O son of a Sūta, speak what is pleasing for the sake of the king, not what is unpleasant;
and you, my son, must never speak anything harmful to the sons of Pṛthā. O high-minded one, turn Duryodhana away from the path of unrighteousness."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"The learned Bhīṣma, son of Śantanu, and the venerable sage Droṇa,
as well as you yourself, speak words that are most beneficial and true to me."

"Just as those heroic sons of Kuntī, the great chariot-warriors, are the sons of Pāṇḍu, so too, according to dharma, are they all my sons; of this there is no doubt. Just as this kingdom is ordained for my sons,"

"In the same way, this kingdom belongs to the sons of Pāṇḍu; of this there is no doubt. O Kṣattṛ, go and bring them here along with their mother, treating them with great honor, together with that Kṛṣṇā of celestial beauty, O Bhārata."
"By good fortune those Pārthas live; by good fortune that Pṛthā lives;
by good fortune those great chariot-warriors have obtained the daughter of Drupada.
By good fortune we all prosper; by good fortune Purocana has been destroyed."
"By good fortune, O one of great luster, my supreme sorrow has been removed.
Go yourself, Vidura, and bring them here without delay.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having been addressed thus, Vidura, the knower of royal dharma, then mounted a swift-moving chariot and, after a few days, arrived at the Pañcāla kingdom. Thereupon, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Vidura departed.
O Bhārata,
having taken various jewels and diverse riches for Draupadī, for the Pāṇḍavas, and indeed for Yajñasena himself, he went into the presence of Yajñasena and the Pāṇḍavas.
Having heard that Vidura had arrived, Drupada, the best of kings and a righteous soul,
honored him according to dharma along with his own sons.
Having gone there, that knower of dharma, who was proficient in all the scriptures, [honored him].
O King, he approached Drupada with propriety;
and Drupada, in turn, received Vidura according to dharma and paid honor to the high-souled Vidura as was fitting.
And they both conducted a courteous exchange of inquiries regarding each other's welfare according to custom.
Then, O Bhārata, he beheld the Pāṇḍavas and Vāsudeva there;
having embraced them out of affection, he then inquired after their health.
O lord of the people, having been honored by them in due order according to the word of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with repeated expressions of affection,
those Pāṇḍavas, endowed with humility, bowed down and were embraced.
Seeing them again and again, O King, he shed tears out of joy. Then, O King, he inquired after the well-being of those sons of Pāṇḍu and presented them with various jewels and riches.
O lord of the people, Vidura then bowed down to Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, and [recalled] how gifts had been bestowed upon the Pāṇḍavas, Kuntī, Draupadī, and the sons of Drupada by the Kauravas.
The high-minded one sat down upon a bright golden seat;
having conversed with one another, he spoke again with joy regarding that which had been said by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the descendants of Ajamīḍha concerning the Pāṇḍavas.
There, in the presence of all who were listening, Amitamati spoke all of that; and being humble and full of discipline,
he addressed Drupada in the presence of the sons of Pāṇḍu and Keśava.
"O King, listen with your ministers and your sons to my words. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his sons, his ministers, and his kinsmen,
has repeatedly spoken of his welfare to you, O King, being well-pleased."
"O lord of men, he is deeply pleased with you because of this alliance;
likewise, the highly wise Bhīṣma, son of Śāntanu, together with all the Kauravas, inquires after your welfare in every respect."
"O Pāñcālya, the great archer Bhāradvāja Droṇa, your dear friend,
has approached you for an embrace and inquires after your welfare;
so too does Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who has entered into a kinship with you."
Everyone among the Kauravas likewise considers themselves to have achieved their purpose; yet,
an alliance with the gods does not bring them such great joy,
nor is the recovery of their kingdom regarded by them as so pleasing.
"O Yajñasena, once you have established this alliance with me,
you should understand this and send forth the Pāṇḍavas;
for the Kurus are in great haste to see the heirs of Pāṇḍu."
These bulls among men have been away for a long time, and they,
as well as Pṛthā, will be eager to see the city; and all the noble Kuru women will likewise be eager to see Kṛṣṇā, the princess of Pañcāla.
Desirous of seeing both our city and our kingdom, they await you; therefore,
may your lordship command the sons of Pāṇḍu without delay regarding their departure with their wives— this is my request.
"O King, once the high-souled Pāṇḍavas have been dismissed by you,
I shall then dispatch swift messengers to Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
the sons of Kuntī, along with Kuntī and Kṛṣṇā, will come."
Drupada said:
"O Vidura, O man of great wisdom, it is exactly as you have told me today.
O lord, I too feel supreme joy now that this alliance has been established."
It would indeed be appropriate for these high-souled ones to go to their home;
however, it was not proper for me to say this myself with my own voice.
But when the heroic Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, deems it right—
Let Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and the twins, those bulls among men,
as well as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, both knowers of dharma, then go with the Pāṇḍavas;
for these two tigers among men are devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, we all, along with our followers, are dependent upon you;
we shall do exactly as you tell us out of affection."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Vāsudeva spoke, "My departure is pleasing to me,
provided that King Drupada, who knows all duties, agrees."
Drupada said:
"Just as the hero of the Daśārhas, that best of men and mighty-armed one, considers it to be timely, so too is that my firm resolve."
For just as the highly fortunate sons of Kuntī are mine now, so too are the sons of Pāṇḍu Vāsudeva’s; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and son of Dharma, does not think otherwise.
01,199.009c Whatever is for their benefit, Keśava, that tiger among men, meditates upon;
01,199.009d Vaiśampāyana said: 01,199.009d Kuntī [said].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the highly effulgent Vidura entered the residence of Pṛthā.
Having touched the feet of Pṛthā and bowed his head to the earth, he stood there;
seeing her brother-in-law, Kuntī grieved again and again:
"O son of Vicitravīrya, how have your sons been saved by you?"

"By your grace, we were saved from the house of lac and have returned to you. A tortoise, wherever he may go, thinks of his sons; one should care for one's sons with such concern that they may remain safe and well."
"Your sons live, O bull of the Bharatas;
you are their protector. Just as a cuckoo always causes its offspring to grow unharmed, even so, my dear, have your sons been well protected by me."
"Many sufferings, even those ending in death, have been endured by me;
beyond this, I know not what must be done—you ought to know.
Having spoken thus, she, afflicted by grief and deeply distressed, lamented.
Having prostrated himself, Vidura said, "O Bhārata, do not grieve.
Your mighty sons shall not perish in this world;
in a very short time, they shall be established in their own kingdom."
"Accompanied by all your kinsmen, do not grieve, O Mādhavī.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, having been granted permission by the high-souled Drupada,"
The Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa, and the high-minded Vidura, taking with them Draupadī Kṛṣṇā and the illustrious Kuntī,
went happily to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) for their recreation.
[He gave] elephants adorned with golden girths and neck-chains, decorated with golden hooks,
equipped with ornaments of Jāmbūnada gold, with temples and trunks flowing [with musth],
and attended by great mahouts, fully provided with all weapons.
The king then gave a thousand elephants clad in excellent armor,
and the Pāñcāla prince likewise gave a thousand chariots, resplendent and adorned with gold and jewels, each yoked to four horses.
The king bestowed fifty thousand noble horses adorned with golden trappings and garlands of excellent chowries;
he also gave ten thousand female slaves wearing exquisite ornaments.
Then he gave a thousand slaves who were excellent archers,
along with golden beds, seats, vessels,
other articles, and herds of cattle.
And the King of Pañcāla, exceedingly delighted, gave ten million [pieces of gold] individually,
as well as a full hundred palanquins and five hundred excellent horses.

In this manner, Pāñcāla bestowed these riches for the sake of his daughter; there, the Saumaki king gave the bride-price (harana) which was to be given by her kinsmen. O Bhārata, Dhṛṣṭadyumna went there, taking his sister with him.
Without sounding the thousands of musical instruments being played by many,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Kaurava, upon hearing that the heroes had arrived,
dispatched Kauravas to receive the Pāṇḍavas.
O Bhārata, Vikarṇa the great archer, Citrasena, Droṇa the supreme archer, and Kṛpa the son of Gautama— those heroes,
those great car-warriors, shone resplendent as they were surrounded by them.
Then they slowly entered the city of Hastinapura. Hearing that the Pāṇḍavas had arrived, the citizens, out of curiosity, decorated the city known as Nāgasāhvaya.
Strewn with loose flowers and sprinkled with water on all sides,
perfumed with divine incense and graced with auspicious rites,
the incomparable city shone with hoisted banners and garlands.
With the blaring of conchs and kettledrums and the sounds of various musical instruments,
the city seemed as if it were bursting with curiosity,
where those tigers among men— the destroyers of grief and suffering— resided.
Then the Pāṇḍavas heard various pleasant words, uttered by those wishing to do them a kindness, which were touching to their hearts:
"This tiger among men, the knower of dharma, is returning once more."
"He who protects us according to dharma, like his own heirs—
today the great king Pāṇḍu has arrived from the forest like a peacock from the woods;
he has come desiring to do what is pleasing for us, of this there is no doubt."
"What indeed has not already been done today that would be most dear to us all,
since our heroic husbands, the sons of Kuntī, have returned to us?
If we have given gifts, if we have offered oblations, or if we possess any ascetic merit— "
"Therefore, let the Pāṇḍavas remain in the city for a hundred autumns.
Then they performed the salutation at the feet of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, of the high-souled Bhīṣma, and of others worthy of such honor.
Having exchanged greetings regarding their welfare with the entire city,
they entered their quarters by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Duryodhana’s queen, the daughter of the King of Kāśī,
together with the daughters-in-law of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons,
received Draupadī, who was like a second Śrī.
She honored Gāndhārī, who was worthy of worship like the goddess Śacī descended from heaven;
there, Mādhavī, together with Kṛṣṇā, paid her respects to Gāndhārī.
Having offered her blessings, she then embraced the princess of Pañcāla.
Having embraced the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇā, Gāndhārī thought,
"Pāñcālī is indeed the death of my sons. Reflecting thus, the daughter of Subala spoke to Vidura with reasoned words.
"O Kṣattṛ, if it pleases you, let Kuntī, the princess, together with her daughter-in-law and her attendants, be taken quickly to the residence of Pāṇḍu at an auspicious hour,
moment, lunar mansion, and date."
"Kuntī shall enjoy herself in her own home with her sons just as she pleases.
"So be it," the Kṣattṛ then replied, and he had everything prepared accordingly.
Then the kinsmen honored the Pāṇḍavas exceedingly.
The citizens and the guild-leaders honored the Pāṇḍavas;
likewise, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Bāhlīka with his son,
then performed the rites of hospitality at the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
While those high-souled Pāṇḍavas were living in this manner,
Vidura acted as the director of all their affairs by royal command.
Those mighty and high-souled ones rested for some time.
Summoned by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and by the son of Śantanu,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Kaunteya, together with your brothers, listen to these words of mine."
"The kingdom was expanded by Pāṇḍu; the world was protected by Pāṇḍu. By my command, O Kaunteya, my brother of great strength has always performed difficult deeds, O lord of the people."
Therefore, O Kaunteya, carry out my instruction without delay. My wicked sons are all possessed by egoism;
they will never obey my command, Yudhiṣṭhira.
"May there never again be conflict between you and those wicked-souled men who are always intent on their own interests and are arrogant; enter Khāṇḍavaprastha,
for while you dwell there, no one shall be able to oppress you."
Protected by Pārtha as the wielder of the thunderbolt protects the thirty gods,
and having obtained half of the kingdom, enter Khāṇḍavaprastha.
Thus spoke Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"If Keśava deems it right, that must undoubtedly be done. Having consulted with Vāsudeva, the Pāṇḍavas sat down together.
"O Kṣattṛ, bring the requisites for the consecration without delay;
today itself I shall consecrate the joy of the Kurus.
Let the brahmins, the foremost merchants, and the leaders of all the guilds assemble."

"Let the subjects and especially the kinsmen be summoned. O father, let the day be declared auspicious, and let a thousand cows be given away. Let the heads of the villages be bestowed upon the Brahmins along with sacrificial fees."
O Kṣattṛ, bring the armlets, the crown, and the hand-ornaments;
the pearl necklace, the long necklace, the gold coins (niṣkas), and the earrings; the waistband, the sacred thread, and likewise the girdle for the abdomen.
"Let one thousand and eight elephants, supervised by Brahmins,
quickly bring water from the Ganges;
let him be adorned with all ornaments and bathed in the consecration waters."
Mounted upon his royal elephant, fanned by divine whisks, and adorned with a white parasol variegated with gold and jewels,
he was being praised by kings and by the words of the twice-born: "Victory!"
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and the best of the Ājamīḍhas,
let the people in the city praise him with joyful hearts, saying:
"Having bestowed the kingdom upon me and having performed such great services for Pāṇḍu."
"This counter-action will surely be accomplished; there is no doubt.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the Steward (Vidura) exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
"O Great King, this is fitting and will bring glory to the Kauravas."

"O Indra among kings, you ought to do exactly as was said, this very day and without delay. Having spoken thus, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi then urged him on; and the Kaurava caused everything to be done as Dhṛtarāṣṭra had commanded.
At that moment, O Great King, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana arrived, honored by all the Kurus along with their circles of friends,
together with the consecrated kings and the Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas.
Then, with the approval of Keśava,
Kṛpa, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Dhaumya, Vyāsa, Keśava,
Bāhlīka, and Somadatta— honored by those learned in the four Vedas— performed the rites according to the prescribed rules.
Then they performed his consecration upon the auspicious throne with great restraint;
having conquered the entire earth and brought the bulls among men under his control,
he performed the Rājasūya and other sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
"Having performed the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*), let them rejoice together with their kinsmen.
Having spoken thus, they all honored him with blessings;
the Kuru prince, consecrated by royal aspersion (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*), was adorned with every ornament.
Praised with cries of "Victory!", the king bestowed inexhaustible wealth;
and the joy of the Kurus, honored by all the consecrated monarchs,
mounted his royal state elephant, resplendent beneath a divine parasol.
Followed by the kings like Mahendra by the gods,
the king then circumambulated the city named after the elephant and entered it, being greatly honored by the citizens.
The Pāṇḍavas congratulated the son of Pāṇḍu, the Mūrdhāvasikta;
meanwhile, all the sons of Gāndhārī, together with their kinsmen, were grieving.
But perceiving the sorrow of his sons, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke to the king.

In the presence of Vāsudeva and before the eyes of the Kurus, you have obtained an inauguration that is difficult for those of unrefined souls to attain. Go this very day, O King; you have accomplished your purpose, O Kaurava.
O King, Purūravas, Nahuṣa,
and Yayāti lived right there in that place called Khāṇḍava, O best of kings; for that,
O mighty-armed one, was the capital of all the Pauravas.
Because the hosts of sages were destroyed out of greed for the son of the sage,
you must therefore cause the city and kingdom of Khāṇḍavaprastha to flourish; let the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras be firmly resolved [to do so].
