"By devotion to you, other beings likewise resort to this auspicious city. Indeed, the city and the kingdom are prosperous and filled with wealth and grain.
Therefore, O sinless son of Kuntī, go there together with your brothers."
Accompanied by chariots, elephants, horses, and also foot soldiers—
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having accepted those words and having bowed down to the king, they all [departed].
Then those bulls among men set out for that formidable forest; meanwhile,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with Saubala, proclaimed throughout the city that the citizens ought not to go along with the Pāṇḍavas.
Having obtained half of the kingdom, they entered Khāṇḍavaprastha.
Then those Pāṇḍavas, having gone there with Kṛṣṇa at their head,
those infallible ones indeed adorned that city like heaven itself.
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, thought of Vāsava; O King, Mahendra, being thus thought of, commanded Viśvakarman: "O Viśvakarman of great wisdom, from this day forward, that city..."

"By the command of Mahendra, Viśvakarman went to Keśava, who is worthy of prostration, and having bowed down, he said, 'What shall I do? "It shall become a divine city on earth known as Indraprastha."
But Vāsudeva, the imperishable one, having heard that, said to Viśvakarman:
"Build for the King of the Kurus a great city named Indraprastha, resembling the city of Mahendra and created by Indra."
Then, having performed rites for peace in that auspicious and holy region and having had the benediction recited according to tradition, saying "Let it be Indraprastha," those great chariot-warriors,
led by Dvaipāyana, laid out the city.
Then Viśvakarman constructed a supreme city,
adorned with moats resembling the ocean and provided with a rampart that stood encompassing the very heavens.
That best of cities shone like Bhogavatī with its elephants, being as bright as pale clouds and resembling a mass of snow;
it was adorned with formidable gateways that resembled the two-winged Garuḍa.
It was well-guarded by gate-towers resembling masses of clouds and like Mount Mandara,
featuring various well-placed, firmly fixed, and well-shielded weapons; indeed,
it was covered with spears like two-headed serpents.

Equipped with practice-platforms and guarded by warriors, that preeminent city shone; adorned with sharp goads, *śataghnī* weapons, and networks of mechanical engines, it gleamed with great iron wheels.
With its well-proportioned great thoroughfares, free from the afflictions of malevolent deities,
it shone brilliantly with various excellent white mansions;
crowded with palatial towers and lofty buildings, it was adorned with diverse market-stalls.
As if in rivalry with one another, the palaces rose high;
likewise, pavilions, assembly halls, stables, and water-stations were erected on all sides. Thus Indraprastha shone forth, resembling the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa.

Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and sovereign of the Pauravas, having performed auspicious rites and honors by means of Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, entered the city— which was endowed with every excellence and constructed by Viśvakarman.
Placing Dvaipāyana at their head and abiding by the counsel of Dhaumya,
O King, that subduer of foes, together with his brothers and Keśava,
[entered] the city which had beautiful arched gateways and was provided with thirty-two gates.

The one of great splendor entered the gate of the city of Vardhamāna; the loud sounds of conchs and kettledrums were heard intensely on all sides, and the voices of thousands of Brahmins crying "Victory! were heard as well.
Being praised by many bards, genealogists, and panegyrists, the king,
mounted upon his state elephant, passed along the royal highway and entered his magnificent palace, where auspicious rites had been performed.
Having entered the palace, the king, honored with marks of hospitality,
worshipped the foremost of Brahmins along with Keśava in due order.
Thereupon, the kingdom flourished, filled with multitudes of men and women.
Abounding in herds of cattle, there was then an abundance of crops,
like a mass of clouds in the sky increased and enveloped by lightning. There,
in that delightful and auspicious region, stood the residence of the Kauravya.

Filled with wealth, it shone like the abode of the Lord of Riches (Kuvera). Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and sovereign of the Pauravas, had performed auspicious rites and honors by the Brāhmaṇas who were masters of the Vedas.
Placing Dvaipāyana at their head and abiding by the counsel of Dhaumya,
O King, that conqueror [Yudhiṣṭhira], together with his brothers and Keśava, set forth;
and the voices of the Brahmins were heard by the thousands, crying out, "Victory!"
Being praised by many bards, panegyrists,
and heralds, the king, seated upon his state elephant, passed along the royal highway and entered his excellent palace, which had been consecrated with auspicious rites.
Having entered his palace, the king, honored by the citizens,
worshipped the foremost of Brahmins along with Keśava in due order.
Thereupon, the kingdom flourished, filled with throngs of men and women.

O King, there the twice-born ones arrived—the best among those who know all the Vedas—as well as those proficient in all languages; they took pleasure in making it their dwelling place. And merchants seeking wealth came from every direction to that land.
Then, experts in all the arts arrived there to dwell; and all around the city were delightful gardens filled with mangoes,
hog-plums, kadambas, aśokas, and likewise campakas.
They were covered with coconut trees, breadfruit trees, and plantains;
with *aśoka*, *tilaka*, *lodhra*, blue *aśoka*, and *campaka* trees;
as well as with *puṃnāga*, *nāgapuṣpa*, breadfruit, and jackfruit trees.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *kadamba* trees, with *bakula* and *ketaka* trees,
all beautiful, in full bloom, and bent down by the weight of their fruit;
and with *prācīnāmalaka*, *lodhra*, and *aṅkola* trees, all in splendid flower.
It was filled with *jambū* trees, *pāṭala*s, *kubjaka*s, and *atimuktaka*s; with *karavīra*s, *pārijāta*s, and various other trees,
all perpetually endowed with flowers and fruit and teeming with flocks of diverse birds.
Resounding with flocks of intoxicated peacocks and ever-intoxicated cuckoos,
it was filled with houses as spotless as mirrors, various bowers of creepers,
enchanting painted chambers, and likewise with artificial mountains.
With various ponds filled with the finest water,
and with exceedingly beautiful lakes fragrant with lotuses and lilies, frequented by swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and adorned by ruddy geese;

And there were various beautiful lotus ponds surrounded by groves; in the center of the palace, Viśvakarman constructed for the king a delightful and divine residence, resembling the dwelling of Indra.
Stairways made of gold and jewels, variegated with every kind of gem, and various enchanting monastery grounds were constructed; likewise, thousands of rows of palaces shone forth in splendor.
The royal roads are continuous, white, and adorned with jewels among women; there are delightful ponds, both broad and vast,
and the river named Nandinī embraces that city.

It was crowded with people of the four castes, filled with garlands and artisans, and provided with all kinds of articles suitable for enjoyment; it was constantly frequented by noble people and filled with throngs of men and women.
Filled with rutting elephants, and abounding in cattle, camels, donkeys, and goats,
it was always frequented by the virtuous and had been constructed by Viśvakarman.
For those who dwelt in that great kingdom, which was inhabited by holy people, [it was a place of prosperity].
O great king, the joy of the Pāṇḍavas increased constantly as Saubala, Karṇa, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Kṛpa were present there,
while Bhīṣma and the king established the rules for the conduct of dharma.
The Pāṇḍavas became residents of Khāṇḍavaprastha;
accompanied by those five great archers who were like Indra himself,
that best of cities shone like Bhogavatī with its serpents.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O lord of men, having honored and dismissed Viśvakarman,
and having likewise honored and dismissed Dvaipāyana, [he departed].
The king spoke to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, who was ready to depart and had made his preparations:
"O sinless Vārṣṇeya, it is through your grace that the kingdom has been obtained by me;
O hero, it is solely through your favor that this desolate realm, so difficult to traverse, has been secured."

"By your grace alone, O Mādhava, we shall remain established in our kingdom; you are the refuge of the Pāṇḍavas at the time of their end. You are our mother, our father, and our god; we know no other than Pāṇḍu."

O sinless one, having understood this, you must perform what is to be done for the Pāṇḍavas. O highly fortunate one, it was through your power that the kingdom was obtained according to your own dharma;
O Lord, why should the kingdom of your fathers and grandfathers not belong to you?
What can the ill-behaved sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra do to the Pāṇḍavas?
Rule the earth as you desire and always bear the burden of dharma.
O Kaurava, support the Brahmins; this is instruction on dharma in brief.
"Today itself the illustrious Nārada will arrive in haste; honoring his words, you must indeed carry out his command. Having spoken thus and then saluted Kuntī, Janārdana departed.
He spoke with gentle words: "I shall depart; salutations be to you!
Having reached the house of lac, O Keśava, it was discovered by me, and it was also known by your noble kinsman Kuntibhoja, O sinless one."
O Govinda, with you as our protector, even great suffering has been overcome;
how much more so for those who are without a protector and especially for the poor? By the sight of you, all my sufferings are pacified.

"O one of great wisdom, remember these; by them the Pāṇḍavas live. Having thus addressed her and having paid his respects to his father's sister, Vāsudeva, together with his followers, resolved to depart.
Having settled them there, O King, the heroic Keśava, together with Rāma and with the consent of the Pāṇḍavas, then departed for Dvāravatī. Janamejaya said:
"O ascetic, having thus obtained that kingdom at Indraprastha,
what did those high-souled Pāṇḍavas do thereafter?
For they were all indeed great souls, my own grandfathers."
And how did Draupadī, their lawful wife, attend upon them?
Or how was it that those illustrious lords of men, though living together with the single Kṛṣṇā, did not fall into mutual discord?
"O one rich in asceticism, I wish to hear all this in detail—
the conduct of those who were united with that Kṛṣṇā toward one another.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Authorized by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Pāṇḍavas— those tigers among men and scorchers of foes, who had obtained the kingdom— rejoiced together with Kṛṣṇā. Having secured the kingdom, the highly energetic Yudhiṣṭhira remained true to his promise.

Together with his brothers— who were highly wise, devoted to truth and righteousness, and had conquered their enemies— he protected the earth according to dharma. Having attained the highest joy, those sons of Pāṇḍu dwelt there.
Performing all the affairs of the city, those bulls among men sat upon costly royal thrones. Then,
when all those high-souled ones had taken their seats, they sat down.
Then Nārada, desiring to see the King of Dharma, arrived by means of that vehicle which is frequented by constellations, traversed by Suparṇa,
radiant as the moon and sun, and served by great ṛṣis.

Honored by the spirits, the radiant one of great asceticism, beholding the earth— the sustainer of beings— adorned with garlands of cities and kingdoms, arrived through the divine celestial path that is difficult for those who have not practiced austerity to attain.

A Brahmin who has reached the end of all the Vedanta, one who has gone to the further shore of all branches of knowledge, endowed with supreme austerity and encompassed by Brahmanic asceticism, firm in policy and statesmanship, that great sage was renowned.

Having reached that which is higher than the high, he had fully realized the Dharma; with his self-cultivated, dust-free, tranquil, gentle, and upright nature, that twice-born one was approached by all gods, dānavas, and humans through the power of righteousness.
Among various beings whose sinful karma has been exhausted,
and among the various gods for whom he has established boundaries in every way,
there are hundreds of soma-drinkers in sacrifice who have performed meritorious deeds and maintained the sacred fires.
He was a knower of the *Ṛg*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* Vedas, skilled in the principles of logic and traditional history;
upright, noble-minded, pure, a frequent traveler on the path, and sinless.
He was endowed with a smooth crest-lock and possessed supreme splendor.
Wearing two magnificent, supreme garments— pure white, fine, divine, radiant, and auspicious— bestowed by Mahendra,
he indeed held a divine golden vessel with a spout shaped like a cricket’s head.
Wearing two auspicious, divine earrings resembling fire and the sun,
and raising a silver parasol of wondrous and supreme splendor,
he attained a preeminent spiritual luster that is difficult for anyone else to achieve.
In the palace of the protector of the earth, he was like Bṛhaspati, fully immersed in learning;

he was a master who had reached the further shore of the entire collection of the Vedas— both those in continuous recitation (*saṃhitā*) and those in their separate forms— as well as of the Dharma of the two-footed and the sequential Dharma.
He was an expert in the *gāthās*, *sāmans*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters, as well as in the most beautiful *sāmans*.

Being wise and skilled in what ought to be done, he himself [bestowed] everything upon those seeking liberation; that best among the intelligent fixed his mind upon the manifold aspects of the Dharma.

Having realized the meaning, he cuts through the doubts regarding the scriptures according to his own system; he is eternally capable of defining the meaning, a cutter of doubt who is himself free from doubt;
by nature skilled in the Dharma, he is proficient in the various teachings.
Through the methods of elision, augmentation, and transposition within grammatical operations,
he observed words that have a single phonetic form but diverse meanings, as well as those with identical meanings but distinct sounds,
and the expression of different meanings through various linguistic usages.
He is the authoritative standard for the world in all matters of legal jurisdiction;
he is eternally honored by all castes in all their variations,
and in every diverse accent and in every variety of meter.
In all positions,
in all traditional recitations, and in all verbal roots, he who knows the reality of intentions explains the designations while teaching every verb, recollecting the words as its constituent parts.
Examining the reality as it is, which has been pointed out by the law of time,
he who understands what is intended to be done and how it is concealed by the world— [he understands] the explained convention and the speech that reaches the heart.
One who possesses the application of vowels and grammatical refinement for both oneself and others,
who is a knower and understander of these vowels, and who understands the tones of the teachings as well as the unity and plurality of the spoken sentences.
He is the knower of the ultimate truths, of various transgressions,
and of the manifold teachings— both frequently through their non-differentiation and repeatedly through their differentiation— and he has thoroughly examined the diverse expressions and instructions.

Skilled in words of manifold meanings therein, and in all their secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), he is an adornment of speech through its phonemes, accents, and meanings; and he has fully explained the suffixes as they are fixed according to each verbal root (*dhātu*).
There are five classes of syllables known as vowels;
then the celestial sage Nārada arrived there by chance. Seeing that the rishi had come, he went out to meet him and saluted him.
Yudhiṣṭhira offered him his own beautiful seat;

the great ṛṣi sat down upon it, which was covered with a black antelope skin. Then, once the celestial ṛṣi was seated, he himself [offered] the guest-offering (arghya) according to the prescribed rite.
The wise Yudhiṣṭhira gave [him gifts] and offered him his kingdom.
Having accepted that honor, the Ṛṣi became pleased in mind;
having honored him with blessings, he said to him, "Be seated."
Then, having been granted permission, King Yudhiṣṭhira sat down;
he then sent word to Kṛṣṇā that the Blessed One had arrived.
Upon hearing this, Draupadī also purified herself and became composed.

She went to the place where Nārada was staying together with the Pāṇḍavas. Having saluted the feet of that celestial sage, the daughter of Drupada, who practiced righteousness, stood there with her hands joined in reverence and properly attired.
And that righteous-souled Nārada, the best of sages and a speaker of truth,
having pronounced various blessings upon the princess,
said to that blameless lady, "May you depart," O venerable one.
Then, after Kṛṣṇā had departed, the venerable Ṛṣi spoke in private to all the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira:
"The illustrious daughter of Pañcāla is the sole lawful wife of you all."
"Let a policy be established such that no dissension may arise among you.
Once upon a time, there were two Asura brothers, Sunda and Upasunda, who lived together and were renowned throughout the three worlds as being incapable of being slain by anyone else."
Sharing a single kingdom, a single house, a single bed, a seat, and food,
those two struck each other for the sake of Tilottamā. Therefore,
let that friendship which arises from mutual reflection be preserved.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, act in such a way that there may be no division among you here;
O great car-warriors, ensure that it is distributed equally among all.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, whose sons were the two Asuras Sunda and Upasunda?
How did their division arise, and how did they slay one another?
And to whom did this Apsaras Tilottamā, the daughter of a god, belong?"

Nārada said:
"O Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira, together with your brothers, listen to this ancient history from me in detail, exactly as it occurred."
In ancient times, within the lineage of the great asura Hiraṇyakaśipu,
there was a lord of the Daityas named Nikumbha, who was radiant and powerful.
To him were born two sons of great heroism and fearsome prowess.
Sunda and Upasunda were two lords of the Daityas, fierce and cruel-minded;
those two Daityas, of one resolve and united for a single purpose,
lived together constantly, sharing equally in both sorrow and joy.
They eat together and do not go apart from one another;
they act for each other's pleasure and speak kindly to one another. Having identical character and conduct, they are as if two made into one.

Having grown up, those two of great heroism, being of one mind even in their undertakings, resolved with single-minded intent upon the conquest of the three worlds. Having undergone initiation, they went to the Vindhya mountains and there performed fierce austerities.
After a long time, those two became devoted to asceticism;
exhausted by hunger and thirst, they wore matted hair and bark garments, their entire bodies covered with grime, and subsisted on air alone.

In the summer, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they remained joined by the five fires, standing with their feet raised and heads bent down; and during the rainy season, they lay within the midst of water. Offering their own flesh as oblations, they stood balanced on the tips of their big toes.

With arms raised and eyes unblinking, they maintained their vows for a long time. Through the power of their asceticism, the Vindhya mountain, having been scorched for a long duration, emitted smoke; that was like a marvel.

Then the gods became afraid upon seeing the fierce asceticism of those two; thereupon, for the sake of obstructing their penance, the gods created impediments. They repeatedly attempted to entice both of them with jewels and with women.
Those two of great vows did not break their vow;
then the gods again employed an illusion against those two high-souled ones,
[creating] sisters, mothers, wives, and likewise attendants for them.
Being pursued by a demon with a spear in his hand, they were terrified;
their ornaments and hair disheveled, and their garments fallen away,
they all ran toward them and cried out, "Save us!"
Those two of great vows did not break their vow,
as long as neither of them experienced agitation or distress;
then those women and all that being vanished.
Then the Grandfather himself, the progenitor of all the worlds, approached the two great asuras and invited them to choose a boon.
Thereupon, those two brothers, Sunda and Upasunda, were possessed of firm prowess.
Having seen the divine Grandfather, they then stood with palms joined in reverence; and then, together, they both spoke to the Lord, the God:
"If the Grandfather is pleased with this austerity of ours..."
"If our lord is pleased with us, we two shall both become masters of illusion, masters of weapons, powerful, able to assume any form at will, and even immortal.
The Grandfather said:
"Except for immortality, everything else you have requested shall be granted. Choose another boon, one that provides a regulation regarding death such that you may be equal to the immortals;
for this great austerity was undertaken with the thought, 'I shall accomplish this.'"
"O Daitya lords, by this very reason, immortality is not ordained for you two.
You have undertaken this ascetic penance for the sake of conquering the three worlds;
for this reason, O lords of the Daityas, I shall not grant your desire."
Sunda and Upasunda said:
"O Grandfather, among all beings whatsoever in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving,
let there be no fear for us from anyone except from one another."
The Grandfather said:
"I grant you both this desire that was requested and spoken of as you wished;
and this ordinance regarding death shall come to pass for you exactly as it has been ordained."
Nārada said:
Then the Grandfather, having granted this boon to those two and having turned them away from their asceticism, departed for the world of Brahmā.
Having obtained all the boons, even those two lords of the Daityas,

who were now invulnerable to all the worlds, returned to their own abode. Seeing those two great Asuras having obtained the boons and having their desires fulfilled, [the gods were filled with anxiety].
All their friends were filled with joy at those two. Then, casting off their matted locks, they both became adorned with crowns, wearing costly ornaments and spotless garments.
The two lords of the Daityas, filled with supreme joy, as did their circle of friends, held an untimely Kaumudī festival that fulfilled all desires, exclaiming:
"Let there be eating! Let there be feasting! Let there be constant delight! Let there be singing!"
"Drink! Give!"—such were the words heard in house after house.
Thus did the voices of those great-souled ones resound here and there in their joy, accompanied by great drinking bouts and the loud clapping of hands.

The entire city of the Daityas became joyful and exceedingly delighted. Through those various and manifold diversions of the Daityas, who could assume any form at will, as they sported together, their many years passed as if they were but a single day.
Nārada said: As soon as the festival had concluded, both of them, desiring the three worlds,
consulted together and then issued orders to their army.
Permitted by their friends, the elders of the Daityas, and their ministers,

they performed the rites for departure during the night under the asterism Maghā and then set forth. They were accompanied by [an army] bearing maces and spears, and holding tridents and clubs in their hands.
Setting out with his lawful wife and a vast army of Daityas,
they proceeded with great joy while being praised by *cāraṇas* with auspicious hymns and invocations for victory.
Then those two Daityas, capable of going anywhere at will and intoxicated by battle, flew up into the air and went to the very abode of the gods.
Having learned of their arrival and of that boon from the Lord, [the gods were alarmed].
Then, having abandoned the celestial realm, the gods went to the world of Brahmā. Those two,
possessing fierce prowess, having conquered Indra’s world as well as the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, also defeated the beings that move through the sky.
Having conquered the *nāgas* dwelling within the earth, those two great asuras also defeated all the *mleccha* tribes inhabiting the ocean. Thereafter,
those two of fierce command began to conquer the entire earth.
Having summoned their soldiers, the two of them spoke these very sharp words:
"The royal sages and the twice-born increase the splendor, strength, and prosperity of the gods through great sacrifices and offerings to the gods and ancestors."
"Since all these enemies of the Asuras have thus grown so powerful,
their destruction must be carried out by all of us together with our whole being.
Having thus instructed them all on the eastern shore of the great ocean, [he departed].
Adopting a cruel resolve, they went forth in every direction.
Seeing all those twice-born ones who were performing sacrifices and those who were officiating at them, the two powerful brothers then slew them all by force.
The soldiers of those two, acting with confidence, seized the *agnihotra* fires of the sages of purified souls in their hermitages and cast them into the water. Furthermore,
there were the curses uttered by those high-souled ones whose wealth was their asceticism when they were provoked to anger.
By virtue of the boon granted to them, even as those two yawned, [the weapons] did not strike;
when the curses they released failed to take effect, like arrows shot at stones,
the twice-born then abandoned their religious observances and fled.
Those on earth who were perfected through austerity, self-controlled, and devoted to tranquility,
fled in fear of those two like serpents at the sight of Vainateya;
their hermitages were plundered, broken, and left with their jars and ladles scattered about.
The entire world was empty, as if struck by Time itself;
with the royal sages and the seers having vanished from sight, both great Asuras, having made their resolve, began to manifest their powers, seeking slaughter.
Becoming two elephants in rut with temples flowing with ichor,
they sent even those hidden in fortresses to the abode of Yama.
Then, becoming lions, and again tigers, both of them became invisible once more.

By various such means, those two cruel ones slaughtered the sages upon seeing them. At that time, the earth became one where sacrifices and Vedic recitations had ceased, where kings and twice-born brahmins had perished, and where festivals and sacrifices were utterly destroyed.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", stricken with fear, the markets and shops were closed;
religious rites for the gods ceased, and auspicious marriages were abandoned. Agriculture and cattle-rearing were halted, and cities and hermitages lay in ruins.
The earth became strewn with skeletons of bones and took on a terrifying appearance; with ancestral rites ceased and the auspicious sounds of *vaṣaṭ* no longer heard,
the world then became fearful in form and difficult to behold.
The moon, the sun, the planets, the stars, the constellations,
and the dwellers of heaven fell into despair upon seeing that deed of Sunda and Upasunda.
Thus, having conquered all the quarters by their cruel act, the two Daityas—
Free from rivals, they established their residence in Kurukṣetra.
Nārada said:
Then all the celestial rishis, the Siddhas, and the supreme rishis...
Seeing that great slaughter, they then experienced supreme distress; yet, having conquered anger, mastered their selves, and subdued their senses,
they then proceeded out of compassion for the world to the abode of the Grandfather.
Then they beheld the Grandfather seated together with the gods,
surrounded on all sides by the Siddhas and the Brahman-sages. There was the god Mahādeva, and there was Agni along with Vāyu.
The Moon and the Sun, Dharma, Parameṣṭhin, and likewise Budha;
the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, the forest-dwellers, and those who subsist on rays of light;
the unborn, the undeluded, those whose wombs are filled with splendor, and the ascetics.
All these sages were worshipping the Grandfather (Brahmā). Then, having approached him together, all those great seers recounted the entire conduct of Sunda and Upasunda.

They reported everything in its entirety to the Grandfather— exactly how it was done, precisely what was done, and in whatever order it occurred. Then all the hosts of gods and those supreme ṛṣis [remained there].
Placing that very matter before him, they urged the Grandfather [Brahmā].
Then the Grandfather, having heard those words of everyone at that time,
reflected for a moment upon the determination of what ought to be done.
Aiming for their destruction, he summoned Viśvakarman;
and having seen Viśvakarman, the Grandfather, possessed of great ascetic power, commanded him: "Let a desirable woman be created here."
Having paid homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and having welcomed his words,
he [Viśvakarman] fashioned a divine woman after reflecting with great effort upon whatever exists in the three worlds, whether stationary or moving.
He diligently gathered from here and there every beautiful thing that was to be seen;
he even set jewels by the millions upon her limbs,
creating her, who possessed a divine form, out of a mass of precious gems.
Created with great effort by Viśvakarman,
she became peerless in beauty among women in the three worlds. There was not even the slightest part of her body that lacked perfection of form.
Where the gaze of those who look upon her does not falter,
she stands like Fortune incarnate, possessing a lovely form and a beautiful body;
she approached the Grandfather and said, "What shall I do?"
Becoming delighted upon seeing her, he joyfully granted her a boon:
the state of being beloved by all beings and a form of incomparable beauty through his own splendor.
By that granting of the boon and by the act of the Creator at that time, she...
It captivated the eyes and the minds of all living beings.
Because she was fashioned by bringing together every jewel bit by bit (*tilaṃ tilaṃ*),
the Grandfather gave her the name Tilottamā.
Having paid homage to Brahmā with palms joined in reverence, she spoke these words:
"O Lord of Beings, what task is to be done by me, for which purpose have I been created here today?
Nārada said:
Then the Blessed Lord, the God, spoke to her—she who was auspicious, beautiful in all her limbs, and gladdening to the mind: "Let this task be accomplished.
The Grandfather said:
"Go, O Tilottamā, and by means of your desirable form, O blessed lady, entice the two Asuras, Sunda and Upasunda. Indeed,
because of the excellence of your beauty, they will surely fall [into passion] at the mere sight of you."
"Act in such a way that there may be a conflict between them, as they have with one another.
Nārada said:
"Having promised 'So be it' and having paid homage to the Grandfather,"
There he formed a circle for the gods, circumambulating it clockwise. The Blessed One sat facing the east, Maheśvara to the south, the gods to the north, and the sages were on all sides.
As she was performing that circumambulation of the mandala,
Brahmā and the Lord Viṣṇu stood there having treated her with utter contempt; Indra and the Lord Sthāṇu likewise remained steadfast through their fortitude.
Then, as she went by his side with an intense desire to see him,
another face with curved eyelashes emerged from his right side;
and as she turned behind him, a western face emerged.
As she departed for the northern side, her northern face emerged; from the sides,
the back, and the front of even Mahendra’s eyes— a thousand large eyes with red corners— appeared on every side.
In this way, in ancient times, Sthāṇu became Mahādeva with four faces;
likewise, he became the thousand-eyed slayer of Bala.
And so it was for all the hosts of gods and the ṛṣis in every respect.
The faces turned toward whichever direction Tilottamā went;
the gaze of all those great-souled ones fell upon her body,
with the sole exception of the god Pitāmaha.
As Tilottamā was departing, all the gods and the supreme ṛṣis considered that task already accomplished by her perfection of form. Then, when Tilottamā had gone, the Creator of the World—
The illustrious Grandfather dismissed all those gods and hosts of sages, saying, "The task is accomplished. Nārada said:

Having conquered the earth, the two Daityas became free from rivals and devoid of anxiety; having brought the three worlds under their undisputed control, they felt they had accomplished all that was to be done.
[They then surveyed] the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, kings, and Rākṣasas.
Having taken all the jewels, the two attained supreme satisfaction; since there were no one here to restrain them,
they then became effortless and sported like immortals.
With women, garlands, perfumes, and abundant foods and delicacies,
as well as various heart-pleasing drinks, the two attained supreme delight in the inner apartments,
the forest gardens, and the mountain groves.
They roamed like two immortals through regions as they desired.
Then, on one occasion, they went for recreation upon the back of the Vindhya mountains, where the surface was level with its rocky slabs and the *śāla* trees were in full bloom at their tips.

When all divine objects of desire had been brought there, the two of them sat together with their women upon excellent seats, filled with great joy. Then, the women attended upon them with instrumental music and dance.

They approached her with songs joined by hymns of praise for the sake of pleasing her; O Lord, even the mere mention of her name brings about dissolution and transformation, so what need be said of beholding her, who is made radiant by her playful charms?
Skilled in secret dalliance, speaking with soft and faltering words— surely such a woman, deeply impassioned and beautiful of eye,
would bring even the mind of a sage under her sway, for she is full of passion.
Clear and producing loveliness, like the moon’s orb at twilight; indeed, even great men are shattered by women who delight and utterly subdue the mind, just as mountains are split by waters.
Then Tilottamā, gathering flowers there in the forest,
assumed a captivating appearance with a single red garment;
she was picking *karṇikāra* blossoms growing along the riverbanks.
He slowly went to that place where those two great asuras were. Having drunk the excellent beverage, their eyes became bloodshot with intoxication;
upon merely seeing that woman of beautiful limbs, they both became deeply agitated.
Leaping up and leaving their seats, the two went to where she stood; both intoxicated by desire, they both sought her favor. Sunda seized that fair-browed woman by the hand with his right hand.
Upasunda also took Tilottamā by her left hand;
both of them were intoxicated by the granting of the boon, as well as by their innate strength,
the pride of wealth and jewels, and the intoxication of drinking wine.
Drawing the two lords of the Daityas toward her again and again with a sidelong glance,
that beautiful woman caught Sunda with her right glance,
while seeking to seize Upasunda with her left.
Intoxicated by all these forms of pride—perfumes, ornaments, and beauty—they fell into infatuation.
Intoxicated by these various haughtinesses, they frowned at one another;
possessed by intoxication and lust, they then spoke to each other.

"She is my wife; she is your elder," Sunda said. "She is my wife; she is your daughter-in-law," Upasunda replied. "She is not yours; she is mine!"—thus they spoke, and wrath took possession of them both.
Intoxicated by her beauty, their affection and friendship vanished; for her sake, both of them seized two terrible maces. Having grasped those two terrible maces, they were deluded by desire for her.
"I first! I first! they cried, and struck one another down.
Struck by their maces, those two formidable warriors fell upon the surface of the earth, their limbs smeared with blood like two suns fallen from the sky.
Then those women fled, and that entire host of Daityas,
trembling with despair and fear, went to Pātāla.
Thereupon, the Grandfather (Brahmā) was there together with the gods and the great ṛṣis.
The pure-souled one arrived, intending to worship Tilottamā. Having been gratified by Brahmā with a boon, she chose [a boon] out of affection; thereupon, the Grandfather, being pleased, spoke to her.
"O beautiful lady, you shall wander through the worlds frequented by the Ādityas;
and because of your splendor, no one at all shall be able to look upon you clearly.
Having thus granted her this boon, the Grandfather of all the worlds [departed].
Having entrusted the three worlds to Indra, the Lord departed for the world of Brahmā.
Thus, having become united and single-minded in all their purposes, they both,
enraged over Tilottamā, struck one another down.
Therefore, out of affection, I say to you all, O best of the Bharatas:
act in such a way that no division may arise among you all on account of Draupadī;
may prosperity be yours, if you desire to do what is pleasing to me.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, it should not be as it was with Sunda and Upasunda.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having been thus addressed by the great seer Nārada, those high-souled ones—"
O King, having come together, they made an agreement with one another in the presence of that celestial seer Nārada of immeasurable power:
"The stainless Kṛṣṇā shall dwell for one year in the house of each one."
"Whoever among us, while sitting together with Draupadī, should look at one another,
he shall dwell in the forest for twelve years as a celibate student (brahmacārī).
When that agreement had been made by the dharma-practicing Pāṇḍavas,"
Then the Lord, the Master, having been honored there by the Pāṇḍavas,
and the great sage Nārada as well, departed joyfully for his desired destination. Thus was the agreement previously made by them, urged by Nārada.
And none of them, O Bhārata, were at that time divided among one another. All this has been related to you in detail, O lord of men,
exactly as it occurred at that time, O Janamejaya.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus made this agreement, the Pāṇḍavas dwelt there,
bringing other rulers of the earth under their control by the prowess of their weapons.
Kṛṣṇā became subject to the will of all those five sons of Pṛthā, those lions among men of immeasurable splendor;
and she, together with those five heroic husbands, [was likewise subject to their will].
She became supremely delighted, like the Sarasvatī river among the nāgas,
while the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were conducting themselves according to dharma;
all the Kurus flourished, free from faults and endowed with happiness.
Then, after a long time, O lord of the people, some thieves stole the cows of a certain brahmin, O best of kings. While that wealth was being carried away, the brahmin was overwhelmed with rage.
Having arrived at Khāṇḍavaprastha, he shouted to the Pāṇḍavas:
"The wealth of cattle is being carried away by base, cruel, and undisciplined men!
O Pāṇḍavas, run forth from this territory and recover it by force!"
The sacrificial oblation of a negligent Brahmin is plundered by crows;
a lowly jackal invades the empty cave of a tiger.
[Such is the fate of] a king who takes a sixth share as tribute yet provides no protection.
They call him the perpetrator of every sin in all the world when,
while the property of a Brahmin has been stolen by thieves and his means for dharma have been destroyed, he cries out in distress: "Let the taking up of arms be done for me!"
Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī and a Pāṇḍava, heard those words of that weeping brahmin from nearby;
and having heard them, the mighty-armed one said to the twice-born man, "Do not fear."
And where the weapons of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas lay,
there sat Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, together with Kṛṣṇā;
that son of Pāṇḍu was unable either to enter or to depart.

As that distressed man was being urged on again and again by those words while his wealth was being carried away, the son of Kuntī, grieving there in that outcry, reflected upon the suffering of the ascetic brahmin.
"It is certain that his tears must be wiped away; otherwise, a very great demerit would accrue to the lord of the earth from looking on while he weeps,
if I do not provide protection for him today at the gate."

"Furthermore, there would be a lack of faith among all of us, even in our protection; it would be established in this world that unrighteousness belongs to us. And there is no doubt that if I were to depart without having taken leave of the king,"
It would be disagreeable both to King Ajātaśatru and to me;
however, if the king were to enter [the city], my forest-dwelling would come to an end. Everything else has been avoided, except for this insult to the lord of the earth.
"Let there be great unrighteousness, or let my death occur in the forest;
even with the destruction of this body, righteousness alone is superior.
Having thus resolved, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, [proceeded].
Having tightly covered his face with his upper garment and entered [the assembly], O lord of the people, he took leave of the king; then,
taking up his bow, he spoke joyfully to the Brahmin.
"O Brahmin, come quickly while those seekers of another's wealth are not yet far gone;
let us go together before I recover your property from the hands of the thief today."

That mighty-armed Pāṇḍava, equipped with bow, armor, chariot, and banner, pursued them; having conquered the thieves and destroyed them with his arrows, he recovered that wealth and brought it back to the Brāhmaṇa, thereby drinking in fame.
Then, having given that wealth of cattle to that twice-born man,
the heroic Savyasācin Pārtha, the scorcher of foes, returned to his city.
Having saluted all his elders and being greeted by them in return, he entered.
He said this to Dharmarāja: "Let a vow be prescribed for me.
The time limit has been exceeded by me because of the sight of you; I shall go to dwell in the forest, for such was the agreement made by us."

Thus addressed with these sudden and unpleasant words, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, afflicted by grief, spoke to his brother Guḍākeśa, the steadfast one, with a faltering voice: "How can this be? he said to his brother.
The distressed king spoke these words to Dhanañjaya:
"O sinless one, if I am an authority to you, then hear my words:
O hero, regarding that which you did to me, an act of displeasure, upon entering [the city]."
"I permit all of that, for there is no offense in my heart; indeed,
the entry of an elder into a younger's space is not a violation,
whereas the entry of a younger into an elder's space is a transgression of the sacred law."
"Turn back, O mighty-armed one; do as I say. For there is no loss of dharma for you, nor has any violation of mine been committed.
Arjuna said:
"I have heard from you, O Lord, that one should not practice dharma through deceit.
I shall not waver from the truth; by the truth, I touch my weapon. For once it has been accepted, O King, the vow is not performed by oneself [if it is subsequently abandoned]."
The bridge would be broken, unrighteousness would prevail, and I would incur great infamy.
O increaser of my fame, you must grant me your command;
it is my firm resolve that nothing whatsoever shall be done without your permission.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having taken leave of the king, he was initiated for the vow of celibacy and went to dwell in the forest for twelve years.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As that mighty-armed one, the bringer of glory to the Kauravas, was departing,
high-souled Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas followed him.

O King, there were those learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, as well as contemplators of the supreme self; pure devotees of the Blessed One, Sūtas, and those versed in the Purāṇas; other storytellers, ascetics, and forest-dwellers.
And those twice-born ones who recited divine narratives sweetly—
surrounded by these and many other companions whose speech was gentle, the son of Pāṇḍu set forth like Vāsava accompanied by the Maruts.
O bull of the Bharatas, he beheld delightful and variegated forests and lakes, rivers and oceans, as well as various regions and sacred fords, O best of the Bharatas.

Having reached Gaṅgādvāra, the lord established his camp. Listen to me, Janamejaya, regarding the wondrous deed that the pure-souled one, the preeminent chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas, performed there.

O Bhārata, when the son of Kuntī had settled there along with the brahmins, those learned men established their sacred fires in numerous places. As those fires were being kindled, set ablaze, and offered oblations, [the night passed].

O King, that gateway to the Gaṅgā shone most brilliantly with those high-souled ones who had offered floral oblations at the riverbanks, who had performed their ablutions, who were learned, self-restrained, and established on the path of the righteous.

While that settlement was thus in turmoil, the son of Pāṇḍu, the son of Kuntī, descended into the Gaṅgā for his ritual ablution. Having performed his ablutions there, he offered libations to his ancestors.
O King, as he desired to emerge from the water with the intention of performing his fire-ritual,
the mighty-armed one was drawn away by Ulūpī, the daughter of the Naga king,
who was filled with desire for him within the depths of the water, O great monarch.
Having been taken and led to his father’s house,
this son of Pāṇḍu saw there the well-composed fire in the most magnificent palace of the Kuru prince Nāga.
There, Dhananjaya, the son of Kunti, performed the fire-rite;
the consumer of oblations was gratified by the offering made by him without hesitation. Having completed the fire-rite, he then [addressed] the daughter of the Naga king.
As if laughing, O son of Kuntī, he spoke these words:
"O timid one, what is this rash act you have committed, O beautiful lady?
What is this fortunate region, who are you, and whose daughter are you?"
Ulūpī said:
"O Pārtha, there is a serpent named Kauravya born in the lineage of Airāvata;
I am his daughter, a female serpent named Ulūpī."

O son of Kuntī, as soon as I saw you descend into the river that flows to the ocean for the sake of your consecration, I was overwhelmed by the god of love. O joy of the Kurus, I am thus tormented by the bodiless one on your account.
"Delight this devoted woman today by giving yourself to her in private.
Arjuna said:
"O blessed lady, this vow of celibacy of mine is for twelve years."
"I have been commanded by Dharmarāja, and I am not my own master.
Furthermore, O water-dweller, I desire to do what is pleasing to you;
never at any time has an untruth been spoken by me before."
"And how might that not be a falsehood, yet still be pleasing to you, and so that my dharma is not violated? O serpent, act in such a way.
Ulūpī said:
"O son of Pāṇḍu, I know how you roam the earth,
and how your preceptor ordained this vow of celibacy for you—
each of you acting toward one another regarding the daughter of Drupada."

"Whoever among us, out of delusion, should enter [the city], shall practice the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) in the forest for twelve years; this is the covenant you have made. Therefore, for the sake of Draupadī, there is this mutual exile."
By the command of Nārada and out of a desire for dharma,
one full year was spent there, divided into five parts by the son of Kuntī, with Draupadī herself, according to the permission of Nārada.
What was done there was for the sake of dharma; here, dharma is not defiled. Since your mind was not incited by you toward the pursuit of desire, no transgression whatsoever is fitting for you.
"O large-eyed one, protection must be afforded to those who are distressed. By providing me with protection, your dharma will not be violated;
even if there should be the slightest transgression of this dharma."
"And that would indeed be your duty, O Arjuna, having given me my life;
honor me, your devotee, O Pārtha, for this is the opinion of the virtuous, O Lord. If you do not do so, consider me as dead."
"O mighty-armed one, practice the supreme dharma by granting me my life;
O best of men, today I have come to you for refuge.
O son of Kuntī, you always protect those who are miserable and without a protector."
Thus, I come to you for refuge and cry out in my distress;
longing for you, I entreat you, so please do what is pleasing to me. Therefore, by giving yourself to me, you ought to fulfill my desire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the daughter of the lord of serpents, the son of Kuntī performed all of that accordingly, having righteousness as his motive.
Having spent that night in the abode of the Nāgas,
the majestic one begot upon her a most charming son,
the highly fortunate Irāvān, who possessed great strength and prowess.

At dawn, having stayed overnight at Abhyuṣitolūpī, the wise Arjuna reached his own abode; when the sun had risen, he departed from the residence of the Kauravya and proceeded toward the hermitage at Gaṅgādvāra.
Then Pārtha departed for his own auspicious abode;
having returned there once more with her to Gaṅgādvāra,
the virtuous Ulūpī left him and went to her own home.
"O Bhārata, having granted him the boon of invincibility in all waters, [he said]:
'Without a doubt, all aquatic creatures shall become subject to him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having related all of that to the brahmins, O Bhārata,
the son of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt then departed for the slopes of the Himavat,
reaching both Agastyavaṭa and the mountain of Vasiṣṭha.
And at Bhṛgutuṅga, the son of Kuntī performed his own purification;
he gave away thousands of cows at sacred fords and shrines,
and that best of the Kurus bestowed dwellings upon the twice-born.
Having bathed at the holy ford of Hiraṇyabindu,
that best of men beheld the foremost of mountains and sacred shrines;
then, O Bhārata, that best of men descended together with the Brāhmaṇas.
Desiring to reach the eastern direction, that bull among the Bharatas departed;
the best of the Kurus visited the sacred fords in their proper order,
reaching the lovely Utpalinī River and the Naimiṣa forest.
O Bhārata, he saw the Nandā, the Aparanandā, the illustrious Kauśikī, the great river Gayā, and also the Gaṅgā;
thus he beheld all the sacred fords as well as the hermitages.
Purifying himself, he bestowed wealth upon the Brahmins; he visited all the sacred fords and shrines that exist throughout Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga.

Having seen them according to the prescribed rites, he then gave them wealth as well. O Bhārata, at the gates of the Kalinga kingdom, the Brāhmaṇas who had followed the Pāṇḍavas took leave of the son of Kuntī and returned.

Permitted by them, the heroic Dhanañjaya, son of Kuntī, set out toward the ocean with a small number of companions. Having passed beyond the Kaliṅgas, he traversed various countries and sacred shrines.
Beholding those righteous and delightful sights, the Lord proceeded;
then, having bathed at Śūrpākāra, he took refuge on the coastal marshland of the ocean. Having seen Mount Mahendra, which was graced by ascetics, he went forth.
Then, having bathed in the Godāvarī and passed beyond it, the one of great strength reached the Kāverī at its confluence with the ocean;
there he bathed and worshipped the gods and the ancestors together with the sages.
Traveling slowly along the seashore, he went to Maṇalūra.
There are all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and holy shrines (*āyatana*).
Then, in the thirteenth month, [he reached] the Lord of Maṇalūra.
Having approached, the mighty-armed one went before the lord of the earth,
O King— the ruler of Maṇalūra, Citravāhana, who knew the dharma,
was a leader in all scriptures, was skilled in all weapons, and was stainless.
He was preeminent in righteousness, truth, self-restraint, purity, and especially in valor;
on this earth, he was the supreme knower of the duty of the kṣatriyas and served as the standard of comparison for the chanting of the names of the righteous royal sages.
And he accepted that Pāṇḍava according to the prescribed rites.
He had a daughter named Citrāṅgadā, who was beautiful to behold;
he saw her wandering at will within that city.
Having seen that woman of beautiful hips, the daughter of Caitravāhana, he desired her.
Approaching the king, he made known his purpose:
"O King, please grant this woman to me, a high-souled Kṣatriya."
Having heard that, the king said, "Whose son are you, and what is your name?
The Pāṇḍava replied to him, "I am Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī.
Then the king spoke these words to him with conciliation:
In this lineage, there was indeed a king named Prabhankara who,
being childless and desiring offspring, performed supreme austerity.
By that fierce asceticism and by his prostrations, Śaṅkara [was pleased].
By him, the Lord Mahādeva, the husband of Umā, was propitiated. That Blessed One granted him a single offspring for each generation in his lineage;
therefore, there has always been but one child born at a time in this family.
"O Supreme Person, sons were born to all those ancestors of mine, but this daughter was born to me; she will certainly ensure the continuation of my lineage. It is my conviction that she is my son."
"O bull of the Bharatas, she is designated as a *putrikā* according to the rule of the cause [of lineage].
Therefore, O Bhārata, whatever one son is born to her by you, let him be the bride-price for her;
let him be the perpetuator of the family here."
"O Pāṇḍava, accept her on this condition.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," and having accepted the maiden,
Pārtha performed the marriage rites in the thirteenth month.
The son of Kuntī lived in that city for three full winters.
When a son was born to him, he embraced that excellent woman,
took leave of the king, and departed to return home.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O bull of the Bharata race, that best of the Bharatas proceeded to the most meritorious sacred fords on the southern shore of the ocean, which were graced by ascetics.
There, however, the ascetics avoided five sacred fords (tīrthas) that had previously been frequented by practitioners of austerity:
Agastyatīrtha, Saubhadra, and the most purifying Pauloma.
Kāraṃdhama, Prasanna, and that which is the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha),
as well as Bhāradvāja’s Tīrtha, which greatly pacifies all sins—
the best of the Kurus beheld these five sacred fords.
Then, having observed those secluded sacred fords and seeing that they were being avoided by sages whose minds are fixed on dharma, the son of Pāṇḍu,
the joy of the Kurus, joined his palms in reverence and questioned the ascetics.
"Why are these sacred fords (*tīrtha*) avoided by those who discourse on Brahman?
The ascetics said:
"Five crocodiles dwell in these [waters] and carry off those whose wealth is their austerity."
"Therefore, O joy of the Kurus, these sacred fords (tīrthas) are avoided.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, the mighty-armed one was restrained by those whose wealth is asceticism (tapodhana).
That best of men went to see those sacred fords. Then, having reached the supreme ford of the great seer belonging to the son of Subhadrā,
the hero, the scorcher of his foes, plunged in with speed and performed his ablutions.

Then, while he was within the water, a great crocodile moving through the depths seized that tiger among men, Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī. Taking hold of that struggling aquatic creature, the son of Kuntī—
The mighty-armed one, the best among the strong, rose up by his own strength; but as soon as that crocodile was pulled out by the illustrious Arjuna,
it became a beautiful woman adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
O King, blazing with splendor, divine in form, and enchanting,
Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, beholding that great marvel and being exceedingly pleased, spoke these words to that woman.
"Who indeed are you, O auspicious one, and from where do you come, moving as you do in the water? And for what purpose did you previously commit this great sin? The woman replied:

"O mighty-armed one, I am an Apsaras who wanders through the forests of the gods; I am named Varga, O one of great strength, and I am eternally beloved by the Lord of Wealth. I have four other auspicious friends, all of whom can travel wherever they desire."
Together with them, I set out for the abode of the world-protectors. Then we all beheld a Brahmin of rigid vows, handsome, engaged in study, wandering alone in solitude.
O King, by his ascetic power, that forest was enveloped in splendor;
like the sun, he illuminated that entire region.
Having beheld such asceticism of his and his wondrous appearance, [the gods were amazed].
O descendant of Bharata, desiring to create obstacles to his asceticism, we descended upon that place—
myself, Saurabheyī, Samīcī, Budbudā, and Latā—
and together we approached that brahmin.
Singing, laughing, and enticing that twice-born man, they cast glances at him and bared their limbs, as if unwillingly, through the playful display of smiles and amorous gestures.
Displaying their arms, thighs, hips, and teeth, those beautiful women stood all around that twice-born man, seeking to entice him; yet,
O hero, he did not set his mind upon us in any way whatsoever.
The one of great splendor did not waver, remaining firm in his stainless austerity.
But that brahmin, O bull among kṣatriyas, became enraged and cursed us:
"You shall become crocodiles in the water and roam there for a hundred years."
Vargā said:
"Then, O best of the Bharatas, we were all deeply distressed and went for refuge to that Brahmin, whose wealth was his asceticism, who was steadfast and infallible."
"Arrogant because of our beauty, our youth, and our passion, we have committed an improper act; O twice-born one, you ought to forgive us.
For this alone is sufficient punishment for us, O you whose wealth is asceticism."

"Since we have come here to seduce you, whose soul is so disciplined, [we must consider that] those who contemplate dharma regard women as incapable of being slain. Therefore, O knower of dharma, it does not behove you to harm us according to the law."
O knower of dharma, a Brāhmaṇa who is friendly toward all beings is so called;
may this saying of the wise prove true and auspicious. Furthermore, the disciplined protect those who have come to them for refuge.
"We have come to you for refuge; therefore, you ought to forgive us.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus addressed, that righteous-souled Brahmin, a performer of auspicious deeds,"
O hero, he who possesses a splendor equal to the sun and the moon showed his favor.
The Brahmin said:
"A hundred, a thousand, the universe, and 'all'—these are all words for the inexhaustible."
This number, however, is one hundred; it does not signify an inexhaustible quantity.
And when you have become crocodiles, seizing men in the water, some best of men shall pull you out from the water onto dry land.
Then you shall all regain your own forms;
never before have I spoken an untruth, even when laughing.
And from this time forward, all these sacred fords (tīrthas) [shall be established].
"By this name, these bathing places for women shall become renowned everywhere;
they shall be meritorious and purifying for the wise.
Vargā said:
Then, having saluted that brahmin and performed a circumambulation of him,
we departed from that place in great distress and reflected:
"Where indeed might we all find that man within a short time?"
"May we meet again with him who can restore us to that former form. O Bhārata, having reflected thus, in what seemed like a mere moment,
we beheld the illustrious celestial sage Nārada.
Seeing that celestial seer of immeasurable splendor, we were all filled with joy;
yet, O Pārtha, having saluted him, we stood there with distressed faces. He questioned us regarding the root of our sorrow, and we explained it to him.
"Where shall we all go so that we may find them again?
Having heard what had occurred, she spoke these words:
"On the southern shore of the ocean, there are indeed five sacred fords (tīrthas)."
"Go without delay to those meritorious and delightful places;
there, O tiger among men, the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya, pure in soul, will swiftly liberate you from this suffering— of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, Nārada vanished right there before them all. O hero, having heard his words, we have all come here;
and now, O sinless one, this truth has been realized today as I have been liberated by you.
"These four friends of mine, however, remain elsewhere in the water. O hero, perform an auspicious deed and liberate them all.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O lord of the people, that best of the Pāṇḍavas, undepressed in spirit and endowed with prowess, liberated them all from that curse;
and rising from those waters, he regained his own body.

O King, those Apsarases then appeared just as they had before. Having purified the sacred fords (tīrthas) and given them leave to depart, the Lord went again to the city of Maṇalūra to see Citrāṅgadā.
Upon her he begot a son, King Babhruvāhana. Seeing him, O King, the Pāṇḍava went toward Gokarṇa and spoke to Citravāhana.
"O lord of men, let us accept this Babhruvāhana as the bride-price for Citrāṅgadā;
by means of him, I shall be released from my debt. Then the son of Indra spoke these words again to Citrāṅgadā.
"Stay right here, O blessed lady, as the one who increases Babhruvāhana’s prosperity. You have come to my residence at Indraprastha; there you shall find delight.
[There you will see] Kuntī, Yudhiṣṭhira, and Bhīma—my two younger brothers."

When you have arrived there, you shall see your other kinsmen as well; O blessed and blameless lady, you will rejoice together with your relatives. Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, is established in dharma and steadfast in truth.
Having conquered the entire earth, he will perform the Rājasūya sacrifice;
kings known as rulers upon the earth will come there,
and your father will arrive bringing many jewels.
"You have set out on this same caravan with Citravāhana’s army;
I shall see you at the Rājasūya sacrifice. Protect my son, do not grieve.
For he who is named Babhruvāhana is my very life-breath moving outside of me."

Therefore, indeed, cherish your son, who increases the lineage of Pūru; the heir of Citravāhana, a delight to the Pauravas by virtue of his righteousness— a beloved son of the Pāṇḍavas— protect him always.
"Do not grieve over separation, O blameless one," having thus spoken to Citrāṅgadā,
[he showed her] the primordial abode of Paśupati, which grants liberation through mere sight.
Where even a sinful man attains the state that grants fearlessness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
He [visited] the holy fords and sacred shrines in the western regions.
He of immeasurable prowess traveled in due order to all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and shrines (*āyatana*) that exist on the western ocean;
having visited them all, he arrived at Prabhāsa.
At night, he reflected upon the story told by Gada,
as well as the sweetness, the perfection of beauty, and the virtues of Subhadrā;
he pondered what means there might be to obtain her.
Having assumed a change of dress and taken on the form of a wandering mendicant,
he remained unrecognized by the Kukuras, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis due to his disguise;
wandering about and subsisting on alms, he maintained the appearance of a parivrājaka.
By whatever means possible, having entered that great house and seen Subhadrā, the uniquely beautiful sister of Kṛṣṇa,
and having ascertained the intention of Vāsudeva, I shall accomplish what is beneficial and auspicious.
Having thus made this resolution, he then became initiated;
carrying the triple staff, with a shaven head, a water-pot, and a rosary as his finger-ring,
Pārtha bore the burden of yoga within the hollow of a banyan tree.
Even as he was entering while Vāsava was pouring down rain,
Bībhatsu thought of Keśava, the lord of gods and destroyer of afflictions,
the auspicious Śambhu who removes the distress of those who bow before him, yet who deceives by means of his illusory form.
Knowing his thought through divine knowledge, Keśava,
who was lying upon a blessed bed accompanied by Satyabhāmā,
suddenly laughed and rejoiced, O King.
Again and again Satyabhāmā spoke to Puruṣottama:
"O Blessed One, while lying comfortably upon your bed, you were overcome with anxiety;
you laughed in many ways, again and again."

"O Kṛṣṇa, if it is to be heard, or if you have grace toward me, O Lord of the World, you ought to speak; for I truly desire to hear it. My paternal aunt’s son is Arjuna, the younger brother of Bhīmasena."
At that time, O Pārtha, he had gone on a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) for a specific reason and according to his agreement; then,
having completed his pilgrimage, the descendant of Bharata returned at night,
thinking of Subhadrā and me as well for her sake.
While thinking only of that auspicious lady, he assumed the form of an ascetic;
disguised in the garb of an ascetic, having reached Dvārakā,
he beheld the fair-complexioned Mādhavī by whatever means possible.
"Having understood the doctrine of Vāsudeva, I shall strive toward my heart's desire. Having thus resolved, the Pāṇḍava Partha,
bearing the marks of an ascetic, remained in the shade of a banyan tree while Indra was pouring down rain.
"Even while bearing the burden of yoga, he has experienced mental suffering.
If Mādhava knows me to be such as this, remembering me, he might see your brother. Thus [Kṛṣṇa] showed [himself] to Satyabhāmā.
Then, rising from his bed, Madhusūdana set out;
he heard that Bībhatsu, the unconquered, had reached the region of Prabhāsa and was wandering among the sacred fords (tīrthas).
But at the word of the *cāraṇas*, that Janārdana, Mādhava, then approached the son of Kuntī alone, remaining unrecognized. At that time, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava beheld one another at Prabhāsa.
Having embraced one another and inquired after each other's welfare in the forest,
those two dear friends, the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, remained there.
Then Vāsudeva questioned Arjuna regarding that mode of life.
"For what purpose, O Pāṇḍava, do you wander through these sacred fords?
Thereupon Arjuna related everything exactly as it had occurred;
and having heard this, the lord Vārṣṇeya said, "It is even so."
Having stayed at Prabhāsa as long as they desired, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava went to Mount Raivataka for their residence.
Indeed, they had already gone to that mountain at the previous word of Kṛṣṇa.
The men adorned themselves and brought forth food;
having accepted it all and partaken of it, Arjuna the Pāṇḍava,
together with Vāsudeva, watched the actors and dancers.
Having taken leave of them all and honored them, the son of Pāṇḍu,
possessed of great splendor, approached a divinely prepared and well-adorned bed.
Then, the mighty-armed one lay down there upon that auspicious couch.
O Bhārata, he recounted to the Sātvata the sight of sacred fords, mountains, rivers, and forests;
and even as he was telling these stories, O Janamejaya, he was overcome by sleep.
On that bed comparable to heaven, the son of Kuntī was carried away;
O sinless one, being awakened by sweet singing, the sound of the lute,
as well as by hymns and auspicious praises, he woke up.
Having performed his necessary duties and being greeted by the descendant of Vṛṣṇi,
he took leave of the Vārṣṇeya and then chose to stay for the night.
Having said "So be it," Vāsudeva indeed ordered food to be prepared.
Having suddenly dismissed Pārtha, who was disguised in the form of a eunuch,
Hari departed for Dvārakā by means of his gold-adorned chariot.
O Janamejaya, Dvārakā was indeed fully adorned.
Even in the pleasure gardens,
people desiring to see the son of Kuntī gathered by the hundreds of thousands and quickly came to the royal highway to honor the son of Kuntī.
O Vārṣṇeya, unable to endure even half a moment’s separation from Govinda,
they stood gazing intently, overcome with curiosity;
there were hundreds and thousands of women in their lines of sight.
A great assembly of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas took place. Thus honored by all the sons of the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas,
he greeted those worthy of greeting and was greeted in return by everyone.
The hero was saluted with great honor by all the youths; having embraced them all— who were of his own age— again and again,
he remained in Kṛṣṇa’s delightful palace, which was filled with jewels and provisions for enjoyment.
He dwelt there for many nights together with Kṛṣṇa;
then the greatly effulgent Kṛṣṇa entered his own delightful palace.
All the queens honored Kṛṣṇa, who had returned from his journey.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O King, after a few days had passed on that Raivataka mountain,
there occurred a very great festival for the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
There, at that great mountain festival, the heroes of the Bhoja, Vṛṣṇi, and Andhaka clans gave gifts to thousands of Brahmins. And all around that mountain were palaces variegated with jewels.
O King, that place was adorned on all sides with lamp-trees;
there, musicians played their instruments,
dancers danced, and singers sang songs.
The highly energetic princes of the Vṛṣṇis, adorned with ornaments,
moved about everywhere in vehicles whose parts were variegated with gold.
The citizens likewise moved on foot as well as in various kinds of carriages.
Accompanied by their wives and retinues by the hundreds and thousands,
the lord Haladhara, intoxicated and joined by Revatī,
wandered there, O Bhārata, followed by Gandharvas.
In the same way, the powerful Ugrasena, king of the Vṛṣṇis,
accompanied by thousands of women and being sung to by Gandharvas, arrived;
as did the son of Rukmiṇī and Sāmba, both intoxicated and fierce in battle.
Wearing celestial garlands and garments, they sported like immortals.
Akrūra, Sāraṇa, Gada, Bhānu, Viḍūratha, Niśaṭha, Cārudeṣṇa, Pṛthu, and Vipṛthu were there as well.
Satyaka and Sātyaki, who were companions of Bhaṅgakāra,
as well as Hārdikya Kṛtavarman and others who have not been mentioned— these,
surrounded by women and Gandharvas respectively, [departed].
Then they beautified that festival on Mount Raivataka;
Vāsudeva, endowed with all virtues, went there with his women,
and having given gifts to the twice-born, he beheld a wandering mendicant.
Then, while that most auspicious tumult was occurring,
Vāsudeva and Pārtha together wandered about;
and as they were thus walking there, [they saw] the beautiful daughter of Vāsudeva.
Then they both beheld Bhadrā, adorned and standing in the midst of her companions.
As soon as Arjuna saw her, the god of love arose within him.
Kṛṣṇa perceived that Pārtha’s mind was thus fixed with single-minded intent.
Then, O Bhārata, Puṣkarākṣa spoke as if laughing:
"Why is the mind of this forest-dweller thus agitated by desire?
O Pārtha, she is my sister, the uterine sibling of Sāraṇa."
"May you be blessed! She is named Subhadrā, the beloved daughter of my father.
If your mind is inclined toward her, I shall speak to my father myself.
O Bhārata, he spoke thus to the lotus-eyed one, as if smiling.
Arjuna said:
The daughter of Vasudeva and the sister of Vāsudeva—
endowed with such beauty, whom would she not enchant?

"Indeed, every auspicious deed would certainly be accomplished for me if this daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, your sister, were to become my queen. For the host of gods, always mindful of you, conquers the asuras."
"O Lord, through the sight of you, there is indeed nothing that cannot be attained; what need is there to speak of it?
But tell me, O Janārdana, what means might there be for its attainment?
I shall undertake all of that, provided it is possible for a human being."
Vāsudeva said:
"O bull among men, the svayaṃvara is the marriage rite for Kṣatriyas; yet that, O Pārtha, is fraught with uncertainty because it lacks a fixed cause."

"Even the forcible abduction of Kṣatriya women for the sake of marriage is praised among heroes; thus do those who know the Dharma understand. Therefore, O Arjuna, you have forcibly carried off my auspicious sister."
"Indeed, let her choose for herself; for who knows what she intends to do? But when the time has ripened, you shall assume the form of an ascetic.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, having determined what was to be done,
O King, dispatched swift messengers at that time to Dharmarāja,
who was staying in Indraprastha, with all that news.
Upon hearing this, the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava gave his permission;
and Bhīmasena, having heard it, considered his purpose accomplished. Having spoken thus with the men, he attained great joy.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O Janamejaya, when that conversation had been concluded and he was granted permission, Dhanañjaya learned that the maiden had gone to Raivataka.

Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
reflecting upon Bhadrā, he sat down upon a stone slab in a delightful forest region, thickly covered with many trees.
With *sāla*, *tāla*, and *aśvakarṇa* trees, as well as *bakula* and *arjuna*;
with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *ketaka*, and *pāṭala*; and with *karṇikāra*, *aśoka*, *aṅkola*, and *atimuktaka*.
On that stone surface, which was thus covered by these and other [offerings],
he, reflecting again and again upon Subhadrā of auspicious speech,
beheld the Vṛṣṇi heroes who had arrived there by chance.
And Baladeva, Hārdikya, Sāmba, and Sāraṇa; Pradyumna and Gada, Cārudeṣṇa and Viḍūratha; Bhānu and Niśaṭha, as well as Pṛthu and Vipṛthu.
Seeing many others in that same way, he harbored sorrow in his heart. Then all those Vṛṣṇis, filled with longing and endowed with humility, stood surrounding the ascetic as they beheld him together.
Then Arjuna, with a joyful mind, addressed them, saying: "Welcome!
Let everyone sit upon this delightful stone surface.
Having been thus addressed by the ascetic, those bulls among the Yadavas were filled with delight.
They all sat down close together, saying, "A very warm welcome.
Then, once those Vṛṣṇi heroes were seated, the Pāṇḍava,
concealing his true feelings, addressed them with inquiries after their welfare.
Having spoken auspicious words in every respect, Baladeva said this: "O Brahmin, show me favor; from where have you come?
O best among speakers, tell me of the holy places you have seen."
O Bhārata, he described to the Yādava the mountains, sacred fords, forests, and shrines; indeed, he recounted to him the sight of the holy fords, the mountains, the rivers, and the woods.
While narrating those stories, O Janamejaya, at the conclusion of his discourse,
he presented a tale connected with dharma to the hero of the Vṛṣṇis.
Having heard that meritorious discourse on dharma, the hero of the Vṛṣṇis honored it.
Then, O Bhārata, all the Yādavas deliberated:
"This illustrious twice-born man, bearing the marks of an ascetic, is a guest from another land;
relying upon what dwelling might he live here free from disturbance?"
Thus did those Yādavas speak to the son of Rohiṇī;
they all beheld Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of the Yādavas, as he approached. "Come, O Keśava, dear one! the son of Rohiṇī spoke these words.
"This learned twice-born man, bearing the marks of a mendicant,
has come to our city as a guest from afar to dwell here for the duration of the rainy season;
tell me, Janārdana, in what place he resides."
"O illustrious one, while you remain here, I am bound to you by dharma.
However, tell me where I myself may dwell in a pleasant place. Being well-pleased by those words, he embraced Janārdana.
The mighty Baladeva, having reflected, spoke these words:
"The wise one should dwell in the garden for four months and years,
staying in the maidens' quarters of Subhadrā and eating food according to his desire."
"It is my firm conviction that we should dwell in the vine-arbors;
all the Yādavas consider it so, provided they receive your permission.
You are powerful, handsome, eloquent, illustrious, and deeply learned."
But it is my opinion that it is not proper [to go] near the maidens' quarters.
You are my teacher, my instructor, and my leader; you know the scriptures and are the best among those who know the Dharma.
I shall not contradict what you have said; I will do as you say.
In discerning what is auspicious and inauspicious, there is no one else on earth like him; this illustrious guest from afar is learned in all dharmas,
steadfast, endowed with discipline, truthful in speech, and has conquered his senses.
"Indeed, who can discern the mind of this one who bears the marks of an ascetic?
O lotus-eyed one, having led him to the auspicious inner apartments of the maidens,
report this to Subhadrā at my command."

"Honor him with foods to be chewed, foods to be eaten, drinks, and other desired offerings. Having agreed, saying "So be it," Keśava, accompanied by the ascetic, made a covenant with him and became exceedingly joyful.
Having sported on the mountain as they desired, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava then entered that city, taking the Pāṇḍava by the hand;
and having entered, they went to a beautiful house furnished with every enjoyment.
He announced Pārtha to Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
Having heard the words of Hṛṣīkeśa, both of them spoke at length:
"This great desire revolves within our hearts."
"When shall we see Bībhatsu, the Pāṇḍava, returned home?"—
while they were thinking thus, Pārtha dispelled their sorrow and honored them with unsurpassed, previously unknown marks of worship.
Seeing that ascetic, the most excellent of dear guests, who had arrived,
Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to his uterine sister Subhadrā:
"O blessed lady, this is a guest from afar, a self-restrained sage observing vows."
"Let him receive constant honor while residing in your maidens' quarters;
for an ascetic who is recognized by a noble person should always be honored. Therefore, O Vārṣṇeyī, support this ascetic always with food and edibles."
"Whatever this seer says must certainly be done; of this there is no doubt.
O blessed lady, together with your friends, you must remain obedient to his will. For in the past, O blessed one, there were ascetics who were devoted to the practice of seeking alms."
O illustrious lady, those maidens residing in the inner apartments of the Daśārhas,
remaining unwearied, would provide them with various foods and delicacies at the proper times.
She said to Kṛṣṇa, "So be it; I shall do as you have told me.
I will satisfy that bull among the twice-born with my conduct and my actions.
In this manner, Dhanañjaya remained for some time in that form.
Honored with the finest foods and delicacies by Bhadrā, he dwelt there;
and as he constantly gazed upon Bhadrā, who was endowed with every virtue and was the sister of Vāsudeva, the god of love arose within him.
As if concealing his outward appearance upon beholding that woman of excellent complexion,
Pārtha, fallen under the sway of desire, sighed long and hot;
he did not regard Kṛṣṇā as the sister of Vāsudeva on account of her beauty.

When the time had passed, Dhanañjaya— though restrained by the goad of desire— no longer remembered Subhadrā, even though she was like Indrasenā come to his heart, or the daughter of Varuṇa herself in person; for he was preoccupied with his brothers' wealth.
