Beholding Bhadrā, who was devoted to the delights of play and surrounded by hundreds of female companions,
Arjuna rejoiced as the sacrificial fire rejoices at seeing Svāhā.
This took place in the presence of the illustrious Pāṇḍava and Subhadrā.
The origin and the power [of the disease] were previously described by Gada;
and having heard the roar of a thunderbolt, the wise Keśava also gave a detailed account in the past, using Arjuna as a comparison.
In their anger and intoxication, the Vṛṣṇis directed their boastful talk toward Arjuna;
comparing their own manly deeds to his, those archers grew increasingly arrogant.
Even in mutual quarrels and disputes, the Vṛṣṇis [continued this way].
"Even Arjuna is not my equal; how much less you," they said.
And as the Vṛṣṇis took their newborn sons, they uttered these blessings:
"O child, may you become an archer equal in prowess to Arjuna."
Therefore, Subhadrā desired that bull among the Bharatas on account of his manliness;
she was captivated by the beauty and the skill of him who is true to his word,
having heard [of them] from the companies of wandering bards and guests and from Gada.
While the bull of the Bharatas was out of sight, Subhadrā remained devoted to him;
whenever anyone happened to see Bhīmasena while traveling through Kurujāṅgala,
Bhadrā would always ask him about Bībhatsu.
Through frequent questioning and likewise through constant hearing,
the Pāṇḍava came to perceive Bhadrā as if before his very eyes;
her two arms, resembling serpents, were calloused from the striking of the bowstring.
As she looked upon him, the thought "This is Pārtha" arose in her mind without a doubt;
for Subhadrā had heard of the bull of the Bharatas according to his true form,
and seeing him in that very form, she attained supreme joy.
Once, as he was seated, she asked the joy of the Kurus:
"How are the regions? How are the mountains and the various provinces?
And how are the lakes, the rivers, and the forests for one who travels?"
"Which directions have you ever traveled, and how have you always wandered?
Thus addressed, he then spoke many playful and false words to Bhadrā;
being exceedingly pleased, he told her many such stories.
Having heard of his various deeds in the world, the maiden’s heart became filled with the thought of him.
And on a certain junction of the lunar phases (*parvan*), Subhadrā [beheld] the bull of the Bharatas.
Having reached a secluded spot in private, she spoke joyfully:
"While wandering through the worlds as an ascetic, did you, O Blessed One, see Pṛthā, our father’s sister, who dwells in Khāṇḍavaprastha?"
Is the noble Yudhiṣṭhira well with all his brothers who are self-restrained? Is Bhīma devoted to dharma for the sake of the wise Dharmarāja?
And has Dhanañjaya, having fulfilled his vow, been freed from the fault of his transgression?
Restraining his desires for sensual enjoyments, indifferent to what is pleasant or unpleasant— where indeed does Pārtha wander today, dwelling through many difficult nights?
For he is accustomed to comfort, undeserving of suffering, long-armed, and a subduer of enemies.
"Has the Blessed One heard of or seen Pārtha Arjuna?
Hearing her words, he spoke to her as if smiling:
"Noble lady, Pṛthā is well, along with her son and her daughter-in-law."
He rejoices as he beholds his sons, and he beholds Kurukṣetra. Having been granted leave by his mother and his uterine brothers, Dhanañjaya,
the Pāṇḍava, dwells alone in Dvārakā bearing the insignia of an ascetic.
"O Mādhavī, why do you not recognize me, even though you see me constantly? Having heard these words of his, the sister of Vāsudeva stood there sighing heavily, scratching the earth.
Then, exceedingly thrilled, Arjuna Dhananjaya— the best among all wielders of weapons— joyfully addressed her, saying,
"I am he," just as your heart had turned toward me upon hearing [my name], O beautiful lady.
My constant devotion is directed toward you, and it is a hundred times greater than that.
O blessed lady, on an auspicious day, I have been chosen by you in accordance with dharma;
I shall become your husband, just as Satyavat was chosen by Sāvitrī.

Having spoken thus, Pārtha then entered the bower of creepers. Thereupon, the graceful Subhadrā, filled with a sense of bashfulness and lying upon her celestial bed in a manner unbecoming of her, fainted away.

Having perceived through his divine eye what had occurred in the maidens' quarters, Kṛṣṇa instructed Rukmiṇī regarding the food and other provisions for Arjuna. From that time forward, Dhanañjaya indeed remained preoccupied with thoughts of that auspicious lady.
At that time, the Lord remained in that grove for the sake of his task;
Subhadrā, too, was not at ease regarding Pārtha—
she was emaciated, her face pale, and she was wholly devoted to anxiety and grief.
Sighing deeply, the noble-minded Bhadrā was distressed in her mind;
she found no pleasure whatsoever in beds, seats, or enjoyments. Neither by night nor by day did she sleep, appearing like one who has gone mad.
To Bhadrā Devakī, who was thus overcome with grief, he spoke these words:
"Do not grieve, O daughter of the Vṛṣṇis; take heart, O beautiful lady.
I shall present you to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, those bulls among men."
"Afterwards, I shall learn of your news; do not grieve, O Mādhavī. Having spoken thus, her mother, who desired her welfare, then informed Ānakadundubhi of Bhadrā's situation.
In secret, she sat upon a single seat there and spoke of Bhadrā and Svastā;
meanwhile, we have heard that the illustrious Arjuna, the ascetic, is now in the grove,
along with Akrūra, Kṛṣṇa, Āhuka, and Sātyaki.
"O one of great wisdom, let it be announced, if it is something that should be heard by our kinsmen.
Vasudeva, having heard this from Akrūra and Āhuka,
then informed Kṛṣṇa and consulted with him many times.
"This is the task; this is what must be done; this indeed has been thus resolved.
Akrūra, Ugrasena, Satyaka, and Gada, along with Pṛthuśravas, Kṛṣṇa, and Śini, were all assembled together.
O Bhārata, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Devakī, and Rohiṇī,
together with Vāsudeva and abiding by the counsel of the family priest,
deliberated upon the marriage for the twelfth day.
O Bhārata, this was unknown to the son of Rohiṇī and to Uddhava;
however, the elder brother of Gada, desiring to perform the marriage of Subhadrā,
spoke of it as a great festival for the purpose of worshipping Mahādeva.
For thirty-four days and nights, for the sake of pacifying Subhadrā’s distress and for the welfare of Savyasācin, he caused a proclamation to be made throughout the city:
"On the fourth day from now, you must go to Antardvīpa."

"Accompanied by their wives, their retinues, their sons, and their kinsmen, all the social orders must depart; all the Yādavas must depart. Thus addressed, they all acted accordingly in every respect.
Then, O Bhārata, on the Antardvīpa of all the Daśārhas,
there was a supreme festival for thirty-four days and nights.
[There were] Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Āhuka, Akrūra, Pradyumna, Śini, and Satyaka.
The Kukuras, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis set out for the ocean with joyful hearts;
the Vṛṣṇis, together with the Brāhmaṇas, departed on ships equipped with masts and banners, as did all the inhabitants of the city.
Then, having arrived in haste, Subhadrā spoke to the lotus-eyed one— who is worshipped by the hosts of the Daśārhas— in accordance with the instruction of the ascetic:
"That Blessed One will remain here for twelve days, occupied with his duties."
"Who could perform the rites of attendance for him while he remains here?
To her Hṛṣīkeśa replied: "Who else, especially, other than you, is worthy to attend upon that seer? No mortal man is fit for this."
"By our own counsel, you alone must remain under the command of this great seer; perform all his duties, keeping both fame and dharma in view,
for the sake of that foremost guest and for all these ascetics."
"O blessed lady, remain devoted to your duties and maintain self-control.
Having thus instructed Bhadrā and provided for her protection, Madhusūdana departed amidst the blaring of conchs and the great sounds of kettledrums.
Then, having reached that island, all the Kukuras and Andhakas, headed by Ugrasena and devoted to the practice of charity and righteousness, took up residence there;
it was seven yojanas in width and ten yojanas in length.
That great island, with its mountains and vast forests,
became a pleasure ground for all the Sātvatas, provided with networks of embankments and lotus-pools,
as well as clusters of ponds, marshes, and enchanting groves.

That island, with all the Kukuras and Andhakas who were equal to Vāsudeva, became endowed with supreme excellence, like heaven with the immortals. For thirty-four days and nights, they remained devoted to the practice of giving and righteousness.
Led by Ugrasena, all the Kukuras and Andhakas went forth for recreation;
adorned with various garlands and ornaments, and anointed with diverse forms of unguents,
all the Yādavas, joined together in drinking, set out toward the pleasure gardens.
There they became engaged in delighting themselves with true songs, dances, and instrumental music;
for when the bull of the Daśārhas, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, had departed from there,
Pārtha considered the time for Subhadrā’s marriage to have arrived.
Having decided upon their departure from that city of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, Pārtha, the son of Pāṇḍu, then spoke these words to Subhadrā:
"Listen, O blessed lady, to what has been ordained by the sages according to the scriptures and according to the facts."
The father, brother, mother, maternal uncle, paternal uncle, and even the preceptor of a maiden possess authority over her giving away in marriage. Meanwhile,
her father Āhuka was desirous of witnessing the great festival of Paśupati.
"O blessed one, I have gone to the intermediate island with my sons, grandsons, and kinsmen;
O large-eyed lady, my relatives are indeed staying in a foreign land.
Therefore, O Subhadrā, the fifth form of marriage, the Gāndharva, shall take place."
Regarding the union with a maiden, four types of rites have been proclaimed.
O Mādhavī, listen now to the practice of those virtuous ones, just as it is:
having invited a suitor according to the prescribed rule, she is given by her father to him as he requests.

She is called a "wife" by the wise; she is submissive and devoted to her husband. For the sake of maintaining dependents and for her own nourishment, when she remains with her husband, she is considered by the wise to be a "consort" (*bhāryā*).

Having chosen her according to the Dharma and brought her to his own home, she who is given to him in accordance with the law during her youth becomes a wife appointed by her father; and she who gives birth to a husband is known by the name of "jāyā" (she who gives birth).
*Dārāḥ*, *patnī*, *bhāryā*, and *jāyā*—these are the four kinds [of wives].
These four alone are witnesses to the sacred fire when joined with the ritual according to the Dharma;
[the others] are through the Gāndharva marriage, out of passion, or for the sake of obtaining a son.

She who is favored by her own will is submissive and fruitful. The Gāndharva marriage, however, is devoid of ritual; it proceeds solely from passion. It is recorded as the union of one with desire with another with desire, in secret, without mantras.
"O Mādhavī, I have said that even an actionless deed must be performed by you. For today,
indeed, the solstice, the month, the lunar mansion, the fortnight, the lunar day,
the *karaṇa*, the *muhūrta*, and the excellence of the *lagna* are all perfectly aligned."
O large-eyed one, for marriage, the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is praised,
as well as the month of Vaiśākha among months, the bright fortnight among fortnights, the asterism Hasta among constellations, and the third lunar day among dates.
The ascendant is indeed Capricorn, the most excellent; likewise, the *bava* lunar day is auspicious.
The *maitra* moment is favorable for our marriage ceremony. O blessed lady, all these perfections shall come to pass tonight.
The Blessed One, the sun, the best among those who give heat, is setting;
for Nārāyaṇa, the omniscient creator of the universe, would surely not remain unaware of this.
Since we have fallen into this crisis of dharma, what indeed should be done to bring about what is auspicious?
"Do not address me, who am deluded by the god of love arising from the mind, with such lamentation. Give me an answer; why will you not speak, O Mādhavī?
Having heard Arjuna's words, she reflected upon Janārdana.
With eyes clouded by tears, she did not utter a single word;
Arjuna, the best among victors, began to rave with the madness of passion. Then, having entered the bower of creepers, he thought of his father.
Knowing that the son of Kuntī was thus reflecting, the Lord of Śacī,
accompanied by Śacī and by hosts of sages, Siddhas, and Apsarases led by Nārada,
as well as Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī, arrived at Kuśasthalī.
Having reflected upon Subhadrā’s thoughts, Janārdana then considered that Rauhineya’s consciousness was stolen by sleep,
and [he remained] together with Akrūra, Śini, Satyaka, and Gada.
Accompanied by Vasudeva and the wise Āhuka,
Devaka, he arrived at night at the city of Dvārakā, surrounded by his kinsmen;
having honored the Lord of Gods along with Nārada and other great sages.
Having offered words of auspicious inquiry, the Lord of the Gods entreated him;
Kṛṣṇa replied, "So be it," regarding the marriage ceremony.
Āhuka, Vasudeva, along with Akrūra and Sātyaki, [were present].
Having bowed their heads in prostration to the Subduer of Pāka (Indra), they said:
"O God of gods, homage be to you! O Lord of the world, O Master of the universe!
We, together with our kinsmen, are blessed among all beings, O All-pervading One."
"O Viśvajit, we have gained confidence through your words.
Having spoken thus, they propitiated him and honored him with great effort;
then, by the command of Mahendra, they all departed together with the great ṛṣis.
They performed the marriage of Śakra’s son according to the sacred scriptures;
Arundhatī, Queen Śacī, Rukmiṇī, and Devakī,
together with celestial women, carried out the auspicious rites.
The great seer Kāśyapa was the *hotṛ* priest, and Nārada and others were the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*). At that time, they all bestowed auspicious blessings upon Arjuna.
Then, having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), Mahendra [anointed] the subduer of Pāka.
Accompanied by all the world-protectors and praised by all the gods,
he adorned that son of Pṛthā— like a second Vāsava— with crowns, armlets, necklaces, and other ornaments, as well as bracelets and earrings.
Then Purandara, having embraced his son, attained great joy;
likewise, Queen Śacī and the women of the Yadava clan, together with Bhadrā, Arundhatī, and others,
performed the auspicious marriage rites.

Accompanied by celestial nymphs, they joyfully honored her with ornaments; the divine women regarded Subhadrā as if she were Paulomī herself. Then the marriage ceremony proceeded, performed with every excellence.
Having taken her hand in marriage according to the rites of mantra and oblation,
just as Śatakratu took Śacī,
the beautiful Subhadrā attended upon Jiṣṇu with exceeding devotion.
"Bhadrā is the equal of Pārtha in beauty as well as in age;
and Pārtha is also the equal of Subhadrā in beauty and auspicious marks.
Thus spoke the gods at that time, joyful, with Indra at their head.
Having thus settled the gods together with the Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases,
and having taken leave of all the Yādavas, they departed as they had come.
Then the Yādavas, having taken leave of Pārtha, went to Antardvīpa.
Then Vāsudeva, the joy of the Yadus, spoke to Pārtha:
"O bull of the Bharatas, having mounted my chariot yoked with Sainya and Sugrīva, you shall stay here for twenty-two days, O Pārtha."
"O Pārtha, enter Khāṇḍavaprastha in happiness along with Subhadrā;
O Bhārata, I shall come later accompanied by the Yādavas.
You, however, should dwell in the house of Rukmiṇī, devoted to the garb of an ascetic."
Having spoken thus, Janārdana departed for Antardvīpa.
Then Pārtha, having performed the marriage, had accomplished his purpose;
yet, a sudden passion for her arose within Pārtha.
That hero, the bull among the Bharatas, was united with that auspicious lady,
just as Rāma was endowed with Sītā when she had reached maturity; for he, the victorious one, recognized her as Modesty, Fortune, and the very act of humility itself.
She, being virtuous and peerless in beauty among twelve excellent women, caused him—
who was already radiant by nature with his own splendor— to shine even more intensely,
like the autumnal sun when its thousand rays are rising.
But that high-minded woman, devoted to that tiger among men,
remained within the maidens' quarters and became entirely intent upon him.
Meanwhile, Dhanañjaya set out from the city of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas.
Having made this decision, Pārtha said this to Subhadrā:
"Distribute among the leading hosts of the twice-born according to their merit;
provide them with foods to be chewed and eaten, and with all desired objects, so that they may depart."
"Go yourself quickly, O blessed lady, to the residence of the Great King, for his own sake, to inform him of the completion of the great vow,
with these supreme, excellent horses endowed with splendor, strength, and speed."

"Quickly bring the chariot here, joined by Sainya and Sugrīva," she said to her companions, O fortunate lady, "for the sake of sport. Having spoken thus, take the chariot and all the weapons and go forth at once.
"You should place the chariot-poles, banners, quivers, and bows, as well as all the great maces with their raised handles, upon this excellent chariot.
Thus addressed by Arjuna, Subhadrā, who speaks auspiciously, [responded].
She went quickly with her friends to the king’s palace;
standing there, as if in play, she spoke these words to the guards:
"I shall go by this chariot to complete my great vow."
When Subhadrā had spoken thus— [referring] to the chariot of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, joined by Sainya and Sugrīva, and equipped with weapons— the people, with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O blessed lady, let this chariot be used by you as you desire."

Having prepared the excellent chariot and addressed her with kind words, the beautiful woman, having had everything arranged as instructed, quickly took Subhadrā along with her friends and spoke to Arjuna.
"This chariot, the best among those for riders, has been brought here at your command.
Go in safety as you wish to the Kurus, O delighter of the Kauravas. Having presented that chariot to her husband, Subhadrā, who was esteemed as auspicious, [departed].
Then, filled with joy, she gave various kinds of wealth to the brahmins; she provided savory foods and desired delicacies,
as well as diverse garments, according to their wishes and her own faith.
Having been gratified with various kinds of food and having received those riches,
the Brahmins departed for their own homes after pronouncing supreme blessings.
However, Dhanañjaya had already been requested by Subhadrā beforehand.
"O Pārtha, there is no one on earth equal to me in holding the reins; therefore,
let Mādhavī, the sister of Vāsudeva, mount first and take hold of the horses' reins after the rites for success have been performed."
Leaving behind that banner with its raised great bow,
Dhananjaya, dressed in white garments, ascended the excellent chariot,
as well as the crown and ornaments bestowed by Mahendra.

Having adorned himself, the son of Kuntī then prepared to depart. Thereupon, a tumultuous clamor arose within the maidens' quarters upon seeing Pārtha mounted on his chariot, sword in hand and bearing his bow.

In the maidens' quarters, the girls spoke to the sister of Vāsudeva, who stood upon the chariot with Arjuna, holding the reins and possessing beautiful hips: "O Subhadrā, O lady of auspicious speech, all your desires have been fulfilled."
Having obtained as your husband the heroic Arjuna, who is dear to Vāsudeva,
you are the most excellent among all women, O sister of Kṛṣṇa,
since your husband Arjuna is the best among all men.
"A hero has been born to you, O blessed one, a great chariot-warrior for all the world. Go in safety to your home; may you be reunited with your kinsmen.
Thus addressed, she was gladdened by her joyful female companions.
She urged on the auspicious horses, endowed with auspicious speed;
then, with a chowrie in her hand, she became a female companion who was a hunchbacked woman. Then [the chariot] emerged with a roar from the gate of the maidens' quarters.
The people beheld that most excellent chariot, sounding like a thundercloud;
the city-dwellers heard the great roar of the chariot held by Subhadrā, which was like the sound of a cloud in the sky.

Standing upon his excellent chariot together with Subhadrā, Arjuna shone forth, endowed with supreme splendor like Mount Kailāsa with the Gaṅgā; Pārtha, that great car-warrior, gleamed resplendent accompanied by Subhadrā.
Like Śakra, the father of Pārtha, when accompanied by Śacī,
many people, having approached and beheld the illustrious Subhadrā being led away according to dharma, raised a great clamor of joyful shouts.
Subhadrā, the auspicious lady of sweet speech, the glory of the Daśārha clan, being full of desire, goes forth with the desiring Pārtha.
Then others, filled with rage, cried out, "Seize her! Slay her! Do not delay!"
As they were thus being restrained, that roar became exceedingly great;
by that clamor of the people, the hero was like an elephant afflicted,
and he rained down showers of arrows, yet he did not provoke anyone to anger.
He released sharp arrows, blazing with their own luster,
at the clusters of excellent palaces, the mansions, and the dwellings,
as well as at the pillars of the palace rows, the altars, and the banners.
He released sharpened arrows, yet he did not provoke anyone;
having agitated that best of cities like Garuḍa agitating the ocean,
that bull of the Bharatas departed, looking back toward the gate of Raivataka.

By the command of the Lord of Men, the powerful Vipṛthuśravas, accompanied by a great force, remained constantly on Mount Raivataka during Vāsudeva’s absence, acting as his counterpart to the wielder of the plow.
Then he became the protector of the city, increasing its prosperity;
having learned of the departure of the Pāṇḍavas, Vipṛthuśravas set out. Hearing the roar of the city, he urged on his own army.
Having traversed that path, he beheld that bull among men who had emerged from the gate of Dvārakā, like the sun emerging from a cloud,
resembling a rain-cloud accompanied by lightning as he bore his bow and arrows.
Upon encountering Pārtha, amazement seized the warriors as they beheld that army with its surging chariots, elephants, and horses. Then Subhadrā, who speaks auspiciously, spoke with great joy:

O bull among men, my intention to capture your chariot while you were fighting in battle has been formed by me for a long time— [the chariot] of that great-souled one who is filled with vigor, splendor, brilliance, and strength.
"May you indeed become the charioteer for Pārtha," he said, as he was training him.
Thus addressed, that bull among men, being pleased, replied to his beloved:
"Drive the horses without delay; let them enter the army of Viṣṭhala."

"O blessed lady, behold the strength of my arms as I fight against many who seek to slay me, and see my arrows being discharged! Having been addressed thus by Pārtha, O bull of the Bharatas, Bhadrā then—
Then, having urged on the horses with confidence,
they entered the army; that joyful host of Vipṛthu, with its great musical instruments sounding and its lofty banners raised, followed after Pārtha alone.
Joyful, they surrounded Dhanañjaya with various kinds of chariots drawn by excellent horses of great speed, raining down showers of arrows; but he,
a master of great weapons, warded off their missiles with his own divine weapons.
The conqueror of enemy cities covered the vast sky with his arrows;
with sharp shafts, the mighty-armed one cut through their arrows, as well as their crowns, armlets, and even their bows.
Desiring to strike down his enemies, Pārtha severed with sharpened arrows the yokes, shafts, fenders, and various mechanical devices;
he rendered those great car-warriors bowless, stripped of armor, and deprived of their chariots.
Having performed this, Pārtha, being pleased, said, "Look! and showed it to her.
Seeing that great marvel, Subhadrā said to Pārtha:
"I have attained my purpose; may you be blessed, O Pārtha, depart as you please."
Seeing the army closely engaged with the son of Pāṇḍu,
Vipṛthu hurriedly approached and said, "Stay!
But the Yādavas did not disregard those words of their commander.
Like great waves driven by the wind upon the ocean reaching the shore,
that bull among men quickly descended from his excellent chariot;
approaching that tiger among men, he embraced him with great joy.
Approaching Pārtha, he said:
"I have known this long-term residence of yours; nothing that you have done remains unknown to me, for I am the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace."
Janārdana was delighted by his union with Subhadrā, O Dhanañjaya; and when you had arrived at Dvārakā wearing the marks of an ascetic, your sister was sent forth by the bull among all the Vṛṣṇis.
O hero, O Dhanañjaya, you ought always to honor this daughter of the Daśārhas— devoted, virtuous, and auspicious— just as Śacīpati honors Śacī;
be the kinsman and the refuge of Subhadrā.
You possess kinship with Rāma and with Mahendra’s younger brother [Kṛṣṇa].
Indeed, Madhusūdana always made me his counselor;
and, dear one, it was through Subhadrā and you that Dhanañjaya [acted].
Having pointed out this divine, excellent chariot equipped with all weapons, as well as this very escort, O hero, the elder brother of Gada,
who brings happiness to the Vṛṣṇis, then departed for Antardvīpa.
"Let your brothers behold you here, who have been confined for so long, now reunited with your beloved, like the gods beholding the wielder of the thunderbolt.
For when the bull of the Daśārhas, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow, has arrived..."
They shall follow after Bhadrā with jewels and riches. Go on your path unharmed; be happy, O Dhanañjaya!
May you be reunited with friends whose sorrows have vanished, for you yourself are free from grief.
Then, having taken leave of Vipṛthu and having saluted him with joy, Pārtha, adhering to the counsel of Kṛṣṇa, mounted Kṛṣṇa’s chariot;
for that chariot had already been prepared for Pārtha by Kṛṣṇa.
Filled with every kind of jewel and endowed with all objects of enjoyment,
having been authorized by Vāsudeva and having declared that his task was accomplished,
the bull of the Bharatas, having ascertained Kṛṣṇa’s intention, departed.
Thus, accompanied by their families and amidst great festivities, the Vṛṣṇis also entered the city in a golden chariot prepared according to ritual prescription,
yoked with the horses Sainya and Sugrīva, and adorned with garlands of tinkling bells.
Equipped with every weapon, sounding like the roar of clouds,
brilliant as a blazing fire, and destroying the joy of his enemies—
he was armored, wearing a breastplate, armed with a sword, and having fastened his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors.
O Bhārata, having placed Mādhavī upon the chariot, he set out accompanied by his retinue under the pretext of a hunt; at that same time,
Subhadrā, having worshipped Raivata, the lord of mountains, [set out].
Having caused all the deities and the Brahmins to pronounce blessings,
and having circumambulated the mountain, he set out toward Dvārakā;
at that time, he [saw] Subhadrā, Kṛṣṇa’s sister, surrounded by women.
Rushing toward her, the son of Kuntī, afflicted by the arrows of love, forcibly placed Subhadrā— whose every limb was beautiful— upon his chariot.
Then that tiger among men, taking her who possessed a radiant smile, [departed].
He set out toward his own city in a chariot that traveled through the sky. Seeing Subhadrā being carried away, all the soldiers ran toward the city of Dvārakā, crying out in distress.
Having approached the Sudharmā assembly hall together,
they reported all of Pārtha’s prowess to the guardian of the hall. Having heard them, the guardian of the hall then [sounded] the war-drum.
He struck [the drum] which produced a great sound and was adorned with gold.
Then, at that noise, the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas were agitated;
they suddenly rose up together from the inner island.
Then, setting aside their food and drink, they entered the assembly hall.
There, the seats were made of gold, furnished with costly coverings,
variegated with gems and coral, and radiant with the brilliance of blazing fire.
Those tigers among men, the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇi and Andhaka clans,
occupied hundreds of thrones like sacrificial fires taking their places upon their altars.
As they sat together, they resembled a gathering of gods.
The keeper of the assembly hall, together with his followers, related the deeds of Jiṣṇu.
Having heard that, those Vṛṣṇi heroes, their eyes reddened with intoxication,
unable to endure the conduct of Pārtha, rose up in arrogance.
"Yoke the chariots quickly, and bring forth the spears! ...
[Bring forth] the elephants and likewise the horses!
Bring the armor quickly!"
Some cried out for costly bows and large armor,
while others shouted for charioteers to yoke the chariots;
some themselves led forth horses adorned with gold.
As the chariots, armor, and banners were being brought forward,
there arose a great tumult amidst the shouting of the heroic men.
Then Vanamālin, intoxicated and resembling the peak of Mount Kailāsa, [advanced].
Clad in blue garments and intoxicated with pride, he spoke these words:
"O you of little wisdom, why do you act thus while Janārdana remains silent?
Without understanding his true intent, you have become enraged and your thundering is in vain."
"Let this high-minded one first declare his own intention;
then, without weariness, do that which he deems fit to perform.
Then, having heard those words from Halāyudha, which were worthy of acceptance, they [acted accordingly].
Then they all became silent and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
Having heard these identical words of the wise Baladeva, they all sat down once again in the midst of the assembly hall.
Then Kāmapāla spoke to Vāsudeva, the scorcher of foes:
"O Lord of the three worlds, O Kṛṣṇa, creator of the past, the present, and the future,
why do you sit silent, looking on, O Janārdana?"
"O Acyuta, for your sake we have all honored Pārtha;
yet that evil-minded defiler of his lineage does not deserve such honor.
For who, having eaten from a vessel, would then dare to break it?"
Thinking himself born of noble lineage,
yet desiring a connection with someone else while honoring his own previous ties— who indeed, being motivated by such interests, would act with such recklessness?
Having insulted us and disregarded Keśava,
he has today forcibly carried off Subhadrā— his own death.
For how could he have placed his foot upon the very crown of my head?

"O Mādhava, O Govinda, if he does not desist when forbidden by you, I shall endure his assault no more than a serpent endures the touch of a foot. Today, alone, I shall rid this earth of the Kauravas."
"For this transgression of Arjuna is not to be tolerated by me;
together with my brothers, I shall slay that defiler of his lineage. As he was thus roaring, with a voice like the sound of clouds or kettledrums—
Then all those Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas followed that course.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When all the Vṛṣṇis had spoken these words repeatedly, [the Lord spoke].
Then Vāsudeva spoke these words, consistent with dharma and artha:
"What was previously spoken by me was not heard by all the Yādavas acting together;
that which has once passed away never returns at any time."
"Listen all together to my reasoned words:
Guḍākeśa has not shown contempt toward this lineage;
rather, he has undoubtedly offered it even greater honor."

The son of Pṛthā does not consider you Sātvatas to be ever greedy for wealth; moreover, the Pāṇḍava considers the *svayaṃvara* to be inviolable. Who would approve of the giving away of a maiden like an animal?
"What man on earth would even sell his own offspring?
It is my conviction that the son of Kuntī perceived these faults;
therefore, the Pāṇḍava forcibly took the maiden in accordance with righteousness."
"This alliance is indeed fitting, for Subhadrā is illustrious,
and Pārtha is likewise such a man who has carried her off by force—
he who was born in the lineage of Bharata and the high-souled Śantanu."
Who would wish to be the son of Kuntibhoja’s daughter other than Arjuna?
And I do not see anyone who could defeat Pārtha by prowess,
except for the three-eyed Hara, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes.
O worthy one, even among all the worlds, including those of Indra and Rudra,
there is no chariot like that, nor are there horses such as mine; furthermore, my weapons are complete, and my two quivers contain inexhaustible arrows.
Pārtha is a warrior swift with weapons; who indeed could be his equal? Pursue Dhanañjaya and, with the utmost conciliation, bring him back—rejoicing; this is my supreme resolve.
"If Pārtha, having conquered you by force, should go to his own city, your fame would perish instantly; but there is no defeat in conciliation.
My son is the daughter's son of my father's sister; he does not deserve to enter into enmity with his kinsmen."
Having heard those words of Vāsudeva, O lord of men, they acted accordingly.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having sounded their drums, those Yādavas made preparations for war.
Then Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, hearing that great sounding of the kettledrums,
spoke in haste to Subhadrā:
"All the Vṛṣṇis are arriving, along with their friends, well-wishers, and kinsmen."
Desiring to fight for your sake, those lowest of men— with eyes reddened by intoxication, heedless, impure, deluded, and drunk on liquor—
along with the Vāminas and Vāśinas and others, I shall strike down with my excellent arrows.
"Or else, I shall lead those intoxicated by pride to the abode of Yama.
Having spoken thus to his beloved, the mighty son of Pṛthā turned back;
and seeing him returning, Subhadrā was overcome with terror.
"Do not speak thus, O Pārtha," she said, then falling at his feet.
"Is Subhadrā indeed Kali incarnate for the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis?
Thus did those citizens, O Lord, utter such public gossip among the people.
"They increase my grief; therefore, do not think of sin. Through your favor, I shall be freed from the fear of censure.
Having been addressed thus by his beloved Bhadrā at that time, Pārtha [replied]:
Then Pārtha, whose prowess is truth, resolved to depart. Having addressed his beloved with a smile and embraced her,
Pārtha raised her up once more and said, "Go, go!"
Then Subhadrā, acting with haste, grasped the reins with her hand and urged on the swift horses,
having made herself ready; thereafter, the Vṛṣṇi heroes, clad in armor, remained composed.
Having seen the prowess of Pārtha, they arrived at the royal highway on swift, excellent horses for the purpose of bringing back Pārtha;
[they were seen] upon the pillars of the rows of palaces, on the altars, and on the banners.
Seeing Arjuna’s arrows, they were struck with the utmost wonder;
the Yādavas, believing Keshava’s words to be true,
passed beyond Mount Raivataka after hearing the speech of Vipṛthu.
Having heard that Arjuna had performed [the feat], the Vṛṣṇis were desirous of going;
but having heard that Pārtha had gone far away, the lords of men turned back after passing the city gardens and the vast Girivraja.
Having reached Sānu, Muñjavat, as well as forests and groves,
and the lotus-lakes and ponds in the holy kingdom of Ānarta,
they proceeded toward the Dhenumatī tirtha and the Aśvarodha lake.
Then, having observed the mountain Āvarta and Arbuda, the best of peaks,
and having approached the summit from afar, he crossed the Kāravatī river,
reached the kingdoms of the Sālveyas, and passed beyond the Niṣadhas.
Beholding the vast city of the gods on all sides with a perfectly concentrated mind,
the mighty-armed one passed beyond it and beheld the forest of the gods;
the great seers of the forest of the gods paid him honor as he approached.
Having passed through forests, rivers, mountains, and mountain cascades, Pārtha, with Subhadrā as his charioteer,
reached the territory of the Kauravas and became free from apprehension.
The mighty-armed one, whose disposition was like that of a lion among his brothers,
[beheld] from afar the city resembling that of the Daśārhas, endowed with groves;
at a distance of one *krośa* from the city, there was the beautiful cattle-pen of Pārtha.
There, Bībhatsu went to where he was settled with the daughter of the Yadus;
then, having honored Subhadrā, Pārtha spoke these words:
"Go to the city of Vṛjinī in the guise of a cowherd girl."
"O Kṛṣṇā, who speaks of love, let my words be pleasing to you.
If she sees you while you have gone there with me and speaks harshly,
but sees you having gone there in another disguise, she will speak kindly to you."
"But that which she says first cannot be revoked;
therefore, casting aside both pride and arrogance, go there yourself.
Having heard those words of his, Subhadrā replied:
"I shall do exactly as you say, O Pārtha.
Having heard the words of Subhadrā, the son of Indra (Arjuna) was well-pleased;
he quickly summoned the cowherds and spoke these words.
"Let all the young women who are there, all those women of Vraja, come together with Bhadrā as she departs for Indraprastha, the best of cities, to see the illustrious Kṛṣṇā."

Having heard this, the women of Vraja were brought there by the cowherds; then Arjuna, having turned back, performed his marriage ceremony there with that blameless lady who was surrounded by those women of Vraja.
Having dwelt there for nights exceeding a year, and having sported as he pleased while being honored by the descendants of Vṛṣṇi, the lordly son of Kuntī then spent the remaining time at Puṣkara.
When the twelfth year was complete, he entered Khāṇḍavaprastha;
having approached the king with humility and composure,
Pārtha, after honoring the Brahmins, went to Draupadī.
Draupadī replied with affection to that joy of the Kurus:
"Go there yourself, O son of Kuntī, to where that daughter of the Sātvatas is;
for even when a load is well-fastened, its previous binding becomes loosened."
Then Dhanañjaya comforted Kṛṣṇā as she lamented in many ways,
and he repeatedly asked her for forgiveness; and in haste, he also consoled Subhadrā, who was dressed in red silk.
Pārtha, having assumed the form of a cowherd girl, sent her forth;
that illustrious woman, shining even more with that appearance,
went toward the city of Vraja, situated in the midst of the cowherd girls.

Then the illustrious lady, the wife of a hero and a woman of noble form, quickly reached and entered Khāṇḍavaprastha, the most excellent of cities, Indraprastha; having arrived at her magnificent residence, she settled there.
The illustrious Bhadrā, with her large copper-hued eyes, paid homage to Pṛthā;
and Kuntī, filled with supreme affection, smelled the head of that woman who was beautiful in every limb, bestowing upon her incomparable blessings.
Then, approaching in haste, Bhadrā, whose face resembled the full moon, paid homage to Draupadī and said, "I am your servant. And Kṛṣṇā rose up to meet her, that sister of Mādhava.
She embraced her and spoke with affection: "May your husband be without rival;
may you, O blessed lady, be the mother of heroes and likewise remain dear to your husband. With vigor and composure, she uttered these supreme blessings.
Likewise, the auspicious Muditā said to her, "So be it.
Then, having embraced Subhadrā, the daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, who possessed a beautiful countenance,
and having placed her on her lap, Muditā praised Vāsudeva.
Then, upon reaching the city of Vṛjinavatī, a tumultuous roar of joy arose in an instant from the Ānarta warriors;
those men, radiant as the sons of gods, bore banners made of Jāmbūnada gold.
The people followed behind Pārtha, as the immortals follow Puruhūta;
they beheld the many magnificent vehicles belonging to the inhabitants of the city of the Daśārhas, yoked with cattle, camels, and excellent horses.

Then, in that best of cities, a great joy arose among the youths upon seeing Pārtha returned from Prabhāsa like their own kinsman. Surrounded by the hosts of the Daśārhas, he entered that preeminent city.
Cheered with supreme affection by the citizens of that foremost city,
Dhanañjaya reached the gate of the inner apartments; having descended from his chariot and approached Dhaumya, Dhanañjaya paid homage to him and to his mother.
Having touched the feet of the king and of Bhīma, Dhanañjaya— being greeted by the twins with joy— embraced them and congratulated them; then,
having reunited with his brothers, he paid homage to all those headed by the Brāhmaṇas.
He honored the citizens and the people of the countryside as was fitting; then,
having bestowed the wedding procession and the dowry upon his preceptor while he remained there,
they approached Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, and paid him their respects.

Even before their arrival, that high-souled and highly illustrious king was worthy of worship, just like the elder brother of Gada; and they were duly honored by the Pāṇḍava, who himself was worthy of honor.
Having been granted permission by the illustrious king, they entered with joy.
Regarding that noble Subhadrā— who was worthy of no despondency, who increased their delight,
and who was the sister of Kṛṣṇa— the sons of Pṛthā considered her to be Śrī herself in bodily form.

Through her own virtuous conduct, Subhadrā became exceedingly dear to her elders, her fathers-in-law, and likewise to her brothers-in-law. Thereupon, those great car-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu, were filled with joy in their hearts.
And Kuntī, O Janamejaya, became exceedingly joyful;
likewise, those headed by Yudhiṣṭhira became joyful, O Janamejaya,
as did Kuntī and Kṛṣṇā, who were constantly so.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
after the great festival of the Vṛṣṇis had concluded,
he who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace heard that Bhadrā had been carried off by Arjuna.
Long ago, O bull of the Bharatas, a doubt arose among the citizens; for Vāsudeva, knowing [the truth], had instilled it in him,
just as it was previously made known to the world by Vipṛthu.
Having been consoled and granted permission, he was united with Bhadrā; and by him,
whose banner bears the foremost of birds, the large-eyed maiden was intended to be given to that worthy lord of men, the son of Pṛthā.
Having honored the best of the Pāṇḍavas, he dispatched Arjuna;
together with Bhadrā, Bībhatsu was conducted to the city of Vrajin. But the lotus-eyed one, having heard that he had arrived at his own excellent city...
Then Keśava, desiring to depart for Khāṇḍavaprastha, took leave of Arjuna, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, who was staying at Indraprastha;
first, Madhusūdana paid his respects to King Āhuka.
King Vipṛthu, Akrūra, Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and Vidūratha were honored beforehand by their father, that lord of men;
and Janārdana was likewise delighted by the Vṛṣṇi king, who was himself filled with joy.
Having consecrated it with mantras and received permission, he marshaled the army.
Then, having mounted their vehicles, the inhabitants of the city of the Daśārhas let out a lion’s roar in an instant, filled with great joy.
Harnessing their excellent horses, as well as their carriages, draft animals, and chariots,
and [preparing] their elephants, the Vṛṣṇis, filled with supreme joy, assembled;
then the pure-souled Keśava arrived together with Rāma.
Surrounded by the great ministers of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, by heroic great chariot-warriors, and by hundreds of brothers, youths,
and soldiers, Śauri, the scorcher of foes, was protected by that vast army.
There arrived the wise and highly illustrious lord of gifts,
Akrūra, the subduer of enemies and commander-in-chief of the Vṛṣṇi heroes;
as well as the immensely energetic Anādhṛṣṭi and the highly renowned Uddhava.
The highly intelligent and illustrious Satyaka, who was a direct disciple of Bṛhaspati,
as well as Sātyaki, Kṛtavarman the Sātvata,
Pradyumna, Sāmba, Niśaṭha, and Śaṅku.
The valiant Cārudeṣṇa, Jhillī, Vipṛthu,
the mighty-armed Sāraṇa, and Gada, the best among the learned—
these and many other Vṛṣṇis, Bhojas, and Andhakas likewise [were there].
Taking many wedding gifts and various provisions, they arrived at Khāṇḍavaprastha; led by the Vṛṣṇis,
they set out with lion-like roars, eager to behold Subhadrā.
In a short time, those Yādavas, together with Kṛṣṇa,
reached the city and attained the highest joy from the sons of Pṛthā.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, hearing that Mādhava had arrived—
Then, for the purpose of receiving [the gifts] from Kṛṣṇa, he dispatched the twins;
by them that prosperous Vṛṣṇi host was received and entered Khāṇḍavaprastha, which was adorned with flags and banners.
The roads were sprinkled and swept, beautified by heaps of flowers,
and graced with the cool, holy-scented juices of sandalwood;
and in every place, they were made fragrant by the burning of aloe-wood.
O Janamejaya, the sky became as if overflowing with fragrance;
crowded with well-groomed people and adorned by merchants,
the mighty-armed Keśava entered it together with Rāma.
Surrounded by the Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Mahābhojas,
and being honored by thousands of citizens and Brahmins,
that Supreme Person entered the king’s palace, which resembled the abode of Purandara.
Yudhiṣṭhira met with Rāma according to the prescribed rites; having smelled Keśava on the head, he embraced him with his arms. Kṛṣṇa, in turn, honored the delighted Yudhiṣṭhira with humility.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, duly honored Bhīma, that tiger among men, as well as those foremost of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas,
receiving them with hospitable rites according to the rules and their respective status.
He honored some as if they were his gurus, treated others like companions,
addressed some with affection, and was himself saluted by others. Then Pṛthā and the sons of Pṛthā, together with Kṛṣṇā, were filled with joy.
Having approached the lotus-eyed one, their senses became filled with joy;
seeing Saṃkarṣaṇa and Janārdana arrived out of delight,
Pṛthā considered her son Yudhiṣṭhira to have found his kinsmen.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa and Akrūra, those two immeasurable ones, like those who are undepressed,
brought a flood of wealth for Subhadrā, the daughter of Bhadrasena—
corals, garments, and ornaments by the thousands.
With carpets, rugs, and blankets, with tiger skins spread out before them,
and with various floods of jewels, the residence of Yudhiṣṭhira became radiant with light; it was filled with couches, seats, and vehicles.

Then, for seven nights, there took place a supreme festival of marriage, bringing joy to the young men, for Subhadrā, who was named Bhadravatī. Thereafter, Vāsudeva bestowed excellent wealth upon those who had come as suitors.
The highly illustrious one indeed brought away Subhadrā, who was to be given by her kinsmen,
along with chariots having golden parts, adorned with garlands of networks of small bells, each yoked to four horses and accompanied by charioteers esteemed for their skill.
O lord of men, Kṛṣṇa gave hundreds upon hundreds of horses born in Bāhlīka, Sindhu, and Kamboja for the purpose of being taken away;
he also gave a thousand cows and even ten thousand more.
The pure-souled and illustrious one gave twenty-one thousand milch cows from the Mathurā region,
possessing holy luster, as well as white mares with a radiance like the rays of the moon, to the son of Pṛthā.

Out of affection, Janārdana gave a thousand elephants adorned with golden ornaments; Kṛṣṇa, the dark-eyed one, gave a thousand elephants that were ever-intoxicated, mounted by riders, and resembled clouds in hue.
O Bhārata, [he saw] horses born in Kamboja, Araṭṭa, Bāhlīka, and Sindhu,
equipped with golden armor, resounding with the ringing of bells,
covered with white chowries, and adorned with all kinds of weapons.
At that time, he gave fifty thousand noble horses;
he also gave a hundred horses resembling the moon with black ears,
as well as tame mules possessing the speed of the wind.
Madhusūdana gave five hundred and five white palanquins with black-antelope hair, as well as a thousand palanquins from the easterners,
the westerners, and the Bāhlīkas, O Janārdana.
He indeed gave an unsurpassed dowry of a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], as well as attendants well-trained in bathing and massaging, endowed with youth,
and likewise skilled in serving food and cooking.
Expert in the kindling and extinguishing of fires, in directing [the ritual] wherever it may be, in the anointing with fragrances, and in their grinding—
he was skilled in every rite.
The lotus-eyed one bestowed a thousand Gaurī women— well-attired, radiant, adorned with hundreds of gold necklaces, healthy, well-clothed,
and skilled in service.
Janārdana also gave as an unsurpassed dowry for the maidens one hundred thousand excellent horses of the *pṛṣṭhya* breed born in Bāhlīka,
as well as the finest gold, both wrought and unwrought, possessing the brilliance of fire.
Janārdana, the descendant of Daśārha, gave ten *bhāras* of human ornaments; Keśava gave as wealth a hundred *bhāras* of the finest jewels and a hundred bright pearl necklaces.
O Bhārata,
he then gave as the bride-price a thousand coral trees, as well as other items, including a thousand couches with golden footstools and costly coverlets.
Of elephants with temporal juice flowing in three streams,
resembling mountain peaks, never retreating in battle,
adorned with golden girths and neck-chains, and decorated with golden goads;
The lover of thousands gave a thousand excellent elephants— fitted with sharp bells, adorned with golden garlands, equipped with elephant-riders,
bound with bells, and stationed within the range of the earth.
He gave twenty thousand buffaloes yielding abundant milk;
then, by the command of Vasudeva, Vāsudeva bestowed them,
while Rāma, the wielder of the plow, gave to the son of Pṛthā a gift to be accepted at his feet.
Delighted and bringing forth the joy of kinship, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) [appeared] like a vast ocean:
a flood of great wealth and jewels, with garments and blankets for its foam, great elephants for its crocodiles, and crowded with banners for its aquatic plants.
The great river, having struck the ocean of the Pāṇḍavas,
entered it while filling it to the brim; bringing grief to their enemies,
Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira accepted all of that.
Then Baladeva [consumed] honey day and night, constantly and in great excess, along with his younger brothers— honey produced from grapes and especially the wine of Kāpiśā.
They drank delightful liquor mixed with divine honey, served in vessels of ruby and sapphire, as well as in goblets made primarily of silver and gold.
And the righteous-souled Pāṇḍava also honored those great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas. Those high-souled ones, the best of the Kurus, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, gathered together.
They roamed about in the abode of the immortals like men of meritorious deeds,
here and there amidst great drinking bouts, with the sounds of excellent cymbals and costly liquors.
Having drunk again and again of the Maireya wines,
the Kurus and Vṛṣṇis sported as they pleased and according to their inclination.
Thus those heroes of supreme valor passed many days in recreation.
Having honored the sons of Pṛthā, as well as Pṛthā herself and Bhadrā, those bulls among the Yadus,
permitted by Keśava and desiring to go toward their city,
were honored by the Kurus and departed once more for the city of Dvāravatī.
Placing Rāma at their head, the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas departed.
Then the mighty Rāma, having honored Subhadrā and embraced his sister, said to Draupadī, "Please accept her," and entrusted her to her care.
Having saluted the feet of his paternal aunt, he then departed.
At that time, Pṛthā, filled with joy, honored him;
and the foremost heroes of the Vṛṣṇis were highly esteemed by the sons of Pṛthā and the citizens.
Having received splendid jewels bestowed by the best of the Kurus,
Vāsudeva, O Bhārata, remained right there with Pārtha for twenty-four days and nights, enjoying himself, he of great strength.
The high-minded one dwelt in the beautiful city of Śakraprastha;
O Bhārata, he roamed along the banks of the Yamunā with Pārtha,
piercing deer and boars, and took delight together with Kirīṭin.
Then Subhadrā, the beloved sister of Keśava, gave birth to the son of Subhadrā,
who was as radiant as Jayanta born of Paulomī;
he was long-armed, possessed of great strength, with eyes like those of a bull, and a subduer of his enemies.

Subhadrā gave birth to the hero Abhimanyu, a bull among men; because he was both fearless (*abhī*) and full of spirit (*manyumān*), they called that crusher of enemies, the son of Arjuna and bull among men, "Abhimanyu."

That great chariot-warrior was born to Sātvatī from Dhanañjaya, like fire produced by friction from within a *śamī* tree during a sacrifice. Upon his birth, the mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira became the son of Kuntī.
He gave ten thousand cows and as many gold coins to the twice-born;
from his childhood, he had been beloved by Vāsudeva,
as well as by all his ancestors, like the moon is to all creatures.
From birth onwards, Kṛṣṇa performed his auspicious rites for him;
and that boy grew like the moon in the bright fortnight.
That subduer of enemies mastered the tenfold science of archery, consisting of four branches.
From Arjuna, who was a knower of the Vedas and knew all divine and human matters, that mighty one learned everything regarding the specialized knowledge of weapons, their excellence,
and all practical applications; he trained him in these particulars with great distinction.
In both theory and practice, he made himself as it were equal [to his father];
beholding his son, the son of Subhadrā, Dhanañjaya was filled with joy—
he who was endowed with every physical strength and marked by every auspicious sign.
Invincible, with shoulders like those of a bull and a mouth wide open like a serpent, possessing the pride of a lion, a great archer with the prowess of an elephant in rut,
with a voice like the roar of clouds or a drum and a face resembling the full moon.

Bībhatsu beheld his son, who was equal to Kṛṣṇa in heroism, prowess, beauty, and appearance, just as Maghavan beholds his own son; and so too did the princess of Pañcāla, endowed with auspicious marks, behold him in relation to her five husbands.
She obtained five heroic and auspicious sons, like five mountains:
Prativindhya from Yudhiṣṭhira, Sutasoma from Vṛkodara,
Śrutakarman from Arjuna, and Śatānīka, the son of Nakula.
Sahadeva begot Śrutakīrti; these five great car-warriors, heroes, the princess of Pañcāla bore, just as Aditi bore the Ādityas.
According to the scriptures, the Brahmins addressed that Prativindhya to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Let this Prativindhya be skilled in the knowledge of weapons used by enemies.
And when a thousand *soma* sacrifices had been performed, Kuntī bore to Bhīmasena a great archer named Sutasoma, whose splendor was equal to that of the moon and the sun."

"Having returned after performing great deeds of renown, the Diademed One (Arjuna) said, 'A son has been born to you'; thus he became known as Śrutakarman. He was the descendant of Kuru and the joy of the Kurus, born of the royal seer Śatānīka."
Nakula begot a son who bore his own name and increased his fame. Then Kṛṣṇā gave birth to a son from Sahadeva under the constellation presided over by Agni; therefore, they know him as Śrutasena.

O Indra among kings, the illustrious sons of Draupadī were born at intervals of one year each, devoted to one another’s welfare. Their birth-rites, as well as their tonsure and initiation ceremonies, were performed in due order.
O best of the Bharatas, Dhaumya performed for them the rites according to the prescribed rules.
Having completed their study of the Vedas and having observed their vows with great care,
they then received from Arjuna the entire science of archery, both divine and human.
"O tiger among kings, the Pāṇḍavas attained great joy, being accompanied by sons who were like the offspring of gods, broad-chested, and possessed of great strength. Vaiśampāyana said:

Residing in Indraprastha, they slew other lords of men by the command of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and of the son of Śaṃtanu (Bhīṣma). Relying upon the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), the entire world lived in happiness.
Like an embodied being cherishing his own body, which is the fruit of meritorious deeds and auspicious marks,
that bull among the Bharatas pursued virtue, pleasure, and wealth with equanimity,
honoring them as if they were three kinsmen equal to himself.
Among those [virtues] which were equally distributed among him as if they were embodied beings upon the earth,
the king shone like a fourth [personification].
The Vedas found in him their supreme student, and the great sacrifices their performer.
The [four] castes obtained that protector, that auspicious lord of men;
like those four castes, they rejoiced in that lord of men. His prosperity was firmly established, and his intellect possessed its ultimate refuge.
Through that king, Dharma became complete and possessed of all its kin;
accompanied by his four brothers, the monarch shone even more brightly,
like a great sacrifice extended by the four Vedas being employed.
The Brahmins, headed by Dhaumya— eminent sages equal to Bṛhaspati— stood surrounding him, just as the immortals attend upon Prajāpati;
they gazed with exceeding love upon the King of Dharma, who was like the stainless full moon.
The eyes and hearts of the subjects rejoiced equally [in him].
He indeed delighted them with affection through unsurpassed gifts of love;
yet the subjects did not rejoice merely because of his divine nature.
Whatever was pleasing to his mind, he performed that through action;
for nothing improper, nor anything untrue, nor falsehood, nor anything disagreeable ever issued from the speech of the wise Pārtha, who spoke so beautifully.
For he, the mighty Pāṇḍava, shines over the entire earth for the welfare of the whole world as well as his own;
O Bhārata, it is like forests in full bloom through the splendor of their grain.
Desiring to act, that best of the Bharatas, possessed of great splendor, took his delight;
and thus all the Pāṇḍavas, joyful and free from anxiety,
dwelt there, terrifying the lords of the earth with their own majesty.
Then, after a few days had passed, Bībhatsu said to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Kṛṣṇa, the days are hot; let us go toward the Yamunā. There, O Madhusūdana, surrounded by our friends, we shall enjoy ourselves."
"We shall return again in the evening; may this be pleasing to you, O Janārdana.
Vāsudeva said:
"O son of Kuntī, this also pleases me—that we [should remain] in the water."
"O Pārtha, surrounded by our friends, let us enjoy ourselves as we please.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Bhārata, having taken leave of Dharmarāja and having obtained his permission,"
Then Pārtha and Govinda, surrounded by their circle of friends, departed;
and while sporting in the groves at Khāṇḍavaprastha,
Mādhava beheld the lovely river Yamunā with its flowering parks.
The abode of all beings, Khaṇḍava, where the wielder of the sword and shield [Arjuna] dwelt— he,
together with Savyasācin, beheld that region resounding with the cries of bears and jackals, and echoing with the calls of swans and cranes.
It was a dwelling frequented by troops of monkeys and the abode of all manner of rakshasas; it was surrounded by leopards, jackals, lions, bears, boars, ruru deer, elephants,
and thousands of various other animals and birds.
It was worthy of honor by all the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas; it was the abode of the high-souled Takṣaka, the lord of the serpents,
and was filled with bamboo, śālmalī trees, garlands, and creepers, and surrounded by cane thickets.
It was covered with *śāka*, *padmaka*, and *tāla* trees, with *rohiṇa* trees having hundreds of branches;
it was so densely obscured that it could not be seen,
filled with thickets of hollow bamboos inhabited by venomous serpents.
Devoid of the great splendor of the sun, crowded with thickets of trees,
and surrounded by *snuhī*, cane, *kuliṅgākṣa*, and *hintāla* plants;
it was infested with swarms of venomous fanged beasts and shunned by all human beings.

The Lord of all gods, the master of all worlds, who knows the divisions of every realm, wearing yellow garments, wandered through that forest in many ways— the great abode of the *rakṣasas*, the lords of serpents, and the birds, as well as of all elemental beings (*bhūtas*).

Madhusūdana beheld that destruction of Khāṇḍava, which was filled with excellent trees, yakṣas, hosts of spirits, and birds; he had reached that supreme pleasure grove abounding in various kinds of trees.
It was filled with various lofty mansions resembling the palace of Purandara,
and was provided with costly, flavorful foods, drinks, and edibles,
as well as diverse garlands, for the sake of the two descendants of Vṛṣṇi and Pṛthā.
They entered that place filled with various auspicious jewels;
and all the people, O Bhārata, sported there according to their pleasure,
as did the women with broad hips and lovely, full breasts.
With their gait faltering from intoxication, those lovely-eyed women sported;
some in the forest, some in the water, and some in the houses— those women sported according to the location and according to their pleasure for Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
Satyabhāmā, the beautiful wife of Vāsudeva who is ever dear to him,
as well as Draupadī and Subhadrā, used to give those women— intoxicated with joy— costly garments and ornaments.
Some women danced with great joy, while others shouted; some laughed, and others drank excellent wine. Some wept there, and others struck one another.
Some whispered secret counsels to one another,
while some were gathering garlands and some were arranging them.
Everywhere there was the charming sound of flutes, lutes, and drums.

That most prosperous forest was indeed filled with sound. While things were thus proceeding, the two delights of the Kurus and the Dāśārhas went to a certain nearby spot that was exceedingly beautiful.

Having gone there, O King, those two high-souled Kṛṣṇas, conquerors of enemy cities, then sat down together upon two costly seats. There, they recounted their past exploits, heroic deeds, and enjoyments.
Having spoken many things, those two, Pārtha and Mādhava,
rejoiced; seated there in delight like the two Aśvins upon the vault of heaven,
the brahmin then approached Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya.

Near the lion-throne sat those two, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya. Resembling a massive śāla tree, with the luster of molten gold, tawny like a lion, with a lion’s beard, he was equal to him in stature and height.
Resembling the rising sun, clad in black garments, wearing matted locks,
with a face like a lotus petal and tawny in hue, he went toward Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha as if blazing with splendor, desiring to consume the Khāṇḍava forest.
Seeing that best of the twice-born blazing as he approached, the powerful one [Kṛṣṇa] thought in his mind, "This is Pāvaka (Fire). Then Arjuna and Vāsudeva quickly sprang up and stood ready.
Vaiśampāyana said: He spoke to Arjuna and Vāsudeva, the descendant of Satvata,
those two heroes of the world who were standing near the Khāṇḍava forest.
"I am a Brahmin who eats much; I always eat without measure. Let the Vārṣṇeya and the son of Pṛthā give me a single meal that will satisfy me.
When he had spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava then said to him:
"By what food might your honor be satisfied? We shall strive to provide that food.
When they had spoken thus, the Blessed One then said to those two heroes who were speaking: "What food shall be prepared?"
"I do not desire food; know me to be the Fire-god (Pāvaka). Grant me that food which is appropriate for me.
"Indra always protects this Khāṇḍava forest."
I am unable to burn it while it is protected by that great-souled one;
Takṣaka, his serpent friend, always dwells here,
and for his sake, the wielder of the thunderbolt protects the forest along with his hosts.
There, many beings were being protected by chance—
many indeed of terrible form and fierce prowess. Desiring to burn him, I was unable to consume him due to the splendor of Śakra.
Seeing me ablaze, he rained down water from the clouds;
therefore, though I desired to burn the forest, I was unable to consume it.
Now he has encountered you two, who are skilled in weapons and have become my allies.
"I shall burn the Khāṇḍava forest; this is the food chosen by me.
For you two, being experts in the highest weapons, shall properly ward off those streams of water and all creatures from every side."
Janamejaya said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
Rudra said:
Vaiśampāyana said:
"For what purpose does the blessed Agni desire to burn the Khāṇḍava forest?"

"O Brahmin, protected by Mahendra and filled with various creatures, this reason— that the sacrificial fire, being highly enraged, consumed the Khandava forest— does not appear to me to be a small one."

"O Brahman, O Sage, I desire to hear this in detail and according to its true nature: how the burning of Khāṇḍava occurred in the past. Very well, I shall relate to you this ancient tale, which is praised by the seers."

O best of men, this ancient story concerning the destruction of Khāṇḍava is heard, my dear: there was a king renowned as Śvetaki, who was like Indra, the one with the green horses, and endowed with great strength and prowess.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, and wise, such that no other person existed like him; he performed great sacrificial sessions and rituals accompanied by abundant gifts.
Day after day, O King, his mind was focused on nothing else.
During sacrificial sessions, at the commencement of ritual acts, and in various kinds of gifts—
while he was thus engaged, after some time had passed,
it is said that he desired to perform a sacrificial session lasting for a hundred years.
The officiating priests did not agree to perform the sacrifice for that high-souled one;
yet the king, together with his circle of friends, made a great effort through prostration, conciliation, and gifts, he of great renown.
Unweariedly, he entreated the officiating priests again and again;
yet they, possessed of immeasurable power, did not carry out his intention.
Then that royal sage, filled with wrath, spoke to those who were staying in the hermitage.
"O Brahmins, if I have fallen and am not established in service, I should be quickly abandoned by you and censured by the brahmins; therefore,
you ought not to obstruct my supreme faith in the sacrifice."

O best of the twice-born, it would be improper for me to abandon you; O brahmins, since I have sought refuge in you, you ought to show me favor through words of consolation, gifts, and the like, acting according to the truth and the requirements of the situation.
"O best of the twice-born, having propitiated you, I shall state what our task is;
or else, if I am abandoned by you on account of hatred,
O ascetics rich in austerity, I shall go to other officiating priests for the sake of performing the sacrifice."
Having spoken these words, that king fell silent.
O scorcher of foes, when they were unable to persuade the king to perform the sacrifice,
those officiating priests, filled with anger, spoke to that best of monarchs.
O best of kings, your duties indeed proceed incessantly; therefore, we have become exhausted by constantly carrying out these tasks. You ought to release us from this exhaustion caused by such toil.

"O sinless one, resorting to a state of mental confusion and driven by haste, go to the presence of Rudra; for he will perform the sacrifice for you. Having heard these words of reproach, O King, Śvetaki became enraged.
Having gone to Mount Kailāsa, he undertook fierce austerities; with self-restraint and firm vows, worshipping Mahādeva,
the king remained there for a long time, devoted to fasting.
Sometimes at the twelfth mealtime, and sometimes even at the sixteenth,
the king took food consisting only of roots and fruits;
with arms raised and eyes unblinking, he stood motionless like a pillar.

For six months, King Śvetaki remained perfectly composed in meditation. O Bhārata, as that tiger among kings was thus performing great ascetic penance, Śaṅkara, with supreme affection, revealed himself to him.
And the Blessed One spoke to him in a voice that was affectionate and deep:
"I am pleased, O tiger among kings, by your asceticism, O scorcher of foes! Choose a boon, O ruler of the earth; may it be well with you, whatever you desire."
Having heard these words of Rudra of immeasurable splendor,
the royal sage prostrated before the high-souled one and replied:
"If the Blessed One, who is worshipped by all the worlds, is pleased with me..."
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord of the suras, perform the sacrifice for me yourself.
Having heard these words spoken by that king,
the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke these words with a smile:

"O King, it does not fall within our domain to perform sacrifices for such as you; yet, O King, you have performed very great austerities seeking a boon. Therefore, O scorcher of foes, I shall officiate at your sacrifice on certain conditions."
"O Indra among kings, if you remain composed and steadfast in celibacy for twelve years, and constantly satisfy the fire with streams of clarified butter,
then whatever desire you pray for from me, O King, you shall obtain it."

Thus addressed by Rudra, Śvetaki, the lord of men, performed all that exactly as it had been spoken by the wielder of the trident. When the twelfth year was complete, he returned once more to Maheśvara.
And as soon as Śaṅkara, the creator of the worlds, saw King Śvetaki,
that best of monarchs, he spoke with supreme delight:
"O best of kings, I am gratified here by you through your own deed."
O scorcher of foes, officiating at sacrifices for Brahmins is prescribed by the sacred law;
therefore, O scorcher of foes, I myself do not officiate for you today.
However, on the surface of the earth, there is a highly fortunate and most excellent of the twice-born who is my own portion.
"He who is renowned as Durvāsas shall indeed officiate at your sacrifice by my command;
let the materials for the rite be gathered, O one of great splendor.
Having heard these words uttered by Rudra, [he acted accordingly].
Having returned once more to his own city, he again accumulated the necessary provisions;
then, having gathered those provisions, he approached Rudra once more, saying,
"My provisions and all my requisites have been gathered."
"O Mahādeva, by your grace, may my initiation take place tomorrow.
Having heard these words of that high-souled king,
Rudra summoned Durvāsas and spoke these words.
"O best of the twice-born, this highly fortunate king Śvetaki is a ruler of the earth; O chief of sages, perform a sacrifice for him at my command. To these words, the sage said to Rudra, "So be it."

Then, for that high-souled king, a sacrificial session (satra) was undertaken according to the rules, at the proper time, as prescribed, and accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). When that sacrificial session of the high-souled king had been completed—
Permitted by Durvāsas, the officiating priests, all those who had been initiated there, and the members of the assembly of great luster departed;
and that illustrious king also then entered his own city.
Then a transformation occurred in the Blessed One Fire; deprived of his brilliance, exhaustion overcame him. And having perceived himself to be bereft of luster, the consumer of oblations—
He went to the holy abode of Brahmā, which is honored by the worlds;
there, he spoke these words to the Brāhmaṇa who was seated: "O Lord of the World, I have been deprived of my splendor and my strength."
"By your grace, I desire my own nature to be stable.
Having heard these words, the Blessed One, the creator of all worlds,
spoke these words to the bearer of oblations as if smiling:

O highly fortunate one, for twelve years you offered oblations poured as a stream of clarified butter; because of that, O carrier of the sacrificial offerings, exhaustion has suddenly come upon you due to the depletion of your vital energy.

"Do not fall into distress, O Agni; you shall return to your natural state. By the command of the gods in the past, you reduced to ashes that most terrible forest of Khāṇḍava, the abode of the enemies of the gods."
O Vibhāvasu, all beings dwell there; you shall be satisfied by their fat and will return to your natural state. Go quickly to burn them, and then you shall be liberated from your sin.
Having heard these words falling from the mouth of Parameṣṭhin,
the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) exerted his supreme speed and rushed forth;
having reached the Khāṇḍava forest, he maintained that highest velocity.
Suddenly the fire blazed up, enraged and fanned by the wind;
seeing Khāṇḍava aflame, those who were dwelling there exerted the utmost effort to extinguish the fire.

Then, taking up water quickly, hundreds and thousands of elephants, acting with haste and filled with wrath, sprinkled the fire. Likewise, many-headed serpents rained down showers of water from their heads.
Overwhelmed by rage, they rushed forward with haste toward the fire and discharged [their weapons];
likewise, other creatures, with various efforts to hurl their weapons,
quickly brought the fire to its destruction, O best of the Bharatas.
In this manner, repeatedly blazing up again and again,
the fire-god was extinguished seven times at Khāṇḍava;
having thus fallen into despair, he was constantly filled with exhaustion.
Enraged, the bearer of oblations approached the Grandfather and reported everything exactly as it had happened to Brahmā. Having reflected for a moment, the Blessed One spoke to him.
"O Anala, a means has been perceived by me whereby you shall consume the Khāṇḍava forest this very day, even as Śatakratu looks on—
those two who were the ancient gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa, O Vibhāvasu."
Having arrived in the world of men for the sake of the purpose of the gods—
those two whom the world regards as Arjuna and Vāsudeva—
they are both together here, O Fire, in the vicinity of the Khāṇḍava forest.
"Ask those two for assistance in the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest;
then you shall consume that grove, even though it is protected by the gods. For they will both strive with great effort to ward off all living beings."

"And there is no doubt in my mind that you two, together, will defeat the king of the gods. Having heard these words, the bearer of oblations (Agni) quickly approached Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha and spoke to them regarding the matter at hand.
"I have already told you this before, O best of kings.
When this was said, Bībhatsu replied to Jātavedas,
O tiger among kings, speaking words appropriate for that moment.
While the performer of a hundred sacrifices was unwilling, he desired to burn the Khāṇḍava forest.
"I possess many supreme and divine weapons,
with which I would be able to fight even many wielders of the thunderbolt."

"O Blessed One, I have no bow equal to the strength of my arms when I exert effort in battle, such that it might withstand my force. And I have need of many inexhaustible arrows for one who shoots with speed."
I have no two arms with which to fight Purandara;
nor is my chariot capable of bearing the arrows I desire to discharge.
Furthermore, I long for divine horses, white as snow and swift as the wind.
And his chariot has the roar of a thundercloud and a splendor equal to the sun;
likewise, by virtue of Kṛṣṇa’s prowess, there exists no weapon equal to it,
with which Mādhava might slay the nāgas and piśācas in battle.
"O Blessed One, you ought to tell me the means for the successful accomplishment of this task,
by which I might ward off Indra as he rains down upon the great forest.
O Pāvaka, we two shall perform whatever must be done through human effort."
"O Blessed One, you ought to grant the means that are capable [of this].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the smoke-bannered consumer of oblations, [replied].
He thought of Varuṇa, the world-protector, desiring to see the god Āditya who dwells in the water as the lord of the waters. And he,
knowing that thought, revealed himself to Pāvaka.

Having honored the Lord of Waters— the great lord who is the fourth among the guardians of the world— Agni, whose banner is smoke, spoke to him. As soon as he was addressed, Varuṇa, of great splendor, arrived.
Then, O tiger among kings, the Fire-god spoke these words:
"Give back quickly both that bow and the two quivers which were given to you by King Soma, as well as the chariot marked with the emblem of the tawny horse."
"Give this to Savyasācin,
who is joined with divine horses;
for Pārtha will accomplish a most great task with the Gāṇḍīva."
"Let Vāsudeva give me that discus for my sake.
Varuṇa replied to Pāvaka, "I shall give it.
Then [he gave] that wonderful, highly powerful [discus], which increases fame and renown.
Invincible by all weapons and a crusher of all weapons,
it is the preeminent among all arms and a terrifier of enemy armies;
equal to a hundred thousand, it is the increaser of the kingdom.
Variegated with diverse colors, beautiful, smooth, and without blemish;
worshipped by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas for eternal years—
that divine bow, the best of bows, was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times.
He indeed gave him that jewel of a bow and two inexhaustible great quivers,
as well as a chariot yoked with divine horses and bearing the banner of the foremost of monkeys,
equipped with silver steeds adorned with Gandharva-like golden garlands.
Resembling pale clouds, equal in speed to thought or the wind,
equipped with all necessary implements, invincible by gods or dānavas,
radiant, of great roar, and captivating to the hearts of all beings.
The lord of the world, Bhauvana, the Prajāpati, created by means of his own ascetic power that [palace] whose form was indescribable like that of the sun;
ascending which, the lord Soma conquered the Dānavas.
Resembling a mountain cloud and blazing as if with splendor,
it destroyed the golden earrings from the ears of the wives of the enemies of the gods.
That auspicious [bow], equal to the weapon of Śakra, was mounted upon that best of chariots.
The banner-pole was made of refined gold, exceedingly beautiful and unsurpassed.
Upon it stood a divine monkey named Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, possessed of great splendor, able to assume any form at will, and marked with the characteristics of lions and tigers.
And with a roar, he became most terrible, surrounded by ten million spirits; he who was formerly born from the wind and was the destroyer of the hosts of *rākṣasas*,
standing there as if roaring, shone resplendent upon the summit.
Upon that banner were various great beings,
by whose roar the consciousness of the enemy armies was destroyed.
He [approached] that supreme chariot, adorned with many banners.
Having circumambulated [the deity] and bowed down to the gods,
