Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes, equipped with his armor, sword, and bound leather arm-guards and finger-protectors,
took his leave of Viṣṇu.

Pārtha ascended the chariot like a man of merit ascending a celestial mansion (vimāna). Taking hold of that divine Gāṇḍīva, the best of bows fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times, Arjuna became filled with joy.

Having paid homage to the consumer of oblations (Agni), the valiant one then took up that [bow], exerting his strength, and joined it with a string; as the bowstring was being fixed by the powerful Pāṇḍava, indeed—
Those who did not hear that clamor there had their minds truly distressed;
but having obtained the chariot, the bow, and likewise the two inexhaustible quivers,
the son of Kuntī became ready and joyful for the task of assistance.
Then Pāvaka gave to Kṛṣṇa the discus with a vajra-navel, his beloved Āgneya weapon; and he [Kṛṣṇa] then became ready for action.
And Pāvaka said to him: "O Madhusūdana, by means of this..."
"You will undoubtedly conquer even non-human beings in battle. By means of this [weapon], you shall always be superior to men, gods, rākṣasas, piśācas, daityas, and nāgas in combat."
"You will undoubtedly become [the foremost] in the destruction of the most eminent enemies.
This weapon of yours, which is by name the Sudarśana discus— that,
O Lord, you must now apply against this Daitya, just as in the past."
O Mādhava, when this wheel is discharged by you in battle against the enemies, that powerful weapon will reduce everything to ashes;
and having slain those foes in the conflict, it shall return to your hand again, unhindered.
And Varuṇa gave to him that terrible mace named Kaumodakī, which resounded like a thunderbolt and was the destroyer of the Daityas; it belonged to Hari and was given for the sake of Agni’s approval,
by a friend who does what is pleasing to his friend.
The descendant of Vṛṣṇi, being well-pleased, spoke to Pārtha Dhanañjaya:
"O Pāṇḍava, you are unconquered and invincible; you are a conqueror.
O Phalguna, you are unconquered! Having said this, the heroic one took up the reins.
"Victory! Janārdana replied to Bībhatsu.
Having circumambulated him clockwise, he touched the chariot with his hand;
delighted, Kṛṣṇa became the charioteer of that chariot.
Having paid homage to the Purifier (Agni), he worshipped the bow Gāṇḍīva;
having mounted his chariot, Bībhatsu strung that great bow. From Kṛṣṇa’s arms, the bowstring was released with a most terrible sound.
Cooing like a lioness greedy for deer, she flew down swiftly.
Then Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, delighted, spoke to the fire-god;
they were masters of weapons, equipped with arms, chariot-warriors, and possessed of banners.
"O Blessed One, we are capable of fighting even against all the gods and asuras combined,
let alone against the wielder of the thunderbolt alone who desires to fight for the sake of the serpent.
Arjuna said:
Discharging the discus weapon in battle, the heroic Vārṣṇeya—
Janārdana— there is nothing in the three worlds that he cannot conquer.
Taking up the bow Gāṇḍīva as well as the two inexhaustible great quivers, [he stands ready].
"O Fire, I too am capable of conquering the worlds in battle— including the gods, asuras, and humans—
let alone the wielder of the thunderbolt alone."

"O Lord, having surrounded him on all sides with a great forest fire, let it blaze forth at will this very day; we are capable of assisting in the task. Should he approach the Khandava out of negligence, [we shall prevail]."
Even Mahendra, together with his hosts, will not be able to protect them;
he shall witness the slaughter of the divine armies, whose earrings are shattered by the arrows.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by the descendant of Daśārha and by Arjuna,
the Blessed One assumed his fiery form and proceeded to burn the forest.

Then, having surrounded it on all sides, the seven-rayed Fire-god blazed forth in anger, consuming Khāṇḍava as if displaying the end of a Yuga; O bull of the Bharatas, he entered that forest, having seized it completely.
O Bhārata, as he burned, consuming all beings with a roar like the thundering of clouds, his form shone like the great,
golden-peaked Meru, the lord of mountains, possessed of immense luster.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Those two tigers among men, stationed on their chariots on both sides of the forest,
wrought a great slaughter of living beings in all directions.
Janamejaya:
For what purpose did the blessed Agni desire to burn the Khāṇḍava forest? Vaiśampāyana: [He replied: For what purpose did the blessed Agni desire to burn the Khāṇḍava forest?
"I wish to hear this; speak, O best of Brahmins.
There was once a great king named Śveta, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage. While that king was performing a twelve-year sacrificial session,"
The sacrificial fire, being offered oblations there by continuous streams of clarified butter,
became pale in hue, as if afflicted by jaundice;
the carrier of offerings was no longer able to accept the oblation of anyone else.
Constantly exhausted and with his body worn out, he then approached Brahmā. Having gone to the divine Grandfather and paid homage to him, Pāvaka then informed him of the pain in his own body.

Brahmā said: "Having known this and having burned the Khāṇḍava forest, you will become free from disease and perfected in splendor; of this there is no doubt. As soon as those words were spoken by that supreme Brahmā, Parameṣṭhin...

Desiring to burn the Khāṇḍava forest, he went there and proceeded to set it on fire; however, he was then extinguished with water by the gods who were the guardians of the forest. Thus, while carrying out the burning of Khāṇḍava, he suffered defeat seven times.
Then he went again to Brahmā and informed the Lord; and having been commanded by him as well, he of the white body [approached] those two,
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who in the Dvāpara age were Kṛṣṇa and Phalguna.
"Those two great-souled ones will soon be near the Khāṇḍava forest;
seek out those two great heroes, for they will provide you with assistance.
Indeed, wherever living beings dwelling in Khāṇḍava are seen,"
Fleeing here and there, those two heroes pursued one another;
for they could find no opening between the two chariots due to the swiftness of their maneuvers.
Those two preeminent car-warriors appeared as if they were whirling in circles.
While the Khāṇḍava forest was burning, thousands of beings then flew up,
uttering terrible cries toward the ten directions;
many had a single part burnt, while others were scorched throughout.
With eyes burst open, bodies shattered, and limbs mangled, they were deprived of their senses; some, embracing their sons, and others their fathers or mothers,
were unable to let go out of affection and perished right there.
Others, with distorted appearances, rose up by the thousands here and there, reeling about, only to fall back again into the fire;
their wings, eyes, and feet scorched, they writhed upon the surface of the earth.
In every place, O Bhārata, embodied beings were seen perishing as all the reservoirs of water were being boiled;
thousands of tortoises and fish were seen deprived of life.
With their bodies ablaze, the living beings in that forest appeared like fires incarnate during that destruction of life;
Pārtha, however, cut those who were thus leaping up into pieces with his arrows.
Then, laughing, he cast them into the blazing fire;
those arrows, their entire bodies pierced through, let out great roars and,
leaping upward with force, fell back again into the flames.
The cry of the forest-dwellers, struck by arrows and being consumed by fire,
was heard like the roar of the ocean being churned;
perceiving this, they leapt up from the mountain.
And from the fire, as it blazed up, great flames leapt into the sky,
causing intense agitation among the inhabitants of heaven. Greatly distressed by those flames, the gods, led by the sages, [were filled with alarm].
Then all those high-souled dwellers of heaven went for refuge to the thousand-eyed Purandara, the king of the gods. The gods said:
"Why are all these men being consumed by fire? O Lord of the Immortals, has the destruction of the worlds arrived?
Thus did all those people, overcome with fear, cry out in lamentation.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard that from them and having personally investigated the matter himself, the slayer of Vṛtra,
whose vehicle is drawn by bay horses, set out for the purpose of releasing the Khāṇḍava forest.
Having completely covered the sky with a vast net of clouds of various forms, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of the gods, poured down rain. Then,
he released streams of water as thick as axle-trees by the hundreds of thousands.

The thousand-eyed Indra rained down upon the Khāṇḍava forest toward the fire. But those streams, before they could reach it, were dried up in the sky itself by the splendor of Jātavedas; not a single one reached the fire.

Then Namuci, the slayer of enemies, becoming violently enraged at the radiant one, again rained upon him, discharging a great volume of water. The flames became intertwined with the torrents, and were filled with smoke and lightning.
That forest became terrible, filled with the roar of thunder.
Vaiśampāyana said:
As he rained down water, the Pāṇḍava warded it off.
Displaying his supreme weapons, Bībhatsu,
the Pāṇḍava, covered the entire Khāṇḍava forest on all sides with a rain of arrows;
he then withdrew that rain from the forest.
Not a single creature was able to emerge from there.
Seeing that water thus obstructed by the iron arrows of Savyasācin,
the gods and the sages stationed in heaven were filled with wonder.
While the sky was being covered by arrows discharged by Savyasācin,
Takṣaka, the mighty king of serpents, was not there;
for at that time he was in Kurukṣetra while that forest was being consumed by fire.
But there was the powerful Aśvasena, the son of Takṣaka;
he made a strenuous effort to escape from the fire,
yet, tormented by the arrows of the son of Kuntī, he was unable to emerge.
His mother, the daughter of a serpent, saved him by swallowing him;
having first swallowed his head, she now swallowed his tail.
Greedy for her son, that female serpent then began to ascend upward.

With a sharp, broad-edged crescent-headed arrow, the Pāṇḍava severed her head as she was moving away; the Lord of the Gods beheld her. Desiring to liberate him, the wielder of the thunderbolt [assailed] the Pāṇḍava with a rain of wind.
At that moment, Aśvasena caused him to be bewildered, yet he himself was released. Seeing that terrible illusion and having been deceived by the serpent,
O Bhārata, he cut down those who were moving through the air into two or three pieces.
And filled with rage, Bībhatsu cursed that crooked-moving one, saying,
"May he find no firm footing," while Pāvaka and Vāsudeva did likewise.
Then Jiṣṇu covered the sky with thousands of sharp arrows.
Remembering that deception, he fought on, filled with rage.
And the King of the Gods, seeing Phalguna thus provoked,
discharged his own blazing weapon, which overspread the entire sky.
Then he released the wind Subhadrajava, which was ablaze.
Thereupon, that wind of great roar agitated all the oceans;
standing in the sky, it produced turbulent clouds that discharged torrents of water.

Then Arjuna, skilled in decisive action, also discharged a supreme weapon, having consecrated it with mantras, in order to counter those terrible clouds that were releasing lightning and the roar of thunder. He invoked the Vāyavya weapon.
By that [power], the strength and vigor of Indra’s thunderbolts and clouds were destroyed;
those torrents of water went to dryness, and the lightning flashes perished.
In an instant, the sky became completely tranquil, with its dust and darkness subsided.
The orb of the sun remains in its natural state, possessing the quality of pleasantly cool breezes; and the fire-god,
appearing in various forms, rejoices without resistance as he is drenched by those torrents of fat exuded from the bodies of living beings.
Blazing with incomparable flames and filling the world with its roars, the fire blazed up;
and seeing that forest protected by the two Kṛṣṇas, the arrogant birds,
such as the Suparṇas and others, then flew up into the sky.
Then Garuḍas, with wings, beaks, and claws like thunderbolts,
descended from the sky, desiring to strike Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava;
likewise, swarms of serpents gathered near the Pāṇḍava.
Emitting terrible poison, they rushed forth with flaming mouths;
seeing those sky-dwellers full of rage who had taken refuge on the enemy's side, Pārtha cut them down with arrows and weapons resembling the sun.
Helpless, they fell into the blazing fire to bring about the destruction of their bodies.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and pannagas, rose up, uttering an incomparable roar, desiring battle.
With iron clubs, maces, discs, stones, and *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons raised in their arms,
their vigor intensified by rage, they sought to slay Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha;
as they shouted and loosed a rain of weapons, [the Lord acted].
Bībhatsu [Arjuna] struck down their heads with sharpened arrows,
and then Kṛṣṇa, of great splendor and slayer of enemies, wrought a great slaughter among the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas with his discus.
Then others, pierced by arrows impelled by the force of the wheel,
stood their ground despite their great prowess, like the shore [resisting the tide];
drenched in blood, they lay there resembling indragopaka insects.
Then Śakra, the great lord of the thirty gods, becoming enraged,
mounted his white elephant and charged at those two.
Seizing his thunderbolt with speed, he discharged the weapon Vajra.
"These two are slain," said the slayer of the Asuras to the gods.
Then, seeing the great thunderbolt raised by the Lord of the Gods,
the deities each took up their own respective weapons.
King Yama took up the Staff of Time, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) a palanquin,
Varuṇa a noose, and likewise Śiva a discus;
Skanda, having taken up his spear, stood firm like Mount Meru.
The King of the Yātus took up a spear and a sword, while Samīra took an elephant-goad; the two Aśvins also took up blazing medicinal herbs;
Dhātṛ took up a bow, and Jaya likewise took up a mace.
The immensely powerful Tvaṣṭṛ, filled with rage, seized a mountain; Aṃśu took up a spear, and the god Mṛtyu a battle-axe;
Āryaman, too, moved about brandishing a terrible iron club.
Mitra stood there, grasping a discus with edges as sharp as razors;
and Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Savitṛ, O lord of the people, being greatly enraged and with bows and swords drawn,
rushed toward Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha.
The Rudras, the Vasus, and the mighty Maruts,
as well as the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas, blazing with their own splendor—
these and many other gods [honored] those two Supreme Persons.
Desiring to slay Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, they advanced with various weapons;
there, O Bhārata, wonderful omens were seen in that great battle, resembling the end of a Yuga and portending the destruction of all beings.

But seeing Śakra thus enraged along with the gods, the two undecaying ones (Nara and Nārāyaṇa), fearless and invincible in battle, stood ready with their bows strung. Then, having seen those gods approaching one by one, they [prepared for combat].

Then, filled with rage, the two [Nara and Nārāyaṇa] warded them off with arrows resembling thunderbolts. Repeatedly thwarted in their resolve and struck down many times, the gods abandoned the battle out of fear and sought refuge with Śakra alone.
Seeing the gods repelled by Mādhava and Arjuna,
the sages stationed in the heavens were struck with wonder;
and Śakra, too, repeatedly witnessed their prowess in battle.
He became exceedingly pleased and once more fought those two. Then the subduer of Pāka discharged a truly massive shower of stones, desiring once again to test the prowess of Savyasācin.
The highly indignant Arjuna countered that shower of arrows with his own;
and seeing that his effort was being rendered fruitless, Śatakratu,
the king of the gods, then further increased that rain of shafts.
Then the son of Pākaśāsana, gladdening his father, caused that shower of stones to dissolve with his high-velocity arrows; meanwhile,
he uprooted a great peak from Mount Mandara with his two hands.
Desiring to kill the son of Pāṇḍu, Śakra released the mountain together with its trees.
Then Arjuna, with swift, straight-flying arrows whose tips were ablaze,
shattered that mountain peak into a thousand pieces.
As that mountain was shattering,
its form then shone like the sky being torn asunder along with the sun, moon, and planets.
By that great mountain falling violently downward into the forest fire, [the flames were extinguished].
Furthermore, the creatures dwelling in Khāṇḍava were slain there.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus, the inhabitants of Khāṇḍava were terrified by the falling of the mountain.
Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Nāgas, hyenas, bears, and forest-dwellers; rutting elephants, tigers, lions, and maned beasts;
as well as deer, buffaloes, and birds by the hundreds.
Other species of living beings, likewise agitated, fled away;
gazing upon that forest fire and the two Kṛṣṇas with weapons raised,
they became as if terrified by the sound of their leaping.
Then, beholding the forest burning in many ways and seeing Kṛṣṇa with his weapons raised, they let out a terrible roar;
by that fierce roar and by the roar of the fire, [the world was filled].
The entire sky resounded as if with clouds of portentous omens;
then the mighty-armed Janārdana Kṛṣṇa discharged his own great, blazing discus, radiant with its own splendor.
By him, those low-born creatures, including the Dānavas and night-stalkers, were all cut down by the hundreds; in an instant they fell into the fire.
There, the Rākṣasas were seen being torn asunder by Kṛṣṇa’s discus.
Smeared with fat and blood like clouds at twilight,
O Bhārata, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi moves about there like Time itself, slaughtering thousands of Piśācas, birds, Nāgas, and beasts.
For every time that discus of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of enemies, was hurled,
it would return again and again to his hand after having slain many creatures.
And so it was, O Bhārata, as he continued to strike down all beings.
Then the form of the Soul of all beings became exceedingly fierce;
and among all the assembled gods and dānavas on every side,
there was no one who could be a victor over Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava in battle.
When the gods were unable to protect that forest from their power or to extinguish it, they turned away;
and Śatakratu, beholding the hosts of deities with their faces averted, [acted accordingly].
He remained there, filled with joy, praising Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava. But when the gods had withdrawn, an incorporeal voice, deep and resonant as a thundercloud, spoke, addressing Śatakratu.
Your friend Takṣaka, the best of serpents, was not present;
for at the time of the burning of Khāṇḍava, he had gone to Kurukṣetra.
Moreover, these two, standing ready for battle in this conflict, cannot be conquered by you.
O Śakra, listen to these words of mine regarding Vāsudeva and Arjuna:
those two are the gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa, renowned in heaven;
you yourself well know what their prowess and what their valor are.
These two, invincible in battle and unconquered, cannot be defeated even by all the worlds; they are the two ancient and most excellent sages,
worthy of the highest worship by all gods and asuras alike.

"O Vāsava, since this place is filled with Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, humans, Kinnaras, and Pannagas, you ought to depart from here along with the gods. Furthermore, behold this ordained destruction of the Khāṇḍava forest."

Having heard these words and recognizing them as true, the Lord of the Immortals cast aside his anger and resentment, and then departed for heaven. Beholding that high-souled one thus departing, the denizens of heaven—
O King, they followed Śatakratu swiftly and together;
and beholding the Lord of the Gods then departing with the deities,
the heroic Vāsudeva and Arjuna let out a lion’s roar.
O King, when the king of the gods had departed, Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava were filled with joy;
they then once again set the forest on fire without any apprehension.
Just as the wind disperses the clouds, Arjuna [dispersed] the gods.
With volleys of arrows, he scattered the creatures dwelling in the Khāṇḍava forest;
not a single being was able to escape from there,
as they were being cut down by the shafts discharged by Savyasācin.

Even the greatest beings there could not even look at Arjuna in battle, whose arrows are never in vain; how then could they engage him in combat? He pierced one with a hundred shafts and a hundred with a single feathered arrow.
Deprived of their strength, they fell into the fire as if struck down by Time itself;
they found no refuge on the riverbanks or in the rugged terrain,
and even in the abodes of the ancestors and gods, a great torment arose.
Thousands of hosts of spirits, distressed, raised a great cry;
likewise, the elephants, beasts, and birds shrieked.
At that sound, the fish dwelling in the Ganges and the ocean were terrified.
Neither did they move about in the waters, nor did other beasts and birds,
nor the hosts of *vidyādharas*, nor those who dwelt there in the forest; for neither the mighty-armed Arjuna nor the exceedingly powerful Kṛṣṇa could be seen.
No one at all was even able to look upon him, much less fight him;
yet Hari, with his discus, slew those Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Nāgas who emerged there, even though they had retreated to a single narrow path.
With their heads and bodies severed by the force of the discus,
those massive-bodied beings fell lifeless into the mouth of the blazing Fire-god;
and he was filled with floods of flesh and blood, as well as streams of fat.
Above, a smokeless fire was seen moving through the sky,
with blazing eyes and a blazing tongue, its great mouth wide open in a blaze;
with flaming hair standing erect and tawny eyes, it drank the fat of living beings.
Having obtained that ambrosia prepared by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, the consumer of oblations became joyful,
satiated, and attained supreme bliss. Then,
from the abode of Takṣaka, [he took] the Asura named Maya...
Madhusūdana suddenly beheld him fleeing;
Agni, whose charioteer is the wind, desiring to consume him,
took on a physical form with matted hair and roared like a rain-cloud.
Having recognized Maya as the foremost of artisans among the lords of the Dānavas,
Vāsudeva, desiring to slay him, stood with his discus raised;
like a fire licking with its tongue, he pursued Maya to consume him.
Seeing the raised wheel and the fire desiring to consume him, O Bhārata, Maya cried out, "Arjuna, run toward me!
Hearing his terrified voice, Dhanañjaya said, "Do not fear."
O Bhārata, Pārtha, as if bringing Maya back to life, replied to him: "Do not fear," said Pārtha, who is devoted to compassion. When Pārtha had granted safety to Maya, the brother of Namuci—
The descendant of Daśārha did not wish to kill him, nor did the fire consume him.
Vaiśampāyana said:
For fifteen days, the wise fire [remained] in that forest.
Protected by Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha from Indra, the son of Pāka,
he burned that forest; yet, while it was burning, the fire did not consume Aśvasena, Maya, and the four Śārṅgaka birds.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahman, why did the fire not burn the Śārṅgaka birds while that forest was being consumed? Tell me this quickly."

O Brahmin, the reason for the non-burning of Aśvasena, the Dānava Maya, and the Śārṅgaka birds has been proclaimed; however, the reason for the Śārṅgaka birds' immunity from destruction has not yet been told.
This matter of the Śārṅgaka birds' indestructibility is truly marvelous, O Brahmin.
"Tell me how they were not destroyed in the conflagration of the fire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen to the reason why the fire did not burn the Śārṅgaka birds when things had come to such a pass."

While that forest was burning, O Bhārata, [there arose] a terror for all living beings; I shall relate all of that to you exactly as it happened. He was the foremost among those who know dharma, an ascetic of rigid vows.
There was a great seer renowned as the learned Mandapāla.
O King, he had set out upon the path of the sages who maintain their vital energy in an upward flow; he was devoted to Vedic study, delighting in dharma, ascetic, and possessed of conquered senses.

O Bhārata, having reached the culmination of his asceticism and cast off his body, he went to the world of the ancestors, yet he did not obtain the fruit thereof. Seeing even those worlds won by his austerity to be fruitless, he—
He questioned the dwellers of heaven who were standing near Dharmarāja:
"For what reason are these worlds, earned by my asceticism, shrouded?
What have I failed to do therein, the fruit of which is this?"
"In that regard, I shall do that for the sake of which this has been undertaken;
tell me without delay that deed by which I may attain the worlds with their fruits. O dwellers of heaven, declare the fruit of this asceticism."
The gods said:
"O Brahman, hear that by which men are born as debtors;
[they are so] through ritual acts, through the life of celibate studentship, and through progeny—of this there is no doubt."
All that is removed by sacrifice, austerity, and sons;
you are an ascetic and a performer of sacrifices, yet offspring do not exist for you. These worlds of yours have been closed off on account of your lack of progeny.
"Beget offspring; then you shall enjoy eternal worlds. O sage, because a son saves his father from the hell named Put, therefore, O best of the twice-born, strive for the continuation of progeny."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of the gods, Mandapāla reflected:
"Where indeed might offspring be quickly produced, and in great numbers?"
Reflecting thus, he approached the birds that breed in great numbers;
having become a *śārṅgaka* bird, he united with Jaritā.
From her he begot four sons who were exponents of the Veda.
Leaving them right there, he went toward Lapitā; the sage had gone to the forest with his young sons still within their eggs and with their mother,
O Bhārata, once that illustrious one had departed for Lapitā.

Agitated by affection for her offspring, Jaritā reflected deeply, O King; though abandoned by him in the forest, she, being distressed, did not desert her sons— the ṛṣis still within their eggs, who were not to be abandoned— in Khāṇḍava.
She, overwhelmed with affection, supported these offspring as they were born through her own labor.
Then, while wandering in that forest together with Lapitā, the seer Mandapāla saw the fire approaching to consume the Khāṇḍava forest.

Having understood his intention and knowing that his sons were still children, the great seer Mandapāla began to praise him for the sake of their safety. That brahminical seer praised Jātavedas with hymns.
Entrusting his sons to the world-protector of great majesty, Mandapāla, filled with fear, said:
"O Agni, you are the mouth of all the gods; you are the bearer of the sacrificial oblation."
O Purifier, you move hidden within all beings.
The seers speak of you as one, yet they speak of you again as threefold;
having fashioned you into eight forms, they made you the carrier of the sacrifice.
"The supreme seers declare that this entire universe was created by you;
for without you, O Consumer of Oblations, the whole world would instantly cease to exist.
Having offered salutations to you, the Brahmins attain the destination won by their own deeds."
They go together with their wives and even their sons to the eternal state. O Agni, they call you the clouds suspended in the sky with lightning;
the years, having issued forth from you, consume all beings.

O Jātavedas of great splendor, this entire creation is yours alone; all that exists, both moving and unmoving, is ordained by your very action. In the beginning, the waters were created by you, and this entire world rests within you.
In you, the sacrificial offering to the gods (*havya*) and the offering to the ancestors (*kavya*) are duly established.
O Agni, you alone are the blazing fire; you are the Ordainer (*dhātṛ*); you are Bṛhaspati.
You are the two Aśvins, the Yamas, Mitra, Soma, and you are also the Wind (*anila*).

You, O Janārdana, arose as Brahmā, the cause of the world's maintenance; at the time of dissolution, you are the fire of time in the form of Rudra. O Lord, Master of the Universe, you protect the embryo enveloped by the fetal membrane.
O God of gods, you are the praiseworthy Self of the universe; let there be salutation unto you!
O Consumer of Oblations, protect my sons, my grandsons, and my wife;
protect my home, my field, and my cattle; protect me, O All, at all times.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, having been thus praised by Mandapāla, the Purifier (Agni) was gratified with that sage of immeasurable splendor.
With a pleased soul, he said to him, "What desired thing shall I do for you?
To the carrier of oblations (Agni), Mandapāla replied with joined palms,
"While burning the Khāṇḍava forest, spare my sons."
Protect my wife, protect my home, and always protect my cattle. Let all missiles fall upon others than us, O Lord;
O Consumer of Oblations, be auspicious to us everywhere and at all times.
"So be it," having thus promised, the Blessed One, the carrier of oblations,
blazed up in the Khandava forest at that time with the desire to consume it.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, when Śukra was set ablaze, those Śārṅgaka birds were deeply distressed;
pained and extremely agitated, they found no refuge.
Seeing their young sons, their ascetic mother—
O lord of men, the singer, tormented by grief, lamented:
"This terrifying fire, burning the dry forest, approaches from here;
fierce and illuminating the world, it increases my sorrow."

"And these young ones of dull intellect are tormenting me— featherless and lacking feet, yet the refuge of our ancestors. And here he comes, terrifying us, licking his lips as he approaches the trees."
Because of my lack of strength, my sons are not capable of fleeing with me;
nor am I able to carry my children and escape elsewhere. Yet I cannot abandon them, for my heart seems to burn with grief.
"How might my sons be released from this blazing fire?
What shall I, unfortunate and grieving along with my children, do?
Which son indeed shall I abandon, and which shall I take as I depart?"
"What indeed would it be that I could do, my sons? How do you think I should act? As I reflect upon how to bring about your liberation, I find no way at all.
Therefore, covering you with my own limbs, I shall die together with you."
"O Jaritāri, this lineage is established by virtue of its seniority. Sārisṛkva shall beget offspring who will increase the family of his ancestors;
Stambamitra shall perform austerities; and Droṇa shall be the most excellent knower of Brahman."
Having spoken thus, your pitiless father departed long ago.
"I am not able to wander together with children in the forest of asceticism;
taking whom could one go? Who possesses the highest excellence?"
"What indeed must be done so that our purpose may be accomplished?"— thus she was distraught,
and by her own wit she could not see a means of liberation for her sons from the fire.
To her who was speaking thus, those Śārṅga birds then replied to their mother:
"O mother, abandon this affection and fly away where the fire does not reach;
for if we are destroyed, you will still have sons,
but if you, mother, are destroyed, there would be no continuation of our lineage."

"Having considered both these matters, that which would be beneficial for our lineage is the supreme time to act; O Mother, let this be yours. Do not, out of affection for our sons, bring about the destruction of the family."
"For this deed of our father, who desired the welfare of the world, shall not be in vain.
Jaritā said:
"This is the burrow of a mole in the ground, near the base of this tree."
"Enter it quickly; you shall have no fear of the fire here.
Then, my dear sons, I shall cover the opening with dust. In this way, I believe we shall counteract the blazing path of black-trailed Agni."
"Therefore, I shall come after the fire has passed to scatter a heap of dust [over it]. May this means for liberation from the consumer of oblations be pleasing to you.
The Śārṅgaka birds said:
"May the flesh-eating rat not destroy us while we are still hairless and made of raw flesh;
seeing this danger, we shall not be able to remain here.
How might the fire not burn us, and how might the rat not devour us?"
"How may our father not be rendered fruitless? How may our mother be preserved? The destruction of the mouse would be in the hole; the destruction of the fire-birds would be in the sky.
Having considered both these outcomes, burning [the body] is better than devouring it."
Death for us would be contemptible if it were by being gnawed by a rat in a hole; however,
the abandonment of the body through fire is desired by the learned,
for when one is consumed by fire, there is certainly a fixed and certain destination in the world of Brahmā.
Jaritā said:
"A hawk seized that mouse as it emerged from this hole;
having caught that tiny creature with its two feet, there will be no fear from that."
The Śārṅgaka birds said:
"We do not know for certain that the mouse was carried off by the hawk in any way;
there may be others here as well, and we have fear even of them."
For fire might arrive unexpectedly, yet the turning back of the wind is observed;
O mother, death from those dwelling in the hole would be certain for us.
Yet, O mother, a doubtful death is preferable to one that is certain.
"Move through the air according to the proper way, and you shall obtain beautiful sons.
Jaritā said:
"I indeed saw a hawk approaching from nearby toward the hole."
The powerful hawk seized the moving mouse as it emerged from its hole and carried it away;
as that hawk was flying off, I swiftly followed behind him,
offering blessings to him as he bore the rat from its burrow.

Homage be to you, O King of Hawks; we have been protected by you as if by a king. O King of Hawks, you who fly forth having seized our enemy—having ascended to the heavens, may you become golden and free from foes.
When he had been devoured by that hungry bird, I took leave of him and returned home.
"Enter the cave, my sons; have confidence, for there is no fear for you."
"Without a doubt, while I was looking on, my mouse has been carried off by a hawk.
The Śārṅgaka birds said:
"O mother, we truly do not know that the mouse was carried away from here before now."
"Without knowing [the way], we shall not be able to enter the hole.
Jaritā said:
"I indeed know that mouse was carried off by the hawk."
"Therefore, there is no fear; let my words be carried out.
The Śārṅgaka birds said:
"You cannot dispel this great fear through mere pretense."
When cognitions are thus confused, that state is not produced by the intellect alone;
nor have we been of assistance to you, nor do you know who we are. Why do you oppress us? Who are you, and who are we to you?
"You are young and beautiful, capable of seeking out a husband;
follow your own husband, and you shall obtain excellent sons.
We too, having entered the fire, shall attain auspicious worlds."
"Then, if fire does not consume us, you shall indeed become our very life-force once more;
we shall be reunited, so do not grieve.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been addressed thus, Śārṅgī then left her sons in Khāṇḍava and went swiftly to a safe place where there was no refuge for fire.
Thereupon, the bearer of oblations, blazing with sharp flames, approached.
Where those young cranes, the sons of Mandapāla,
were staying, they saw the Fire blazing with his own splendor;
distressed and piteous, they addressed him from nearby with these words.
Then Jaritāri caused his speech to be heard by Pāvaka.
Jaritāri said:
"The wise man remains vigilant before the onset of a time of distress."
Having encountered a time of hardship, he never experiences distress at any time.
"How indeed can our father, fallen into suffering, come under [the power of] others?"—thus [he thinks].
But he who, being senseless, does not perceive the hardship before it has arrived...
In that time of distress, being afflicted, he did not understand anything at all.
Sārisṛkva said:
"You are steadfast and wise, and this is a life-threatening crisis for us."
"Indeed, among many, there is one who is both brave and wise; of this there is no doubt.
Stambamitra said:
"The eldest brother is indeed a protector; the eldest delivers one from distress."
"If the eldest does not understand, what will the younger do?
Droṇa said:
"The fire, blazing and swift, is coming toward our abode."
"The seven-tongued fire, emaciated, approaches licking [everything].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by his brothers, Jaritāri [spoke] to Vibhāvasu.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he offered praise; hear how it was, O King.
Jaritāri said:
"You are the self of the wind, the purifier, and the body of the plants."
O *śukra*, the waters are your womb, and you are the womb of the waters.
Your flames move upward and downward, and they spread forth to the sides,
O one of great heroism, like the rays of the sun.
Sārisṛkva said:
"Our mother has approached our father, yet we do not know him;
nor have wings been born to us, O Lotus-bannered One."
O Agni, no protector is found for us other than you;
therefore, O sole hero, protect us!
O Agni, that auspicious form of yours and those seven flames of yours—
Therefore, being praised today, protect us who seek refuge;
O Jātavedas, you alone are the one born for ascetic heat,
for there is no other heater found among the cattle, O God.
"Protect us, the seers and children;
O bearer of oblations, pass us by!
Stambamitra said:

O Agni, you alone are everything; this entire world is centered within you. You sustain all beings, and you support the universe. You are Agni, the bearer of oblations; you yourself are the supreme offering.
The wise worship you in many ways and also as one alone.
O bearer of oblations, having created these three worlds,
when the time arrives, you burn them again, being well-kindled.
O Agni, you alone are the source of this entire world, and you alone are its foundation once again. O Lord of the Universe, you abide within as the food consumed by all living beings.
"Ever increasing, you digest everything; everything is established in you.
Droṇa said:
"Becoming the sun with its rays, O Jātavedas..."
O Śukra, having taken up the waters from the earth and all the juices born of the earth, you release them again at the time of emission and nourish all beings here with rain.
From you, O Śukra, these plants with green foliage are born again, as well as the lotus ponds and the great ocean, the vast receptacle of waters.
This indeed, O Tigmāṃśu, is the abode and the ultimate refuge of Varuṇa.
May Śiva be our protector; do not destroy us today!
O tawny-eyed one, red-necked one, black-trailed consumer of oblations, go beyond and release us, as if toward the dwellings of the ocean.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Droṇa of unwearied deeds, Jātavedas (Agni),
his mind composed by Mandapāla’s promise, spoke to Droṇa.
"You are indeed the seer Droṇa; this Brahman has been uttered by you. I shall fulfill your desire, and no fear shall exist for you.
For you were previously introduced to me by Mandapāla."
"You were to avoid my sons while burning the forest," he said;
and as for those words of his and what has been spoken by you here—both of these are very heavy upon me. Tell me, what shall I do for you?

"I am greatly pleased; may it be well with you, O Brahmin; by your hymn of praise, O Lord," said Droṇa. "O Jātavedas, O Lord of all gods, O you of great fame, [be gracious] toward those devoted to you."
"O Śukra, these cats constantly terrify us;
O Havyavāha, place them along with their kinsmen between your fangs.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having granted permission to the Śārṅgaka birds, Agni acted accordingly;
and being fully kindled, O Janamejaya, he consumed the Khāṇḍava forest.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O descendant of Kuru, Mandapāla, reflecting then upon his sons, spoke to Aśītāṃśu; yet he did not cease to feel distress.
Distressed on account of his sons, he said this to Lapitā:
"How is it that my little sons, though capable of leaping, are now unable to do so?
As the sacrificial fire grows and the wind blows swiftly,
my children will be incapable of escaping."

How indeed will that ascetic mother, overwhelmed by sorrow and seeing no means to protect her sons, be unable to save them? How indeed [will she fare] regarding my children, who are powerless to escape or to fall [from this height]?
Tormented on all sides and crying out, she ran toward [him], asking:
"How is my son Jaritāri? And how is Sārisṛkva?
How is Stambamitra? How is Droṇa? And how is that poor woman?"
O Bhārata, as the ṛṣi Mandapāla was thus lamenting in the forest, Lapitā replied to him as if with indignation:
"You have no regard for your sons; you spoke of them as mere ṛṣis."
"Those who are radiant and heroic have no fear of fire;
yet they were offered into the fire by you in my presence,
and so it was promised by the high-souled Agni himself."
A world-protector would never speak a falsehood under any circumstances;
those speakers are capable [of speaking truth], yet your mind is not set upon them. It is only by thinking of that enemy of mine that you are consumed with grief.

"Surely you have no affection for me as you once had for her; for it is not right for one who possesses wings [and thus the power to help], being capable of looking on while a friend is suffering, to remain devoid of affection toward that friend in any way whatsoever."
"Go back to Jaritā herself, for whose sake you are grieving.
I too shall wander alone, just as that coward does.
Mandapāla said:
I would not conduct myself in this world as you imagine;
I wander for the sake of offspring, yet that [offspring] has fallen into distress.
He who, being dull-witted, abandons what is present to cling to a future goal—[he acts thus].
"Let the world despise him as it wishes; do as you please. For this blazing fire, licking the trees, produces an inauspicious heat in my heart toward one who is hateful."
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the fire had passed beyond that region, Jaritā,
longing for her sons, then went quickly toward her children.
Seeing all those sons in the forest— safe, released from the fire, yet wailing piteously—
she wept again and again at that most incredible sight.
And one by one, he approached those sons as they were crying out;
Jaritā, however, embraced them and kissed them out of maternal affection.
Then, O Bhārata, Mandapāla also arrived there suddenly.
Then all those sons did not at all welcome him, because of the great weight of Mandapāla’s status and especially because of his ascetic power.
"By your grace, we have all grown wings; we now offer our salutations."

When they had spoken thus, the great ascetic Gautama, having greeted them in return, embraced his sons and smelled the heads of those young boys; indeed, Gautama experienced that same joy which comes from the touch of one's children.
Out of respect for Mandapāla, they approached his feet;
though he was lamenting one by one and repeatedly calling out to Jaritā,
they did not say a single word to that ṛṣi, whether good or bad.
Mandapāla said:
"Which of your sons is the eldest, and which is the one after him? Which son is the middlemost, and which is the youngest?"
"To me who speaks thus, afflicted by grief, why do you not reply? O consumer of oblations, I have done this; I find no peace at all because of it.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Mandapāla touched her in that manner.
Jaritā said:
"What business do you have with your eldest son, or with the one born after him? What business do you have with your middle son, and what with your youngest, O ascetic woman?"
"You who previously departed, having abandoned me who am inferior in every way—
go back to that very Lapitā, the youthful woman of lovely smiles.
Mandapāla said:
For women in this world, there exists nothing other than the presence of another man— save for the rivalry with co-wives— for such is the nature of things;
it is indeed a kindling of the fire of enmity and a cause of intense agitation.
For among women, rivalry between co-wives is indeed always destined to occur; thus,
even Arundhatī— the virtuous, auspicious lady renowned throughout all the worlds— suspected Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
She utterly despised that hero, the sage who dwelt in the midst of the Seven Seers, though he was one whose nature was perfectly pure and who always delighted in what is dear and beneficial;
by that malice toward him, her radiance became like smoke and ruddy.
"Visible yet invisible, neither beautiful nor ugly, she appears like a mere sign;
just as you have come here for the sake of offspring, so too,
having desired me while things stood thus, you now behave exactly as she did."
"A man should never place his trust in his wife under any circumstances;
for a wife who has borne sons no longer regards her husband's business as her own.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all those sons attended upon him properly;
and he, O King, began to console his own sons.
Mandapāla said:
"For the sake of your protection, I have petitioned the Fire-god;
and the Fire-god has already given his promise, saying, 'So be it.
Having understood the words of Agni and your mother's knowledge of dharma,"
"Your supreme prowess is such that I have not come here before.
O dear sons, you should not feel any distress regarding death;
for the Fire-god knows the sages, and that Brahman is known to you as well."
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus comforted his sons and taking his wife with him, O Bhārata,
Mandapāla then departed from that region for another land.
The Lord of fierce rays also, together with the two Kṛṣṇas, consumed the kindled Khāṇḍava forest, bringing security to the world;
and there the Fire-god drank from the streams flowing with fat and marrow.
He attained supreme satisfaction and revealed himself to Arjuna.
Then the Blessed Lord, the ruler of the gods, descending from the sky and surrounded by the hosts of Maruts, spoke these words to Pārtha and Mādhava:
"You two have performed this deed which is difficult even for the immortals to achieve. Choose boons, for I am pleased; choose even those that are rare and superhuman.
Pārtha, however, chose from Śakra all the divine weapons in their entirety.
Arjuna said:
The King of the Gods said:
"O God, best among speakers, I choose the Pāśupata weapon."
"O you whose vehicle is the tawny horse (Indra), grant me other divine weapons as well!
O Pārtha, let the weapons of Indra and the others be received according to the prescribed rites.
Tryambaka will bestow upon you the divine Pāśupata weapon."
"Śakra then set a time for him to receive that [weapon],
saying: 'When the Blessed Lord Mahādeva becomes pleased with you,
then I shall bestow all the Pāṇḍava weapons upon you in their entirety.'"
O descendant of Kuru, I myself shall know that time;
and through great ascetic power, I shall bestow those [weapons] upon you—
all those belonging to Agni as well as those belonging to Vāyu.
"And you shall accept all my wealth, O Dhanañjaya.
Vāsudeva also felt eternal affection for Pārtha;
then the Lord of the Devas, being pleased, granted him that boon.
Having granted them the boon, the Lord of the Maruts, together with the gods, was pleased;
having taken leave of the Fire-god, he returned once more to the third heaven.
And Pāvaka, too, having consumed that forest along with its beasts and birds, [departed].
Having eaten the flesh and drunk the fat and blood, he was thoroughly satiated; after six days had passed,
O lord of the people, he spoke to them with supreme joy.
"I have been gratified by you two foremost of men according to my pleasure. I grant you leave, O heroes; go wherever you desire.
[Take with you] the divine bow Gāṇḍīva and the two inexhaustible great quivers."
"O great chariot-warrior, this chariot marked with the banner of the monkey has been given to you. By means of this bow and this chariot, O Bhārata,
you shall conquer your enemies in battle, including the gods, asuras, and humans."
Thus, having been granted permission by the high-souled Pāvaka,
Arjuna, Vāsudeva, and the Dānava Maya—
these three, O bull of the Bharatas— then circumambulated him.
Together they sat down upon the delightful bank of the river. Then Maya, having honored Pārtha in the presence of Vāsudeva with folded hands and gentle words, spoke to him again and again.
Janamejaya said:
"O Vaiśampāyana, for what purpose did the blessed Lord Agni burn that Khāṇḍava forest? Vaiśampāyana said: [The Blessed Lord Agni burned that Khāṇḍava forest.]
"By doing what displeasure to whom, or by desiring to please whom, does Fire act thus? For Fire ought not to persist in such persistence for a trivial cause;
this is my thought regarding his burning of Khāṇḍava, O best of Brahmins."
Listen to me, O King, as I explain everything exactly as it happened; hear, O lord of the earth, the reason why Agni consumed the Khandava forest.
There was once a king, O Indra among kings, known by the name Śvetaketu.
An Atiratha among the Ikṣvākus, a performer of sacrifices who gave away abundant dakṣiṇās,
that wise king Janamejaya then undertook the initiation for a thousand-year sacrifice and, together with his officiating priests, performed the rite.
At that sacrifice of his, great seers gathered together,
as did thousands of Brahmins learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
then his officiating priests had their eyes clouded by smoke.
After a long time, having become weary, they abandoned that lord of men.
Thereupon, that king sought to propitiate the officiating priests,
but they did not show favor to him, as he had fallen into the state of being deprived of his sight.
Then, with their consent, the lord of men, having had his sacrifice interrupted,
completed it together with other officiating priests;
and through that great sacrifice, being highly praised, he ascended to heaven.
Accompanied by all the officiating priests and joined by the members of the assembly,
the bearer of oblations drank at the sacrificial session for a thousand years.
Through that offering, the Fire-god attained supreme satisfaction.

And Agni did not wish to take the sacrificial offering of anyone else; a lack of appetite came upon him, and he then went to the Grandfather (Brahmā). Having approached the Grandfather, he reported this matter to him.
"O Blessed One, Śvetaketu has indeed attained supreme satisfaction;
yet a sharp aversion has entered him, which I am unable to dispel.
Then the Grandfather of all beings spoke to that Fire-god:
"I shall destroy your lack of appetite; you must observe this agreement. Then the bearer of oblations spoke to Brahmā.
Thereupon Brahmā said to him: "If you will burn the Khāṇḍava forest..."
For there dwell many enemies of the gods; however,
by my grace, O Agni, your appetite shall be fully restored,
and after you have waited for some time, you shall then consume them.
"And even when born in human form as the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
you, O bearer of oblations, shall together with them consume the forest.
"So be it," the Fire replied to Brahmā.
O King, having learned that those two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, had been born [as Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna],
and having recollected those words of the Self-born One, the bearer of oblations (Agni) then went to consume the forest.
O King, this has been told to you, how it happened in the past,
where that serpent Maya and the Śārṅgaka birds were released from the fire.
